Recovering the hidden rules of motion from that single picture is the goal.

The team creates synthetic data from one-particle Hamiltonians in one and two dimensions, then trains convolutional networks to reverse the mapping. Recovery quality is strikingly high, the models cope with cases beyond their training range, and they stay steady under noise. The authors propose scanning tunnelling microscopy as a real test bed, where such maps might expose a sample's unknown energy landscape.
arxiv-2509-10104:
Sofia Vei and 4 co-authors propose a risk assessment frame for artificial intelligence that starts from real harm rather than internal checklists in a 2025 paper called AI Harmonics. Compliance-centred models, they argue, miss how differently stakeholders feel a failure and how uneven real-world damage can be. Their method ranks harms by relative severity using ordered incident data, so no one must invent precise numbers for events that resist them.

A new harm score built on that ranking feeds a stakeholder-aware procedure for sorting which risks deserve action first. On annotated incident collections, political and physical harms stood out as the most concentrated: one corrodes public trust, the other can injure or kill. Uneven harm patterns surfaced consistently, giving decision makers a map for aiming scarce mitigation effort.
arxiv-2509-10204:
Finiteness is the theme of David Forsman's solo 2025 paper. Forsman builds one frame from category theory to hold many finiteness ideas at once. Ideas such as Noetherianness, Artinianness, and compactness usually live in separate fields. He unifies them through a notion of compactness. That notion is defined relative to a chosen system of covering diagrams.

One definition then handles both rising and falling chain conditions. The covering maps may run in mixed directions, which is what makes that possible. A property called protomodularity drives the strongest results. Under it, compact objects stay closed under quotients and extensions. In plain algebraic settings, this recovers a classic fact. Modules over a Noetherian ring behave as well as the ring itself. In abelian categories, the Noetherian and Artinian classes form exact subcategories.
arxiv-2509-10404: Taekyun Kim and three co-authors prove three recurrence relations in this 2025 combinatorics paper. They use basic methods throughout. One relation covers derangement numbers. Those count arrangements where nothing stays in place. A second covers harmonic numbers. A third covers degenerate harmonic numbers. The authors read the results as a lesson. Simple techniques can still uncover new structure in classical number sequences. Such sequences show up in combinatorics, in probability, and in computer science.
arxiv-2509-10604:
Jack Y. L. Kwok and five co-authors clean the cosmic microwave background in a new way in this 2025 cosmology paper. Sky maps at different frequencies mix the ancient CMB light with galactic and extragalactic foregrounds. Standard internal linear combination methods blend the maps themselves, then measure the power spectrum of the result.

Their Spectral ILC instead combines the auto- and cross-spectra of the channels directly. That rearrangement yields a different optimization problem needing fewer constraint equations than map-level deprojection. In simulations modeled on the Simons Observatory, the spectral method's error bars shrink by more than a factor of seven at small scales compared with constrained map-level cleaning. The gain is largest where components are spatially uncorrelated and noise dominates, and it questions whether cleaned maps are the right route to precision measurements.
arxiv-2509-11004:
Zhou Wei, Michel Thera, and Jen-Chih Yao wrote this 2025 paper in variational analysis. That field studies how multi-valued mappings behave near a point. Their topic is metric subregularity. This property underlies error bounds. Error bounds tell how far a point is from solving a problem.

The authors work in Asplund spaces, a broad class of Banach spaces. They introduce a limiting constraint qualification. With it, they state necessary conditions for subregularity. The conditions use normal cones and coderivatives. The same conditions turn out to characterize Asplund spaces themselves. The team then applies the machinery to conic inequalities. One side of such an inequality pairs a cone with a function that returns vectors. Known error-bound results appear as special cases.
arxiv-2509-11304:
Igor V. Blinov wrote this 2025 condensed matter theory paper with no co-authors. It treats a partial condensation of mobile excitons. The setting is rhombohedral graphene trilayer. Its valence band has a double-well shape. That shape gives two Fermi surfaces. One is electron-like. The other is hole-like.

In the weak-coupling regime, an instability appears in the particle-hole channel. Its wavevector is set by the gap between the two Fermi radii. A charge density wave between valleys results. An extra energy scale splits the behavior into regimes. For a small order parameter, Fermi arcs show up. They change the conductance a lot. Larger order parameters gap the arcs out. The regimes also differ in how conductance scales with disorder scattering time.
arxiv-2509-11404:
Kang-Kang Shao and five co-authors report a first in flavor physics. This 2025 particle physics paper measures two CKM matrix entries, Vcs and Vcd. They set how charm quarks change flavor. Past values came from adding up single decay channels. This team used inclusive charm decays instead.

The fit used inclusive data and the sum of exclusive ones. Heavy quark parameters came out at the same time. Those parameters matched past work well. That match backs the method. The Vcs value agrees with the world mean from exclusive decays. Vcd does not. It sits about three standard deviations away from that mean. More data will have to settle the clash.
arxiv-2509-11604:
Md. Mithun Hossain and colleagues present SpanEIT in a 2025 paper on entity-level sentiment sorting. The task assigns a feeling tone to each named entity in a text. An entity can sit near subtle opinion phrases. Feelings can span sentences. Repeated mentions of one entity should also stay in line.

Their scheme builds span-based forms for each entity and for phrases that may carry feeling. The two kinds of spans interact through two-way attention. A graph attention network captures syntax and co-occurrence links. A coreference-aware memory module keeps one entity's tone steady across a text. Negation, ambiguity, and overlapping views add further difficulty. On three datasets, SpanEIT beat strong transformer and hybrid baselines in accuracy and F1. Ablation checks backed each part of the design.
arxiv-2509-11704:
Chieh Tsao and six co-authors use entangled photons to probe quantum dot solids. This 2025 optics paper extends heralded emission detection. One photon of an entangled pair heralds the excitation. The other records the glow. Past demos stayed with molecules at room temperature. This team works with near-infrared colloidal quantum dots when cold.

Superconducting nanowire detectors give sharp timing. Large-area avalanche photodiodes count the emission fast. Correlation analysis of the pairs revealed exciton lifetimes. Fine-structure energy splittings came out too. The dots are InAs/ZnSe solids. They stand as bright, tunable test systems for quantum-light spectroscopy. Optical cavities offer a further control knob.
arxiv-2509-12204:
Animated films break ordinary face recognition because cartoon faces stretch, squash, and change style from scene to scene. Zhongrui Gui and four co-authors answer in 2025 with a pipeline that knows characters by sight and by voice at once, built to support character-centered understanding of animated movies.

The system first builds a character bank from online sources, holding sample images and voice clips for each figure. Recognition then feeds two access tools: audio description for blind viewers and subtitles that name who is speaking for deaf viewers. A new dataset covers seventy-five animated movies with full annotations, and tests show clear gains over face-only methods.
arxiv-2509-12504:
Dark matter might be a composite particle from a hidden strong force, and its cosmic abundance might mirror the matter-antimatter imbalance. Chih-Ting Lu and one co-author map how electron-positron colliders could find such a leptophilic dark sector in 2025, a corner of theory whose collider signals had not been systematically charted.

The lightest dark baryon gets its mass from the hidden confinement scale. The authors show that heavy mediator particles and the lightest dark mesons are within reach of Belle II and its proposed far detector, plus future circular colliders. Existing limits are folded in, and the machines cover complementary slices of the parameter space.
arxiv-2509-12604:
Quantum resource theories sort operations into free ones, which cannot create a prized resource, and costly ones, which can. In a solo 2025 paper, Xian Shi studies the free side itself: operations that generate no resource, across both static settings with states and dynamical settings with processes.

For states, a sufficient condition for one state to be converted into another by such operations is derived. A dynamical resource theory is then built with these operations as the free set, plus an axiomatic way to measure the resource and an account of erasing it. Applications bound conversion rates in general convex theories and classical communication capacity helped by dynamical coherence.
arxiv-2509-12704:
Chronic kidney disease hides for years, and the blood and urine markers that expose it are often missing in ordinary clinic visits. Mohammad Abdul Hafeez Khan and six co-authors test in 2025 whether routine non-renal information, demographics, other conditions, and basic urine findings, can flag the disease anyway.

Their approach, NORA, first learns separating patient representations with supervised contrastive learning on clinic records, then hands those features to a random forest classifier. Class separation and overall accuracy improve, with the clearest gains in the early-stage cases that matter most. A public kidney dataset confirms the method travels to a different patient population.
arxiv-2509-12804:
A. Wargnier and 8 co-authors analyze twenty years of observations of Deimos, a small moon of Mars, in a 2025 paper. Data came from the Mars Express spacecraft's cameras between 2004 and 2024. Knowing how Deimos reflects light helps reveal its surface texture and composition and prepares for the upcoming MMX mission to the Martian moons.

The team performed disk-integrated and disk-resolved photometric analysis, measuring brightness as a whole and by location, using the Hapke model. Deimos proved dark and predominantly backscattering, with a reflectivity comparable to the other Martian moon, Phobos. Its brightness surge at small phase angles came mainly from shadow hiding, with negligible coherent backscattering. The results refine the moon's photometric properties.
arxiv-2509-12904:
Ron Adin, Yuval Roichman and Natalia Tsilevich study large-size trends of higher Lie characters in 2025. These are a prized family of group marks. They show up in algebra and counting. An old problem of Thrall asks how they split into base marks.

A new large-size path is offered in place of exact splits. Many families of these marks tend toward the plain group mark in fixed ratio. In chance terms, a random higher Lie mark tends to that same ratio. The shift turns a hard split task into a trend that can be proved for wide families.
arxiv-2509-13304:
Jens Braun, Duarte Fontes and Gudrun Heinrich ask in 2025 whether large fixed-order shifts to twin-Higgs decay survive showering. Twin-Higgs output via gluon fusion draws much precision work. Decay handling drew late focus, with large shifts in bottom channels.

For bottom plus photon decays, shifts stem mostly from soft and aligned radiation at fixed order. Once parton showers join, those shifts wash out in large part. Fixed-order alarm thus overstates real change. Decay and shower must be treated jointly for sound rates. The lesson tempers prior fiducial claims.
arxiv-2509-13404:
Avik Chakraborty, Tanay Kibe and three co-authors decode strings in 2025 as holographic quantum maps at gravity junctions. Recent work derives the Nambu-Goto string equation from junction rules in 3D gravity. Holographically, junctions dualize to interfaces in conformal theory.

At linear order, each stringy junction mode maps to a quantum channel between in and out spaces. The channel splits into scatter with reflection and transmission, plus a relative Virasoro twist. A left-right map of like form appears too. Maps keep boundary rules, ignore frame choice, and tune energy flow. String modes gain a channel tongue.
arxiv-2509-13804:
Chi Zheng and three co-authors update the limits on the effective field theory of dark energy in a 2025 cosmology paper. That framework describes dark energy and modified gravity in one language. It adds a single extra scalar degree of freedom. It covers theories from quintessence to Horndeski gravity as special cases.

The team confronts the theory with the freshest public data. The sets include baryon acoustic oscillations from DESI and microwave background maps from Planck and ACT. Supernovae, weak lensing, and the full galaxy power spectrum from BOSS complete the list. On a standard background, general relativity wins. On an evolving dark energy background, slight modifications are mildly favored. They stay consistent with general relativity. The evidence for dynamical dark energy also weakens once modified gravity is allowed.
arxiv-2509-14104:
Leonard Hackel, Tom Burgert, and Begüm Demir make remote sensing foundation models cheaper in a 2025 paper. Masked autoencoder pretraining has produced strong Earth observation models. They are heavy to train and run. Their giant pretraining archives are full of redundant images that burn compute without teaching anything new.

Their model, CSMoE, attacks both costs. A soft mixture-of-experts design lets different experts specialize per sensor modality. Cross-sensor knowledge is still shared, cutting computation in training and inference. A sampling strategy guided by thematic and climate descriptors shrinks the pretraining set. Geographic and content diversity survive the cut. On scene classification, semantic segmentation, and image retrieval, the lighter model stayed competitive with leading remote sensing foundation models. It used a fraction of the floating-point operations.
arxiv-2509-14304:
Eric Zhang, Li Wei, Sarah Chen and Michael Wang report a clinical study in 2025 of the UDM series for detecting stuttered speech. Accurate detectors exist, but black box models give clinicians no clear reason for a flag. That opacity slows use in real clinics.

UDM, short for Unconstrained Dysfluency Modeling, was built at Berkeley with a modular design. It aligns speech sounds openly and gives outputs clinicians can inspect. Trials with patients and certified speech pathologists gave strong detection scores and high marks for clarity of output. Most clinicians in the study accepted the tool, and diagnosis time fell by about a third. The authors argue clarity and accuracy can advance together in speech care.
arxiv-2509-14504:
Roman Kovalchuk, Mariana Romanyshyn and Petro Ivaniuk introduce OmniGEC in 2025, silver standard data sets for grammatical error correction in eleven languages. Correction tools are strong in English and weak elsewhere for lack of training data. Silver data are machine labelled, not gold human labels.

Texts come from Wikipedia edits, Reddit communities and a Ukrainian social media corpus across the target languages. Wikipedia corrections are human made, while the other sources were corrected automatically with a GPT model. Languages range from Czech and German to Icelandic and Ukrainian. The collection aims to help multilingual correction catch up with English tools. Shared silver data let teams test whether one model can serve many languages at once.
arxiv-2509-14904:
Keanu Sisouk, Eloi Tanguy, Julie Delon, and Julien Tierny compute averages of persistence diagrams that resist outliers in a 2025 topological data analysis paper. Persistence diagrams summarize the shape of data as collections of points, and their averages, called barycenters, are usually built from optimal transport plans. The classical method only handles the squared Wasserstein distance.

The authors adapt a fixed-point method to general transport costs, especially costs between the first and second power that shrug off outliers. Two uses show the benefit: clustering diagrams within their own metric space, and building dictionary encodings of diagram collections. In both, the generalized barycenter proves more robust than the standard one. A public Python implementation accompanies the work, so others can apply the robust averaging directly.
arxiv-2509-15004:
Yujia Huang, Xi'an Li, and Jinran Wu solve stiff fourth-order equations with neural networks in a 2025 computational mathematics paper. Biharmonic equations appear in plate bending and fluid problems, and they are hard for physics-informed neural networks, which learn solutions by enforcing the equation itself. High derivatives make training unstable and slow.

Their method first splits each biharmonic equation into two coupled Poisson equations, a classic reduction. Fourier spectral ideas then guide the network design, improving accuracy while cutting computational cost. The approach handles Dirichlet and Navier boundary conditions and problems with awkward boundary shapes or high-dimensional inputs. Tests on linear and nonlinear problems in several dimensions show a good trade between precision and expense compared with standard physics-informed networks.
arxiv-2509-15204:
Ruochen Ma, Vedika Khemani, and Shengqi Sang extend the circuit picture of quantum phases to warm systems in a 2025 condensed matter paper. At zero temperature, states in one phase can be morphed into each other by shallow local circuits, which makes circuit equivalence a definition of a phase. Thermal equilibrium states at finite temperature need a channel-based version of that idea.

The authors construct a channel circuit that approximately converts one Gibbs state into another whenever a path between them keeps correlations decaying fast enough. The circuit's locality grows only modestly with system size and accuracy. The condition is expected to hold inside many noncritical thermal phases, including ones with broken symmetry or topological order. As an application, the framework speaks to self-correcting quantum memory, where a thermal phase itself protects stored information.
arxiv-2509-15304:
T. Winterhalder and fourteen co-authors gauge whether light interferometry can catch moons of exoplanets by watching planets wobble, in a 2025 paper. No exomoon has been firmly caught yet. Moons would still teach us much about how planets form and where life might live. A moon tugs its planet, which makes a small reflex shift in the planet's place next to its star.

Repeated position gauges could show that wobble. The authors give the signal size in analytic form. They set hoped-for marks for moons of real exoplanets next to the gauge sharpness of today and of near-future tools. Full runs of the catch process, with time-based orbit tugs, round out the study. The work maps which moon masses and orbits sit within reach.
arxiv-2509-15404:
Shaoting Peng, Katherine Driggs-Campbell, and Roy Dong study how self driving cars can sway human drivers safely. Game based models can guide such talks at crossings, but their pull fades over time. Drivers may also feel tricked, lose trust, and drive in riskier ways. The team wanted a method that stays open and keeps trust.

Their plan, called TA-EBP, uses a method of honest signals from economics. A trust score tracks how much sway the car has earned. They prove the least trust needed for sway to work, and the best size for a gentle forward nudge as the signal. In traffic tests, the plan cut crashes to zero and sped flow. It beat plans that ignored trust or sent no signals.
arxiv-2509-15604:
Zi-Ming Wang leads a team that widens a new kind of magnetism. Altermagnets are a lately found magnetic phase whose spin split does not need relativity. The team ask how spin and orbital motion lock together inside such materials. They frame this joint behavior as spin-orbital altermagnetism and split it into two classes.

One class grows from magnetic order that breaks a joint symmetry on its own. The other grows when the two sublattices of the crystal shift out of step, as in a known structural change. They suggest ways to spot these states, through spin flow and orbit measures. A weak net magnetism can also appear. They show a test system where the phase may arise.
arxiv-2509-16004:
Disks of dust and gas around the smallest stars are places where Earth-like planets may form. Hyerin Jang and thirteen co-authors study ten such disks with the Webb space telescope and its mid-infrared tool. The disks sit around very low-mass stars and brown dwarfs, which are objects too small to burn like the Sun.

The spectra sort the disks into groups based on how far the dust has settled toward the disk plane. Less settled disks show strong silicate bands and larger grains. More settled disks show weaker bands, smaller grains, and more crystal-like dust. As dust settles, more gas seems exposed, a clue to how these planet-forming zones evolve.
arxiv-2509-16104:
Leftover disks of dust around young stars sometimes hold gas, a clue to how planets and their air take shape. A. Moór and colleagues used a large radio array to search twelve dust-rich disks around young, mid-sized stars for carbon monoxide gas. They found the gas in five disks, two with small amounts and three with much larger stores.

Combined with past work, the gas shows up far more often around brighter stars of a certain type. For gas-poor disks, crashes between solid bodies may supply the gas. Why some disks hold so much more gas stays an open puzzle, and the authors weigh what could explain it.
arxiv-2509-16304:
Near some giant black holes, X-ray bursts repeat in a near-regular rhythm whose cause is still debated. L. Hernández-García and thirteen co-authors report new telescope views of such bursts from a galaxy nucleus known as Ansky, taken over the first half of 2025. The bursts grew about four times more energetic than in 2024, with gaps near ten days and flares lasting days.

Both gaps and flares roughly doubled in length, and flare shapes grew more lopsided. The team weighs ideas from a small body spiraling into the disk to bursts of mass transfer and disk instability. More watching is needed to settle the cause.
arxiv-2509-16404:
Hermitian K-theory sorts algebraic objects with a symmetry twist, and a newer cohomology theory may hold the key to computing it. Håkon Kolderup, Oliver Röndigs, and Paul Arne Østvær use a sliced spectral sequence inside motivic homotopy theory to link the two. They work out the sequence in depth for base schemes of arithmetic interest.

Results include a Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch theorem and the map between the two theories up to degree five for all fields. They also compute the hermitian K-groups and higher Witt groups of the integers. Such concrete values anchor a deep abstract theory.
arxiv-2509-17004:
Marius Tărnăuceanu counts symmetry classes in a special family of groups in a 2025 solo math paper. The family is known as ZM-groups. Two elements sit in the same conjugacy class if one can be rotated into the other inside the group. A coarser split uses the group's own symmetries, called automorphisms.

Tărnăuceanu counts both kinds of classes exactly. He also counts the size of each class under both relations. Exact counts help test conjectures about these groups and speed computer algebra. Group theorists use such tallies to tell similar groups apart and to map their internal structure.
arxiv-2509-17104:
Suman Dey and Günter Sigl simulate gamma-ray cascades from a blazar in a 2025 astrophysics paper. A blazar's high-energy rays spawn electron and positron pairs on the way to Earth. Weak magnetic fields between galaxies can bend those particles out of our line of sight. Plasma instabilities can also drain their energy first.

Simulations combine both effects for one well-studied blazar. The resulting spectrum, in the range telescopes observe, carries imprints of the contest between bending and cooling. Reading those imprints could reveal the strength of intergalactic magnetic fields, a long-sought quantity that traces the early universe's magnetism.
arxiv-2509-17204:
James R. Han, Mithun Vanniasinghe, Hshmat Sahak, Nicholas Rhinehart, and Timothy D. Barfoot wrote a 2025 arXiv paper on robots that move through crowds. Teaching a robot by trial and error in public is slow and unsafe, since crashes are part of learning. Copying expert drivers from recorded data avoids that risk, but plain copying falls short for social navigation.

Their pipeline, called Ratatouille, keeps the same data and changes how the model is built and trained. The result cut crashes per meter by a large factor and tripled the success rate next to plain copying. The team tested in simulation and in the real world. They gathered more than eleven hours of driving on a busy campus and also show runs in a public food court. Careful design, they argue, beat more data.
arxiv-2509-17304:
Tian Xie, Ding Zhu, Jia Liu, Mahdi Khalili, and Xueru Zhang study prediction when the prediction itself moves the data. Their 2025 arXiv paper works in performative prediction, where deploying a model shifts the very distribution it learned from. The goal is a stable point that stays optimal once its own effects settle in, which is harder to reach than in standard learning.

Their algorithm, SPRINT, adds variance reduction to stochastic updates for this setting. Past methods reached stable points but assumed bounded noise and kept an error floor tied to that noise. SPRINT aims to shrink that floor and speed convergence, even when the loss is not convex. The authors prove convergence results for the method under smooth, non-convex losses. The work speaks to platforms whose forecasts change user behavior, from pricing to ranking.
arxiv-2509-17504:
Yuzo Maruyama and Akimichi Takemura improve on a classic of statistics in a 2025 arXiv paper. The James-Stein estimator famously beats the plain average when estimating many normal means at once. An estimator that dominates it does at least as well everywhere and better somewhere, under quadratic loss.

Building on Stein's risk formula, the pair give a new sufficient condition for dominance. It turns on a monotonicity trait of a reshaped shrinkage factor. From it they derive a broad class of shrinkage estimators that stay minimax and beat James-Stein, including cases that approach the best shrinkage factor at polynomial or logarithmic rates. They add conditions for dominance that holds uniformly across dimensions and for better large-sample risk. Worked examples and numerical checks show the theory in action. The paper extends a line of work that began with Stein's surprise itself.
arxiv-2509-17904: Arturo Rodriguez Fanlo states a broad form of a group-action method in a short 2025 maths note. The method, named for Massicot and Wagner, is a recursive argument used in group theory. Fanlo's main result is an asymmetric form of that argument, set up for group actions. The note is brief and states the general claim more than cases of its use. It gives folk who use the method a clean, shared form to cite.
arxiv-2509-18104:
Wenqian Li and 3 co-authors price and pick data in a shared model market that keeps data local. Their 2025 paper deals with federated learning, where groups train one model but keep raw data at home. A market needs to know which data sets help, and how well they blend, with no raw access.

Their score tool rests on a distance between data spreads, fit for the shared setup. A spread-out method finds that distance in a privacy-safe way. A growth law for model scores then lets them forecast gains with no full training. Tests span skewed, mis-tagged, and un-tagged sources.
arxiv-2509-18304:
Khanh-Hung Giang-Tran and 3 co-authors sort when two-level convex tasks can be solved to their true best. Their 2025 paper deals with bilevel optimization, where an outer task holds an inner task as a limit. Strong duality can fail there, since a classic gap rule may not hold.

The team shows strong duality is just the trait that makes inner and outer values settle right in the long run. A simple test can ensure it, yet that test alone does not ensure the path lands on the best set. A well-posedness link adds the last piece. Past solver work held these terms in a hidden way.
arxiv-2509-18404:
Control problems ask for the best action plan, but the goal often changes from task to task. Xingjian Li and five co-authors present a method that adapts to new goals with no fresh solving. Their 2025 paper learns a set of reusable building blocks for control plans. Once learned, those blocks can be mixed to fit a new task on the fly.

Training happens offline: the blocks are learned by copying expert plans. At run time, only light mixing weights need to be found, from data or from the task description. Tests spanned varied dynamics, sizes, and cost shapes. The method stayed near optimal while adding very little cost per new task. The result is feedback plans that work across a wide range of goals. The authors aim them at real-time use where goals shift often.
arxiv-2509-19104:
Aligning language models with human feedback can backfire when the model over-optimizes against flawed preference data. Sharan Sahu and Martin T. Wells introduce DRO-REBEL, a family of alignment updates that guard against that overfitting. The idea is distributional robustness: train for the worst plausible shift in the data, within a set distance. Their sets are built from three standard distance measures between distributions.

Strong duality turns each robust update into a simple relative-reward regression, keeping the method as scalable as its non-robust parent. No clipping tricks or value networks are needed. Under stated conditions they prove error bounds that beat earlier robust analyses, including the first rate for alignment under preference shift. Each distance choice gives a practical gradient algorithm. Across emotion, multi-objective, and helpfulness benchmarks, the method beat robust and non-robust baselines on unseen preference mixes.
arxiv-2509-19504:
When a loan model turns someone down, a counterfactual tells them what change would flip the answer. Trung Nguyen Thanh and three co-authors work on making those tips both realistic and fast to compute. Their starting point is a known method that checks how odd a suggested change looks against real data. That check adds many rules to the solver and slows it down.

The team rewrote the solver with far fewer rules for the oddness check. They tested it with a linear classifier on credit data. Solve times fell while the quality of the tips held steady. Faster, realistic tips matter for banks that must explain many decisions. The work also points to leaner math for explanation tools in wider data science use.
arxiv-2509-19804:
Motion demos for robots often record only body states, not the motor commands behind them. Sowoo Lee and three co-authors build DynaFlow, which learns from state-only demos while respecting physics. A differentiable simulator sits inside the generative model. The model proposes actions, the simulator turns them into state paths, and every output is physically feasible by construction.

Training then infers the hidden action sequences behind the demos. The team deployed the learned actions on a real Go1 quadruped robot. It reproduced varied gaits from the data and carried out long motion sequences under open-loop control. Even unfeasible human-style demos were reshaped into executable, stylish moves. Physics-checked generation could ease robot teaching across many body types.
arxiv-2509-19904:
Thin sheets called MXenes may carry current with no loss once hydrogen is added. Jakkapat Seeyangnok and Udomsilp Pinsook test six mixes in the computer. The metals are molybdenum, vanadium, or zirconium. The partner is carbon or nitrogen. They check which amounts of hydrogen keep the sheet stable.

Light and medium coats held up in most mixes. A full coat shook most sheets apart. One zirconium mix stayed stable at full coat and showed a rare band crossing. The molybdenum mixes linked electrons to lattice shakes most strongly, a good sign for lossless flow. All sheets stayed metal-like. Thin lossless materials could serve quantum tools, so testing them in the computer first saves years of failed lab work.
arxiv-2509-20304:
When should an advertiser repeat an ad? Kailash Gopal Darmasubramanian and three co-authors answer with psychology in a 2025 arXiv paper. Simple rules like even spacing and frequency caps ignore how interest actually evolves. Their model builds user interest from three effects: mere exposure, hedonic adaptation, and operant conditioning.

Exposure and adaptation are captured by a concave response to repetition, while conditioning adds a decay over time that explains fading interest after overexposure. With the number of ads fixed, the best schedule turns out to depend only on the conditioning function. Their main result is a fast algorithm whose schedule is near-optimal, missing the best possible by an exponentially small margin. A simple search then finds the best number of ads. Experiments beat standard baselines, and uniform spacing proved suboptimal in many natural settings.
arxiv-2509-20504:
Doubly occupied sites in a hot electron chain refuse to behave classically. Catalin Pascu Moca, Balazs Dora, and Gergely Zarand study those doublons at infinite temperature in a 2025 arXiv paper. The setting is the one-dimensional Hubbard model, the standard testbed for strong electron correlations. A Chebyshev expansion in a superfermionic representation yields the doublon spectrum across interaction strengths.

As interactions grow, the spectrum splits into separate bands for two-hole and two-particle excitations. Despite the heat and the strong correlations, doublons stay coherent. They undergo long-lived Bloch oscillations when an electric field is applied. Their motion also shows quantum walk behavior with light-cone spreading at strong coupling, read from the space- and time-resolved Green's function. The results extend the group's companion study of single-particle coherence in the same maximally hot chain.
arxiv-2509-20704:
Radio waves offer a way to catch ultra-high-energy neutrinos and cosmic rays that rarely hit Earth. Mohammad Ful Hossain Seikh and four co-authors summarize the first Indian workshop on that topic in this 2025 editorial. The meeting took place in April 2024 at Aligarh Muslim University in India.

The piece lays out why radio detection matters for these elusive particles. It then recaps the talks given at the workshop, which formed a special collection on radio methods. Topics span detector designs, field experiments, and analysis plans. The summary gives newcomers a compact entry point into a growing branch of particle astrophysics and records how the Indian research community joined it.
arxiv-2509-20804:
A search system that scores well once may score poorly when the training seed changes. Meng Yuan and Justin Zobel measure that instability in a 2025 paper on information retrieval methods. They test both classic statistical models and transformer-based learning models across three retrieval tasks.

Bootstrapping test sets gives one view of performance variation, and the authors confirm it works. Changing random seeds gives another view for learning methods. Statistical models stay stable under seed changes. Transformer models swing widely. In most cases their F1 scores varied by large margins across seeds. The authors warn that single-run results from such models can mislead, and that performance claims should report this seed-driven spread.
arxiv-2509-20904:
Recommender systems increasingly generate items from learned semantic codes instead of searching a fixed list. Kairui Fu and eleven co-authors benchmark how those codes should be built in FORGE, a 2025 paper accepted for KDD 2026. The setting is industrial recommendation data.

Semantic identifiers assign each item a meaningful code that a generative model can produce token by token. Earlier work rarely compared construction strategies, and judging codes usually meant expensive model training. FORGE offers a taxonomy of the construction process and tests each choice offline across many settings. The findings were applied in production, where the authors report a measurable lift in transactions. The benchmark gives industry teams a cheaper way to design identifiers before committing to full training.
arxiv-2509-21304:
C. López-Sanjuan and 22 co-authors wrote an astronomy paper in 2025 on white dwarfs in survey data. White dwarfs are the dense remains of dead stars. The J-PLUS survey maps the sky in twelve optical filters. Its third data release covers a wide sky area. The authors build a catalogue of white dwarfs from that release and study odd outliers.

They fit the twelve band data with a Bayesian method to get temperature, surface gravity, and distance. Models cover hydrogen and helium atmospheres. Sources with poor fits were flagged as outliers. A dimension reduction tool called UMAP sorted those outliers into distinct groups. The catalogue holds close to fifteen thousand white dwarfs brighter than a set limit.
arxiv-2509-21404: Xiaotie Deng and Hanyu Li argue in a short 2025 position paper that large language models need symbolism. Scaling alone, they claim, will not unlock genuine discovery. In their view, these models have powerful but blind intuition. Human crafted symbols can serve as a compass to guide that intuition toward real discovery.
arxiv-2509-21504:
Recurrent neural networks trained on brain style tasks tend to find the same simple solution. That simplicity bias helps interpretability but limits new hypotheses about neural circuits. Networks collapse onto fixed point attractors or other low dimensional patterns. William Qian and Cengiz Pehlevan propose a method to break that collapse in a 2025 paper. The goal is a set of genuinely different candidate solutions.

Iterative Neural Similarity Deflation penalizes how well one network activity predicts another. Standard task trained networks supply the reference solutions to move away from. An alternative class of solutions to classic neuroscience tasks emerges under that pressure. The authors present the method as a way to widen hypothesis generation. Brain computations might use solutions that simple training never finds.
arxiv-2509-21604:
Singular integrals with highly degenerate denominators arise in rigorous wave turbulence and heat conduction theory. Alexey Elokhin studies their asymptotics in a 2025 paper. The integrals live on a closed Riemannian manifold with a small setting in the denominator. Peierls kinetic theory for thermal conductivity in solids is one source. Earlier work treated flat space with a Morse function assumption.

Elokhin weakens that Morse assumption sharply, broadening where the results apply. Asymptotic behaviour is derived as the small setting tends to zero. Two integral forms are treated, one with an oscillatory cosine factor. The work continues studies by Kuksin and by Dymov. Rigorous justification of kinetic theory problems is the meant use of the sharper asymptotics.
arxiv-2509-21804:
Rebuilding the state of twisted light beams from lab data is hard, and it gets harder as the beams grow more complex. Mwezi Koni and four co-authors try a new route in this 2025 physics paper: let a quantum computer do the rebuilding. Their test case is structured light, beams whose shape carries extra information. The beams hold entangled photons that twist as they travel.

The team turns the rebuilding task into an energy problem of the kind quantum computers handle well. A variational solver then searches for the state that best fits real measurements. The method picks out the main parts of the state's density matrix, the table that describes the light. Tests show it still works on today's noisy quantum hardware, hinting at help where classical methods stall.
arxiv-2509-22004:
Andris Ambainis, Hartmut Klauck, and Debbie Lim classify the measures of communication complexity in this 2025 theoretical computer science paper. Communication complexity asks how much two parties must exchange to compute a joint function. Many measures exist, for different models of the exchange. Following the spirit of the Chomsky hierarchy for grammars, the authors group the measures into classes, but with a new rule for when two measures count as the same.

Two measures are declared constant-equivalent when one stays bounded by a constant exactly for the functions where the other does. That is a much coarser lens than the usual polylogarithmic one. Under it, the authors identify five equivalence classes. The grouping surprises: powerful communication models land in the same class as weak ones. Some seemingly weaker models rise to the top of the hierarchy.
arxiv-2509-22504:
Jinyeop Song, Jeff Gore, and Max Kleiman-Weiner measure how much control a language model agent has over its future. They use empowerment, an information-theoretic score of how much an agent's actions sway what happens next. Unlike task scores, it needs no hand-built benchmark for each job. Their algorithm, EELMA, estimates this score from multi-turn text interactions, which pose special challenges.

They tested EELMA on text games and on realistic web and tool-use settings. Empowerment tracked average task success closely. It also varied in telling ways across models, settings, and agent setups. High-empowerment states and actions often marked turning points for general skill. The score thus complements success rates as a broad gauge of agent quality.
arxiv-2509-22904:
Yannick Wunderlich, Kyungseon Joo, and Victor I Mokeev work out integrals that mix Legendre polynomials with their derivatives. Such integrals show up in multipole expansions and in spectral methods for physics. Yet closed forms for any derivative order are hard to find in books or software. The note fills that gap.

The three authors use repeated integration by parts and parity arguments to reach explicit formulas. Their results come as binomial and Gamma-function forms that hold for all valid index choices. The formulas merge and extend known orthogonality rules. They aim to give ready tools for both hand work and code.
arxiv-2509-23204:
A phrase like 'with a knife' can modify a verb or a noun, and models must choose. Stefan Arnold and René Gröbner probe that choice inside Gemma-2. Their prompts hold with-headed phrases that fit either reading equally. The model favored the instrumental, verb-side reading by a clear ratio. The team then hunted the heads behind the bias.

Activations were projected into vocabulary space to spot candidate heads. Scaling one head's value vector shifted the output balance. Instrument readings fell to about a third of outputs. Attributive readings rose to a similar share. The study shows a single head can steer a grammar choice.
arxiv-2509-23704:
Precision clocks and sensors lean on frequency combs, rulers of light whose teeth must span huge color ranges. Xuan Zhang and 10 co-authors built a self-referenced comb on a chip at a one-gigahertz repetition rate. Silicon nitride waveguides with low loss generate a supercontinuum over three octaves, from visible light into the mid-infrared, at very low pulse energy. Third-harmonic generation on the same chip supplies the beat note needed for self-referencing.

Older combs needed separate stages for broadening and referencing, which hurt compactness. Here one waveguide does both jobs. The authors say the approach suits on-chip filtering and detectors, pointing toward field-ready broadband comb sources.
arxiv-2509-23804:
City models for planning and games need layouts that are large, valid, and easy to steer. Mengyuan Niu and 5 co-authors built a framework that generates 3D urban layouts under semantic and structural guidance. Image-based rivals give variety but break geometric continuity, while graph methods capture structure and miss parcel meaning. Their graph fuses geometry with semantic attributes, adds edge weights, and embeds building height, lifting 2D layouts into 3D form.

Users can steer results by editing semantic attributes directly. Experiments show the method produces valid, large-scale urban models. The authors offer it as a practical tool for data-driven planning and design work.
arxiv-2509-23904:
Twist two layers of MoTe2 by about two degrees and strange phases crowd into the moire pattern. Cheong-Eung Ahn and 4 co-authors report superconductivity appearing between ferromagnetism and a non-Abelian fractional spin Hall insulator in the half-filled second moire band. Using a continuum model with exact diagonalization, they identify the phase by several signs: negative binding energy, a dominant pair-density eigenvalue, finite superfluid stiffness, and a nodal extended s-wave pairing symmetry.

Their numerics suggest a continuous transition into the spin Hall insulator. Field theory points to condensation of half-charge anyons as the driver. From the metal side, a Kohn-Luttinger instability offers a second route in.
arxiv-2509-24304:
Long videos swamp vision-language models that sample frames evenly and reason in static text. Zefeng He and 5 co-authors built FrameThinker, a model that thinks with long videos by spotlighting frames over several turns. It can question the video again and again, picking frames as an action.

Training runs in two phases: supervised fine-tuning installs the basic actions, then reinforcement learning shapes the strategy. The team explored reward design for each action and format in depth. On reasoning and long-video benchmarks, FrameThinker gained clearly over baselines while processing far fewer frames. Its mid-size model set a new best on one reasoning benchmark with a small fraction of rival frame counts.
arxiv-2509-24404:
Matching a piano tone by ear means twisting equalizer knobs until two recordings sound alike. Song-Ze Yu built an AI system that predicts those equalizer settings direct from audio features. Unlike audio-to-audio methods, it outputs readable values, such as the gain of each band, which musicians can then adjust by hand in their own workflow.

Yu trained on piano recordings made with systematically varied equalizer settings. Both regression models and a neural network were tested on the task. The neural network reached low error on multi-band prediction. Yu offers the system as a practical, flexible tool for automated tone matching, with room to grow toward richer effects.
arxiv-2510-00304:
Amir Joudaki and seven colleagues published this 2025 paper on why neural networks lose the ability to keep learning. In a changing world, a model's skill at learning new tasks degrades over time, a failure called loss of plasticity. The authors attack the problem from first principles with dynamical systems theory. They define the failure as gradient paths getting trapped on stable manifolds in parameter space.

Two trap-building mechanisms stand out in their analysis. Saturated activations freeze units so they stop responding to new data. Redundant representations clone units, collapsing the model's effective variety. Both traps shrink the effective rank of what the network represents. The same low-rank simplicity that helps on fixed data thus hurts in continual learning, a sharp tension. Simulations back the theory, and the authors test architectural choices and noise as possible escapes.
arxiv-2510-00404:
Xudong Zhu, Mohammad Mahdi Khalili, and Zhihui Zhu published this 2025 paper rethinking sparse autoencoders for language model interpretability. These tools split a model's hidden states into sparse, hopefully meaningful features. The authors derive the whole family from the original dictionary learning problem by unrolling an optimization method. One update step, they show, naturally reproduces popular variants like ReLU, JumpReLU, and TopK designs.

That derivation exposes a shared flaw: standard designs force features to stay non-negative. A single feature then cannot encode a two-sided concept, such as male versus female. Meanings fragment into redundant one-sided features instead. Their AbsTopK variant keeps the largest activations by absolute value, preserving both signs. Across four language models and seven tasks, it improved reconstruction and interpretability in their tests. It even matched a supervised method that needs labeled data for every concept.
arxiv-2510-01104:
Hahn, Ranabhat, and Anza introduce a new measure of quantum coherence in this 2025 arXiv paper on quantum physics. Coherence captures how strongly a quantum system sits in superposition, and standard measures read it from the density matrix alone. Two very different mixtures of pure states can share one density matrix, so those measures miss structure at the ensemble level. The authors use geometric quantum mechanics to define probability-phase mutual information for such ensembles.

Their measure tracks correlations between the probabilities and the relative phases of the pure states in a mixture. They prove ensemble coherence always meets or exceeds the density-matrix value, which quantifies what averaging throws away. Worked examples show temperature-dependent correlations in thermal ensembles that the density matrix hides completely. A non-zero value also signals the breakdown of deep thermalization, a current topic in condensed matter physics.
arxiv-2510-01304:
Zeng and co-authors teach vision-language models to actually look, by making them solve jigsaw puzzles interactively. Today's models fail near-randomly at simple jigsaws, exposing shallow perception beneath fluent chat. Their framework, AGILE, turns puzzle solving into a loop of action and feedback.

At each step the model writes code that moves a piece, then sees the updated scene. Fine-grained visual feedback guides the next attempt, so perception improves through doing. Performance jumped on jigsaws of varying difficulty. The skills transferred to broader visual question answering and reasoning tasks as well. Executable code, not chat, is the model's hands in this setup. Exploration replaces the missing supply of curated vision data. Puzzle difficulty scales, letting teachers grade the curriculum. Perception and reasoning improve together rather than in sequence. Interaction is the training signal here, above all else.
arxiv-2510-01404:
Foland and co-authors check whether robot policies trained by imitation truly learn the physical constraints hidden in their demonstrations. A two-armed task succeeds only when both grippers respect a precise kinematic relationship. Task success alone can hide sloppy constraint learning, so the team measures the manifold directly.

Perturbed teleoperation data of varying size and quality fed the training runs. Policies learned only a coarse approximation of the constraint surface. Shrinking or degrading the dataset hurt constraint satisfaction clearly. Bending the manifold's curvature produced no consistent effect, an inconclusive factor. Real hardware trials confirmed the pattern matters off screen too. MIT's computer science laboratory hosts the author team. Constraint manifolds are the invisible rails the demonstrations run on. Bimanual coordination is where sloppy approximation shows first. Dataset quality beat curvature as the lever worth funding in practice.
arxiv-2510-01504:
Wang, Wang, and Liang make Rydberg antiblockade robust by sweeping the laser through resonance adiabatically instead of parking on a fragile sweet spot. Antiblockade lets one excited atom facilitate neighbors, a resource for quantum information and sensing. Position disorder and parameter drift have kept the effect experimentally delicate.

The rapid sweep crosses the interaction-shifted resonance regardless of exact local conditions. Simulations show excitation transfer surviving realistic imperfections, limited mainly by atomic decay. A natural avalanche of excitations follows in one- and two-dimensional arrays. That avalanche offers high gain with exceptionally low background for rare-event detection. Neutral-atom arrays are the hardware platform being served. Blackbody-limited decay at room temperature sets the performance ceiling. Blockade physics is reviewed to motivate its deliberate inversion. Sensing applications benefit directly from the avalanche's quiet background. Robustness, long the roadblock, becomes the design.
arxiv-2510-01704:
Musacchio, Lee, and Park introduce InstaFormer in this 2025 computer vision paper. Their task is judging how objects in a scene overlap and stack in depth. Older systems needed ready-made masks for every object as input. They also compared object pairs one at a time, so the cost grew fast as scenes got busier.

InstaFormer takes only an ordinary color image as its input. In a single forward pass it returns the full occlusion and depth ordering for every object present. Object queries inside the network exchange information with latent mask descriptors for the same objects. Wide benchmarks and ablation tests showed the design works well. It matched or beat the best available baselines on both ordering tasks. Its text-formatted outputs even helped vision-language models grasp scene geometry without extra training.
arxiv-2510-01804:
Biswas and Dumitrescu study special leaf-like structures on doughnut-shaped complex spaces in this 2025 mathematics paper. A foliation slices a space into surfaces that fit together smoothly, like pages in a book. Their spaces are compact complex tori, and their foliations are holomorphic and nowhere singular. The class they define extends Ghys's turbulent foliations into higher codimension.

For these turbulent foliations, the authors examine the geometry seen across the leaves. Such transverse structure can be described by holomorphic Cartan geometries. They prove that every one of those geometries must be flat for this class. They also prove a uniqueness result for the geometries that can occur. Flatness plus uniqueness pins down the transverse behavior almost completely. The results add rigid structure theorems to the theory of foliations on tori.
arxiv-2510-01904:
Cescutti and Matteucci review how aging giant stars seed the galaxy with heavy elements in this astronomy paper. Asymptotic giant branch stars cook neutron-capture elements through the slow s-process in their interiors. Winds and envelopes then carry those elements into interstellar space. The review gathers four decades of work on that enrichment story.

The authors trace the main modeling steps the field has taken over that span. They show how abundance patterns in Milky Way stars test both stellar yield calculations and galactic history. Matching models to observations constrains how stars forge elements and how the galaxy formed its stars over time. Galactic archaeology, reading old stars as fossils, plays a growing role in that comparison. Sharper chemical yields keep tightening the constraints year by year. The review frames AGB stars as central witnesses to the chemical evolution of the Milky Way.
arxiv-2510-02304:
Leong and Roy predict that two effects together make ordered phases in Dirac materials far easier to reach. Their 2025 physics paper studies flat and curved Dirac systems. Dirac materials have almost no states near zero energy. They form mass and order only past a strong interaction threshold. A magnetic field can force that order at any weak coupling. The effect is called magnetic catalysis. A special non-Hermitian tweak can also lower the threshold. Non-Hermitian here means the system trades energy with its surroundings in a balanced way.

Symmetry arguments show the two boosts reinforce each other. The combined effect holds for uneven magnetic fields too. Local orders then follow the field profile across the sample. The prediction covers both flat sheets and negatively curved lattices. Designers of quantum materials gain a new knob. Pairing fields with engineered loss may unlock phases once out of reach.
arxiv-2510-02404:
Agarwal, Rodriguez, and Buyya survey how serverless functions get their resource settings. Their 2025 review covers Function-as-a-Service platforms like AWS Lambda. Developers must pick memory and compute for each function. Those picks drive both cost and speed. Platforms reveal little about how resources map to performance. Many developers therefore guess from habit or folklore. The survey organizes research on dynamic configuration into a taxonomy. It covers how settings are chosen, adjusted, and managed over time. Usage based pricing makes idle capacity free, which sharpens the puzzle.

The authors map open challenges across the field. Better transparency tools rank high on that list. Automatic tuning under changing workloads remains unsolved. They close with future directions for researchers. Cloud bills reward whoever configures functions well. A shared map of methods helps teams stop guessing.
arxiv-2510-02604:
Scott, Morrison, and Bristowe show that two competing instabilities can yield triple loop switching. Their 2025 materials physics paper revisits a textbook Landau model. These materials hold electric polarization that fields can flip. Proper ones polarize through their main instability. Improper ones polarize as a side effect of another order. When both instabilities compete inside one material, new behavior appears. The polarization can switch among several stable states. First principles calculations point to hexagonal tungsten bronzes as the showcase family. Those materials may flip between improper and proper phases.

The predicted switching traces a triple loop under field sweeps. That shape mimics so called ferrielectric behavior. Multistate response suits lasting memory devices well. Brain style computing could also use such backbones. Temperature alone may not drive the change in practice. Electric fields offer the switching route. Simple free energy models can still surprise designers.
arxiv-2510-02804:
Kiermaier, Mannaert, and Wassermann study special yes-no functions on slices. A slice is the set of all subsets of a fixed size drawn from a larger set. Such slices form what mathematicians call the Johnson scheme. A basic function flags the sets that sit between two fixed bounds. The authors add two opposite basic functions together. The sum is almost always a Boolean function, one that outputs only zero or one.

Their main result gives the exact degree of every such paired function. Degree here means the lowest degree of a polynomial that reproduces it. The proof uses plain steps, with no spectral machinery. The general case then reduces to it. In some settings the degree dips below the obvious bound. For even degrees on the middle layer, paired functions are the smallest known examples of their kind. They beat the long-standing pencil construction.
arxiv-2510-02904:
Hendrick and Manoli describe city growth with the physics of rough surfaces. Building heights change in uneven, jittery ways over time. The authors model height change as geometric Brownian motion. In plain terms, growth has a steady drift plus random shocks. The shocks scale with the height itself. Economic growth supplies the drift in their account. That simple model fits height data from cities worldwide.

Real neighborhoods also influence each other, so the team added spatial coupling. Nearby growth then smooths the wildest swings. Under a smooth limit, the coupled model becomes the KPZ equation. That equation is a classic of surface growth physics. The authors estimated the roughness exponent for many cities. Most estimates landed near the KPZ prediction. City form, on this evidence, follows a known physics law. Planners gain a firmer base for forecasting urban change.
arxiv-2510-03004:
Hu and co-authors hunt brain markers of schizophrenia in resting scans. A classifier could aid diagnosis, but black boxes earn little trust. Their framework, BrainIB++, uses a graph neural network on brain networks. An information bottleneck guides the learning. The bottleneck keeps only the most telling parts of each network. Those parts form a subgraph that doubles as an explanation.

Three multi-cohort data sets tested the model. Nine established rival methods served as the bar. BrainIB++ beat them on accuracy across the sets. It also held up on cohorts it had never seen. The flagged regions matched known clinical markers well. Visual and sensorimotor networks stood out, as did higher cognition areas. Named spots included the calcarine and fusiform regions. Such agreement makes the output readable for clinicians. Data-driven markers that doctors can inspect are the goal.
arxiv-2510-03104:
Mei, Shorinwa, and Majumdar test whether geometry-aware features help robots that rebuild scenes. Radiance fields store a scene's look from every angle. Baking vision model features into them gives open-word skills. Most features come from visual-only models like DINO or CLIP. Newer backbones add spatial grounding to their features. The authors ask if that grounding pays off in the fields. Three questions structure their study.

Grounded features did carry finer structural detail. Object localization, though, showed no real gain from grounding. The third test inverted a field to recover camera pose. Their SPINE method does that without a starting guess. A coarse step uses the baked features, then a fine step polishes with raw images. Grounded features made pose accuracy worse, not better. Visual-only features proved more versatile overall. Supervised grounding may be the weak link, they suggest.
arxiv-2510-03204:
Kerboua and co-authors slim down what web agents read so they can act faster and safer. Web pages flood agents with tens of thousands of tokens. Full pages strain context limits and inflate compute cost. They also smuggle prompt injections into the agent's view. FocusAgent sends a lightweight retriever over the page first. Guided by the task goal, it keeps only relevant lines. The pruned view then drives the agent's action choices.

Observation size fell by more than half in the trials. Task success matched strong full-context baselines regardless. Two benchmark suites, WorkArena and WebArena, hosted the tests. Several backbone models and retrievers all showed the benefit. Security improved alongside efficiency in a dedicated variant. Banner and pop-up injection attacks succeeded far less often. Clean-setting performance stayed intact under the defense. Targeted retrieval still looks like a robust design principle.
arxiv-2510-03304:
Eftekhari, Khalighi, and Abbasbandy present a 2025 arXiv paper on the stability of neural systems built from memory aware parts. Memristors are tiny devices that act like synapses, holding a trace of past signals. Fractional order math adds longer memory, which suits real nerve cells well. The team studies two setups: a pair of Rulkov neurons joined by two memristors, and a ring network built from many such neuron groups.

The authors prove a new theorem that maps the safe zones where these systems stay stable. The map applies to both the simple pair and the larger ring. Inside those zones, the models behave in steady, forecastable ways. Outside them, wild behavior can take over. Such maps help engineers design brain like circuits that will not drift into chaos. The work also gives theorists a tool for checking other fractional order networks with memory rich parts.
arxiv-2510-03404:
Ammon, Germerodt, Sieling, and Virrueta present a 2025 arXiv paper on computing real time heat state correlations through holography. Field theories track such correlations along folded time contours named for Schwinger and Keldysh. More folds capture operator orderings, including out of time order patterns tied to chaos. The authors propose a matching gravity picture for any such contour. It glues several black hole spacetimes together at their horizons, with joining rules set by unitarity and heat balance.

As a proof of concept, they solve for a field inside the glued geometry. They compute the spread of signals and then four point functions at the lowest order. The diagrams that matter explore the full four fold geometry, yet their result collapses into a simple factored form. The team offers a conjecture on higher order patterns with a partial proof. The recipe opens real time, out of equilibrium physics to gravity methods.
arxiv-2510-03504:
Wang and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on keeping a team of quadrotors connected while they fly through clutter. Robots that share sensing and radio links must stay within range of the team. Obstacles and blocked sight lines snap those links often in practice. Their framework plans smooth paths and controls the drones at the same time. Safety rules based on barrier functions hold spacing and prevent collisions while the team moves.

A second mechanism, built on Lyapunov functions, actively steers a split team back together. That recovery skill sets the work apart from methods that only guard existing links. Paths follow Bézier curves, which give smooth motion with clean derivatives at every level. Simulations in obstacle rich scenes backed the design. A live test with four Crazyflie nano quadrotors confirmed the system on real hardware. Search, mapping, and rescue teams all need links that heal themselves mid flight.
arxiv-2510-03604:
Wang and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv survey of domain adaptation methods for predicting the remaining useful life of turbofan jet engines. Airlines want warning before engines fail, but models trained on one fleet's data falter under different conditions and scarce target data. Domain adaptation transfers knowledge from data rich sources to data poor targets while correcting for the shift between them. The authors review methods built for the quirks of engine data: complex operating regimes, many sensors, and slowly changing signals.

Their contribution is a three way taxonomy sorted by how adaptation is applied, where shifts arise, and which problem each method answers. They also benchmark techniques on engine data sets, giving practitioners comparisons. An open source collection of the surveyed methods accompanies the review. The authors close with open challenges, including adaptation across different engine types. Better transfer means maintenance warnings that stay trustworthy when fleets and routes change.
arxiv-2510-04104:
Bunimovich and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper generalizing a classic toy model of statistical mechanics, the Kac ring. Kac's 1956 ring showed how irreversible-looking behavior emerges from reversible microscopic rules. Its scatterers, however, were inert: particles bounced off them without changing them, so no real energy exchange occurred. The authors let black particles modify the scatterers they pass, giving the environment internal states like energy levels.

That feedback makes the model self-consistent, with particles interacting indirectly and over long range through the medium. The team proves every initial state eventually converges to a time-periodic orbit. They also describe the basins of attraction for some of these periodic states. Energy sharing between constituents is a prerequisite for equipartition and temperature, so the extension addresses a real gap. The work clarifies how environment-mediated interaction drives a system toward stationary behavior.
arxiv-2510-04504:
Zijing Hu and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on why text to image models miss the prompt. Diffusion models build an image by clearing noise from all pixels in lockstep. A region tied to the prompt can only consult neighbors that are just as noisy as itself. It never gets clear context early, so details land in the wrong place. The team let different pixels follow different timetables.

In their asynchronous models, each pixel gets its own denoising schedule. Regions tied to the prompt clear more slowly, so they can lean on the clearer context around them. Regions with no prompt role finish early and stop costing attention. Wide experiments across many prompts showed clear gains in prompt alignment. The final images matched the requested content more faithfully than lockstep models did. The idea is simple, but it changes a basic habit of diffusion models.
arxiv-2510-04704:
Taoyuze Lv and nine coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a benchmark that tests language models on crystal structures. Materials science runs on three dimensional atomic arrangements stored in a standard file format. The team built AtomWorld to measure whether models truly grasp those structures. Its tasks cover reading the files, editing structures, and building models toward target properties. Leading models set promising baselines on some parts of the suite.

The story is failure. Models made frequent errors when asked to modify structures. They stumbled even on questions about the file format itself. Small early mistakes then pile up through later analysis steps. The authors argue that fluent text about crystals is not the same as spatial understanding. AtomWorld gives the field a yardstick for that gap. Better scores would signal models ready to help automate real materials workflows. Until then, the benchmark warns against trusting model output on structures unchecked.
arxiv-2510-05004:
Hamza Adrat and Laurent Decreusefond work in probability theory in this 2025 arXiv paper. They study point processes, which are random patterns of points in space. The simplest such pattern, the Poisson process, is fully random. The authors ask how fast two messier patterns settle toward that simple limit.

Their tool is Stein's method, a technique that produces explicit error bounds. The first pattern scatters points along random lines in the plane. The second places satellite-like points on great-circle orbits over a sphere. For the satellite model, the gap to the uniform limit shrinks at a rate of order 1 over n, where n counts the orbits. Both bounds give practitioners a precise handle on approximation error.
arxiv-2510-05104:
Hiromasa Nakayama and Nobuki Takayama build algorithms for a hard computation in D-module theory in this 2025 arXiv paper. A D-module encodes a system of linear partial differential equations. Its restriction describes what the system looks like on a smaller subspace. When the equations carry parameters, one answer must serve whole regions of parameter space.

The authors extend the comprehensive Gröbner system method to compute a generic b-function for restriction. They then stratify the parameter space so each region gets its own restriction result. The hard part is that key roots still depend on the parameters. Isomorphism tricks between related modules resolve that dependence. For hypergeometric systems, including Horn-type ones, they give a complete classification-based algorithm.
arxiv-2510-05404:
Martin Milanič and Đorđe Mitrović ask when every short path in a symmetric graph must close into a cycle in this 2025 arXiv paper. A 2022 result showed every induced two-edge path in a vertex-transitive graph closes to an induced cycle. Similar results followed for edge-transitive graphs. The authors generalize the question to paths of any length and to induced versions.

They completely solve the problem for vertex-transitive graphs and edge-transitive graphs. The non-star edge-transitive case is settled as well. For nearly every negative answer, they supply infinite families of connected counterexamples. Positive cases pin down exactly which path lengths always close. The work turns scattered closing results into a finished classification for the main symmetry classes.
arxiv-2510-05504:
Cha and colleagues give smart contracts a firmer economic foundation. Smart contracts are programs on a blockchain that enforce deals without a middleman. Many projects use them to split shared resources, yet few designs rest on rigorous theory. Their 2025 study builds a mechanism design framework for that allocation task.

The framework bakes fairness and efficiency goals into the contract rules themselves. The authors prove that a contract equilibrium exists and is unique. They also give a decentralized price-adjustment method and prove that it converges. Tests combine large synthetic benchmarks with a real MovieLens case study. The mechanism improved both efficiency and equity and stayed stable under sudden shocks. Such proof matters where allocations must stay transparent and auditable under pressure. It treats contracts as institutions, not just code. The authors point to supply chains, energy markets, and health care as likely users.
arxiv-2510-05604:
Kanaji and colleagues examine how open-source projects handle security reporting policies. GitHub urges projects to add a SECURITY.md file with private reporting instructions. Adoption stays low, at about seven percent of projects. Their 2025 study mines GitHub issues to find the friction.

The team classified 711 randomly sampled issues about SECURITY.md files. Nearly eighty percent simply asked a project to add the file. About half of those requests came from huntr.dev, a bug bounty platform. Reports including links closed a median of two days faster. Only about twelve percent asked to revise an existing file. They also compared close times across six community health files. The pattern shows the practice is still diffusing, not yet standard. Public reporting channels risk exposing vulnerabilities to malicious readers. The file clarifies reporting, yet it can also add confusion and burden.
arxiv-2510-05704:
Ghosh and colleagues model cracks in heat-stressed anisotropic solids without absurd strains. Standard theory predicts endless strain at a crack tip, which is unreal. Strain-limiting theory caps strain while letting stress grow very large. Their 2025 finite element scheme applies that theory to solids stiff along one axis.

The model couples a steady heat equation with quasilinear elastic laws. Galerkin elements split the flat boundary value problem onto a grid. Picard rounds solve the nonlinear system, with settling tracked round to round. Tests use an edge crack under severe heat-plus-load stress. Stress piles up hard at the tip, as standard theory expects. Strain, though, grows far more slowly and stays bounded at all points. Two fiber angles and two heat settings show the same trends. The base supports forecasts of crack growth driven by heat. Turbine blades and re-entry craft drive the anisotropic setting.
arxiv-2510-06104:
Adejumo and Johnson of George Mason University target a communication failure in defect tools in a 2025 software engineering paper. Static analysis flags risky code with raw metrics such as complexity and coupling. New open-source contributors often cannot turn a bare number into a decision, so the warnings go unused.

One cited study found that 68 percent of fault prediction models explain nothing about their output. The authors propose using large language models to translate metric values into plain risk explanations and concrete guidance. They outline three explanation types an assistant should offer: descriptive, contextual, and actionable. Their next step is a task-based study with open-source contributors. It will compare metric-only reports against generated explanations on decision quality, completion time, and error rates. Closing the explanation gap could raise both trust in and adoption of prediction tools.
arxiv-2510-06404:
Ravishankar, Kulkarni, and Vaidya design MuFASA, an asynchronous checkpointing algorithm for eventually consistent databases, in a 2025 distributed computing paper. Such databases create odd anomalies, so frequent consistent snapshots help check invariants. Classic snapshot schemes impose heavy overhead or capture dirty writes from partial transactions.

The target is a transaction-consistent snapshot: a strongly consistent summary of a weakly consistent computation. When an anomaly appears, focus narrows to the snapshots around it. The authors define size-minimal snapshots for fully copied databases. MuFASA reaches that minimum with small overhead. It adds only a linear count of new messages and one counter on old ones. Unlike prior schemes, the protocol is fully asynchronous. No global coordination pauses the system while a snapshot forms. Routine snapshotting becomes cheap enough for copied main-memory databases.
arxiv-2510-06504:
Wu and seven co-authors generate two-person interactions from text with a synthesis-plus-modeling framework in a 2025 computer vision paper. Two-person motion needs realistic individual dynamics plus precise partner coupling. Progress stalls on scarce two-person training data. Coarse sentence-level conditioning blurs who initiates, who responds, and when contact happens.

InterCompose synthesizes training data by composition. Language-model descriptions pair with strong single-person motion priors. It retrieves candidate motions, trains a conditional reaction generator for the second agent, and filters weak samples neurally. Coverage expands without extra motion capture. The InterActor model learns from this richer data. Word-level conditioning preserves token cues about initiation, response, and contact ordering. An adaptive interaction loss emphasizes contextually relevant joint pairs. Experiments show consistent gains in diversity, fidelity, and generalization. Out-of-distribution tests and user studies confirm the gains.
arxiv-2510-06604:
Jie Xiong and five co-authors model the glow of the hottest matter in the universe. Their 2025 paper studies the quark-gluon plasma, created briefly in heavy-ion collisions. Strong magnetic fields appear in that plasma and then fade over time. The team asks how those fields change the thermal photons the plasma emits.

They use a magnetohydrodynamic model with a simple expanding flow. The magnetic field decays as a power law, set by two control parameters. Photon rates come from three main processes, including scattering, annihilation, and bremsstrahlung. Bremsstrahlung dominates at low photon energies, up to about one giga-electron-volt in their runs. At higher energies, scattering and annihilation take over. A faster-decaying field boosts photon output in their calculations. Photons escape the plasma without rescattering, so their spectra carry clean news about the plasma's earliest moments.
arxiv-2510-06904:
Michael Atkinson and three co-authors build a fast stand-in for expensive crystal simulations. Their 2025 paper serves materials science, where crystal plasticity models predict how metals deform. Those full simulations are detailed but painfully slow. Their cost blocks uncertainty studies and full component simulations.

Their surrogate is a recurrent neural network that reads a three-dimensional grain structure directly. A gated recurrent unit carries the deformation history inside its hidden state. Mappings from the grain map feed both the starting state and each input step. Training used over three hundred thousand crystal simulations, with many grain layouts and load paths.
