The surrogate reproduces averaged stress responses for unseen histories well. It captured load-path dependence better than microstructure dependence, the authors note. More varied grain examples should close that gap. Plugged into a larger simulation as the material law, it solved equilibrium problems with varied inputs.
arxiv-2510-07404:
Gharahi and Ottaviani characterize a recursive class of tensors through a single elegant test. Their 2025 paper studies persistent tensors, which survive a substitution process and thereby certify lower bounds on tensor rank. The symmetric case corresponds to special polynomials called persistent. The authors prove that a symmetric tensor is persistent exactly when the determinant of its Hessian matrix is a pure power of a nonzero linear form. The converse direction is verified for cubic tensors and for tensors in up to three variables, using classical work by Segre.

The Hessian of such a tensor itself factors as a pure power of a lower-degree form. Small-dimensional normal forms make the class concrete. The authors also place persistent polynomials inside prehomogeneous geometry and tie them to semi-invariants and homaloidal polynomials.
arxiv-2510-08004:
Wang, Deng, and Zheng wrote this 2025 paper on detecting depression in older adults from sound, video, and personality. Self-report questionnaires miss people who understate symptoms. Their entry to a multimodal challenge instead reads behavior directly. For audio, a co-attention module fuses three feature families, from classic speech descriptors to self-supervised representations. For video, features from face analysis and two image networks combine into one visual stream.

Personality is the extra ingredient. An interaction encoder models how personality traits modulate the audio and visual evidence. Depression expresses differently across personalities, so the same flat voice can mean different things. On the challenge's elderly track, the full system significantly improved detection performance over unimodal approaches. The authors present personality as context that screening tools should never discard. Earlier and kinder detection could route older adults to help before depression deepens.
arxiv-2510-08204:
Soham Ghosh, Saloni Bhogale, and Sameer Deshpande propose sparseVCBART in a 2025 arXiv paper on flexible regression models. Varying-coefficient models let each input affect the outcome through a curve that shifts with other factors. They sit between rigid classic models and opaque machine learning tools. When inputs outnumber cases, older fits cannot tell which inputs matter or what drives the shifts.

Their method models each coefficient curve with ensembles of regression trees, grown under Bayesian rules. Priors that shrink weak signals toward zero help keep only real effects in view. The authors prove the fitted posterior settles near the truth at a near-best possible rate. Tests showed accuracy on par with top rivals and much tighter, better-calibrated error ranges. They also used it to study how talks between people shift prejudice across groups.
arxiv-2510-08304:
Matteo Amestoy and co-authors build a new health statistics method in a 2025 arXiv paper on the exposome. The exposome covers all non-genetic exposures a person meets in life, from air to diet. Such data are hard to analyze: exposures overlap strongly, repeat over time, and interact with personal traits. Their method, Profile-LMM, merges profile regression with linear mixed models.

Profile regression groups exposures into latent profiles, which tames the overlap problem. The mixed model part handles repeated measures and within-person change over time. The method also allows profiles to interact with individual characteristics. On simulated data, it recovered true parameters and the hidden exposure clusters accurately. The team then applied it to the large Lifelines cohort in the Netherlands. They found exposure combinations linked in a significant way to diastolic blood pressure.
arxiv-2510-08504:
Bayu Dirgantara and J. Julio constrain a neutrino mass model using the electron's magnetic moment in a 2025 arXiv paper. The anomalous magnetic moment, or g-2, measures how a particle's magnetism departs from theory. Their model generates neutrino masses radiatively through loops involving heavy scalar leptoquarks. Two leptoquark types, one singlet-like and one doublet-like, sit at the TeV scale.

Texture choices decouple the electron and muon sectors. Both moments can then gain chiral enhancements from different heavy quarks while dodging the muon-to-electron photon decay limit. Fitting neutrino oscillation data forces one-loop and two-loop mass terms to coexist, which constrains parameters. The muon g-2 correction ends up negligible under those constraints. The electron g-2 gap implied by rubidium measurements can close within two sigma, if neutrino mass ordering is inverted. Tau decay rates sit within reach of next-generation tests.
arxiv-2510-08604:
Raffaele Mura and co-authors craft jailbreak prompts that look natural enough to slip past filters in a 2025 arXiv paper. Jailbreaks trick safety-aligned language models into producing restricted content. Existing automated attacks append odd suffixes or long templates, which raise the prompt's perplexity sharply. A simple perplexity filter on inputs can therefore catch many of them.

Their attack, LatentBreak, instead swaps words in the original prompt for semantically equivalent ones. Each swap is chosen to pull the prompt's latent representation closer to that of harmless requests. The prompt keeps its intent and reads naturally, with low perplexity throughout. Evaluation against perplexity-based filters on several safety-aligned models favored LatentBreak over competing algorithms. Its prompts were also shorter than rivals' outputs. The work is a white-box attack, assuming access to model internals for latent measurements.
arxiv-2510-08704:
N. Kaiser computes loop integrals for sunset diagrams in two spatial dimensions plus time in a 2025 arXiv set of notes. Sunset diagrams are Feynman diagrams where several internal lines connect the same two vertices. Their loop functions reduce to n-body phase-space integrals, which Kaiser evaluates iteratively for every number of bodies. The results display a simple power-law pattern worth noting.

The phase space depends only on the total mass, the sum of all particle masses, through a clean power formula. Because of that simplicity, the loop integrals for sunset diagrams with any number of internal lines become elementary functions. Arctangents and logarithms suffice, apart from polynomial terms set by regularization choices. An outlook computes the same phase spaces in four spatial dimensions for two to five bodies. A digression to one spatial dimension shows the three-body phase space already involves a complete elliptic integral.
arxiv-2510-08804:
Raghavan and Mallick present MOSAIC, a team of language model agents built for scientific coding, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Scientific programs differ from everyday coding tasks. They demand rigorous algorithms, deep subject knowledge, and chains of subproblems where later steps build on earlier ones. There are often no simple test cases to check against. A single model working alone tends to lose the thread or invent facts.

MOSAIC splits the work among specialized agents arranged as students and teachers. The agents draft a rationale, write code, reflect on it, and debug it step by step. A consolidated context window keeps the whole chain in view, which the authors say curbs invented details. The framework needs no extra training. On scientific coding benchmarks it beat existing approaches in accuracy and robustness, and its step-by-step trail made its reasoning easier to follow.
arxiv-2510-09004:
Mou and co-authors show that a small patch can make a language model safer without making it dumber, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Safety training usually mixes refusal examples with general data and searches expensively for the right blend, because too much safety data dulls everyday skill. The team instead trains a low-rank adapter, a tiny add-on module called LoRA, on safety data alone. Refusals learned that way left general performance intact in their tests.

Evidence from theory and experiment explains why: the adapter stores safety behavior in a low-dimensional subspace set almost at right angles to the model's core space. Because the two barely overlap, strengthening refusals does not disturb the machinery of general competence. They present the adapter as a plug-and-play safety patch: cheap to train, easy to attach, and removable. Code is released for others to verify the claim.
arxiv-2510-09304:
Marwan Soliman, Pauline Kergus, Diego Regruto, Luiz Villa, and Zohra Kader wrote a 2025 arXiv paper on the control of power converters. Converters manage the flow of electrical energy between sources and loads, and each use needs a control law, meaning a rule that keeps output steady. Switching parts inside the devices make that control hard for classic methods.

The authors study a data-driven method called Virtual Reference Feedback Tuning, which builds the control law from measured data rather than from a full model of the device. They apply the method to a buck converter circuit, a circuit that lowers voltage, supplied by the OwnTech foundation. Their study tests whether feedback built from data can handle the fast switching that makes these converters tricky to govern.
arxiv-2510-09604:
Colin Holm-Hansen, Yingtian Chen, and Oleg Gnedin publish a catalogue of fake stellar streams in a 2025 arXiv paper. Real stellar streams are ribbons of stars torn from globular clusters, and their shapes trace the Milky Way's mass and may reveal dark matter's nature. To use them, astronomers need realistic models of stream populations across a whole galaxy.

The team built mock streams inside four Milky Way-mass simulated galaxies. Their pipeline models how globular clusters form and dissolve, builds time-varying gravitational potentials, and sprays particles to grow each stream. They generate mock observations for the Gaia, LSST, and Roman surveys. The two newer surveys should raise the observable star counts in streams by orders of magnitude, with LSST alone seeing a thousand or more stars in dozens of streams beyond the disc. Stream widths and lengths beyond the inner galaxy follow clean power laws in the mock data.
arxiv-2510-10204:
Chattopadhyaya and Jan Manschot study Appell functions for general lattices in this 2025 arXiv paper in mathematical physics. Appell functions are special functions that appear in string theory and number theory. The authors attach them to an arbitrary positive definite lattice, a regular grid of points with a notion of length.

They also fix a choice of independent vectors inside the lattice, up to the lattice's dimension. The resulting functions generalize earlier constructions tied to specific lattices. Such functions encode partition-like counts that appear in black hole physics and modular forms. A lattice-general theory lets one framework serve many models, instead of rebuilding the analysis for each grid that nature or theory supplies.
arxiv-2510-10304:
Hu, Benjamin Van Durme, Jacob Andreas, and Harsh Jhamtani improve sample efficiency in language model agents in this 2025 arXiv paper. Agents acting in new environments learn slowly from step-by-step interaction. That inefficiency hurts most where each interaction is costly, such as work with humans or physical systems that must be reset.

The authors rewrite past trajectories in hindsight, recasting what the agent did as training signal for better behavior. Hindsight turns even failed episodes into lessons by relabeling what they achieved. Learning from rewritten experience squeezes more value from each interaction. The method targets online learning, where the agent must improve while it works, not in a separate training phase.
arxiv-2510-11504:
PET scanners image the body by detecting pairs of photons born when a positron annihilates with an electron, but random background events blur the picture. Ana Marija Kožuljević and co-authors study a quantum trick for cleaning that background in this 2025 arXiv medical physics paper. The two annihilation photons are entangled in polarization, and if both scatter inside detectors, the difference of their scattering angles peaks sharply.

The team built a demonstrator with two polarimeter modules of scintillating crystals on a rotating gantry and measured a gallium-68 source at activities between 200 and 380 megabecquerels. Comparing polarization-correlated two-hit events with conventional single-pixel hits, they found the signal-to-random-background ratio was larger for the correlated events in every selected sample. They also showed that this ratio tracks the polarimetric modulation factor, so that factor could serve as an estimator of the random background.
arxiv-2510-11604:
Acquiring a new online shopper costs far more than keeping an existing one, yet the algorithms that predict who will leave are black boxes that cannot say why. Sanjula De Alwis and Indrajith Ekanayake propose a churn analytics framework built for explanation rather than mere prediction in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their complaint is that standard churn models identify likely leavers without revealing what drives attrition, when intervention works best, or which segments deserve priority.

The framework combines three components. Explainable AI methods describe which features drive each customer's risk. Survival analysis models time-to-event data, estimating when churn will happen, not only whether. And RFM segmentation groups customers by recency, frequency, and monetary value. From the three views the authors derive personalized retention strategies. They argue this shift lets organizations cut attrition and build loyalty instead of spraying generic discounts.
arxiv-2510-11804:
Yuwen Cui and nine colleagues survey a cat-and-mouse contest over privacy on the Tor network. Tor routes traffic through several relays to hide who visits what. Yet website fingerprinting attacks can still guess the visited site from traffic patterns alone, with accuracy climbing even in open-world tests. Their 2025 arXiv paper gathers a scattered literature into one map, which the authors say has been missing.

The survey sorts prior work into three domains: datasets, attack models, and defense mechanisms. Defenses include adaptive padding, traffic regularization, traffic morphing, and adversarial perturbation, each reshaping traces to mislead attackers. The authors compare strengths and weaknesses under varied threat models. They stress that defenses trade privacy against usability and performance, so no single winner exists. Open challenges include multi-tab browsing and attacks using only coarse traffic features. A public GitHub page lists representative studies and their datasets for future researchers.
arxiv-2510-11904:
Yiqi Wu, Simon Portegies Zwart, and H. A. Dijkstra simulate the climate of water-covered planets with tilted axes. A planet's obliquity, its axial tilt, shapes seasons and habitability, yet tilts are nearly impossible to observe directly for exoplanets. Their paper, published in New Astronomy and posted on arXiv in 2025, runs an intermediate-complexity global circulation model on aqua-planets. They vary tilt, rotation speed, and planet mass.

High obliquity breaks the symmetry between the hemispheres. The ratio of polar temperatures between north and south drifts further from equal as tilt and rotation rate grow. Cloud cover reorganizes into distinct latitude bands, with more clouds over the warmer hemisphere. The steady climate proves sensitive to tilt and spin but independent of the planet's mass. The useful upshot: a measured north-south climate asymmetry on a water world could betray its tilt and rotation rate to distant observers.
arxiv-2510-12804:
Gao studies a shape reconstruction problem in convex geometry in this 2025 arXiv paper. The question asks which convex body has a prescribed curvature measure, a record of how its surface bends. The body sits in a half-space and meets the boundary like a droplet, forming a capillary surface. The version treated here mixes two exponents in a dual curvature measure.

Gao reduces the problem to a Monge-Ampère type equation, a nonlinear equation linking a surface's curvature to a given density. It is posed on a spherical cap with a Robin boundary condition, which mixes values and slopes at the edge. For contact angles in the stated acute range, Gao proves that a unique smooth solution exists. That solution is exactly the capillary convex body the problem asks for.
arxiv-2510-13004:
Muldrow, Ludden, and Petersen compare fuel use for forced and unforced satellite rendezvous motion in this 2025 arXiv paper, a preprint of a space flight mechanics conference paper. A chaser satellite circling a target can follow natural motion trajectories that standard equations predict will cost no fuel. In reality, model mismatch means correction burns are needed, and the authors measure how big that mismatch is.

They compared predictions from the classic Clohessy-Wiltshire equations against a higher-fidelity model across several test cases with similar mission parameters, counting the impulse maneuvers required to hold the supposedly free trajectories. Their central demonstration is that unforced motions are not inherently more fuel efficient than forced ones. That finding permits extended orbital operations where forced paths prove cheaper, which matters as servicing, refueling, and debris removal missions multiply.
arxiv-2510-13104:
Pothagoni and colleagues ask how crystal orientation should be fed to neural networks in this 2025 arXiv paper, published in Acta Materialia. Networks now classify material microstructures from images. Electron backscatter diffraction maps add orientation data. Its texture and phases carry key information. Four ways of feeding in that data were candidates. Each of the four was tried in turn, on the same task, with the same networks.

The team trained networks to classify five synthetic microstructures with varying textures and grain shapes under each option. A spectral embedding of orientations won by far. It places them in a space respecting the symmetries of the crystal. The gap between the best and the rest was large. The lead held even with the small data volumes typical for practical experiments. The authors conclude that this choice significantly affects classification accuracy. It will matter more as rational materials design produces unknown textures.
arxiv-2510-13404:
Hussain and co-authors fuse images from several light bands to improve scene understanding in poor visibility. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets surveillance and self-driving systems that struggle in fog or low light. Short-wave infrared imaging sees through haze and separates materials clearly. Yet public short-wave datasets are scarce, which slows work in this area. Colour and thermal cameras each miss part of the scene on their own.

The team first creates synthetic short-wave images from thermal data using contrast enhancement methods. These synthetic images mimic structural cues without claiming to copy true spectra. A neural network then merges synthetic short-wave, thermal, and colour images through separate encoders and a gated fusion head. Tests on five public benchmarks and one private dataset show better contrast and sharper edges. The fused images also keep structural detail while running in real time.
arxiv-2510-13704:
Obando-Ceron and co-authors add simplicial embeddings to actor-critic agents and reap faster learning per interaction. Their 2025 arXiv paper addresses a trade-off in deep reinforcement learning: speed versus sample efficiency. Massive parallel training cuts wall-clock time but can still burn huge numbers of environment steps. Better-shaped internal representations offer a cheaper route to efficiency.

Simplicial embeddings are light layers that force feature vectors onto simple geometric structures. The constraint yields sparse, discrete-like features for the agent's value and policy networks. Those features steady the critic's bootstrapping, the self-referential update at the heart of actor-critic methods. They also strengthen the gradients that improve the policy. Plugged into FastTD3, FastSAC, and PPO, the layers improved both learning speed and final scores. Gains appeared across continuous and discrete control tasks, with no runtime penalty.
arxiv-2510-14104:
Giacomo Cacciapaglia, Francesco Sannino, and Jessica Turner examine the 'weak axion,' a hypothetical particle from the electroweak sector rather than the strong force, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Electroweak theory motivates a good-quality axion. It is tied to breaking the symmetry combining baryon and lepton number. Its mass is generated by electroweak instantons, and it avoids coupling with light.

The strongest limit on the decay constant, a scale for how weakly the particle interacts, comes from a loop-induced coupling to electrons. Stellar cooling pushes that scale above a thousand trillion electronvolts. The same symmetry breaking would induce proton decay through higher-dimensional operators. Limits from the Super-Kamiokande detector constrain the new-physics scale severely. Within the allowed space, signals such as a proton decaying into a positron plus the axion are undetectable. Future proton-decay searches at next-generation neutrino experiments are the most promising test.
arxiv-2510-14304:
Kyungryul Back and co-authors propose a decoding trick that uses watermarking questions to steer vision-language models toward truthful, visually grounded answers, in this 2025 arXiv paper. These models often hallucinate, leaning on one modality or on memorized training patterns instead of what the image actually shows, which undermines trust in their descriptions.

Their training-free method works in three steps. First, it chooses a mature layer and an amateur layer among the model's decoding layers. Second, it identifies a pivot layer by asking a watermark-related question that tests whether the layer is visually well-grounded. Third, it applies tri-layer contrastive decoding, which contrasts the layers' predictions to favor grounded tokens when generating the final output. On public benchmarks including POPE, MME, and AMBER, the method reached state-of-the-art performance in reducing hallucinations and produced more visually grounded responses, all without retraining the underlying model.
arxiv-2510-14504:
Matt Grenander, Shay Cohen, and Mark Steedman make sequence-to-sequence coreference resolution, deciding which words in a text refer to the same entity, fast enough for dialogue, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Generative coreference models that output labeled text hold state-of-the-art accuracy, but they reprocess the prefix for every sentence, which is wasteful when text arrives incrementally, as in conversation.

Their compressed representation extracts and reorganizes entity-level tokens from the input and discards the majority of tokens, shrinking what the model must carry forward. On the OntoNotes benchmark, their model scored less than one F1 point below a full-prefix incremental baseline while compressing the input. On LitBank, where single mentions are also annotated, the model passed state-of-the-art performance. The results indicate that discarding a portion of tokens is a strategy for incremental coreference, opening generative resolvers to streaming applications.
arxiv-2510-14804:
Gao proves, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a result about the variety of clique sizes a hypergraph can have. A hypergraph generalizes a graph: its edges can join more than two vertices at once, and it is called k-uniform when every edge joins exactly k of them. A clique is a maximal complete substructure, a set of vertices so fully connected that nothing can be added. Different cliques can have different sizes. How many distinct sizes can occur?

Gao shows that for every uniformity from three upward, a hypergraph on n vertices has strictly fewer than n distinct clique sizes, with the shortfall growing as n grows. In particular, the number of sizes is at most n minus a term that tends to infinity. The case of three-uniform hypergraphs settles a question posed by Erdős. The result limits the combinatorial complexity of these structures cleanly and generally.
arxiv-2510-14904:
Fiastre, Yang, Schmid, and their co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a model that finds, follows, and describes every object moving through a video. The task, dense video object captioning, demands detection, tracking, and a natural-language caption for each object's whole trajectory. Hand-labeling such data is so expensive that earlier systems trained the pieces separately, which limited their quality.

The team's workaround removes the human labelers. They used a top vision-language model to generate captions for entities already localized in space and time, extending two datasets, LVIS and LV-VIS, into captioned versions. On this synthetic data they trained MaskCaptioner end to end, so detection, segmentation, tracking, and captioning improve together. With pretraining on the new caption sets, the model reached state-of-the-art results on three existing benchmarks for the task, VidSTG, VLN, and BenSMOT. The datasets and code are publicly released.
arxiv-2510-15004:
Zhang and co-authors improve, in a 2025 arXiv paper, the training data behind automatic code translation. Translating programs between languages needs parallel corpora, aligned source and target code. Whole-program pairs give context for semantic alignment, but their length dilutes the fine-grained signal. Snippet pairs, short aligned fragments, teach alignment sharply, yet they are scarcer, and earlier augmentation work manufactured more program-level data.

The authors use large language models to generate snippet-alignment data. They then explore how to combine the two data types. Their answer is a two-stage strategy: learn from both corpora in sequence, not from program pairs alone. On the TransCoder-test benchmark, the augmented snippet data plus two-stage training improved translation performance over fine-tuning solely on program-alignment data. The paper argues the field has undervalued the small units: fine-grained alignment data, cheaply synthesized, lifts the translator.
arxiv-2510-15304:
Fei Wang and five colleagues shrink large language models by merging layers instead of simply deleting them. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that pruning whole layers throws away skills stored in the removed parts, and that plain averaging of neighboring layers blends weights badly. The team's method, CoMe, treats layers like puzzle pieces whose best channels deserve to survive.

A sensitivity score, built from activation strength and weight size, ranks channels across adjacent layers. The top channels are then concatenated, or stitched together, into merged layers, shrinking the model step by step. A final training phase uses hierarchical distillation, where the smaller model learns from its full-size parent layer by layer. Across seven benchmarks CoMe led rival pruning methods. Cutting thirty percent of a LLaMA-2 model's parameters kept about eighty-three percent of its original average accuracy, a strong retention rate for that size reduction.
arxiv-2510-15804:
Shauli Ravfogel, Gilad Yehudai, Tal Linzen, Joan Bruna, and Alberto Bietti wrote a 2025 paper on language models. It asks why models sort statements into true and false internally. The sorting follows simple geometric directions. Probing studies had found these truth subspaces. They could not explain how training creates them.

The authors build a transparent one-layer transformer. It reproduces the phenomenon end to end. In their setting, factual statements appear beside other factual statements. False ones cluster together too. Predicting future words then rewards marking truth. The team checked the pattern in pretrained models. It held there as well. In the toy system, learning had two phases. Facts were memorised first. A linear true-false split then emerged gradually.
arxiv-2510-15904:
Subhradip Chakraborty, Ankur Singh, Xuming Chen, Gourav Datta, and Akhilesh R. Jaiswal turn ordinary cache memory into a computing engine for neural networks. Deep workloads demand ever more on-chip SRAM, which now fills a large share of the die. Their NVM-in-Cache design adds resistive memory devices into a standard six-transistor SRAM cell, forming a compact hybrid cell with no area overhead.

In processing-in-memory mode the cell performs many multiply-and-accumulate operations in parallel directly on the cache power lines, while stored cache data stay intact. Simulations in a twenty-two nanometre process show strong throughput and very high efficiency per watt. Running a ResNet-18 network on CIFAR-10 with many rows in parallel gives accuracy in the low ninety percent range, the five authors report.
arxiv-2510-16004:
Andreas Radler, Vincent Seyfried, Johannes Brandstetter, and Thomas Lichtenegger argue that a neural twin must stay on the true system's path, not merely start well. Neural surrogates simulate dynamical systems fast, and a twin goes further by eating live measurements at test time to update its state for context-specific decisions. Drifting off trajectory ruins that promise over time.

Their family of methods, PAINT, trains a generative network to model the distribution of states in parallel across time, rather than stepping forward one state at a time. At test time, states are predicted from measurements inside a sliding window. Theory shows PAINT stays on-trajectory while autoregressive models generally do not. On a hard two-dimensional turbulent fluid problem, PAINT tracks the true state from sparse measurements with high fidelity, the four authors report.
arxiv-2510-16104:
Aritra Banerjee and four co-authors study how strings move near a BTZ black hole. A BTZ hole is a simple three-dimensional black hole much used in theory. String behavior in the thin zone just outside such a hole's horizon had never been mapped in a full, tidy way. The team uses the string-Carroll expansion, a math frame built for zones where light seems to crawl.

Working step by step in powers of an effective light speed, they sort the paths that closed strings can take there. The sorting brings out traits of whole families of string paths at once, plus some traits no one had noted before. Because near-horizon zones match this frame by nature, the method should port to other black holes too. The work gives theorists a firmer grip on strings in curved space near horizons.
arxiv-2510-16204:
Rajesh Asapanna and three co-authors study how noise hurts quantum walks. In a quantum walk, a particle steps across a lattice under quantum rules. Their testbed is a lattice of light, built from pulses looping in a double fiber ring. Noise that changes with time usually scrambles the walker's quantum state, an effect called decoherence.

They find a sheltered case: when the noise stays fixed within each driving cycle, whole bands of motion stay decoherence-free. Fully random noise, by contrast, wrecks coherence within a few steps. Edge states, special states bound to the lattice rim, lose coherence under either kind of noise. The team backs the claims with an exact equation for the dynamics and with lab tests using laser pulses. The results hint at noise patterns that quantum devices could live with.
arxiv-2510-16704:
Tianxin Wei and four co-authors study domain generalization, where a model trained on some data sources must still work on a new, unseen source. Contrastive learning, which pulls similar items together, seems like a natural helper. In practice the team found it often makes generalization worse.

Their analysis traces the failure to weak links between examples of the same class across domains. They answer with domain-connecting contrastive learning. On the data side, stronger augmentation and cross-domain positive pairs rebuild those links. On the model side, an anchoring step draws on class structure already present in pre-trained features. Experiments support the approach as a way to learn features that travel across domains.
arxiv-2510-16904:
Markus Weyrauch, Moritz Linkmann, and Jacob Page merge two estimation methods in a 2025 paper. Turbulence is the chaotic swirling seen in fast-moving fluids. Estimating its full state from coarse readings is hard. One classic method fits readings over time, but stays coarse. Learning methods sharpen images, yet need costly fine reference data.

The authors use the classic fitting method to train a sharpening network. No fine reference data is needed at any point. Their flow solver runs on graphics hardware and allows gradient training. The trained network beat the classic method at early times. The classic method stayed steadier near the end of its window. Mixing both, network first and fitting second, more than doubled accuracy.
arxiv-2510-17104:
Noah Franz and fifty-six co-authors report a hunt for a rare flash linked to crashing neutron stars in this 2025 paper. A weak gravity-wave alert pointed to a wide sky zone in August 2025. A fast-fading source in that zone looked at first like the sought flash. Many teams then tracked it in light of many kinds.

Close study showed the source was a type IIb supernova, a star blast with some traits of the flash. The team also built a score to rank such finds by place and fade speed. At all times, at least four other finds scored much the same. The score can help crews drop false leads fast in future hunts.
arxiv-2510-17404:
Fractons are odd excitations that can barely move, first found in certain quantum error correcting codes, and they have drawn interest from high energy physics as well. Ling-Zheng Xia, Lixin Xu, and Wei-Jia Li build a holographic model of a fractonic solid, using a black hole in a higher dimensional space to describe the material behaviour. Their aim is a full account of how such a solid vibrates and spreads energy at low energies.

By computing the natural vibration patterns of the black hole, Xia and his co-authors recover every collective mode of the solid. The list holds two sound like waves, one spreading mode, and one unusually slow mode that fades with the fourth power of its wave number. That slow mode stays present even when the crystal symmetry is openly broken.
arxiv-2510-17504:
Machine translation systems often stumble over specialised terms, which must be rendered the same way every time in technical and legal texts. Jingshu Liu, Raheel Qader, Gaëtan Caillaut, and Mariam Nakhlé describe the entry that the Lingua Custodia team built for the WMT 2025 shared task on terminology. The task covered three language pairs: English into German, English into Spanish, and English into Russian.

The team started from two recent instruction tuned language models, Qwen3 and Gemma3 in their smaller sizes, and fine tuned them further in a two stage process aimed at honouring supplied terminology. A system description of this kind lets other builders see which base models and training stages a competitive terminology entry used. Note that the arXiv listing abstract for this record does not match the paper itself, so this description follows the hosted text.
arxiv-2510-17704:
Erhard Scholz asks whether one relativistic scalar field can mimic dark matter effects. His model sits inside integrable Weyl geometry, a framework that extends Einstein gravity. The field carries a Bekenstein-type term, named for a pioneer of such theories. A second term gives the field extra mass energy.

Both terms switch on only when the field gradient stays spacelike and small. In the weak-field limit, the model yields MOND-like motion for falling bodies. MOND is a modified-gravity idea built to explain galaxy rotation without dark matter. The mass term also changes how the field bends light. Scholz presents the model as a bridge between two rival pictures.
arxiv-2510-18004:
Francis Ndikum Nji, Vandana Janeja, and Jianwu Wang group complex data that vary across both space and time. Uses range from snowmelt and sea ice tracking to crop health and disease spread. Older grouping tools miss long-range links, local shape, and the errors made during grouping itself, the authors argue.

Their A-DATSC model adds attention, an adversarial setup, and a deeper encoder to the standard subspace approach. Samples are projected into a latent space where hidden groups form simpler patterns. For analysts facing four-dimensional records, the paper offers a design built for the tangled time behavior that simpler methods flatten away.
arxiv-2510-18304:
Liangyu Chen, with James Burgess and three co-authors, studies image resolution for biomedical AI in a 2025 paper. Biomedical images, from scans to microscope slides, carry fine detail that low-resolution inputs can erase. Most multimodal language models were built for small, general-purpose pictures instead.

The team varied resolution during training and testing across several biomedical tasks. Training and testing at native resolution, meaning the image's original size, clearly improved results. Mismatched resolutions hurt performance badly, sometimes severely. Mixing resolutions during training softened that harm while keeping costs manageable. Their advice favors native-resolution testing and mixed-resolution training data for medical models.
arxiv-2510-18404:
Sungwoo Hong, with Hyungyu Kim, Sung Mook Lee, and Dongmin Seo, extends the theory of unusual symmetries in four-dimensional quantum field theory. The symmetries in question are called non-invertible, meaning they cannot simply be undone like ordinary symmetries. Earlier work covered simpler cases, and Hong and his co-authors aim to handle theories with several instantons and several axions at once, while making the ideas more usable for particle physics.

Building on two known constructions, the team introduces a method called partial gauging and shows how it produces the needed boundary theories and inflow terms. They work out how the symmetry operators act on line-like objects and on axion strings, connecting the effects to the known Witten effect. The result unifies several separate earlier constructions into one framework, stated through concrete equations that other researchers can apply.
arxiv-2510-18904:
Shriyansh Agrawal and six co-authors present DuoLens, a framework for spotting machine-generated text and code across many languages. Detectors in wide use often cost a lot of computing power or miss too much. The team argues that smaller encoder models can do better when they are trained for the job.

Fine-tuned versions of RoBERTa and CodeBERTa, trained on special data for code and natural language, beat large language models at this binary choice task while using far less compute. Their scores stay high across domains. This makes DuoLens a practical option for checking multilingual writing and source code at scale.
arxiv-2510-19104:
Florian Lengyel studies maps between simplex objects. The maps multiply values point by point. He builds them with a promonoidal method from category theory. The result links products of simplices to one larger simplex. It gives a concrete kernel on the simplex category.

For the simplest case, the map is a homotopy. That is, it bends a constant map into the identity map. Lengyel gives its shape with a piecewise-linear formula. He uses barycentric coordinates and a prism split. The work ties abstract machinery to geometry you can check by hand.
arxiv-2510-19304:
Mingyu Jo and four co-authors introduce Loopholing, a mechanism that helps discrete diffusion models keep the information they normally throw away while generating. These models decode in parallel, a promising alternative to step-by-step generation, but each sampling step collapses a rich distribution into a single choice, starving later steps of information.

Loopholing carries that lost information through a fixed latent pathway beside the sampling steps. Training uses a self-conditioning trick that avoids replaying the whole denoising path. The result cuts generative perplexity sharply against earlier baselines, sometimes beating them outright, and narrows the gap with sequential generators.
arxiv-2510-19404:
K Somesh and seven co-authors measure a heavy-fermion ferromagnet called UGe2. They use very strong magnetic fields. The fields come in pulses and reach sixty tesla. Resistivity is the key reading. How it changes depends sharply on field direction. The crystal axis matters a lot.

Along the easy axis, resistivity falls strongly. The ferromagnetic transition signature vanishes in modest fields. Along the hard axes, resistivity barely changes. The transition survives to far higher fields. The contrast shows direction can matter as much as strength. Both magnetism and the heavy electron state are destabilized.
arxiv-2510-19704:
Markus Bläser, Sagnik Dutta, and Gorav Jindal pin down the exact difficulty of several problems in optimization and computational algebra by tying them to Hilbert's Nullstellensatz problem. That problem asks whether a system of polynomial equations has a common solution, and many efficient algorithms secretly rest on it. The authors treat it as a complexity class and test familiar problems against it.

Transforming one polynomial into another by an affine change of variables turns out to be at least as hard as the Nullstellensatz problem over any field. For real polynomials, deciding stability, convexity, and hyperbolicity are all complete for the universal theory of the reals. The results tell algorithm designers exactly how hard these problems are, guiding where to look for efficient methods.
arxiv-2510-19804:
Boris Alexeev and Dustin G. Mixon present a counterexample to a favorite conjecture of Paul Erdős about Sidon sets, a problem carrying a one-thousand-dollar prize he offered. Erdős repeatedly proposed, starting in 1976, that every finite Sidon set, a set whose pairwise sums are all distinct, can be extended into a perfect difference set. The authors show the set one, two, four, eight, thirteen cannot be so extended.

While preparing the work they discovered Marshall Hall Jr. had published a different counterexample three decades before Erdős first posed the problem. Suspicious of the apparent oversight, they took unusual care: a large language model helped produce formal Lean proofs verifying both Hall's counterexample and their own. The episode closes a half-century-old question and raises a historical eyebrow.
arxiv-2510-20204:
I. Ishant and four co-authors give close proof on field-made states in the metal CePdAl. Bulk tests had hinted at odd states when a field is applied. One hint was a quantum spin liquid, a state long sought in such metals. But no close probe had checked what the states are. The team used muon spin tests on single crystals at fields along one axis.

At low fields, the low-heat states show long-range magnetic order. Past a key field, the signs change. At one field, the muon rate grows by a power law at low heat, while the shift stays flat. That pair of signs fits a critical spin liquid. At a still higher field, a non-Fermi liquid state shows up with no strain left.
arxiv-2510-20604:
Changan Liu and three co-authors present efficient algorithms for computing random walk centrality, a graph measure that averages hitting times to a node from all other nodes. The measure captures rich structural information and has wide uses in graph mining, but existing computation methods are too demanding for large networks. A novel formulation of the centrality underpins both of their scalable algorithms.

One algorithm uses approximate Cholesky factorization with sparse inverse estimation, while the other samples rooted spanning trees. Both run in near-linear time and carry strong approximation guarantees, two properties that rarely come together for this measure. Extensive experiments on large real-world networks, including one with over ten million nodes, demonstrate the efficiency and approximation quality of the pair.
arxiv-2510-20704:
Gabriele Parisi, Vincenzo Nugara, Salvatore Plumari, and Vincenzo Greco compute the shear viscosity, or inner friction, of a hot fluid made of two particle types that interact with different strengths. Such mixed fluids appear in quark gluon matter and other hot systems where each part alone is easier to study.

Within a classic kinetic framework, the team compares quick blends of single type viscosities against a full two type treatment. In most cases a weighted average of the parts matches the full result well, though the match is not guaranteed. A direct simulation check confirms the two type values, and for quark gluon matter the heat trend of the blend fails, proving that cross type collisions can matter a great deal.
arxiv-2510-20904:
Amir Michaelis and two co-authors model a quiet route to a Type Ia supernova, in which a white dwarf gains helium steadily from a companion until a double detonation destroys it. Such explosions serve as cosmic distance markers, so their true channels matter for cosmology.

Building on earlier one dimensional work on repeating helium flashes, the team grows a white dwarf from a lower mass to near the limit through steady accretion, yielding realistic layered helium profiles. Mapped into multi dimensional fluid simulations with nuclear burning, a modest hot spot near the helium shell base reliably triggers the shell blast and then the core blast. The path shows even calm accretion can end in a full supernova.
arxiv-2510-21104:
The ARA Collaboration, with seventy seven names on the author list, reports the first experimental evidence for in ice Askaryan radiation from high energy cosmic ray cascades in the Antarctic ice sheet. Askaryan emission is coherent radio light from charge excess in a cascade, long predicted but elusive in ice.

In two hundred eight days of phased array data, thirteen impulsive radio events from below the surface receive a detailed reanalysis. Event rate, arrival directions, pulse shape, spectrum, and polarization all match in ice Askaryan expectations. The result validates radio detection of ultra high energy particles in polar ice, a technique central to future neutrino observatories.
arxiv-2510-21204:
Xiyuan Zhang and thirteen co-authors study foundation models for tables, which learn from made-up data and then handle real tables they have never seen. Earlier work in that line, started by a model called TabPFN, left open which kinds of synthetic data teach these models best.

The team tests synthetic data sources, called priors, and picks out traits that help a trained model generalize to real tasks. Guided by those traits, they build Mitra, a model trained on a chosen mix of varied synthetic priors. Across classification and regression benchmarks, Mitra beats leading rivals such as TabPFNv2 and TabICL, and it needs fewer example rows to reach good accuracy.
arxiv-2510-21304:
Hagit Attiya, Constantin Enea, and Enrique Román-Calvo tackle a core trade-off in distributed storage: systems want to stay available during network splits, yet also keep data consistent. Classic results cover simple read-write stores, leaving unclear which richer objects and consistency levels can run without coordination between servers.

They build a general framework where a store's specification joins the meaning of its operations with a chosen consistency model, covering counters, sets, self-healing data types, and transactional databases. Inside it, they prove a theorem with a clean test. An available implementation exists exactly when the specification is arbitration-free, meaning it never needs a single global order to settle what readers may see. The result unifies several earlier theorems under one rule.
arxiv-2510-21404:
Xueguang Xie and six co-authors build a learning-based simulator for elastoplastic materials. Such materials stretch and then keep a permanent bend. Purely data-driven models often fail on new settings. They can also break physical rules. The team therefore embeds those rules directly into the model's design.

Two neural networks learn the elastic and plastic response laws separately. Measured physical parameters enter as conditions. One trained model can then cover many materials without retraining for each. The setup is fully differentiable, and the parameters stay explicit. The same framework can work backward, reading unknown material properties out of recorded motion. Experiments report top results on rebuilding motion and long-range prediction. They also cover new shapes and precise parameter estimation.
arxiv-2510-21704:
Christy Li and six co-authors send an AI agent to interrogate vision models about their secret habits. A recognition model may lean on an unintended visual cue, a background, a texture, a watermark, and such hidden reliance breeds overfitting and spurious success that only shows up when conditions change.

Their agent works like a scientist: it proposes hypotheses about which attributes drive a model's predictions, designs experiments to test them, and grades its own conclusions with a self-evaluation protocol. When the evidence contradicts a finding, the agent reflects, discards, and starts a new round. On a fresh benchmark of one hundred thirty models rigged with known dependencies across eighteen categories, self-reflection steadily improves the agent's detection and clearly beats non-reflective versions. The agent also exposes genuine attribute reliance inside leading models, including a major vision encoder and a popular object detector.
arxiv-2510-22204:
Weixian Qian leads an eight-author team teaching drones to judge landing spots with reasons attached. A careful human pilot would demand no less. Learning-only assessors stumble when conditions shift. They also cannot explain a verdict. That is a poor mix for aircraft choosing where to set down.

Their framework, NeuroSymLand, splits the job in two. A light segmentation model builds a scene map as a graph. Objects, attributes, and spatial relations fill the graph. Safety rules then run directly over that map. The rules were drafted by a large language model and refined by humans. Ranked landing candidates come out with plain explanations. Each site shows which constraints it passes or fails. The design targets marker-free assessment on modest onboard hardware.
arxiv-2510-22304:
Odin Zhang leads a thirty-seven-author team presenting ODesign, a generative model meant to design the partners in biomolecular handshakes. Nearly every biological process runs on molecules binding molecules, and designing binders on purpose would let scientists program new functions. Earlier generative tools each handled one kind of molecule and offered little control over where the grip lands.

ODesign works at all-atom resolution across all pairings. A user marks an epitope, the patch to be gripped, on an arbitrary target, and the model generates diverse binding partners with fine-grained control. On protein benchmarks at entity, token, and atom level it beat specialist baselines in controllability and performance. It stretches beyond proteins to nucleic acids and small molecules, enabling interaction types, like RNA designed to bind a chosen protein, that earlier tools could not attempt.
arxiv-2510-22404:
H Z Q Chen and four co-authors present MCTR, a lossless method to compress data sets of k-mers, the short fixed length pieces used in genomics. Keeping every piece and its count while shrinking storage is the hard part. MCTR first builds a shortest set of strings that covers the data using an Eulerian cover of a de Bruijn graph.

Those strings are then compressed further with the Burrows Wheeler Transform, and the original multiset can be rebuilt exactly. Tests on simulated and real data confirm exact recovery but show a rival lossy tool runs faster and squeezes noisy data more. The trade off favours fidelity.
arxiv-2510-22604:
Some sets of motion problems can be solved in a neat, exact way. Such sets have a long past in the study of dynamics. Ghorbanali Haghighatdoost wrote a 2025 review of that past. He wrote it alone. It starts with the Moscow School of A T Fomenko. It ends with a new school he set up in Azerbaijan.

The review tracks tools that sort such systems by their shape. Tools named include foliations, atoms, and molecules. Newer frames use groupoids and fractional calculus. His own thesis work pushed the theory to new systems. It mapped their singular points and split points. Later work in Iran joined shape, geometry, and analysis in one plan.
arxiv-2510-23104:
Yi-Li Hsu, Katelyn X Mei, and Lucy Lu Wang test whether organizing medical documents in a hierarchy improves multi-document summaries. Clinicians often face stacks of related records, and flat summaries can lose how documents link to each other. A hierarchical structure may help a model organize and contextualize facts across sources.

The authors try two ways of adding hierarchy across three large language models. They grade the summaries with automated scores, model-based scores, and domain expert review. Their findings show where structure truly helps medical summarization, a task where missed context can affect care decisions.
arxiv-2510-23204:
Giulia Pusceddu and four co-authors test whether robots that show value awareness sway human choices. Participants worked with two Furhat robots on a labeling task for images tied to human values. One robot was programmed to understand and prioritize human preferences; the other was not.

Participants clearly told the value-aware robot apart from the other. Their explicit choices, though, did not show a clear conformity effect when the robots disagreed. The study separates perceived awareness from actual influence, a useful caution for designers who expect socially aware robots to persuade users in group decisions.
arxiv-2510-23304:
Riccardo Romanello and six co-authors use reinforcement learning to build quantum circuits with as few CNOT gates as possible. CNOT gates create entanglement, a key resource for quantum algorithms, and some circuit families use only CNOT gates. Minimizing their count is an open problem whose difficulty is not fully known.

Instead of training many agents for different circuit sizes, the authors train an approach that generalizes across cases. A leaner CNOT circuit runs faster and errs less on noisy hardware. Their learning method offers a practical tool for compiling quantum programs efficiently.
arxiv-2510-23404:
Nicholas Miesch, Edward Shuryak, and Ismail Zahed extend a light-front theory of hadrons to pentaquarks and their mixing with ordinary baryons. Their earlier work built Hamiltonians and wave functions for mesons and baryons with confinement and chiral symmetry breaking. For three-quark baryons, the longitudinal wave function lives on an equilateral triangle of momentum fractions.

Here they generalize to n-quark states and specialize to five-quark pentaquarks, determining their masses and mixing. Pentaquarks are exotic states confirmed in recent years, and a unified light-front treatment helps predict which reported peaks are genuine new particles.
arxiv-2510-23504:
Usama Zidan, Mohamed Gaber, and Mohammed M Abdelsamea present iPac, a graph neural network method for medical image classification that builds graphs from image patches with their context. Graph networks are promising for images, yet they often ignore the structure and relations among visual entities. iPac constructs a new graph representation of each image.

Its stages partition the image into patches, extract features, cluster them, and build a graph that carries intra-image patch context into the network. Classification then uses relations between regions, not just isolated features. Relational reading may catch disease patterns that flat models miss.
arxiv-2510-23604:
Yi-Jie Wang and five co-authors work out on paper the phase diagram of a spin-valley Anderson impurity, a model for a single magnetic atom coupled to an electron sea. The model matters because magic-angle graphene behaves like a lattice of impurities bathed in Dirac electrons. Two Hund-type couplings, one favoring a valley doublet and one a singlet, shape the behavior.

The authors derive the whole diagram analytically, using bosonization tricks and checking against renormalization group runs. One coupling drives a BKT transition out of the heavy Fermi liquid into a doublet phase with a kink in the spectrum. The other drives a second-order transition into a singlet phase with a non-Fermi-liquid point. Pairing tendencies across the diagram trace to multiplet splitting, and pseudogap shoulders turn out to be multiplet excitations. They close by applying the results to magic-angle graphene.
arxiv-2510-23804:
Adela DePavia and two co-authors probe a quirk of Adam, the workhorse optimizer of machine learning: its hidden bias can flip when the data are rotated. Earlier work suggested Adam has a richness bias, learning curved decision boundaries closer to the best possible than gradient descent finds. But Adam rescales each coordinate separately, which makes it sensitive to feature orientation.

The authors show that even small rotations of the data distribution can make Adam drop its rich boundary and settle for a linear one, worse than what gradient descent reaches. The competitive advantage reverses from a change of coordinates. As a remedy, they use a recent reparameterization that rotates the optimization objective, giving any first-order method built-in indifference to data rotations. Experiments confirm the fix restores Adam's pull toward rich boundaries. The lesson: an optimizer's bias is not a fixed trait but depends on representation.
arxiv-2510-23904:
Kexin Quan and four co-authors introduce MultiColleagues, a multi-agent system designed to act as a brainstorming colleague rather than a task manager. Most AI tools execute steps well but rarely contribute ideas of their own or solve problems jointly with people. MultiColleagues instead has several agents converse with each other, trade ideas, and pull the user into the ideation process.

The team tested it in a within-subjects study with twenty participants, against a single-agent baseline. Users felt a stronger social presence from the multi-agent system. They rated their outcomes higher in quality and novelty, and their ideas came out more elaborated during the sessions. The authors read the results as evidence that agents can move past being process partners. With this setup, a group of agents can share intent, lift group dynamics, and help people push ideas further than a lone assistant does.
arxiv-2510-24204:
Renato Neves proves an adequacy theorem linking a formal meaning for probabilistic concurrent programs to what can be observed from them, working alone. The language extends probabilistic Guarded Command Language with concurrency, and its meaning rests on mixed powerdomains, which combine nondeterminism with probability. Observable traits are treated as open sets of a topological space, following Smyth's idea.

The proof needs a topological version of König's lemma adapted to probabilistic programming, which Neves also proves in the paper. One payoff is that whether a concurrent program satisfies an observable property of a certain form is semi decidable. This relates to Escardó's conjecture about may and must probabilistic testing.
arxiv-2510-24404:
Shantonu Mukherjee proposes a pairing between skyrmions and vortices in a two dimensional ferromagnetic superconductor, working alone. He formulates an interaction between ferromagnetic and superconducting orders that obeys the needed symmetry principles. This allows a duality similar to boson vortex duality in superfluids, where the two topological excitations interact through an emergent gauge field.

The static potential attracts a skyrmion and a vortex of opposite topological charge, so bound pairs can form. Mukherjee further argues that such pairing makes a Magnus force on the vortex induce a transverse, Hall like drift of the skyrmion. The theory predicts a coupled motion that experiments on ferromagnetic superconductors could test.
arxiv-2510-24804:
Xiaoyang Hu, the sole author, finds a human like quirk in vision and language models: they adapt to clash. In a classic test, a word names a hue that clashes with the ink hue, which slows a reply. People do better on a clash trial right after a clash trial, as if control ramps up.

Twelve of the thirteen models Hu tested showed that same clash after clash gain. One case most apt hit a score cap. To find the base of the act, Hu used sparse tools to pick out key inner nodes in one model. One clash tuned node group, when cut, raised clash errors a lot while calm trials held near steady.
arxiv-2510-25004:
Guifre Molera Calves, Shinji Horiuchi, Edwin Peters, Ed Kruzins, and Nick Stacy read space junk by the fine shifts in radar waves bounced off it. Their plan uses more than one site: a strong beam sent from a deep space post, caught by far scopes turned to radar work. Tiny wave shifts, called micro Doppler marks, tell how each piece spins.

From 2021 to 2025, the team watched twenty spent rocket parts at mixed heights and sizes. Spin reads came out to the second, and size reads fell in a tight band of true size. Shape maps were built from the reads by a new image step. Mass spread traits could also be drawn out.
arxiv-2510-25404:
Jamison Meindl led seven co-authors in presenting SemanticOpt. Yunsheng Tian, Tony Cui, and Veronika Thost helped. Zhang-Wei Hong, Jie Chen, and Wojciech Matusik joined. Mina Konakovic Lukovic closes the author team. Their 2025 paper tackles expensive black-box tuning. Each test may cost much time or money.

Current optimizers mainly use numeric or categorical readings. Bayesian tuning is a leading example there. They ignore broader domain knowledge from experts. Papers and past tests also go unused. Language models can interpret such semantic information well. Yet even strong models solve tuning unreliably alone. SemanticOpt fine-tunes models on structured tuning trajectories. Natural language context augments those trajectories for training. It jointly uses numeric and semantic evidence. Predictions stay interpretable and aligned with Bayesian surrogates. Their benchmark pairs real problems with semantic information. SemanticOpt beat classic and language model methods on average.
arxiv-2510-26204:
Ashish Bhoopesh Gulaguli, Shashwat Singh, and Rakesh Kumar Bansal extend a sequential change detection method from independent data to data with memory. Sequential change detection watches a stream and raises an alarm as soon as its statistical pattern shifts. A complication is that neither the before nor the after distribution is known in advance, so both must be learned from the stream itself.

The earlier method, from twenty twenty two, used Page CUSUM statistic, a running score that accumulates evidence for a change. It pairs that score with the empirical distribution for the before state. A universal code models the after state. Gulaguli and the team carry that construction over to the Markov setup, where each observation depends on the previous one, which covers many real monitoring tasks.
arxiv-2510-26404:
Su Ruibo writes on a basic task in scientific computing: solving the Poisson equation on a round-edged convex region. The Poisson equation is a standard tool for things like heat spread and electric fields. The finite element method chops the region into small flat-sided pieces and solves on that stand-in shape. Su asks how big the error from that swap can be, stated in exact terms before any computing is done.

The paper gives explicit error bounds that depend only on broad facts about the region's shape, not on fine detail. The bounds hold for any convex region and for any family of triangle-like meshes used to fill it. Such clear bounds help users judge whether a mesh is fine enough before they trust the numbers it gives.
arxiv-2510-26804:
Miheer Salunke and four co-authors model hearing overload in autism in a 2025 study. Sound overload is when noise feels too strong and hard to bear. It affects many autistic people, yet past models often fixed traits that vary by person.

Their method, called a universal differential equation, mixes known body rules with a learned part. A differential equation is a rule that links change over time to current state. The mix beat a pure learned model and used far fewer free parts. It also found body traits with small error and flagged pulse patterns with risk. The goal is care and wearables shaped to each person.
arxiv-2510-26904:
Simone Romiti applies physics-informed neural networks to lattice gauge theories. These theories place the strong and related forces on a grid, and their spectra are usually found by heavy numerical methods. Physics-informed networks instead bake the governing equation into their training loss.

Romiti encodes the Schrödinger equation and the symmetries of the eigenstates directly into the loss, so the network explores the spectrum without supervision. It learns eigenfunctions and eigenvalues at arbitrary gauge couplings, moving smoothly from the analytically known strong-coupling regime toward weaker couplings. Tests on the single-plaquette U(1) and SU(2) pure-gauge theories reproduce the hierarchy of energy levels and their wavefunctions. The paper presents the method as a flexible route into gauge theory spectra.
arxiv-2510-27104:
Michelle Mastrianni, Rucha Deshpande, Frank Samuelson, and Yee Lam Thompson build a framework to predict how AI triage tools affect patient waiting in radiology. Such tools fast-track scans for one disease, but hospitals now run several at once across many conditions. Speeding one queue can quietly slow another, including urgent cases outside the target.

Their software, multi-QuCAD, models multi-tool, multi-disease workflows with queueing theory, the math of waiting lines, using disease rates, reading times, and cleared device performance. Tests range from two diseases to nine and compare scheduling rules. Target conditions gain time, but non-target urgent cases can face large delays. A hierarchical protocol saves most time for top priorities while delaying lower ones more, guiding safer combined deployment.
arxiv-2510-27304:
Rodrigo Carnier, Laura Lahesoo, and Kensuke Fukuda compare batch and streaming learning for spotting anomalies in Internet of Things traffic. Batch models need heavy maintenance and adapt poorly when attack patterns shift, a failure called concept drift. Streaming learning updates incrementally and can detect drift, promising more robust defense as device traffic grows.

The team streams carefully mixed datasets sample by sample, framing detection as binary classification. Batch models indeed fail under drift, but current datasets prove too uniform to expose streaming model limits fully. Tree-based methods stay competitive against non-tree rivals, confirming their batch-era advantage. An adaptive random forest reaches high F1 scores at a third of its batch counterpart cost, while an adaptive tree cuts cost fourfold with a small stability trade-off.
arxiv-2510-27404:
Ruifeng Leng, Cheng-Yang Lee, and Siyi Zhou widen a quantum framework to fast particles in this 2025 paper. Most quantum systems use Hermitian Hamiltonians, energy rules that keep chances adding up right. Pseudo-Hermitian systems bend that rule yet can still give real energies and sound evolution. The trick is a metric, a custom inner ruler for states.

The trio extend the trick to relativistic quantum field theory, the physics of fields and fast particles. In their setup, incoming and outgoing states carry different metrics, joined by a projector that keeps total chance conserved. Each symmetry of the system comes with two matching operators, one per side. Their scattering math stays Lorentz invariant, unchanged across moving frames, and unitary. The fundamental CPT symmetry holds too, as in the standard theory.
arxiv-2510-27504:
Junkang Liu leads six co-authors in DP-FedPGN, a differentially private federated learning algorithm that seeks globally flat minima. Client-level differential privacy prevents inference attacks and leakage, but private training usually sharpens the loss landscape and hurts generalization. Sharpness-aware methods find locally flat spots, which may not reflect global flatness under privacy noise.

Their algorithm adds a global gradient norm penalty to the local loss, steering toward a globally flat minimum while also shrinking local update norms and thus clipping error. Theory analyzes how the penalty mitigates privacy-driven degradation, removes heterogeneity impact, and keeps fast convergence, with strict Renyi differential privacy guarantees. Tests on image and language tasks with ResNet and transformer models improve significantly over state-of-the-art private methods.
arxiv-2510-27604:
Alex Alarcon and five co-authors present DiffstarPop in 2025, a fast model of how galaxies form stars over time. Each galaxy has a star formation history, the rate at which it made stars in each era. In the base model, that history is summed up by a few values with clear physical sense, such as how well gas turns into stars and when that process stops.

DiffstarPop links those values to how each dark matter halo, the unseen mass well that holds a galaxy, grew over time. The link is tuned to match three distinct galaxy models. Code in JAX can draw a million such histories in about one second on a standard chip. Fast draws enable broad tests of galaxy growth.
arxiv-2511-00104:
Jorge Castelo Mourelle, Nicolas Sanchis-Gual, and Jose Font explore whether bosonic dark matter inside white dwarfs could explain mismatches between their mass estimates. Masses from electromagnetic methods sometimes differ from gravitational redshift measurements by five to fifteen percent across datasets. Thermal effects, model uncertainties, and measurement errors explain many cases but perhaps not all.

A gravitationally coupled bosonic dark matter component is tested as an alternative explanation for the remaining discrepancies. Astrophysics readers get a dark matter probe hidden in stellar remnants. White dwarfs are sensitive laboratories because their structure balances gravity against quantum pressure precisely.
arxiv-2511-00304:
Cesar Mello and Fernando Medina da Cunha build a theory for a grim feature of cancer cells. Their outer membranes cluster nutrient transporters into sugar-rich domains, giving the cells backup routes to feed. Their framework links surface chemistry to transport through a combined model of charged particle flow, surface attraction forces, and the cell's energy and redox balance.

From that structure they derive bounds on total intake. Two levers, membrane geometry and field strength, suppress intake in a steady regime up to a sharp knee, beyond which intake collapses. A combined intake index tracks energy carriers such as ATP: once intake falls below a upkeep level, energy falls and damage becomes hard to reverse. Healthy membranes sit above that level, which marks a possible window for selective treatment.
arxiv-2511-00604:
Ola Groettvik describes the qualification system for MOSAIX, a prototype sensor chip for the ALICE experiment's Inner Tracking System upgrade at CERN. The upgrade will use stitched, wafer-scale monolithic pixel sensors for the first time in high-energy physics. MOSAIX is the final full prototype before production, a long thin chip packing one hundred forty-four independently powered pixel matrices and eight fast data transmitters.

Groettvik presents the test system and verification strategy built to qualify the chip, with special care for proving the test infrastructure itself before real chips arrive. A field-programmable gate array controls the sensor and parses its output stream. A second such chip emulates MOSAIX, standing in for the real device so the whole chain can be exercised early. The contribution documents a careful dress rehearsal for production testing.
arxiv-2511-00704:
Morgan Lee and six co-authors test whether knowledge tracing models survive changing students. Knowledge tracing predicts what a learner knows from their practice history, and the field has long assumed the learning process sits still. Online platforms keep changing, though, and student populations drift with them. The team runs four well-studied tracing models over five academic years of platform data.

Performance was checked within single years and across years, where drift bites. Every model family degraded when concept drift struck. Bayesian knowledge tracing, the oldest and simplest approach, stayed the most stable on newer data. Complex attention-based models lost predictive power significantly faster, a humbling result for sophistication. Platform builders, the authors imply, should budget for drift rather than assume a model trained once stays trained.
arxiv-2511-00804:
Abhiram Kusumba and colleagues introduce EraseFlow, a method for removing unwanted concepts from text to image generators. Erasing harmful or proprietary content is now a basic safety need, yet older methods often wreck image quality, depend on fragile adversarial training, or demand costly retraining.

EraseFlow treats unlearning as exploration over the full denoising paths a diffusion model takes, not just final images. It trains a policy with GFlowNets, which sample whole paths in proportion to their reward, steering generation away from the target concept while keeping the model's prior intact. Because no hand built reward model is needed, the approach generalizes to concepts not seen in training and, the authors report, beats prior baselines on the erasure versus quality trade off.
arxiv-2511-01104:
Yujian Liu and colleagues train language models to write testing harnesses, not just test cases. Ordinary automatic test generation produces input and expected output pairs, which limits the variety of tests and gives little help when a failure needs debugging.

A harness is code that synthesizes inputs and validates observed outputs, so it can express complex cases and check invariants rather than one fixed answer. HarnessLLM is a two stage pipeline: supervised fine tuning first, then reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards with a custom reward design. The resulting models beat input output based testing at finding bugs and at strategy diversity. Their generated tests also help at generation time, improving code produced by models that validate drafts against the harnesses.
arxiv-2511-01604:
Jose Maria Balmaceda, Dom Vito Briones, and Joris Buloron describe a three-dimensional analogue of an association scheme, a combinatorial structure that organizes the relations among a set's elements. Where a transitive group action yields a classical scheme, a two-transitive action yields an association scheme on triples.

The paper works out one family in detail: the schemes arising from finite unitary groups acting on their isotropic lines. The authors compute the relations of these schemes and their intersection numbers, the counting data that encode how the relations combine. The construction ties finite group actions to triple combinatorics, extending the classical correspondence between unitary group geometry and ordinary association schemes.
arxiv-2511-01804:
Viraj Patel, Lisa Kreusser, and Katharine Fraser reconstruct blood flow fields from ultrasound data that is sparse and noisy. Flow patterns reveal cardiac function, and ultrasound is safer than radiation-based imaging and friendlier to patients with implants, but its signal fades with depth. Particle image velocimetry on echocardiograms helps, yet measuring blood velocity accurately remains hard.

Their model is a physics-informed neural field with multi-scale Fourier feature encoding: a continuous function that estimates the flow while respecting the physics of fluid motion, needing no ground-truth supervision. On synthetic and real datasets, it achieved consistently low error both when denoising and when filling in missing regions, verified against reference flow fields and measured flow rates. The work adapts techniques proven in other imaging areas, notably flow MRI, to ultrasound.
arxiv-2511-01904:
Doulaye Dembélé proposes judging classifiers by the entropy of their eigenvalues. Classification quality is usually scored from a contingency table, but many standard measures misbehave when the classes are imbalanced, exactly the situation in face recognition, text mining, and medical pattern tasks. Dembélé's measure builds the score from the eigenvalues of the problem's natural matrix summary, summarized through their entropy.

For binary problems, the paper derives relations between the eigenvalues and familiar quantities: sensitivity, specificity, the area under the receiver operating curve, and the Gini index. A side result estimates the confusion matrix in a way meant to blunt the curse of imbalanced classes. Worked data examples are used to argue that the eigenvalue entropy measure outperforms the gold-standard measures it is compared against, particularly when class proportions are skewed.
arxiv-2511-02304:
Beyazit Yalcinkaya, Marcell Vazquez-Chanlatte, Ameesh Shah, Hanna Krasowski, and Sanjit Seshia teach teams of robots to cooperate on jobs that unfold over time. In one, an agent presses a button to unlock a door while another holds it open. Tasks with that temporal structure are naturally written as automata, which break a team objective into smaller sub-tasks per agent. Earlier learning approaches handled only one task at a time and used samples inefficiently, retraining from scratch for each new job.

Their framework learns a single policy conditioned on the automaton, under centralised training but decentralised execution, so each agent acts on its own information at run time. The authors identify obstacles to making this work, solve them, and prove the approach optimal. Learned value functions can also assign tasks to agents at test time, and experiments showed genuine multi-step coordination emerging.
arxiv-2511-02504:
Le Chen, Yi Zhao, and eight co-authors teach two robot hands to play the piano, at a scale no previous system attempted. Bimanual piano playing is a brutal control problem: high-dimensional, full of contacts, and demanding fast, precise finger work. Their agent, OmniPianist, learns without a single human demonstration, and ends up able to perform nearly one thousand different pieces of music.

Three components make it work. An optimal-transport strategy invents efficient fingerings automatically. Then more than two thousand specialist agents are trained by reinforcement learning, each on distinct pieces, and their experience is pooled into a dataset of over a million playing trajectories. Finally a flow-matching transformer learns from that dataset by imitation, producing one generalist player. Experiments and ablations support the claim that the recipe scales, a step toward human-level dexterity in robot hands.
arxiv-2511-02904:
Jacob Bringewatt, Henry Froland, Andreas Elben, and Niklas Mueller sharpen a method for measuring quantum states without mapping them in full. Classical shadows estimate many properties of a state from repeated random measurements. Their 2025 paper adds prior knowledge, namely symmetries, to cut the number of samples needed when the properties of interest respect a gauge rule.
