Language models can check each other's homework: a verifier model scores candidate answers and picks the best. Jack Lu and four co-authors ask in 2025 when that verification actually pays off, looking closely at how verifiers judge answers from their own and other model families.

Earlier studies mostly examined self-verification, a model grading itself, and rarely crossed family lines. Verifiers improve solvers by selecting high-quality answers from a pool, but only if their judgment is trustworthy. Knowing when verification helps, and when it merely adds cost, guides how reasoning systems should spend their compute.
arxiv-2512-02404:
One classic object in algebra counts the elements of a Weyl group, weighted by a statistic called the major index. Summing that weight over the whole group gives a polynomial known as the Mahonian polynomial. A signed version of the sum, weighted by the sign of each element, raises further counting questions.

The 2025 study works out these polynomials for classical Weyl groups, the symmetry groups behind much of modern algebra. Exact formulas of this kind feed into combinatorics, where such sums track how permutations and reflections are distributed. They also give checks for computer algebra systems that handle group data. Pure counts of this sort form the base on which much of group theory rests.
arxiv-2512-02704:
Senrong Xu and six co-authors question a popular way to sharpen uncertainty sets from machine learning models. Conformal prediction wraps any black box model and returns sets with rigorous coverage guarantees. A correction step can fine tune the model to make those sets smaller and more efficient.

The authors argue that this correction may clash with entropy, a measure of information content. Chasing smaller sets could distort what the model expresses. The tension matters for high stakes uses, such as medicine, where an efficient but misleading uncertainty set is worse than a wider honest one. Wide sets that stay true beat tight sets that lie, a trade this work puts in plain sight for all to weigh.
arxiv-2512-02904:
Marie Louise Schubert and a large team design a fully differentiable digital twin for solar cells. The key target is energy yield: the total electric energy a cell makes in a year at a real location. Computational guidance is crucial for photovoltaics, especially for emerging cell technologies.

Existing simulations usually cover isolated aspects, like optics or electronics alone. A twin through which gradients flow end to end lets designers optimize the whole device at once. Faster, joined up design could raise yearly yield per panel, the number that decides real world value. Yield per year is the score a buyer sees on the bill, so a twin that lifts that score earns its keep in cash terms.
arxiv-2512-03104:
Black holes that spin and bulge in odd ways may hide neat math. Takeshi Fukuyama studies the Tomimatsu-Sato family of spacetimes in this 2025 work. That family extends the Kerr black hole to higher orders of shape change, and its algebra has long looked messy.

Fukuyama writes a key quantity as a ratio of two tau functions. In that form, he finds a fixed split of the math into a cubic part and a quartic part. The split suggests a hidden order in these spacetimes. It may help others solve and classify such black hole models. For relativity scholars, the split offers a fresh handle on a family long seen as unwieldy.
arxiv-2512-04104:
Technology-facilitated abuse, where digital tools are used to harass, monitor, or control a person, takes forms that shift faster than support services can catalogue. Dipankar Srirag and colleagues build a unified taxonomy of that abuse. They then audit how well Australian institutions explain it online, in a 2025 preprint.

The taxonomy, distilled from peer-reviewed literature, organises abuse types, prevention, detection, and support across the abuse life cycle. The audit crawled three hundred six government, charity, and service domains, gathering more than fifty thousand pages, and classified them with zero-shot topic models. Coverage proved narrow. About seventy percent of abuse-related pages focused on harassment, comment abuse, or sexual abuse. Under one percent addressed covert surveillance, economic abuse, or long-term control. Support leaned on information pages over counselling, and much writing sat at a reading level many at-risk users would struggle with.
arxiv-2512-04204:
Fast radio bursts arrive in (at least) two flavours, repeating and apparently one-off, and astronomers still argue about what separates them. Yang Liu and colleagues let a machine look for the dividing line, guided by human physical reasoning, in a 2025 astrophysics preprint. Their aim: a simple classifying equation, not a black-box score.

The workflow has three stages. Deep learning first sifts the CHIME catalogue and finds six independent parameters describing the bursts completely. Humans then build dimensionless groups from those parameters, via Buckingham's pi theorem and correlation analysis. Finally, symbolic regression searches for the governing equation. The result sorts bursts into two distinct Gaussian distributions, evidence for two physical classes. Applied to the newer CHIME catalogue, the equation stays consistent, suggesting it captures real physics. The authors present the human-machine division of labour as a template for other sciences.
arxiv-2512-05204:
Todor Krasimirov-Ivanov, Alba Cervera-Lierta, Paolo Stornati, and Federico Centrone design a quantum optical neural network that could be built with today's photonics. Continuous-variable quantum optics suits neural networks well: light's quadratures play the role of signals, Gaussian operations act like weighted connections, and subtracting photons supplies the needed nonlinearity. The catch has been feasibility — many proposals demand parts that do not exist in the lab.

Their architecture uses coherent light as input, a general Gaussian transformation followed by multi-mode photon subtraction as the processing layer, and homodyne detection to read results out. The authors derive the design's formulas in closed form, show its neurons provide flexible activation shapes, and prove a single layer can approximate any function. A custom high-performance library mimics training exactly, and experiments on learning and state-preparation tasks show strong expressivity and generalization for the resources spent.
arxiv-2512-05504:
Théo Marty completes the classification of partial sections of flows begun in the first part of this series. A partial section is a surface that a flow's paths cross transversally without the surface having to span everything. Classifying such surfaces for arbitrary continuous flows continues the classical Schwartzman-Fried-Sullivan theory of cross-sections. The groundwork — Lyapunov maps and recurrence — was laid in part one.

Here Marty gives a dynamical criterion for when partial cross-sections exist at all, as a direct consequence of the earlier work. He then describes all of them through a cohomological criterion in the spirit of Fried's, and characterizes how many partial cross-sections live in a given cohomology class. Together the two papers reduce a geometric classification problem to computable algebraic data. It is the kind of result that lets later researchers test a flow for sections by calculation rather than by construction.
arxiv-2512-05704:
Balázs Tóth, Ádám Gali, and Gergő Thiering present Exe.py, a Python code for computing the fine structure of defect based qubits in solids. Certain point defects with threefold symmetry make promising qubits. Their energy levels split in fine detail through the Jahn-Teller effect, where the defect distorts and breaks its own symmetry, tangled with spin-orbit coupling. Getting those splittings right from first principles is needed to judge a defect's worth.

Exe.py builds on density functional theory output and follows the approach of an earlier method. An excited state calculation lets it reach excited states as well. It predicts fine structure parameters of the zero phonon lines, including how they shift in a magnetic field. The team demonstrates it on a family of diamond defects: the silicon, germanium, tin, and lead vacancy centers, plus a nitrogen based defect. It also handles trigonal molecules.
arxiv-2512-05904:
Abdul Mannan, Alessio Del Dotto, and Massimo Ferrario analyze how an electron beam holds together as it rides a plasma wave toward high energy. In the bubble regime, a driving pulse expels plasma electrons, leaving an ion filled cavity behind it. A witness bunch inside feels nearly linear fields. The team models the cavity as a uniform charged ellipsoid and studies the beam slice by slice.

Each thin slice of the bunch is treated as a small cylinder with its own envelope equation, describing how its width breathes as it travels. Together they reveal how the width oscillates, how emittance degrades, and how energy spread grows. The analysis also gives matching conditions: the beam settings at injection that keep transport and acceleration clean. Plasma accelerators promise tabletop machines for high energies. Slice by slice envelope physics is how designers learn to keep quality through the ride.
arxiv-2512-06104:
Isaac Liao and Albert Gu take a swing at one of deep learning's core assumptions: that intelligence requires massive pretraining. ARC-AGI is a benchmark of visual puzzles where rules are inferred from few examples. CompressARC, their model, has only seventy six thousand parameters and no pretraining at all. It solves puzzles by compression, seeking the shortest description that generates the answer. Training happens on the single target puzzle itself, its solution withheld.

Yet it cracks one fifth of the evaluation set. Description length becomes a second road to generalization. The numbers are modest; the existence proof matters. It reasons from the single case in front of it.
arxiv-2512-06404:
Mohammad Soleymanibrojeni and seven co authors present GENIUS, an AI agent system that runs atom level simulations of materials with little expert help. Such simulations forecast how new materials will behave, yet setting them up and fixing their errors still takes a specialist. That gap slows the push to design materials on computers.

GENIUS pairs a knowledge graph about a leading simulation code with a tiered team of language models, watched over by a state machine that handles error recovery. Given a plain prompt, it writes input files, checks them, runs them, and repairs failures on its own. Across a broad bench of tasks it brought most runs to completion, and repaired most of those by itself. Next to plain setups it cost about half as much and nearly wiped out made up steps. The authors cast it as a way to open hard simulations to non experts.
arxiv-2512-06504:
Andrii Lysyi and five co authors automate the drone inspection of solar panel farms. Human crews and simple drone passes miss faults, repeat alerts for the same panel, and chew bandwidth sending video back. Their system aims to cover the whole chain, from flight to a geo located repair alert, with no hands in between.

A thermal view of each panel is embedded in a form that ignores the color palette used to display heat. It is then fused with a normal color view through a gate that weighs the two. When a fault looks doubtful, a control loop sends the drone back for a targeted second look, steered by a compact rotation update. Alerts for the same panel are clustered by map distance so each fault is reported once. On a public benchmark the system scored well, beating earlier methods by a clear double digit margin in detection quality.
arxiv-2512-06904:
Ao-Sheng Xiong and co-authors work on a measurement puzzle from heavy-ion collisions, where pairs of particles called hadrons fly out of the wreckage. Watching how their momenta correlate lets physicists probe the forces between them. The link runs through a source function, which describes where the pair was born. That source cannot be measured directly, and it is usually just assumed to be a smooth bell shape.

The team asks whether the true source can be recovered from the data instead. They build a toy model around a classic smoothing method named for Tikhonov. Pairs are sent through a simple square-well force with four strengths, and the resulting correlations are computed. Feeding those curves back through the method rebuilds the assumed bell-shaped source well. The test suggests real data could one day yield realistic sources rather than guessed ones.
arxiv-2512-07004:
Faizan A Khattak and Mantas Mikaitis build exact software models of the matrix multipliers built into NVIDIA graphics chips. These tensor cores multiply matrices in hardware and now speed up far more than artificial intelligence, reaching into general scientific computing. A catch is that they do not follow the standard rules for decimal arithmetic, and each chip generation behaves a little differently, so results can fail to reproduce across machines.

To pin the behavior down, the authors craft test inputs designed to expose bit-level choices: how rounding works. How wide the accumulator runs, where numbers normalize, and whether extra carry bits exist. They then compare model against real hardware on millions of random inputs, refining until the match is bit exact. The finished models cover four data-center chips, from the V100 to the B200, across the low-precision formats developers actually use.
arxiv-2512-07104:
Quan Zhou and Sibo Zheng test whether the newest sky survey data really prefer a dark energy that changes over time. The DESI survey's distance measurements recently hinted at such dynamical dark energy over the standard constant kind. But distance data alone are not the whole story: a changing dark energy should also leave marks in how matter clumps at low redshift. Measured by the same survey's full-shape analysis of galaxy positions.

The authors build the needed statistical machinery for the survey's first-year matter spectrum, then combine it with the newer distance release and other probes in a large sampling analysis. Adding the clumping data tightens the limits on the two numbers that describe how dark energy evolves. The improvement holds across three widely used comparison data sets, and is sharpest for one supernova sample.
arxiv-2512-07304:
Mark Myers and co-authors make realistic noise affordable in classical simulations of quantum circuits. A fast method called stabilizer simulation has taught the field much of what it knows about error-correction circuits, but it can only swallow simple Pauli-type noise. Real devices suffer richer, coherent errors that can bite harder, and those were largely beyond simulation's reach. Through stratified importance sampling, the team shows general noise can be run inside the stabilizer frame in reasonable time.

Non-unitary noise costs nearly the same as the easy Pauli kind. Coherent, unitary noise takes about ten times longer, a bargain next to older methods that often failed to converge at all. As a demonstration, they simulate a popular family of quantum error-correcting codes, the rotated planar surface codes.
arxiv-2512-07604:
R. Fedriani and seventeen co-authors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on a busy star-forming region. The region, named IRAS 18162-2048, holds a deeply buried young protostar. Around it sit other young stars at very different stages of growth.

The team observed the field with the Very Large Telescope, the VLA radio array, and ALMA. Near-infrared light reveals two sources, while the main protostar stays hidden even there. One source shows a hydrogen line profile that marks it as a young, hot, massive star. Glowing hydrogen molecules nearby carry a pattern that points to ultraviolet light, not shocks. Radio images confirm the same star as a compact source that has begun to ionise its surroundings. It now hosts a small ionised region and a wider zone shaped by its radiation. Young and older objects side by side suggest several generations of star birth.
arxiv-2512-07804:
Conor Bready, Harrison Tuckman, and Eric Neuscamman wrote this 2025 computational chemistry paper. Coupled cluster theory is a workhorse for predicting molecular behavior. A newer variant, Aufbau suppressed coupled cluster, targets excited states of molecules.

The authors derive and implement its one-body reduced density matrix. From that matrix flow the quantities chemists actually want to read. Excited-state natural orbitals come first among those products. Atomic populations and dipole moments follow from the same object. The team uses the natural orbitals to refine the method's own solutions. Re-solving in fresh orbital bases, round after round, removes dependence on the starting guess. They test the scheme on simple valence and Rydberg systems. Dipole moments in small molecules get a careful accuracy check. Where high-level comparison data exist, the new method matches top rivals. That match holds when the response stays perturbatively complete, they stress.
arxiv-2512-07904:
Omar Mustafa and Abdullah Guvendi wrote this 2025 theoretical physics paper on quantum oscillators in exotic gravity. Their arena mixes a global monopole's spacetime with Eddington-inspired Born-Infeld gravity. Both Schrödinger and Klein-Gordon oscillators are placed inside that arena.

The radial equations are first reduced to confluent Heun form. Forcing the Heun series to stop yields polynomial wave functions. That truncation is the key that unlocks exact solutions here. It quantizes the oscillator frequency and restricts the allowed angular momenta. In the simplest case, a degree-one polynomial gives a closed formula. The frequency and a finite cap on angular momentum follow directly. The cap is set jointly by the gravity deformation and the monopole's deficit. The same method then tackles the relativistic oscillator version. A Wu-Yang magnetic monopole couples into that relativistic sector. Particle and antiparticle energies come out in closed form, perfectly charge-symmetric.
arxiv-2512-08004:
Zhibo Yu, W N Brandt, Fan Zou, and colleagues, astronomers who study active galaxies, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their question is why the growth of supermassive black holes has fallen so sharply since cosmic noon, roughly ten billion years ago. They use the best current measurements of black hole accretion, drawn from nine well studied extragalactic fields.

The team finds that the main driver is a drop in the typical Eddington ratio, the rate at which active nuclei feed compared with their limit. The decline is not mainly a shift of activity toward smaller black holes. As feeding rates fell, the bulk of cosmic accretion moved from fast feeding nuclei to slow ones. In smaller galaxies, weaker outburst brightness, rather than a shorter duty cycle, explains most of the fall.
arxiv-2512-08104:
Harish Karthikeyan, Yue Guo, Leo de Castro, and colleagues, researchers in artificial intelligence security, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their framework, AgentCrypt, addresses privacy when AI agents work together. Access controls alone are not enough, because agents can leak private context later while reasoning, messaging people, or calling tools.

AgentCrypt adds a deterministic protection layer on top of any agent platform, with three levels of protection. The first allows open exchange, the second applies context aware masking, and the third uses homomorphic encryption so agents can compute on data they cannot read. Because protection sits outside the probabilistic model, tagged data stays private even when the model makes mistakes. The team implemented the system on two agent frameworks and released a benchmark of privacy critical tasks. The goal is collaboration on data that would otherwise stay locked in silos, with guarantees regulators can check.
arxiv-2512-08804:
Tian Yu Chen, Yong Zhuang Li, and Xiao Mei Kuang study how a black hole in a non minimal Einstein Yang Mills theory would look when lit by a thin accretion disk. Matter in the disk follows stable circular orbits outside a key inner boundary. Inside that boundary, matter plunges quickly into the black hole.

By tracing orbits of both massive and massless particles, the authors find that the inner orbit boundary and the photon sphere depend strongly on the non minimal coupling value. Compared with two standard black hole types, the coupling widens the range of impact parameters and slightly strengthens the redshift in the images. Because the coupling also changes the event horizon, the final image is weaker than the standard cases under the chosen emission model. That holds at all viewing angles between disk and observer. The work shows how a coupling change leaves clear optical fingerprints.
arxiv-2512-09404:
Mohid Farhan and three co-authors fit dark matter and dark energy into a single particle physics model, the Three-Higgs Doublet Model. That model extends the Higgs sector of the Standard Model to three doublets. The two dark components of the universe, the matter shaping galaxies and the energy speeding up cosmic expansion, are treated separately.

In their construction, dark matter and dark energy live in separate inert doublets of the model. A symmetry suppresses the dark matter's interactions so it behaves as required, while a shift symmetry lets the other component mimic dark energy for this cosmic epoch. Using a software tool, they compute the dark matter's leftover abundance from the early universe and show it can match observations and earlier literature even with dark energy included. They also compute the model's renormalization group equations to check the setup stays stable across a wide range of energies.
arxiv-2512-09704:
Shruti Paranjape, Marcus Spradlin, Anastasia Volovich, and He-Chen Weng study the algebraic structure inside scattering amplitudes for gluons, the force carriers of the strong interaction. Recent work connected the symbol letters of massless scattering to cluster variables of partial flag varieties, algebraic objects with rich combinatorics. This paper examines cluster adjacency, the rule saying which quantities can appear next to each other, for a family of amplitudes.

Split-helicity amplitudes, where the gluons' spins split into two groups, can be written in closed form using zigzag diagrams, which makes them a test case. The authors check in several cases, and conjecture in general, that the poles appearing in each term of these amplitudes satisfy cluster adjacency. The test uses a set of permutations built from arc permutations of the corresponding zigzag. Results of this kind suggest the complicated formulas of particle scattering are governed by a cluster algebra geometry.
arxiv-2512-09804:
Jens Albrecht and five colleagues release OnCoCo 1.0, a public dataset for sorting messages in online counseling chats into fine grained types. Automated analysis of counseling text has relied on category systems built for motivational interviewing, mostly from face to face sessions. Those systems are too narrow for written psychosocial counseling. The team built a broader coding scheme and labeled a set of real counseling messages with it, then released both the data and trained models openly.

The scheme separates dozens of counselor message types from dozens of client message types, covering a few thousand messages in total. The authors fine tuned several models on the data to show it works in practice. Researchers and practitioners can use the resource to study how counselors and clients talk, and to build tools that support mental health dialogue analysis. It extends what language resources exist for social and mental health conversation.
arxiv-2512-10404:
Laszlo Wolf, Geoff Brennecka, and Vladan Stevanović search for better piezoelectric materials, the kind that turn pressure into electric charge inside devices such as acoustic wave filters. Their paper studies an alloy that mixes aluminium nitride, already widely used, with silicon carbide, both common and already familiar in electronics.

Working from first principles across the full mix range, the team first mapped which crystal structures actually compete, finding wurtzite, zincblende, and rhombohedral forms to be the relevant ones. They then predicted stiffness, piezoelectric, and dielectric behaviour for the wurtzite form using special model structures. Reading those results through the needs of a bulk acoustic wave filter, they chart trade-offs between sound speed and piezoelectric response and point to the mixes worth pursuing.
arxiv-2512-10604:
Sandor Katz and Daniel Nogradi reformulate quantum chromodynamics, the theory of quarks and gluons, on an unusual lattice: the four-dimensional sixteen-cell honeycomb. Lattice calculations chop space-time into a grid, and the usual cubic grid breaks rotational symmetry badly, forcing small spacings and costly extrapolations to the continuum. A honeycomb with more symmetry should soften those errors.

Working in quenched QCD, where the gluon sea is simplified, they test both gluonic and fermionic observables. Scaling behaviour on the honeycomb proved clearly better than on the cubic lattice, so much larger spacings still allowed controlled extrapolation to the continuum limit. Chiral and topological properties improved markedly as well. The six-page study makes the case that prettier geometry is not decoration: it buys cheaper, cleaner access to real QCD results.
arxiv-2512-10904:
Jorge Sanchez and a large team read the recipe of a planet's rocks straight from its air. The ratios of rock-forming elements govern a planet's interior mineralogy. The elements are magnesium, silicon, and iron. They are usually assumed to mirror the host star. That assumption is barely tested, because those elements hide in rock. Ultra-hot Jupiters solve the problem: at dayside temperatures above three thousand kelvin, refractory elements stay gaseous and spectroscopically visible.

With the IGRINS spectrograph on Gemini South, the team took detailed emission spectra of WASP-189b and detected neutral iron, magnesium, and silicon, alongside water, carbon monoxide, and hydroxyl. The magnesium-to-silicon, iron-to-magnesium, and silicon-to-iron ratios all matched the star's values, while refractories ran twice as rich relative to volatiles. Accepted by Nature Communications, the result is the first evidence that giant planet atmospheres preserve stellar rock-forming ratios.
arxiv-2512-11104:
Brennan Flannery and colleagues combine several pathology foundation models into one representation for grading and staging cancer from microscope slides. Each model was trained in a similar way, yet what they share, repeat, or uniquely capture was unclear. Their fusion method uses information measures to prune redundant features while keeping complementary ones.

The study covered kidney, prostate, and rectal cancers, sorting slides into low versus high grade or stage. Fusion of small tile level embeddings beat every single model and simpler combinations such as voting or plain joining of features. The models' overall feature spaces aligned strongly, but their local neighbourhoods differed, confirming they hold complementary fine detail. Attention maps from the fused system concentrated on tumour regions and ignored benign areas more cleanly, aiding both accuracy and interpretation.
arxiv-2512-11204:
A. Fraser Gillan and colleagues search for hidden comet like activity among asteroids that follow Jupiter crossing orbits. Wide field surveys find new Jupiter family comets each year by spotting a dust coma or tail, yet they also find many similar looking asteroids with no reported activity. Some of those quiet bodies may simply be too faint in survey images for weak activity to show.

Using deep imaging from a mid sized telescope in the Canary Islands, the team observed sixteen such asteroids plus seven known comets for comparison. Three asteroids showed surface brightness patterns consistent with low level activity, including one Jupiter Trojan. Within the distance range where activity appeared, the active share rose to about a third of targets. The authors estimate sizes for the active nuclei and note their colours match a primitive asteroid type, suggesting many more weakly active bodies await discovery.
arxiv-2512-11304:
S. C. Park, Tuomas Virtanen, and Christian Webb prove a precise link between two classic models of statistical physics: the near-critical Ising model and the sine-Gordon model at a special setting. The Ising model describes interacting spins on a grid, tuned here close to its phase change with plus boundary conditions. The sine-Gordon model is a continuous field theory long suspected to mirror the same physics.

The authors show that doubled correlation functions of the main Ising fields, covering spin, disorder, fermions, and energy, exactly match sine-Gordon correlations at the free fermion point. The proof leans on how correlations vary smoothly with a mass parameter and on known critical-case results. The match is a rigorous instance of bosonization, a deep duality between matter descriptions.
arxiv-2512-11404:
Kengo Shinoda and colleagues calculate how a dying star's hydrogen envelope decides whether the leftover core becomes a neutron star or black hole. When a massive star explodes, some material falls back onto the core. In hydrogen rich stars, a reverse shock bouncing off the boundary between hydrogen and helium layers can drive much more fallback, but its effect across explosion strengths was never mapped systematically.

One dimensional simulations of metal poor stars, with and without hydrogen envelopes over a huge energy range, revealed a universal transition. When the explosion carries only a few times the envelope's binding energy, the reverse shock returns to the centre and the remnant grows sharply. Stronger explosions blow the shock out, and stripped and unstripped stars leave nearly equal remnants. Normalising by envelope binding energy collapses all models onto one relation, summarised in a simple formula.
arxiv-2512-11804:
Oscar Ivan Agudelo Rico and Matteo Rizzi study the Jacobi operator of minimal hypersurfaces that grow toward a cone at infinity. Minimal surfaces are soap film like shapes with zero mean curvature. The Jacobi operator, built from the surface Laplacian plus a curvature term, tests whether such a shape is stable or can flex.

The pair prove Fredholm traits for this operator, meaning its key equation behaves like a finite dimensional one in the ways that matter. Under clear nondegeneracy rules on the surface and on the data falloff, they build a right inverse, so the Jacobi equation can be solved. Worked cases show where the results apply, aiding the study of cone tipped minimal shapes.
arxiv-2512-12004:
Troy Allen presents EnviroLLM, an open source toolkit for tracking what local AI use costs in power and speed. People run large language models on their own machines for privacy, yet they have no easy way to see energy use or judge trade offs between models.

EnviroLLM watches processes live, benchmarks models across Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, and OpenAI style APIs, and stores results with charts for long term study. It adds judge based quality scores next to energy and speed numbers. Personalized tips then suggest better models or settings for the user hardware. The tool aims to make home AI use measurable, so greener and faster choices stop being guesswork.
arxiv-2512-12704:
Sougata Bhattacharyya and Sovik Roy view Dicke states through topology in a 2025 paper. Dicke states are symmetric quantum states of many qubits where a fixed number are excited. The authors treat qubits as topological loops and link the states' recursive measurement behavior to the stability of n-Hopf links, which are chains of interlocked rings.

They use Schmidt rank to measure how bipartite entanglement survives splitting, and the l1 norm of coherence as a measure of link fluidity. Unlike GHZ states, which they compare to Borromean rings that fall apart when one ring is cut, Dicke states keep a robust, self similar linking. Local measurements preserve the global link structure through residual coherence that does not vanish.
arxiv-2512-12804:
Sander Beckers develops a new semantics for probabilities of counterfactuals in a 2025 philosophy paper. Counterfactuals are what-if claims, like what would have happened under a different cause. Pearl's standard semantics for them needs structural causal models, but Beckers shows some such models cannot be extended into realistic ones, leaving them outside Pearl's scope even in simple settings.

His generalization keeps the Markov condition, realistic variables only, and causal completeness. It drops so called response variables. He proves it matches two other recent proposals that avoid such models. The result is a compromise in the Pearl Dawid debate: against universal determinism, as Dawid urges, but for a general counterfactual semantics, as Pearl holds.
arxiv-2512-12904:
Ben Dong, Hui Feng, and Qian Wang present OptHQC, a faster version of HQC, a code based scheme for quantum-safe key exchange. Such schemes guard future messages against quantum computers, but they run slower than classic methods. Speed is thus a major barrier to wider use.

The team studied each computing block of HQC and sped up all three stages: key generation, encryption, and decryption. They used sparse data tricks, chip level acceleration for hashing, and lookup tables for the heaviest steps. On a standard CPU, the result ran about 55 percent faster on average than the reference version of HQC.
arxiv-2512-13204:
Samuel Magorrian and co-authors tune the elastic properties of ultra-high temperature ceramics, materials built for extreme heat. These ceramics resist huge temperatures but are brittle and hard to shape. Mixing several metals into one compound offers a way to adjust traits such as stiffness.

The team fine-tuned a universal machine learning potential on carbide mixtures with group IV and V metals. Elastic constants strayed from simple mixture rules in both high-entropy and low-entropy blends, an effect traced to lattice mismatch strain. They flag a three-part mixture of hafnium, vanadium, and zirconium carbides as a good balance. Variants could run up to 40 gigapascals softer than zirconium carbide.
arxiv-2512-14204:
Robson Christie, Jaewoo Joo, Greg Kaplanek, Vincent Vennin, and David Wands study quantum tunneling in the early universe in a 2025 paper. They model a scalar field in an uneven double well potential during inflation, coupled to an environment of spectator fields.

From that setup they derive Markovian and non Markovian master equations and solve them numerically. Decoherence, the loss of quantum interference, proves key to suppressing interference between the two vacua. Heavy fields settle into the true vacuum with high probability, while light fields can get stuck more often in the false one. Once decoherence occurs, tunneling nearly stops. They call this cosmic lockdown, a form of the quantum Zeno effect.
arxiv-2512-14404:
Hangjun Cho and co-authors revisit how data-driven models of dynamical systems choose their building blocks. Methods like SINDy pick a few terms from a large dictionary of candidate functions, using an algorithm called Sequential Threshold Least Squares. Which terms survive depends on reconstruction errors, which the authors call scores, and on how similar the dictionary terms are to each other.

Working out the theory behind those scores leads to a screening step that prunes the dictionary before fitting. Experiments on ordinary and partial differential equations showed better accuracy and models that are easier to read. The guidance is aimed at people who use SINDy in practice.
arxiv-2512-14604:
Many people leave text behind repeatedly over time, in reviews, posts, or medical notes across visits, but at irregular, sparse intervals. Such sparse longitudinal text could guide policy and targeted recommendations, yet its uneven timing makes it hard to analyze with standard tools.

One answer offered is LLmFPCA-detect, which pairs large language models with multivariate functional principal component analysis to hunt for anomalies in these data. The language model turns raw text into usable signals, and the functional method handles observations scattered over time. The goal is to flag unusual patterns in text histories that would be hard to spot by reading alone.
arxiv-2512-14704:
Tourists now leave digital traces throughout their trips, and those traces have reshaped how tourism behavior is studied. Earlier work on these data leaned heavily on quantitative measures, counting visits, movements, and other trace counts to reach its conclusions.

A profiling approach based on interest analysis is presented instead, grouping tourists by what they care about rather than only by what they did. Interest profiles can help destinations and businesses match offers to travelers more intelligently. The study reflects a broader shift in tourism research, from raw digital trace counts toward richer readings of traveler behavior and motivation.
arxiv-2512-14804:
Janka Lengyel and colleagues map the messy flow of air behind wind turbines. The wake trailing each turbine shapes how a whole wind farm performs, yet its layout is still only partly known. The team uses LiDAR scans taken from a turbine top to watch the wake in two dimensions.

Their analysis measures roughness and bursts of extreme flow at each spot in the wake. It finds four distinct wake zones, with strongly linked patches two to five rotor widths downstream. What older work called an intermittency ring turns out to be a set of local bubbles instead. The method offers a cheap way to check wake models and to guide how farms are laid out and run.
arxiv-2512-14904:
Marc Kegel and two coauthors define a distance between shapes that carry a contact structure, a geometric twist used in three dimensional topology. The contact surgery distance counts the fewest contact surgeries, cut and paste moves, needed to turn one such space into another. A plainer version of the question, for smooth spaces without the contact twist, was already known.

Their main result bounds the new distance: it exceeds the smooth surgery distance by at most 5. Along the way, they classify the rational homology 3-spheres on which one invariant of a plane field, called d3, already fixes two others, the Gamma invariant and the Euler class. The work ties a hands on surgery count to classical invariants of three dimensional spaces.
arxiv-2512-15104:
Attila Lovas and two coauthors prove sharp rates for how fast Markov chains settle down when their world keeps changing. The chains live on general state spaces in a stationary random environment, driven by a random map that contracts, up to a bounded perturbation. Such chains model systems buffeted by outside randomness they cannot control.

The authors prove the chains converge to a limiting law and give explicit convergence rates. They also show the processes are strongly mixing and estimate the mixing coefficients, which measure how fast the past is forgotten. The results extend what was known in a significant way. For some additive autoregressive processes with outside covariates, the mixing rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors. The work serves probabilists who need firm numbers, not just limit statements, for chains in random surroundings.
arxiv-2512-15304:
Axel J. M. Deenen and a coauthor predict a diode effect for supercurrents made from shape alone. The superconducting diode effect lets current pass more easily one way than the other, a prized trick for superconducting electronics. Their device is a hollow helix made of an ordinary superconductor, with no exotic material asymmetry.

Using time dependent Ginzburg-Landau simulations, they show the helical shape plus field induced Meissner screening currents give unequal critical currents for the two polarities. Efficiency peaks where one direction first nucleates vortices, marking a crossover between screening dominated and vortex dominated behavior. The mechanism is robust, they argue, and sits within reach of experiments. Three dimensional superconducting diodes of this kind could serve multi level integrated quantum circuits.
arxiv-2512-15404:
József Kovács and eight coauthors present a database that helps astronomers turn a star's measured colors into its true brightness and size. To get a star's total light output and radius, one needs its full flux across all wavelengths. In practice that comes from a bolometric correction applied to measured magnitudes.

The Gothard Observatory database gives computed magnitudes and corrections for 752 filters. Those filters come from 78 ground and space instruments. The values were computed from the BOSZ library of computed stellar spectra, in the Vega magnitude system, using the species Python package. The grid spans temperatures from 2800 to 16000 kelvin. It covers a wide span of surface gravity and metal content, and dust reddening up to three point one magnitudes. Applied to 192,000 APOGEE stars, the corrections yield total outputs. The authors show that ignoring carbon can skew those outputs by up to zero point two percent.
arxiv-2512-15504:
Kai Hippi proves a quantum mixing result for compact hyperbolic surfaces in a 2025 math paper. Quantum mixing describes how observables spread evenly over a surface at high energy, a large scale analogue of a theorem by Zelditch. The assumptions here hold for both arithmetic surfaces and random surfaces of large genus.

Rather than using ball averaging or Nevo's ergodic theorem, Hippi builds a new method on the hyperbolic wave equation. It uses the quantitative exponential mixing of the geodesic flow established by Ratner and Matheus. The result complements large scale quantum ergodicity theorems by Le Masson and Sahlsten. Together they give a fuller picture of observable behavior in the large scale limit.
arxiv-2512-15604:
Naomi Clare Robertson and Alex Hall compare cosmic shear nulling methods for Stage IV surveys in a 2025 paper. Cosmic shear measures how galaxy shapes are bent by gravity, but gas feedback in galaxies biases the signal at small scales. Nulling methods transform the data to mute the modes most hit by that feedback.

The study compares three approaches: the BNT transform, a new LU based method acting on the two point statistics, and a cross correlation method using large scale structure tracers. A Fisher forecast gauges the bias left in key parameters. All three cut bias well. The LU method cuts most but loses precision, while BNT keeps more information and has firmer theory footing.
arxiv-2512-16004:
Furkan Sik and two co-authors present a new numerical method in this 2025 arXiv paper on applied mathematics. Their topic is the finite element method, a standard way to solve physics equations on a mesh. They add wavelets, which are math tools that split a solution into coarse and fine parts, adapted to the problem at hand.

Their method works on meshes made of many-sided polygon pieces built by merging smaller triangles step by step. Each scale can be solved on its own and then added in, with no need to redo coarser levels. Smooth regions use fewer, larger pieces, while sharp regions keep small ones. The result is near-linear computing cost and lower memory use.
arxiv-2512-16104:
G Abellan and three co-authors analyze collapsing stars with math in a paper made public on arXiv in 2025. When a massive star's core collapses, gravity can form a black hole. The team models a star whose pressure differs by direction. They use one coordinate system for both inside and outside the star. That avoids seams where two charts are stitched.

Within that single chart, they derive exact solutions for the whole collapse. They track how horizons form. They find a phase with two apparent horizons inside the matter. The event horizon settles at the Schwarzschild radius. They also give threshold rules. These link a star's initial compactness to instant horizon formation. The model breaks standard energy conditions. The authors flag that as a limit of idealized matter models.
arxiv-2512-16304:
Jiajun Yuan and five co-authors restore damaged speech in research shared on arXiv in 2025. Recordings made at very low sampling rates, common in archives and surveillance audio, lose the cues that make words clear. Generative repair models often invent plausible sounds that change the words, which is dangerous for evidence and history.

Their framework, CogSR, aims at precise offline restoration. A large audio-language model reasons step by step about the content, acting as a semantic anchor, while explicit acoustic cues pin down the speaker's identity. A rectified flow generator then rebuilds the missing high frequencies under that guidance. Tests showed the method removes ambiguity even under severe degradation, producing speech that is both realistic and faithful to the words spoken. The authors target high-value legacy recordings where accuracy matters more than speed.
arxiv-2512-16404:
Robert Rugg, Shambel Akalu, and Amare Abebe make a modified gravity theory computable in their arXiv paper from 2025. F(T) gravity replaces Einstein's curvature with torsion to explain cosmic acceleration. Their power-law version is nonlinear, and the standard Boltzmann solver CLASS, which computes how cosmic structure grows, cannot handle nonlinear models directly.

The workaround is a second-order Taylor expansion of the field equations around the standard cosmological model. That is safe when the extra parameter n, which measures departure from the standard model, stays small. Supernova data indicate n is at most 0.05, small enough that the power spectrum comes out accurately with negligible truncation error. The framework lets cosmologists test this gravity theory against the same data pipelines used for the standard model.
arxiv-2512-16804:
Oem Trivedi argues that atomic clocks give a sharp Solar System test of scalar-tensor dark energy, where a scalar field drives the late speedup of the universe. Clock rates and Newton constant drift both tie back to that one field.

By linking those local measures to the field motion, Trivedi derives a direct bound on the present-day equation of state of dark energy. The bound forces any locally coupled scalar into a very slow roll, the strongest of its kind. It does not depend on the shape of the field potential, and it rules out wide classes of models. Lunar laser ranging and light path data tighten the result further.
arxiv-2512-16904:
Pierre Fernandez and coauthors test post-hoc watermarking, where a language model rewrites existing text while planting a hidden statistical mark. Marks can guard copyrighted works or reveal use in training data, but quality and detectability trade off.

The team varies how compute is spent: bigger rewriting models, beam search, many candidate drafts, or entropy filtering at detection. On open text such as books, their plans give strong detection with meaning kept intact. The simple Gumbel-max scheme beat newer rivals under nucleus sampling, and beam search helped most methods. Verifiable text such as code proved hard, and smaller models oddly beat larger ones there.
arxiv-2512-17004:
Yannis Bennacer, Olivier Mousis, and Vincent Hue ask why Io is dry while Europa kept its water, though both are Galilean moons whose bulk density falls with distance from Jupiter. Early Jupiter shone brighter and may have driven air loss on both moons.

The team models how protosatellites formed and heated, counting heating from rock impacts and pebbles plus young Jupiter glare, and tracks water loss by dehydration and air escape. Europa kept most volatiles in nearly all runs, since big dehydration would start only after ten million years. Io, by contrast, could not lose much water by escape, so it likely formed dry. A dehydration line in the Jovian disk may explain the split.
arxiv-2512-17204:
Ethan Silver, Plamen Krastev, and Edo Berger search LIGO data from the first three observing runs for binary black hole mergers with convolutional neural networks. Neural searches promise faster detection and follow-up than classic pipelines, vital when sky partners must be alerted fast.

Training data were built from real LIGO noise. The pipeline found 57 of the 75 cataloged binary black hole events in two-detector data, with 57 false positives that parameter checks and human review can mostly clear. Time-shifted data runs set the false alarm rate. The results mark a step toward low-latency machine learning searches for multi-messenger astronomy.
arxiv-2512-17304:
M F Fauzi, H S Ramadhan, and A Sulaksono compare two rival pictures of how dark matter might gather around a black hole. One picture, the vacuum model, gives the matter negative outward pressure. The other, the Einstein cluster model, gives it none. Both are widely used, so the team asks whether telescopes could ever tell them apart.

They track three signals: the photon sphere where light can orbit, the size of the black hole shadow, and the bending of light near the halo. The two models bend the photon sphere in opposite ways. The Einstein cluster also shifts the shadow size more strongly away from a plain black hole. Both models show a distinct lensing effect tied to the halo.
arxiv-2512-17704:
Mohammad Aqib, Hemangi Madhusudan Shah, and Dhriti Sundar Patra pin down when a certain self-similar shape in geometry must in fact be a plain, rigid one. Almost Ricci-Bourguignon solitons are spaces whose curvature flows almost as if the space were merely rescaling itself, a near-miss of the famous Einstein shapes. On a compact such space, the team asks what extra conditions force the near-miss to collapse into something trivial or special.

Their theorems slot these solitons into the wider family of Einstein-type metrics and state clean tests for triviality. Side-by-side comparison with the classic Barros and Ribeiro results shows exactly where the new tests reach further. Rigidity results like these tell geometers when apparent freedom is an illusion.
arxiv-2512-17804:
Arthur Couteau, Panayotis Dimopoulos Eggenschwiler, and Patrick Jenny audit turbulence's energy economy transfer by transfer. In stirred fluid, big eddies hand their energy to smaller ones in a cascade, but the bookkeeping between individual wave modes was usually blurred into group averages. Their simulations itemize every exchange within each interacting trio of modes.

A simple potential, built from the modes' own energy content, predicts where the fiercest transfers cluster. Shifting where the stirring injects energy moves that cluster with it: the energy-rich scales, not the trio's geometry, set the map. Direct swaps with the energy-rich range are choked by the fluid's incompressibility, leaving only residue near home. A classic closure theory, EDQNM, matches the audit well. Turbulence modelers gain a sharper ledger.
arxiv-2512-17904:
Stéphane Bessy, Daniel Gonçalves, Amadeus Reinald, and Dimitrios M. Thilikos study a wiring puzzle on flat maps. Given a directed graph drawn without crossings, can added arrows make every point reach every other point, while the drawing stays flat? They show that even telling whether any fix exists is NP-hard, meaning no fast general method is likely.

When the number of added arrows is capped at a budget k, the picture changes. Their method solves the capped problem in time that grows fast only in k, not in the graph's size. The key is that each face of the drawing admits only a few useful partial fixes. It is the first method of its kind for a hard flat wiring problem.
arxiv-2512-18004:
Shubham Kumar Nigam, Parjanya Aditya Shukla, Noel Shallum, and Arnab Bhattacharya tackle a backlog in India's courts: piles of handwritten legal papers in Marathi. Police reports, charge sheets, and witness statements must be read and translated before many people can use them. Marathi has few digital training sets, and handwriting varies a lot.

The team compares two routes. One reads the page with a text scanner and then translates the text. The other uses a vision language model to go from page image to translation in one step. Their tests on real legal pages weigh accuracy and ease of use, aiming at tools that can run on modest hardware in district courts.
arxiv-2512-18104:
Andreas E. Robertson leads a seven author team making digital twins of materials that admit their own doubt. Real materials vary from batch to batch in grain pattern and makeup, and no model can erase that spread. Their network, the VDMN, bakes chance into a layered model that mirrors how tiny structures carry load.

A fast math scheme passes the spread through the network as it works, in both directions: predicting behavior and working back to hidden traits. In tests it forecast the bend and stretch spread of 3D printed polymer blends, matching lab results. It also pulled apart mixed sources of doubt in the base traits, a step toward twins that know their limits.
arxiv-2512-18404:
Jifeng Chu and three co-authors study Sturm-Liouville operators, a classic family of differential operators whose vibration-like solutions are called eigenfunctions. Each eigenfunction crosses zero at points called nodes, and the authors ask how far those nodes can move when the potential varies. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, treats each node as a nonlinear function of the potential.

Working with potentials inside an L1 ball of fixed radius, they solve the optimization problems that push each node to its extremes. Strong continuity of the nodes in the potential makes the argument work. The result is a set of explicit, sharp bounds for all nodes, written as elementary functions. Such bounds tell engineers and physicists exactly how much a spectrum can shift when a system is perturbed.
arxiv-2512-18504:
Jensen Zhang, Ningyuan Liu, and Keze Wang study why vision-language models stumble on concepts outside their training data. They trace the failure to an asymmetry. The image encoder can extract useful features from unseen pictures. The text encoder, though, is stuck with a fixed vocabulary and cannot coin anchors for new ideas. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, fixes the text side at inference time.

Their framework, GTMA, builds a continuous pseudo-word embedding matched to the visual anchor of an out-of-distribution image. That sidesteps the vocabulary limit. A gradient-based policy tunes the invented word, with regularization to keep it plausible. On ImageNet-R and VISTA-Beyond, GTMA lifts zero-shot and few-shot accuracy on new concepts by up to 15 to 20 percent over the base model. Accuracy on familiar concepts holds steady.
arxiv-2512-18604:
Wencan Mao, Quanxi Zhou, and colleagues in Japan, Chile, and China plan flight paths for farm drones that spot weeds and gather data from field sensors in one trip. Uncertain conditions, partial views, and limited batteries make the planning hard. Their 2025 paper casts the problem as a Markov decision process and solves it with multi agent reinforcement learning. Each drone learns its own policy while sharing the field.

Their algorithm, ITDQN, adds two ideas to deep Q learning. An elite imitation mechanism lets agents copy top performers, cutting exploration costs. A mediator Q network sits over a double deep Q network, speeding and stabilizing training. Tests in simulated and real world settings confirm it works. ITDQN beats the double deep Q network baseline by 4.43% in weed recognition rate. It also leads by 6.94% in data collection rate. Smarter routes mean more weeds mapped and more sensor data harvested per battery charge.
arxiv-2512-18704: Mariagrazia Bianchi and Nicola Sambonet complete a theorem in the representation theory of finite groups, following earlier work by Gluck and Wolf. Their note, posted to arXiv in December 2025, finishes the Itô-Michler theorem for projective representations of a p-solvable or pi-separable group. They then relate the projective irreducible modules of such a group to those of its Sylow p-subgroups and Hall pi-subgroups, tying global structure to local pieces.
arxiv-2512-18804:
Guangtao Lyu and six co-authors generate 3D dances from music, betting on tempo as the one cue that never lies. Genre labels, used by earlier systems, are noisy or missing and let the dancing drift off the beat. Tempo, by contrast, sits steadily between 60 and 200 beats per minute across datasets. Their model, TempoMoE, posted to arXiv in December 2025, builds rhythm into a diffusion generator.

Motion experts are grouped by tempo range, and multi-scale beat experts track both quick steps and long phrases. A hierarchical routing unit reads the music and blends the right experts on the fly, with no manual labels. Experiments give state-of-the-art dance quality and rhythm alignment. The design lesson travels: anchor generative models to stable physical quantities, not to shaky human annotations.
arxiv-2512-19004:
Tongyuan Miao, Gary Huang, Kai Jun Han, and Annie Jiang speed up diffusion language models by starting the race partway down the track. These models generate text in parallel but begin from a fully masked blank, wasting many denoising steps. Their idea, posted to arXiv in December 2025, is context-aware initialization: a small auxiliary model injects prompt-based priors into the starting point, through discrete token injection or embedding-level interpolation.

A confidence-based remasking step keeps the model skeptical of bad priors, since unmask-only decoding can lock in early mistakes. On the GSM8K math benchmark, denoising iterations drop by about 35 percent in function evaluations. The honest caveat: naive warm-starting can also hurt final accuracy, so the authors frame calibration and revision mechanisms as the research agenda. Faster generation only counts if the text stays good.
arxiv-2512-19104:
Haishan Ye studies optimization when a system can only say which of two options looks better, never by how much. Rank-based zeroth-order methods work from such ordinal feedback, and they are used in learning from human preferences. Their theory, though, has lagged behind their practical success, especially with noisy goals.

Ye gives a simple, efficient rank-based algorithm and proves explicit query counts for reaching a target accuracy. The bounds hold for convex and nonconvex smooth goals, under standard assumptions on noise and curvature. The counts match the best known results for methods that see exact values. Ordinal feedback alone, the result shows, loses nothing in query efficiency.
arxiv-2512-19304:
Emir Devlet Ertörer and Cem Ünsalan put a binary neural network for reading handwritten digits onto a small FPGA chip. Binary networks swap heavy floating-point math for bitwise logic, saving power and time. That thrift suits tight embedded hardware, if the design is done well.

The accelerator was written by hand in Verilog, with no high-level synthesis tools, for a Xilinx Artix-7 board. It classifies in real time at eighty megahertz with low power and steady timing. On the MNIST test set it reached eighty-four percent accuracy. Code and training scripts are public, and the authors stress the clarity that manual hardware design gives.
arxiv-2512-19404:
Madhumitha K. V., Harshitha A., Swati Nayak, and Sabitha D'Souza define a new matrix for graphs and study its spectrum. The starting point is the Lanzhou index, a sum over vertices that weighs each degree by the degree in the complement graph. Their matrix fills an entry for each edge from the endpoint weights, and zero elsewhere.

Spectrum work follows: bounds on the Lanzhou energy and on the spread of eigenvalues, plus exact spectra and inertia for standard graph families. They also characterize when the eigenvalues sit symmetrically about the origin. The paper extends spectral graph theory to a fresh index-based matrix.
arxiv-2512-19704:
Markus Köhli, Martin Schrön, Steffen Zacharias, and Ulrich Schmidt present URANOS, a Monte Carlo code for following neutrons through matter from thermal to fast energies. It grew out of work on the CASCADE detector and aims at small to medium projects that need speed plus an interface a newcomer can actually use. The geometry engine is voxel-based: designs are drawn as stacked pictures, each pixel a material.

Inside, ray casting drives transport through elastic and inelastic collisions, absorption, and evaporation-like processes, with cross sections drawn from evaluated databases. Boron-lined detector physics gets special care, tracking charged particles after conversion and projecting their diffusing tracks onto readout units. Freely available, URANOS targets detector response studies, laboratory setups, and cosmic-ray neutron transport in the environment.
arxiv-2512-19804:
Shane Coffing and three co-authors build a faster way to forecast tsunamis, with honest odds attached. Small models can stand in for the full wave physics. They run far faster than the full sums, but the classic kind follows one fixed path. Their model instead keeps the physics in an initial-value problem. Fixes to its operators tune it so its paths match real wave paths.

A Bayesian pooling step is layered on top of the start values. That yields new paths that work across a range of nearby starts. The result is a stand-in the team calls a randPROM. It gives full, odds-based forecasts of waves. They test it on a made-up Fiji case and on the real 2011 Tohoku tsunami. It cut the number of full runs by a lot, while its calls on arrival times and heights stayed sound.
arxiv-2512-20004:
Rahul Yumlembam, Biju Issac, Seibu Mary Jacob, and Longzhi Yang both wield and attack graph-based malware detectors for Android. Their detector turns each app into a graph of API relationships, embeds it with a graph neural network, and mixes those embeddings with permission and intent features for classification. Accuracy exceeded ninety-eight percent on both the CICMalDroid and Drebin benchmark datasets.

Then the team turns adversary. Their attack, VGAE-MalGAN, trains a generative model to fabricate API graphs that slip past graph-based detectors, with a substitute detector mimicking the target during training. Detection rates fell significantly against the forged samples. Retraining on the adversarial examples, however, restored much of the robustness, making the paper a small arms race in one study.
arxiv-2512-20104:
Subrata Kumer Paul leads an eight-author team running a factorial experiment on the knobs practitioners twiddle by habit. Human activity recognition from video serves healthcare, surveillance, and smart environments, yet most studies chase new architectures while the interaction between activation functions and optimizers goes unmeasured. Their grid crosses three activations, ReLU, sigmoid, and tanh, with four optimizers, SGD, Adam, RMSprop, and Adagrad, on two recurrent architectures.

ConvLSTM consistently beat BiLSTM on both HMDB51 and UCF101 data, reaching up to 99 percent accuracy with Adam or RMSprop, thanks to stronger spatio-temporal learning. BiLSTM approached 98 percent on UCF101 but slumped near 60 percent on HMDB51, showing fragile cross-dataset robustness and little sensitivity to the activation-optimizer pairing. The study offers practical guidance for healthcare-oriented recognition systems.
arxiv-2512-20204:
Marko Čechovič and co-authors built a corpus for meetings where participants share no common language. Volunteers held dialogues helped by automatic simultaneous speech translation. The corpus holds five hours of recordings in twelve original languages, with transcripts and translations into English, both machine-made and corrected, plus written minutes of each meeting.

The team also tackles a practical hazard: misunderstandings that creep in when translation mediates a conversation. They marked the mix-ups by hand and tested whether large language models can spot them automatically. The best model found most annotated spans but also raised many false alarms. The corpus gives speech and translation teams realistic material for testing cross-lingual meeting systems.
arxiv-2512-20404:
Junyi Liu and Stanley Kok summarize messy, emotional text while keeping the feelings in the summary. Social media posts, reviews, and forum threads are short, noisy, and fragmented, unlike the tidy news articles most summarizers were built for. Yet for brand monitoring and market analysis, the sentiment is often the whole point.

Their approach adds sentiment signals to both an extractive method, TextRank, and an abstractive one, UniLM. Sentiment shapes which sentences get picked and how new summary text is generated. The result is concise summaries that preserve emotional nuance and thematic relevance. For information systems work, such summaries promise faster interventions and sharper strategic decisions in fast-moving online environments.
arxiv-2512-20604:
Alexandros Christoforos and Chadbourne Davis make diffusion models write long texts without drowning in cost. Text diffusion builds a passage by step-by-step denoising, but dense attention, where every position looks at every other, makes long texts slow and hungry for memory. Their method, MoE-DiffuSeq, trims the attention pattern and adds a mixture of experts, a design that routes each piece of text to a few chosen subnetworks.

Sparse attention cuts the squared cost, while the expert routing adds skill only where it is needed. A soft absorbing state inside the process reshapes how attention behaves during denoising, which speeds up rebuilding and sharpens each token as it is refined. On long-text benchmarks, the system beats prior diffusion models and sparse-attention rivals in training speed, sampling speed, and output quality. Long science texts, big code bases, and extended chats are the intended uses.
arxiv-2512-20804:
Alexander Reichmann and four co-authors work on growing silicon carbide crystals inside a computer. Growers need these crystals for electronics, but atom-by-atom simulation forces unrealistically fast deposition. Atoms slammed down that quickly form messy layers and many defects, more like sputtering than real growth.

The team instead use a method that places each atom directly at its lowest-energy spot, stretching the effective time scale. They grew crystals on stepped silicon carbide surfaces cut at two angles, testing settings and atom-interaction models. Their tuned setup reproduced stable step-flow growth that ordinary simulation could not. They also measured dislocations, surface roughness, and atom movement in the results.
arxiv-2512-21604:
Alan A. Dzhioev, Andrey V. Yudin, Natalia V. Dunina-Barkovskaya, and Andrey I. Vdovin compute the neutrinos a massive star emits in its final stages before exploding as a supernova. Detecting these pre-supernova neutrinos would give an early warning of the collapse, so observers need reliable predictions of their spectra and brightness.

Using the MESA stellar evolution code, the authors model realistic temperatures, densities, and electron fractions inside the star. They include neutrinos from thermal processes and from weak-interaction reactions in hot nuclei. They then compare two treatments of those nuclear reactions: a thermal quasiparticle random-phase approximation and the standard effective Q-value method. The consistent treatment of Gamow-Teller transitions raises both the energy output and the average energies of the emitted neutrinos and antineutrinos. That difference directly changes how detectable the pre-supernova signal would be.
arxiv-2512-21704:
Taufiq Iqbal Baihaqi, Parada T. P. Hutauruk, and their co-authors measure a physics cross section with a neural network instead of a theory model. The process is coherent diffractive production of J/psi mesons at the HERA collider, where a photon strikes a proton and a J/psi emerges with the proton intact.

Earlier analyses fitted the data with theoretical models, whose built-in assumptions limit their reach and make answers model-dependent. The authors train a neural network on the same dataset as a model-independent alternative. Their best network reproduces the differential cross section across the kinematic range. They then merge HERA data with LHC data at various energies to predict the total photoproduction cross section. From the fit they extract the exponential slope parameter and show it depends on both photon virtuality and energy. The study shows neural networks as extraction tools for observables.
arxiv-2512-21904:
Fano fibrations, produced from compact Kähler manifolds by Kawamata's theorem, carry singular geometry on their base that interacts with canonical metrics. In the first of two papers, Alexander Bednarek constructs a (1,1)-form on the regular part of the base variety. The form is related to the Weil-Petersson metric and arises for a fibration generated by an ample rational line bundle.

The singular Kähler metric built by Zhang and Zhang on the base is shown to satisfy a twisted Kähler-Einstein equation involving that form. For a submersion, the Chern classes of the total space and the base decompose in terms of the same form. The results set up the companion paper's analysis of finite-time singularities in the Kähler-Ricci flow.
arxiv-2512-22104:
Lorenzo Magnea and Enrico Zunino mine decades of gauge-theory calculations for clues about celestial holography. That idea says the long-distance behavior of gauge and gravity theories is governed by a 2D conformal theory living on the celestial sphere. For non-abelian theories, soft radiation patterns are a key testing ground, and many high-order results already exist.

The authors translate known results, including soft emission currents for up to three particles and three-loop single emission, into celestial language. They show all logarithms in the single soft current can be absorbed into coupling scale choices, casting doubt on needing a logarithmic celestial theory. They also find that operator product expansions from collinear limits carry energy-dependent coefficients that break holomorphic factorization and, in double limits, associativity.
arxiv-2512-22204:
Fatma Almaz and Bilal Tekyoldaş study special curves built from lightlike, or null, curves inside lightlike cone space, a setting from semi-Riemannian geometry. Null curves have tangent vectors of zero length, and the indefinite metric gives them richer geometry than curves in usual Euclidean or Minkowski space. The authors analyze a null curve using its natural Frenet frame of four vectors.

From combinations of those frame vectors, tangent, normal, and binormal, they construct Smarandache curves, then compute their bending, torsion, and other geometric invariants. The results show how the original curve's traits transfer to the constructed curves and how the cone space's metric shapes them. The work connects degenerate geometry with the dynamics of lightlike particles in theoretical physics.
arxiv-2512-22604:
Wei-Hong Liang, Zhuo-Ran Hu, and Eulogio Oset test a picture of an exotic particle by watching how B mesons decay into it. The particle, Ds0*(2317), might be a molecule loosely bound from a D meson and a kaon, possibly with a Ds-eta component, rather than a compact quark state. The authors study B meson decays ending with that particle alongside an anti-D meson.

Their method concentrates the messy weak-interaction physics into measured branching fractions of related decays that produce D-kaon pairs, then follows how those pairs propagate and bind into the resonance. With just two free parameters, the approach describes six measured decay rates at once. That consistency supports the molecular interpretation of the Ds0*(2317) state.
arxiv-2512-22804:
Bor-Yiing Su, Peter Dykas, Mike Chrzanowski, and Jatin Chhugani present early work on training neural networks in mixed numerical precision without losing accuracy. Low-precision formats speed training and save memory, but picking which tensors can safely use them is tricky. Their framework, Mixture of Representations, inspects each tensor, and even parts of tensors, and picks a number format based on the values it actually contains.

Concrete algorithms switch dynamically between the compact FP8 format and the wider BF16 format, at both whole-tensor and sub-tensor levels. In their experiments the approach keeps model quality on par with established methods while putting more than ninety-eight percent of tensors into FP8. Because it needs no fine-grained partitioning schemes, the authors argue it can pair with other low-precision techniques and make training robust across datasets and partition choices.
arxiv-2512-22904:
Jin Wu and Chanjin Zheng address cognitive diagnosis, the task of estimating which skills each student has mastered from their answers. Deep learning models capture complex links among students, questions, and skills, but real education data are long-tailed, with few records for many skills, and the data keep changing as courses evolve. Both facts drag accuracy down.

Their framework, MetaCD, pairs meta-learning with continual learning. Meta-learning finds a starting point for the model that adapts to a new task from only a little data, easing the long-tail problem. A parameter protection mechanism, borrowed from continual learning, guards important weights so the model can absorb new skills without forgetting old ones. Across five real-world datasets, MetaCD beat competing baselines on accuracy and on generalization to later tasks, balancing flexibility on new material with stability on what came before.
arxiv-2512-23604:
Vignesh Manoharan and Vijaya Ramachandran bring a classic network question to parallel computers. A distance sensitivity oracle preprocesses a graph so it can instantly report the shortest path between two points when any single edge fails. The problem matters for communication networks and has been studied heavily for sequential machines and recently for distributed ones, but not for the PRAM model of parallel computation.

The authors present the first PRAM algorithms that build such oracles for directed weighted graphs, answering each query in constant time with one processor after preprocessing. They also give the first work-optimal parallel algorithms for several related problems in the same fine-grained complexity class, including replacement paths, second simple shortest paths, and minimum weight cycles. A brief announcement appeared at SPAA 2025.
arxiv-2512-23804:
Zhendong Li, Akwum Onwunta, and Bedřich Sousedík speed up hard design problems whose rules involve random inputs. In PDE-constrained optimization under uncertainty, one picks controls for a system ruled by partial differential equations while the material traits are not known for sure. A discretize-then-optimize pipeline with stochastic Galerkin projection then yields huge, badly conditioned linear systems that solvers struggle with.

Preconditioners, rough inverses that reshape the system for the solver, are the fix, and the authors build layered ones that use the sparse shape of the Galerkin system. Their design rests on cut-down stochastic expansions, trading build cost against how much faster the solver runs. Tests on steady and time-dependent control problems showed much faster convergence than existing methods, and the gains held up across the tested problems. For engineers who must design under doubt, that means answers far sooner.
arxiv-2512-24004:
P. C. Hinton and five co-authors ask whether Earth actually needs its magnetic field to keep its air. Textbooks credit that bubble with shielding the atmosphere from the solar wind, yet unmagnetized planets complicate that story. Using RHybrid, a hybrid plasma code treating ions kinetically and electrons as a fluid, the team simulated an unmagnetized Earth-like planet under typical solar wind conditions. They varied how strongly its ionosphere emits ions.

They tracked both escaping planetary ions, oxygen and hydrogen, and solar wind protons deposited into the atmosphere, then netted the two fluxes. Deposition proved comparable to escape, and across the simulated emission rates the atmosphere lost less than three percent of its mass over a billion years. That suggests the built-in field may be unnecessary for retention. The authors also guess that ionospheric emission evolves toward a critical rate where the net flux vanishes.
arxiv-2512-24204:
Pavel Slepov studies jet quenching in a quark-gluon plasma. Jets lose energy as they cross the hot medium. The plasma here is anisotropic, with a preferred direction. Slepov uses gauge-gravity duality to model it. A lightlike Wilson loop on the boundary defines the quantity of interest. Its dual is a two-dimensional worldsheet in a five-dimensional bulk.

The paper generalizes the loop's orientation. The jet quenching parameter then depends on that orientation. At a first-order phase transition, the parameter jumps. The size of the jump also depends on orientation. These patterns appear across several holographic models. Both light and heavy quarks show them. The models include temperature, chemical potential, and magnetic field. Spatial anisotropy is present throughout. The underlying action is an Einstein-dilaton system with three Maxwell fields.
arxiv-2512-24304:
Antoni Wójcik and Jan Wójcik defend a quantum bound under attack. A recent paper by Chatterjee and others reported breaking the temporal Tsirelson bound. The setting was the Leggett-Garg scenario. An experiment backed the claim. The dynamics were described as a superposition of unitary time evolutions. The two authors dispute that reading of the work.

They show the evolution fits a standard frame. No superposition of evolutions is needed to describe it. The apparent breach has a simpler source. The measured quantities do not match what the Leggett-Garg setup assumes. Once that mismatch is seen, the bound stands unbroken. The paper defends the bound by careful bookkeeping of what was actually measured.
arxiv-2512-24404:
Soham Pahari and M Srinivas reason about places using pictures alone. Most AI reasoning systems lean on text as their main medium. That limits them in spatial tasks like navigation and geo-localization. Ground-to-aerial localization is the target problem here. Given street-level images, the system must find where they sit from above.

Their framework, ViReLoc, plans and localizes in the visual domain. Step-by-step inference is encoded as images, not words. Reinforcement-style objectives train the planning. Contrastive learning aligns the ground and aerial views. Adaptive feature interaction reduces the gap between viewpoints. Experiments span diverse navigation and localization scenarios. Spatial reasoning accuracy improved consistently. Cross-view retrieval improved as well. The authors note a side benefit: no live GPS data is needed, which suits more secure navigation.
arxiv-2512-24904:
Alberto Sarmiento, Douglas Danton, and Viviane Pardini Valerio construct unusual expansive homeomorphisms on compact surfaces, solving a question posed by Artigue. Expansivity means nearby orbits in the end split by a fixed amount. Their examples are cw-expansive, yet have a fixed point whose local stable set is linked but not locally linked, a strange shape.

Generalizing an earlier building gives, on surfaces of genus at least two, maps that are two-expansive but not expansive. New sphere and torus examples are cw-two-expansive without being N-expansive for the related range. Dynamics readers get counter-cases that split closely related expansivity notions.
