Results span a broad class of settings and architectures, including deep neural networks. By tying lower bounds to the algorithm as actually run, the authors aim to give a truer map of where gradient methods stall.
arxiv-2602-06004:
Andrew Sack introduces pointed building sets, a new combinatorial frame built from families of lattices tied by compatibility rules. To each such set he assigns a complete lattice, called its ornamentation lattice. The paper's goal is to lay out the theory of these generalised ornamentations from the ground up.

Special cases already help explain three known families: the operahedron lattices, affine Tamari lattices, and hypergraphic posets of path hypergraphs. Other natural classes recover classics such as the Tamari lattice, topologies ordered by coarsening, and naturally labelled partial orders. Inverse limits and group actions round out the theory, yielding infinite analogues of the Tamari lattice. The work gives one roof to lattices that had looked separate.
arxiv-2602-06204:
Fine-tuning a huge model cheaply often means training small low-rank adapters, a method called LoRA. Nan Chen and 2 co-authors study a practical nuisance: the best learning rate changes when the adapter rank changes, forcing fresh tuning every time. They build a theory, called Maximal-Update Adaptation, to predict the right rate.

Their analysis shows two regimes. In one, the best rate stays roughly fixed across ranks. In the other, it falls off in inverse proportion to rank, depending on how the adapter starts and scales. They also find a setup where a rate tuned for LoRA transfers to full fine-tuning, which could slash tuning costs. Experiments covered language and vision tasks.
arxiv-2602-06904:
A. Niemiec and seventeen co-authors weigh six of the most massive galaxy clusters known, using weak gravitational lensing. Clusters trace the large-scale structure of the universe, and their mass distribution over cosmic time depends on key cosmological parameters, so accurate masses matter. But the Frontier Fields clusters have complex, lumpy shapes that simple mass profiles fit poorly.

The BUFFALO survey extended Hubble imaging of these clusters, and the team combined it with spectroscopy to build lensing catalogues with about 50 background sources per square arcminute. That density lets them measure individual cluster masses robustly and test how sensitive the results are to centering, redshift uncertainty, foreground contamination, and boost corrections. The largest biases arise for the most disturbed clusters, such as the merging Abell 2744, and the framework will matter for future wide-field surveys like Euclid and Rubin.
arxiv-2602-07204:
A Joyce manifold carries a special geometric structure, and its symmetries raise sharp questions about dynamics and moduli.  Ollie Thakar constructs infinitely many diffeomorphisms of such a manifold that achieve the lowest topological entropy allowed by homology, imitating a recent construction for K3 surfaces.

The paper further shows these maps act freely on a component of the Teichmüller space of G_2 structures, which forces the moduli space to have infinite fundamental group.  A proposed analogy with algebraic surfaces is also examined, with a theorem marking its limits.  Geometers get new extremal cases and a clearer map of where the analogy holds.
arxiv-2602-07304:
A random walk sweeps out a range, and the shape of that range fluctuates in ways that depend on dimension.  Arka Adhikari and one co-author study fluctuations of graph distance and cut-point counts in random media built from walk ranges.

They find a sequence of dimension-dependent phase transitions in how those fluctuations scale, with a distinct transition in dimension six and non-standard rescaling exactly at six.  The paper is short and technical, but it pins down where the qualitative action changes and how.  Probabilists studying random walks and random media get a precise phase diagram for a natural fluctuation problem.
arxiv-2602-07404:
Adaptive trials assign treatments as results arrive, aiming to estimate effects efficiently or find the best treatment.  Evan T.  R.  Rosenman and one co-author improve that adaptivity by borrowing strength across arms with Stein-like shrinkage estimators.

Classical Neyman-style adaptive allocation minimizes error for a Horvitz-Thompson estimator but ignores information shared across treatment arms.  Shrinkage estimators use that shared information, cutting expected squared error against estimating each effect alone. Their risk can be computed efficiently as expectations of ratios of Gaussian quadratic forms.  Trial builders get adaptive designs that learn from every arm at once.
arxiv-2602-07704:
Election polls can mislead even after standard weighting, because the people who refuse to answer may differ from those who reply. Lukáš Lafférs and two co-authors tackle this nonignorable nonresponse problem for survey questions with ordered answers, such as ratings of trust or satisfaction.

Their method uses clues observed among respondents, like how an interviewer rated a person's cooperativeness, to project toward nonrespondents, while still folding in known population shares. The estimator runs by maximum likelihood in a short R routine and is tested on the 2024 American National Election Study. Pollsters and survey researchers gain a practical fix for a bias that weighting alone cannot remove.
arxiv-2602-07904:
Bayesian tuning hinges on picking the right acquisition function at each step, yet no single rule wins everywhere and the best choice shifts during a run. Giang Ngo and four co-authors propose LMABO, which casts a pretrained language model as a zero-shot online strategist. It reads a structured summary of the optimization state and selects from a portfolio of acquisition functions.

Unlike adaptive methods that look only at past function values, the language model weighs budget remaining, surrogate characteristics, and progress as one. Across fifty benchmark problems, LMABO beats strong static, adaptive, and other language-model baselines. The authors argue the advantage comes from synthesizing the full state into a coherent plan, a case for language models as orchestrators rather than mere predictors.
arxiv-2602-08104:
Multi-agent reinforcement learning systems fail in safety-critical settings, yet diagnosing which agent failed first and how failure spread remains underdeveloped. Risal Shahriar Shefin and three co-authors introduce a two-stage gradient-based framework for interpretable failure analysis.

Stage one detects the initial failure source, dubbed patient zero, through Taylor-remainder analysis of policy-gradient costs at the first threshold crossing. Stage two validates that detection and traces propagation through geometric analysis of critic derivatives, building contagion graphs that explain why downstream agents sometimes appear to fail first. Safety engineers for multi-agent systems gain diagnostics that attribute failure and map its spread, not just a flag that something went wrong.
arxiv-2602-08204:
Indoor tracking for next-making wireless networks needs accuracy without draining spectrum and energy, yet machine-learning trackers usually demand large labeled datasets. Geng Wang and six co-authors propose LocDreamer, a world-model method that jointly learns target tracking and scheduling of localization anchors.

The world model captures latent target motion and environment structure, making made readings to imagine arbitrary anchor deployments. Those imagined data train both the tracker and a reinforcement-learning scheduler that activates only the most informative anchors. On a real indoor dataset, the approach improves data efficiency and generalization over conventional methods while cutting energy and signaling costs. Wireless engineers gain tracking that learns from imagination, not just labels.
arxiv-2602-08504:
Electing a committee or dividing a budget fairly means choosing a subset of candidates under rules about which subsets are allowed, and fairness should survive beyond simple yes-or-no votes. Piotr Skowron develops a general theory of fair shares for scored ballots, where voters give each candidate a number for how much they value that pick. His arXiv paper extends recent fairness axioms to that richer setting.

Earlier rules handled only approval ballots, where each voter lists candidates they accept. Skowron proposes fair-share rules for scored ballots and methods that produce fair-share rankings, so every prefix of the ranking also meets the fairness test. The frame covers committee elections with diversity rules, participatory budgeting, and public decisions. Readers get a rigorous base for fair selection under realistic rules.
arxiv-2602-08704:
In opinion dynamics, some people sway others far more than their network position alone suggests. Moses Boudourides studies source-specific influence in the Friedkin-Johnsen model for directed, weighted nets, where agents differ in susceptibility to influence. His arXiv paper treats agents who never budge as boundary nodes and the rest as interior nodes.

That framing yields a Green operator and a full response matrix showing how a fixed opinion at each source reaches every target. From it, the author defines broadcasting and reception measures that separate structural position from model-implied influence. Existence, uniqueness, transient, and steady-state results follow, plus spectral analysis for the homogeneous undirected case. Readers get a susceptibility-aware toolkit for influence, source selection, and intervention.
arxiv-2602-09104:
Lewis R. Prole and fifteen co-authors analyze massive black holes in the SEEDZ simulations of cosmic dawn. The biggest holes reach about a million solar masses by redshift 12.5, through short bursts of super-Eddington accretion lasting 5 to 30 million years. What stops the growth is the black hole's own feedback, not nearby supernovae or an empty gas reservoir.

For the most active holes, feedback fully evacuates the host halo, ejecting gas into intergalactic space, even though the feedback model is relatively weak. The injected energy exceeds the halo's binding energy. Two readings follow: early feedback is far weaker than assumed, or some JWST galaxies formed in two steps, quenching first, then regaining gas through mergers or cosmic-web accretion.
arxiv-2602-09204:
Autonomous surface vessels in changing seas must navigate under uncertainty, and Ozan Kaya and three co-authors offer a hybrid risk-aware architecture for the job. The system builds probabilistic risk maps capturing obstacle proximity and the behavior of moving objects, then plans with a risk-biased rapidly exploring random tree, refined by B-spline smoothing for continuous trajectories.

Three rewiring modes trade off path length against risk: shortest path, lowest risk, or a combination. Tests with static and dynamic obstacles show safe navigation, smooth paths, and adaptation as risks shift. Against conventional lidar-only or vision-only navigation, the method improves operational safety and autonomy, a promising step for uncertain marine missions.
arxiv-2602-09404:
Protostellar jets are thought to carry away the spin that would otherwise stop a young star from gathering mass, but how they launch remains poorly pinned down. Somnath Dutta's single-author 2026 paper reports high-resolution observations of protostar HOPS 10 that complicate the standard picture. Combined data trace both the entrained outflow and the collimated jet in fine spatial and velocity detail, revealing an unusually one-sided jet.

The fast jet appears on one side only, the clearest monopolar example reported to date, while the slower outflow shows on both sides. Since the system is seen nearly edge-on with little obscuring dust, a hidden counterjet cannot easily explain the asymmetry, and shock-tracer emission confirms a genuine jet rather than cloud contamination. Dutta argues intrinsically asymmetric mass loading along the disk's magnetic field lines best explains the one-sided launch.
arxiv-2602-09604:
ARM vector extensions and RISC-V vector extensions support flexible vector lengths, raising the question whether one portable design can run fast everywhere. Ruimin Shi and five co-authors answer with a vector-length agnostic design for quantum state-vector simulation in their 2026 paper, implemented in Google's Qsim. Key techniques include vector-length-adaptive memory layout, load buffering, fine-grained loop control, and gate-fusion-based arithmetic intensity adaptation.

Five quantum circuits of up to thirty-six qubits were evaluated on three ARM processors, including NVIDIA Grace, AWS Graviton3, and Fujitsu A64FX. New metrics and hardware counter events quantify vectorization activity, yielding generic insights for future agnostic designs. The single-source implementation speeds simulations by up to four and a half times on one processor, two and a half times on another, and one and a half times on the third.
arxiv-2602-09804:
Toshiaki Hishida studies the motion of a viscous dense fluid filling a three-dim outer domain subject to the Navier slip-with-friction edge rule as well as outflow at far off. His 2026 paper treats the Oseen system as the linear form, treating the solver set under a link among edge shape, friction number, and outflow. Smoothness of the solver near the origin in the complex plane is then studied.

From that smoothness, bounds for the Oseen flow are built, given a floor rule linking friction and outflow holds at every edge point. The paper thus connects edge shape, friction, and far-field outflow to the long-time flow of Oseen flow in outer domains, giving precise decay behavior under a stated edge rule.
arxiv-2602-09904:
Online courses widened access after the pandemic, but they leave learners to watch their own focus without a teacher in the room. A 2026 paper led by Anna Bodonhelyi, with four co-authors, targets two quiet failures of attention: drifting minds and outright disengagement. Its tool watches video cues, reading faces and gaze to spot behavioral disengagement, mind wandering, and boredom as they happen.

Ordinary detectors would need students' video shipped to a central server, raising privacy worries. The team instead trains across devices with federated learning, so raw data stays local while models still improve, and it adds features to cope with eyeglasses. Tests on five data sets, comparing several federated methods, show strong promise for private, real-time support that keeps remote learners engaged.
arxiv-2602-10004:
Large reasoning models often keep reasoning long after they have already reached the right answer. A 2026 paper led by Junda Wang, with four co-authors, introduces ESTAR, an early-stopping method for token-aware reasoning. It combines a trajectory classifier that spots safe stopping points, fine-tuning that teaches models to emit their own stop signals, and reinforcement learning that truncates rollouts at those signals with compute-aware rewards.

Across four reasoning data sets, ESTAR cut reasoning length nearly fourfold while leaving accuracy essentially unchanged. Cross-domain generalization stayed strong. Early stopping, the authors conclude, is a simple yet powerful lever for making large reasoning models cheaper to run without making them weaker.
arxiv-2602-10404:
Adapting broad organic-chemistry language models to smaller, domain-specific reaction data sets is a key challenge: new reaction knowledge must be learned without losing general chemical understanding. A 2026 paper led by Jiayun Pang, with three co-authors, tests low-rank adaptation, a light-touch alternative to full fine-tuning, for reaction prediction on limited, complex data sets. Using United States patent reaction classes and hard carbon-hydrogen functionalization reactions, they test forward prediction, retrosynthesis, and reagent prediction.

Low-rank adaptation matches full fine-tuning on accuracy and better preserves multi-task work, curbing catastrophic forgetting. Both approaches work beyond their training data, producing plausible alternative solvent picks. Fine-tuning on carbon-hydrogen functionalization shows the two approaches encode different reactivity patterns, suggesting low-rank methods may adapt better to specific reactions. The results support modular, light-touch fine-tuning as a practical route for chemistry work.
arxiv-2602-10504:
Ming Dong and four co-authors test whether detoxifying language models by editing their knowledge works in a 2026 paper. Current tests lean on automatic toxicity classifiers, assuming lower scores mean genuinely safer conduct. That assumption, the paper argues, is shaky.

The authors propose a toughness-oriented system that probes beyond classifier scores along three axes: tuning, composition, and cross-lingual toughness. They identify pseudo-detoxification, where apparent improvements come from broken making rather than real suppression of unsafe content. Strength also degrades when several unsafe conduct are edited jointly. The message is cautionary: a clean classifier score is not proof of a safe model.
arxiv-2602-10804:
Douglas M. Gingrich derives algebra rules for collapsing dust in quantum-inspired gravity in a 2026 paper. Starting from a wide class of spherically symmetric spacetimes, he writes covariant Hamiltonian constraints that generate metrics for many such gravity models under dynamical flow. Solving those constraints yields simple rules for the dust ball's outer edge and its apparent horizons.

The dust density need not be homogeneous inside the collapsing ball, a generality the algebra approach preserves. Applying the rules to several quantum-inspired metrics, the paper recovers known bounce results by new means and obtains new ones. The work gives teams a compact tool for asking whether quantum-inspired gravity swaps singularities with bounces.
arxiv-2602-10904:
Kenta Tabata and four co-authors build and test a manta-ray-like under-sea robot in a 2026 paper. Inspired by manta rays, the robot uses flapping motion for push to cut sea-floor stir and improve speed over screw push. Side fins driven by servo motors and a sleek control box reduce water drag.

A Raspberry Pi-based control system with motion and pressure sensors watches and steers swimming in real time. Pool tests gauged swimming and diving skills, showing steady motions under tuned control. The robot suits places like tanks and fish farms where minimal stir and quick turns matter, showing nature-based design in working hardware.
arxiv-2602-11004:
Self-driving cars must see fast, yet their computers are limited. Liangkai Liu and four co-authors propose PP-DNN, a perception system that cuts image work without cutting scores. It picks key frames and key regions on the fly, guided by how scenes change.

A region finder spots key frames and zones from frame-to-frame likeness and traffic context. A cost predictor then forecasts the arithmetic load, a scheduler shares work across models, and a separate predictor covers quiet frames. Built into a robot operating system pipeline, it was tested on two driving sets. It raised fused frames sharply, cut fusion delay and its swing, and improved finding completeness and cost-effectiveness over the rival.
arxiv-2602-11104:
Flocks that move on their own can clump, then unclump as drive grows. Letian Chen and Luke K. Davis study that reentrance in a Hamiltonian flocking model, a conservative system known to mimic bird flocks. Grouping here recalls motility-induced phase separation in active matter.

Simulations show the uniform phase returns at high self-drive. The cause is a contest between spin-velocity coupling and mobility-limited frustration. Strong coupling damps sideways diffusion and traps the system, closing the window where separation can form. The work bridges reentrant conduct across balance and non-balance materials with one conservative model.
arxiv-2602-11204:
Public pretrained encoders can be fooled by attacks built without knowing downstream tasks. Zhuxin Lei and two co-authors propose ZePAD, a defence that needs only one tuning to protect many downstream tasks while preserving benign results. It pairs two branches: one strengthens adversarial resistance, the other preserves benign memory.

Two adversarially tuned encoders power the enhancement branch, while the memory branch trains on local data. Surprisingly, ZePAD can also detect downstream-agnostic attacks from branch confidence alone, with no separate finding training. Tests across many self-supervised methods and data sets validate the design, with gains in both benign and adversarial results in some cases. The paper claims a zero-sacrifice defence that persists across tasks.
arxiv-2602-11304:
Analyst agents drown in tool outputs, documents, and fast-changing data. Anushri Eswaran and four co-authors study their failure modes in crypto, a high-density test domain. They build CryptoAnalystBench from nearly two hundred production queries across eleven categories, with an agentic harness and a judge rubric spanning relevance, timeliness, depth, and consistency.

Human annotation yields a taxonomy of seven higher-order error types that factuality checks and judge scores often miss. Those failures persist even in leading systems and can compromise high-stakes decisions. A refined judge rubric captures key failures reliably, though not precise scores. The benchmark, pipeline, rubrics, and taxonomy are released to guide safer analyst agents.
arxiv-2602-11404:
Ordinal mechanisms are usually judged by worst-case distortion, which can look bleak. Ioannis Caragiannis and two co-authors evaluate distortion under random preferences instead, where agent values are drawn from spreads. They first prove no ordinal mechanism can beat a specific bound, about one point five eight, even in the simplest one-item-per-agent case.

They then propose a mechanism that achieves that optimal bound even when each agent's spread is agent-specific and unknown to the mechanism. Refining further, they optimize the distortion gap, the slack against the best distortion for the instance at hand, with a mechanism reaching a near-optimal gap just above one. Simple one-pass mechanisms are also evaluated, completing a random picture of ordinal sharing.
arxiv-2602-12004:
Text-to-image models now serve medical purposes like data augmentation and teaching, yet existing checks miss whether generated images carry the intended clinical meaning. Robert Cronshaw and six co-authors propose CSEval, a framework that uses language models to judge medical semantic match between images and their prompts. It targets anatomy and disease rather than mere realism or diversity.

Experiments show CSEval catches semantic inconsistencies other metrics overlook and correlates with expert judgment. As a scalable, useful add-on to current evaluation, it supports safer adoption of generative models in healthcare. A lifelike image with the wrong anatomy or disease is worse than a plainly flawed one.
arxiv-2602-12104:
Liquidations keep decentralized lending protocols solvent, but their mechanics open doors to predatory price manipulation and extractable value. Agathe Sadeghi and one co-author model the profit-maximizing liquidator when prices come from a constant-product market maker, including sandwich attacks that manipulate the price feed to trigger liquidations.

They derive closed-form bounds on liquidation and prove that market-maker transaction fees are a critical security lever. Fees do more than pay liquidity providers: set right, they can make manipulation unprofitable outright. The result suggests fees can harden price oracles from within, without the delays of time-weighted averages or median prices.
arxiv-2602-12504:
Standard IV methods find a local average treatment effect only under monotonicity, which rules out defiers who do the reverse of what a tool pushes. Johann Caro-Burnett works alone here, giving the Difference-in-Instrumental-Variables target, which uses two tools with clashing compliance patterns. That design finds a pinned, clear causal effect without forcing monotonicity.

The target is a mix of edge treatment effects on compliers and defiers, weighted by gaps in treatment take-up across tools. When the one-way rule does hold, it matches the standard IV target. Use needs only simple linear changes and standard two-stage least squares steps, and repeat-data uses show its value in settings where tools push action in reverse ways.
arxiv-2602-12604:
Differential privacy limits how much any single point can sway a stats output, by adding tuned random noise. Joowon Lee led this work with one co-author, Guanhua Chen, studying private guessing in two-step procedures common in cause reading and personal care rule learning. Data-driven weights first force factor balance, then a value of focus follows from weighted sample fitting.

Their method, DP-2ERM, makes the final tool private directly through goal noise tuned to data-driven response of the full line. Analysis joins fixed weight-noise bounds for flipped tendency, spread balancing, and max gap weighting, with chance response bounds for the second-step answer. The final tuning is tighter than step-wise mixing, and tests plus a standard care-rule use show an improved privacy-use trade-off.
arxiv-2602-12804:
Reconfigurable surfaces can boost wireless links, but oscillator phase noise threatens the gains, especially for the standard OFDM waveform. Stephen McWade and Arman Farhang compare OFDM with OTFS, a waveform built to tolerate time-varying channels, in surface-aided systems with phase noise. No earlier work had fully analysed phase noise for surface-aided OTFS, so the paper fills that gap and proposes a joint estimation method.

The method uses Wiener filtering to estimate the surface channel and the phase noise together, exploiting the statistics of both the noise and the Doppler-spread channel. Numerical tests show surface-aided OTFS beating surface-aided OFDM clearly under phase noise. The proposed estimator also improves bit error rates by up to 3 decibels over existing methods, a solid margin for practical receivers.
arxiv-2602-13004:
Granger causality maps predictive links in time series, but in federated settings parties cannot pool their data, and clients often see other traits. Ayush Mohanty and two co-authors study doubt in federated Granger causality, where cross-client edges must be inferred indirectly through repeated client-server rounds. Point guesses alone cannot say which edges are real, since doubt from data and model settings propagates through the process.

The paper derives explicit variance recursions and long-run variances for those rounds, separating data-driven aleatoric doubt from setting-driven epistemic doubt. It proves the initial setting doubt's contribution fades asymptotically. Edge-given variances then enable principled selection of genuine edges over spurious ones. Mock tests improve edge recovery over plain rivals, and real industrial data yield close root-cause identification with clear structures.
arxiv-2602-13104:
Random forests are usually backed in the long run, but O'Connell builds a finite-sample, design-based theory. Each tree is treated as a random if-then guesser on fixed side factors, with the forest as their Monte Carlo mean. A variance rule splits Monte Carlo error exactly from a co-swing floor that persists even with endless trees.

The floor comes from two sources: reuse of sightings, where the same training results weigh across many trees, and split line-up, where trees grown on their own find similar forecast rules. The floor stays above zero under minimal rules, and line-up lives on even when sample splitting removes sighting overlap fully. A new step-aligned mock redraw method guesses the floor, splitting forecast doubt into clear parts. Final ranges achieve nominal cover, with cautious bias for smooth results and long-run fairness for sorting, including high-D settings.
arxiv-2602-13504:
AI-written news is widely discussed but rarely measured outside English, and Turkish media had no empirical study beyond journalist interviews and fake news detection. This paper fills the gap by fine-tuning a Turkish BERT model on 3,600 labeled articles from three major outlets with distinct editorial lines, classifying AI-rewritten content. On held-out data, the model scored 0.9708 F1, with symmetric precision and recall across both classes.

Deployment on over 3,500 unseen articles from 2023 to 2026 found stable patterns across sources and time, with mean confidence above 0.96 and an estimated 2.5 percent of examined news content rewritten or revised by language models on average. The study moves the debate from perceptions to evidence. Ozancan Ozdemir is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-14204:
Asem Abdelraouf and one co-author prove a 2026 arXiv realization theorem for hypergeometric local systems. Irreducible systems defined over fractions are built through families of affine kinds in algebraic tori. Such families are well studied and show up in mirror symmetry, a link between shape theory and physics.

The result holds always when the fibers are one-dimensional or even-dimensional. For fibers of odd size above one, it holds under a monodromy rule. The theorem ties abstract local systems to concrete shape families, giving a bridge between hypergeometric theory and algebraic shape work that other researchers can build on directly.
arxiv-2602-14304:
Wendy L. Freedman and five co-authors gauge a 2026 arXiv distance-scale link between two star groups. Hubble views of 92 galaxies with strong I-band asymptotic giant branch stars weigh IAGB brightness against tip-of-the-red-giant-branch brightness in the same frames. That shared-frame weigh is free of dimming shared by both groups.

The IAGB brightness curves fit single even Gaussians well. The IAGB minus TRGB gap is minus zero point five eight nine magnitudes, with a shared spread of zero point one one nine magnitudes. Taking minus four point zero five for the TRGB gives a modal IAGB absolute brightness of minus four point six four, plus or minus zero point one two. The crowd spread gives a mean error of just zero point zero one two magnitudes, a tight differential zero point.
arxiv-2602-14404:
William L. Tong and two co-authors study a 2026 arXiv question about reasoning traces and length generalization. Reasoning models generate intermediate traces before final answers, but how those traces help, and where they fail, remains unclear. The paper introduces PITA, a dataset of over 23 million propositional logic statements with proofs.

The benchmark asks: if a model learns truth or falsity on statements with proofs up to a fixed length, how well does it handle longer proofs? Task depth counts steps to solve an example, while task breadth counts unique examples per task. Varying both across PITA subsets, reasoning-trace models generalized well on broad, shallow subsets but deteriorated on narrow, deep subsets relative to non-trace baselines, mapping the limits of trace-based reasoning.
arxiv-2602-14504:
Naveed Ahmed and one co-author probes a 2026 arXiv number problem: error guessing for convection-dominated transport. Left-over-based after-the-fact error guessing is studied for finite element splits of flow-spread formulas, steadied by algebraic flux fix and tied algebraic steady tricks. Plans hold BJK and Monolithic Convex caps, plus MUAS, SMUAS, and BBK methods.

Score of guessers and caps is tested on tuned meshes for two-size test problems, including edge layers, inner layers, and a non-linear flow problem with answer-tied transport. Exactness, discrete max rule keeping, tuned mesh acts, and thrift are weighed. Results show steady-guess links hang strongly on mesh lining and flow character, with cap acts splitting sharply for moving or curved layers.
arxiv-2602-14604:
Methane ice in cold space holds clues to how complex molecules form. Varvara Karteyeva, with four co-authors, reports lab spectra of methane mixed with water, carbon dioxide, methanol, and ammonia. The mixes were cooled to 6.7 and 10 kelvin, matching dark clouds and young stars.

Band strengths in the mixes run about 20 percent higher than the standard pure-methane value at 10 kelvin. That shift matters when reading data from the James Webb Space Telescope. The team tests the new spectra on open telescope data for the protostar region B335. They also probe how methane shifts between its cold phases.
arxiv-2602-14904:
Damian Arellanes notes that big-compute models still lack a set form like Turing gear for big-scale thought. State- and data-first models, many in fifty years, slight flow order, the trait that sets work order, while only flow-first models treat flow plain.

He offers join-by-colimit gear for high-level devices, giving linked devices a firm, joint base that lone-device classics lack. Real-world kits, told as linked devices, not lone boxes, thus gain a math of joining. Big-scale thought gains a would-be set form.
arxiv-2602-15004:
Schmude and colleagues adapt PDE foundation models into skillful weather emulators for Mars. The models start from pretraining on numerical solutions to a wide set of partial differential equations. The team builds on Poseidon, a foundation model for two-dimensional systems, and extends it to three dimensions while keeping its pretrained knowledge. They also test how it copes with sparse starting conditions.

Training draws on four Martian years of data with a median budget of 13 GPU hours. Combining pretraining with the dimensional extension lifts performance by about 34 percent on a held-out year. The authors read this as proof that PDE foundation models can anchor real-world problems where training data and compute are both scarce.
arxiv-2602-15104:
Zhou and colleagues present ABCMB for the cosmic microwave background, a solver of Einstein-Boltzmann type that can be differentiated. The package is analysis-ready, capturing key effects to linear order in cold dark matter cosmology. It returns the CMB power spectrum, with lensing, polarization, massive neutrinos, recombination, and Big Bang nucleosynthesis handled by a treatment at the current state of the art.

ABCMB agrees with the CLASS code at sub-percent level and runs on GPUs with competitive, sometimes faster, runtimes thanks to favorable scaling with maximum multipole moment. Refactored around object-oriented design, it improves extensibility, so new physics can be added without editing source files. It also supplies accurate, stable gradients, making Fisher analyses straightforward and opening efficient gradient-based sampling methods.
arxiv-2602-15204:
Garner and colleagues present a distributed memory method for anisotropic mesh adaptation that avoids joint chatter and global syncing. Meshing work is separated from speed concerns through two parts: a multicore cc-NUMA-based shared-memory mesh making software and a side-by-side runtime system that helps apps exploit overlap on new high-performance compute designs.

First, an initial mesh is split, and its boundary elements are adapted on a single node. Subdomains are then spread among cluster nodes so inner elements are adapted while already-adapted boundary elements stay frozen, preserving mesh fit. Lessons cover redesigns of the shared-memory software and use of its trial running model by the method for good speed. The method generates meshes of up to about 1 billion cells with quality and speed matching current state-of-the-art HPC meshing software.
arxiv-2602-15304:
Akter and colleagues present a mixed setup combining Federated Learning and Split Learning for care models without pooling data. Joint medical choice support is often limited by rules blocking sharing person files across sites. The method keeps feature-pulling bases on sites while holding forecast heads on a server, allowing code learning and showing an edge where rules can be used.

Rather than taking spread teaching as closed by nature, the team checks leaks using member guessing on cut-layer codes and studies shields based on signal capping and bell-curve noise. They test three sets under non-IID site splits using a line, scoring along four sides: forecast value, lift-based order under room limits, checked leaks, and message cost. Findings show mixed versions achieve forecast scores and choice-facing order versus solo shared or split, while giving a privacy-value balance cutting checked leaks without pooling data.
arxiv-2602-15504:
Velutharambath and Wührl ask what patients expect from treatment, and how those hopes show up in words online. Hopes shape how well a treatment works, yet most study of them happens in clinics, while forums like medical subreddits may hold hopes people do not voice elsewhere. No prior work, the authors note, had mapped what kinds of hopes users discuss online or how they phrase them.

To open that task, which they call Expectation Detection, they build RedHOTExpect, a corpus of 4,500 Reddit posts, silver-labelled by a large language model and hand-checked to about 78 percent label accuracy. They find hope-filled, proactive phrasing more marked in posts on bodily or treatment-linked illness than in mental-health posts, and a tilt toward hoped benefits over bad outcomes. The corpus is public for reuse.
arxiv-2602-15604:
Shailesh and colleagues use metallicity gradients to read recent galaxy history in the EAGLE simulations. Disc galaxies show radial gradients in metals for stars and gas alike, and young stars plus star-forming gas trace the last two billion years. The team derives oxygen profiles for young stars under two billion years old and for star-forming gas. Galaxies are then sorted by the signs of the two slopes into four groups: NN, NP, PP, and PN.

Each group tells a different story. NN galaxies grow steadily inside-out with high star formation efficiency. NP and PP systems show recent feedback-driven disruption, with PP systems shaped mainly by supernova feedback. PN galaxies show past violent events followed by gradient recovery. The match or mismatch between stellar and gas gradients thus helps date major events, shaped by inflows, feedback, and gas cooling.
arxiv-2602-16104:
Darren Gerrity and Ivan Soprunov study volume polynomials for four planar lattice polytopes and their square-free parts. The question is motivated by pairwise intersection numbers of four curves in the algebraic torus with prescribed Newton polytopes and generic coefficients. For arbitrary convex bodies in the plane, Plucker-type inequalities fully characterize the possible square-free polynomials.

The lattice case breaks that neat picture. The interior of the region cut out by those inequalities contains integer polynomials that are realizable by lattice polytopes and others that are not. Extra arithmetic constraints on mixed areas of lattice polytopes drive the gap. A discrete diagram, mapping a pair of lattice polytopes to their mixed area plus lattice widths in a given direction, makes those constraints visible. The paper thus shows discreteness adds genuine obstructions beyond the continuous theory.
arxiv-2602-16404:
J. G. Patel, writing alone, proves a result about algebras that admit many different norm topologies. The paper works with an algebra and with the subalgebra formed by spanning all products of pairs of elements from the algebra. Patel shows that this product subalgebra has infinite codimension in the full algebra exactly when the algebra has the discontinuous square annihilation property.

In that case, the algebra admits infinitely many non-equivalent algebra norms, so a single algebraic structure can carry infinitely many different norm topologies. The equivalence gives readers a clean test: the codimension condition and that property stand or fall together, and either one guarantees many norms.
arxiv-2602-16504:
Ashley Babjac and Adrienne Hoarfrost introduce GRIMM, a benchmark for enzyme function prediction built on genetic stratification. Most biological sequences encode unknown functions and look little like characterized proteins. So predicting enzyme function from sequence is hard, and models trained on public data can overstate performance and fail to generalize.

GRIMM clusters sequences by similarity and assigns whole clusters to training, validation, or test sets only, so no cluster appears in more than one split. It offers a closed-set test with the training label mix and an open-set test with novel labels, as a realistic proxy for discovering new enzyme functions. The approach is lightweight, needing only clustering and label annotations, and it generalizes to other sequence classification tasks.
arxiv-2602-16604:
Elena Magnanini extends the classic edge-triangle exponential random graph model to a block setting with varied vertex types. Vertices carry types from a base split, and link values depend on those types. The paper proves a large deviation rule for the run of measures and derives a variational form for the limiting free energy.

In the ferromagnetic case, where triangle values are not negative, the variational task shrinks to a scalar task. That names the block twin of the replica symmetric regime. Under further limits akin to Dobrushin's uniqueness zone, the maximizer is unique and a law of large numbers holds for edge density. Network theorists get a rigorous block version of a classic model.
arxiv-2602-16704:
Hee Seung Hwang and co-authors introduce REFINE, a reinforcement learning frame for fast weight models trained by next-sequence prediction. Fast weight designs offer an alternative to attention transformers for long contexts, holding memory steady regardless of context length. Yet next-token training optimizes single-token guesses and ignores coherence across later tokens, leaving fast weight models with weak long-range grasp.

REFINE picks informative token spots by prediction entropy, rolls out multi-token sequences, assigns self-supervised sequence-level rewards, and optimizes with group relative policy optimization. It applies at mid-training, post-training, and test-time training. Tests on LaCT and DeltaNet models show REFINE beats supervised fine-tuning with next-token training on retrieval and related tasks, giving long-context builders a stronger training objective.
arxiv-2602-16904:
Matthew Weaver offers a new method for implicit equations of translation surfaces using iterated homogeneous resultants. Such a surface is built from two space curves by translating one along the other. Such surfaces are common in geometric modeling, and since their form is parametric, an implicit equation is wanted. Goldman and Wang studied them thoroughly, finding syzygies that yield the equation through an inhomogeneous resultant.

That method may fail when the parameterization has ill-behaved basepoints. The new code uses iterated homogeneous resultants, with smaller Sylvester matrices overall, potentially running faster. It succeeds in many cases where the prior method cannot be used. It works where the old method fails. The gain is speed and wider use. Modelers get a tougher tool. The paper is short and direct.
arxiv-2602-17104:
Sie Hendrata Dharmawan led a two-author paper arguing that simpler can be stronger in spectral community detection. The work targets the two-community stochastic block model under constant edge density, a standard testbed for finding hidden groups in networks. Rather than piling on preprocessing steps, the authors strip the spectral algorithm down to its essentials and lean directly on the adjacency matrix.

The key move exploits traits of the second eigenvector to reach error bounds near the information-theoretic limits, tighter than previously reported results. Theory backs the tighter rates, and experiments confirm the method works in practice. The paper's lesson is pointed: cutting non-essential steps can buy both speed and accuracy, a case for simplification over added complexity in this corner of network science.
arxiv-2602-17204:
Herzallah Alharazin led a ten-author team on an ongoing first lattice study of the doubly charmed tetraquark known as T_cc, tackled as a three-body problem. The work studies the D D pi system in the isospin-zero, charm-two sector. There the tetraquark appears as a pole in the elastic scattering amplitude. The approach folds in two-body and three-body effects together and handles left-hand cuts from single pion exchanges.

Two lattice ensembles with a moderately heavy pion mass supply the data. The team uses two-hadron, three-hadron, and tetraquark operators to extract finite-volume energies. Extra inputs from two-body subsystems feed the three-body analysis. The paper presents preliminary results for those subchannels plus exploratory three-body spectra for simple K-matrix choices, allowing a first comparison with the lattice spectrum.
arxiv-2602-17604:
Tomislav Begušić and Garnet Kin-Lic Chan document the phase-aware form of Majorana stabilizer states. Stabilizer states are central to quantum error correction and fast circuit simulation. They matter because they can be highly entangled, yet still shown and changed fast under Clifford gates.

The paper extends that story to the Majorana Clifford group used in fermionic quantum work. It gives the phase-aware account of the matching states, with methods for their amplitudes and inner products. Update rules for shifting the states under Majorana Clifford gates complete the toolkit. Readers who study many-body fermionic systems gain a precise guide for this representation.
arxiv-2602-18004:
Ryan Kelly and team improve neural posterior estimation, or NPE, for simulation-based inference (SBI) when the simulator is misspecified. Standard neural methods falter for two reasons. Incompatible data summaries break NPE through extrapolation. Prior-predictive draws can produce extreme summaries that trouble SBI for the data at hand. Current preconditioning schemes target settings where the model is right, leaving their behavior when the model is wrong unknown.

Their fix, preconditioned robust NPE, weights training data by how close they are to the data at hand and fits a robust posterior model. A forest-proximity variant scores runs by tree-based nearness, giving outliers less weight and keeping work on the data at hand. Across two synthetic cases and one real case with incompatible summaries and extreme prior draws, the approach beat standard baselines on stability, accuracy, calibration, and posterior-predictive fit.
arxiv-2602-18304:
Darsh Asher and five co-authors expose a hardware leak that steals private backend data through timing alone. Their 2026 paper targets backend enrichment, where models trained on confidential data fetch hidden features that shape answers while staying invisible to the caller. The attack, FeatureBleed, is the first of its kind at the hardware level.

FeatureBleed exploits zero-skipping in AI accelerators, reading private retrieved features purely from end-to-end timing, with no power traces, clock tricks, or shared-cache channels. Tests span clinical records, medical images, and census data, plus three hardware backends and three model types, with an attacker edge up to nearly ninety-nine points. Turning off zero-skipping costs dearly in energy and speed, but a padding defense that equalizes runtimes to the worst case protects for only about seven percent overhead and no extra power.
arxiv-2602-18604:
J. D. Nölke and seven co-authors map the magnetism of dark halos. Their 2026 paper notes areas around active regions show emission well below quiet Sun at low temperatures near or below one megakelvin. These areas are called dark halos, canopies, or moats. To understand them, the team studies photospheric field and coronal emission at varied temperatures.

Solar Orbiter Polarimetric and Helioseismic Imager and Extreme Ultraviolet Imager data identify EUV-dark areas near NOAA 12893. The dark halo's unsigned flux density matches quiet Sun levels overall but drops thirty-eight percent from inner to outer boundary, shifting above to below quiet Sun levels. Coronal emission at or below one megakelvin sits about forty percent below quiet Sun, independent of distance. At or above one point six megakelvin emission exceeds quiet Sun levels, declining outward. A few hot loops extend across the halo, while short loops dominate at lower temperatures.
arxiv-2602-18804:
Prime modules are a classical tool in algebra, but many arguments need a local version that sees only part of the ring. Sholastica Luambano, with one co-author, introduces I-prime and (I, J)-prime modules in 2026, together with their duals, I-coprime and (I, J)-coprime modules, for a commutative unital ring with fixed ideals.

Category-theoretic techniques reveal their structural properties, and the main results are versions of Greenlees-May Duality and the Matlis-Greenlees-May Equivalence carried into this prime and coprime setting. The work generalises earlier results on I-reduced and I-coreduced modules. Its payoff is a bridge: these locally prime modules become a tool for studying classical globally prime modules, linking local and global primality.
arxiv-2602-18904:
Vector-quantised autoencoders give high-quality latents, but their quantisers cannot be differentiated and tend to collapse. Hao Lu, with five co-authors, replaces quantisation at its root in 2026. PCA-VAE uses an online PCA bottleneck trained by Oja's rule. It learns an orthogonal, variance-ordered latent basis with no codebooks, commitment loss, or lookup noise.

Even so, PCA-VAE beats VQ-GAN and SimVQ on reconstruction quality for CelebA-HQ. It does so using far fewer latent bits. Its dimensions are naturally interpretable, capturing pose, lighting, and gender cues without adversarial regularisation or disentanglement objectives. The result suggests PCA is a viable replacement for vector quantisation. It is mathematically grounded, stable, bit-efficient, and semantically ordered. Simple can beat complex here. Fewer moving parts mean fewer failure modes.
arxiv-2602-19004:
Wearable motion sensors and video should describe the same movement, but aligning them precisely is hard. Duc Duy Nguyen, with two co-authors, introduces MoBind in 2026. It is a layered contrast learning frame for joint representation of IMU signals and two-dimensional pose series from video.

MoBind addresses three challenges. It filters out irrelevant visual background. It models structured multi-sensor IMU setups. It achieves fine-grained, sub-second time alignment. Motion cues are isolated by aligning IMU signals with skeletal motion series rather than raw pixels. Full-body motion is split into local body-part paths, each paired with its IMU. A layered contrast strategy first aligns token-level time segments, then fuses local and global motion. Tests on three datasets show MoBind beats strong baselines across retrieval, synchronisation, localisation, and action recognition.
arxiv-2602-19104:
Giant black holes show lumpy, choppy surroundings. Giuseppe Ficarra, with three co-authors, models that lumpiness in 2026 with high-resolution simulations. A Fishbone-Moncrieff torus orbits a Kerr black hole. The Black Hole Accretion Code drives the general Einstein magnetohydrodynamics.

Two cases are compared. One accretes smoothly. The other adds plasma density bubbles with pressure-balanced magnetic islands of varied amplitude. Power spectra from the lumpy case slope more steeply. They deviate from the usual inverse-frequency noise pattern. Correlation times also grow, suggesting macro-structures get absorbed at the horizon. Near-horizon turbulence holds larger coherent energy shapes in the lumpy case. Infall rate shifts accordingly. Event Horizon Telescope observations thus gain a new interpretive lens.
arxiv-2603-01704:
Changjiang Du defines and proves a convergence trait for modules used in p-adic Hodge theory in this 2026 work. The setting involves number fields built over the p-adic numbers, with several variables tracked at once. Such modules encode Galois representations, the symmetry data that number theorists study most.

Du works over a multivariable ring and defines what overconvergence means for this class of modules. Basic traits of the new notion are then explored step by step. The main proof shows overconvergence holds at the perfectoid level, a very large and rigid limit setting. The proof leans on the geometry of the relative Fargues-Fontaine curve, a central object in modern p-adic geometry. Results of this kind extend the bridge between Galois data and explicit analytic objects.
arxiv-2603-01904:
Tao Feng, Henk Hollmann, Weicong Li, and Qing Xiang classify the symmetry groups of a special family of error-correcting codes. Their 2026 work concerns irreducible cyclic codes, whose check polynomial cannot be factored over its field. A code counts as standard when its permutation symmetries are just the cyclic shift and the Frobenius map.

The team gives a complete classification of all non-standard cases among non-degenerate codes. Their proof leans on the classification of finite simple groups, a landmark of modern algebra. Apart from a few explicit exceptional families and their descendants, every such code proves standard. Degenerate codes flip the pattern, with all but four exceptions proving non-standard. Consequences include a description of related sequence subgroups and a settled conjecture for the non-standard cases.
arxiv-2603-02004:
Gershom Seneviratne, Jianyu An, Vaibhav Shende, and colleagues teach navigation robots to avoid obstacles the way humans prefer. Their 2026 work starts from a gap: vision-driven policies move well, yet they cut close to hazards in messy real spaces. Human intuition about safe clearance is hard to encode as a simple reward.

Their method, CHOP, shows annotators the executed path beside counterfactual paths the robot could have taken. People label pairwise preferences by expected collision risk and path efficiency. Those aggregated labels then fine-tune the navigation policy toward human safety taste. On a public navigation data set, near-collisions and path deviation fall sharply across several top models. Gains transfer to a real quadruped robot, with better goal success and clearance in live runs.
arxiv-2603-02204:
Amir Asiaee, Kaveh Aryan, and James Long improve forecast ranges under experiments in this 2026 paper. Conformal prediction gives ranges that cover the true value at a set rate. Ranges shrink when test cases are matched with like calibration cases. In gene experiments, likeness means a treatment left the target untouched, but that fact is often unknown.

The team proves how wrong matches weaken coverage, with an exact formula for the loss. They then learn only the needed fact: whether each gene sits downstream of a treatment. One method reads overlap patterns across treatments to find those links. Tests on fake gene models confirm the corrected ranges hold their rate. Even with heavy mismatch, coverage stayed at the target level.
arxiv-2603-02504:
Pratibha Zunjare and Michael Hsiao make language models prove their math in this 2026 paper. Models often produce fluent but logically broken solutions to math problems. Their framework, NeuroProlog, compiles word problems into executable Prolog programs. Formal checks then guarantee the reasoning, not just the final answer.

Training mixes three tasks in one symbolic space, a strategy they call the Cocktail effect. Tasks cover formula translation, problem-to-program synthesis, and program-answer alignment. Joint training lets symbolic grounding in one task lift the others. At run time, an error-aware decoder repairs programs step by step. Gains over single-task training were significant across four model scales. Their best setup beat larger program synthesis systems with far fewer parameters.
arxiv-2603-03204:
Ana Achúcarro, Perseas Christodoulidis, Jinn-Ouk Gong, and Oksana Iarygina rescue a class of early-universe models from a feared instability. In multi-field inflation, a negative mass for sideways perturbations usually signals disaster. Several known models seemed to break that rule, and their 2026 paper explains why they survive.

In what they call ultra slow-turn models, the trajectory's turn rate shrinks exponentially fast, switching off the would-be instability before it grows. The total entropy perturbation, they argue, is the reliable judge of stability, not the sideways mass alone. Popular string- and supergravity-inspired scenarios, including fibre inflation and modular inflation, fall into this safe class. The criterion should help model builders sort viable universes from unstable ones.
arxiv-2603-03404:
Tetiana Obikhod and Ievgenii Petrenko analyze one of the rarest Higgs boson production modes at the Large Hadron Collider: a Higgs made together with a single top quark. Because the top quark is the heaviest known particle, this channel probes its coupling to the Higgs, the top Yukawa coupling, with unusual directness. Their 2026 paper builds on the ATLAS experiment's search strategy at current collider energies.

Improved modeling aims to sharpen sensitivity to new physics and tighten Standard Model limits. Simulations map the expected rates for the channel's sub-modes, and a flipped-sign coupling scenario shows clear rate enhancements from constructive interference, matching expectations. Key motion and angle distributions agree with ATLAS projections. The work also optimizes event selection and error estimates, and projects what the future high-luminosity collider run could achieve.
arxiv-2603-03704:
Yoonwoo Kim and five colleagues let a language model whisper common sense into a robot's map of the unseen. A robot planning in a cluttered room cannot see every object, and naive planners ignore the stray objects they stumble on. Their 2026 framework, CoCo-TAMP, builds two commonsense rules into state estimation: objects have likely homes, and similar objects cluster together while dissimilar ones separate.

Writing those rules by hand would be endless, so a large language model supplies them on the fly. Its guidance shapes a hierarchical estimate of where task-relevant objects probably are, focusing the search. In simulation, planning and execution time fell by nearly two thirds against a commonsense-free baseline. In real-world robot demonstrations, the saving grew to nearly three quarters. Long-horizon chores become tractable when the robot guesses like a person.
arxiv-2605-00604:
Man Yung Wong shows that mixture-of-experts language models fumble exactly at the seams between domains, and borrows ideas from neuroscience to fix the routing. At a domain transition, standard affinity routing gives the correct expert almost no probability. The gate, choosing experts by resemblance alone, is stateless and cannot see a transition coming.

Wong adds three light mechanisms. A leaky membrane potential per expert accumulates routing context over time. A precision weight tracks each expert's recent prediction errors. An anticipatory predictor forecasts the next state. In controlled experiments the combination raised the correct expert's probability by more than a hundredfold. An ablation shows memory and anticipation interact super-additively. Anticipation alone does nothing, since pre-transition tokens look identical to ordinary ones. In a character-level model, the full gate often picks the right expert before its domain even appears.
arxiv-2605-00804:
Haoyu Wang and four co-authors present Prop-Chromeleon, a mixed reality system that turns everyday objects into touch props for virtual scenes. Mixed reality often looks convincing but feels empty, because virtual objects give no physical feedback. Given a text prompt, the system generates virtual content and anchors it to the shape of a real object the user can hold.

The team studies how generation behaves under different object shapes and prompts, using shape similarity scores and judgments of prompt fit. In a user study, the adaptive props improved perceived realism, immersion, and enjoyment over static baselines. The results suggest shape-aware generation can support both believable touch interaction and creative play.
arxiv-2605-00904:
Ujunwa Mgboh, Rafi Ibn Sultan, Joshua Kim, Kundan Thind, and Dongxiao Zhu test how robust transformer-based fluence map prediction is in radiation therapy planning. Learning-based prediction offers a fast alternative to iterative planning for intensity-modulated therapy, but its behavior under realistic shifts is unclear. Their two-stage pipeline maps anatomy from CT and contours to dose, and then to beamlet fluence maps.

They compare transformer designs with hierarchical, global, and hybrid attention, trained with a physics-informed loss for energy consistency. Performance degrades smoothly under moderate geometric changes and noise, but fails sharply under severe rotations and noise. Hierarchical models show slower error growth, and a common image score alone misses clinically relevant errors, so physics-based evaluation is needed.
arxiv-2605-01104:
Keyu He, Qianou Ma, Valerie Chen, Wayne Chi, and Tongshuang Wu present RECAP, an open-source platform for capturing, replaying, and analyzing how programmers work with AI coding assistants. Chat logs or version histories alone cannot show which prompt led to which edit, what was tried and discarded, or how strategy evolved. RECAP records AI chat sessions and fine-grained code edits inside VS Code without disrupting workflow.

Recordings merge into a unified timeline for interactive replay, with an extensible analysis layer for tasks such as behavioral classification and AI reliance measurement. Deployed in a university software engineering course, the platform captured thousands of prompts and code edits from dozens of students over a multi-week project. That enables interaction analyses no single data source could support.
arxiv-2605-01204:
Hiroto Sawada and two co-authors present FLRSP, a way to make federated learning safer. In federated learning, many clients train a shared model together without handing their data to a central server. The risk is that the updates clients share can leak: an attacker who intercepts them may rebuild the original training data. Past defenses against such attacks usually cost accuracy, so safety and quality traded off against each other.

FLRSP breaks that trade-off by sharing only a random subset of each client's model parameters. Each client computes its full update locally, sends a randomly chosen part of it, and the server folds those parts into the global model. In tests on image classification with a residual network and a vision transformer, under two standard federated rules, the method kept accuracy high while resisting leading reconstruction attacks better than earlier defenses.
arxiv-2605-01604:
Mukund Pandey argues that benchmark culture cannot grade AI agents once they run live in production. Standard suites are built for single sessions in the lab, while deployed agents act for long stretches, chain tool calls, and drift, with no ground truth waiting at the end.

From systems running at billion-event scale, Pandey draws a taxonomy of seven failure modes found only in production, such as compounding decision errors and tool failure cascades. He then shows the standard scores fail empirically: some modes slip past every common metric, and others surface only after several grading cycles of delay. His proposed framework grades agents on five dimensions, continuously, on live traffic rather than in episodic runs, and ships with an open reference implementation. The paper is a field report and a design brief for anyone shipping agents.
arxiv-2605-01704:
Kwan Soo Shin warns that language models debating copies of themselves polish the wording of one view rather than testing it. Across rounds of closed-system reasoning, where agents only rework each other's output, accuracy can hold while the reasoning underneath rots. He names that failure the Reasoning Trap, with multi-agent debate as its sharpest case.

His framework prices the rot. A faithfulness score checks each atomic claim against the given evidence. A theorem built on the data processing inequality shows the evidence signal can only shrink along a closed chain of reworkings. Companion results mark the exits: open systems that fetch fresh evidence can recover. His Socratic, evidence-first protocol rebuilds faithfulness in tests on two fact-checking sets, where debate had preserved answers while gutting their support. He closes with a falsifiable conjecture extending the bound to any closed protocol of the same shape.
arxiv-2605-02004:
Zhongqi Yang and colleagues build personal health models that learn from other users without being misled by them. People differ a lot in body and behaviour, yet a single user's data is often scarce and noisy. Past methods used only similar users or a shared population model, which can bias a personal fit.

Their framework trains a personal model with support users weighted by fit, using both similar and dissimilar people. Similar users aid transfer, while dissimilar users give a contrast that suppresses false patterns. An iterative method updates model and weights together. On six tasks from four real health data sets, the method beat population and personal baselines, with error cuts up to ten percent.
arxiv-2605-02104:
Manuela-Simona Cojocea rethinks probability by letting a distribution function generate geometry, not just label points. An admissible chart maps a value range into the probability interval, and pulling back the interval's distance gives value space a new metric. Swapping the chart while keeping the data and its law fixed changes that metric structure, so the setup is not a mere relabelling.

Charts preserve order but alter distance, spread, closeness to a boundary, and centrality. Averaging in chart coordinates and pulling back gives a Fréchet centre that matches Kolmogorov-Nagumo means. The geometric view explains why those means depend on the chart: a new chart changes the loss being minimised, not just the coordinates.
arxiv-2605-02204:
Shunpu Tang and colleagues warn that semantic communication, a new paradigm for next-generation networks, can leak private meaning to a reasoning eavesdropper. Semantic systems send meaning rather than raw bits through joint source-channel coding. Past attacks used fixed solvers and often needed instant knowledge of the wiretap channel, which may lead designers to understate the risk.

Their eavesdropper is orchestrated by a large language model and runs as a closed loop of three agents. An optimisation agent inverts both semantic and channel effects to recover private content without wiretap channel knowledge. A perception agent judges how well the recovery worked, guiding further rounds. The work aims to guide safer semantic system design.
arxiv-2605-02304:
Axel Álvarez studies how repeating patterns in group actions can be sorted by order, in a work of pure mathematics on dynamics. The tools at the center are regionally proximal relations, which track when points in a system keep coming close in a strong sense. Álvarez builds a new topology on part of the universal minimal system to handle the higher-order case.

With that tool, he gives an algebraic account of the relation for abelian actions and extends known results on recurrence sets to wider groups. He then shows that the maximal factor of one order acts as the key factor for cubic patterns, and for progressions in finitely generated abelian actions. The work ties two higher-order relations together on minimal points.
arxiv-2605-02404:
Michael Helcig, Eldar Kurtic, and Dan Alistarh explore statistically lossless quantisation of large language models, a middle ground between lossy compression and exact preservation. Methods such as GPTQ and AWQ compress well but lose fidelity, while fully lossless methods give no inference speedup. The authors examine three senses of losslessness for a quantised model.

Task-lossless compression keeps zero-shot benchmark accuracy within natural sampling variance, and they find it achievable at aggressive bit widths. Distribution-lossless compression is stricter: the quantised model's next-token distribution must be practically indistinguishable from the original. They propose expected acceptance rate, the best token-agreement probability under optimal coupling, as a direct fidelity metric for that stricter goal. Further results develop the idea.
arxiv-2605-02504:
Freja Thoresen and Dan Saattrup Smart build a multilingual test for false model output, focused on faithfulness errors. A faithfulness hallucination is fluent text that drifts from the source given to the model, or that clashes with itself. Most tests of this fault cover English only, so it was unclear if findings held for languages with less training data.

Starting from a multilingual question dataset, the pair create synthetic error sets for hundreds of languages and train token-level detectors for thirty European languages. They then test five models in English, Danish, German, and Icelandic. The smallest model erred most, with errors peaking in Icelandic, while larger models did better on most languages. Rates were consistently higher in lower-resource languages.
arxiv-2605-02604:
Zhou Bingtao, Xiang Mian, and Ning Qian question a quiet assumption in domain adaptation, the task of moving a vision model to a new setting without access to its original training data. Standard source-free methods still start from a model pretrained on that source data, so they are not truly source-free. The authors also note that swapping the source model changes final results very little.

They propose a stricter setting that starts from a randomly initialized model, guided only by a vision-language model and unlabeled target images. Their two-stage framework first warms the model up under that guidance, then finds a cleaner shared region between the guide and the learner for distillation. On three standard benchmarks, the method matched or beat approaches that still rely on source models.
arxiv-2605-02804:
Jim O'Regan and Jens Edlund build speech embeddings that keep separate traits in separate lanes of one vector. A voice carries content, identity, dialect, and gender at once, but a standard embedding mixes them into a single point, so similarity searches cannot say which trait should count. Their framework gives each trait its own subspace.

A shared acoustic encoder feeds a small projection head per trait. Each head is trained by distillation from a specialist teacher or by contrast over pairs sharing a label. Retrieval then scores each lane apart and adds them with signed weights, so a search can stress what was said, stress how it sounded, or suppress one trait to surface another. On cross-corpus tests with shared sentence prompts, signed weighting reduced same-speaker bias and found matching content across recording conditions.
arxiv-2605-03004:
Mauricio Lopez-Hernandez and Josue De-Santiago test whether the universe's slowing of expansion looks the same in every direction, using exploding stars as distance markers. The deceleration parameter sums up whether cosmic expansion is speeding up or slowing down. If the cosmos is isotropic, that value should not depend on which hemisphere of the sky supplies the supernovae.

Using a large modern supernova sample, the authors compare hemispheres under three redshift corrections. A directional variation persists in all frames, strongest where corrections for our own motion are incomplete, and weaker but present in the most corrected frame, aligned with the known cosmic microwave dipole. Inferring the dipole from the supernovae themselves gives a motion estimate mildly at odds with the microwave value. Adopting that estimate in the corrections removes the pattern.
arxiv-2605-03304:
Jiachen Shen, Jian Shi, Dan Wang, and Han Zhu model how the EU carbon border charge could reshape electricity prices across linked national markets. Static studies miss cross-border spillovers, which matter greatly in Europe's interconnected grid.

Their spatio-temporal graph neural network tracks prices and carbon intensity together across eight countries. In simulated scenarios, the charge did not act as a flat tax: low-carbon France and Switzerland gained an edge with possible price drops, while high-carbon Poland faced rising costs on two fronts. A shift in the market merit order drove the split.
arxiv-2605-03504:
M. Rubio, S. Rodríguez-Aparicio, J. M. Montanero, and M. A. Herrada study how a soluble surfactant changes droplet pinch-off at an interface. In the diffusion-limited regime they consider, flow-driven transport keeps feeding surfactant to the surface, challenging simpler pictures of how tension evolves during breakup.

Over most of the breakup, sorption holds surface tension nearly constant, with diffusion hindering supply only at the very end. Droplet shapes differ markedly from the insoluble case, where depletion raises tension locally. Experiments on millimeter droplets with two fast surfactants matched the model with no fitted parameters almost to the final microseconds.
arxiv-2605-03704:
Agnieszka Kałamajska, Dalimil Peša, and Artur Rutkowski study a singular semilinear elliptic equation. Its reaction term divides by a power of the unknown solution, so it blows up where the solution vanishes. The operator is of second order, in nondivergence form. The solution must be zero on the domain's edge.

They prove a solution exists when the domain is C1,1 smooth and the operator's terms are C1. Uniqueness among L1 solutions follows in the slightly stronger C2 case as well. Their proofs combine recent nonlinear forms of the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality with bounds for Green functions and new Kato-type inequalities. Together these tools tame the singularity at the edge.
arxiv-2605-04404:
David Gonzalez and Julia Knight work in mathematical logic, on the problem of classifying countable structures up to isomorphism and measuring how hard each classification is. A central tool is a standard embedding that turns any graph-like structure into a labelled tree while preserving the complexity of its description.

Earlier work showed this embedding preserves Scott complexity, a measure based on the simplest sentence that pins a structure down. Gonzalez and Knight refine that result: for a computable bound, having a computable Scott sentence transfers in both directions between a structure and its tree, with matching complexity. They also describe the classes of trees that arise from the embedding.
arxiv-2605-04504:
Jingtao Zhou and three co-authors improve prompt learning for vision-language models, a cheap way to adapt such models by tuning a few prompt tokens rather than the whole network. Past methods mostly tune the text side and treat the image encoder as a fixed whole-image extractor, missing fine detail.

Their method splits the visual signal into broad semantic parts and fine high-frequency detail using a frozen generative model. Text prompts are anchored to stable broad features, while shuffled-detail training forces the model to truly use fine granularity. Added as a plug-in to existing text-focused methods, it lifted results across eleven benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-04804:
Sofia Kankkunen, Merja Tornikoski, and Talvikki Hovatta examine long-term radio changes in active galactic nuclei, galaxies powered by supermassive black holes with fast jets. Radio records for fifty-four sources from the Metsähovi Radio Observatory are split into single flares. The aim is to link flare timing to the engines driving the jets.

They find the bend seen in earlier timing analysis best matches the average length of the brightest flares. Flare timing also rises with black hole mass divided by how fast matter falls in, suggesting a link to the central engine. Links with flare rise times were weaker and may reflect distance effects.
arxiv-2605-05004:
M Zotov and seven co-authors report the first detection of extensive air showers with a small-aperture fluorescence telescope, carried out at the Mount Aragats research station. Air showers are cascades sparked by ultra-high-energy cosmic rays entering the atmosphere. Their instrument uses two small Fresnel lenses and fast timing to catch the faint fluorescence light.

Two independent selection methods, a conventional cut-based analysis and a neural network approach, both found more than fifteen high-confidence shower tracks on clear, moonless nights. The authors detail how true tracks were separated from look-alike background signals. The result proves compact fluorescence telescopes can work, informing future ground and space missions.
arxiv-2605-05504:
Plasmons are ripples of electric charge that travel through a thin sheet of electrons. I. M. Moiseenko and D. A. Svintsov develop an exact theory for what happens when such a ripple hits the edge of a gate. Their setting is a two-dimensional electron system, part covered by a gate and part bare.

Using the Wiener-Hopf technique, they derive formulas for how much of the wave reflects and how much passes through, from either side. The amplitudes and phases depend in a rich way on the gate spacing and conductivity. The results support designs for tunable terahertz detectors and modulators.
arxiv-2605-05704:
An AI agent with tools can be manipulated into harmful actions, but blanket refusal rules also block harmless requests. Zhe Liu and seven co-authors propose SafeHarbor, a guardrail that draws precise decision boundaries instead. Static guidelines cannot adapt to context, so their system builds rules from experience.

A hierarchical memory stores past cases, and enhanced adversarial generation produces training confrontations that sharpen the boundary. New requests are judged against remembered near-misses, not just fixed policy text. The goal is an agent that refuses what is genuinely dangerous while staying useful for everything else.
arxiv-2605-06204:
Congye Wang asks when trimming suspicious calibration points actually helps conformal prediction. Conformal methods give prediction sets with coverage guarantees, but contaminated calibration data can distort them, and trimming looks like an obvious cleanup. Wang shows the effect runs through the law of the retained points, not through the taint level alone, which reframes trimming as conditioning rather than cleanup.

An exact finite sample identity reduces clean target coverage after trimming to a one dimensional transfer problem on score distributions. A piecewise bound splits the cost into a clean side covariance term and a retained taint term. Trimming helps when its score separates retention chances while staying neutral on clean data. Otherwise it cannot cut taint much, and the paper offers certificate templates for independent audits.
arxiv-2605-06304:
Simone Azeglio and three co-authors derive a multi-scale geometry for how neural populations encode sensory information. A representational geometry measures distances between stimuli by how reliably brain activity separates them. Different constructions of that distance can lead to qualitatively different conclusions about the neural code, which has made the approach hard to trust without firmer foundations.

Starting from how distances must contract when stimulus resolution is lost, the authors show a unique Riemannian geometry emerges. It extends the classic Fisher information metric across scales, from fine details to coarse global distinctions.
