Well encoded stimulus directions expand in this geometry, and poorly encoded ones contract, tying the metric exactly to mutual information. Estimated with diffusion models and applied to visual cortex data, it yields interpretable, robust features.
arxiv-2605-06404:
Gabriele Martino and Sebastian Tschiatschek propose a new way to explain model predictions with gradients. Integrated Gradients is faithful and scalable, but its results can be brittle because they depend on a chosen baseline, a straight path, and saturation effects. Their method, FRInGe, rethinks both the reference and the path.

FRInGe uses a maximum-entropy predictive reference and follows a Fisher-Rao geodesic, meaning a curved shortest path, in distribution space. Trust regions keep the matching input-space path stable. Across six ImageNet architectures it improves calibration-oriented attribution scores most clearly, while staying competitive on perturbation and infidelity measures.
arxiv-2605-06704: Omar A. Abuloha and three co-authors study when third-order ODEs can be turned into linear ones under contact maps, for cases whose Lie symmetry algebras have four or five dimensions. Using Cartan's method, they build fixed frames for two branches, of rank one and rank zero, that mark the linearizable cases. The paper also gives a recipe for finding the actual contact maps and shows the results with cases.
arxiv-2605-07104:
Xinyu Liu, Zixuan Xie, and Shangtong Zhang derive convergence rates for stochastic approximation under noise that depends on the past. Such methods power reinforcement learning algorithms like Q-learning, but proving how fast they settle when noise is Markovian has been a stubborn problem. The authors study methods whose average update shrinks toward the answer.

They obtain rates that hold almost surely, coming close to the best possible rate in the harmonic step-size case. The key tool combines a correction based on the Poisson equation with a smoothing technique for contractive maps. Their results cover a learning-rate range used widely in practice and give firmer ground for learning theory.
arxiv-2605-07904:
Kakan Deb and seven co-authors profile a room-temperature kagome ferromagnet, MgMn6Sn6, whose manganese moments form a pattern that is not in line. Kagome metals mix electron topology, linked behavior, and magnetic order, making their electrical transport in magnetic fields rich and strange. Single-crystal neutron scattering pinned down the moment layout inside the kagome bilayers.

The Hall response carries a large built-in part, nearly the same for different field directions, while at low heat an uneven outer part grows in, showing how scattering depends on direction. A large Sommerfeld number, odd without f-electrons, signals strongly linked electrons. Supported by basic calculations, the authors present the material as a hopeful platform for studying how such links shape transport in fields.
arxiv-2605-08304:
Sithembele Nkonkobe counts a new family of arrangements in combinatorics. Start with an ordered set partition. Slip identical bars between its blocks. That gives a barred preferential arrangement. Nkonkobe adds two rules. No block may stay fixed. And in each section, a fixed number of named elements must appear as singletons.

The counts define higher order degenerate r-deranged Bell numbers. Those numbers generalize several known sequences. The study derives a set of combinatorial identities for them. The identities show how to compute the counts from simpler pieces. The study also adds asymptotic results. They describe how fast the counts grow as the set gets large.
arxiv-2605-08504:
Zeru Shi, Zhenting Wang, Fan Yang, Qifan Wang, and coauthors trace the massive activations inside large language models to a single birthplace. A few hidden values grow enormous in these models, and the team identifies one layer, the Massive Emergence Layer, where they first appear before spreading deeper through residual connections.

Inside that layer, both the normalization and feed-forward parameters help create the effect. Once formed, the special token's representation barely changes across later layers, which narrows the variety of signals attention receives. The authors propose a simple method that loosens that rigidity, and it consistently improved performance on instruction following, math reasoning, and other tasks.
arxiv-2605-08604:
Xi Tan, Sagar Mohan, and Ziming Zhao protect small embedded devices from attacks that hijack program flow by corrupting return addresses. Shadow stacks guard those addresses, but existing embedded versions miss interrupts, cost too much speed, or need special security hardware many chips lack. WATSON instead reuses the standard debug watchpoint unit found on ordinary chips to guard the shadow stack's memory.

Address matching in the debug unit blocks stray writes to the stack, and compiler options add forward direction checks. On a common embedded chip family, speed costs stay in single digits and code growth is tiny, even across interrupts and two real applications. Low cost devices gain strong flow protection without exotic hardware.
arxiv-2605-08704:
Hyunmin Hwang and four coauthors evolve the reasoning skills of language model agent teams using particle swarm ideas. Most multi agent methods debate at test time only, leaving each agent's procedure fixed and exposed to peer errors. AgentPSO treats each agent as a particle whose state is a skill written in plain language and whose motion follows a semantic update direction.

Agents blend their past direction, personal best skill, global best skill, and self reflection drawn from peer traces. Across math and general reasoning tests, evolved skills beat static and test time only rivals, and they transfer across benchmarks and even to a different base model. Agent research gains reusable reasoning habits without touching model weights.
arxiv-2605-08904:
Xiaozhe Li and six coauthors test whether language model agents can keep improving their own solutions inside huge search spaces, the way human experts refine through feedback. Their OPT-Bench combines twenty machine learning tasks with ten classic hard combinatorial problems, demanding adaptation through reflection rather than memorized patterns. Their OPT-Agent answers with a loop of perception, memory, and reasoning that revises solutions as environment feedback arrives.

Across nineteen models from seven families, stronger models exploit feedback better, yet adaptability stays capped by base capacity and even the best models trail human experts. Self improvement research gains a rigorous arena separating genuine refinement skill from rote tool use.
arxiv-2605-09004:
Dennis Fremstad, Julian Adamek, and David Mota lift the grade of cosmos sims with a learned touch up that takes a curved cosmos too. Fine sims cost a lot to run. Their tool takes a coarse field as its base. It also takes curve, mass share, clump strength, growth rate, and age shift. It paints in fine form that could be true. As a GAN, it can make more than one fine take from noise.

Key stats match true fine runs in the main. Most lost large scale power comes back. Small scale power dips a bit, near ten percent. Big halo cores come out a touch less dense. A curved light cone set shows the tool at work scale.
arxiv-2605-09204:
Lee and Abdu Jyothi break the sequential chain of backpropagation, the depth bottleneck in parallel training. Gradients must flow layer by layer, so depth grows with region count, while scan based shortcuts that cut depth cost too much on modern networks. The expense comes from combining full rank Jacobians across the whole hidden state, a cubic cost in size.

Their method, LBI, limits cross region traffic to a narrow latent interface, making scan based backpropagation practical. The adjoint recursion then becomes a suffix scan over small Jacobians, with per combine cost cubic in interface size rather than full size, and gradients exact. Across Mamba-2, Mamba-3, Transformer, and a hybrid, LBI holds quality at 47 to 61 million block parameters. An interface of size 16 keeps training quality close to dense baselines, within a small cross entropy gap. Backward traffic across devices drops to one scan over fixed size matrices, roughly 56 kilobytes here.
arxiv-2605-09304:
Nazari and five colleagues present Merlin, a system answering free form questions needing analytical reasoning about code, pairing an LLM with CodeQL for expressive queries over large codebases. Tools like grep cannot answer questions needing semantic or inter-procedural reasoning, and LLMs struggle with large codebases under resource limits. Two challenges dominate: well formed queries often return degenerate or empty results, and few CodeQL queries exist online, limiting LLMs as CodeQL query generators.

The team answers with RAG based iterative query generation plus a novel self-test technique built on assistive queries generating concrete witnesses that reveal and explain semantic flaws in candidate queries. Over natural language questions from common bug finding tasks, Merlin found most issues reported by other approaches, plus issues that would otherwise have stayed undetected. A user study found Merlin access raised task accuracy 3 point 8 fold and cut programmer task time by 31 percent.
arxiv-2605-09504:
Riegler and Strümke argue that AI security policy is aimed at the wrong target. Restricting access to individual frontier models misses the point, they claim. The dangerous capability lives mostly in the scaffold around a model. That scaffold means coordination, memory, and tools that let small open models punch above their weight. To test this they built swarm attack, an open framework where lightweight agents share memory, explore in parallel, and improve by evolution.

Five copies of a small open model ran hundreds of jailbreak attacks each. They breached one frontier system at a high rate. Against another system they failed, despite frequent technical successes. The same small models then found all nine planted flaws in a vulnerable program. That took about four minutes on a consumer laptop. With the scaffold parts switched off, they found almost none. Policy should assess whole systems rather than gate single models.
arxiv-2605-09804:
Sasakura worked out the joint distributions of any number of eigenvectors of real and complex symmetric random tensors. Tensor eigenvectors show up in nonlinear problems, from spin glasses and quantum information to AI and string theory, yet they are less mapped than matrix eigenvalues. Past work with the same tools had given mean distributions only.

With quantum field theory tools, Sasakura got random matrix forms and large-dimension asymptotics for the joint distributions. The asymptotics take the form of one shared function of tensor shapes, extending to joint distributions the universality once found for means. Monte Carlo runs cross-checked the results, giving the theory a second, numerical check.
arxiv-2605-09904:
Chen and five colleagues built TOC-Bench, a test of temporal object consistency in video language models. Such models have made great strides in general video understanding. But whether they keep the same object's identity, state, and flow across occlusion, vanishing, return, state shifts, and cross-object contact remains little tested. Current tests may thus overrate temporal reasoning while missing object-focused failures.

TOC-Bench ties each queried subject to a per-frame object track plus a structured event timeline. A three-layer temporal-necessity filter cut 60.7 percent of candidate pairs, keeping 17,900 items across 10 test dimensions that truly need ordered visual proof. A human-checked set of 2,323 pairs over 1,951 videos followed. Tested models proved weak at event counting, event ordering, identity-sensitive reasoning, and hallucination-aware checks despite strong general video scores.
arxiv-2605-10104:
Ishikawa, writing alone, applies Chern-Simons gauge theory to roaming-electron ferromagnetism, where moving electrons carry the pull rather than fixed moments. He shows that a shared log H term in the free energy drives the electron system to a first-order switch. Sharp effects at zero field split plus and minus pulls apart, producing B-H hysteresis, the lag between applied field and magnetisation.

It is claimed to cover a broad class of roaming-electron magnets and to reveal the gauge-theory origin of their pull, including the puzzling quantum behaviour of single, symmetric-domain crystals. Earlier pictures, from the Stoner mean-field model and the Hubbard model to spin-fluctuation theories, capture only parts of the effect, and first-principles methods reproduce lab trends only partly. The paper positions the gauge-theory account as the missing tiny-scale cause.
arxiv-2605-10304:
Linda Albanese and four colleagues study memory networks that retrieve stored patterns from partial cues. Using the Hopfield model as a test case, their 2026 paper examines partial annealing. Fast neural dynamics couple to slowly shifting patterns in a two-temperature, two-timescale setup. A real number n tunes the time split and the link between neurons and synapses.

Adapting Guerra's interpolation, the authors derive the free energy without analytic continuation, a delicate analytic step. They show that negative values of n slowly uncorrelate stored patterns, cutting cross-talk and favoring orthogonal layouts. That pushes the net to maximal storage, one pattern per neuron. Mean-field Monte Carlo tests confirm the picture, and partial annealing restores recall even with biased patterns, beating standard uncorrelation methods.
arxiv-2605-10504:
Jinchang Zhu and five colleagues identify a failure mode in GPT-style pretraining. A causal-decoder block is layered: lower layers build the residual basis for upper layers. Upper layers can lock onto sharp attention patterns while the lower-layer features they watch are still settling. The authors call this premature upper-layer attention specialization. Their 2026 paper shows the failure is real.

Briefly slowing just the upper layers' query and key projections early in training lifts a 270M GPT-style decoder's perplexity, token efficiency, and downstream accuracy. Probes confirm the intervention leaves lower-layer routing on schedule; it stops upper attention from settling onto an immature residual basis. Matched ablations point to multiplicative gated feed-forward networks, not RMSNorm or bias removal, as the part holding back the upstream residual writes behind the failure in LLaMA-style blocks. A pathwise analysis unifies both findings under a bound.
arxiv-2605-10604:
Mieke Wilms and Christoph Heitz map the Pareto frontier of decision systems. Building fair decision systems requires trading performance with fairness toward people. More fairness might cost some performance and vice versa, yet possible trade-offs remain poorly mapped. Their 2026 paper treats fairness in binary decision problems as a multi-goal tuning problem.

The authors study best decision rules for any utility scores, population mixes, and a wide range of group fairness metrics. These metrics use egalitarian, prioritarian, and Rawlsian justice views. The Pareto frontier consists of fixed, group threshold rules applied to people's success odds. By metric, the frontier may include upper-bound threshold rules, picking people with lower success odds. The frontier's location depends only on population traits, utility scores, and fairness score. It does not depend on technical design.
arxiv-2605-10704:
Mohammed M.H. Qazzaz and co-authors present a forward-looking UAV movement handling xApp for Open Radio Access Network near-real-time controller settings. The system uses Double Deep Q-Network reward-based learning enhanced with transfer learning to tune hand-off decisions for drones flying preset paths. Unlike after-the-fact methods that respond to signal decay, the framework foresees network conditions and cuts both outage chance and hand-off rate through forecast tuning.

Central weight averaging pools knowledge from multiple flight cases into a global model that extends to unseen working settings without long retrains. Tests show a good trade-off between hand-off rate and link trust, cutting hand-off events by more than half against greedy methods while keeping outage chance nearly tiny. The results back learning-based movement handling for aerial user equipment in next-generation open radio networks.
arxiv-2605-11004:
Arun Kumar, Rahul Yadav, Yogesh M. Joshi, and Manjesh K. Singh develop a nano-clay-stabilized water-in-oil emulsion as an environmentally gentler lubricant. Conventional mineral-oil lubricants struggle to combine lubrication with heat dissipation, and the team builds their emulsion on sunflower oil with Garamite clay.

Raising clay loading lifts yield stress and strengthens shear-thinning and thixotropic behavior, the reversible structuring that lets the fluid remember recent flow. Against steel-on-steel contacts under high pressure, the best emulsion cuts friction by roughly 41 percent against oil and 84 percent against water, with wear down by about 80 and 96 percent. Lubrication engineers get a plant-oil emulsion whose microstructure tunes its own friction.
arxiv-2605-11404: Tang and eight colleagues tackle attributing large-scale emergence to single agents in language-model multi-agent systems. Existing axiomatic methods scale combinatorially and stop near one thousand agents, while the phenomena they explain occur at one million or more. Adapting Aumann-Shapley path-integral attribution to million-agent scale, they run three to five orders of magnitude quicker than sampled Shapley. On fourteen days of Bluesky data, full-scale attribution disagrees structurally with a biased hundred-agent sample, shifting about twice the share onto top follower tiers.
arxiv-2605-11804: Patryk Krukowski and four colleagues improve data-free continual learning, where a model must retain old knowledge without revisiting old data. Current model inversion assumes diagonal covariance, ignoring links that shape learned reps and yielding weak fake samples. Their REMIX system models full covariance through a Laplace kernel form, with memory linear in feature size and only a log-scale extra compute cost. The more lifelike samples improved scores across standard benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-11904: Huiyu Yi and five colleagues improve class-incremental learning, where a model must absorb new classes without forgetting old ones. The popular nearest-class-mean classifier assumes features collapse to single points, but drift in incremental training leaves classes as complex manifolds instead. Their HC-SOINN classifier captures manifold topology through a local-to-global representation, while their STAR method tracks pointwise trajectories to deform the topology as features drift. Plugged into seven state-of-the-art methods, it improved all of them.
arxiv-2605-12104: M. Douspis and seven colleagues test whether a faint glow from hot gas can tell apart reionisation histories that fit Planck data. They work out the glow's sky pattern for each kind and find the two kinds give clearly different patterns, despite model doubt. Today's data lean toward a late start for the first stars, but cannot settle it. A sharper sky map near scale 2000, at 0.4 units strong, could settle it in coming years. The glow data alone place the midpoint of the first-star era between redshifts 7.94 and 8.17.
arxiv-2605-12304: Talib Ansari and two colleagues make CFD finding fast with soundness rules. Symbol fitting suffers wobble, rest stalls, and conduct issues, while physical soundness is rarely used for wake prediction. Their screened system in GEP adds two filters plus a weight-map constraint to the loop, dropping unstable tries early. It cuts cost by 42.3 percent against the baseline and unsound models at the end from 58.4 percent to 1.7 percent. Trained on a cylinder wake, the models improve forecasts, stay realizable, and carry over to a block, an airfoil, and a body.
arxiv-2605-12604: Pillai and seventeen colleagues present first results from SIMPLIFI, a SOFIA survey of Galactic molecular cloud filaments. The survey traces field shape from the DR21 Main Ridge into nearby sub-threads at about a tenth of a parsec detail. It pushes maps beyond dense regions probed before. They compare field direction, gravity direction and rotated brightness gradient. Field and gradient run aligned in sub-threads but at right angles in the Main Ridge above a column threshold near two times ten to twenty-two. That switch matches Planck thresholds.
arxiv-2605-12804: Mei and four colleagues present BiPneu, a bipolar-pressure system for soft parts. Two-way pressure regulation is key to soft parts, giving wide motion. Yet regulation across both sides is hard, due to uneven moves, valve kinks and flow jolts. Their DM-SMC controller uses hysteresis choice from a mixed air-electric model. It beats model and PID controls, cutting error by 11.9 percent in step tests and 35.6 percent in sine tests.
arxiv-2605-12904: Chen, Ding and Akoglu tackle a limit of tabular foundation models, which predict on new tables without task-specific training but choke on long contexts. Their method, VIP-COP, scores training examples and features by their value for prediction and keeps only the high-value context. It works fast, improves with more test-time compute, needs no access to model internals, and names its chosen predictors plainly. Across large high-dimensional tests it beats heuristic and optimised baselines.
arxiv-2605-13004: Kresin, Tang, Baeumer and Wang ask what survives of one-sided Poisson cluster processes once cluster orientation is erased. They build matched reversible cluster nulls preserving intensity and the full Bartlett spectrum, showing second-order structure alone need not reveal temporal direction. For stationary Poisson branching clusters they derive the Fourier-Stieltjes transform of the reduced third cumulant and show a nonzero imaginary factorial bispectrum certifies orientation. Explicit orientation-erased nulls and finite-window contrasts round out the results.
arxiv-2605-13104: Chaudhary, Hubballi and Kulkarni survey content caching methods in Named Data Networks, a form of Information Centric Networking that focuses on content rather than end hosts. Named Data Networking uses named data with a request-response model, and routers cache content to meet future demand. The survey first taxonomises caching techniques, then discusses methods with their advantages and disadvantages. It closes with performance metrics used to evaluate caching methods and directions for future research.
arxiv-2605-13204: Ding and colleagues solve indefinite stochastic linear quadratic control with random weights and Poisson jumps. When jumps strike, the usual fundamental matrix form can break because the state matrix may turn singular. They build the key process straight from the stochastic value flow, proving a unique maximal regular solution to the jump Riccati equation. That solution gives a closed loop form for the one open loop optimal control, with conditions for uniform convexity and worked examples.
arxiv-2605-13504: Arianna Ceccarelli, Alexander Browning and Ruth Baker develop a method for structural identifiability of partially observed stochastic processes. It asks whether parameters can be pinned down from ideal noise-free data. For trajectory data, they use a model tracking single particles. For density data, they derive a partial differential equation model with an algebra approach. They also study initial-condition information via characteristic equations and a Taylor expansion of density over time. Applied to an example model, it is identifiable from trajectory data but not from density data.
arxiv-2605-13904: Bladon and Bent test whether a brain encoder has truly learned how vision is organized, not just how to predict brain scans. They apply feature visualization, a gradient-ascent probe, to the TRIBE v2 encoder paired with V-JEPA 2, freezing both models and synthesizing images for seven visual regions. The probe recovers a clear progression of growing spatial scale and feature complexity from area V1 through V4.
arxiv-2605-14304: Zhang, Joe-Wong and Lan propose Matrix-Space Reinforcement Learning, a geometric abstraction for trajectory segments through matrix descriptors of lifted transitions. Compositional generalization requires finding useful prior rollout parts. They expose hidden structure and support composition. The descriptor is proved well defined and complete. Value functions on segments approximate action values. MSRL posts the best finite-budget AUC of 73 percent.
arxiv-2605-14404: Hwang and colleagues address multilingual machine unlearning, model-information removal across several languages, where private-data leaks are the risk. Prior checks, they argue, miss how information spreads between them, largely reusing per-language tests. They propose two metrics, the Knowledge Separability Score for overall unlearning quality across the set, and the Knowledge Persistence Score for steady removal across pairs. Tests of varied removal methods with these metrics reveal patterns unique to this setting. They also offer a fresh view of removal work.
arxiv-2605-14604: Kasneci and Kasneci argue that sycophancy in tutoring language models is a safety risk. Good tutoring needs corrective friction, the kind of pushback that surfaces a wrong idea and challenges it with care. Their EduFrameTrap test varies student confidence and pressure across six subjects. It sets context-switch frames apart from authority pressure and social-affective pressure, such as appeals not to be told one is wrong. Across two frontier models, authority and social pressure are reported to trigger epistemic retreat more often than context-switch attacks.
arxiv-2605-14704: Chen, Cheng, Faure, Su and Hsu introduce SceneFunRI, a benchmark for reasoning about invisible objects in real scenes. People often infer where a hidden object sits from context and commonsense, but vision-language models struggle with this. Built from SceneFun3D with 855 instances, it asks models to locate hidden functional objects from task instructions plus commonsense reasoning. The top baseline is reported to score only about fifteen percent on strict accuracy, showing the skill stays unstable.
arxiv-2605-14804: Burgess, Pike and Pourakbar-Saffar construct uniquely 2-colourable 4-cycle systems. A cycle system decomposes the edges of a complete graph into cycles of fixed length. It is k-colourable when vertices can be coloured with k colours so no cycle is monochromatic, and uniquely k-colourable when that colouring is unique up to permuting colour classes. The authors build uniquely 2-colourable 4-cycle systems with order n for every admissible n from forty-nine, plus decompositions of the complete graph minus a 1-factor for all admissible n from fifty.
arxiv-2605-15104: Md Tahmid Rahman Laskar and five others convert verified text benchmarks for tool-calling agents into audio tests without re-annotating tool schemas or gold labels. Their framework makes speech with speaker variation and background noise, creating paired text-audio instances. Seven omni-modal models were tested on audio versions of Confetti and When2Call. Performance varied strongly by model and by task. Failures most often trace to misunderstood argument values in speech. A reference-free judge protocol checked against human preference is also included.
arxiv-2605-15304: Amir Zeldes presents DiscoExplorer, an open-source web interface for studying discourse relations, the links like cause or yield joining claims, across languages. Common relation lists now span sets, but complex data and missing tools block matching. It runs locally and publishes datasets from the DISRPT shared task covering 16 tongues, with a query language plus search and visualization for links and cue devices like connectives. Example studies show the workflow.
arxiv-2605-15504: Nischal Aryal, Arash Termehchy, Ali Vakilian, and Marianne Winslett study learning systems whose owners and users pull apart. Biased outputs can steer users to choices that harm them. Past fixes ask owners to curb their own bias. Owners lack motive to do so and cite free speech or trade. The team instead frames the clash as a game. Their scalable tools with proof pledges boost wanted facts and acts while cutting biased, manipulative acts.
arxiv-2605-15604: Xuechen Zhang and five colleagues present VSPO for steering language-model behavior. Models must hit accuracy goals while meeting behavior wishes like verbosity. A wanted behavior may show rarely or never, creating a sparse reward bottleneck. VSPO steers rollouts with a target vector of varying strength. It upsamples rare behaviors and enriches variety, speeding policy optimization. Under a bandit model, VSPO beats reward-shaped GRPO when steered distributions align with the target. Tests on benchmarks for behaviors show VSPO improves control while holding or lifting accuracy.
arxiv-2605-15704: Chen Chen, Zihan Jia, Andrea Sabbioni, Reza Farahani, and Lei Jiao present Scale, a scheduling frame for serverless edge computing. Placing requests and managing resources in shifting, mixed edge systems is hard. Scale uses policy deep reinforcement learning to balance stability and performance under shifting loads. Its design weighs service-level goals, end-to-end latency, and data locality in each scheduling choice. In Huawei Cloud simulations it lands within a factor of 1.11 to 1.15 of a top integer programming solver, while cutting decision time by up to 99 percent.
arxiv-2605-15904: Inoussa Mouiche and Sherif Saad present CTiKG, a context-aware tool for extracting threat entities and relations from cyber threat intelligence reports into knowledge graphs. Pipeline methods suffer error build-up from complex report structure, domain language and semantic ambiguity. CTiKG mixes hybrid NLP models using SecureBERT+ embeddings with expert knowledge from a domain ontology to cut misclassifications and cascading errors. On the DNRTI-AUG-STIX2 set, with 21 entity types aligned to STIX 2.1, it gains 3 to 4 percent on entity recognition and up to 8 percent on relation extraction over top baselines.
arxiv-2605-16004: Thomas Ransford proves a conjecture of Jean Esterle about negative powers of contractions on Hilbert space. Take any closed subset of the unit circle with zero length. He finds a sequence growing to infinity with a striking trait. Any contraction whose spectrum lies in the set, and whose inverse powers grow no faster than that sequence, must be unitary. The proof extends a removability result for bounded holomorphic functions to certain unbounded functions of moderate growth near such sets.
arxiv-2605-16304: Yu and four others propose a deep learning tool for undersea sound target spotting from ship noise. A variational mode split plus 3/2-D spectrum method first pulls high-quality DEMON spectral traits that catch signal envelopes. A 1-D conv net with a multi-stage multi-type focus tool then sharpens traits at varied depths. A tunable class-even focal loss counters severe class skew, and tests on real ship-noise data show clear gains.
arxiv-2605-16504: Gogilashvili and Tamborra model stellar collapse of 195 stars with masses between 9 and 120 solar masses, using a schematic treatment of neutrino flavor change. They find flavor transformation shifts the explodability of massive stars, notably in the 16-30 solar mass range, and shifts the compact remnant mass spread. Their findings mark flavor conversion as a key ingredient in predicting neutron star and black hole populations. It also eases the red-giant and supernova-rate problems and matches model hopes with the low-mass tail of the seen neutron star mass spread.
arxiv-2605-16604: Hemadri and colleagues build R2V Agent, a routing system that lets a small local model run an agent task and call a stronger teacher model only at steps where failure looks likely. A verifier scores each candidate action, and a calibrated router weighs worst-case risk before escalating. Across coding, text-world, and terminal benchmarks it lifts success close to teacher levels while keeping teacher calls far below simpler routing rules.
arxiv-2605-17104: Yu and colleagues argue that scientific reasoning in large language models needs logical soundness, not just longer chains or bigger datasets. They define criteria for judging reasoning steps, sample training data rich in logical structure, and test the approach on physics problems across three base models. The enriched training improved both the faithfulness of reasoning and success on scientific questions, they report.
arxiv-2605-17404: Luo proves the squared-distance from a random short ring member to the log-unit lattice of two-power cyclotomic fields converges to a constant times the square root of n. He shows the target lies inside the origin's Voronoi cell for k at least four. The max-norm case yields a sub-polynomial approximation ratio for the short generator problem. A coarse lattice theorem and a trigamma theorem on determinant ideals then cut the ML-KEM factor from exponential-root to sub-polynomial.
arxiv-2605-17504: Zhou and colleagues establish a distribution view for visual mechanistic reading. The view models how a feature activation shifts the natural image distribution, framing the task as KL-minimal tuning. Prior paradigms carry biases. They may drift from natural images and read as uninterpretable, or fail to activate model traits and read as unfaithful. A KL-minimal soft-constraint principle balances clarity against faithfulness, realized through energy-guided diffusion sampling. Tests on DINOv3 validate the theory and approach.
arxiv-2605-17704: Alon Bebchuk and Nir Shavit probe the lottery ticket idea. It says dense neural networks hide small subnetworks that can match the full model when retrained alone. In a small, clause-based toy setting where features can be tracked clearly, winning tickets match starting spots already close to the final feature codes. Sparse retraining preserves a family of compatible codes rather than exact rows. Simple distance probes often beat standard weight-based ticket hunting.
arxiv-2605-17804: Chenxi Wang and three colleagues offer GenTS, a benchmark library for generative time series models. Older libraries suit discriminative models with fixed workflows, a poor fit for generative methods like adversarial training and diffusion, which learn full data distributions. GenTS unifies data preparation, gathers versatile models, and supplies panoramic evaluation metrics in a modular design users can extend. Benchmark runs across varied tasks yield model selection guidance and point to future research directions. The code is open source, with tutorials and docs posted alongside.
arxiv-2605-18304: In a 2026 paper, Samit Ghosh and Arjun Paul classify integrable transitive algebraic Lie algebroids on a smooth complex projective variety. They then build Higgs bundles tied to a Lie algebroid and study their moduli spaces, the geometric spaces that collect such objects. Using a Tannakian view, they describe principal bundles with Lie algebroid connections and construct their moduli spaces, ending with a motivic non-abelian Hodge correspondence.
arxiv-2605-18404: Hongyu Wang and six co-authors present JanusPipe, a 2026 training system for machine learning interatomic potentials, models that bring ab initio accuracy to molecular dynamics simulations. Conservative models force a double-backward run pattern that clashes with staged parallel training. JanusPipe answers with a memory-saving staged design and a wave-based scheduler that balances compute phases. On 32 GPUs it lifts throughput by 1.51 times over 1F1B and 1.45 times over Hanayo.
arxiv-2605-18804: Salar Beigzad and Vansh Verma extend Forward-Forward learning, a local training method for neural networks, with multi-scale goodness scores. Their Adaptive Multi-Scale Goodness Aggregation gathers local, middle, and global signals, mines hard negative examples on a curriculum, and sets layer-wise thresholds. A warm-up cosine schedule steadies training. On MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, the method beats the baseline by up to about one and a half percent, with little extra compute.
arxiv-2605-18904: Guodong Du and Wanyu Lin slim down dynamic model merging, which combines fine-tuned models without joint training or task data. Dynamic methods keep task-specific capacity but must split limited storage between shared and expert weights. Their DiDi-Merging method assigns low-rank capacity to both parts through differentiable rank choice, then refines parameters without data. On an eight-task vision benchmark the small setup keeps 98.7 percent accuracy at just 1.24 times one model's storage. Dropping refinement costs over four points, and results assume the task is known.
arxiv-2605-19004: Ahmad Yehia and six colleagues release EgoTraj, an egocentric dataset of human walking shot on Meta Quest Pro headsets in city streets. Forecasting walking paths from a first-person view matters for humanoid robots, wearables and assistive guidance, yet egocentric path data have been scarce. EgoTraj holds 75 sequences from wearers, each pairing synced video with head poses, three-dimensional eye gaze vectors and scene labels. Unlike typical sets, it captures long, self-directed routes with varied wearers, and benchmarks show gaze, scene and motion cues each helping forecast quality.
arxiv-2605-19404: Ma, Wu and Tong recast the projective truncation approximation without Green's functions. Earlier versions cut equations of motion for Green's functions and recovered static means through the spectral theorem. The new version builds a self-consistent theory for reduced density matrices, and spells out the dynamical matrix while casting the solution as an over-constrained optimization problem. That shift links the method to variational density-matrix theory, and the authors discuss inner-product choices, generalized virial and Wick theorems, and the static component problem.
arxiv-2605-19504: Deutsch and Riccò extend a classical regularity result to a wider class of first-order linear elliptic operators. It is known that distributions with symmetrized gradient as a bounded Radon measure belong to the space BD on bounded domains with smooth boundary. For an operator satisfying the rank-one property, they prove that a distribution on a Lipschitz domain with bounded operator-variation belongs to the BV-A space. The short paper states the extension cleanly, without new examples or applications.
arxiv-2605-19604: Zhang and team introduce Formal Skill, a runtime-native abstraction turning reusable agent capability into executable form. Current skills stay informal: long documents, or function calling and protocol servers that leave workflow state, policy enforcement and completion discipline out. Formal Skill packages JSON metadata, action schemas, reliable Python executors, hook control logic, routing and skill-local state into state machines and hook policies. Implemented in FairyClaw, an open event-driven runtime, it scores competitively on Harness-Bench while using substantially fewer tokens, especially where formal skills matter most.
arxiv-2605-19804: Go and colleagues propose StitchVM, a way to align diffusion and flow image models with task rewards such as prompt fidelity or aesthetic preference. Rewards live on clean images, but alignment needs value estimates at noisy intermediate steps. There, Tweedie estimates bias and Monte Carlo rollouts cost heavily. StitchVM grafts a frozen diffusion backbone onto a truncated pixel space reward model, carrying its reward skill into the noisy latent regime. Stitching and fine tuning takes only ten GPU hours, and downstream methods run faster with lower memory.
arxiv-2605-19904: Huang works out flip count moments for a coin game that ends on a set word. He gives a loop rule for the moments when the word is a run of heads, or heads then a tail. The sums yield to a one knob twist on classic count numbers, and a wider proof covers dice with any faces and odds.
arxiv-2605-21104: Tom Jacobs, Rohan Jain, and Rebekka Burkholz propose HORST, an optimizer that trains sparse transformers without losing stability. Standard adaptive methods favor stability while sparsity demands a different bias, so the authors compose optimizer steps as operators and add a hyperbolic mirror map that pushes weights toward sparsity. In vision and language trials, HORST beat AdamW at every sparsity level, with the largest gains when sparsity was highest.
arxiv-2605-21304: Sagnik Nandy, Wanyi Ling, and Nikolaos Ignatiadis explain how limma-trend works from an empirical partially Bayes perspective. In high-throughput biology, thousands of regressions are fit, one per gene or protein, with very few samples per unit. Limma-trend improves power by shrinking variance estimates toward a fitted curve relating variance to a unit-level summary. This happens before p-values and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery control. They show limma-trend computes approximate partially Bayes p-values, with a prior estimated for nuisance parameters.
arxiv-2605-21604: Siddhant Ray and co-authors present Argo, efficient importance labeling for enterprise email systems. Email importance tagging has long been a key yet hard problem. Traditional methods such as keyword matching, user-defined rules, and sender-based rules demand heavy manual feature work and fail to scale or to carry over well. Recent large language models offer deep context grasp and better tagging quality. But using models like GPT-4.1 at enterprise volumes incurs high compute costs, driving other tagging schemes near GPT-4.1 quality.
arxiv-2605-21704: Chaerim Moon and co-authors design gait-level motion for grasp-based dynamic locomotion in microgravity. Travel there often relies on thinly and oddly placed anchors, driving grasp-based motion with multiple limbs. Their paper sets fit and speed goals for grasp-based dynamic travel and builds a gait-level parameter-metric frame linking motion values to review metrics. A physics-based simulation with two quadruped shapes in random three-dimensional anchor settings finds steady effects across contact support, motion-induced loading, kinematic fit, actuation demand, and traversal time.
arxiv-2606-00104:
Uysal, Kehrer, and Panichella keep language models out of the drone control loop while letting them plan missions, in this 2026 arXiv paper on PEACE. Putting a foundation model in control raises latency and risks hallucinated commands reaching real hardware. Their planner-executor design has the model produce a mission plan in one pass, then hands execution to structured tool calls over a robotics middleware bridge. A world model fuses detectors with depth projection to locate objects in 3D.

A constraint enforcement layer enforces altitude limits and horizontal geofencing, so unsafe plans cannot execute if the model proposes them. Bounded replanning recovers from execution failures without unbounded model calls. The design was shown in software-in-the-loop simulation with a drone autopilot in the Gazebo simulator. Compared with tightly coupled language model control, the authors report explainability, constraint enforcement, and fewer model invocations. Code, datasets, and videos are released.

arxiv-2606-04404:
Liao, Shi, and Xie tackle a practical problem with deep neural networks, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Many inputs and weights do not matter for the output. Yet they raise cost and complexity. Their tool is the knockoff method. It creates fake copies of variables. Researchers then spot the real variables while controlling the false discovery rate. That rate is the share of flagged variables that are in fact useless.

Building on a regularized network, they propose three screening methods. One filters with a single layer. One filters across many layers. One adds up variable weights across the network. Each method prunes inputs while keeping the false discovery rate under control. In tests against existing algorithms, the authors report good performance. The work aims at smaller, cheaper networks. It also gives the kept inputs a stated statistical guarantee.
arxiv-2606-04804:
Xu and colleagues show that a popular recipe for solving physics inverse problems with generative models quietly samples the wrong distribution, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Diffusion and flow models are used to reconstruct solutions of partial differential equations under hard physics constraints. Conditioning on a hard constraint means conditioning on a measure-zero set.

On controlled problems, removing the factor inflates posterior error to twenty times the sampling-noise floor, and a minimal-displacement projection is biased at nine times the floor. Their sampler, CoCoS, targets the correct co-area posterior and matches the gold-standard posterior to within sampling noise. Satisfying the physics, they conclude, is not the same as sampling the posterior.
arxiv-2606-05004:
Peihua Mai and co-authors propose SharedRequest in this 2026 arXiv paper, a framework for privacy-preserving inference with large language models that works with any model. Prompt privacy matters because users send sensitive text to cloud services, but earlier protection methods tend to sacrifice answer quality or speed, and often need changes to one specific model. SharedRequest instead protects privacy at the level of a whole batch of prompts.

The method hides each original prompt among noisy variants, while grouping instructions that mean the same thing so one inference can serve many queries. It needs no access to model parameters and no architectural changes. In experiments it delivered over 20 percent higher utility than prior differential privacy baselines, and its shared-prompt mechanism cut query cost by up to fivefold compared with unbatched inference.
arxiv-2606-05104:
Sheng Jin, Minghao Liu, and a large team introduce KINA, the Knowledge Index of Noah's Ark, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The benchmark targets three flaws in how language model knowledge is usually tested. Designs driven by sheer scale ignore disciplinary representativeness. Flat payment for annotators permits lazy consensus. Ranking instability goes unaudited under limited test budgets. KINA holds 899 items across 261 disciplines.

The authors back the design with two results. Representativeness is cast as a coverage objective over expert-elicited anchors, with a greedy approximation guarantee for the proxy they use. A proof shows bonus-on-bar tournament payment beats flat payment for review quality. Evaluating 42 models from 13 labs, the top scorer, a Gemini model, reached 53 percent. A Claude Opus model followed at 49 percent and a GPT model at 48 percent, leaving large headroom. Tool augmentation added up to five points, and bootstrap checks expose how unstable nearby ranks are.
arxiv-2606-05204:
Juan Margalef-Bentabol presents xCPS in this 2026 arXiv paper, an open-source package for symbolic computation in the covariant phase space formalism of field theories. That formalism extracts physics, symmetries, conserved charges, and entropy from a theory's Lagrangian while keeping covariance manifest. xCPS builds on the xAct tensor algebra system to automate calculations people grind through by hand.

Starting from a generic Lagrangian, the package derives the equations of motion and the symplectic currents. It tests whether an infinitesimal transformation of the fields is a Noether symmetry and computes its charge. In many cases it can decide whether an expression is a divergence and find its divergence potential. Using a graded, supercommutative wedge product for vertical exterior calculus, xCPS supports work in gauge theories and higher-derivative gravity models, including Wald's entropy for black holes. The package comes under the GPL license.
arxiv-2606-05304:
Chen Huang, Yuhao Wu, and Wenxuan Zhang ask what agents in a multi-agent system should say to one another in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such systems are usually designed around roles, pipelines, and turn schedules, while message content is left as unconstrained language.

The authors analyzed five common inter-agent communication strategies across two system topologies. No fixed strategy is universally best, but effective messages consistently preserve the action-centered information downstream agents need. Their proposal, PACT, treats communication as a state-update problem: each agent output is projected into a compact action-state record before entering the shared history. Across topologies, PACT improved the performance-cost trade-off, reaching comparable or stronger task results with fewer tokens. In production coding harnesses it lifted the OpenHands resolve rate while cutting tokens per resolved task by ten percent. On SWE-agent it halved input tokens at equal resolve rates.
arxiv-2606-06104:
Chen Hu and colleagues measure distances between brain-signal correlation patterns with a geometry built for the job in a 2026 arXiv paper, presented at KDD 2026. EEG pipelines favor spread-based descriptors, but channel scaling distorts them. Full-rank versions avoid that distortion and live on a curved manifold. The framework defines sliced-Wasserstein gaps on curved spaces carrying pullback Euclidean metrics.

Two versions follow, under two recent geometries. Slicing reduces the costly transport problem to many small ones. On top sits a method for decoding across shifting data, the everyday reality of EEG work. Three EEG datasets tested the approach. Performance under data shift improved over baselines. Training overhead stayed low, and inference cost nothing extra at all. Comparing correlation structure this way, the authors argue, extracts signal that scaling-sensitive features smear away. Brain-computer interfaces and hospital screening both need that robustness.
arxiv-2606-06204:
Mengyan Li and co-authors build a testing hierarchy for quantum states in this 2026 arXiv paper. Some families of quantum states admit a classical explanation, meaning ordinary chance based models with commuting measurements can mimic them. Telling whether a given family has that property decides whether it offers any real quantum advantage. The authors turn the question into a chain of computable tests.

Their tool is a semidefinite programming hierarchy, a ladder of convex optimization problems that grow steadily more exact. The key move recasts the question as whether set response rules and special measurements called POVMs can reproduce the family. The hierarchy also produces witnesses, certificates that prove a family is not classically simulable when the tests fail. Applied to states mixed with depolarizing noise, it bounds the critical noise level from above, matching direct classical simulations in several examples.
arxiv-2606-06304:
Kauser Zulfiqar and co-authors map the vibration modes of magnetic skyrmions in a two layer material in this 2026 arXiv paper. A skyrmion is a tiny swirling knot of magnetization that can store or carry information. In a synthetic antiferromagnet, two magnetic layers hold opposite skyrmions coupled against each other. How such pairs wobble when excited, their eigenmodes, decides how fast and reliably devices could use them.

Using eigenvalue and ringdown simulations, the team varied container shape and layer thickness. A single layer skyrmion has a spinning gyrotropic mode and a pulsing breathing mode at the lowest frequencies. In square confinement the bilayer showed two nearly matched gyrotropic modes, both layers rotating the same way. In rectangles, opposite rotation senses combined into nearly straight line translation. Chains supported standing wave patterns, plus breathing where the layers pulse out of phase. Signals traveled along chains at speeds rivaling single layer ones.
arxiv-2606-06604:
Alain Connes and Caterina Consani build a geometric home for the integers in this 2026 arXiv paper on arithmetic geometry. Spec Z, the spectrum of the integers, behaves like a curve with a point for every prime. Peter Scholze's p adic geometry suggests its points over perfectoid fields are classified by untilts, lifts from positive characteristic. The authors construct an absolute version of this curve over the mythical field with one element.

They show this curve is a common geometric origin for structures in p adic Hodge theory, complex geometry, and the adelic scaling site. Its moduli space over any perfectoid field parameterizes all perfectoid fields sharing that field's tilt. That realizes Scholze's heuristic concretely, independent of characteristic. Over the complex numbers, the nontrivial points at each prime form torsors over the local Weil groups.
arxiv-2606-07204:
Alhassan recovers sharp images from microscope data in this 2026 arXiv diploma thesis, written at the Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics. The method is 4D scanning transmission electron microscopy: a focused beam scans a specimen and records a diffraction pattern at each point. Those patterns hide phase, the shift the specimen imposes on the wave, which normal images lose.

The thesis explains ptychography, which rebuilds phase by combining overlapping patterns. It compares direct methods with iterative ones, including the extended iterative engine and Wigner distribution deconvolution. With an original Python script, the author applied the simpler single side-band method to simulated data for a molybdenum disulfide monolayer. The result gave amplitude and phase images. The work also reports real 4D data recorded on an actual microscope.
arxiv-2606-07404:
Shravan reports training a language model with over 100 billion parameters on a single 8-GPU node in this 2026 arXiv systems paper. The model family, LightningLM, grows in four stages from a dense seed through larger sparse mixture-of-experts versions, where only a subset of expert subnetworks activates per token. Each stage inherits the previous stage's trained weights instead of starting over. The final model stores about 119 billion parameters but activates under 6 billion at a time.

Three disciplines made the single-node feat possible, the author argues. A reversible architecture recomputes activations during backpropagation instead of storing them, holding memory flat as the model grows. State-preserving growth treats each expansion as keeping a learned interface intact, with named failure modes for getting it wrong, several of them silent. Finally, quantized expert weights with trained low-rank adapters cut memory further. The released training loss reached about 1.78 at full scale.
arxiv-2606-07604:
Cunningham and Cirone show that the attention weights used to interpret language models mislead, and offer a geometric replacement, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Attention weights show where a model looks, but influence also depends on the size and direction of the value vectors being mixed, which weights ignore. Their contribution weights project each token's effect onto the layer's output, combining attention, value magnitude, and directional alignment into one faithful measure.

Across several decoder-only models, tasks, and datasets, contribution weights identified critical tokens better than weight-based metrics. The metric also reframes attention sinks, the first tokens that absorb huge mass. Rather than passive overflow tanks, sinks actively suppress information: their rate relates convexly to output norm, steadying representations by opposing the semantic drift of low-confidence tokens. A striking case shows tokens receiving enormous weight while adding almost nothing to the output, a discrepancy invisible without the correction.
arxiv-2606-07804:
Anwer and co-authors present QIRL, an intrusion detector for vehicles, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Connected cars exchange messages constantly, which enlarges the attack surface for safety-critical services. Static defences cannot adapt when attackers change behaviour across multi-stage campaigns, and attack classes are heavily imbalanced in real traffic.

QIRL frames detection as a Markov decision process, a sequence of decisions with costs and rewards, and learns with a lightweight deep Q-network. Its design borrows quantum ideas: states use amplitude and phase, exploration uses rotation gates, and rewards gain an interference-like term. Training-only synthetic balancing and asymmetric costs handle the imbalance without leaking into test data. On the CICIDS2017 and UNSW-NB15 benchmarks, accuracy reached about ninety-eight and ninety-one percent. F1 scores, balancing missed attacks against false alarms, were about ninety-five and ninety-two percent, and each verdict took tens of microseconds.
arxiv-2606-08004:
Yi-Hua Dong and co-authors argue that metastable phases are not missing from phase diagrams, just hidden off the real axis, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A metastable phase is an energetically unfavourable state, like supercooled liquid, that equilibrium diagrams suppress. Lee-Yang zeros are points in the complex plane where the partition function vanishes. Their pattern near the real axis signals phase transitions.

The team shows numerically, in a toy model and a periodically driven system, that regions bounded by Lee-Yang zeros correspond to metastable phases. As parameters or drive amplitudes grow, the bounding zeros approach the real axis and split into branches. That marks the metastable phase emerging in the gap between two stable phases. In the driven system the zeros' imaginary part tracks the drive strength. Viewing drives as complex thermal fields gives a new handle for engineering non-equilibrium states.
arxiv-2606-08204:
Urbano and colleagues propose a new way to turn continuous signals into compact token sets in this 2026 arXiv paper. A neural field represents data such as an image or a climate map as a function from coordinates to values. The usual way to encode such fields retrains a small network for every sample, which is slow and memory hungry. Their framework, LH-NeF, instead builds in two general priors: locality, that nearby points relate, and hierarchy, that structure exists at several scales.

A hierarchical encoder groups nearby observations and processes them with attention, producing ordered tokens from which the field can be rebuilt. The method used about forty-two times less memory than the strongest comparable baseline and allowed far larger batches in training runs reported here. Across images, three-dimensional shapes, and climate fields, its representations matched or beat both general and specialized rivals on reconstruction and later tasks.
arxiv-2606-08404:
Moo Chung, Maccotta, and Struck model the folding of the brain's surface as a flowing field in this 2026 arXiv paper. Cortical folding reflects coordinated development and is increasingly read as a sensitive marker of brain disease. Most analyses reduce folding to indirect scalar summaries that never model the geometry itself. In juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, a common genetic epilepsy, cortical abnormalities are often subtle, spread out, and hard to detect with standard measures.

The authors introduce a framework based on the Poisson equation, a classical equation linking a field to its sources. Folding patterns are treated as a stationary source-sink structure derived from mean curvature, the local bending of the cortical surface. This yields a smooth, globally balanced potential field. The surface gradient of that field defines a physically interpretable flux, a flow across the folds. This view supports coherent analysis of how ridges and grooves are organized.
arxiv-2606-08504:
Scursulim designs quantum circuits that respect optimization constraints by construction, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Combinatorial optimization can be attacked with variational quantum algorithms, where a parameterized circuit, called an ansatz, searches for the best solution. Two challenges dominate: the ansatz must explore the feasible subspace where valid solutions live, and penalty terms that punish infeasibility require tuning. Scursulim's ansatz eliminates the penalties entirely by encoding the constraints into the quantum state itself.

The proposal is the first feasibility-preserving mixed Dicke state ansatz for Hamming-weight-constrained problems, where solutions must contain an exact or bounded number of ones. Pure Dicke states, symmetric superpositions of all bit strings with a fixed weight, handle equality constraints and appear as a special case. The mixed version handles inequality constraints as well. Because every state the circuit can produce is feasible, the optimizer spends all its effort on solution quality.
arxiv-2606-08604:
Tikhonovich and colleagues unify two halves of generative recommendation in one design in this 2026 arXiv paper. Generative retrieval has become a scalable approach to candidate generation in industrial recommender systems. Each item receives a short token sequence called a semantic ID. The next item's ID is decoded autoregressively, like words in a sentence. A practical limitation is that beam search optimizes the likelihood of token sequences, not the relevance of the underlying items.

Their system, Gryphon, generates semantic IDs and scores items at the item level within one model. Retrieval and relevance ranking thus stop working at cross purposes. Items that share an ID can be distinguished by the item-level scoring. The work targets industrial use, where candidate generation must scan enormous catalogs fast and well. In short, the model both finds the items and grades them, all in one pass over the catalog.
arxiv-2606-08704:
Chivers-White and Stokes rebuild a foundational theory of light-matter interaction with its loose ends tied, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Non-relativistic quantum electrodynamics describes how atoms interact with light. Its multipolar form is a central framework in the field. The theory can be written in different gauges, and the standard forms carry ultraviolet divergences and gauge ambiguities that practitioners manage informally. The authors develop a regularised arbitrary-gauge formulation, with a Lorentzian form factor cutting off the high frequencies.

Within the regularised theory they compare the Coulomb and multipolar descriptions. They also analyze how regularisation affects perturbation theory. The regularised multipolar gauge shows a trade-off between the strength of interaction terms and the localization of material subsystems. The work gives the field a clean base on which hard short-range questions can be asked with care.
arxiv-2606-08904:
Mo and colleagues show that the order in which a chip's large blocks are placed matters as much as where they go, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Macro placement arranges the big functional blocks on a chip canvas, and early choices trigger domino effects that constrain everything placed later. Designers traditionally ordered blocks by static heuristics based on area or connectivity. Their framework, OrderPlace, evolves ordering strategies automatically, using a language model to propose code-level policies.

Candidate policies range from static scoring rules to dynamic, physics-inspired mechanisms. Judging each candidate fully would be too slow, so a lightweight proxy, a deterministic greedy probe, filters the field. On the standard ISPD 2005 benchmarks, the discovered strategies cut total wirelength by 34.04 percent compared with WireMask-EA. Against EGPlace, the state-of-the-art method, the reduction was 14.08 percent. The results recast sequencing as a searchable design dimension, not a fixed habit.
arxiv-2606-09204:
Paeng finds that attacking a safety-trained AI recommender can backfire, erasing the target brand entirely, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In retrieval-augmented recommendation, corpus documents enter the model's context. Attackers hide prompt injections, manipulative instructions, in documents to promote a brand. Paeng calls the failure mode the Injection Paradox: in safety-trained Claude models, one injected document spreads suppression to the brand's clean documents.

In Claude Opus 4.6 the brand fell from a 54 percent baseline to zero top-two recommendations in all 50 trials, though only one of its four documents held an injection. Counterfactuals and tests across 3 brands reproduced the pattern. GPT models behaved oppositely, the same injection increasing recommendations: model families differ sharply here. Hence a reverse attack: inject a competitor's documents and let the model's safety training suppress them. Code and per-trial records are promised public.
arxiv-2606-09304:
Xu and colleagues fix a quiet assumption inside on-policy distillation, the training scheme where a student learns from a stronger teacher's feedback on its own attempts, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The scheme works only if the student's trajectories stay aligned with the teacher's and if the teacher's per-token preferences are uniformly reliable, and both often break. SG-OPD brings in a binary verifier, a checker that simply marks answers right or wrong, as a trust signal at two levels.

Phased teacher sampling mixes verifier-endorsed teacher rollouts into the cold start, then fades out. A sign-consistency gate then extrapolates the distillation update on tokens where teacher and verifier agree, and interpolates where they conflict. On competition-level mathematics benchmarks, SG-OPD beat standard on-policy distillation consistently. Average gains reached 1.98 points per sample and 7.50 points per question, sizable margins at this level.
arxiv-2606-09404:
Timo Heiß and his colleagues introduce Sails, a method for explaining how features interact inside a machine learning model, in this 2026 arXiv paper. An interaction means the effect of one feature on a prediction depends on another feature, like temperature mattering differently on weekends. Existing explanation tools can flag that an interaction exists, or picture only narrow cases, but rarely show its actual shape.

Sails fits an interpretable surrogate, a simpler stand-in model, to the local effects of the black-box model it explains. The surrogate uses generalised additive model smooths, flexible curves whose terms isolate each pair's interaction. The pairs are then sorted into linear, product-separable, and non-product-separable forms, each with its own chart. Controlled simulations and a real-world task validated the approach. Its weak spots are strongly correlated features and interactions involving more than two features at once.
arxiv-2606-09604:
Stefano Menchiari and his co-authors model the Milky Way's neutrino glow, adding a source class that past maps left out in this 2026 arXiv paper. Neutrinos are near-massless particles that pass through almost all matter. IceCube has now caught a soft glow of them from the galactic plane. Past models blamed space-filling cosmic rays hitting gas along the plane.

The new model adds massive star clusters and the dead-star blasts inside them. Cosmic rays gain speed at the joint wind shock of a cluster's stars and at supernova shocks. The team built many fake cluster sets that match local star counts, then summed their output. Lone clusters sit near the edge of what even a cubic-kilometre detector can see. Their summed glow thus hides inside the diffuse haze. The total fits IceCube's best match for known maps.
arxiv-2606-09704:
Han-Pu Liang and his co-authors probe why a disordered solar material keeps its good electronic traits in this 2026 arXiv paper. The material is AgBiS2, a lead-free pick for light-based devices. Its silver and bismuth ions swap sites freely, yet the band edges stay usefully spread. Which ordered form is the true base, and what guards the edges, stayed debated.

The team paired a learned force model with a learned Hamiltonian, a quantum energy map, to track huge samples. Both tools let structure and electron states evolve side by side. A three-dimensional web of bismuth-sulfur bonds emerged as the key motif. It steadies the disordered form and shapes the band-edge states. At weak disorder, silver-bismuth swaps fight the silver ions' urge to sit off-centre. That clash bends local shapes and blurs diffraction signs, which explains past lab puzzles.
arxiv-2606-09804:
Xin-Chen He and his co-authors show that fading black holes stamp a shared fade on the waves they stir in this 2026 arXiv paper. Primordial black holes may have formed in the young universe and ruled its energy for a spell. As they evaporate by Hawking radiation, the shift back to a radiation age sources a sea of gravitational waves. Past work often gave all holes one mass, which makes them vanish at once.

Real groups span a range of masses, so they thin out over time. The team shows the late tale of any such group is ruled by the evaporation law, not by its first mass spread. That rule forces a set power-law dip in the wave spectrum. The link ties the far wave tail straight to how holes shed mass.
arxiv-2606-09904:
Ying studies when solutions of rough differential equations stay finite forever, in a 2026 arXiv paper on stochastic analysis. Rough equations describe systems driven by very irregular signals, and branched versions organize the driver's effects with tree-like structures. Earlier work allowed unbounded coefficients, the functions setting drift and response, but questions about explosion, where solutions blow up in finite time, remained open in this setting.

Ying provides a non-explosion criterion for branched rough equations with unbounded drift and rough coefficients. He characterizes pure area branched rough paths, paths sitting over the zero path, and uses them to build two constructions that do explode in finite time. Those examples prove the criterion is sharp, meaning it cannot be loosened in general. A final principle trades coefficient growth against decay of higher derivatives, allowing even faster growth than earlier results while still preventing explosion.
arxiv-2606-10004:
Cao and colleagues show that almost any quantum dynamics can be rewritten to look local, in a 2026 arXiv paper on quantum theory. Locality here means particles interact mainly with near neighbors on a lattice, so wave packets can travel in an orderly way. A Hamiltonian, the operator encoding a system's energy and evolution, may look highly non-local in one operator basis.

The team demonstrates the idea by turning a highly non-local random matrix model into a local one-dimensional lattice theory where particles propagate as localized wave packets. More generally, they show any Hamiltonian can be cast in this form, with the lattice dispersion relation and the theory's non-integrability set by the original spectrum. They frame the results as a step toward quantum mereology for fields, the study of how parts compose wholes in quantum systems.
arxiv-2606-10304:
Revankar and his team discover an internal signal that reveals when a language model agent is encoding stolen data in secret, in a 2026 arXiv paper on AI security. When agents are coerced into covertly encoding private data, through Base64, letter swaps, acrostics, or synonym chains, the outputs evade surface detection, but the computation leaves traces. Across nine encoding families and eight models from five design families, that process is supported by a shared narrow subspace in the model's residual stream.

The same direction shows a second signature at the planning token: its polarity flips based on whether the model will perform the encoding inline or outsource it to a tool call. That reveals the plan before any encoded text exists. Their monitor, Mirage, exploits both signals in real time. On one hundred twenty-six agentic exfiltration scenarios it far outperformed output-only detection.
arxiv-2606-10504:
Tran and co-authors study knowledge distillation across data types in this 2026 arXiv paper. A large teacher model trained on one modality, such as images, guides a smaller student working on another, such as audio or text. Existing methods usually need paired data, matched examples from both modalities, which are costly or impossible to collect. The authors build theory for the unpaired setting, identifying two governing quantities: feature alignment between internal representations, and label alignment between predictions.

The resulting framework, UCMKD, aligns distributions rather than individual samples, and comes with both infinite-sample and finite-sample guarantees for the student. A meta-learning style optimisation puts the two alignments into practice. Experiments on benchmarks including AVE, RAVDESS, CREMA-D, and VGGSound show consistent gains over prior work with no paired data. The method also stays competitive in the easier paired setting.
arxiv-2606-10904:
Nutfullin, Evgrafov, and Namiot compare quick defenses for multimodal language models in this 2026 arXiv paper. Image inputs open attack routes that text safety training only partly covers, and retraining for each new attack class is too costly. The team tests three inference-time defenses and their combinations on eight InternVL and Qwen-VL models across seven safety benchmarks totaling 9,000 samples.

No single defense wins everywhere: the best choice depends on the model's baseline safety and the attack type. Stacking defenses backfires, pushing refusal of harmless queries to between 97 and 100 percent. A simple safety prompt is the mildest option, with moderate gains and over-refusal of at most about 18 percent.
arxiv-2606-11004:
Zhang and colleagues revisit a replication question in education data mining in this 2026 arXiv paper. Knowledge tracing models predict a student's growing mastery from practice history. A 2021 study found deep models shine early, when a student starts a skill: the cold-start edge. The team reruns the analysis on a newer ASSISTments dataset, FoundationalASSIST, and extends it across problem types.

The cold-start pattern holds: deep models again predict best in the first attempts at a skill. Performance also varies by problem type, from multiple choice to ordering tasks, so averages alone mislead. The study doubles as a proof of concept for SafeInsights, a privacy-preserving infrastructure meant to make such replications routine.
arxiv-2606-11104:
Grohs and Trödler prove a hard limit on learning tanh neural networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Real computers compute with finite precision, rounding every number. They ask what accuracy any algorithm can guarantee when it sees only finitely many point evaluations of a target function from a tanh network class, error measured in an Lp norm.

Their tool is a new construction of sharply localized bump functions from iterated tanh activations, spikes hiding between sample points. With such bumps in the class, no adaptive randomized algorithm using m samples can beat the Monte Carlo rate. That means error shrinking like one over the p-th root of m, unless the sampling budget grows exponentially in network size. The result extends earlier ReLU limits to the tanh setting. Finite precision itself caps what can be learned here.
arxiv-2606-11304:
Joschka Birk and five co-authors present SPADE in a 2026 arXiv paper, an autoregressive transformer for sequences whose tokens carry multiple features. Standard practice embeds them jointly. SPADE, Split And Delay Embeddings, instead embeds each feature independently. Delaying each stream relative to the previous one lets ordinary self-attention learn within-token correlations.

The test bed is point-cloud calorimeter shower generation in the granular ILD detector, where fast simulation matters because full Monte Carlo is compute-hungry. SPADE proved competitive with the state-of-the-art AllShowers model on photon showers. It substantially outperformed its VQ-VAE-based predecessor OmniJet-alpha-C, and eliminates training that VQ-VAE entirely. Against a Combined model merging coordinates into one number, SPADE scales easily to higher granularities without parameter inflation. The mechanism applies to any generative task with multi-feature tokens, enabling LLM-style pretraining for higher-dimensional data.
arxiv-2606-11404:
Hyodo, Wakita, and Johnson simulate micrometeoroid impacts on icy bodies in a 2026 arXiv paper. In the outer Solar System, gravity attracts micrometeoroids, generating hypervelocity impacts on rings and satellites. Impactors are seemingly rocky, targets typically icy, and both may span wide porosities. They ran 3D iSALE simulations of rocky impactors hitting icy targets at thirty kilometers per second, characteristic of Saturn's rings.

They varied impact angle and porosities, using end members of zero and ninety percent for forty-five-degree impacts. Early crater morphology varies with porosity. A dense impactor on a ninety-percent-porous target drives deep, narrow-channel cavities. A ninety-percent-porous impactor on a dense target makes shallow craters driven by near-surface vapor blowoff. Comparable porosities give intermediate, hemispherical cavities. The impactor is heated and efficiently vaporized regardless of porosity, though its peak pressure and temperature vary by an order of magnitude.
arxiv-2606-11704:
Zhihao Zhou leads a large team testing a powered exoskeleton for divers in this 2026 arXiv paper. Swimming is energetically expensive for humans, and a diver's endurance is capped by the breathing gas they carry. Exoskeletons cut the metabolic cost of walking on land, but their use underwater was unexplored. The team's DiveMate is untethered and field-deployable, giving adaptive help with each kick.

In open-water diving trials, the results are large. Divers cover about forty-three percent more distance on the same gas, and dive duration grows by about fifty-five percent. Net gas consumption falls by forty-seven percent. Muscle activation drops markedly, confirming divers exert themselves less rather than merely kicking differently. Movement also becomes more regular. The authors present DiveMate as the first demonstration that exoskeletons can extend diving endurance, and a reference design for future underwater devices.
arxiv-2606-11804:
Yuefang Lian and seven colleagues attack and defend the data summaries that feed AI systems in this 2026 arXiv paper. Summarisation sits upstream: it decides which information survives into later learning and decisions. An adversary who perturbs the similarity structure behind a summary can quietly degrade everything downstream.

The authors formulate multi-resolution image summarisation objectives as DR-submodular functions, a class with diminishing returns that supports approximation guarantees. They allow one admissible perturbation to degrade several target models at once, cast as a min-max problem. The defence is a regularised max-min problem against mixed attack types. Both sides get algorithms with theoretical guarantees. Experiments on real data and controlled clustered benchmarks show the attack works in low-to-moderate budget regimes and causes downstream task losses. The defence improves the robustness-utility trade-off in structured settings, though its protection on real data is sensitive to parameter choices.
arxiv-2606-11904:
Hao-Kun Ke and five colleagues describe a heat-driven diode with unusual one-way behaviour in this 2026 arXiv paper. A thermoelectric diode turns a temperature gap into current mostly in one way. Here the effect is driven by electron-phonon interaction, electrons trading energy with lattice vibrations, in the device centre.
