The one-way behaviour is intrinsic: forward and backward electron transport stay asymmetric even when the temperature gap is not reversed.

It stems from the unequal chances of phonon emission and absorption, plus structural reflection asymmetry. One novel phenomenon is a heat-driven effect powered by the temperature gap between the leads and the device region. The other blocks electron backscattering in the load resistor, lowering its resistance. Under suitable conditions the interaction yields a larger current than no interaction at all, with no superconductivity or magnetic fields needed.
arxiv-2606-12104:
Hložný and Milivojević map the exotic superconducting phases that a twist can create in layered materials, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their stack pairs graphene, a single sheet of carbon atoms, with niobium diselenide, a superconductor, in a van der Waals heterostructure, meaning layers held together by weak attraction. Rotating one layer by about twenty-three degrees lowers the shared symmetry. Superconductivity leaks into the graphene by proximity, a neighbor effect where pairing crosses the boundary.

Using the Bogoliubov-de Gennes formalism with parameters from first-principles calculations, the authors build every gap function the lowered symmetry allows. These gap functions mix singlet and triplet pairing, two ways electron pairs can align their spins. Channels that keep time-reversal symmetry stay topologically plain. Channels that break that symmetry produce a rich phase diagram of chiral topological phases, labeled by Chern numbers of minus four, minus two, two, and four.
arxiv-2606-12204:
Pei and co-authors trace how one missing electron reshapes magnetism on a kagome lattice, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The kagome lattice is a pattern of corner-sharing triangles, frustrated because neighbors cannot all align at once. The host is a doped Mott insulator, where strong repulsion freezes electrons until a few are removed. The study follows a single hole, one missing electron, as spin polarization drops from nearly full to none.

Near full polarization, the hole spreads by binding flipped spins into singlet bonds, paired spins pointing oppositely. The authors call this object an RVB polaron. Its effective bandwidth, the energy range it can move through, is extremely small, so it traps itself. Toward zero polarization, antiferromagnetic correlations in an enlarged repeating cell take over. These echo classical Potts and Heisenberg models on the same lattice, linking short-scale pairing to long-scale order.
arxiv-2606-12704:
Tompa and colleagues compare ways to fine-tune foundation models that predict interatomic forces, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A machine-learned interatomic potential, or MLIP, estimates energies and forces between atoms so teams can simulate materials without heavy quantum work. Foundation versions are pretrained broadly, then fine-tuned, meaning adapted with extra training, for a specific chemical system. Guidance on which strategy to use has been scattered.

The team tests 7 strategies, from full retraining of everything to layer freezing, low-rank adaptation, and replay methods that rehearse old data. Trials span 5 chemically diverse benchmarks, 3 generations of foundation models, and training sets of 5 to about 950,000 cases. They find prerequisites matter more than strategy: a good foundation model, correct atomic reference energies, and sound settings outweigh the choice among methods. Naive fine-tuning converges best for single systems, while multihead replay alone always preserves broader robustness.
arxiv-2606-12804:
Inahama defines a spectral distance between compact sub-Riemannian manifolds, extending a classical Riemannian construction to spaces where motion is allowed only along restricted directions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sub-Riemannian geometry studies such limited spaces, where the natural volume, called Popp's volume, is fixed by the geometry itself. Because of this, the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the div-grad sub-Laplacian, the analogue of the Laplace operator, should carry shape information.

Inahama embeds the manifold into the Hilbert space of square-summable series using the sub-Laplacian's eigenfunctions, weighted by their eigenvalues. The spectral distance between 2 manifolds is then defined through the Hausdorff distance between their images, minimised over all choices of eigenfunction bases. The main result is that this value is a genuine distance: it vanishes exactly when the 2 sub-Riemannian manifolds are isometric.
arxiv-2606-12904:
Nakayashiki and Watanabe ask whether a reader's highlighting signature is a durable trait or a passing state, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Here each reader's first 6 months of highlighting are frozen as a profile, and its advantage in predicting that reader's later selections is tracked at time gaps out to 24 months.

The advantage, measured against negatives from the reader's own interest neighbourhood, shows no detectable decline at any horizon: retention over 6 to 12 months is 1.00, with a confidence interval from 0.85 to 1.18 across 212 readers. About 90 percent of the signal survives after excluding all sources the profile was built from, so it is not just repeated domains. Within-person drift is slow. Profiles built from a reader's earliest documents, a median of 20 months before evaluation, rank their next reads at roughly 3 times the average precision of non-personal priors tested.
arxiv-2606-13004:
Asensio Ramos and colleagues present 3DStokesFlow, a simulation-based inference framework that rebuilds the 3D structure of the solar atmosphere from Stokes profiles, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reading the state from polarised light data is ill-posed: noise and degeneracies make pixel-by-pixel inversion codes slow, while machine-learning Bayesian methods work only in 1-dimensional setups and ignore spatial links between pixels.

It uses conditional flow matching, a generative strategy. Multi-scale spatial patterns are pulled from the iron line pair at 630 nanometres. Those features condition a generative model that samples the spread of atmospheric parameters. It is trained on 3D quiet-Sun magnetohydrodynamic runs. Checks on synthetic data show the model captures the 3D stratification of all thermodynamic and magnetic fields. Applied to Hinode/SP data, it finds focused electric currents at magnetic boundaries.
arxiv-2606-13104:
Khurana and colleagues present AuthorityBench, a benchmark tracking how citation-based authority signals distort language models' behaviour, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Models are now widely deployed in citation-augmented settings, but whether a citation's presence changes how a model treats a claim, independent of factual content, was poorly understood. The benchmark uses a balanced 2-by-2 factorial design crossing claim veracity with citation veracity, the first benchmark to separate those 2 factors.

The benchmark contains 220,564 prompts across 4 domains, general knowledge, science, law, and medicine, with spread over 40 templates, 4 venue prestige tiers, and an author name dataset. Testing 7 models, the authors find that citation presence, whether the citation is real or fabricated, raises hallucination rates relative to a no-citation baseline. The effect is strongest when fabricated citations accompany true claims. That raises hallucination by 3 to 22 percentage points and reaches 35 to 77 percent in the general knowledge domain, while legal claims are robust.
arxiv-2606-13204:
Yin and colleagues propose CoDeR, a dense retrieval method that splits topical relevance from constraint compatibility, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Retrieval systems treat semantic similarity as a proxy for relevance, but for constraint-sensitive queries the proxy fails. A document can be topically close while backing the opposite constraint. It may satisfy an attribute the user wanted excluded or affirm a relation they wanted negated. The authors call this failure constraint-violating evidence exposure.

CoDeR keeps a topical encoder and adds a compatibility scorer, a bi-encoder trained on satisfying and violating evidence. The compatibility signal can rescore candidates or retrieve a matching candidate set, giving the ranking with no large language model calls at inference time. On 3 diagnostic sets targeting antonymy, negation, and exclusion, CoDeR reduced the rate of violating hits in the top 2 results by 20.59, 23.53, and 5.77 points relative to the non-CoDeR baselines.
arxiv-2606-13404:
Gestsson and Olaya-Castro develop a way to measure how quantum coherence drives energy transfer in this 2026 arXiv paper. When light excites a molecule, the energy moves between sites, and wavelike superpositions called coherences may speed or steer that motion. Despite much debate, a tool for assigning coherence its share of the transfer rate has been missing. The authors use Nakajima-Zwanzig projection tools, a method that separates a system's motion from its environment's memory effects. From it they derive a memory kernel identity, a relation isolating its contribution.

The identity yields a rate of transfer with the coherence term made explicit. They apply the approach to a dimer, two coupled sites, interacting with a phonon bath, the vibrations of the material around it. The calculation shows how coherence in the energy basis changes the transfer. The framework offers a dial for a quantity previously discussed only in words.
arxiv-2606-13504:
Boubakour, Szikman, and Elouard give a thermodynamics for quantum master equations in this 2026 arXiv paper. Master equations describe how an open quantum system relaxes through contact with its environment. When some frequencies are too small, the secular approximation fails, and two repairs apply: the partial secular and the geometric-arithmetic approximations. Both keep the dynamics valid, but the system relaxes to a state that is not the Gibbs state of its Hamiltonian. Naive thermodynamics would break down.

Starting from a second-law expression that includes system-environment correlations, the authors use perturbation theory to keep the entropy production positive despite the approximations. A finding is that the interaction energy between system and bath enters the balance even at weak coupling, alongside the Lamb shift. These contributions appear as work the system performs on the bath. The framework lets researchers discuss heat, work, and efficiency for a class of dynamics.
arxiv-2606-13604:
Wu, Hou, and Xie describe a learning system that tunes a food-delivery marketplace in this 2026 arXiv paper. Dispatch in a three-sided marketplace, joining customers, couriers, and merchants, is judged by outcomes such as delivery speed, courier utilisation, and merchant congestion. They present a deployed reinforcement learning system at DoorDash that adapts dispatch weights at store level. Rather than replacing the assignment optimiser, a learned policy picks a multiplier that shifts its trade-off between delivery quality and batching efficiency. That interface keeps production constraints and safeguards intact.

The policy is learned offline from logged marketplace data, so no risky live exploration is needed. A shared value function is trained centrally while execution stays decentralised across stores, using conservative double Q-learning targets to tame noisy, delayed feedback. The work is a case study in adding reinforcement learning to a production system: change the weights, not the machinery.
arxiv-2606-13704:
Pérez-Ortiz argues that AI must be designed for the planet, not only for people, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The paper introduces Planet-Centered AI as a design philosophy. It is grounded in systems thinking, treating Earth as an interconnected whole. The author diagnoses limitations across current AI frameworks, most of which remain human-centered. He shows why those limits become serious under planetary conditions marked by systemic risk, non-stationarity, and doubt. Optimising human objectives can unsettle the systems those objectives depend on.

The paper sets out how a planet-centered approach reshapes the AI lifecycle, from problem framing and model design to evaluation and deployment. It emphasises alignment with global agendas, system-aware thinking, and evaluation over time. It advances a falsifiable claim: systems optimised without regard for systemic consequences will fail global goals. Position papers of this kind aim to redirect research agendas.
arxiv-2606-13804:
Keila Lucas and colleagues test a large language model at detecting flaws in manual software test cases in this 2026 arXiv paper. Manual testing, where testers follow natural-language instructions, remains essential for issues automation misses. But manual test cases often contain test smells: quality problems such as ambiguity, redundancy, or missing checks that undermine reliability. Existing detectors depend on hand-engineered rules and generalise poorly across test suites. The authors' earlier work assessed small language models on test steps from real-world Ubuntu test cases spanning seven smell types.

This study asks whether a large model, a current Gemini flagship preview, does better. Scaling from small to large models is not guaranteed to help a classification task of this kind, and the cost difference is large. The comparison gives testing teams evidence for procurement decisions: whether flagship-model detection justifies its price for keeping test suites clean.
arxiv-2606-13904:
Wijaya and colleagues build a diagnostic tool that shows exactly where question-answering agents over data lakes go wrong. Such agents must find relevant tables in a huge lake, plan an analysis, and compute an answer. One accuracy score cannot say whether search, planning, analysis, or moment-to-moment choices failed. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents SANA, which rebuilds tasks into runtime profiles and swaps in ideal versions of each part in turn.

Applied to the LakeQA and KramaBench benchmarks, the diagnosis differed by setting. Data analysis was a consistent bottleneck on both: agents reaching the right sources still failed to carry out the needed computation. Search was a major limit in LakeQA's large lake but minor in smaller KramaBench. Planning was least limiting; agents drafted sound plans yet often failed to follow them. Even with all parts idealized, a residual gap remained, pointing to the agents' action policies.
arxiv-2606-14004:
Meza, Ferrer, and Riera extract pure melody-of-speech representations ignoring who talks and what is said. Prosody, the rhythm and tune of speech, carries emotion and helps resolve meaning. Big self-supervised speech models mix prosody with speaker identity and word content, which breaks when those factors shift. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds autoencoders of just pitch and energy signals, producing global prosodic embeddings, one summary vector per utterance.

The team compared recurrent and transformer autoencoders, trained by standard or masked reconstruction. They built a benchmark of three tasks under three protocols of rising difficulty, testing whether embeddings preserve prosody while shrugging off speaker and content changes. Their embeddings proved robust to such mismatches versus audio-based methods. They also retained at least as much prosodic information as rival purely prosodic embeddings. Uses include speech synthesis input and measuring prosody's role in a task.
arxiv-2606-14604:
Nicolaou and co-authors compare deep learning models for forecasting health behavior in a 2026 arXiv study. Wearables and phones produce rich daily series like step counts, screen time, and sleep, which could trigger proactive health support. Yet nobody had systematically compared modern forecasting architectures on such data, across populations, personalization levels, and multi-day horizons.

The team benchmarked six architectures, two zero-shot foundation models, and statistical baselines on three public datasets covering over eight hundred participants, scoring forecasts from one to eight days ahead. No single architecture dominated: PatchTST led the trained models, with three runners-up statistically tied. The foundation model TimesFM matched or beat trained models without any training, especially with little data. Personal fine-tuning cut per-feature errors by roughly sixteen to sixty percent, helping sleep forecasts most and step counts least.
arxiv-2606-14804:
Das asks whether machines can make genuinely new math conjectures in a 2026 arXiv paper. A conjecture is a precise claim not yet proved. Automated discovery tools now propose claims at scale. But judging whether a claim is truly novel and non-trivial still falls to humans. The test case is the Birch test. It asks if a machine can find new, deep structures with no human help.

Das studies HypothesiX, an agent that mines conjectures. Its claims about twin primes are checked against the Birch test's demands. Twin primes are prime pairs two apart, like eleven and thirteen. The paper then proposes a numeric score for non-triviality. It measures how far a new claim sits from clusters of known conjectures in an embedding space. The score can also flag where a faulty claim goes wrong. That helps when proof-checking tools fail to verify it.
arxiv-2606-14904:
Lin and co-authors watch hollow pentagons stir themselves into motion in a 2026 arXiv paper. The pentagons form a single layer on a plate. Air flows upward through the plate, lifting them slightly. The airflow couples the particles, so each one's motion depends on its neighbors. Shape matters: hollow pentagons pull together, while solid ones push apart.

Under strong airflow, sparse hollow pentagons drift diffusively for long times, like particles in a thermal bath. Under weaker airflow, two states coexist. Some pentagons sit isolated and still. Others pack into dense clusters that move faster than diffusion allows. This emergent activity is collective: locally disordered clusters catch the airflow and move in correlated ways. Langevin simulations of attractive active pentagons reproduce the basic behavior. Their activity comes from local packing density, matching the experiment's picture.
arxiv-2606-15204:
Danchev and coauthors generalize a family of ring classes in a 2026 algebra paper. A ring's units are its invertible elements, and several recent classes tie units to special subsets. UQ rings require a unit power minus one to land in the quasi-nilpotent elements. The new n-UQ rings impose that condition with an arbitrary fixed exponent. The authors run a structural analysis of this broader class.

They test whether the class survives constructions like matrix rings and group rings. It also persists under trivial extensions and power series rings. New characterizations link n-UQ rings to reduced, clean, and exchange rings. Semi-regular and potent rings enter the picture as well. The authors prove the older n-UJ and n-UU classes sit strictly inside n-UQ. So one framework now covers several separate theories. The results clarify how unit behavior interacts with quasi-nilpotency in noncommutative rings.
arxiv-2606-15604:
Song adapts a general segmentation foundation model to radiotherapy planning in 2026, targeting the internal target volume drawn on four-dimensional CT scans. Such scans capture the full breathing cycle, but current contouring treats each phase alone, inviting phase-specific artifacts. Song fine-tunes Segment Anything Model 3 with low-rank adaptation, a parameter-efficient method, using only seven annotated volumes.

Hard negative mining sharpens boundary decisions in low-contrast chest regions, and at inference a phase-coherent filter exploits the fact that real anatomy persists across neighbouring phases while artifacts flicker. The system reaches median Dice scores of 0.968 on pulmonary and 0.910 on cardiac structures. It also wipes out the severe false positives that the unadapted model makes in zero-shot use. With seven volumes it keeps over ninety-five percent of full-data accuracy, and the pipeline trains on one consumer-grade GPU.
arxiv-2606-16504:
Zhao and co-authors insert a correction layer in 2026 between robot policies and their controllers, fixing commands that hardware cannot faithfully execute. Imitation-learned policies, including vision-language-action models, output high-level action references for low-level controllers. Missing higher-order reference signals, plus the policy's blindness to control dynamics during training, open an execution gap: realized actions drift systematically from commanded ones. For precision manipulation, that drift is decisive.

Their framework, APEX, treats both policy and controller as black boxes and sits between them, plug-and-play. A dynamic filter reconstructs the missing higher-order signals, producing a dynamically feasible reference. An online adaptive law then refines that reference from low-level state feedback, with a provable convergence guarantee. In tests, APEX raises replay success from 62.5 percent to 81.3 percent, per the report. Across four policy classes, from ACT to diffusion policies, it adds 4.8 to 25.8 percentage points.
arxiv-2606-16704:
Xi and colleagues study topological magnons in a frustrated magnet in 2026. A magnon is a wave of tilting spins moving through a magnetic material. Frustrated magnets have competing interactions that no spin pattern can satisfy, so at zero field there may be no clean state to expand around.

Their model places spins on a triangular lattice with Kitaev and off-diagonal exchange terms. A ground-state search plus spin-wave theory finds that an in-plane field selects a compact seven-site pattern with noncoplanar spins. That pattern hosts magnon bands whose Chern numbers, the integers marking band topology, can be tuned by the field. Raising the field drives two bands to touch and swap Berry curvature, flipping part of the Chern vector, and the thermal Hall response crosses near zero. About half the spectral weight sits on the topology-carrying bands, giving a way to spot them.
arxiv-2606-16904:
Agosti and colleagues tackle a backward problem for a coupled phase-field system in a 2026 paper on inverse problems. The system pairs a Cahn-Hilliard equation, which models how mixtures separate, with a reaction-diffusion equation. Running it backward means recovering earlier states from one observation at the final time.

Their main result is a Carleman estimate, a weighted energy inequality, for this fourth-order and second-order pair with cross-diffusion terms. From it they derive conditional stability bounds: Holder-type control of past states at positive times, and weaker logarithmic control of the starting state itself. Applied to a tumour growth model coupling tumour volume fraction with nutrient concentration, the estimate yields backward uniqueness and stability for early tumour states. It drops an earlier smallness restriction on the chemotaxis coefficient that biology rarely respects. The bounds also support fast convergence of iterative reconstruction algorithms on finite-dimensional sets.
arxiv-2606-17004:
Kashani, Tavasoli and Shakeri personalize automated insulin delivery in a 2026 paper on diabetes technology. Artificial pancreas systems dose insulin automatically, but they are tuned for an average patient. Real insulin needs swing with meals, activity and shifting sensitivity, within and across people, so fixed settings leave performance on the table.

The method adapts controller parameters daily from the wearer's own glucose data. Adaptation is cast as projected gradient descent on a daily risk metric, with gradient estimates built to filter noise and metabolic variability. Contraction theory proves the optimization stays stable and the loop converges while adapting. Tests run on the hundred-adult cohort of the standard UVA/Padova diabetes simulator, under varied meal timing, size and sensitivity. Glycemic risk falls and time in the healthy glucose range climbs steadily, gaining several points by week seventeen. Personalization, the results suggest, compounds rather than saturating early.
arxiv-2606-17204:
Kapusta and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on the critical point of quantum chromodynamics. At that point the smooth crossover between hadronic matter and quark-gluon plasma meets a first-order line. Heavy-ion experiments hunt for signs of it in collision data. Realistic models of the search must include phase boundary effects.

The team builds an equation of state that adds a surface energy term. They then study how its coefficient changes the size of the critical region. The temperature must sit within about one percent of its critical value, they find. Only then could the critical exponents show up in their setup. That makes measuring the exponents in collisions doubtful, though first-order signs may still be within reach.
arxiv-2606-17304:
Kesseli and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on CoRoT-2b, a young hot Jupiter whose hottest spot sits oddly to the west. Tidally locked hot Jupiters should show their hottest region at the substellar point or shifted east by super-rotating jets. Earlier space telescope phase curves showed robust evidence of the opposite pattern for this planet, and this study, the second in a series, hunts for the cause with ground-based spectrographs.

Phase-resolved spectra from instruments on the Very Large Telescope and Gemini South cover phases before and after eclipse. The planet's signal was detected in both phase ranges, allowing separate atmospheric retrievals for each epoch. Both retrievals agree on composition, but the later phases favour a hotter, flatter temperature profile, matching the western hotspot picture. Tests of rival explanations favour rotation slower than synchronous, with measured spin broadening well below the locked value.
arxiv-2606-17704:
Yerin and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper proposing a new probe of Josephson junctions based on the diode effect in a driven SQUID. A junction's current-phase relation hides its inner physics in higher and fractional harmonics. Static patterns from different mixtures look nearly identical, though, so the harmonics resist clean extraction. The authors instead drive an uneven SQUID with an oscillating flux and watch the diode effect, the imbalance between forward and reverse critical currents, as drive strength and frequency vary.

Two analytic reductions predict that each harmonic dresses with its own Bessel function under the drive. Computer solutions confirm distinct fingerprints: weak, sparse, dense, or intermodulated arc patterns for different harmonic mixtures. The signatures survive in both damping regimes tested on the model system. That robustness makes the scheme a candidate probe for unconventional superconductors, where the hidden harmonics carry the physics of interest.
arxiv-2606-17804:
Makartsou and colleagues propose a 2026 device concept for controlling the phase of spin waves, the ripples that can carry information through magnetic films. Their design places a narrow Permalloy racetrack holding magnetic domain walls above a YIG film. Stray fields from the pinned walls change the local magnetic field in the film below, and that alters the wavelength of passing spin waves.

Micromagnetic simulations show that moving the domain walls gives phase shifts up to ninety degrees in either direction, without reshaping the waveguide. Within the studied gigahertz band, multi-domain settings gave robust shifts of opposite signs, while wall-free settings gave almost none. A semiclassical model confirms the stray field as the cause, pointing toward compact programmable parts for magnonic circuits and in-memory computing.
arxiv-2606-17904:
Gil de Avalle and colleagues test what maintenance chatbots do when a worker's question steps outside the manual, in a 2026 paper. Advisory models are often chained to approved procedure documents to stop them inventing facts. Real operators, though, ask off-script questions mid-repair, and a safe system must notice and decline rather than force-fit an answer.

Their benchmark, DiagFlowBench, turns fifty industrial diagnostic flowcharts from a consumer manufacturer into more than sixteen hundred multi-turn dialogues mixing proper and out-of-scope turns. Ten commercial and open models varied wildly in how often they abstained. The common failure was subtle: models picked a real step from the manual that simply did not fit the situation. The authors argue reliability tests must measure how safely a model fails, not just whether it follows the book.
arxiv-2606-18004:
Jin and colleagues catch an extra flicker in a black hole binary just before it changes state, in a 2026 astrophysics paper. Using NICER observations of MAXI J1820+070, they track the shift from the hard-intermediate state to the soft-intermediate one. At that moment the broadband noise collapses and the steady jet quenches. The famous Type-C quasi-periodic oscillation vanishes, replaced by a Type-B.

About half a day before the transition, a new oscillation appears in the high-energy power spectrum, running at a few hertz and unrelated by harmonics to the Type-C signal. It seems to glide smoothly into the Type-B oscillation seen right after the jump. Its position on standard diagnostic plots matches Type-B oscillations in other binaries. The authors propose this signal is a precursor, meaning Type-B behavior can switch on earlier than textbooks assumed.
arxiv-2606-18104:
Veronese and colleagues trace the faint outer gas of sixteen nearby galaxies to find where galactic discs truly end, in a 2026 astronomy paper. The data come from MHONGOOSE, a MeerKAT radio survey of southern star-forming galaxies spanning a wide range of hydrogen masses. By stacking spectra, the team pushes the measured atomic hydrogen profiles down to column densities far below what single pointings reach.

High-mass galaxies show an inner plateau, then a knee, then a continued fall with no unambiguous sharp edge. Low-mass galaxies decline more steeply and also show no clear cutoff. When each profile is scaled by the radius where a fixed low surface density is reached, the shapes line up as self-similar. The long-debated idea of a universal break density, first raised from the galaxy NGC 3198, finds no clean support here.
arxiv-2606-18204:
Archey and colleagues hunt for the commutative heart inside a class of operator algebras built from self-similar graphs, in a 2026 mathematics paper. A Cartan subalgebra is a maximal well-behaved commutative piece from which the whole algebra can be reconstructed, and finding one is a standard route to classifying these algebras. Self-similar graph algebras arise when a group acts on a graph in a self-replicating way, enriching the usual graph algebra picture.

The authors isolate a distinguished piece of the path groupoid, the symmetric cycline subgroupoid. For abelian acting groups it is open, abelian, and normal. Specializing to the integers, they describe its dual bundle, giving a new groupoid model for the algebra. For a large class of examples they also prove the subgroupoid is maximal among open abelian ones, and closed. That maximality is exactly what promotes its function algebra to a Cartan subalgebra.
arxiv-2606-18304:
Ding and colleagues slim down mixture-of-experts models by pruning inside the experts, not just between them, in a 2026 machine learning paper. MoE models are cheap to run per token but heavy to store and serve. Earlier compression removed whole experts or ranked them by importance. Yet the authors observe that information inside an expert concentrates in a few channels. Even prized experts carry deep redundancy that expert-level cuts cannot reach.

Their framework scores channels by attribution and recasts the pruning target as maximizing channel-score coverage, with an efficient approximation and an alignment-aware redistribution that keeps the pruned model friendly to low-bit kernels. On DeepSeek and Qwen MoEs, the method held accuracy under half or quarter pruning combined with four-bit quantization. It shrank one thirty-billion-parameter model's memory footprint more than fivefold, beating prior baselines across benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-19004:
Lai and colleagues present Spotlight in 2026, a system that cuts the cost of reinforcement learning post-training for Diffusion Transformers. Such training is very costly and can need thousands of top-end graphics processors. Cheap spot instances could help, but they sit idle in this workload because rollouts end at near the same time. Spot cuts also break the parallel groups that training relies on, slowing recovery.

Two insights drive the design. First, seed exploration can use slightly stale model weights, since the ranking of seeds stays much the same from one round to the next. Idle spot units can thus explore while training runs. Second, parallel groups can be rebuilt fast by reusing state already on the node, dropping recovery from minutes to under a second. A bandit planner picks seeds to raise reward spread within the time budget.
arxiv-2606-19104:
Chowdhury presents PHANTOM in 2026, a public MATLAB and Octave toolbox linking linear field statistics to dark matter halo observables. Cosmologists often need power spectra, mass functions, and halo profiles in one consistent setup. Python tools cover much of this ground, but many analysis pipelines are written in MATLAB. PHANTOM fills that gap with a cosmology module and a halo module that share one consistent cosmology object throughout.

The cosmology side solves for the linear power spectrum, variance, and correlation function. The halo side covers mass functions, linear bias, density profiles, and concentration-mass relations for cold, warm, and fuzzy dark matter. Core routines are validated against leading Python packages with sub-percent agreement on shared models. Users can pull field statistics, halo statistics, and observables like enclosed mass and lensing convergence on their own grids. One entry point keeps background and halo results consistent by design.
arxiv-2606-19404:
Khazem proposes free-energy signatures in 2026 as a thermodynamic diagnostic for hallucination in large language models. Recent work shows the spectrum of attention-derived graph Laplacians carries strong signal about reasoning quality. Prior spectral diagnostics summarize that spectrum by a few eigenvalues or hand-picked scalars. Most of its structure goes unused, though wrong reasoning may mark the whole spectrum.

The descriptor treats each layer's attention Laplacian as a Hamiltonian. It extracts thermodynamic potentials, including the partition function, free energy, spectral entropy, and heat capacity, plus a random-matrix spectral form factor. Proofs show the signatures are stable under attention perturbation, enrich finite spectral summaries, and give a training-free detector a finite-sample bound. Across six open models and six benchmarks, a light probe on the signatures gives the strongest aggregate detection scores among attention-spectral baselines. It needs no update to the underlying model, suiting deployment screening.
arxiv-2606-19604:
Nikhil Krishna, Mariola Kłusek-Gawenda, and Rafał Staszewski test whether collider data can weigh in on the proton radius puzzle in 2026. The proton charge radius came out smaller in muonic hydrogen studies than in older measurements. Exclusive dilepton production in proton-proton collisions offers a fresh probe of that size.

A dipole form factor model frames the comparison. The standard parameter choice faces two test scenarios tied to rival radius values. Sensitivity peaks at large dilepton masses and at forward or backward rapidities. Fitting current ATLAS and CMS data within the model yields an effective radius near 1.002 femtometres. The fit uncertainty runs about 0.038 femtometres. Real sensitivity to the radius scale clearly exists in this channel. Yet the authors stress the result does not yet settle the proton radius puzzle.
arxiv-2606-19704:
Dhaval Patel leads a large team arguing in 2026 that agent leaderboards mislead deployment choices. Benchmarks for language model agents multiply, yet each covers only a few deployment dimensions. Aggregate scores hide the gaps that real use exposes.

Fourteen parallel studies probe one MCP-based industrial agent benchmark, AssetOpsBench. New asset types, workflow layouts, search tweaks, and code-level speed fixes all face tests. Seven prior agent benchmarks join the consolidation. Rankings from aggregate scores fail to transfer to out-of-distribution settings. Public-to-hidden competition records show the same rank instability directly. The team propose ranking by predictive validity: how in-sample rank correlates with out-of-sample rank. A twelve-tier test rig exposes the traits that suites like HELM fold into one mean score and hide from view. Three falsifiable criteria and a pre-registered pilot make the position testable.
arxiv-2606-19904:
Anping Zhang and six colleagues add realistic timing to city-scale crisis simulators in 2026. Human helping arrives in bursts: frantic spells split by long quiet gaps. Language model social simulators are usually graded on whether each act looks plausible, not when it lands.

A multi-year log of offline volunteering in Shenzhen, spanning the pandemic, grounds the study. Burstiness proves common for people and tracked groups alike. It is mostly self-exciting and homegrown, amplified by the pandemic rather than daily cycles. A standard language-model-only simulator reproduces almost none of that timing. Its agents act on a near-regular clock with no self-excitation channel. A data-calibrated gate that decides when agents act, leaving choices to the model, lifts timing past the burst threshold. Content quality survives the change intact.
arxiv-2606-20104:
Petr Ivashkov, Randall Balestriero, and Bernhard Schölkopf argue that a world model for acting agents should remember what actions do, not just what scenes look like. Their 2026 paper introduces sensorimotor world models, latent models that predict future states from current ones plus actions. Such models often fail in training because a latent state that is easy to predict can collapse, throwing away the information a planner needs.

Their fix is a single regularizer based on inverse dynamics. The latent state must keep enough information to recover the action that caused each transition. That pressure blocks collapse and steers the representation toward controllable features, ignoring distractors no action can change. The model trains end-to-end from offline, reward-free trajectories, with no frozen encoders or moving averages. Across simple 2D and 3D control tasks, the learned spaces stayed compact and readable, and planning performance rivaled more complex systems.
arxiv-2606-20204:
Chloe Wilkins and four colleagues link the composition of the solar wind to how close its source sits to the Sun's open-closed magnetic boundary. Their 2026 paper attacks the slow solar wind's origin, a long-standing puzzle. Plasma may escape there through interchange reconnection, where open and closed field lines swap partners, but hard evidence tying wind composition to that boundary has been scarce. The team matched a decade of Ulysses spacecraft measurements to two coronal field models tracing each parcel's source.

Composition depended strongly on source distance from the boundary. Ion charge-state ratios, abundances, and variability all peaked within a band about twenty-five megameters wide around the boundary, matching reconnection scales. Farther away, coronal hole wind looked uniformly fast and steady. Strong neighboring closed fields also pushed nearby wind toward slow-wind character. The slow wind's makeup is governed largely by boundary topology.
arxiv-2606-20304:
Morteza Kimiaei improves derivative-free optimization for noisy, high-dimensional problems where only function values can be measured. His 2026 paper starts from matrix-adaptation evolution strategies, robust solvers that learn a full scaling matrix from ranked samples. Under heavy noise, ranking misleads: selection picks the wrong points and the learned scaling degrades. Kimiaei replaces the full matrix with a diagonal approximation built from conjugacy-type conditions.

The update uses consecutive normalized recombination steps, applied conservatively, so unreliable selection has limited influence. No gradients or interpolation models are estimated, and no dense covariance is learned from noisy rankings. The method is cheaper than full matrix adaptation, while keeping a stable scaling in noisy settings. Experiments on noisy benchmarks show it holding up where the underlying framework falters.
arxiv-2606-20604:
Rahman Sanya builds a human-augmented machine learning pipeline that turns social media conversation into a public policy agenda. His 2026 paper addresses agenda setting, the policy stage where issues are identified, traditionally a slow, labor-intensive, and costly process to scale across large regions.

The approach runs in five stages: data cleaning and preprocessing, keyword extraction and issue identification, narrative creation, narrative validation, and agenda validation. Experiments on a Twitter dataset validate the method's output against human judgment. Machine scale plus human checks could let governments hear public concerns as they form, not months later. Agenda setting becomes a measurable, repeatable pipeline.
arxiv-2606-21104:
Harrison Gimenez proves an ancestor property result in a solo 2026 mathematics paper about the weak right order of right-angled Coxeter systems. Coxeter systems are groups generated by reflections with set relations. The weak right order ranks elements by reduced word length from the identity. An element has the ancestor property when its interval holds a unique longest involution. Hart and Rowley conjectured it for finite systems.

Gimenez shows the property holds for any non-identity fully commutative element in an arbitrary Coxeter system. Every element of a right-angled system is fully commutative. The property therefore holds for all non-identity elements there. An axiomatization of right-angled systems as reflection systems is also given. Settling the conjecture in a broad class clarifies the order structure that underlies Coxeter group combinatorics and its links to geometry.
arxiv-2606-21804:
Patel and colleagues ask in 2026 whether code written by artificial intelligence agents is harder to maintain than code written by people. A patch can pass its tests yet still plant confusion that hurts the next programmer who must extend it. As coding agents take on more repository work, that downstream cost matters as much as first-attempt success.

Their framework, CodeThread, turns single-step benchmark tasks into two-step ones, so an agent must first implement a change and later build on the result. Across four frontier coding agents and four benchmarks, agents solved follow-up tasks less often when building on agent-written code. Resolve rates dropped by up to 13.1 percent compared with building on human code. Standard maintainability metrics did not explain the gap. The clearest signals were subtler habits, such as altered input validation and error handling, plus larger downstream code size.
arxiv-2606-22104:
Dhariwal and colleagues investigate, in 2026, how swapping the halide in a family of calcium-based perovskites changes their value as solar cell materials. The compounds share one structure with fluorine, chlorine, bromine, or iodine in the halide role. Using first-principles calculations, the team compared structural stability, electronic band structure, and optical behaviour across the four variants, hunting for the composition best suited to photovoltaic use.

The iodide compound had the most stable configuration of the four. All four materials showed direct bandgaps between 2.0 and about 3.79 electronvolts, a range suited to absorbing sunlight. A spectroscopic efficiency screening, which estimates the maximum solar efficiency a material's absorption allows, ranked the iodide highest at 29.6 percent. The fluoride scored lowest at only 0.6 percent efficiency in the same screening. The authors conclude that halide substitution is a powerful tuning knob for this perovskite family, with the iodide variant the clear candidate for solar applications.
arxiv-2606-22304:
Alharthi and colleagues argue, in 2026, that generative models fail to be idempotent because their encoders and decoders learn mismatched manifolds. Idempotency means applying the model twice changes nothing once a sample lies on the target data surface. In practice the model drifts when applied repeatedly, because the encoder projects inputs onto one latent surface while the decoder rebuilds from a different one.

Their training framework closes the gap by forcing encoder and decoder to learn matching views of the same underlying surface. Aligning the two geometries encourages stable projections. In tests, the approach achieves much lower idempotency error than existing methods. It regenerates the same outputs when run again and again. Demonstrations cover image creation and image editing. This also improves identity preservation and information stability, yielding more realistic editing models.
arxiv-2606-22504:
Igor Santos-Grueiro tackles a security flaw in coding agents in this 2026 paper. Agents often receive broad tool access for a whole task, even when a resource is needed for only one subgoal. He calls the leftover exposure lingering authority: a capability stays available after the episode that justified it has closed.

His system, Portico, is a reference monitor that hands the agent revocable capabilities. A task contract compiles into starting capabilities, grant rules, closure tests, and global deny rules. Grants materialize as opaque, epoch-bound handles. Closure removes them from the agent's next interface and rejects stale replays before any side effect. In controlled tasks, Portico executed no contract-forbidden effects. On the closure tests it rejected all ten post-closure reuses, while a non-revoking comparator allowed all ten. Scripted and live model traces over file writes, git changes, and network access showed the same split.
arxiv-2606-22804: This paper builds Co-VStream, edge-cloud collaboration for understanding of long video streams. The building builds. Their collaboration is edge-cloud. The understanding is long video streams. It is AI. Co-VStream streams. The Co-VStream understands long videos.
arxiv-2606-23004:
Hal Simpson and Paul Truman classify a special family of braces in a 2026 algebra paper. A brace is a set carrying two group operations, one like addition and one like multiplication, tied by a mixing rule. Braces were invented to study solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation. This paper looks only at finite braces. It narrows further to braces where both groups are cyclic, meaning each is generated by repeating a single element. The authors call the two-sided cases biskew braces.

Simpson and Truman rework the known classification of these bicyclic braces. Their viewpoint uses regular subgroups of permutation groups, which act on elements in a tidy transitive way. That lens makes the classification easier to organize and check. Within it, they identify exactly which bicyclic braces also qualify as biskew braces. The result completes the census of this small but structured family.
arxiv-2606-23204:
Iris Dominguez-Catena, Daniel Paternain, and Mikel Galar audit the LAION-5B image dataset for demographic bias in a 2026 paper. LAION-5B is a vast web-scraped image and text collection that trains many modern AI systems. Its uncurated scale raises concerns about who gets represented and how. The team studies its two main parts, an English subset and a multilingual one. Using three face analysis models, they measure the age, gender, race, and expressed emotion of faces found in the data.

Dominguez-Catena and colleagues find strong skews. Young adults, white individuals, and males are heavily overrepresented. Middle-aged or older women and minority racial groups are consistently underrepresented. Emotion labels also follow stereotypes, with anger tied mostly to males and happiness to females. The patterns repeat across both models and both dataset parts. Given LAION-5B's reach, such skews can shape many downstream systems.
arxiv-2606-23304:
Dominik Lüthi and colleagues try to improve the transfer of graphene nanoribbons onto device platforms in a 2026 nanoscience paper. Graphene nanoribbons are atom-thin carbon strips whose electronic traits are set by their width. Aligned ribbons grow on a stepped gold surface, then must move to device-ready substrates intact. That transfer is a central bottleneck. The team tests whether chevron-shaped ribbons parked along the gold step edges act as passivators, nudging the target ribbons toward terrace centers.

Lüthi and colleagues also build an automated Raman mapping framework that classifies each pixel by two spectral signals. That gives a scalable score for transfer coverage and local ribbon integrity over large areas. Mapping shows strongly patchy transfer, with wide dead regions and only one high-yield sample in the series. Chevron passivation changes local growth but does not yet deliver reproducible, high-quality transfer.
arxiv-2606-23404:
Jun Zhang and colleagues present ReasoningLens, a tool for auditing the long reasoning traces of modern models, in a 2026 paper. Large reasoning models produce enormous chains of thought. The key logic often hides inside walls of step-by-step text. That makes errors hard to spot by eye. ReasoningLens gives each trace a clear structure. High-level strategy sits at the top. Low-level steps sit below it, in an interactive view. An agentic auditor then hunts for errors on its own, with tool-based checks of the steps that look wrong.

Zhang and colleagues release the tool as open source, with a dataset and a demo video. The tool also builds profiles of each model. These profiles show the blind spots a model falls into again and again across many traces. The aim is to help researchers debug and improve the next generation of reasoning models.
arxiv-2606-23904:
Fraija, Betancourt Kamenetskaia, Galván, and Dainotti model the fading glow of gamma ray bursts years after the explosion. By then the ejected material has slowed to everyday speeds, in their 2026 paper on high energy astrophysics. A burst's afterglow is synchrotron light from ejecta plowing into surrounding gas. The slower, quasi spherical outflows follow their own late time rules, the deep Newtonian phase, and a long lived central engine can keep pumping energy in. The authors build an analytic framework for this regime in a stratified environment.

The model yields multiwavelength light curves and closure relations, the linked decay rates observers use to test theory. Applied to the burst GRB 171205A, it fits the late time data. Short bursts tied to kilonova candidates, plus radio limits gathered years later, further constrain the outflows' dynamics and energy injection histories.
arxiv-2606-24004:
Krishnan, Goyal, and Savelka compile a handful of human preference judgments into a written specification that steers a language model, no retraining required, in a 2026 paper on AI alignment. Shaping model behavior today means either hand crafting prompts through trial and error, or fine tuning on roughly a thousand preference pairs, which is expensive and opaque. Spec learning takes a brief instruction plus about twenty preference pairs and compiles them into a natural language specification. That specification then prompts the unchanged model at inference time.

On specialized domain datasets, responses under the compiled specifications often beat direct preference optimization, the standard fine tuning method. The specifications have a second virtue: they are human readable. A person can inspect what preference signal the model is following, debate it, and edit it. The alignment signal moves from the weights into the input, staying transparent.
arxiv-2606-24504:
Succi, Coveney, and Hansen ask why large language models improve so slowly with scale, and whether the slowness condemns the current path. Scaling laws tie model loss to size through a small exponent. Enormous growth thus buys modest gains, an unsustainable regime in energy terms. One comforting story blames a numerical bias. Fits neglect the loss floor reachable only with infinite data, the pedestal effect, artificially shrinking the exponent.

That comfort fails, the authors argue in 2026. Correcting for a nonzero asymptotic loss does not remove the unsustainability. The measured exponents are genuinely small. The energy trajectory of ever larger models stays implausible, regardless of fitting choices. A second thread connects exponent size to data smoothness, through an analogy with models of fluid turbulence, where roughness controls scaling. Succi's trio writes as physicists auditing an industry mantra. Bigger is better only while the exponents, and the power grid, cooperate.
arxiv-2606-24604:
Hariharan, Gowda, and R forecast Alzheimer's disease courses as distributions of odds, rather than single verdicts. Progression modelling is useful only if it describes how a patient may evolve, and how sound that forecast is. Most deep learning reduces the task to one step sorting into flat classes: normal, mild impairment, dementia. Their 2026 framework combines three pieces, respecting the disease's ordered nature.

A Temporal Fusion Transformer encoder is adapted with an ordinal output layer and asymmetric loss weighting, plus oversampling of converters to sharpen response to the mild impairment to dementia step. Conditioned on the learned patient profile, an autoregressive mixture density network generates five year likely paths for diagnosis state, clinical rating, memory score, and hippocampal volume. On the ADNI cohort, the model beats linear, recurrent, and transformer baselines for the next visit call. The strongest gains land exactly on the transition clinicians most need to foresee.
arxiv-2606-24704:
Iryna Karpenko solves initial boundary value problems for the sine Gordon equation in light cone coordinates. The sine Gordon equation is a classical integrable wave equation. In light cone variables it takes a simple mixed derivative form. Karpenko works on the two quarter planes, right and left of the origin, with data decaying at infinity. The tool is the Riemann Hilbert problem framework, a modern method for integrable equations. The two half line problems turn out to differ sharply.

For the right problem, the initial data alone determine the solution uniquely. No boundary data at the origin are needed for a well posed problem. The left problem behaves differently. There the boundary values at the origin must be prescribed alongside the initial data. Without them the problem is not well posed. Karpenko demonstrates both facts within one Riemann Hilbert treatment.
arxiv-2606-24804:
Elizabeth Skoropata leads a large team using terahertz light to stir new collective vibrations in a polar nanolattice. Phonons, the vibrations of a crystal, are usually steered by changing the unit cell through strain, doping, or light. Structure above the unit cell offers another lever, largely unexplored. The sample is a strontium titanate thin film with an ordered network of interfacial dislocations. Time resolved X ray diffraction watches the motion unfold.

Breaking symmetry at all scales creates a dynamical electric polarisation. It also mixes phonon modes in ways the team can control. New collective modes appear in the THz range. Their atomic displacements swirl in circular, vortex like patterns never reported before. Skoropata and colleagues see a route to control of electric, magnetic, and ferroelectric systems through growth topology.
arxiv-2606-24904:
Yang Jiao studies how measurement windows can fake or hide hyperuniformity, an exotic state of disordered matter. Hyperuniform systems suppress large scale density fluctuations completely, like crystals, while lacking any long range order, like glasses. Detecting the state depends on the small wavenumber behaviour of the structure factor. Real measurements, though, cover only finite patches of a sample. Worse, observations may mask parts of the configuration entirely.

Jiao builds a unified theory for finite windows and for spatially correlated binary masks. The measured structure factor is the true one convolved with the spectral density of the observation function. For generic hyperuniform systems a universal quadratic leakage term appears at the smallest wavenumbers. It mimics a fixed exponent regardless of the true one. The true exponent survives only in an intermediate window of scales. Stealthy hyperuniform systems, with a spectral gap, suffer related distortions.
arxiv-2606-25004:
Gefei Tan, Adrià Gascón, Sarah Meiklejohn, and Mariana Raykova propose directional sharpness as a certificate of machine learning model quality. Generalisation itself cannot be certified directly: it depends on unseen data. Proxies disappoint. Test accuracy misleads when training was perturbed, deliberately or by accident. Sharpness, a curvature measure with an empirical link to generalisation, is costly to compute and can fail when training deviates from the prescribed procedure. Directional sharpness is designed to stay reliable and cheap under such changes.

Evidence from experiments and proofs supports two claims. It tracks generalisation more strongly than existing metrics. It also flags weak models more reliably. An auditor holding the training data can evaluate it quickly. Zero knowledge proofs extend the reach, certifying quality without revealing the training data at all. Tan and colleagues position the metric for real auditing pipelines.
arxiv-2606-25504:
Robot navigation among people needs practice crowds, but hand building each test scene is slow and rigid. Duc Tai Nguyen, Volodymyr Shcherbyna, and Anh Do Duc present GROVE in 2026, a pedestrian simulator driven by plain language. Users pick a preset such as emergency, queuing, or normal flow, or type a free prompt describing the scene they want. Separate modules handle long term human behaviour, medium range walking, and short range robot interaction, each steered by the prompt.

Each module picks among leading existing approaches according to the scenario, aiming to close the gap between simulated and real crowds. The simulator plugs directly into common robot platforms including Isaac Sim, Gazebo, and RViz. Qualitative comparisons across homes, hospitals, and offices show varied, realistic crowd behaviour that stresses navigation policies harder than the hand made scenes of earlier tools.
arxiv-2606-25704:
Two small self propelled robots joined by a spring sound like a toy, yet their joint motion mimics swimming microbes. Priyanka, Nitin Kumar, and Harsh Soni study this robotic dimer in 2026 as active Brownian particles, each pushing along its own chosen heading. When the two propulsion directions match, little happens. Tilt them apart, and the mismatch creates a steady torque: the pair begins to rotate persistently, with no outside steering at all. Geometry, it turns out, writes the choreography.

Three regimes appear as the two angles vary: run and tumble wandering like bacteria, smooth circular trajectories, and spinning in place. Spring stiffness and rotational noise tune how stable each regime is, shifting the borders between them. The results show mechanical coupling plus activity generating varied self organised behaviour from minimal parts, bridging artificial active matter and the chiral swimming of cells such as algae and sperm.
arxiv-2606-25804:
PET scanners image the body from pairs of gamma rays born when positrons annihilate. Those two photons are quantum entangled, their polarisations locked at right angles. Mihael Makek and colleagues built a demonstrator in 2026 that reads that correlation through Compton scattering. It uses single layer scintillator polarimeters. The question: do entangled events sharpen the picture? They imaged germanium line sources at clinical activities, plus a standard NEMA phantom filled with a gallium solution. Single pixel events set the reference image quality.

Single pixel resolution came out at about two and a half millimetres. Polarisation correlated Compton events resolved between roughly three point six and four point nine millimetres, depending on selection cuts, but carried up to twenty percent more signal over random background. The phantom scan combined both event types. The team estimate up to ten percent more sensitivity is available from the entangled events while keeping image quality high.
arxiv-2606-26004:
Daniele Licciardello and Luca Martucci map the symmetry structure of the axiverse. The axiverse is the crowd of light axion-like fields that string theory predicts. Such fields could solve the strong CP problem and supply dark matter. The pair study four-dimensional effective theories with many axions coupled to abelian gauge sectors. Supersymmetric versions with one unit of supersymmetry get broad coverage too.

Generalized symmetries take centre stage. Both invertible and non-invertible symmetries are identified, along with how each breaks. The breaking mechanisms stack into hierarchies of energy scales. Quantum gravity enters through wormholes, which threaten non-invertible axion shift symmetries. A recently proposed Imaginary Distance Bound sharpens that threat. In the supersymmetric axiverses, wormhole arguments give towers of instantons a starring role. Infinitely many superpotential terms follow from them, reshaping what low-energy axion physics can look like.
arxiv-2606-26104:
Jasmine Brazilek and Harper Dunn measure how writing style in advocacy texts steers a model's moral leanings. Ten linguistic features face testing on animal-welfare material. Stance-contrast probes with matched vocabulary isolate each feature's effect. Fine-tuning data built from each feature then shifts a small model's preference for pro-animal-welfare reasoning. 

Nine features move the needle. Seven push toward stronger pro-welfare reasoning: immediate time framing, depicted harm severity, narrative structure, evaluative claims, emotion words, moral vocabulary, and assertive certainty. Two push against it. Hedged language and concrete sensory description each dilute the stance. First-person perspective shows no clear effect. A larger model from a different family repeats the pattern. Nine of ten effects point the same direction there, though more weakly. The practical moral for advocates is in the title's spirit: assert a position instead of describing a scene.
arxiv-2606-26304:
Ryan Campbell and Sarah Jaeggli report a curious polarization pattern inside a sunspot. The Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope watched a sunspot penumbra, the streaky ring around the dark core, with spectropolarimetry. Four-lobed Stokes U profiles, a rare shape in the linear polarization signal, appear in coherent patches. The pattern survives careful correction for instrumental crosstalk, so it lives in the Sun, not the telescope.

Layered inversions reproduce the signal. Gradients in velocity and magnetic field with height do the work, especially the magnetic azimuth twisting along the line of sight. Holding that azimuth fixed in synthetic tests warps the U profile while leaving the other Stokes signals nearly untouched. A classifier trained on circular polarization maps confines the magnetic complexity to the penumbra's edge by a light bridge. Four-lobed U profiles may serve as a flag for twisted fields in future solar data.
arxiv-2606-26504:
Josh O'Connor examines duality-based particles and the exotic branes they probe. Extended objects called branes populate string theory and M-theory. Their charges group under hidden duality symmetries. Double and exceptional field theories make those symmetries visible before the curling up of extra dimensions. They replace ordinary internal coordinates with broader ones.

O'Connor works with a worldline action, the rule governing a particle's path through this extended spacetime. Choosing a physical slice recovers known particles. Some are massless in ten or eleven dimensions. Others appear as massive particles in lower dimensions, their masses set by winding and wrapping charges. The framework unifies those cases in one duality-based description. It gives a tool for studying exotic branes, odd objects with less familiar charges.
arxiv-2606-26904:
Yangfan He, Yujin Choi, and Jaehong Yoon present Robust-TO, a video understanding framework that distrusts damaged frames. Video reasoning models normally treat every frame as equally reliable. The authors name the resulting failure the Blind Trust Problem. Blur, glare, and occlusion can cut accuracy sharply on real-world tasks while the model stays unaware its evidence degraded.

Robust-TO routes questions to specialist perception tools through one evidence interface. A reliability-relevance score picks trustworthy frames for each tool. Every tool returns a prediction, its time span, and a calibrated reliability score. Reasoning then weights evidence in three trust tiers. A training reward balances correctness, evidence reliability, and cost together. Across two benchmarks spanning eight tasks, the framework held up far better under realistic damage than standard models.
arxiv-2606-27904:
W Ursae Majoris stars are contact binaries, two stars sharing one envelope. Low mass ratio members form a poorly bounded subclass. A Poro and five colleagues analyse them statistically in 2026. A sample of 818 contact binaries sets the definition. The empirical threshold for low mass ratio lands at a ratio near zero point two seven. Rotational stability is examined next through Monte Carlo analysis.

Gyration radii of both stars enter the stability test. The primary's radius stays nearly constant across the sample. The secondary's radius and the spin-to-orbital angular momentum ratio fall slightly as mass ratio rises. The secondary's internal structure thus drives stability trends. The team also compiled a dedicated sample of 115 such systems. Gaia DR3 parallaxes supply their absolute parameters. Empirical relationships among those parameters are derived. The datasets and summaries are offered as benchmarks for modelling and evolutionary studies of these binaries.
arxiv-2606-28104:
Traditional Chinese Medicine rehabilitation involves techniques like acupuncture and Tuina massage. Judging trainee performance visually is hard, because hands occlude each other and interact with objects. Francis Xiatian Zhang and six colleagues propose CME-AQA in 2026, a cross-view multimodal assessment framework. Visual and pose information are fused for context. Training uses both first-person and third-person videos, which improves robustness at inference. Two new datasets support the work.

Each dataset records sixty-one subjects in synced first- and third-person views, with expert scores. One covers acupuncture, the other Tuina. On key rating tasks like needle depth and quick needle insertion, the framework improves weighted F1 by over ten percent relative to the best competing method. Mean absolute error also falls for insertion time and manipulation frequency. Tests on a CPR dataset give comparable performance on several posture criteria.
arxiv-2606-28204:
Jack Geary, Boyan Gao, and Henry Gouk study strategic classification, where people change their features, such as reported income, to earn a favorable decision from an algorithm. Most theory assumes a simple linear decision rule because predicting how people respond to a complex, nonlinear rule is computationally hard.

Geary and colleagues recast a person's best response as a constrained optimization problem and build a Lagrangian, a standard reformulation that folds constraints into the objective. That version yields to fast first-order methods and matches the known answers for linear rules. Using the implicit function theorem, they also train the classifier while accounting for the responses it will provoke. Their models earned better strategic accuracy on common benchmark datasets.
arxiv-2606-28504:
The Euclid Consortium, with M. Libralato as lead author and a long collaboration roster behind the work, reports a first detection in the globular cluster 47 Tuc. The convective-transition gap is a sharp break in the brightness distribution of a cluster's faintest dwarfs, tied to a change inside the stars themselves, and only two detections existed before this one.

Euclid's combination of star counts, resolution, and photometric precision revealed a statistically significant discontinuity in the main-sequence luminosity function of 47 Tuc. Coming after the gap's discovery in the metal-poor cluster NGC 6397, its appearance in metal-rich 47 Tuc suggests the feature is more general than thought. The gap also promises a diagnostic of clusters' internal chemistry and their multiple stellar populations.
arxiv-2606-29004:
Lin, Jeong, Cai, Wang and Porikli tackle a gap between how motion estimation models are trained and where they are used. Optical flow, the pixel-by-pixel motion in video, is costly to label by hand, so models learn from synthetic scenes but must work in the real world. Their method, SciFlow, is a training scheme that works with any network and teaches itself.

During training, SciFlow blends features from open-world images into synthetic images as semantic interference, a deliberate cross-domain disturbance. The network thus learns to handle real-world looks while still training on known motion. A geometric consistency check keeps the self-teaching honest, discarding signals that break basic motion geometry. In experiments, SciFlow made models much more robust when conditions changed. It enabled synthetic-to-real transfer with no ground truth from the open world.
arxiv-2606-29204:
Ciavarelli, Ercolessi, Noferini and Bellini present a unified simulation framework for how light anti-nuclei form in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Anti-nuclei, bound states of anti-protons and anti-neutrons, are rare products of high-energy collisions. In the coalescence picture, they form when anti-nucleons emerge close together in space and momentum and bind.

Their afterburner framework describes nucleon-nucleon final-state interactions and light nuclei production by coalescence inside one model. An afterburner is a simulation stage added after the main generator, handling these late interactions. The model reproduces anti-nuclei spectra qualitatively without fine-tuning, a sign the mechanism is captured rather than fitted. It also matches correlation observables. It deals with proton-proton events, and can extend to heavier collision systems.
arxiv-2606-29404:
Neumann proves a convergence test for Mayer cluster expansions, series that rewrite a gas's behaviour as sums over small clusters of particles. His setting is lattice gases, models where particles sit on a grid, with forces that can involve many bodies at once and even carry complex values. The goal is absolute convergence of expansions for the log-partition function and for correlation functions.

His new sufficient condition absorbs several classical results as special cases. A partition scheme for spanning hypergraphs, structures that generalize ordinary graphs, suits the method to strong multi-body forces. One use is higher-order hard-core repulsion in hypergraph independence polynomials, counts of sets with no linked pair. The approach also combines with the Gruber-Kunz condition to extend polymer expansion results. Neumann reports that the combined results rival recent work by Nguyen and Fernández from 2024.
arxiv-2606-29504:
Rashidi tests whether keystrokes on a phone can be reconstructed from over-the-shoulder video alone, without recording the screen. His framework combines four detection routes. Hand landmarks come from MediaPipe, skin colour filtering uses HSV values, frame differencing catches motion, and Canny edge analysis traces outlines. Detected touch points then map onto a reference screen layout.

Evaluation uses a staged 120-frame first-person video of passcode entry. MediaPipe and skin detection fail under partial hand occlusion and ambient noise. Motion-only and edge-only setups reach F1-scores, a balance of precision and recall, of only about eighteen percent. The combined setup scores slightly lower still, and its sequence similarity stays near three percent. On five real third-person videos, the detector fires far too often, up to hundreds of points per frame. Rashidi concludes the staged result does not survive uncontrolled footage.
arxiv-2606-29604:
Mack, Panickssery, and Turner present Causal Perturbative Elicitation, a method for surfacing latent behaviours hidden inside a language model. Their method, called CPE, needs no labelled examples of the behaviour it finds. It breaks down the workings of a deep transformer slice with a tensor-decomposition-based algorithm, yielding low-rank adapters.

CPE learns many adapters from a single example. On the Countdown task it nearly matches a supervised method given equal wall-clock time. It also surfaces hidden failure modes. On a password-locked coding benchmark, CPE restores most of the locked performance, exposing sandbagging, where a model underperforms on purpose. Applied to a model organism built to fake alignment, CPE almost wipes out the alignment-faking behaviour. The authors offer CPE as a tool for exploring the range of conduct a model could show.
arxiv-2606-29904:
Yamamoto and three colleagues compare the internal timing of Mamba, a state-space language model, with human reading times. In Mamba each word triggers a state update whose step size, the discretization timestep, is set dynamically by the input.

Using a naturalistic dataset of people reading text, the team shows that Mamba's per-word timestep significantly predicts how long humans spend on each word. The link survives even after controlling for known predictors such as GPT-2 surprisal, how unexpected a word is. The authors argue that Mamba's layered memory, which weighs short-term and long-term retention differently at each layer, offers a new lens on how humans process language in real time.
arxiv-2606-30004:
A. Maltsev, writing alone, studies when ultra-complex conductivity diagrams can arise in crystals. Such diagrams describe how a conductor responds to strong magnetic fields. They would allow striking effects to be observed in the laboratory. Yet they seem to occur only rarely in real substances. Maltsev asks in 2026 how that rarity can be estimated for cubic lattices.

The setting is the tight-binding approximation for electrons in a crystal. Two lattice types are treated: simple cubic and body-centered cubic. At leading order, quirks of the electron spectra block any probability estimate. Maltsev therefore adds higher-order corrections to the approximation. Those corrections yield sharper analytical formulas for the electron energy bands. With those formulas in hand, the emergence probability becomes estimable. The result clarifies when exotic conductivity behavior is worth hunting experimentally.
arxiv-2606-30104:
Ayşe Yüce, Chris Leffler, Sarun Varghese, Myra Spiliopoulou, and Sebastian Stober compare how brain signal models extract features over time. EEG foundation models learn general representations from large brain recordings. Much EEG information lives in temporal dynamics, the way signals evolve. Yet the effect of the temporal extractor itself is rarely isolated. The team runs a controlled comparison inside one unified model.

Three extraction strategies compete on equal footing. A simple linear baseline faces a convolutional encoder. A frozen pretrained time-series model, MOMENT, is the third contender. Two downstream tasks judge representation quality: motor imagery and emotion recognition. On motor imagery, simple temporal features perform competitively with richer ones. The emotion dataset, by contrast, benefits from richer temporal modeling. MOMENT transfers well despite never being designed for EEG.
arxiv-2606-30404:
Samira Huber and four colleagues give robots a memory of human routines, not just maps of rooms. People follow daily patterns in homes and offices. They arrive, leave, and linger at predictable times and places. A useful robot should answer where someone likely is. It should also predict when they usually leave. HUMEMBR is built for exactly those questions.

The system constructs memory continuously as the robot observes. A parallel mechanism retrieves and answers queries from that memory. Structured representations of routines accumulate over long periods. Experiments compare it against full-context language model baselines. HUMEMBR reasons better about long-horizon behavior, the results show. It also uses substantially fewer tokens doing so. The team deployed it on a physical robot. Two different real environments hosted the live tests. Diverse queries and navigation tasks were handled successfully.
arxiv-2606-30704:
Gan Luo and three colleagues train language models to write workflows, step-by-step recipes that solve a whole class of tasks. Single answers from a model vary by instance and are hard to debug. Workflows add structural consistency and reusability, but designing them by hand takes expertise. Earlier automatic methods either solved single instances without learning task-level patterns, or failed to generalise beyond their training setup.

Their system, MetaFlow, treats workflow generation as meta-learning: given a task and a set of allowed building blocks, the model composes a strategy. Training runs in two stages: supervised fine-tuning on synthetic workflows, then reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where execution feedback grades each workflow. Across question answering, code generation and maths reasoning benchmarks, MetaFlow matched baselines on trained tasks in a single pass. It also generalised to unseen tasks and new building-block sets with no retraining.
arxiv-2606-30904:
Izidor Benedičič, J. Paul Attfield and Denis Arčon use diamond defects as tiny magnetic sensors inside a strongly correlated oxide. The material, manganese-doped CaFe3O5, mixes charge-ordered and charge-averaged regions at the nanoscale, a segregation that powder measurements struggle to resolve. The team pressed nanodiamonds carrying nitrogen-vacancy centres, quantum sensors read out by light, into a powder pellet and tracked static and dynamic magnetic fields across the weak ferromagnetic transition.

The resonance spectra split and broadened on cooling below the transition, shifting by about 15 MHz in an order-parameter-like rise. The spin-lattice relaxation rate spiked sharply at the transition, growing by roughly a factor of ten. Detailed fits of the spectra and recovery curves backed the picture of nanoscale segregation between the two electronic phases.
arxiv-2606-31004:
Mert Onur Cakiroglu, Zhihe Lu, Mehmet Dalkilic and Hasan Kurban audit whether AI-video detectors generalise, or merely exploit dataset quirks. Leaderboards such as GenVidBench reward high scores, yet protocols leave confounds uncontrolled. As a warning, a classifier using three clip-length features scores 0.998 on a leave-one-generator-out test while measuring nothing about motion. Surveying 20 papers, the team found none applying all six controls, so they combined them into one audited protocol and ran it on six feature sources across two benchmarks.
