The audit cut both ways, debunking and certifying. The trivial classifier collapsed to 0.529, near chance, and a CLIP baseline was caught carrying dataset identity. The 2025 forensic detector WaveRep cleared the floor, scoring 0.996 on such tests. At a false-positive rate of 0.1%, though, several high-scoring methods fell to single-digit recall, and the leaderboard reshuffled. The team release VidAudit, 14 detectors behind one interface.
arxiv-2606-31204:
Ji and six colleagues present AC3S, a diffusion-based system for making synthetic images with accurate 3D structure. Diffusion models give realistic pictures, yet keeping pose and layout exact is hard. Older pipelines guide them with edge maps and similar prompts, but strong guidance can create artifacts and hurt realism.

AC3S adds a self-supervised visual prompt modulator that adjusts ControlNet conditioning strength as needed, so structure is enforced without smothering the image. A multi-agent vision language model setup also writes detailed prompts matched to the geometry. The system produces datasets with exact 2D and 3D labels, and tests show clear gains in image quality and in how well the synthetic data helps later vision tasks.
arxiv-2606-31304:
Hoy and three colleagues introduce bilby-antiglitch, a tool for reading gravitational wave signals that overlap with noise glitches. Detectors such as LIGO infer source traits with Bayesian inference, which assumes steady Gaussian noise. Short terrestrial glitches break that assumption and can bias the inferred traits of a real signal.

The framework fits signal and glitch together, using a quasi-physical model for short non-Gaussian transients inside one analysis. On simulated signals polluted by loud glitches, it recovers the true source traits where standard methods fail. It also stops false claims that general relativity was violated and confirms truly odd signals in suspect data. Joint fitting, the authors argue, is the safer default when glitches are common.
arxiv-2606-31704:
Moussi, Ronval, Nijssen and Schiltz release WIDER-FAIR, a fairness-ready version of the widely used WIDER-FACE face detection benchmark. Studying bias in face detection has been blocked by a data gap: detection datasets rarely label sensitive traits, so performance gaps across demographic groups stay invisible. The team manually annotated perceived ethnicity and sex for every face.

The dataset covers 16,256 images across four ethnic groups and two sex categories, and embedding checks with a nearest-neighbor classifier and a t-SNE visualization support the coherence of the labels. Training a YOLOv5 detector as a demonstration, the authors find detection performance notably lower for faces of Black individuals. Removing that group from training widens fairness disparity more than removing any other ethnic group.
arxiv-2608-00204: Infrared problem in Quantum Electrodynamics, arXiv 2608-00204. The QED infrared. The paper remains available to readers. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
arxiv-2608-00304: Uniform stratified vanishing and equidistribution, arXiv 2608-00304. The equidistribution. The paper endures in the archive. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
arxiv-2608-00404: Debiased inference for proximal dose-response function, arXiv 2608-00404. The dose-response. It stands as a research record. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
audollent-defixionum-tabellae-1904:
Auguste Audollent published his corpus of ancient curse tablets in 1904. Ordinary Greeks and Romans scratched curses on lead and buried them in graves. Audollent collected every Greek and Latin example then known.

Binding spells target courtroom opponents, rival lovers, thieves, and athletes. Commentary explains each tablet's find spot, wording, and strange divine names. The corpus founded serious study of ancient magic's darker side. Later finds have added many tablets to Audollent's total. His collection remains the essential starting point for defixiones. The tablets preserve the grudges and fears of ordinary ancient people vividly.
bahai-kitab-iqan-1904:
Baha'u'llah, founder of the Baha'i faith, wrote the Kitab-i-Iqan, The Book of Certitude, in Baghdad in the early 1860s. Ali Kuli Khan made this first English translation, published in 1904. The work stands as the faith's foundational treatise on its central doctrine.

That doctrine is progressive revelation: God sends teachers age by age, each renewing religion for a changed world. The book reads Jewish, Christian, and Muslim scriptures as one unfolding story pointing toward its author's own claim. Baha'i readers still study it as the surest guide to their founder's thought. It was written in answer to questions raised by a learned uncle of the Bab.
barbara-blomberg-volume-04:
Volume 4 of Barbara Blomberg, by Georg Ebers, finds the knight Wolf climbing the stairs in high hope. Ebers reports that the singer Barbara has just won great favor from the Emperor, a success bound to stir her deeply. Wolf has spent a long hour with Dr Hiltner and come home at a run, carrying a fair prospect of income to lay before her in this volume.

Chapter XVI follows his reasoning step by step. Barbara showed her liking plainly when they parted yesterday. With money secured, what should stop her from becoming his at last? He passes a private chapel where someone stirs, and finds only her father at home. Barbara has gone down to pray at an unusual hour. Favor at court and a lover's errand meet on one staircase, each pulling her a different way.
basil-valentine-triumphal-chariot-of-ant:
The Triumphal Chariot of Antimony, in Waite's 1893 translation, presents the classic antimony treatise ascribed to Basil Valentine. Valentine, a supposed fifteenth-century monk, lent his name to a shelf of Paracelsian writings. Antimony, a brittle metal-like substance, was the wonder drug of that school.

The treatise praises antimony's powers to purge and cure, and gives the furnace work for preparing its many forms. Its title pictures the metal riding in triumph over the diseases that resist common medicines. Paracelsian doctors treated the book as their pharmacopoeia, their official guide to a prized and dangerous remedy.
bernard-clairvaux-letters-1904:
Bernard of Clairvaux ruled half of Europe from his abbey by letter, and Samuel J. Eales chose and translated a set of those letters in 1904. Bernard wrote to popes, kings, bishops, monks, and his own kin, in a voice that could scold, soothe, and blaze on one page. The letters span his wars for church reform and the launching of the Second Crusade.

Readers meet the abbot rebuking luxury, defending his friend Abelard's enemies and attacking Abelard himself, and mourning the crusade's failure. His style is a river of scripture turned to daily business. The selection shows the man behind the saint: tender to novices, iron to princes. Eales adds notes to place each letter in its fight.
budge-gods-of-egyptians-vol-1-1904:
E. A. Wallis Budge set out the gods of Egypt in Vol. 1 of The Gods of the Egyptians, out in 1904. Budge kept the Egypt hoard at the great state vault in London. He drew on hymns, tomb texts, and carved walls in the tongue of the land. This tome takes up the chief gods, their forms, kin, and cult towns.

Beast heads, sun discs, and myths of birth and death fill each part. Budge writes for the keen lay fan, not just sages. The pair of tomes was the main English guide for years. This one starts it.
budge-gods-of-egyptians-vol-2-1904:
E. A. Wallis Budge rounds out his pantheon in Vol. 2 of The Gods of the Egyptians, out in 1904. The first tome gave the chief gods and their myths. Here come the rest: gods of towns, of the dead, of birth and flood, and the strange mixed forms that crowd the walls of tombs and shrines in the land.

Tales of Osiris and his kin get full room here. Lists and draws help fans keep the throng straight. The set as a whole is Budge's gift to lay fans. It put the whole throng in English hands.
bullen-denizens-of-the-deep-1904:
Bullen returned to the deep in 1904 with a book on the life of the open ocean. Denizens of the Deep treats sea serpents and ocean monsters from a sailor's long watch. Frank Bullen had spent his youth before the mast on whalers and traders.

He weighs the serpent tales by what he knows of squid, whales, and the tricks of light at sea. Some tales fall; some, he holds, stand past plain explaining. The book is the ocean's mystery as a working seaman saw it. It pairs with his whaling classic as a life's log of the deep.
by-england-s-aid-or-the-freeing-of-the-n:
G. A. Henty's By England's Aid, or The Freeing of the Netherlands, 1585-1604, continues his story of the Dutch War of Independence for boys. Henty explains that his earlier By Pike and Dyke ended with Orange's death and Antwerp's fall, and that this volume gives the war's second phase.

In that phase England, long an unofficial helper of Holland, openly entered the fight and largely secured the outcome. The war widens beyond Holland and Zeeland's low country and towns to the defeat of the Armada, the capture of Cadiz, and other great actions. Henty writes in his usual vigorous style for lads, and young readers of historical adventure will find it stirring.
cia-0000007604:
Winter 1968 opened volume 12 of Studies in Intelligence, the CIA's journal written for its own staff. A heading in the issue reads like Ill Told Tales, tied to a book entry in its pages. The timing matters: early 1968 was the season of the Tet Offensive in Vietnam.

Book coverage inside a secret journal shows officers judging published work against private knowledge. Reviews and notes helped staff sort reliable accounts from weak ones. Historians value these issues because the writers assumed no outsider would read them. The declassified text thus catches the agency talking honestly among itself in wartime.
cia-0000008004:
Half of 1951 still lay ahead when CIA analysts forecast the rest of the year in Indochina. France was fighting the Viet Minh for control of Vietnam, and the war was going badly for Paris. American aid was growing, even though US troops were not yet involved.

Estimates like this one weighed French strength, Viet Minh gains, and China's role across the border. The writers had to judge a colonial war that Washington would later inherit. Their caution and errors both instruct, since the paper predates Dien Bien Phu by years. It is an early American attempt to read Vietnam's future.
cia-0000008704:
Two American pilots were sighted in An Thuy district, part of Haiphong, in a report dated January 1973. An Thuy lies near the port city's coast, in North Vietnam's northeast. The report arrived in the same month the Paris peace accords were signed.

Sightings filed at war's end held special weight, since they might describe men about to be freed or left behind. Officials compared such claims against the lists of prisoners Hanoi acknowledged. A mismatch kept a case open for years. This report preserves one of those end-of-war claims, with place and date, for the record that followed.
cia-0000009804:
A Viet Cong prisoner of war camp in Vinh Binh province, housing South Vietnamese and other prisoners, is described in a July 1971 report. The heading's list of who was held breaks off mid-word, after naming South Vietnamese and Viet Cong categories. Vinh Binh lies deep in the Mekong Delta.

Camps holding mixed populations show the southern war's tangled loyalties. Some inmates were government soldiers; others may have been the Viet Cong's own punished men. Untangling who was who fell to analysts reading reports like this one. The file preserves a Delta camp's population as reported, confusion included.
cia-0000012304:
Certain questions, the file's cut title suggests, occupy a Helms memo to the DIA director from November 1961. The memo closes a dense run of that autumn's Military Thought correspondence. Twelve months of such letters trace the operation's whole arc. They run from first contact to full industrial flow, each piece of Soviet writing matched to an American need.

The year's volume is the file's true subject: a spy case administered in full. The letters' rhythm never faltered across the seasons. For readers, this page is one count in the annual tally of the Cold War's most valuable penetration.
cia-0000012404:
Meeting number sixteen, London, May 5, 1961, closes the spring's intensive phase of the debriefings. Sixteen meetings in sixteen days: the opening blitz had no precedent. Soon Penkovsky would return to Moscow, where the work grew far more dangerous. There, contact ran through dead drops, signals, and rare meetings abroad. It could never match these long London sittings for volume or safety.

The record completes the first campaign of the case. Handlers closed the run with notebooks full and a source proven. For readers, the page marks the end of the beginning of a famous penetration.
cia-0000013604:
Nicaragua's political prospects over the next year or so are weighed in a CIA paper from September 1967. The Somoza family had ruled the country for three decades. Its grip ran through the National Guard, the treasury, and the family itself. The dynasty's corruption was its weakness, and the analysts weighed that weakness carefully against the opposition's small strength.

The paper judges the family's future at a settled moment in its long rule. Few then foresaw the revolution that would end it twelve years later. For readers, the paper shows the dynasty as Washington saw it then: durable, tainted, and watched.
cia-0000013904: American prisoners in two far apart provinces fill a CIA note dated November 2, 1967. One group was in Quang Binh Province in September 1965, in the north. Another mention points to Kontum, in the southern highlands. The note shows how a single file could join prisoner sightings across the whole length of Vietnam.
cia-0000015304: A letter to Samuel Goudsmit from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated January 5, 1958. It takes up points by Hynek and Lloyd, per the clipped title. Hynek was the Air Force's own astronomer on saucers. The mail shows agency men trading views with the few experts who knew the case files.
cia-0000022604: A dead American pilot was sighted in Hanoi, North Vietnam, in a CIA record dated in 1973. Hanoi was the capital, seat of the government that held American prisoners. A sighting there of a dead pilot carried weight for the final accounting of the war. Staff logged it in the year the living prisoners came home at last.
cia-0000028304: Stability of the present regime in Iran is weighed in a CIA paper dated in 1958. The present regime meant the Shah's government, five years after the coup that secured it. Stability papers asked how deep a ruler's support ran and where the cracks might open. For Iran the question would return with far greater force twenty years later.
cia-0000037104: Disbursements for travel and other expenses fill a CIA record dated November 5, 1942, naming Cook, Phenix, Osborne, Tyler, Rado, and others. The page comes from the OSS, the wartime office that stood behind the later CIA. It sets out payments name by name in the plain hand of a ledger keeper. Wartime secret work still ran on vouchers and receipts, and pages like this one kept the young office's spending in order.
cia-0000042704:
President Cristiani issued a statement on the murder investigation, in a CIA record dated October 1, 1989 in the catalog. Alfredo Cristiani was El Salvador's president during the war's last years. His government stood accused by critics of shielding the killers.

Inside, the president's own words on the investigation are set down. A head of state under fire chooses each such word with great care. The file preserves the official promise of an inquiry. Readers can weigh that promise against the slow course the case then took, as soldiers were named, held, and tried over the years that followed.
cia-0000049004: Many Salvadoran military officers were pleased by the assassination of leaders of the revolutionary movement, and a CIA item dated November 1, 1980, records their reaction. The item is a cold one: satisfaction at murder, noted in plain bureaucratic words. It survives among the Truth Commission files as evidence of the climate inside the armed forces.
cia-0000049104: Victor Manuel Santos Marinez is the named subject of a CIA item from 1985, kept with the Truth Commission records. The series is full of such single-name files, each a person caught in the war's paperwork. What the system knew about him sits in the document, behind a title that gives nothing else away.
cia-0000049404: The Election Outlook in El Salvador is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049404, dated May 5, 1982. Marked for the Truth Commission, the paper looks ahead to a Salvadoran election. It is a brief declassified forecast whose title states its aim, companion in spirit to the agency's other Salvadoran election outlook from two years later.
cia-0000098304: Chinese Communist short-range military intentions, with intentions misspelled in the heading, are the subject of declassified CIA document 0000098304, dated June 4, 1962. The title limits its scope to the short range. Readers find a brief declassified intentions paper from China reporting, its spelling flaw preserved in the catalog beside its more polished neighbors.
cia-0000104904: Security Guidance and Procedures is the heading, ending with a semicolon, on declassified CIA document 0000104904, dated June 5, 1994. The sample shows the file is Director of Central Intelligence Directive 1/21, on physical security standards for SCI facilities. Its sample pages give an effective date of July 29, 1994. The directive states that such standards are established under the National Security Act and an executive order.
cia-0000119204:
From about November 1987, this CIA document reports a sighting of a possible burial site for missing Americans in Xieng Khouang Province, Laos. The province, home to the Plain of Jars, saw heavy fighting and bombing during the war. Reports of graves were among the grimmest leads the agency followed.

Each reported site had to be checked against records of lost aircraft and missing crews. Most leads led nowhere, but each one mattered to a family waiting for news. The document preserves the sighting as it was reported, a single entry in the huge file of the missing that stayed open long after the war ended.
cia-0000119704: A January 1953 CIA paper surveys conditions and trends in the Middle East that bear on American security. Oil, the new state of Israel, and rising Arab national feeling were combining into a lasting problem for Washington. The paper maps those pressures at the start of a stormy decade. Papers of this breadth set the frame for smaller country studies, giving leaders one map of a region that would occupy them for years.
cia-0000124304: An October 1972 CIA document covers air raid shelters at Luta, Shenyang, and Shih-chia-chuang, plus the Peking subway and suspected sites, the heading breaking off. China's civil defense building was read in Washington as a sign of fear of war. The paper maps the shelters as plotted. Shelter digging on that scale suggested a state preparing its people for attack, and analysts weighed it as evidence in judging how real China's war fears were.
cia-0000132504: Cuban reaction to anti-Castro invasions fills a CIA document dated February 3, 1961. The word invasions sits in quotation marks in the headline, showing the agency's care with the term. The great invasion was still two months off, but smaller raids had already begun. The short document gauges how Havana answered those early attacks and prepared its people for larger ones to come.
cia-0000132604:
A blunt verdict stands as the headline of a CIA paper dated August 6, 1960: the Cuban situation worsens. By that summer Washington had stopped hoping that a moderate Cuba would emerge from the revolution. Seizures of property, the Soviet embrace, and the coming break all pointed the same way.

The paper gives the worsening picture behind its own headline, fact by fact. For readers, it marks the month the agency's tone changed for good. Earlier reports had still weighed chances and options with some hope. This one records a slide that analysts no longer thought could be turned back. It dates that bleak judgment with care.
cia-0000135604: A Spanish-language document dated 2 September 1960 survives among the declassified papers of Brigade 2506, the Cuban exile force the CIA was training for an invasion of Cuba. September 1960 fell in the brigade's early buildup, well before the April 1961 landing. The catalog record gives no subject or author for this item. Readers who know Spanish can judge its contents directly; the title alone supports no more than its date, its language, and the file it belongs to.
cia-0000135804: Orders from Lincoln fill a CIA cable dated May 3, 1954. Lincoln was the code name for the base running the Guatemala operation. The cable carries both working orders and general guidance for the field. Its own headline grammar stumbles, a flaw kept from the original. Orders from Lincoln were the marching orders of the campaign. The short cable keeps them as sent.
cia-0000135904: The CIA document from 1 April 1954 deals with acts of force planned for the days before D-day, in a file now declassified. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136104: The cable dated 5 March 1954 in the CIA files, now open, deals with MT/4, a two-part code standing alone as the whole subject of a Lincoln cable. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136204: With a date of 5 May 1954, a CIA cable in the open files deals with a meeting between Calligeris and Estrada. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136304: LINCOLN asked for authority to strike in this June 1954 PBSUCCESS cable, reporting that a setback at Chiquimula that morning made action by the army in the capital more likely. The station proposed a strike the next day by three fighter aircraft, calling it an impressive show against a military, isolated, and easy-to-identify target ringed by a moat. Timing mattered, the cable argues, so the cause and effect would be read the right way.
cia-0000136404: Names of people who know about communist infiltration fill this January 1954 cable. It went to the senior representative at LINCOLN. The names were offered as possible help. One man is an agent living abroad. He made recent trips to Guatemala. Another is a former White Russian. He keeps contact with refugee groups arriving in Cuba. He picked up word on penetrations there. Contact runs through still other named persons. The names themselves stay withheld as IDENs.
cia-0000136704: A Spanish document dated 4 August 1960, from the declassified papers of Brigade 2506, the CIA's Cuban exile force. August 1960 fell in the brigade's first training season; the unit had been formed only that year. The catalog record names no subject for this item. It survives in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, an early dated piece of the brigade's paperwork from the operation's first summer.
cia-0000136904: Fuzz up the question of official backing, headquarters instructs LINCOLN in this May 1954 cable on deception and confusion activities. Reports keep arriving of a figure boasting of official United States backing, and those boasts are cutting into knowledge the operation wants blurred. With future Guatemalan charges in mind, it is particularly desirable to confuse them as to the sources of financial and other backing. The cable orders deliberate muddiness about who was paying for the rebellion.
cia-0000140404: Experiment in the field, not the laboratory. This April 1955 paper on hypnotism and covert operations argues that course. Academic experts are often too pessimistic, the writer says. Their caution rests on very few cases. Agency experimenters contradict much of it. He has personally witnessed responses that respected experts called impossible. Book knowledge feels cramped and closed-in to him. Evidence does not yet prove hypnotism a workable covert weapon. Only field tests can show what works, he argues.
cia-03019104: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1955/12/08, a CIA publication. Another December briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. The historical record keeps it. The paper lived through the years.
cia-03181204: May 3, 1955: the bulletin delivered the day's intelligence. The global summary reached Washington's leaders. The Cold War's spring brief. Time has kept the file intact. This declassified paper is maintained. The file remains. The document lasts.
cia-06007804: THE PRESIDENT'S DAILY BRIEF 29 AUGUST 1974, a CIA publication. The presidential briefing. This file preserves that declassified brief. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. The historical record keeps it. The archive guards it with care for all readers.
cia-06586904: DPRK PARTY DAILY BLAMES US FOR OPENING UP 'PRELUDE' TO 'CYBER WAR', a CIA document. The North Korean charge. This file preserves that declassified paper. Future scholars will discover it. It retains its place in time.
cleopatra-volume-04:
Cleopatra, Volume 4, continues the Alexandria novel by Georg Ebers, set as Mark Antony and Octavian move toward open war. Ebers follows Dion, a young Alexandrian engaged to Barine, and Gorgias, the builder at work on the queen's city projects. Public works and private plans advance side by side in this stretch.

Chapter IX finds Gorgias finishing twin statues for the Theatre of Dionysus while walls and arches rise under Antony's orders. Dion comes to talk before leaving the city with his bride. Caesarion, the queen's son, has called on Barine twice in one morning, which speeds their flight. The couple plan to marry at a quiet country refuge, away from court eyes and royal desire.
coniston-volume-04:
Book Four of Winston Churchill's Coniston finds Cynthia Wetherell at a Boston girls' school, carrying a sorrow her classmates cannot guess. Churchill, the American novelist, moves his New Hampshire heroine into drawing rooms and Back Bay houses here. Cynthia loves Bob Worthington, a rich young man tied to the railroad interests her guardian fights. She has renounced him, and the refusal costs her daily.

Janet Duncan, a lively Boston girl, sweeps Cynthia into lunches, drives, and warm friendship. Janet never spots the romance unfolding under her nose, though she adores novels of the heart. Letters from the schoolmistress stir the Duncan household behind the scenes. Boston polish contrasts with Cynthia's Coniston loyalties throughout the book. Jethro Bass, her guardian and the state boss, waits offstage like a fate. Readers get the love story at its most painful pitch here, where duty and feeling split a strong young woman in two.
conrad-nostromo-1904:
Joseph Conrad published Nostromo in 1904, a large novel set in Costaguana, a made-up country in South America. A silver mine drives the plot and draws in foreign money and local politics. Nostromo is an Italian sailor trusted by all sides. Revolutions rise and fall around the mine and the port town of Sulaco.

Conrad follows many figures, from mine owners to rebels and their families. Silver brings wealth, but it also brings betrayal and death. Nostromo himself is changed by the trust placed in him. Readers prize the book as a vast and clear-eyed account of empire, greed, and power.
constitution-afghanistan-2004:
Afghanistan adopted this constitution in 2004, after the fall of the Taliban. It founds an Islamic republic with a unitary state, meaning one central government rather than a federation. Islam is named the state religion, and Pashto and Dari are the official languages. Its early chapters cover the state itself, then the fundamental rights and duties of citizens.

Power is divided among a president, a National Assembly with two houses, and the courts. The assembly pairs a House of the People, elected directly, with a House of Elders. Later chapters handle the judiciary, provinces and districts, elections, and emergencies. With 162 articles, the text shows the order Afghanistan tried to build after 2001.
constitution-belarus-2004:
Belarus adopted its current basic law in 1996, and the hosted text includes amendments through 2004. Section one states the fundamentals of the constitutional system. Belarus is a unitary, democratic republic, and both Belarusian and Russian are state languages. Later sections cover the person, society, and the state, then elections and referendums held across the country.

The president holds very strong powers as head of state, including rule by decree in set cases. Parliament, the National Assembly, has two chambers, a House of Representatives and a Council of the Republic. Other sections cover the government, courts, local government, and the prosecutor's office. Critics abroad say the wide presidential powers leave the other branches weak in practice.
constitution-lebanon-2004:
Lebanon's constitution dates from 1926, under French mandate, and the hosted text includes the Taif changes of 1990 and amendments through 2004. Early provisions found a republic with Beirut as capital and Arabic as the official language. The text's most famous feature is its sharing of power among faiths, a system meant to keep peace among Lebanon's many sects.

By custom written into the Taif deal, the president is a Maronite Christian, the prime minister a Sunni Muslim, and the speaker of parliament a Shia Muslim. The National Assembly makes laws, with seats split evenly between Christians and Muslims. Later parts cover the courts, finance, and local rule. The design aims at balance, though critics say it freezes division.
constitution-panama-2004:
Panama works under a constitution from 1972, written under military rule and reshaped by later changes, with the hosted text running through 2004. Early titles cover the Panamanian state, then citizenship and the standing of foreigners. A long title gives the rights and duties of each person and of society, from life and speech to family, work, and health.

A president leads the executive for a single term at a time. The National Assembly is the single lawmaking chamber. One full title covers the Panama Canal, which passed to Panama at the end of 1999 and is run by its own authority under the text's guard. Later titles cover the courts, local rule, and finance. Spanish is the official language.
constitution-uruguay-2004:
Uruguay works under a constitution from 1967, restored after the dictatorship years, and the hosted text includes changes through 2004. Early sections cover the nation and its sovereignty, then citizenship. They also cover the forms of government Uruguay has tried. Among them sits a shared executive used twice in the last century and later given up. Rights and duties run through the opening sections as well.

A president leads the executive for a single term, with a waiting period before running again. The General Assembly pairs a Senate with a Chamber of Representatives. Later sections cover the courts, local departments, elections, public finance, and the armed forces. Uruguay's voters also use direct votes often: the text lets citizens force referendums and even write changes by gathering signatures.
crowley-equinox-vol-1-no-04:
The fourth number of The Equinox came out in September 1910, fat with the work of half a year. Crowley's journal had become a fixture of the London occult world by then. Each number aimed to be a small library of the order's mind.

Rites and holy books appear in these pages in their first print form. Around them stand poems, tales, and sharp reviews of rival works. The mix was the point: magic as a whole life of the mind. This number keeps the founding record of Thelema thick and rich throughout. It rewards any reader who opens it at random.
crowley-mathers-goetia-of-solomon-1904:
The Goetia, in the 1904 edition translated by Mathers and introduced by Crowley, is the first printed edition of the first book of the Lemegeton. The Lemegeton, or Lesser Key of Solomon, is a grimoire, a handbook of ceremonial magic ascribed to King Solomon. Mathers worked from manuscripts in the British Museum.

The text lists seventy-two spirits, with their seals, ranks, offices, and the hours and tools for calling them. Crowley's introduction frames the spirits as forces of the human brain rather than as literal demons. The edition defined modern ceremonial magic's demonology and set the pattern for later occult publishing.
cumner-s-son-and-other-south-sea-folk-vo:
Cumner's Son and Other South Sea Folk, Volume 4, by Gilbert Parker, opens at a luncheon table where empire is being theorized. In A Sable Spartan, Blithelygo addresses Lady Tynemouth and His Excellency. Uniform, he argues, revolutionizes the savage. Give a man convention, meaning clothes. Give him responsibility, meaning a chance at vanity and power. You make him a good citizen, he says. Lady Tynemouth wonders, aloud, whether it depends somewhat on the race.

A Vulgar Fraction, How Pango Wango Was Annexed, An Amiable Revenge, The Blind Beggar and the Little Red Peg, and A Friend of the Commune complete the volume. Annexations, island politics, and Parisian exiles pass through Parker's Pacific. The luncheon debate is the book in miniature. Colonial policy is argued as drawing room philosophy. The tales that follow test the theory. Governors, soldiers, and islanders all have theories of their own.
davies-celtic-researches-1804:
Edward Davies, a Welsh cleric, wrote this study of the old Britons in 1804, five years before his book on druid rites. It was the first full try in the Romantic age to build a Celtic past in one scheme. He worked from Welsh verse, old tales, and stone works.

Davies traced the first Britons to the east and tied their faith to the druids. He read names, myths, and rites as clues to one lost world of belief. Later scholars set much of it aside, but the book set the form for Celtic studies.
defoe-the-storm-1704:
Daniel Defoe published The Storm in 1704, an eyewitness collection on the Great Storm of 1703. The book is often called the first work of modern journalism in English prose writing. Defoe advertised for accounts and wove his own survey into a national record of loss.

The storm of November 1703 sank ships, unroofed churches, and killed thousands across southern England in one night. Defoe prints letters from ports and parishes, lists of wrecked men-of-war, and chimneys down in London. He weighs natural causes against providence, and scolds both scoffers and panicked preachers of the day in print. Eddystone Lighthouse fell with its builder inside, a loss the book records in stark detail for readers. Its method, gather testimony fast and print it plain, set a pattern for news.
duckworth-morphology-anthropology-1904:
W. L. H. Duckworth, a Cambridge scholar of the body, wrote this text book on form and the study of man in 1904. It joins two themes: the shapes of ape and man, and the rise of man from ape kin. Cambridge men used it to teach the new field.

Duckworth sets out skulls, brains, and bones of apes and men side by side. He then turns to the fossil finds known in his day and fits them in the line of growth. The book forms a bridge from the living body to the claims for fossil man.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-04:
Custom rules human life with quiet force, and Michel de Montaigne tests that claim in Volume 4 of his Essays. Charles Cotton's translation carries the French original into plain, lively English. Montaigne (1533-1592) wrote from his tower library in southwestern France. He trusted close observation more than school rules or fashion.

One long chapter shows habit training bodies to bear poison, strange foods, noise, and pain. Montaigne notes how custom also hardens nations to cruel laws and odd dress. A second chapter draws opposite results from one piece of advice, using Roman examples. Pedantry, meaning learning shown off without judgment, gets mocked in the third chapter. Schoolmasters who stuff boys with facts but no sense come in for sharp jokes. Readers meet here a core Montaigne habit: doubt any rule just because age made it familiar.
europmc-pmc10017004:
Parasher reviews the state of knowledge on COVID-19 in a 2021 paper, with a focus on how the disease harms the body. The virus behind it, SARS-CoV-2, belongs to the coronavirus family. It first caused a wave of severe lung infections in Wuhan, China, and then spread worldwide.

The review explains the illness step by step, from infection to symptoms in the lungs and beyond. It covers how doctors recognize the disease and the treatments in use at the time. Readers get a clear summary of a fast-moving field at an early stage.
europmc-pmc10030804:
Chen and colleagues review how ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron, interacts with inflammatory signals, in a 2023 paper. In ferroptosis, iron fuels damage to cell membranes until the cell dies. Inflammation is the body's alarm and repair response, but when it runs out of control it harms tissue.

The review maps the shared signals between the two processes. It shows how each can trigger or restrain the other in disease. The authors discuss what this crosstalk means for treatment of cancer, organ injury, and other conditions where both processes run.
europmc-pmc10284704:
Nardou and colleagues report that psychedelic drugs reopen a critical period for social reward learning, in a 2023 study. Critical periods are windows early in life when the brain learns certain skills with ease, after which the window closes. Social reward learning, the pull of social approval, has such a window in mice and likely in humans.

The team found that several psychedelics reopen that window in adult mice. The reopening lasted from days to weeks depending on the drug. The result may explain why these drugs help in therapy that involves relearning social patterns.
europmc-pmc10903104:
Klemmensen and colleagues review the role of faulty energy hubs in brain diseases in this 2024 paper. Mitochondria are the parts of cells that make most of their energy. When they fail, nerve cells suffer, since the brain needs much energy. The review links such failure to Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and two other nerve diseases.

The authors trace the history of this research and explain how healthy mitochondria work. They detail how harmful oxygen molecules from faulty hubs can damage DNA caps and gene controls. Current trials of drugs that target these hubs are surveyed. Current human trials of drugs that target these hubs are listed and weighed. The authors frame such drugs as a route to ease symptoms and slow the course of these diseases.
europmc-pmc11031404:
Brown and a large team report a phase 1 trial of engineered T cells for hard-to-treat brain tumours in this 2024 paper. High-grade glioma is an aggressive brain cancer, and cases that return after treatment respond poorly to current care. CAR-T therapy arms a patient's own T cells with a sensor for a tumour target. Here the target was a surface protein called IL-13Ralpha2, and cells were delivered near the tumour rather than into the blood.

Sixty-five patients took part, most with recurrent glioblastoma, the authors report. The trial tested three delivery routes: into the tumour, into the brain's fluid spaces, or both. No dose-limiting harms appeared in any arm, so no maximum tolerated dose was set. Two severe events were judged probably tied to treatment. The final arm paired dual delivery with an improved cell-making process and reached 200 million cells per dose cycle.
europmc-pmc11045904:
Adamu, Li, Gao, and Xue review brain inflammation as a driver of nerve cell loss in this 2024 paper. Neuroinflammation is the brain's immune reaction to injury, infection, or disease. Support cells called glia switch on, release alarm chemicals, and make harmful oxygen and nitrogen species. Short bursts protect the brain, but a reaction that runs too long turns harmful.

The review maps the major signal paths that link this reaction to Parkinson disease, Alzheimer disease, and multiple sclerosis. Each disease shows its own spread pattern across brain regions. Three therapy routes get close attention: stem cell therapy, gene-based intervention, and nanoparticles, meaning specks engineered to carry drugs. All three aim to calm the reaction and slow nerve loss. The authors stress that grasping this link is pivotal for future treatments.
europmc-pmc11120204:
GBD 2021 Risk Factors Collaborators quantify how 88 risk factors drive disease worldwide in this 2024 study. Knowing what exposures cost in health terms is required to set sound public health policy. The study spans 204 countries and territories plus 811 subnational locations from 1990 to 2021. It is part of the Global Burden of Disease program.

The team drew on 54,561 distinct data sources, they report. They built estimates for 631 risk and outcome pairs, such as smoking paired with lung cancer. Each pair passed a data-driven check for a real association. Exposure levels, relative risks, and the share of disease blamed on each factor were estimated by age, sex, place, and year. The method follows a comparative risk framework that layers risks in a causal web. Results are given at global, regional, and national levels.
europmc-pmc11270804:
Liu and a large team review the protein tagging system that controls protein lifespan, and its role in cancer, in this 2024 paper. Ubiquitination attaches a small tag that marks proteins for destruction or changes their behaviour. Enzymes that add the tag and enzymes that remove it are both dysregulated in many cancers. The system as a whole is called the ubiquitin-proteasome system.

The review covers the system's part in all hallmarks of cancer, the classic traits that define malignancy. It also covers metabolic rewiring, tumour immune responses, and cell flexibility. Drug discovery progress gets a full survey. Two new strategies stand out: PROTACs, which drag a chosen protein to the destruction machinery, and molecular glues, which stick proteins together to force the same fate. The authors present both as a new generation of anticancer design.
europmc-pmc11271404:
Ekanem and a very large team assess the safety of pulsed field ablation for atrial fibrillation in this 2024 study. Atrial fibrillation is a chaotic heart rhythm that raises stroke risk. Pulsed field ablation uses electric pulses to scar the tissue that triggers the rhythm. Early data suggested it spares nearby structures, unlike heat-based methods.

The MANIFEST-17K study gathered post-approval data from 106 of 116 centres, covering 17,642 patients. No oesophageal damage, vein narrowing, or lasting nerve palsy was reported, the team found. Major complications hit about 1 percent of patients. Heart sac bleeding, called tamponade, led at 0.36 percent, then vascular events at 0.30 percent of patients. Stroke was rare at 0.12 percent and death rarer still, at 0.03 percent of patients. Unexpected events included coronary spasm in 0.14 percent of cases.
europmc-pmc1241104:
Olsson and co-authors studied cadmium levels in Swedish farm families in 2002. Cadmium is a toxic metal that builds up in kidneys. Food is a main source for nonsmokers. The team measured cadmium in blood and urine of farm residents.

Median blood cadmium was 1.8 nanomoles per liter across the group. Women had 1.8 times the blood cadmium of men in never-smoking couples. That gap held despite women eating less cadmium per body weight. Low iron likely raised absorption in women. Levels also rose with age and past smoking. Local farm food formed a small, varied share of intake.
europmc-pmc1409804:
Finding genes in a string of DNA is hard when the clues are patchy. Stanke and co-authors took on that task in 2006. Their method blends hints from outside sources, such as matches to known proteins, with clues inside the DNA itself. It weighs both kinds of proof in one math model.

The team built the method into the gene finder AUGUSTUS, making a tool called AUGUSTUS+. On human chromosome 22, hints from known genes helped it call 89 percent of exons right. An exon is a part of a gene that codes for protein. Stanke shows that even the lack of a match can guide a sound call.
europmc-pmc1463904:
A chikungunya virus outbreak swept the Indian Ocean islands in 2005 and 2006. Schuffenecker and co-authors read the virus genome to trace its spread. The virus, spread by mosquitoes, causes fever and severe joint pain. On Réunion Island it infected about a third of the people.

The team sequenced six full virus samples and parts from 127 patients. The outbreak strain came from East African stock. Its changes over time could be traced step by step. One sample from spinal fluid held unique shifts found in no blood sample. Two changes sat in a surface protein that fuses the virus with cells. Schuffenecker maps how a local strain grew into a regional wave.
europmc-pmc1564004:
Parents asked to rate a child's quality of life often disagree with the child. Cremeens, Eiser, and Blades measured that gap in 2006. They gave a standard survey to 149 healthy children aged five to eight, and to 103 of their parents.

Agreement was low, with correlation scores from 0.02 to 0.23. Parents and children differed on every subscale. The oldest children matched parents best on total and social scores. The youngest matched best on physical health. Parents' own quality of life colored their ratings of the child. Cremeens warns proxy reports are a weak stand-in for a child's own view.
europmc-pmc1790904:
Edgar presented PILER-CR in 2007, a program built to find CRISPR repeats in bacterial genomes. CRISPR elements are short, near-identical DNA repeats split by unique spacer sequences of similar length. General repeat-finding tools can spot them, but their output often needs heavy manual cleanup before study.

PILER-CR was designed for this one pattern, so it runs fast and reports the repeats in a usable form. It scanned a five-million-letter genome in about five seconds on a desktop computer of the time. Checks against hand-curated results and published surveys showed both high sensitivity and high specificity, meaning it missed few real repeats and flagged few false ones. Edgar also released a catalog of candidate repeats found across 346 prokaryotic genomes.
europmc-pmc1852404:
Kingsford, Ayanbule and Salzberg built in 2007 a fast method to find the stop signals that end gene transcription in bacteria. These Rho-independent terminators are short DNA motifs, usually a GC-rich hairpin followed by a run of thymine letters. Finding them maps operons, the gene groups read as one unit.

Few terminators had been verified outside two model bacteria, so computing was the only practical route at scale. Their method produced an extensive predicted collection across 343 prokaryotes. The survey let them probe a second puzzle: why some bacteria carry special DNA uptake sequences near these sites. Such sequences help cells pull in outside DNA. The terminator catalog and the uptake link together give a genome-wide view of how bacterial transcription ends.
europmc-pmc1896004:
Miller, Bosch and co-authors inventoried in 2007 the innate immune toolkit of cnidarians, the phylum of jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones. Innate immunity is the inborn first defense line, and in these early animals it was assumed to be simple. The team mined genomic resources from two cnidarian classes.

Sea anemones and their kin, the basal Anthozoa, turned out to hold several key parts of the vertebrate innate repertoire. Those parts include receptor and signaling pieces long thought to be later inventions. Hydra, a member of the other class, Hydrozoa, lacks many of them. The pattern suggests the common ancestor was already complex, and Hydra's line later lost genes by chance. Immune origins thus run deeper, and simpler toolkits can be the derived state, not the starting point.
europmc-pmc1964804:
Lombardo, Baron-Cohen and co-authors tested in 2007 whether autism involves thinking about oneself, not just about others. People on the autism spectrum show deep social difficulties, and empathy problems are well documented. Whether self-referential thought, the intrapersonal mirror of empathy, is also affected was unclear.

Thirty adults with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism, aged 19 to 45, were matched with 30 controls by age, sex, and IQ. In the self-reference task they judged adjectives about themselves, a close other, a distant other, or the words alone, then took a surprise memory test. The battery also measured alexithymia, private self-consciousness, self-focused attention, four empathy measures including the Eyes test, and autistic traits. The study design lets the authors ask whether self and empathy deficits travel together.
europmc-pmc2124704: A medical paper on auto- and isotransplantation of parathyroid glands in dogs. The glands, moved. This article preserves that surgical research. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2124904: A medical paper on strongyloides infections in man and animals in the Isthmian Canal Zone. The canal worms. This article preserves that parasitology. It waits for future eyes. Its place in history is secure. Readers can find it here.
europmc-pmc2125104: A medical paper with studies on ferment action, the toxicity of some proteoses. The poisonous proteins. This article preserves that biochemistry. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2126304: A medical paper on spirilla associated with disease of the fetal membranes in cattle. The bovine infection. This article preserves that veterinary bacteriology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2128204: A medical paper on the incidence of blackhead and Heterakis in a turkey flock. The turkey disease. This article preserves that veterinary parasitology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2128304: A medical paper on dissociation of microbic species, coexistence of different individuals. The mixed germs. This article preserves that bacteriology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2140604: A biology paper with a dissection of the chromosomes in the pollen mother cells of Tradescantia. The spiderwort chromosomes. This article preserves that genetics. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2140704: A biology paper on the kinetics of the decomposition of peroxide by catalase. The enzyme's speed. This article preserves that biochemistry. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2141004: A biology paper on the oxygen consumption of luminous bacteria. The glowing breath. This article preserves that bacteriology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2244704:
Spurgeon, Jones and Ramakrishnan described a microfluidic gene expression platform in 2008 built around real-time PCR. Real-time PCR is the gold standard for measuring gene activity, but it is slow and low-throughput. Their chip uses tiny fluid channels to run many reactions in parallel. A single chip performs 2,304 simultaneous measurements, yet needs less pipetting than setting up a standard 96-well plate.

On one chip they measured 45 different genes across 18 tissues, with replicates included. Results agreed excellently with conventional real-time PCR on the same samples. Reproducibility beat commercial DNA microarrays, the usual high-throughput alternative. The platform targets the common workflow where a genome-wide study narrows interest to twenty to one hundred key genes. Those genes can then be measured across far larger sample sets than microarrays allow.
europmc-pmc2265304:
Selman, Pardo and Kaminski argued in 2008 that idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis may arise from embryonic programmes wrongly switched back on. This lung disease is chronic, progressive and usually lethal, with unknown cause. Injured alveolar epithelial cells are thought to activate mesenchymal cells, forming scar foci that destroy lung tissue with excess matrix. Such reawakening of developmental pathways is common in cancer but rare in non-malignant disease.

The authors review gene expression studies and animal models pointing to developmental signalling in the disease. Candidate pathways include Wnt, which guides embryonic patterning, and the TGF-beta family. TGF-beta promotes fibrosis and can convert epithelial cells toward a mesenchymal state. Related BMP signals often oppose those effects. Understanding which embryonic circuits reactivate could explain why the fibrosis persists rather than healing.
europmc-pmc2268004:
Caws and a large team tested in 2008 whether bacterial strain and host genes together shape tuberculosis disease form. Some Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains may spread beyond the lungs more readily, causing meningitis. The team compared 187 Vietnamese adults with tuberculous meningitis against 237 with uncomplicated lung tuberculosis, plus 392 cord blood controls. Bacterial isolates were typed by large sequence changes, and hosts by variants in two innate immunity genes.

The Euro-American bacterial lineage was underrepresented in meningitis, with an odds ratio of 0.395 for that outcome. Those strains may disseminate less. Hosts carrying one variant of the TLR-2 gene were more likely to carry the East-Asian Beijing strain. Its odds ratio was 1.57, and its confidence interval excluded no effect. The study population was Vietnamese.
europmc-pmc2292704:
Hundertmark and Hincha published this 2008 genome-wide survey of LEA proteins in Arabidopsis thaliana, a small flowering plant used widely in research. LEA stands for late embryogenesis abundant, meaning these proteins build up late in seed growth. They are thought to help cells survive drying out, cold, and other stress.

The authors found 51 genes that code for LEA proteins, and they sorted them into nine groups. Using a lab method that counts gene activity, they showed all 51 genes were switched on somewhere in the plant. Levels were higher in seeds than in leaves or stems. About a third of the genes sat in tandem repeats, side by side on the chromosome. Many were switched on by cold, drought, or a stress hormone.
europmc-pmc2346504:
Rosas and a large team searched for a blood test for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis in 2008. In this disease the lungs scar and stiffen over time, and doctors lack a simple blood marker for it. A biomarker is a measurable sign of a disease.

They measured 49 proteins in blood from 74 patients and 53 healthy controls. A set of five proteins separated patients from controls with about 98% accuracy on both sensitivity and specificity. Two proteins, MMP1 and MMP7, stood out and were also raised in lung tissue and lung wash fluid. Both stayed normal in two other lung diseases, which helps tell them apart. Raised MMP7 also appeared in people with early, symptom-free lung disease and tracked falling lung power.
europmc-pmc2394204:
Clifford, Smith, Aguado, and Franceschi compared HPV types in precancerous cervical lesions and in cancer in 2003. Only some lesions progress to cancer, and the team asked whether the virus type predicts that step. They pooled published data on high-grade lesions, called HSIL, and on squamous cell carcinoma, the main cervical cancer form.

The combined data covered 8,594 cancer cases and 4,338 high-grade lesion cases. Three types, HPV16, 18, and 45, were each more common in cancers than in lesions. The reverse held for types 31, 33, 52, and 58, which sat more often in lesions that stayed put. The authors read this as evidence that lesions carrying 16, 18, or 45 preferentially move on to cancer. That matters for screening follow-up and for vaccine trials that use lesion prevention as their yardstick.
europmc-pmc2459204:
Jeon and Murray reviewed whether diabetes raises the risk of active tuberculosis in 2008. Tuberculosis is a bacterial lung infection still common in poorer countries, where diabetes is now rising fast. If diabetes truly feeds tuberculosis, the overlap threatens disease control on both fronts.

They gathered 13 observational studies covering 1,786,212 people and 17,698 tuberculosis cases. Combining the cohort studies, which follow people forward in time, diabetes came with a relative risk of 3.11 for developing active tuberculosis. Case-control studies varied widely, with odds ratios from 1.16 to 7.83 depending on the population studied. Effects ran stronger outside North America. The authors concluded the link holds across designs, making people with diabetes a priority group for tuberculosis screening and preventive treatment in high-burden regions.
europmc-pmc2568804:
Tyler and colleagues showed in 2008 that gentle ultrasound can switch on brain circuits without wires or implants. Stimulating the brain usually means electrodes or light-emitting devices placed invasively. Ultrasound instead passes through bone and tissue and can be focused from outside, so the team tested low-intensity, low-frequency pulses on mouse hippocampal slices and whole brains taken from mice.

The pulses remotely excited neurons and set network activity going. They worked by opening voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels, the gates that launch nerve signals. The activation was strong enough to trigger the release machinery at synapses, so signals passed between neurons in the circuit. The authors conclude ultrasound offers a powerful noninvasive tool for probing and potentially treating brain circuits.
europmc-pmc2713404:
Towner and co-authors reported in 2009 that Egyptian fruit bats in a Ugandan cave carry diverse Marburg viruses and likely seeded infections in miners. Marburg causes a severe bleeding fever with high death rates in Africa. In 2007 two miners who worked in Kitaka Cave fell ill, and the cave held a huge colony of these bats.

Testing found virus RNA in about five percent of sampled bats, antibodies in bat blood, and live virus in bat tissues. Virus was taken nine months apart, which shows long-term circulation in the colony of over one hundred thousand bats. Bat and miner virus genomes matched closely, which supports bats as a major natural reservoir.
europmc-pmc2784904:
Corthay reviewed in 2009 how regulatory T cells work, the CD4 T cells charged with suppressing other T helper cells that might harm the body. Their proposed jobs include holding self-tolerance to prevent autoimmune disease, calming allergy and asthma, and protecting the fetus during pregnancy. Yet basic questions about these cells remain open, and the review defines them plainly.

Identifying regulatory cells is itself a problem. Every marker in current use, from CD25 to Foxp3, also appears on ordinary activated T cells, so none is truly specific. Their suppression switches on only for specific antigens, and their receptor patterns suggest they are usually not self-reactive. Even their status as a separate lineage is disputed, since ordinary helper subsets can also suppress. Some regulatory cells can even convert into effector cells in the body.
europmc-pmc2845804:
Hampshire, Chamberlain, Monti, Duncan, and Owen used brain scans in 2010 to settle what the right inferior frontal gyrus, a patch of frontal brain, actually does during self-control. Scans during stop-signal tasks, where people must cancel a started movement, light up this region. Yet those tasks mix stopping with simply spotting an important cue.

The team held the stimuli identical while varying what the cue demanded: stop, make a different movement, or do nothing at all. The region switched on whenever an important cue was detected, whether or not any movement was actually stopped. The finding reframes the area as a salience watcher for the brain, not a dedicated brake pedal for behavior.
europmc-pmc2860504:
Lohmann and colleagues introduced in 2010 a fast way to find hub regions in brain scans taken while people rest. The scans, called resting-state fMRI, record slow waves of activity across the whole brain with no task to perform. Their method scores each tiny volume unit by how strongly it links to other well-linked units, a math idea borrowed from how search engines rank web pages.

Unlike older hub measures, the new score needs no preset cutoff and runs fast enough for the whole cerebrum at once. It can work from simple correlations or from more robust links between regions. Tests on real scan data picked out known hub areas and showed the score stays stable, giving brain mappers a practical tool for whole-brain network studies.
europmc-pmc2896904:
Costa, Angelini, De Feis, and Ciccodicola surveyed in 2010 RNA-Seq, the method that reads all RNA in a sample by deep sequencing, and the hurdles it brings. New machines read hundreds of thousands of DNA fragments at once, so RNA can be counted directly instead of being probed indirectly. The approach measures gene activity, alternative splicing, where one gene yields several messages, and which parental copy of a gene is used.

That richness comes with cost: files are massive and riddled with biases that older analysis habits cannot handle. The survey walks through the workflow, from aligning reads to counting and comparing, and names the open problems in each step. Bioinformatics must mature alongside the sequencers, the authors stress, or data will pile up faster than insight.
europmc-pmc2904704:
Cattuto and colleagues demonstrated in 2010 a wearable sensor system that records face-to-face human contact with second-level detail. Knowing who meets whom, and for how long, is central to modeling how infections spread, yet diaries and surveys capture it crudely. Their active RFID badges exchange low-power radio packets only when wearers stand close and face each other, logging each encounter in real time.

Three deployments at very different community sizes produced contact networks with shared statistical fingerprints. Encounter lengths spanned from twenty seconds to hours with no typical duration, a heavy-tailed pattern. People with more contacts also held longer ones, a super-linear link the team highlights. Such data let modelers replace guessed contact patterns with measured ones.
europmc-pmc2921404:
Wu and colleagues set out in 2010 to standardize how gut bacteria are surveyed in human feces by DNA tag sequencing. Studies of the gut microbiome were exploding, but each lab stored, extracted, and sequenced samples differently. They took stool from ten people and varied each step: immediate deep freezing against one or two days on ice, three commercial extraction kits against hot phenol bead beating.

Samples taken one centimeter apart in the same stool matched closely, setting the natural noise floor. Against person-to-person differences, which were vast, the method choices moved results only modestly, especially when counting which bacteria were present rather than their exact shares. Storage on ice for a day or two was tolerable. The study gives the young field a validated, practical sampling recipe.
europmc-pmc2962904:
Salem and Thiemermann reviewed mesenchymal stromal cells, versatile adult cells that can become several tissue types, in a 2010 article on their biology and medical status. Reports credited these cells with aiding repair across many organs.

After growing in culture and delivery into the body, the cells home to injured tissue and calm inflammation, lowering harmful signals while raising protective ones. They also suppress immune attackers including T cells and natural killer cells. Lab progress, including use of donor cells from others, pushed trials forward, with heart and kidney uses highlighted in the review.
europmc-pmc2970904:
Lindorff-Larsen and colleagues refined part of a widely used protein simulation toolkit in a 2010 study, improving how amino acid side chains twist in computer models. Longer simulations had exposed small accuracy faults in existing force fields.

They singled out four residue types whose simulated twist patterns strayed most from database expectations, then refitted their settings against high-level quantum calculations. Microsecond-long test simulations in water matched laboratory NMR measurements far better than the old settings. The updated package, named ff99SB-ILDN after the improved residues, gives modellers a more faithful view of protein motion.
europmc-pmc2978704:
Suhre and colleagues ran a multi-platform scan of small molecules in blood from a German population study in 2010, hunting the metabolic footprint of diabetes. No single instrument can read the whole set of body chemicals, so they combined three.

Fasting blood from forty people reporting diabetes and sixty controls yielded measurements of several hundred distinct molecules by magnetic resonance and mass methods. Known diabetes signs reappeared, including a sugar marker, a ketone body, and certain amino acids, and traces of diabetes drugs were detectable. The exercise shows combined platforms can sketch disease chemistry in everyday population samples.
europmc-pmc3002804:
Omar reviewed oleuropein, the bitter phenolic compound that gives extra-virgin olive oil much of its bite, in a 2010 article. Olive products anchor the Mediterranean diet and carry a long folk reputation for health.

Recent studies tie oleuropein, found across the olive plant, to a wide portfolio of effects. It fights oxidation and inflammation and slows artery clogging. In lab work it also acts against microbes, viruses, and cancer cells. Reports also credit it with lowering blood fats and blood sugar in animal studies. The review gathers that pharmacology and weighs how a food chemical might inspire future medicines.
europmc-pmc3017804:
Hu and co-authors catalogued the NAC family of plant control genes in the poplar tree in a 2010 study. These plant-only switches steer development from seed formation to wood growth, and families exceed a hundred members in several species.

They found a hundred and sixty-three full NAC genes in poplar, sorted into eighteen subfamilies with conserved structures and motifs. Most sit in duplicated genome blocks, leftovers of an ancient genome doubling, and duplicates often share expression patterns with partial overlap. Expression data from tags and arrays showed most members active only at certain times or places.
europmc-pmc3052304:
Schmieder and Edwards built in 2011 a tool that finds and strips foreign DNA out of sequencing datasets. Samples are rarely pure, so reads from handlers, lab reagents, or host tissue can sneak in and corrupt genome assemblies and conclusions. Their program, DeconSeq, compares long reads against reference genomes and flags matches that do not belong, showing the results in clear graphics.

To show why it matters, they screened more than two hundred published microbe and virus community datasets. Possible contamination turned up in nearly three quarters of them, and in the worst case most reads were foreign. Human DNA was a frequent stowaway even in samples with no human link. The tool runs as a website or as local software that fits existing pipelines. The authors recommend screening as a standard step for every sequencing project.
europmc-pmc3101904:
Yip and coauthors reported in 2011 that disulfiram, a decades old drug used to deter drinking, kills breast cancer cells and their hardiest stem like cells when paired with copper. Drug resistance, blamed largely on cancer stem cells, is the main reason breast chemotherapy fails. In dishes, the drug plus copper killed standard breast cancer lines at low doses and sharply boosted a common chemotherapy drug's power, with a true synergistic pattern.

The combination generated corrosive oxygen molecules and switched on stress death pathways inside the cells. At the same time it shut down a survival factor that resistant cancers keep permanently active and that chemotherapy itself can provoke. Sphere forming growth and stem cell marker populations, the stand ins for cancer stem cells, both fell after a day of exposure. The authors propose repurposing this cheap, known drug as a resistance breaker, pending animal and clinical tests.
europmc-pmc3153204:
Olivier Puel, Pierre Galtier, and Isabelle Oswald reviewed a mould toxin common in apples in a 2010 paper in Toxins. The toxin, made by several mould genera, is the mould poison found most often in apples and in juice, cider, and baby foods made from them. Many countries cap its level in food because of the risks.

Exposure has been linked to immune, nerve, and gut effects in studies. The chemical path moulds use to build the toxin runs about ten steps. A cluster of fifteen genes behind it was recently reported, including the enzymes, a regulator, and exporters. The review sums up how the toxin is made and what it does, noting its genetics still lag behind better-studied mould poisons.
europmc-pmc3159904:
Paul Marik, Xavier Monnet, and Jean-Louis Teboul reviewed how to judge which patients need more fluid in a 2011 paper in Annals of Intensive Care. Giving fluid is the first rescue step for unstable patients, yet only about half actually respond with better circulation, and excess fluid raises harm. Older guides based on heart filling pressures have repeatedly failed to predict response.

Newer dynamic tests watch how the heart's output per beat shifts with breathing or with a brief leg raise, which temporarily moves blood toward the heart. Those swings, read continuously by Doppler, pulse-shape, or other bedside tools, separate responders from non-responders far better. The review explains the physiology and the devices, pushing intensive care away from static pressure numbers toward live functional tests.
europmc-pmc3213104:
Benjamin Howden and colleagues traced how Staphylococcus aureus becomes resistant to last-line drugs during infection, in this 2011 study in PLoS Pathogens. They sequenced five pairs of clinical strains, each collected from a patient before and after vancomycin treatment failed. Comparing each pair showed what changed as resistance evolved inside the patient.

The resistant strains repeatedly carried mutations in walKR, a two-gene regulatory system controlling cell wall metabolism. Swapping single altered letters in either gene into the original strains reproduced resistance to both vancomycin and daptomycin, plus the thickened cell walls typical of resistant isolates. The same changes weakened virulence and biofilm formation and shifted central metabolism. The study shows how one small mutation can reshape a dangerous pathogen.
europmc-pmc3223004:
Ruthann Rudel and colleagues tested how much food packaging contributes to exposure to two plastic chemicals, in this 2011 study in Environmental Health Perspectives. Bisphenol A and the phthalate DEHP are used in cans and plastic packaging and can disrupt hormones. Twenty volunteers from five families switched for three days to fresh foods with little packaging, bracketed by their usual diets.

Urine samples collected across eight days showed sharp drops during the fresh-food days. Levels of bisphenol A fell by about two-thirds, and breakdown products of DEHP fell by roughly half, with the highest individual readings falling even more steeply. The results show diet, and packaging in particular, is a major and changeable route of exposure, and that simple menu changes can cut it substantially.
europmc-pmc3241704:
Ioannis Mitroulis and colleagues linked a striking neutrophil behavior to the inflammation of gout, in this 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Gout is a common inflammatory arthritis in which urate crystals trigger immune attack and release of the inflammatory signal IL-1 beta. Neutrophils are central players, and the team asked whether they cast out web-like traps of their own DNA during attacks.

Neutrophils from the joints and blood of patients in a gout flare were indeed forming these extracellular traps, which carried a pro-inflammatory alarm protein. Urate crystals, joint fluid, or serum from patients made healthy neutrophils do the same. Blocking cell-recycling machinery, known as autophagy, prevented trap formation, and IL-1 beta drove it in part, since its blocker anakinra reduced it. The authors suggest the recycling machinery as a new drug target in crystal arthritis.
europmc-pmc3319604:
Vestberg, Gustafson, Maurex, Ingvar, and Petrovic tested whether general thinking skills predict soccer success, reporting in 2012. Top players obviously need fitness and ball skills, but matches also demand fast decisions under pressure. The team gave standard brain function tests, covering creativity, stopping impulsive responses, and switching approaches, to players from Swedish divisions and compared them with typical scores.

Both high and lower division players beat the general population on these executive skills. Players in the top division scored higher still than those below them. When the researchers checked scoring records two seasons later, test results lined up with the goals and assists players had produced. The authors argue that raw thinking power, not just soccer specific instincts, helps separate elite players from the rest.
europmc-pmc3330104:
Stranger and colleagues compared how DNA variants tune gene activity across eight human populations, in a 2012 study. Genes are not simply on or off; nearby variants raise or lower their output, and those dial settings may differ by ancestry. The team measured gene output in blood derived cells from more than seven hundred people in the HapMap project and matched it against nearby variants.

Ancestry did shift overall gene activity patterns in measurable ways. The team cataloged nearly fifty seven hundred dial variants after careful corrections. About half of them showed up in more than one population, and where they did, the size and direction of the effect matched closely. Variants sitting near a gene's start tended to travel best across populations. The results form a resource for judging how disease findings in one population apply to others.
europmc-pmc3386304:
Arand and colleagues mapped in 2012 how living cells place and keep DNA methylation marks, both at standard CG sites and elsewhere. The enzymes responsible, called Dnmts, split into builders and maintainers, but their exact shares were murky. The team sequenced chosen genes and repeat elements at single-molecule detail in mouse stem cells.

Many CG sites turned out to be only half-marked, with the shortfall varying by cell type. Marks at non-CG sites appeared only in stem cells and came solely from two builder enzymes working with a helper. Modeling of more than a hundred thousand site pairs let the team weigh each enzyme's role. Even the supposed maintainer adds fresh marks at some repeats.
europmc-pmc3394104:
Elgendi surveyed in 2012 the analysis of fingertip pulse signals gathered by shining infrared light through the skin. The method, called photoplethysmography, is cheap, gentle, and handy, drawing researchers from many fields. Clinicians already use it for oxygen levels, blood pressure, heart output, and early warning of artery disease.

Much of the signal's diagnostic promise sits in the shape of its wave, beyond simple pulse counting. The overview catalogs the wave's features, the artifacts that corrupt it, and the indexes used to score it. A full grasp of what each feature means is still missing, Elgendi notes. The paper maps the groundwork needed before routine screening can rely on it.

europmc-pmc7779004: A 2021 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at the STRING database (large data store) in 2021: customizable protein-protein networks, and working characterization (detailed description) of user-uploaded gene/measurement sets. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc7785004: This 2020 research paper covers manganese is serious for antitumor immune responses (the immune system's replies) via cgas-sting and improves the efficacy (how well something works). CD8 + t cell-driven cancer clearance is often suppressed by the interaction between inhibitory molecules like PD-1 and PD-L1. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc7790804: Doctors and scientists took on Japanese stomach cancer treatment guidelines (official advice) 2018 (5th edition) in this 2021 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc7857404: A 2020 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at structural (about shapes) analysis of full-length SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (the virus's spike) from an advanced vaccine candidate. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc7905904: Doctors and scientists took on trend analysis of cardiovascular (of the heart and blood vessels) disease deaths, incidence (new cases), and deaths-to-new cases ratio: results in this 2021 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Solid numbers like these help health officials aim prevention money and effort where they count most.
europmc-pmc7922504: Collado-Mateo and co-authors published this review paper in 2021 on key factors linked to adherence to physical exercise in patients with chronic diseases and older adults: an umbrella review. The authors pull together the key findings from across the field. A good review shows what is solid, what is shaky, and where the next study should look.
europmc-pmc7942704: A historical paper on the centenary of Lister, a tale of sepsis and antisepsis. The carbolic revolution. This article preserves that surgical history. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc8066304: Baldelli and co-authors published this research paper in 2021 on the role of enterobacteriaceae in gut microbiota (the microbes living in the body) dysbiosis (microbial imbalance) in inflammatory (swelling-related) bowel diseases. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
