Hayyim Selig Slonimski was a Russian author, scientist, and inventor. Isidore Singer and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Byelostok in 1810 and died in Warsaw in 1904. He first taught eastern European Jews popular science in Hebrew. He coined many Hebrew technical terms for that purpose.

His strict religious conservatism won readers' full trust. In 1842 he perfected a calculating machine of his own. It won the Demidoff prize of 2,500 rubles at St Petersburg. He later devised a way to send four telegrams at once. In 1862 he founded Ha-Zefirah, a Hebrew weekly for science. He also led the rabbinical seminary at Jitomir for twelve years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomons-adolph:
Adolphus Simeon Solomons was an American communal worker born in 1826. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in New York city on October 26. He was educated at the University of the City of New York. He rose fast in a firm of wholesale importers.

In 1851 Daniel Webster sent him to Berlin with despatches. At Frankfort he first saw a Jewish hospital ward. He resolved to found such a hospital in New York. A charity ball he helped arrange raised the first funds. That money helped start the present Mt Sinai Hospital. He later held government printing contracts in Washington.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stein-philip-14:
Philip Stein was an American jurist born at Steele, Prussia, in 1844. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born there on March 12 of that year. He emigrated to the United States in 1854 as a boy. He was educated at Milwaukee and the University of Wisconsin.

He took his master's degree and joined the bar in 1868. After study at Heidelberg, Bonn, and Berlin, he settled in Chicago. In 1870 he began practice in that city of Illinois. In 1892 and 1898 he won election to the Superior Court. In 1903 he became judge of the appellate court. By 1905 he was presiding justice of that court.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sulamith-14104:
Sulamith was the first Jewish monthly magazine in the German language. Isidore Singer and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Its first volume appeared at Leipsic in July 1806. David Frankel and Joseph Wolf edited it at first. Frankel later edited it alone from Dessau.

The magazine aimed to spread culture and humanity among Jews. It followed the reform path of Mendelssohn's German followers. Pages held biographies, history sketches, sermons, and poems. Education news and Hebrew pieces appeared as well. Contributors included David Friedländer and Ignatz Jeiteles. Volumes ran in loose years until 1840, then revived in 1846. Much content is now dated, the entry notes. The rest still feeds research on modern Jewish history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-temple-of-herod:
Herod's rebuilt Temple in Jerusalem is described in this article. George A. Barton wrote it with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Herod began the work in 20 or 19 B.C. He wanted a shrine as grand as his other buildings.

Jews feared the old Temple would fall and never rise again. Herod stored all materials first to prove his good faith. Priests worked as masons, since only priests could enter the holy place. The main building rose in eighteen months. Courts and outer works took eighty years. The article gives sizes, veils, and the golden candlestick. It also notes the Greek warning sign that barred Gentiles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tirzah-14404:
Tirzah names both an ancient royal city and a daughter of Zelophehad. Immanuel Benzinger wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Jeroboam made Tirzah a royal city of Israel. It housed Israel's kings until Omri's reign. The Song of Songs praises its beauty.

Where the city stood remains uncertain today. Robinson placed it at modern Talluza, near Nablus. Conder instead chose Tayasir, with its caves and tombs. Neither Josephus nor Eusebius gives firm details. The district lay in Manasseh, in Zelophehad's portion. The second Tirzah was his youngest daughter. Numbers names her among his five daughters. Those sisters famously claimed an inheritance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trevoux-hebrew-:
Trévoux, a French town in Ain, barred Jews by its charter of 1300. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Some Jews settled there anyway for a yearly tax. Refugees from Lyons arrived in 1420 after expulsion. They worked at making gold and silver wire.

In 1425 the town forced a large loan contribution from them. Neighbors grew jealous of Jewish commercial success. In 1429 they accused Hebrew books of blasphemy. Investigators seized and burned the books at once. Fines and expulsion followed for the whole community. Some Jews returned within three years. Fresh expulsions came in 1467 and 1488.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-uri-ori-ben-sim:
Uri ben Simeon was a sixteenth-century scholar of Safed who cataloged holy tombs. Schulim Ochser wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was born at Biel and settled at Safed. He abstracted a manuscript of 1537 for his work. That list named tombs of patriarchs, prophets, and sages.

His own travels added descriptions and grave illustrations. The book, Yihus ha-Abot, appeared at Venice in 1659. Hottinger translated it into Latin at Heidelberg. Carmoly later rendered it into French with twenty-seven pictures. A Judaeo-German version appeared at Wilna in 1853. Uri also compiled a forty-year calendar, printed in 1575. Jacob Christmann translated that calendar into Latin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wayikra-rabbah-:
Wayikra Rabbah is a homiletic midrash on Leviticus. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Nathan's Aruk first names the work in later sources. Rashi quotes it often in his commentaries. Zunz dated its origin to the mid seventh century. It arose in Palestine from older materials.

The book is not a running commentary on Leviticus. It holds thirty seven separate sermons, each a chapter. Their themes come from texts across the book. Its editor drew on Genesis Rabbah and the Jerusalem Talmud. Babylonian Talmud phrases appear in it as well. The entry maps its sources, shape, and sermon topics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolper-michael-:
Michael Wolper (born 1852) was a Russian teacher and maker of school books. Herman Rosenthal and Julius Gottlieb wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Wilna, he trained at the rabbinical school there. He left that school in 1872 with his degree. From then on he taught in Jewish grade schools.

By 1905 he also checked the Jewish school at Wilna. He served as censor of Hebrew books as well. His own books teach faith and tongue to the young. One book gives first lessons in the Jewish faith. A second book gives a new way to learn Hebrew. He wrote that book in 1888. With a co-worker he made a short creed book for class use. More Russian-Jewish school books came from his pen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-nappaha-:
Yizhak Nappaha was a scholar of Palestine in the 300s and 400s. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His name means the smith in the tongue of his day. That name stands in the Babylon books, not the Palestine ones.

As a teller of tales he ranks with the first of his age. The Babylon books mix him with more than one like name. That mix came from the free hand of a late sage. So the true name of his sire can not be known now. An older smith of his name was a rich man of old. That man held five courts in the town of Usha. No proof ties the two men as kin to this day. He was a pupil of Johanan, the great sage of the north.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zechariah-mende:
Zechariah Mendel ben Aryeh Lob was a Galician preacher and scholar. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Podhaice early in the 1700s. He died at Frankfort-on-the-Oder in the year 1791.

He came of the house of Solomon Luria and Moses Isserles. That house traced its line back to Rashi of France. His chief teacher was Jacob Joshua of Pene Yehoshua fame. He preached in the Talmud Torah of Frankfort in his prime. He left a great store of works at his death in that town. Just three of them reached print in his life time. One holds notes on the tract Shabbat and feast sermons. One is a mate to that work with more Talmud notes. One is a guide to faith thought and true Cabala lore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zurishaddai-153: Zurishaddai was the father of Shelumiel, a chief of the tribe of Simeon. Emil G. Hirsch and Bernhard Pick wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. When Moses counted the people of Israel, Shelumiel was chosen to help him. The book of Numbers names Zurishaddai each time it names his son in that duty. The entry gives the verses in Numbers chapters one, two, seven, and ten.
journal-of-discourses-vol-04:
Volume Four, from 1857, was preached while a federal army marched on Utah. Johnston's troops drew near, and war talk filled the Salt Lake valley. The Saints readied to burn their homes and flee south.

Young's discourses breathe defiance and faith in the same breath here. Speakers vow to leave a scorched desert rather than yield their faith. Plans for flight, food stores, and guard duty share the pulpit's time. A people under siege hears its prophet plan and pray at once. The sermons catch a kingdom braced for its hardest test yet by arms. Trust in God and trust in Young stand as one here.
kelvin-baltimore-lectures-1904:
Lord Kelvin gave twenty lectures at Johns Hopkins in 1884, and they appeared in print in 1904. The Baltimore Lectures treat molecular dynamics and the wave theory of light. Kelvin built mechanical models to picture how the ether might carry light waves. Twelve appendices extend the lectures with later work and corrections.

Kelvin thinks aloud here, testing models, noting doubts, and pushing analogies hard. His pages show a great physicist before quantum and relativity changed the field. The ether models failed in the end, yet the effort taught much. Historians value the lectures as a record of classical physics at its height. The style stays vivid throughout.
kenelm-chillingly-volume-04:
Volume four of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Kenelm Chillingly opens Book Four in London, a year and a half later. The season has not yet begun before Easter. Fashionable London gathers at an evening reception at Lord Beaumanoir's house. The chapter works through presence chambers and saloons, amassing talk and faces.

Gerard Danvers, a member of Parliament, gets a full portrait here. Danvers mixes energy, ability, and self-reliance with a tolerant indulgence toward others. Townsfolk say he might one day be prime minister. Against this worldly company, Lytton sets Kenelm's sharper questions about success and sincerity. This volume moves the novel from country roads into politics and society.
kent-lectures-homoeopathic-materia-medic:
James Tyler Kent published his Lectures on Homoeopathic Materia Medica in 1904, from lectures given at the Post-Graduate School of Homoeopathics. The first edition staged here is the Calcutta printing of Roy Publishing House. Kent, an American physician, became the defining voice of classical homeopathy in the United States.

Remedy by remedy, from Abies to Zincum, he pictures the patient type each medicine fits: symptoms, temperament, and all. His vivid drug pictures taught generations of homeopaths how to prescribe. The remedy lectures are complete in this scan, though its printed index breaks off at Carbo veg. in the final leaves. Kent's book remains a working manual for practitioners of his school. Few medical lectures have been so often reprinted.
letter-of-aristeas-thackeray-1904:
H. St. J. Thackeray translated the Letter of Aristeas into English in 1904. The Letter is a Hellenistic Jewish work about the making of the Septuagint. It purports to be a courtier's report to his brother.

The tale claims seventy-two scholars translated the Torah in seventy-two days. King Ptolemy's library in Alexandria supposedly commissioned the Greek Bible. Banquets, sage answers, and a tour of Jerusalem fill out the story. Scholars treat the account as charming legend rather than plain history. Its influence on later tradition was enormous regardless. Thackeray's translation presents the founding story of the Greek Bible gracefully.
london-sea-wolf-1904:
Jack London published The Sea-Wolf in 1904, his novel of a shipwrecked intellectual brutalized into manhood at sea. A seal-hunting schooner ruled by the terrifying Captain Wolf Larsen carries the tale. London, who had sailed those waters, loaded the book with sea craft and his creed.

Humphrey van Weyden, a critic and gentleman, is picked up from a ferry wreck and made a cabin boy by Larsen. Larsen, a superman of body and nihilist brain, crushes mutiny, reads Milton, and argues that life is yeast and appetite. Maud Brewster, a poet cast away in turn, joins Humphrey in escape to an island and a slow, tender stand against despair. Larsen, blinded by headaches, dies unbowed, and the pair are rescued from Endeavor Island at the close. The debates between captain and critic still give the sea tale its voltage.
lucretia-volume-04:
Volume 4 of Lucretia opens the novel's second part with a wide retrospect. Years have passed, and Napoleon has fallen from his thrones. The plough has crossed Waterloo, and harvests glitter on that grave. On the terrace at Laughton, one figure now paces alone.

The bride no longer clings to the bridegroom's arm. She is pale and worn, yet still commanding. Lytton pauses to muse on how memory lights only our own track. The story resumes in a changed world and a changed house. Old deeds begin to bear their harvest here. This volume turns the tragedy toward its reckoning.
margery-gred-a-tale-of-old-nuremberg-vol:
Volume four of Margery rides through deep snow to a forest lodge. December wind leaves the riders with red faces and frozen hands. Yet Margery finds joy in the glittering winter woods. Snow crowns every stock and stone like tiny white hats.

Her heart stays heavy with care for her friend Ann. Ann seems doomed to share the sorry life of the Magister. Under God's open heavens, that fate feels impossible to Margery. Friendship, pity, and young love fill these winter chapters. Ebers sets bright nature against a girl's anxious thoughts. The volume carries Gred's story deeper into sorrow.
marlowe-doctor-faustus-1604:
Christopher Marlowe wrote The Tragical History of Doctor Faustus near the end of his short life. He drew on German tales of a scholar who bargained with the devil. The play reached print in 1604, eleven years after Marlowe's death. It became the defining English tragedy of the overreaching mind.

Faustus, bored with law, medicine, and theology, sells his soul for twenty-four years of magic and pleasure. A good angel and a bad angel fight for him while devils stage shows and tricks. The years slip away in pranks until the final hour arrives. Faustus's last speech, begging time to stop, remains one of the most powerful scenes in English drama.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-04:
Volume four of Bourrienne's memoirs holds chapters twenty seven to thirty five. The years in view are 1799 and 1800, by the contents. A new government rises on the ruins of the old in this part.

Bonaparte, now First Consul, writes to all foreign powers at once. He seeks peace, or at least the show of seeking it, Bourrienne says. Talks with England and Austria fail in those first months. Kleber's letter and the Egyptian reports fill the later heads of the volume. Italy was lost, and war with near all Europe ran on. Order, not revolt, was the face the new rule wished to show.
monro-digest-justinian-vol1-1904:
Charles Henry Monro, a Cambridge lawyer, published the first volume of his English translation of Justinian's Digest in 1904. The Digest is the great anthology of Roman law, compiled for the Emperor Justinian in the sixth century from the writings of classical jurists. For centuries, English readers had needed Latin to use it.

Volume 1 opens the work: the nature of law and justice, the courts, and the standing of persons before the law. Monro translates with a lawyer's precision, keeping the jurists' terse style readable. The Digest became the foundation of legal systems across Europe, so an English version served scholars and barristers alike. Monro's volume began the task of making the Corpus Juris of Rome accessible in the language of the common-law world.
my-novel-volume-04:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's fourth book opens with talk of marriage. Mr. Caxton praises how Pisistratus showed a lover's growing love. Signor Riccabocca left off his spectacles to look his best. Uncle Roland doubts this, citing Shakespeare's slovenly lover instead.

Caxton answers that love has many phases and degrees. A scorned lover may pine, while a hopeful one may primp. Blanche tosses her head at Miss Jemima's forward ways. Mrs. Caxton tries to keep the family's dignity intact. The chapter turns courtship into a learned, funny debate, as the tale's own love plot warms beside it.
nassau-fetichism-in-west-africa-1904:
Robert Hamill Nassau summed up forty years on the Gabon coast in Fetichism in West Africa, published in 1904. Nassau, an American Presbyterian missionary and physician, observed native customs across the Ogowe region for decades. Fetishism, in his term, witchcraft, and secret societies form the heart of his account.

He writes as a convinced missionary, yet also as a careful witness who learned languages and sat in village councils. Tales, trials, and charms fill pages drawn from life rather than books. The volume stands as a major period record of religion on the Gabon coast, to be read with its era in mind.
nernst-theoretical-chemistry-palmer-1904:
Walther Nernst systematized physical chemistry in his Theoretical Chemistry, Englished by L. M. Palmer in 1904. The English text was the second edition, drawn from the fourth German edition. The subtitle names his twin guides: Avogadro's rule and thermodynamics. Together they frame his account of matter and its changes.

Nernst applies heat theory to solutions and to electrochemistry in depth. Readers learn how energy rules reactions, cells, and the balance between states. His path here leads toward his later heat theorem, the third law of thermodynamics. The book served as the field's great textbook for years. Its order and scope set a standard.
new-york-at-the-louisiana-purchase-expos:
DeLancey M. Ellis prepared and compiled this report for the New York State Commission to the Louisiana Purchase Exposition. That fair was held at St. Louis in 1904. The report is dated 1907, and the commission sent it to Governor Charles E. Hughes at Albany on March 25 that year.

The letter up front calls it the final report required by statute. Twelve commissioners signed it, among them Edward H. Harriman and Lewis Nixon. Their charge was to account for New York's part in the fair. State reports like this one preserve what a state showed, spent, and claimed at a great national fair.
newton-opticks-1704:
Isaac Newton published Opticks in 1704, a treatise on the reflections, refractions, inflections, and colours of light. Unlike the Principia, Newton wrote Opticks in English and built it from experiments readers could picture. Prisms, slits, and dark rooms are its stage.

Newton showed that white light splits into colors and joins again, proving color lies in light itself, not in the glass. He measured the bending of rays and studied the rings now named for him. Closing queries speculated on gravity, matter, and God's role in nature. The book founded physical optics and set a model for experimental science: ask nature plain questions and record exact answers.
ocean-of-story-kathasaritsagara-tawney-1:
Volume four of The Ocean of Story, from Penzer's ten-volume edition begun in 1924, continues Tawney's rendering of Somadeva. The Kathasaritsagara now braids its hero's fortunes with tale cycles told by sages, wives, and wandering ascetics. Every narrator opens a new door, and behind it waits another narrator with a stranger tale.

Somadeva wrote to divert a queen, and diversion remains the law of the book. Penzer's notes in this volume chase the tale of the grateful beasts and other wanderers across three continents. The translation's calm surface over such abundance is Tawney's quiet triumph. Readers may dip anywhere and surface with a complete story. The ocean, by design, has no dull stretches for long.
openalex-w1267646904:
Gillinder Bedi, Cheryl Corcoran, and eight co-authors wrote this study. It came out in a journal on schizophrenia in 2015. Doctors lack firm tests for mental illness, they note. The team asked if a computer could read speech for risk. They worked with youths at high risk for psychosis.

The team taped talks with thirty-four youths and tracked them for years. Five of them later fell ill in that time. A computer scored how clear and rich their speech was. Those scores flagged each youth who later fell ill. They beat the calls made from clinic talks alone. The team says speech tests could give doctors a firm tool.
openalex-w1969726504:
Hazel McLellan, Paul Birch, and co-authors studied potato blight. Their paper appeared in PLoS Pathogens in 2013. The blight pathogen secretes effector proteins into host plants. Those proteins disarm defenses and aid colonization, they note. Little was known about their host targets before.

One effector, of the RxLR class, drew their focus. It blocks two plant control proteins, called NAC factors. Those factors should move from a cell membrane to the nucleus. The effector stops that move, trapping them outside. Trapped factors cannot switch on defense genes properly. The work exposes a precise act of molecular sabotage.
openalex-w1994728704:
Betty Abelev and colleagues in the ALICE Collaboration published a methods paper in Physical Review C in 2013. It explains how the team measured centrality in lead-lead collisions. Centrality tells how head-on a crash was. The work used collisions at very high energy at the Large Hadron Collider.

The team linked the signals seen in the detector to the overlap of the two lead nuclei. They used a Glauber model, a simple geometric picture of the crash. From it they estimated how many nucleons took part and how many pairs collided. The model values matched values drawn from the data. The method lets ALICE results be compared with other experiments and with theory.
openalex-w1997328904:
Betty Abelev and colleagues in the ALICE Collaboration measured two short-lived particles in lead-lead collisions. Their paper appeared in Physical Review C in 2015. The particles are named K star and phi. The team asked how much of each particle the collisions made.

The team used the ALICE detector and studied particle decays. They measured yields across central and less central collisions. K star yields were lower in central collisions than expected. The authors link that drop to decay products scattering in the hot matter. Phi yields were not reduced in the same way. Flow models matched the phi pattern fairly well. The results showed that mass and outward flow shape the particle patterns.
openalex-w2068012504:
Alejandro Schijman, Margarita Bisio, Liliana Orellana and colleagues compared PCR tests for Chagas disease across many labs. Their study appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2011. Chagas disease is still a major neglected threat. Doctors need tests that find the parasite well. They also need markers of how treatment works.

Labs in many countries joined the test comparison. Each lab checked the same blood sample panels. Methods differed in how they pulled out and copied DNA. Test strength varied between methods and labs. The study picked out the approaches that found more cases. Shared test rules would help trials compare results. The work set the next steps for better Chagas tests.
openalex-w2102356204:
Kerrie Wilson, Emma Underwood, Scott Morrison and colleagues built a framework for spending conservation money wisely. Their paper appeared in PLoS Biology in 2007. Conservation funds are scarce worldwide. Priority lists often name places but not actions. Decision makers need to know what to fund, where and when.

Their framework links places with specific actions. It also weighs the threats each action addresses. Costs and likely benefits enter the calculation. They applied it to Mediterranean-type regions worldwide. Seventeen of the world's hotspots were included. Different actions won funding in different places. Timing mattered as much as location. Smart allocation can save more species per dollar.
openalex-w2462225304:
Matthew Aliota, Stephen Peinado, Iván Vélez, and Jorge Osorio published this study in Scientific Reports in 2016. With no vaccine or drug against the exploding Zika outbreak, one hope was Wolbachia, a bacterium already being seeded into mosquitoes against dengue. Infected Aedes aegypti resist several viruses; whether they resist Zika was unknown.

The team tested mosquitoes carrying the wMel strain, the same stock being released in Medellín, Colombia. Crucially, the mosquitoes fed on a virus-carrying host, mimicking real transmission rather than spiked laboratory blood. The infected mosquitoes showed reduced ability to catch, carry, and pass on Zika. The authors back expanding Wolbachia releases as a multi-virus shield across the Americas.
openalex-w2588121804:
Ana María López-Colomé, Irene Lee-Rivera, and Regina Benavides-Hidalgo, with Edith López, reviewed the protein paxillin in the Journal of Hematology & Oncology in 2017. Paxillin works as a scaffold at focal adhesions, the spots where cells grip their surroundings. It recruits the structural and signaling molecules that let cells move. Its activity switches on when certain parts of the protein gain phosphate groups.

The review explains how paxillin coordinates signals controlling cell migration, including small switch proteins like Rac1 and RhoA. It plays different roles across tissues, development, and the immune response. When its control goes wrong, paxillin helps drive oxidative stress, inflammation, and barrier failure in blood vessels. It is also an essential player in cancer growth and spread, the authors note. Understanding this crossroads protein may suggest new ways to block harmful cell movement.
openalex-w2746235704:
Ubirajara Oliveira, Britaldo Silveira Soares-Filho, and Adriano Pereira Paglia lead a large team assessing Brazil's protected areas in Scientific Reports in 2017. Brazil is a megadiverse country and a top conservation priority. Yet nobody had measured how well its protected area network covers its species. Earlier studies leaned on single groups like birds as stand-ins for all life.

The network holds over seventeen hundred units covering about a quarter of Brazil's territory. It shelters nearly forty percent of the remaining native vegetation. The Amazon holds the largest protected extent, while biomes like the Cerrado hold far less. Worryingly, under one percent of protected areas are well sampled for species records. The team combined distribution data and family trees across vertebrates, arthropods, and flowering plants. Their map exposes both protection gaps and knowledge gaps, showing where new reserves and surveys matter most.
openalex-w3020838504:
Stephen Zhang, Jing Liu, Asghar Jahanshahi, and colleagues posted this preprint on medRxiv in May 2020, before peer review. It surveys the health and job satisfaction of health care staff in Iran at the peak of the country's COVID-19 epidemic. The sample held three hundred four doctors, nurses, radiologists, technicians, and others.

Sizable shares of staff crossed cutoff levels for anxiety, depression, and distress, at roughly three in ten for the first two. Age, gender, schooling, access to protective gear, workplace type, and infection status each predicted some outcomes but not others. Access to protective equipment varied greatly across staff. The authors show that who suffered most depended on a mix of personal and workplace factors.
openalex-w4283589104: Laura Coates, Enrique Soriano, Heidi Bertheussen, and colleagues present the GRAPPA group's updated treatment recommendations for psoriatic arthritis. The guidance, dated 2021, appeared in Nature Reviews Rheumatology in 2022. The preserved sample holds only the publisher's citation page and the article's opening author list. It has no readable abstract, so the guidance itself cannot be summarised from it here.
openalex-w4393120004:
Ben Kirk, Peggy Cawthon, Hidenori Arai, and colleagues present a global expert consensus on what sarcopenia is, in Age and Ageing in 2024. Sarcopenia means losing muscle mass and strength as the body ages. It matters clinically, yet no worldwide agreed definition existed. The Global Leadership Initiative in Sarcopenia gathered representatives of all major scientific societies to settle the concept.

The group used a two-phase Delphi study, in which experts rate statements until they converge. One hundred seven participants from twenty-nine countries took part. Twenty statements won strong agreement. Muscle mass, muscle strength, and muscle-specific strength all belong in the definition, the panel agreed. A shared concept is the base for shared diagnosis and treatment research.
openalex-w7127983704:
Hitomi Kato, Juliana Yumi Ishisaki, Yoshiki Kuwatsuru, and colleagues test magnetic resonance angiography for mapping uterine arteries. Their study appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2026. The patients had symptomatic uterine fibroids. Many are treated by blocking the uterine artery, a procedure called embolization.

The artery's branching pattern varies between women, in four known forms. Knowing the pattern beforehand makes catheter work safer. Invasive angiography had mapped these variants in hundreds of arteries. The team checks whether non-contrast scans classify the anatomy just as well. They confirm the scans' accuracy against standard angiography. A reliable non-invasive map could spare patients a needle-based step before treatment.
openalex-w7204197604:
Elaine Aires Nunes led a Portuguese-language paper, in Brazil in 2026, on making Brazil's laws on African, Afro-Brazil's, and Indigenous history and culture real in public schools. Two laws, from 2003 and 2008, made this teaching mandatory, yet obligation alone does not change classrooms. The authors ground their approach in Vygotsky's historical-cultural theory, where teachers mediate learning, and in key interculturality.

The documentary case study examines a municipal school in Palmas, Tocantins, running a project called Roots and Resistances on Afro-Brazilian and Indigenous art, culture, and identity. Cultural diversity, the authors conclude, is raw content for human development, and hiding it impoverishes the school. Art-based teacher mediation, they argue, can build a democratic, antiracist school.
openalex-w7204254704:
Pedro Gustavo Tavares Souza led a Portuguese-language integrative review, published in Brazil in 2026, on the role of neuroinflammation in neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. Searching six databases for original studies from 2021 to 2026 and screening them by standard review rules, the team included eleven studies.

Inflammation inside the nervous system, the review finds, sits at the center of degeneration. Brain immune cells stay switched on, releasing inflammatory signals, while oxidative stress and several molecular pathways feed continuing neuron damage. The authors also flag treatment prospects based on calming the immune response and on nanotechnology as promising ways to slow these diseases. Neuroinflammation is an important therapeutic target, they conclude, though more work is needed before these approaches reach clinical practice.
openalex-w7204444604:
Brenda Alvares dos Reis led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on advances in managing Crohn's disease, a chronic, immune-driven, progressive inflammation of the intestine that seriously reduces quality of life. Searching two sources for studies from 2021 to 2026, the team focused on diagnostic innovations, biomarkers, artificial intelligence, biological therapies, small molecules, and personalized drug.

Molecular biomarkers, AI-based tools, and new targeted therapies have widened clinicians' ability to predict treatment response and individualize choices, the evidence shows. Precision drug is changing how the disease is managed, the authors conclude, offering a promising route to better medical results and better daily life for patients. The review gives practitioners a compact map of where Crohn's care is heading.
openalex-w7204536504:
Caio de Freitas Almeida wrote a Portuguese-language paper, in Brazil in 2026, on shadow IT in the Military Police of Paraná: systems built by units without the central tools authority's supervision. Such irregular growth can breach office impersonality, create tech liabilities, expose the corporation to cyber vulnerabilities, and risk violations of Brazil's data protection law. The applied study reviews studies and reads the force's 2024 general command ordinance and directive on the subject.

The corporation already has norms and tools for standardization, Almeida finds; the problem is cultural, getting units to comply. Countering shadow IT requires regulated decentralized growth, trained local IT managers, and control in training curricula, so police services stay interoperable and uninterrupted.
openalex-w7204693204:
Carlos Eduardo Rosa Vignoto and Jacqueline Godinho released a Portuguese-language study in Brazil in 2026 on psychotropic dispensing at a community pharmacy in Maringá, Paraná. Psychotropic use has grown sharply in recent decades, making it a public health and pharmaceutical care concern. The team studied special-control drugs dispensed from January to December 2025, over twelve thousand units, examining therapeutic classes, seasonality, control lists, and the generic, similar, and brand-name mix.

Antidepressants dominated, at nearly half of all units dispensed, followed by antipsychotics and anxiolytics. Generics outsold similar and reference products, and most drugs fell on the main special-control list. The profile, the authors note, supports pharmacy planning, stock running, and rational use of controlled drugs.
openalex-w7204998204:
Jhoserd Nilson Xavier de Almeida Lima and Jackeline Maciel de Azevedo released a Portuguese-language study in Brazil in 2026 on teaching botany through the senses in a sensory garden. Botany teaching in basic education struggles with scarce methods and little hands-on work with living plants. The study evaluated the Sensory Garden of the Federal University of Sergipe as a non-formal schooling space for plant kingdom content. Working with second-year high school students from the university's application school through a diagnostic questionnaire, a garden visit, and a post-visit questionnaire.

Students showed difficulty with specific botanical terms and distance from nature, the authors report. Received the garden warmly as a teaching space, and the visit opened discussion of plant preservation. More research on sensory gardens as teaching tools is needed, they argue.
openalex-w7207583204:
Gabrieli Rodrigues Falcao, Gleiciane Santos Feitosa, and Pedro Felipe dos Reis Soares study how a Brazilian university judges its teachers, and whether the feedback those teachers get is usable. Their subject is the faculty evaluation system at the Federal Rural University of the Amazon. Reading an institutional report through the lens of behavior-based management, they test sixteen evaluation items against a strict standard: each item should name a behavior that can be seen and measured.

The original items, they find, were worded in general and abstract terms, leaving wide room for personal interpretation. After the items were rewritten as observable behaviors, fit improved sharply in areas such as knowledge and skills and professional attitude. Their conclusion is practical: turning vague criteria into concrete behaviors makes teacher feedback clearer, fairer, and more useful.
openalex-w7207613304:
Carolyne Assed Caires Duarte leads a team reviewing how COVID-19 damages the kidneys through tiny blood clots and inflammation. Their umbrella review, a summary of earlier systematic reviews, followed standard reporting rules and searched major medical databases. Six evidence summaries met their bar. The focus was acute kidney injury: how often it struck, how it related to death, and how often patients needed dialysis-like treatment.

Kidney injury appeared in about one in eleven hospitalized patients, about one in three critically ill patients, and one in five children with the severe inflammatory syndrome linked to the virus. In children, kidney injury was also tied to higher death rates. The authors caution that the underlying studies overlapped heavily and cannot prove cause, but the pattern supports a real role for vessel damage and clot-driven inflammation.
openalex-w7208792704:
Cristiane Carinhato leads a team on deep-feel class ways and help tech in the aid class for kids with special needs. The aid class works by the side of plain class in Brazil's base schools. The study roots in a plan-first frame for all kinds of kids, and in the guide's role as a bridge. It joins a read of past work with a look at sense-rich class spaces that adapt.

Used with aim, the team finds, play-like sims and deep-feel rooms spark thought. They lower walls of mood and mind. They build kids' free stance and self rule. The team goes a step more. Such ways are not mere toys. They are help tech in their own right. A class for all now needs them, if it is to fit each child and set each child free.
openalex-w7212248404:
Ana Carolina Frazao and Renata Dayanne Peixoto de Lima weigh free speech against the harm of false posts in Brazil. Speech is a base right of a free state, they grant. But it is not a blank check when it hits the rights of others. The pair read two key cases from the top court. Both test when a web firm must pay for the posts its users spread.

Lies and banned posts now cross the land at vast scale. The law must guard both open talk and the worth of each person. The two court themes, the authors hold, mark a real step. They set split rules for when a firm bears the cost of harm. They also press the law arm to write clear rules of its own. The aim is a web that stays free, yet safe to trust.
openalex-w7213882204:
Luiza Fernanda Gama Bastos and Patrícia Fortes Attademo Ferreira draw the line between party loyalty and party coercion in Brazil. Their 2026 dogmatic legal study covers mainly 2021 to 2026, after a constitutional amendment on the subject. Bibliographic, documentary, legislative, and case law methods are combined.

Loyalty and discipline can fit the constitutional order, the authors hold, but they do not license arbitrary leadership action. Tests include whether a rule sits in the party statute, who imposed it, and whether defence rights were respected. Sanction strength and real effects on the mandate also matter. Coercion is their name for discipline that, though formally covered, is used discriminatorily or to make a mandate unworkable.
openalex-w7214987004:
Kazushi Hayashi led a Japanese and Swedish engineering team in a 2026 technical report on pressing composite cathodes for all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries. These batteries promise higher power, longer range, and better safety for electric vehicles, but their solid electrodes must be densely packed to work well. The team adapted sheet metal hydroforming, pressing through a rubber diaphragm with preheating and no fluid, suited to factories that must control moisture strictly.

Using synchrotron X-ray imaging, they compared structures before and after pressing against conventional methods. At room temperature their method cut the void share in the cathode by about half, matching cold isostatic pressing, while uniaxial pressing removed large voids but densified less. Heat helped greatly, reducing voids several-fold further. The fluid-free design, the authors note, fits battery production lines with severe dew point demands.
openalex-w7215826204:
Khalydia Oliveira Aby Faraj led a 2026 integrative review on bioabsorbable fixation plates for jaw fractures in children. Facial fractures are rare in childhood because young bones are flexible, yet the jaw is a frequent site when they occur. Metal fixation is traditional, but a growing child's jaw raises a special concern: hardware should not interfere with growth. The team searched four databases for English-language work from 2014 to 2026.

Bioabsorbable systems dissolve as bone healing advances, and the review found their postoperative complication rate similar to metal fixation, with the advantage of not disturbing mandibular growth. The systems cost more, which the authors note plainly. On balance they judge bioabsorbable fixation a promising alternative for pediatric jaw surgery. It is a case where the material's disappearance is the point: the repair supports healing, then leaves the growing face to itself.
openalex-w7221137004:
Fernanda Tsumay Ikari, Carolina Trevisolli Palomo, and Daniel Augusto Nunes de Lima tested lettuce leaves from community gardens in three Paraná towns for parasite structures, in a 2026 laboratory study. Lettuce is usually eaten raw, so contamination that survives to the plate matters for food safety.

Eighteen leaves were collected in August and September 2026, one garden per town, and examined under the microscope after sedimentation. A single August leaf from Santa Fé carried a larva matching the hookworm family. All other leaves, including every September sample, showed nothing by this method. Given the tiny sample, the authors refuse broad conclusions and instead stress careful growing, handling, and washing of raw vegetables.
openalex-w7221150504:
Anna Luiza Neres Zarelli, Felipe Vivan Estrella, and Mayra Meneguelli Teixeira tested a hormone treatment meant to raise pregnancy rates in beef cows, in a 2026 veterinary study from Brazil. Sixty-eight multiparous Nelore cows on an extensive grazing system received fixed-time artificial insemination; half also got a dose of gonadotropin-releasing hormone at insemination.

Pregnancy was checked by ultrasound about forty-five days later. Just under six in ten of the hormone-treated cows were pregnant, against exactly half of the untreated group. The gap favors the hormone, but the authors are careful: a descriptive study of this size cannot prove the hormone caused the difference. Both groups shared the same feeding, health, and mineral routines.
original-short-stories-volume-04:
Volume four of Maupassant's Original Short Stories contains his most famous tale. The Diamond Necklace stands in the contents between The Wrong House and The Marquis de Fumerol. Twelve tales make up the volume. They include The Story of a Farm Girl, The Wolf, and The Inn, in the standard English translation.

The opening story, The Moribund, begins on a Norman farm under warm autumn sun: heifers grazing, fowls on the dung-heap, apples dropping in the wet grass. Through the gate comes a farmhand who looks sixty at forty, bent and slow in straw-stuffed wooden shoes, while the yellow dog barks for joy. It is Maupassant's peasant world at its most concrete, built to carry a deathbed story.
osler-aequanimitas-1904:
Osler's Aequanimitas gathers his addresses to medical students, nurses, and doctors, first printed in 1904. The title essay praises calm steadiness, the quality its Latin name describes. Osler believed a doctor's temper shapes a patient's trust. His talks mix practical advice with wide reading and warm humor.

Other addresses in the volume treat study, books, and the conduct of a medical life. Generations of students received the book at graduation as a kind of charge. Its essays became the most quoted medical humanism in English. Osler writes as a mentor who expects much and scolds gently. The volume keeps his voice alive. Readers outside medicine enjoy it too.
osler-science-immortality-1904:
William Osler delivered Science and Immortality as the Ingersoll Lecture in 1904. The lecture series asked speakers to address human immortality from their own field. Osler, a leading doctor and teacher, brought a clinical eye to the old question. He asks what science can and cannot say about survival after death.

He sorts people into groups by their stance toward the question. Some hold faith, some doubt, and some rest in calm acceptance. Osler treats each stance with respect and dry wit. His own position stays modest and humane. The address became his most famous piece of philosophy. It shows medicine thinking about its limits.
pargiter-markandeya-purana-1904:
F. Eden Pargiter translated the Markandeya Purana for the Bibliotheca Indica series, completing the English text in 1904 after years of work. The Purana ranks among the oldest of its kind in India, and its crown is the Devi Mahatmya, the great hymn to the Goddess. Kings, sages, cosmic ages, and the deeds of gods fill the frame around that core.

In the Devi Mahatmya the Goddess rises to fight demons no god can master, and she wins in glory. That section shaped goddess worship across India and is still sung aloud at her festivals today. Pargiter's careful version remains the standard scholarly English rendering of the whole Purana for students.
paul-clifford-volume-04:
Volume 4 of Paul Clifford begins at chapter sixteen, in Bath. Clifford and his companions keep a splendid lodging in Milsom Street, over a hairdresser's shop, to please Ned. Yet they slip away to a mean alehouse in a remote suburb, where old Mr. Bags and the gang gather.

Clifford, here called Lovett, lounges silent while Ned jokes and Tomlinson reads a newspaper. The double life is the point: fine gentlemen by day, thieves in low rooms by night. Lytton uses Bath's polish and the alehouse's smoke to show how thin the line between the two worlds is.
pelham-volume-04:
Volume 4 of Pelham brings the hero back to London, and chapter forty-four finds him taking rooms at Mivart's. A year abroad has changed him: pleasure now serves ambition, and his foppery hides a close, keen, inquiring mind. His first visitor is Mr. N—, the tailor, come to renew his measure.

The tailor's advice is pure philosophy of the surface: padding here, an inch across the shoulders, for we must live for effect. Pelham gives exact measure and exact instructions instead. The volume follows his London campaign, where dress, dinners, and politics are all moves in one game.
petrie-methods-aims-archaeology-1904:
W. M. Flinders Petrie laid down the laws of the dig in Methods and Aims in Archaeology, his guide of 1904. Ere Petrie, most digs were hunts for gold and show pieces. He demands that each scrap be kept, drawn, and placed by its layer. A plain pot in place, he says, tells more than a loose gem.

Rules for camps, crews, notes, and print fill the guide. Young dig men learned their trade from it for years. It is the first true field guide of the craft. The laws in it still rule good work on site.
pirandello-late-mattia-pascal-1904:
Luigi Pirandello published The Late Mattia Pascal in 1904, an Italian novel about a man freed by a mistake. Mattia Pascal leaves his unhappy home and his debts behind. While away, he reads that a drowned man has been named as him. Everyone at home thinks he is dead.

Mattia takes a new name and tries to start a fresh life. He soon finds that a man with no past has no rights and no real place. Love and money both slip from his grasp. He returns home to find his wife remarried. The novel mixes comedy and sadness in its study of identity.
plaw-108-200-2004:
Public Law 108-200, the Congo Basin Forest Partnership Act of 2004, authorizes money for protecting rain forests in Central Africa. The findings place the Congo Basin forests in nine countries, including Cameroon, Gabon, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Congress says they are second in size only to the Amazon Basin forests.

The findings praise the forests for soaking up carbon dioxide, cleaning water, and holding soil in place. They hold Africa's richest mix of plants and animals, the act says, including lowland and mountain gorillas, chimpanzees, and the okapi. Their genetic material could feed future advances in medicine, farming, and industry. Logging pressure threatens them, the findings warn.
plaw-108-201-2004:
Public Law 108-201, the NASA Flexibility Act of 2004, gives the space agency more freedom in hiring and pay. Congress passed it so the National Aeronautics and Space Administration could compete for skilled staff. The act amends title 5 of the U.S. Code, the part on federal personnel.

One section raises the pay cap for certain excepted NASA staff to the level III rate of the Executive Schedule. The main section writes a new chapter 98 for NASA in title 5. That chapter sets workforce authorities, with rules on planning, notice to Congress, and reporting. It also lists limits, so the new flexibility comes with checks on how the agency uses it.
plaw-108-202-2004: Public Law 108-202, the Surface Transportation Extension Act of 2004, keeps highway and transit programs running for a short time. Congress passed it while work continued on a full renewal of the Transportation Equity Act for the 21st Century. The act extends advances and funding rules from the 2003 extension act. It raises one minimum guarantee figure for states, moves a bridge set-aside date from February 29 to April 30, and renews contract authority for highway programs paid from the Highway Trust Fund.
plaw-108-203-2004:
Public Law 108-203, the Social Security Protection Act of 2004, tightens rules around people who handle benefits for others. Some Social Security and Supplemental Security Income recipients cannot manage their own money. A representative payee receives and spends the benefits for them, and abuse had drawn concern.

The act's first title protects those beneficiaries. It lets the agency reissue benefits that an organizational payee misused. It adds oversight of payees and bars people convicted of serious crimes, or fleeing prosecution, from serving as payees. Payees who misuse funds can lose their fees and owe the money back. The agency may also redirect payments when a payee fails to give a required accounting.
plaw-108-204-2004:
Public Law 108-204, the Native American Technical Corrections Act of 2004, fixes and updates a shelf of laws about Native Americans. Most of its first title is labeled technical amendments. Each short section names an older law or settlement that needs a correction.

The named items include the Bosque Redondo Memorial Act and the Navajo-Hopi Land Settlement Act. Others cover the Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Indians, a settlement change for Pueblo de Cochiti, and the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians. One section funds repair of Celilo Indian Village. A second part carries new items. They include a water pipeline for the Barona Band of Mission Indians. They also include land and mineral consolidation for the Pueblo of Acoma, and a water study for the Quinault Indian Nation.
plaw-108-205-2004: Public Law 108-205, approved in March 2004, gives small business programs a few more weeks of life. Programs under the Small Business Act and the Small Business Investment Act of 1958 that had been extended through March 15, 2004, now run through April 2, 2004, on the same terms. A second section moves one fee authorization date from October 1, 2003, to May 21, 2004. Congress used these short extensions while a longer renewal was still being debated.
plaw-108-206-2004: Public Law 108-206, passed in 2004, hands a small piece of federal land to Douglas County, Oregon. The Secretary of the Interior must give the county, free of charge, about 68.8 acres of Bureau of Land Management land. The parcel appears on a map dated May 21, 2003, and the county must use it for recreation. Congress says the gift should improve management of and access to the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area. It should also ease traffic and improve safety along Salmon Harbor Drive.
plaw-108-207-2004: Public Law 108-207, passed in March 2004, gives the 9/11 Commission more time and money. The National Commission on Terrorist Attacks Upon the United States was due to report within 18 months of its creation. This law stretches that to 20 months. It also shortens the period between the final report and the commission's shutdown from 60 days to 30 days. A funding section adds money for the commission on top of its earlier appropriations, drawn from intelligence program funds.
plaw-108-208-2004:
Public Law 108-208, the Galisteo Basin Archaeological Sites Protection Act, protects ancient sites in New Mexico. Congress found the Galisteo Basin holds well kept remains of Native American and Spanish colonial cultures. They include the largest ruins of Pueblo Indian settlements in the United States and striking rock art.

The findings warn that nature, city growth, vandals, and uncontrolled digging threaten these resources. The act's purpose is to preserve, protect, and interpret them. It designates a list of Galisteo Basin archaeological protection sites covering about 4,591 acres in all. Federal care for the sites follows from that designation, so the ruins and rock art gain legal protection.
plaw-108-209-2004: Public Law 108-209, the Fort Bayard National Historic Landmark Act, raises the status of a New Mexico historic district. The Fort Bayard Historic District in Grant County, already on the National Register of Historic Places, becomes a National Historic Landmark. The law says New Mexico keeps running the district as before. The Secretary of the Interior may make deals with public or private groups to protect its historic resources and to run educational programs for visitors. Help for activities touching Fort Bayard State Hospital needs the state's agreement.
plaw-108-210-2004: Public Law 108-210, the Welfare Reform Extension Act of 2004, keeps the main welfare program running through June 30, 2004. The Temporary Assistance for Needy Families block grant gives states money to help poor families. The act continues it in the manner authorized for fiscal year 2002, and it pays grants at that level through the third quarter of fiscal year 2004. Other sections extend a national study of child welfare and the child welfare waiver authority to the same June date.
plaw-108-211-2004: Public Law 108-211, passed in 2004, extends school lunch and child nutrition programs through June 30, 2004. An earlier law had carried them only to March 31, 2004. Section by section, the act swaps the old date for the new one. The programs touched include the child and adult care food program, summer food service for children, and commodity distribution payments to states. One section also extends a rule that leaves out some military housing allowances when schools judge which children qualify for meal help.
plaw-108-212-2004:
Public Law 108-212, the Unborn Victims of Violence Act of 2004, is also called Laci and Conner's Law. It amends title 18 of the U.S. Code and the Uniform Code of Military Justice. The law responds to attacks in which a pregnant woman and her unborn child are both harmed.

The act adds a new chapter on protection of unborn children. A person who breaks one of the listed federal laws and thereby kills or injures a child in the womb commits a separate offense. The punishment matches what the same act would draw if the injury or death had happened to the mother. The government need not prove the attacker knew the woman was pregnant.
plaw-108-213-2004: Public Law 108-213, the Energy Efficient Housing Technical Correction Act, fixes one clause in the National Housing Act. Federal housing law let FHA-insured mortgage limits rise to cover the added cost of solar energy systems or home energy saving measures. A few words had limited part of that rule to rehabilitation projects of five family units or fewer. This act strikes those words, restoring the allowable increases for multifamily housing projects as Congress intended.
plaw-108-214-2004: Public Law 108-214, the Medical Devices Technical Corrections Act, repairs wording in a 2002 law on medical devices. That law, the Medical Device User Fee and Modernization Act, charges fees to device makers and updates device rules. The corrections amend the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. They adjust definitions, such as which devices need substantial clinical data to show safety and effectiveness. Other fixes clean up terms for premarket applications and for company affiliates, so the fee program reads as Congress meant it to.
plaw-108-215-2004:
Public Law 108-215, passed in 2004, lets the President accept changes to a border environment deal with Mexico. The deal set up the Border Environment Cooperation Commission and the North American Development Bank. Those bodies fund water, sewer, and cleanup projects along the border.

The amendments let the bank make grants and below-market loans from its paid-in capital, with its board's approval. They also widen the meaning of border region. On the United States side it reaches 100 kilometers from the boundary. On the Mexican side it reaches 300 kilometers. A companion section grants the bank clear authority to pay out grants from its capital resources.
plaw-108-216-2004:
Public Law 108-216, the Organ Donation and Recovery Improvement Act, aims to raise organ donation rates. It amends the Public Health Service Act. Congress states that the federal government should teach the public about donation and the need for more of it.

The act praises families who talk together about donating organs and tissue. It also honors living donors, people who give a kidney or part of an organ while alive. Advances in surgery have made living donation a real option for more patients, Congress notes. Later sections repay travel and living costs for living donors, removing a money barrier that stopped some willing donors.
plaw-108-217-2004: Public Law 108-217, passed in 2004, is another short extension for small business programs. Programs under the Small Business Act and the Small Business Investment Act of 1958 that ran through April 2, 2004, now run through June 4, 2004, on the same terms. A fee authorization moves from May 21, 2004, to October 1, 2004. The act also sets fiscal year 2004 purchase and guarantee authority for investment company programs and deals with combination financing.
plaw-108-218-2004:
Public Law 108-218, the Pension Funding Equity Act of 2004, gives companies temporary relief in funding their pension plans. Pension law used the interest rate on 30-year Treasury bonds to value what plans owe. The Treasury had stopped issuing that bond, and low rates made plan debts look larger.

For plan years in 2004 and 2005, the act swaps in a rate based on long-term corporate bonds. The rate is a weighted average of yields on high-grade corporate bonds over the prior four years. Plans may use a range near that rate when they figure required funding. The change amends both the pension law, ERISA, and the Internal Revenue Code.
plaw-108-219-2004:
Public Law 108-219, passed in 2004, sends a retired government ship to a small Pacific atoll. Title I lets the Secretary of Commerce give the Utrok Atoll local government a decommissioned National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration ship, free of charge and in working order. Utrok's residents were affected by United States nuclear testing.

The ship supports radiation monitoring, rehabilitation, and resettlement work at the atoll. Within 120 days, the Utrok government, working with the Republic of the Marshall Islands, must send Congress a plan for using the vessel. After delivery, the United States is not responsible for running or maintaining it. A second title ratifies certain NOAA appointments, promotions, and actions.
plaw-108-220-2004: Public Law 108-220, approved in April 2004, repays travel costs for troops who came home on leave from war zones. Under the Central Command Rest and Recuperation Leave Program, members flew home on leave. At first they had to pay for their own travel inside the United States. This law orders the Secretary of Defense to reimburse one round trip within the country. It covers leave taken between September 25, 2003, and December 18, 2003. That was before the program was widened to cover domestic travel.
plaw-108-221-2004: Public Law 108-221, passed in 2004, gives an old federal courthouse to Fresno County, California. The General Services Administrator may hand the county the B.F. Sisk Federal Building and United States Courthouse at 1130 O Street in Fresno for nominal consideration. The transfer may happen only after a new federal courthouse is finished and its tenants have moved. The deed must require public use, with substantial use for the administration of justice. If the county stops using it that way, the property can revert.
plaw-108-222-2004:
Public Law 108-222, passed in 2004, provides for handing out judgment funds to the Cowlitz Indian Tribe of Washington. The money comes from an award by the Indian Claims Commission in Docket No. 218, plus interest. The tribe had gained federal acknowledgment on December 31, 2001.

The act starts with careful definitions. The current judgment fund means the Docket No. 218 award and all interest earned up to the act's passage. It then splits that sum into principal, counted a year earlier, and the initial interest earned during the last year. A tribal member is an enrolled member of the tribe. These definitions control how the Secretary of the Interior divides the money.
plaw-108-223-2004: Public Law 108-223, approved in April 2004, names two federal buildings in Washington, D.C., for the Wright brothers. The building at 800 Independence Avenue, Southwest, becomes the Orville Wright Federal Building. The building at 600 Independence Avenue, Southwest, becomes the Wilbur Wright Federal Building. Each designation comes with the standard rule that references to the building in federal laws, maps, or records now mean the new name.
plaw-108-224-2004: Public Law 108-224, the Surface Transportation Extension Act of 2004, Part II, stretches highway and transit programs a little further. Congress passed it in 2004 while a full renewal of the Transportation Equity Act for the 21st Century remained unfinished. It adds this act to the chain of extensions in the 2003 extension law. One change raises the minimum guarantee figure for states to 2.1 billion dollars. Another moves the off-system bridge set-aside date from April 30 to June 30, and contract authority figures are updated to match.
plaw-108-225-2004: Public Law 108-225, approved in May 2004, names a federal courthouse in Miami, Florida. The United States courthouse at 400 North Miami Avenue becomes the Wilkie D. Ferguson, Jr. United States Courthouse. The act is two sections long. After the designation, it provides that any reference to the courthouse in a federal law, map, or record counts as a reference to the Wilkie D. Ferguson, Jr. United States Courthouse.
plaw-108-226-2004: Public Law 108-226, approved in May 2004, names a federal building in Carbondale, Illinois, for a former senator. The building at 250 West Cherry Street becomes the Senator Paul Simon Federal Building. The law follows the short standard form for such namings. Its second section states that any reference to the building in a federal law, map, or record is deemed a reference to the Senator Paul Simon Federal Building.
plaw-108-227-2004: Public Law 108-227, approved in May 2004, names a federal building in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. The building at 228 Walnut Street becomes the Ronald Reagan Federal Building. The act gives the designation in its first subsection. A references part follows, saying that mentions of the building in federal laws, maps, regulations, or records now mean the Ronald Reagan Federal Building.
plaw-108-228-2004: Public Law 108-228, approved in May 2004, pushes back a deadline for selling shares in INTELSAT, the satellite organization. The Communications Satellite Act of 1962 had set dates for an initial public offering as INTELSAT moved toward private ownership. This act strikes December 31, 2003, and inserts June 30, 2005, in one place. In another it replaces June 30, 2004, with December 31, 2005. The short law simply gives the offering more time to happen.
plaw-108-229-2004: Public Law 108-229, approved in May 2004, expands Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore in Michigan. The park's boundary will take in about 104.45 acres of unimproved land near the Crystal River, shown on a Park Service map as the Bayberry Mills proposed expansion unit. The land joins the park once title passes to the United States in fee simple. The Secretary of the Interior may buy it only from a willing seller, and may not gain it by trading away or conveying land already inside the lakeshore.
plaw-108-230-2004: Public Law 108-230, passed in 2004, orders a land conveyance in Mendocino National Forest, California. The Secretary of Agriculture must give the owner of Faraway Ranch in Lake County two tracts of National Forest System land by quitclaim deed. Tract 39 covers about 15.8 acres, and Tract 40 covers about 105.1 acres, both shown on a map dated June 30, 2002. The act's title adds that money from the conveyance goes to National Forest purposes, so the forest gains funds rather than land value lost without return.
plaw-108-231-2004: Public Law 108-231, approved in May 2004, gives a Texas water district more time to pay back the federal government. The Tom Green County Water Control and Improvement District No. 1 owed construction costs for the San Angelo project under a repayment contract with the Interior Department. This law lets the Secretary of the Interior revise that contract. The repayment period for the reimbursable construction costs stretches from 40 years to 50 years, lowering the pace of payments the district must make.
plaw-108-232-2004: Public Law 108-232, the Premier Certified Lenders Program Improvement Act of 2004, loosens a reserve rule for top small business lenders. Premier certified lenders in the Small Business Administration's program must keep a loss reserve against bad loans. For two years, this act lets a lender pull out reserve amounts above one percent of the outstanding balance of the debentures the reserve covers. A third section creates a pilot program for an alternative loss reserve for certain premier certified lenders.
plaw-108-233-2004: Public Law 108-233, the Irvine Basin Surface and Groundwater Improvement Act of 2004, adds a California water project to a federal reclamation law. The Secretary of the Interior may join the Irvine Ranch Water District in planning and building projects in the San Diego Creek Watershed. The projects treat impaired surface water naturally, reclaim and reuse spoiled groundwater, and dispose of brine. The federal share may not pass 25 percent of the total cost, and federal money may not pay for running or maintaining a finished project.
plaw-108-234-2004: Public Law 108-234, approved in May 2004, creates two separate campaign medals for the wars then under way. The President must establish one medal for service in Operation Enduring Freedom and a different one for service in Operation Iraqi Freedom. Members of the uniformed services who took part in each operation earn the matching medal. Eligibility rules come from regulations written by each service secretary. For the military departments, the Secretary of Defense must approve the rules, and they must be uniform across the department.
plaw-108-235-2004:
Public Law 108-235, passed in 2004, takes up Taiwan's place in the World Health Organization. Taiwan was shut out of the WHO even though its population, about 23.5 million, tops that of three quarters of the WHO's member states, Congress found. The findings stress that diseases cross borders fast, so leaving any region outside health forums hurts everyone.

Congress praises Taiwan's health record. Life expectancy there ranks among Asia's highest, and death rates for mothers and infants match Western countries. Taiwan wiped out cholera, smallpox, plague, and polio, and it vaccinates children against hepatitis B. The act addresses steps for Taiwan to take part in the organization's work.
plaw-108-236-2004: Public Law 108-236 is a joint resolution from 2004 marking sixty years since the Allied landing in Normandy. June 6, 2004, was the 60th anniversary of D-Day in World War II. The resolution recalls that the landing, Operation Overlord, was the largest sea invasion ever mounted. On the first day it used 5,000 naval vessels, more than 11,000 aircraft sorties, and 153,000 Allied troops. American forces suffered over 6,500 casualties that day. Congress honors the valor of those who fought at the five beaches and landing zones.
plaw-108-237-2004:
Public Law 108-237, passed in 2004, encourages groups that write voluntary technical standards. Title I is the Standards Development Organization Advancement Act of 2004. Standards bodies bring rival companies together to agree on shared rules, which can raise antitrust worries.

The findings trace earlier laws. In 1993 Congress backed joint research and production ventures that disclose their work to antitrust enforcers. In 1995 it required agencies to lean on voluntary consensus standards. This act gives standards development organizations relief under the antitrust laws for conduct aimed at writing such standards. The idea is that open, shared standards help the national economy without letting firms fix markets.
plaw-108-238-2004:
Public Law 108-238, the National Great Black Americans Commemoration Act of 2004, authorizes help for a Baltimore museum. Congress found that Black Americans have served with honor in Congress, the courts, and senior government posts, yet the public rarely learns their stories in school or museums.

The Great Blacks in Wax Museum in Baltimore is the nation's first wax museum of great Black Americans, the findings say. Its nonprofit owner plans to grow into the National Great Blacks in Wax Museum and Justice Learning Center. The larger site would show wax figures and hands-on exhibits about Black history. This act authorizes federal assistance for that project.
plaw-108-239-2004: Public Law 108-239, approved in June 2004, names a post office in Los Angeles, California. The postal facility at 3751 West 6th Street becomes the Dosan Ahn Chang Ho Post Office. The act uses the standard two-section naming form. Its references section says that any mention of the facility in federal laws, maps, or records now counts as a reference to the Dosan Ahn Chang Ho Post Office.
plaw-108-240-2004: Public Law 108-240, approved in June 2004, renames a post office in River Edge, New Jersey. The postal facility at 121 Kinderkamack Road, known as the North Hackensack Station Post Office, becomes the New Bridge Landing Post Office. The act is short and follows the usual pattern. A second section directs that references to the facility in federal records now mean the New Bridge Landing Post Office.
plaw-108-241-2004: Hattiesburg, Mississippi gains a renamed post office under Public Law 108-241, approved June 25, 2004. The facility at 115 West Pine Street is designated the Major Henry A. Commiskey, Sr. Post Office Building. As with other naming laws, a references section follows. It deems any mention of the facility in federal laws, maps, or records to be a reference to the new name.
plaw-108-242-2004: Public Law 108-242, approved June 25, 2004, names a post office building in Jonesboro, Georgia. The facility at 255 North Main Street becomes the S. Truett Cathy Post Office Building. The first section makes the designation. The second provides that references to the facility in any United States law, map, regulation, or record shall be read as references to the S. Truett Cathy Post Office Building.
plaw-108-243-2004: In Stuttgart, Arkansas, the post office at 304 West Michigan Street takes a new name under Public Law 108-243. Approved June 25, 2004, the law designates the facility the Lloyd L. Burke Post Office. A short references section completes the act. It states that any reference to the facility in federal records now means the Lloyd L. Burke Post Office.
plaw-108-244-2004: Public Law 108-244 gives a Sarasota, Florida postal facility a general's name. The facility at 2055 Siesta Drive becomes the Brigadier General (AUS-Ret.) John H. McLain Post Office, under a law approved June 25, 2004. The second section handles later paperwork. References to the facility in laws, maps, or other federal records are deemed references to the Brigadier General (AUS-Ret.) John H. McLain Post Office.
plaw-108-245-2004: Liberty, New York is the site named in Public Law 108-245, approved June 25, 2004. The postal facility at 14 Chestnut Street is designated the Ben R. Gerow Post Office Building. The act follows the standard two-part pattern for facility namings. Section two directs that any reference to the facility in a federal law, map, or record be treated as a reference to the Ben R. Gerow Post Office Building.
plaw-108-246-2004: Public Law 108-246, approved June 25, 2004, designates a post office building in Strongsville, Ohio. The facility at 15500 Pearl Road shall be known as the Walter F. Ehrnfelt, Jr. Post Office Building. A references section follows the designation. It provides that mentions of the facility in United States laws, maps, regulations, or records count as mentions of the Walter F. Ehrnfelt, Jr. Post Office Building.
plaw-108-247-2004: Tarboro, North Carolina's post office receives its name from Public Law 108-247. The facility at 525 Main Street becomes the George Henry White Post Office Building under the law, approved June 25, 2004. The text is brief. Beyond the designation itself, it only adds the usual rule that references to the facility in federal laws, maps, or records now point to the George Henry White Post Office Building.
plaw-108-248-2004: Public Law 108-248 honors a soldier in the name of his hometown-area post office. Approved June 25, 2004, it designates the facility at 210 Main Street in Malden, Illinois, as the Army Staff Sgt. Lincoln Hollinsaid Malden Post Office. The references section completes the measure. Any federal reference to the facility is deemed a reference to the Army Staff Sgt. Lincoln Hollinsaid Malden Post Office.
plaw-108-249-2004: Manhattan, Illinois gains a memorial post office name under Public Law 108-249, approved June 25, 2004. The facility at 185 State Street is designated the Army Pvt. Shawn Pahnke Manhattan Post Office. The law is two sections long. The second section states that references to the facility in federal laws, maps, or records shall be treated as references to the Army Pvt. Shawn Pahnke Manhattan Post Office.
plaw-108-250-2004: Public Law 108-250, approved June 25, 2004, names a post office in Saint Anne, Illinois, for a Marine officer. The facility at 201 South Chicago Avenue becomes the Marine Capt. Ryan Beaupre Saint Anne Post Office. The designation sits in section one. Section two adds that any reference to the facility in a federal law, map, or record means the Marine Capt. Ryan Beaupre Saint Anne Post Office.
plaw-108-251-2004: Batavia, New York's post office building is named by Public Law 108-251, approved June 25, 2004. The facility at 2 West Main Street is designated the Barber Conable Post Office Building. The act has the usual two sections. The references section deems any mention of the facility in United States laws, maps, or records to be a mention of the Barber Conable Post Office Building.
plaw-108-252-2004: Public Law 108-252 gives the post office in Altamont, Kansas its name. Approved June 25, 2004, the law designates the facility at 410 Huston Street as the Myron V. George Post Office. After the designation, a references section follows the standard form. It says references to the facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, or records shall be read as references to the Myron V. George Post Office.
plaw-108-253-2004: In Roxboro, North Carolina, Public Law 108-253 names the post office building at 223 South Main Street. It becomes the Oscar Scott Woody Post Office Building under the act, approved June 25, 2004. The measure is short. Its second section provides that any reference to the facility in a law, map, or other federal record of the United States means the Oscar Scott Woody Post Office Building.
plaw-108-254-2004: Public Law 108-254, approved June 25, 2004, designates a post office building in Knoxville, Tennessee. The facility at 137 East Young High Pike shall be known as the Ben Atchley Post Office Building. A references section completes the law. It directs that mentions of the facility in federal laws, maps, or records be treated as mentions of the Ben Atchley Post Office Building.
plaw-108-255-2004: Laclede, Missouri's post office takes a famous general's name under Public Law 108-255. The facility at 607 Pershing Drive becomes the General John J. Pershing Post Office, by a law approved June 25, 2004. The street name and the honoree match. The second section adds the standard rule: references to the facility in any federal record count as references to the General John J. Pershing Post Office.
plaw-108-256-2004: Public Law 108-256, approved June 25, 2004, names a post office in Copiague, New York. The facility at 695 Marconi Boulevard is designated the Maxine S. Postal United States Post Office. The act is brief and follows the usual pattern. Its references section states that any reference to the facility in a federal law, map, or record is deemed a reference to the Maxine S. Postal United States Post Office.
plaw-108-257-2004: Fair Lawn, New Jersey's main post office gets a new name from Public Law 108-257. The facility at 14-24 Abbott Road, known as the Fair Lawn Main Post Office, is redesignated the Mary Ann Collura Post Office Building. The law was approved June 25, 2004. Its second section says references to the facility in federal laws, maps, or records now mean the Mary Ann Collura Post Office Building.
plaw-108-258-2004: Public Law 108-258 redesignates a postal facility in Middletown, Rhode Island, for the state's veterans. The facility at 7 Commercial Boulevard becomes the Rhode Island Veterans Post Office Building under the law, approved June 25, 2004. The act has two sections. The references section provides that any mention of the facility in federal records shall be treated as a mention of the Rhode Island Veterans Post Office Building.
plaw-108-259-2004: Cape Girardeau, Missouri's mail plant is named by Public Law 108-259, approved June 25, 2004. The postal facility at 475 Kell Farm Drive becomes the Richard G. Wilson Processing and Distribution Facility. Unlike most naming laws in this group, it covers a sorting facility rather than a retail post office. The references section deems federal mentions of the site to be references to the Richard G. Wilson Processing and Distribution Facility.
