plaw-108-260-2004: Public Law 108-260, approved June 25, 2004, names a post office building in Raeford, North Carolina. The facility at 122 West Elwood Avenue is designated the Bobby Marshall Gentry Post Office Building. The law follows the standard short form. A references section states that any reference to the facility in a United States law, map, or record means the Bobby Marshall Gentry Post Office Building.
plaw-108-261-2004: Edinburg, Texas gains a named post office building under Public Law 108-261, approved June 25, 2004. The facility at 410 South Jackson Road becomes the Dr. Miguel A. Nevarez Post Office Building. Section one makes the designation. Section two provides that references to the facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, or records shall be deemed references to the Dr. Miguel A. Nevarez Post Office Building.
plaw-108-262-2004: Public Law 108-262, the TANF and Related Programs Continuation Act of 2004, keeps welfare programs running through September 30, 2004. The Temporary Assistance for Needy Families block grant continues in the manner authorized for fiscal year 2002. Grants may be paid through the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2004 at the fiscal year 2002 level. A matching change swaps June 30 for September 30 in the Social Security Act. The act also extends the national child welfare study and waiver authority.
plaw-108-263-2004: Public Law 108-263 is the Surface Transportation Extension Act of 2004, Part III. Congress passed it while a long-term renewal of the Transportation Equity Act for the 21st Century was still pending. It chains this act onto the earlier 2004 extensions. The minimum guarantee figure for states rises to a little over 2.3 billion dollars. The off-system bridge set-aside date moves from June 30 to July 31, and highway contract authority is updated for the longer period.
plaw-108-264-2004:
Public Law 108-264, the Bunning-Bereuter-Blumenauer Flood Insurance Reform Act of 2004, targets houses that flood again and again. It amends the National Flood Insurance Act of 1968. Some properties had drawn repeated insurance payments, costing the program heavily.

Title I extends the flood insurance program and creates a pilot program for the worst repeat-loss properties. It lets the Federal Emergency Management Agency fund work that reduces flood risk at single properties with many claims. Other sections improve the existing flood mitigation aid program and set rates meant to reflect real risk. The act also backs digital flood hazard maps and keeps FEMA in charge of mapping mudslide risk.
plaw-108-265-2004:
Public Law 108-265, the Child Nutrition and WIC Reauthorization Act of 2004, renews the federal programs that feed children. Its stated aims are to give children more access to food aid, simplify how programs run, and improve management. It amends the Richard B. Russell National School Lunch Act and the Child Nutrition Act of 1966.

Title I changes the school lunch law in detail. Sections cover nutrition promotion and requirements, direct certification of children for free meals, and simpler household applications. Others deal with runaway, homeless, and migrant youth, food safety, and buying locally produced foods. One section leaves military housing allowances out of eligibility math. Later titles take up the WIC program for mothers and young children.
plaw-108-266-2004:
Public Law 108-266, the Marine Turtle Conservation Act of 2004, sends American help to sea turtles nesting in other countries. Congress found that sea turtle numbers had fallen so far that the long-term survival of six named kinds is in serious doubt. Loggerhead, green, hawksbill, Kemp's ridley, olive ridley, and leatherback turtles are all named.

The findings say six of the seven known sea turtle kinds are listed as threatened or endangered under American law. Turtles live long, mature late, and migrate far, which makes them easy to harm. Illegal trade threatens some kinds, above all the hawksbill. The act's purpose is to help conserve the turtles and their nesting habitats abroad.
plaw-108-267-2004: Public Law 108-267, approved July 2, 2004, renames a foundation for Native American education. The American Indian Education Foundation, created under the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act, becomes the National Fund for Excellence in American Indian Education. The act strikes the old name and inserts the new one in section 501 of that law. Matching changes update the title heading and the section heading, so the whole title now carries the fund's new name.
plaw-108-268-2004:
Public Law 108-268, passed in 2004, moves a Navy site in Washington, D.C., to make room for a new department's home. The Secretary of the Navy must transfer the Nebraska Avenue Naval Complex to the General Services Administrator. The site will house the Department of Homeland Security, the department created after the 2001 attacks.

The Navy hands the complex over in its existing condition. It may keep the part used for Navy family housing. The transfer and the moving of Navy activities must finish within nine months of the act's passage. Other parts of the law provide for the Navy to gain suitable replacement facilities elsewhere, so its work can continue without the Nebraska Avenue site.
plaw-108-269-2004: Public Law 108-269, passed in 2004, directs the sale of a tree nursery site in Bend, Oregon. It amends the Bend Pine Nursery Land Conveyance Act of 2000. When the Bend Metro Park and Recreation District in Deschutes County pays 3,503,676 dollars, the Secretary of Agriculture must convey the Bend Pine Nursery land to the district. The parcel covers about 185 acres and is shown on a site plan map named in the law.
plaw-108-270-2004:
Public Law 108-270, the Western Shoshone Claims Distribution Act, divides judgment money owed to the Western Shoshone people. The funds satisfy awards in Indian Claims Commission and Court of Claims cases, dockets 326-A-1, 326-A-3, and 326-K. Interest earned on the awards counts as part of the funds.

The act defines two pots of money, the joint judgment funds and the judgment funds, by which docket they came from. It sets up a judgment roll, a list kept by the Secretary of the Interior of people entitled to share. An administrative committee and a trust fund also appear in the definitions. Later sections use those pieces to pay out the awards to Western Shoshone members.
plaw-108-271-2004:
Public Law 108-271, the GAO Human Capital Reform Act of 2004, gives the government's watchdog agency more control over its own workforce. The GAO, then called the General Accounting Office, audits federal spending for Congress. The act amends title 31 of the U.S. Code and a law from 2000.

First, it makes permanent two tools from that 2000 law: voluntary early retirement and voluntary separation incentive payments. Congress adds that using them should reshape the GAO workforce, not shrink it. The 2000 law had limited those tools to a period ending December 31, 2003. This act backdates their start to October 13, 2000, and removes the end date.
plaw-108-272-2004: Public Law 108-272 is a joint resolution approved July 7, 2004, about trade sanctions on Burma. Congress approves the renewal of the import restrictions in section 3(a)(1) of the Burmese Freedom and Democracy Act of 2003. That act had banned imports from Burma, also known as Myanmar, to press its military rulers toward democracy. The resolution is one line long. Its approval keeps the import ban in force for another period.
plaw-108-273-2004: Public Law 108-273, approved July 7, 2004, names a federal building in Ponce, Puerto Rico. The United States courthouse and post office building at 93 Atocha Street becomes the Luis A. Ferre United States Courthouse and Post Office Building. The act follows the two-part naming form. Its references part says that mentions of the building in federal laws, maps, or records now mean the Luis A. Ferre United States Courthouse and Post Office Building.
plaw-108-274-2004:
Public Law 108-274, the AGOA Acceleration Act of 2004, extends and adjusts trade benefits for sub-Saharan Africa. The African Growth and Opportunity Act had opened United States markets to goods from eligible African countries. Congress found the act had spurred growth and reform.

The findings report record American exports to sub-Saharan Africa after AGOA began, and a considerable rise in African exports the other way. Eligibility rules had strengthened democratic values, the rule of law, and worker rights, Congress said. Foreign investment grew, above all in cloth and clothing, where tens of thousands of jobs appeared. The act then extends the program before world textile quotas expire.
plaw-108-275-2004:
Public Law 108-275, the Identity Theft Penalty Enhancement Act, adds prison time for thieves who steal identities while committing other felonies. It amends title 18 of the U.S. Code by creating a new crime called aggravated identity theft.

A person who knowingly transfers, holds, or uses another person's identification during a listed felony gets two extra years in prison. If the underlying felony is a terrorism offense, the added term is five years. The added sentence runs on top of the punishment for the main felony. Courts may not put such a person on probation for this count, and the act limits running the extra term at the same time as other sentences.
plaw-108-276-2004:
Public Law 108-276, the Project BioShield Act of 2004, prepares defenses against a terrorist attack with germ, chemical, or radiation weapons. It amends the Public Health Service Act. The goal is to build and stockpile medical countermeasures, such as vaccines and treatments, before any attack comes.

The act gives the National Institutes of Health more flexible contracting and faster scientific peer review for countermeasure work. It also improves research facilities. A second aim is to speed the Food and Drug Administration's approval process for these products. The government can thus promise makers a buyer, which coaxes companies to build drugs that normal markets would never support.
plaw-108-277-2004:
Public Law 108-277, the Law Enforcement Officers Safety Act of 2004, lets qualified officers carry concealed handguns across state lines. It amends chapter 44 of title 18 of the U.S. Code. State laws that bar concealed carry do not apply to a qualified current or former officer who carries the required identification.

The exemption has limits written into the text. States may still let private owners bar concealed firearms on their property. States may also bar firearms on state or local government property, buildings, bases, and parks. The firearm itself must have moved in interstate or foreign commerce. Later parts define who counts as a qualified officer and what identification is needed.
plaw-108-278-2004:
Public Law 108-278, the Tribal Forest Protection Act of 2004, lets tribes help guard federal forests that border their land. Wildfires and pests spread across boundary lines, threatening Indian forest land held in trust. The act responds to that shared risk.

The Agriculture and Interior secretaries may sign agreements or contracts with tribes that meet set criteria. Under those deals, tribes carry out protection projects on nearby federal land. Federal land here means National Forest System land and public lands run by the Bureau of Land Management. The projects protect tribal forest and rangeland by treating the federal ground where fires or infestations often start.
plaw-108-279-2004:
Public Law 108-279, passed in 2004, settles land boundary fights in Barry and Stone Counties, Missouri. The trouble sits near the Mark Twain National Forest and Table Rock Reservoir. Later federal land surveys drew lines that overlapped private claims based on the original government surveys.

The act defines a boundary conflict as that overlap between a private ownership claim and federal ownership of the same land. It sets the Army and Agriculture secretaries as the officials in charge, depending on the land. Original surveys means the old General Land Office work under the Public Land Survey System, on which government land patents were issued. With terms fixed, the act lays out how the disputed lines get resolved.
plaw-108-280-2004: Public Law 108-280 is the Surface Transportation Extension Act of 2004, Part IV. Like the three extension acts before it in 2004, it keeps highway, transit, and safety programs funded from the Highway Trust Fund. Congress passed it while the long-term renewal of the Transportation Equity Act for the 21st Century stayed unfinished. The minimum guarantee figure for states rises to 2.8 billion dollars. The bridge set-aside language is updated, and highway contract authority grows to match the added months.
plaw-108-281-2004: Public Law 108-281, passed in 2004, amends the E-Government Act of 2002 about court rulemaking. The Judicial Conference had raised questions about who writes rules for electronic filing in federal courts. The act strikes one paragraph and replaces it. The Supreme Court must prescribe rules to protect privacy and security in electronic filing and public access to filed documents. The rules should treat privacy the same way across all federal courts where practical. They must weigh the best practices of federal and state courts for guarding private information.
plaw-108-282-2004:
Public Law 108-282, passed in 2004, tackles a shortage of medicines for minor animal species. Title I is the Minor Use and Minor Species Animal Health Act of 2004. Congress found a severe shortage of approved drugs for minor species, and for rare diseases or diseases found in only a few areas.

The findings explain why. Small markets and low profits make approval not worth the cost for drug makers. Studying a drug is also hard when the animal group is tiny or care conditions vary widely. The act creates special procedures so such drugs can be used and sold lawfully. Its stated aim is the public interest and animal welfare. Later titles amend other animal drug rules.
plaw-108-283-2004:
Public Law 108-283, the Northern Uganda Crisis Response Act, requires a report on a brutal African conflict. For more than seventeen years, Uganda's government had fought the Lord's Resistance Army in the north and east of the country. Congress passed the act in 2004 to force attention on the crisis.

The findings say the rebel army used brutal tactics, including kidnapping people and forcing them into sexual servitude. Between 16,000 and 26,000 children were forced to serve in its forces, by the estimates Congress cites. The Secretary of State had listed the group as a terrorist organization. The act then requires an official report on the conflict and the response.
plaw-108-284-2004: Public Law 108-284 is a joint resolution from August 2004 that fills a seat on the Smithsonian Institution's Board of Regents. The citizen regent seat fell vacant when Barber B. Conable, Jr. died. Congress appoints Eli Broad of California to fill it. Citizen regents are the board members who do not sit in Congress. Broad's term runs six years from the date the resolution was enacted.
plaw-108-285-2004: Public Law 108-285, the Helping Hands for Homeownership Act of 2004, supports self-help housing, where families help build their own homes. Its first change is one word: assistance may go to dwellings, plural, in a section of a 1996 housing law. The act also names a rural loan program for Congressman Doug Bereuter of Nebraska. The findings credit him as the author of the section 502 single family housing loan guarantee program. That program had backed more than 316,000 loans since 1991 for rural borrowers who could not get normal financing.
plaw-108-286-2004:
Public Law 108-286, passed in 2004, puts the United States-Australia Free Trade Agreement into effect. Congress must approve and implement such trade deals before they bind the country. Title I approves the agreement and covers its link to United States and state law.

That title also handles early steps toward the deal taking force, first regulations, and how trade disputes get settled. Title II covers customs matters: tariff changes, extra duties on certain farm goods, and rules of origin that decide which goods count as Australian. It also deals with customs fees, wrong information penalties, and policing trade in textiles and clothing. Title III gives relief when imports surge.
plaw-108-287-2004:
Public Law 108-287 is the Department of Defense Appropriations Act for 2005, passed in 2004. It funds military work for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2005. Appropriations acts like this one give agencies legal power to spend money.

Title I covers military personnel. For the Army, it provides about 29.4 billion dollars for pay, allowances, clothing, food, and travel for soldiers on active duty, plus cadets. It also pays into the Defense Military Retirement Fund. Matching sections follow for the Navy and the other services. Later titles fund operations, weapons buying, research, and construction, each as its own account with its own rules.
plaw-108-288-2004: Public Law 108-288, approved August 6, 2004, names a federal courthouse in Pensacola, Florida. The courthouse at 100 North Palafox Street becomes the Winston E. Arnow United States Courthouse. The act is two sections long. The references section says that any mention of the courthouse in a federal law, map, or record now counts as a mention of the Winston E. Arnow United States Courthouse.
plaw-108-289-2004:
Public Law 108-289, the Jamestown 400th Anniversary Commemorative Coin Act of 2004, orders a coin for a founding moment. Jamestown, Virginia was settled in 1607 as the first permanent English colony in America. It served as Virginia's capital for 92 years, the findings note.

Congress says the settlement joined people from across the Atlantic world and mixed English, European, African, and Native American cultures. Institutions born there still shape the country, above all English common law and language. Three groups jointly care for Jamestown's remains: the National Park Service, a Virginia preservation group, and the Jamestown-Yorktown Foundation. A commemorative coin marks the 400th anniversary and supports that work.
plaw-108-290-2004:
Public Law 108-290, the John Marshall Commemorative Coin Act, directs the Treasury to mint coins honoring a great Chief Justice. The findings say John Marshall led the Supreme Court from 1801 to 1835, the longest tenure of any Chief Justice. He wrote more than 500 opinions, including nearly all the major cases of his era.

Under Marshall, the Court gave shape to the Constitution's basic principles, above all judicial review, the power to strike down laws. He had also served as a soldier, a congressman, and Secretary of State. The coin marks the 250th anniversary of his birth. The Treasury may issue up to 400,000 one-dollar coins, each weighing 26.73 grams.
plaw-108-291-2004:
Public Law 108-291, the Marine Corps 230th Anniversary Commemorative Coin Act, orders coins for a famous fighting force. November 10, 2005, marks 230 years since the Marine Corps began. The findings praise its gallant service across that long history.

Congress calls the Corps the nation's leader in amphibious warfare, war fought from sea to shore. It also says the Marines model a warrior spirit known around the world. Coin sales support construction of the Marine Corps Heritage Center, which Congress authorized in 2001. The center preserves the Corps' history for the public. The act sets the coin program in honor of the anniversary year.
plaw-108-292-2004: Public Law 108-292, approved August 6, 2004, names a post office building in Holiday, Florida, for a fallen soldier. The postal facility at 4737 Mile Stretch Drive becomes the Sergeant First Class Paul Ray Smith Post Office Building. The law follows the standard naming pattern. A references section provides that mentions of the facility in federal laws, maps, or records now mean the Sergeant First Class Paul Ray Smith Post Office Building.
plaw-108-293-2004:
Public Law 108-293, the Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Act of 2004, funds and updates the Coast Guard for fiscal year 2005. Title I authorizes the service's appropriations and sets its allowed military strength and training levels.

Title II covers Coast Guard management in detail. Sections deal with long-term leases, enlistment terms, and a bonus for training in critical skills. Others cover housing authority, travel card management, and fellows sent to work elsewhere. One section pays for disabling vessels that may be seized or examined. The act also amends various other laws the Coast Guard administers, as its long title states.
plaw-108-294-2004: Public Law 108-294, approved August 9, 2004, redesignates two postal facilities in Chicago, Illinois. The facility at 7715 South Cottage Grove Avenue becomes the James E. Worsham Post Office. The facility at 7748 South Cottage Grove Avenue becomes the James E. Worsham Carrier Annex Building. Each redesignation carries its own references rule. Federal mentions of either site in laws, maps, or records now point to its new Worsham name.
plaw-108-295-2004:
Public Law 108-295, the SUTA Dumping Prevention Act of 2004, closes a trick used to dodge unemployment taxes. Employers pay state unemployment taxes at rates based on their history of layoffs, called experience. Some firms reshuffled ownership to dump a bad record and win a lower rate.

The act amends titles III and IV of the Social Security Act. State laws must move a business's unemployment experience record along with the business when it transfers to a new owner under much the same ownership or control. A record may not transfer when someone buys a business mainly to grab a lower tax rate and was not already an employer. The change improves how unemployment taxes and benefits are run.
plaw-108-296-2004: Public Law 108-296, approved August 9, 2004, names a post office building in Kansas City, Kansas. The postal facility at 550 Nebraska Avenue is designated the Newell George Post Office Building. The act is short, in the usual form. Its references section says that any reference to the facility in a federal law, map, or record shall be deemed a reference to the Newell George Post Office Building.
plaw-108-297-2004:
Public Law 108-297, the Cape Town Treaty Implementation Act of 2004, aligns American aircraft records with an international treaty. The treaty, signed at Cape Town, covers interests in mobile equipment, with a special protocol for aircraft and engines. It extends modern sale, finance, and lease law across borders.

Congress found the treaty gives lenders and lessors firm, recognized rights. That security makes financing planes and engines more predictable and cheaper. The framework should help aviation and aerospace firms, including exports, the findings say. The act then changes title 49 rules on registering aircraft and recording ownership documents, so the United States system matches the treaty's registry approach.
plaw-108-298-2004: Public Law 108-298, approved August 9, 2004, names a post office building in St. Louis, Missouri. The postal facility at 7450 Natural Bridge Road becomes the Vitilas 'Veto' Reid Post Office Building. The nickname appears inside the official name, in quotation marks. A references section follows, deeming any mention of the facility in federal laws, maps, or records to be a reference to the Vitilas 'Veto' Reid Post Office Building.
plaw-108-299-2004: Public Law 108-299, approved August 9, 2004, moves deadlines for safer travel documents. The Enhanced Border Security and Visa Entry Reform Act of 2002 had required machine-readable, tamper-resistant entry and exit documents by dates in 2004. This act strikes 2004 and inserts 2005 in three places in section 303 of that law. The one-year delay gave governments and travelers more time to meet the document standards set after the 2001 attacks.
plaw-108-300-2004: Public Law 108-300, approved August 9, 2004, names a post office in Montauk, New York. The postal facility at 73 South Euclid Avenue is designated the Perry B. Duryea, Jr. Post Office. The law is brief and follows the standard naming form. A references section says any mention of the facility in federal laws, maps, or records now counts as a mention of the Perry B. Duryea, Jr. Post Office.
plaw-108-301-2004: Public Law 108-301, approved August 9, 2004, raises a cap so the Federal Housing Administration can keep insuring mortgages. Inside the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2004, the FHA's General and Special Risk Program Account had a limit of 25 billion dollars. This act strikes that figure and inserts 29 billion dollars. The change preserves the agency's ability to insure home loans under sections 238 and 519 of the National Housing Act, as the act's title states.
plaw-108-302-2004:
Public Law 108-302, passed in 2004, carries out the United States-Morocco Free Trade Agreement. Free trade deals need an act of Congress to take effect under American law. Title I approves the agreement and sets its place next to United States and state law.

That title also covers first steps before the deal starts, dispute settlement, and arbitration of claims. Title II writes the customs rules. It changes tariffs, adds possible extra duties on some farm goods, and sets rules of origin for deciding which goods qualify as Moroccan. It polices trade in textiles and clothing as well. Title III, on relief from imports, guards American producers if imports surge.
plaw-108-303-2004: Public Law 108-303, the Emergency Supplemental Appropriations for Disaster Relief Act of 2004, sends urgent aid after disasters. Approved September 8, 2004, it adds two billion dollars for Disaster Relief in the Department of Homeland Security for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2004. The money stays available until spent. Up to thirty million dollars may move to the Small Business Administration to cover the cost of running its disaster loan program. Congress marked the spending as an emergency requirement under budget rules.
plaw-108-304-2004:
Public Law 108-304, the Sports Agent Responsibility and Trust Act, brings federal watch over agents who sign student athletes. The act declares certain agent conduct in signing contracts with student athletes to be unfair or deceptive practice. The Federal Trade Commission gains the job of policing that conduct.

Definitions fill the early sections. An agency contract is any spoken or written deal where a student athlete lets someone negotiate a pro sports or endorsement contract. An athlete agent is a person who signs such a deal, or who recruits a student athlete toward one. Family members, lawyers acting as lawyers, and people working only for a pro team do not count as agents under the act.
plaw-108-305-2004: Public Law 108-305, approved September 24, 2004, gives a parcel of land in Ravenna, Ohio, to Portage County. The Secretary of Labor must convey the property at 1081 West Main Street free of charge. The transfer covers all federal right, title, and interest, including federal equity in the site. That interest came from grants to Ohio under title III of the Social Security Act, the Wagner-Peyser Act, or related federal funds sent to the state.
plaw-108-306-2004: Public Law 108-306, passed in 2004, extends small business programs through September 30, 2004. Programs under the Small Business Act and the Small Business Investment Act of 1958 that had run through June 4, 2004, continue on the same terms. A technical amendment repairs a date in an earlier extension law. Another section lets the Small Business Administration hire an agent to assess and collect a yearly loan program fee. The agent may keep the interest earned on the fee while holding it, as payment.
plaw-108-307-2004:
Public Law 108-307, the Harpers Ferry National Historical Park Boundary Revision Act of 2004, redraws the lines of a Civil War era park in West Virginia. It rewrites the first section of the park's 1944 founding act. The Secretary of the Interior may acquire land inside the new boundary shown on a 1979 map.

Land may come by purchase from a willing seller, by gift, or by exchange. One named piece, the Bradley and Ruth Nash Addition, covers about 27 acres outside the old boundary. The Secretary may take that land by donation only, under a 1989 map. The act then provides for further boundary expansion in later subsections.
plaw-108-308-2004: Public Law 108-308 carries the short title Welfare Reform Extension Act, Part VIII. It reauthorizes the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families block grant program through March 31, 2005. Activities continue in the manner authorized for fiscal year 2004, and grants may be paid through the second quarter of fiscal year 2005 at that level. Matching changes move dates in the Social Security Act from September 30, 2004, to March 31, 2005, for extra grants to states with growing populations and for the contingency fund.
plaw-108-309-2004: Public Law 108-309 is a joint resolution making continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2005. Passed in the fall of 2004, it funds the federal government at the start of the new fiscal year, before the regular spending bills were done. Section 101 provides such amounts as are necessary to keep going the projects and activities run under the fiscal year 2004 appropriations acts. Agencies may spend at a rate no higher than the current rate. The resolution names the 2004 acts one by one, starting with agriculture and commerce, justice, and state.
plaw-108-310-2004: Public Law 108-310 is the Surface Transportation Extension Act of 2004, Part V. It is the fifth short extension of highway, transit, and safety programs that Congress passed in 2004. A full renewal of the Transportation Equity Act for the 21st Century was still pending. This part changes the advance rules: the Transportation Secretary must divide the available funds among the states by their share of fiscal year 2004 highway obligation authority. The ratios get the same adjustments that title 23 provides.
plaw-108-311-2004:
Public Law 108-311, the Working Families Tax Relief Act of 2004, extends popular family tax breaks. It amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. Some cuts from earlier tax laws were set to shrink or vanish, and Congress acted to stop that.

Title I repeals the scheduled reductions in the child tax credit, marriage penalty relief, and the 10 percent rate bracket. It speeds up the increase in how much of the child credit can be refunded. It also extends relief from the alternative minimum tax for one year. One section counts combat pay as earned income, helping deployed troops claim credits. Title II sets one uniform definition of a child across the tax code.
plaw-108-312-2004:
Public Law 108-312, the Mount Rainier National Park Boundary Adjustment Act of 2004, shifts the edge of a Washington park toward the Carbon River. Congress found the Carbon River watershed in Pierce County has clean water, strong salmon streams, and key wildlife habitat. It also holds active geology and fine scenery.

The findings call Mount Rainier National Park one of Washington's premier attractions. New campgrounds and visitor contact sites in the Carbon River valley would sit outside old-growth forest and above the flood plain. Joint management across national forest and park lands in the corridor should help the forest ecosystem, Congress said. The boundary change also protects historic and recreational sites such as trails and visitor centers.
plaw-108-313-2004: Public Law 108-313, the Johnstown Flood National Memorial Boundary Adjustment Act of 2004, adds land to a Pennsylvania memorial. The new boundary follows a map of the memorial in Cambria County dated June 2003. The map stays on file at Park Service offices for public inspection. The Secretary of the Interior may buy the added land from willing sellers, take it by gift, pay with donated or appropriated funds, or swap for it. Added lands are run as part of the memorial under the usual laws.
plaw-108-314-2004:
Public Law 108-314, the Martin Luther King, Junior, National Historic Site Land Exchange Act, swaps land in Atlanta, Georgia. The National Park Service owns a vacant lot inside the historic site that has no historic meaning. The City of Atlanta wants that lot to encourage business growth along Edgewood Avenue.

The findings explain the other half of the deal. The site's Visitor Center and Museum is land-locked, with no emergency way in or out. Fire trucks can hardly reach it. Getting city-owned property would give the Park Service easy street access to the center. Both sides gain from the trade, Congress found, and the act's purpose is to authorize the exchange.
plaw-108-315-2004: Public Law 108-315, the Carpinteria and Montecito Water Distribution Systems Conveyance Act of 2004, hands two California water systems to local districts. The Secretary of the Interior may convey the Carpinteria Distribution System of the Cachuma Project to the Carpinteria Valley Water District. The Secretary may likewise convey the Montecito system to the Montecito Water District. Both districts sit in Santa Barbara County. Each transfer follows the terms of a signed agreement between the United States and the district named in the law.
plaw-108-316-2004: Public Law 108-316, passed in 2004, adds a Texas water reuse project to the federal reclamation law. The Williamson County Water Recycling Act lets the Secretary of the Interior join the Lower Colorado River Authority in Texas. Together they may design, plan, and build permanent facilities to reclaim and reuse water in Williamson County. The federal share may not pass 25 percent of the total cost. Federal money may not pay to operate or maintain the finished project.
plaw-108-317-2004:
Public Law 108-317, the Southwest Forest Health and Wildfire Prevention Act of 2004, sets up institutes to fight wildfire risk in the interior West. The institutes demonstrate adaptive ecosystem management, a learn-as-you-go way of caring for land. Congress found wildfire threatens millions of acres of forest and rangeland.

The findings blame past practices: stopping all fires and failing to thin crowded stands let flammable brush build up. At least 39 million acres of National Forest System land in the interior West stand at high risk of wildfire, Congress found. Fires there are growing in number, size, and severity. The institutes aim to restore fire-adapted forests and woodlands to health.
plaw-108-318-2004: Public Law 108-318, approved October 5, 2004, clarifies one number in a Nebraska irrigation law. The Reclamation Project Authorization Act of 1972 covers the North Loup division of the Missouri River Basin project. Its section 501 had set the service area at fifty-three thousand acres, spelled out in words. This act strikes the spelled-out figure and inserts approximately 53,000 acres. The change makes clear the acreage is an estimate, not an exact legal line.
plaw-108-319-2004: Public Law 108-319, approved October 5, 2004, extends the life of the Forest Counties Payments Committee. That committee advises on federal payments to counties with large national forest lands, which cannot tax federal ground. A 2001 appropriations act had ended the committee three years after its passage. This law replaces that end point with September 30, 2007. The change counts as effective from October 11, 2003, so the committee's work never formally lapsed.
plaw-108-320-2004: Public Law 108-320, approved October 5, 2004, is one of the shortest laws in this set. It amends the Stevenson-Wydler Technology Innovation Act of 1980, which runs the Malcolm Baldrige National Quality Awards. Those awards honor organizations for quality and performance. The whole act adds a single line to the award categories in section 17: a new subparagraph reading simply Nonprofit organizations. From then on, nonprofits could receive Baldrige awards alongside businesses and other groups.
plaw-108-321-2004: Public Law 108-321, the Timucuan Ecological and Historic Preserve Boundary Revision Act of 2004, grows a Florida preserve a little. The Timucuan preserve near Jacksonville gains about 8.5 acres in Nassau County, at American Beach. The added land shows on a map dated June 2003. The Secretary of the Interior must redraw the preserve boundary to take in the land. The Secretary must also keep the map on file at Park Service offices where the public can inspect it.
plaw-108-322-2004: Public Law 108-322 is a joint resolution celebrating a new museum on the National Mall. The National Museum of the American Indian officially opened on September 21, 2004. Congress notes it is the only national museum devoted only to the history and art of cultures native to the Americas. The resolution recognizes the unique contribution of Native Americans to the nation's cultural legacy, honors their achievements, and celebrates the opening. It asks the President to issue a proclamation urging Americans to use the museum's resources.
plaw-108-323-2004:
Public Law 108-323, passed in 2004, renews the Tropical Forest Conservation Act of 1998 through fiscal year 2007. That program swaps some of a poor country's foreign debt for promises to protect tropical forests. This act sets the money for debt reduction under two older aid laws for three more years.

The amounts rise year by year: twenty million dollars for fiscal year 2005, twenty-five million for 2006, and thirty million for 2007. Two hundred thousand dollars a year may pay for audits and reviews of the programs, including staff costs. Another section lets debtor countries pay interest and principal in their local currencies, which can then fund conservation at home.
plaw-108-324-2004:
Public Law 108-324 funds military building for 2005 and adds emergency hurricane aid. Its full title joins the Military Construction Appropriations Act, 2005 with an emergency hurricane supplement. Congress passed it in the fall of 2004, after a hard hurricane season.

Division A pays for military construction, family housing, and base realignment and closure in the fiscal year ending September 30, 2005. The Army account covers building, installation, and equipment for posts and facilities, plus Army Corps of Engineers staff. References to this act inside a division count only for that division, the law warns. The hurricane money rides in the same act as an emergency addition.
plaw-108-325-2004: Public Law 108-325, the Craig Recreation Land Purchase Act, arranges a land sale between Alaska and the federal government. If the City of Craig offers to sell certain city land within 180 days of getting an appraisal, the Secretary of Agriculture must accept, if money is available. On transfer, the Secretary pays the city the land's appraised value. The parcels include the Sunnahae Trail and recreation parcel and the Craig Cannery Property, shown on an August 2003 map, plus two lots from the city subdivision plat.
plaw-108-326-2004: Public Law 108-326, approved October 16, 2004, clarifies the tax treatment of bonds issued by the Government of American Samoa. Interest on any bond or other obligation from that government is exempt from income tax by American Samoa, the states, the District of Columbia, and every territory or possession. The act rewrites a subsection of a 1984 law to say so plainly. The exemption covers income taxes only. It does not apply to gift, estate, inheritance, or other wealth transfer taxes. It covers obligations issued after the act passed.
plaw-108-327-2004:
Public Law 108-327, the National Wildlife Refuge Volunteer Act of 2004, renews help from unpaid volunteers at wildlife refuges. It amends the Fish and Wildlife Act of 1956. Volunteers and community partners run projects, staff visitor sites, and care for habitat across the refuge system.

The act authorizes two million dollars a year for fiscal years 2004 through 2009 for the volunteer and partnership work. It also updates a 1998 law on refuge volunteer projects. The word pilot is struck from the project rules, and a cap of twenty pilot projects nationwide disappears. What began as a test becomes a standing part of refuge work.
plaw-108-328-2004: Public Law 108-328, approved October 16, 2004, reauthorizes the New York City Watershed Protection Program. The program, run under the Safe Drinking Water Act, protects the upstate watersheds that supply New York City's drinking water. Section 1443 of that act had covered the years 1997 through 2003. This law strikes that span and inserts 2003 through 2010. The change keeps federal support for guarding the city's water supply going for seven more years.
plaw-108-329-2004: Public Law 108-329, approved October 16, 2004, lets binding arbitration clauses appear in all contracts touching land in the Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Reservation. It amends a law from November 2, 1966. Earlier wording applied the arbitration option to leases and certain contracts. The amendment swaps in broader words so any contract, including a lease, affecting reservation land may carry such a clause. The change counts as effective from the Indian Tribal Economic Development and Contract Encouragement Act of 2000.
plaw-108-330-2004:
Public Law 108-330, the Department of Homeland Security Financial Accountability Act, tightens money management at a young department. The department was built by joining 22 separate federal agencies. Congress found that strong financial leadership is vital to its mission success.

The findings say the department's Chief Financial Officer must be a key figure in management. Under the Chief Financial Officers Act of 1990, such officers are presidential appointees who report straight to the department head. Homeland Security was created after that law, so this act amends title 31 to bring the department under the same rules. It also sets requirements for the department's Future Years Homeland Security Program, its long-range plan.
plaw-108-331-2004: Public Law 108-331, approved October 16, 2004, authorizes a Smithsonian telescope project in Arizona. The Board of Regents of the Smithsonian Institution may carry out construction for the VERITAS project on Kitt Peak near Tucson. VERITAS, the Very Energetic Radiation Imaging Telescope Array System, is a joint project that studies very high energy radiation from space. The act authorizes one million dollars for fiscal year 2005 to carry out the construction work.
plaw-108-332-2004:
Public Law 108-332, the Global Anti-Semitism Review Act of 2004, requires a report on anti-Jewish acts around the world. Congress found that acts of anti-Semitism had grown in frequency and reach over the prior years, even in strong democracies. The findings list recent attacks from late 2003 and early 2004.

In Istanbul, Turkey, car bombs outside two synagogues on November 15, 2003, killed 24 people and wounded more than 250. In Malaysia, a former prime minister told world leaders that Jews rule the world by proxy. In Tasmania, poison burned anti-Semitic slogans into the Parliament House lawns. The act answers by ordering an official worldwide review.
plaw-108-333-2004:
Public Law 108-333, the North Korean Human Rights Act of 2004, aims to promote human rights and freedom in North Korea. Its formal name for the country is the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. Congress passed it in 2004, during a long standoff over the North's weapons programs.

Title I promotes the rights of North Koreans. It backs democracy and human rights programs, radio broadcasting into North Korea, and freer flows of information. It also creates a Special Envoy on Human Rights in North Korea. Title II covers aid for North Koreans in need, both inside the country and outside it. Title III protects North Korean refugees and defectors.
plaw-108-334-2004:
Public Law 108-334 is the Department of Homeland Security Appropriations Act for 2005. It funds the department for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2005. Title I pays for departmental management and operations.

The Office of the Secretary and executive management receives about 85 million dollars. The Office of the Under Secretary for Management receives about 151 million dollars. Of that sum, about 65 million dollars stays available until spent, solely for building alterations named in the act. Small amounts in each account are set aside for official reception and representation costs. Later titles fund the department's agencies, from border security to emergency response.
plaw-108-335-2004:
Public Law 108-335, the District of Columbia Appropriations Act for 2005, funds the government of the nation's capital. Congress holds final budget power over Washington, D.C., so its yearly spending comes through an act like this one. The act covers the fiscal year ending September 30, 2005.

Title I lists federal funds. A federal payment of about 25.6 million dollars supports college tuition for District residents. The money pays the gap between in-state and out-of-state tuition at public colleges nationwide. At private colleges it pays up to 2,500 dollars a year for each eligible resident. Awards may favor students by academic merit and by income and need, the act provides.
plaw-108-336-2004:
Public Law 108-336, passed in 2004, puts into effect an air quality deal between the Southern Ute Indian Tribe and the State of Colorado. The two governments had signed an Intergovernmental Agreement on air quality control on the Southern Ute Indian Reservation. Congress reviewed that agreement before acting.

The findings say the agreement fits the special legal relationship between the federal government and the tribe. Air quality programs built under it, once the Tribe submits them for approval, can be carried out in a way that matches the Clean Air Act. The act's purpose is to allow putting those programs into practice and enforcing them on the reservation.
plaw-108-337-2004:
Public Law 108-337, the Alaska Native Allotment Subdivision Act, lets Alaska Native owners divide restricted land. Restricted land is Alaska land under federal limits on sale and taxation. Owners of allotments sometimes needed to split land for homes or family use, but the restrictions blocked normal subdivision.

With the Secretary of the Interior's approval, an owner may now subdivide restricted land under state law or local platting rules. The owner may then file a certificate of ownership and dedication with the same effect as if the land were held in plain fee simple title. The act also ratifies earlier subdivisions and dedications that the Secretary and the proper authorities had already approved.
plaw-108-338-2004: Public Law 108-338, passed in 2004, gives a small piece of national forest land in Arkansas to a cemetery group. Within 90 days of the act, the Secretary of Agriculture, through the Forest Service chief, must convey the land to the New Hope Cemetery Association for no payment. The parcel, New Hope Cemetery Tract 6686c, covers about 1.1 acres in Pope County. The association must use the land as a cemetery. If the use changes, the land can revert to the United States.
plaw-108-339-2004: Public Law 108-339, approved October 18, 2004, replaces maps in the Coastal Barrier Resources System. Two maps for the Cape Fear Unit NC-07P are swapped out. The new maps carry the title Coastal Barrier Resources System Cape Fear Unit, NC-07P and the date May 5, 2004. The system limits federal aid on fragile coastal barriers. The Secretary of the Interior must keep the new maps on file and open for public inspection under the Coastal Barrier Resources Act.
plaw-108-340-2004:
Public Law 108-340, the Manhattan Project National Historical Park Study Act, orders a study of the sites that built the first atomic bombs. The Secretary of the Interior, working with the Secretary of Energy, must judge whether some sites deserve a place in the National Park System.

The study area names three places. Los Alamos National Laboratory and its townsite in New Mexico come first. The Hanford Site in Washington and the Oak Ridge Reservation in Tennessee follow. The study weighs national significance, suitability, and feasibility, the three tests for new park units. Each site holds buildings and land tied to the secret wartime project.
plaw-108-341-2004:
Public Law 108-341, passed in 2004, transfers federal land in Missouri between two cabinet departments. Administrative control of certain lands moves from the Secretary of the Interior to the Secretary of Agriculture. The reason is the continued federal running of the Mingo Job Corps Civilian Conservation Center in Stoddard County.

The act states that the transfer does not change the Secretary of Labor's role or authority over the Job Corps center. It defines which Fish and Wildlife Service workers at the center count as eligible employees for the transfer's personnel rules. Two fully funded Washington Office Job Corps support staff are named in that definition. Environmental duties for the land are spelled out in the act's definitions as well.
plaw-108-342-2004:
Public Law 108-342, the El Camino Real de los Tejas National Historic Trail Act, adds a Spanish colonial road to the national trails system. El Camino Real de los Tejas, the Royal Road to the Tejas, runs about 2,580 miles in combined historic routes. It reaches from the Rio Grande near Eagle Pass and Laredo, Texas, to Natchitoches, Louisiana.

The routes include the Old San Antonio Road, used in the Spanish and Mexican eras. A map in a 1998 feasibility study shows the trail's course. The Secretary of the Interior administers the trail, and its map stays on file at Park Service offices for the public. The designation honors a road that tied frontier Texas to the wider Spanish world.
plaw-108-343-2004:
Public Law 108-343, the Tapoco Project Licensing Act of 2004, clears the way to relicense a hydroelectric project in the Smoky Mountains region. The Tapoco Project, federal project number 2169, belongs to Alcoa Power Generating Inc. It includes the Chilhowee Dam and Reservoir in Tennessee.

The act's core is a land exchange tied to a settlement agreement. When Alcoa's company conveys land listed in the act to the government, the Secretary of the Interior must at the same time convey other listed land to the company. The lands appear on a June 2004 map of proposed swap areas between the National Park Service and the company. Great Smoky Mountains National Park borders the project, so the swap shapes both power and park land.
plaw-108-344-2004:
Public Law 108-344, passed in 2004, revises and extends federal support for the Boys and Girls Clubs of America. The clubs run after-school programs for young people. The act amends a section of the Economic Espionage Act of 1996 where club funding had been placed.

The changes raise the program's goals and stretch its dates. Where the law said 1,200 clubs, it now says 1,500, and a 4,000 figure becomes 5,000. An end date moves from December 31, 2005, to December 31, 2010. Funding rises step by step: eighty million dollars for fiscal year 2006, climbing each year to one hundred million dollars for fiscal year 2010.
plaw-108-345-2004: Public Law 108-345, approved October 18, 2004, renames a Colorado reservoir. The Ridges Basin Reservoir on Basin Creek, a tributary of the Animas River, becomes Lake Nighthorse. The reservoir was built under the Colorado Ute Indian Water Rights Settlement Act of 1988. The act's second section is the standard references rule. Any mention of the reservoir in a federal law, map, or record now means Lake Nighthorse.
plaw-108-346-2004:
Public Law 108-346, the Arapaho and Roosevelt National Forests Land Exchange Act of 2004, directs a land swap in Colorado. The exchange starts if the City of Golden offers good title to two parcels within thirty days of the act. One parcel, near Evergreen in Park County, covers about 80 acres at Cub Creek.

The second parcel lies near Argentine Pass in Clear Creek and Summit Counties and covers about 55.9 acres. It appears on a September 2003 map of Argentine Pass and Continental Divide Trail lands. Conditions attach to the Argentine Pass land because of the Vidler tunnel, a water tunnel named in the act. In return, the city receives federal forest land under the exchange terms.
plaw-108-347-2004:
Public Law 108-347, the Belarus Democracy Act of 2004, backs democracy and human rights in Belarus. Congress found the United States supports free government there, matching Belarus's pledges as a member of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe. It also declared a vital interest in Belarus's independence.

The findings accuse President Lukashenka of seizing power unlawfully. In November 1996 he used an illegal referendum to impose a new constitution, abolish the elected parliament, and extend his own term, Congress says. Peaceful protests met beatings and mass arrests. Several opposition figures named in the findings had vanished. The act promotes democracy, human rights, and the rule of law in response.
plaw-108-348-2004: Public Law 108-348, approved October 20, 2004, is a short law with a bright purpose. In honor of breast cancer awareness month, the Secretary of the Interior shall let the Gateway Arch in St. Louis, Missouri, be lit with pink lights. The pink lighting lasts for a period in October that the Secretary picks. The act does nothing else. It simply gives the famous arch a role in the yearly campaign to raise awareness of breast cancer.
plaw-108-349-2004: Public Law 108-349, approved October 21, 2004, changes term rules for a congressional watchdog board. The Congressional Accountability Act of 1995 set up an Office of Compliance to police workplace rules on Capitol Hill. Its Board of Directors had faced a one-term limit. This act rewrites one sentence so a board member may be reappointed, but no one may serve more than two terms. The change applies to people serving on the board on or after September 30, 2004.
plaw-108-350-2004:
Public Law 108-350, passed in 2004, lets the Forest Service sell or swap scattered work sites in two Arkansas national forests. The Secretary of Agriculture may sell or exchange federal land and buildings in the Ozark-St. Francis and Ouachita National Forests, on terms the Secretary sets. Money from the sales goes to gain, build, or improve other administrative sites.

The Ouachita tracts list shows what kind of land this is. One tract holds a work center and two residences on about 12.4 acres near Waldron. Another is a ten-acre work center near Booneville. A half-acre residence near Glenwood and a work center of about ten acres follow. Small, scattered offices like these cost more to keep than they are worth.
plaw-108-351-2004: Public Law 108-351, approved October 21, 2004, amends the Lease Lot Conveyance Act of 2002 about where sale money goes. Amounts the United States receives under that act must be deposited in the federal reclamation fund on behalf of the Rio Grande Project. The money becomes available at once to the irrigation districts, credited under a 1924 law. The reclamation fund dates to the Reclamation Act of June 17, 1902, the law that built federal irrigation works across the West.
plaw-108-352-2004: Public Law 108-352, the National Park System Laws Technical Amendments Act of 2004, makes small corrections across park laws. One section lets the Lackawanna Valley heritage area managers make grants, sign cooperative deals, and hire staff. Another fixes spelling, changing Hawaii Volcanoes to Hawai'i Volcanoes in a 1938 act. A third swaps one word for the Lincoln Memorial plaque law, so managers may expend contributions rather than expand them. More sections adjust the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act and other park programs.
plaw-108-353-2004: Public Law 108-353, approved October 21, 2004, names a post office building in Anchorage, Alaska. The postal facility at 4141 Postmark Drive becomes the Robert J. Opinsky Post Office Building. The street name, Postmark Drive, suits a postal building. The act is in the standard naming form. Its references part deems any mention of the facility in federal laws, maps, or records to be a reference to the Robert J. Opinsky Post Office Building.
plaw-108-354-2004:
Northern New Mexico water projects are the subject of Public Law 108-354, passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. The law covers the town of Chimayo, in Rio Arriba and Santa Fe counties, and the nearby city of Espanola. Both places sit in the Santa Cruz River Valley, on the eastern side of the Espanola Basin.

Title I directs the Secretary of the Interior, working with state and local officials, to study whether a water supply system can be built for Chimayo. The study covers drinking water lines, pump stations, and storage reservoirs, and it considers running the system with the Espanola filtration plant. Title II provides for planning, design, and building a water supply, reclamation, and filtration facility for Espanola.
plaw-108-355-2004:
Youth suicide prevention is the focus of the Garrett Lee Smith Memorial Act, Public Law 108-355 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2004. The law amends the Public Health Service Act. It is named in memory of Garrett Lee Smith and deals with children, teenagers, and college students.

Congress opens with stark findings: more young people die by suicide each year than from cancer, heart disease, AIDS, birth defects, stroke, and chronic lung disease combined. Over 4,000 children and young adults took their lives yearly, and rates among Native Americans ran far above the national average. The law backs statewide early intervention and prevention plans, and it authorizes grants to colleges to reduce student mental and behavioral health problems.
plaw-108-356-2004:
Public Law 108-356, enacted by the 108th Congress in 2004, makes three narrow changes tied to the United States Supreme Court. It extends the authority of the Supreme Court Police, adjusts where cases tied to the Court building and grounds are tried, and allows the Court to accept gifts.

First, the police power to protect Court officials away from the grounds, set to end in 2004, is extended to 2008. Second, prosecutions for offenses tied to the building and grounds may be brought in federal district court or in the Superior Court of the District of Columbia. Third, the Chief Justice or a designee may accept gifts and bequests of personal property about the history of the Court or its justices, while gifts of money go into the Treasury.
plaw-108-357-2004:
Tax law for American business is the subject of the American Jobs Creation Act of 2004, Public Law 108-357 of the 108th Congress. The act amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. Its stated aim is to remove barriers in the tax code and make manufacturing, service, and high-technology firms and workers more competitive at home and abroad.

Title I repeals the exclusion for extraterritorial income and replaces it with a deduction tied to income from domestic production activities. Title II adds business tax incentives, starting with a two-year extension of higher expensing limits for small businesses and new depreciation rules for leasehold property. Later titles carry the plan further through the code, section by section.
plaw-108-358-2004:
Congress tightened federal control of anabolic steroids in the Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 2004, Public Law 108-358 of the 108th Congress. The law amends the Controlled Substances Act. It deals with drugs and hormonal substances related to testosterone, the chemicals athletes and bodybuilders have used to build muscle.

The core change rewrites the legal meaning of an anabolic steroid. The new text names covered substances one by one, starting with forms of androstanediol, androstanedione, and androstenediol, each spelled out with its chemical makeup. Estrogens, progestins, and corticosteroids are left outside it, along with one named substance. The act also calls for research and study work on steroids and steroid precursors.
plaw-108-359-2004:
Church pension plans gain access to collective trust funds under Public Law 108-359, a short 2004 law of the 108th Congress. The measure amends the federal securities laws. It concerns retirement plans run for churches and the pooled funds those plans may now join.

The law makes matching changes in three statutes. It revises the Investment Company Act of 1940 so collective trusts can include church plans alongside government plans. It then amends the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 in the same direction. Interests tied to church plans are treated the same way across the securities laws. Each change is a wording fix, but together they open the pooled funds to church plans.
plaw-108-360-2004:
Two federal hazard programs are carried forward by Public Law 108-360 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2004. The enrolled text is headed as the reauthorization of the National Earthquake Hazards Reduction Program. A second title creates a parallel effort for windstorms, even though the catalog title names only the windstorm act.

Title I continues the earthquake program, with its definitions, funding, and agency roles restated. Title II sets up a National Windstorm Impact Reduction Program and a national advisory committee to guide it. That title also requires a report every two years and coordination among agencies. A short third title authorizes funding for commercial space transportation.
plaw-108-361-2004:
California water supply is at the center of Public Law 108-361, the Water Supply, Reliability, and Environmental Improvement Act, passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. The law authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to run water technology and infrastructure programs meant to increase and diversify the nation's water resources.

Title I, called the Calfed Bay-Delta Authorization Act, covers the Bay Delta program in California. It sets out management, reporting duties, a crosscut budget, the federal share of costs, and compliance with state and federal law. Title II adds smaller items, including a Salton Sea study program, a study of water storage and conservation at Alder Creek, and approval for a temperature control device at Folsom Reservoir.
plaw-108-362-2004:
Diabetes research is the focus of the Pancreatic Islet Cell Transplantation Act of 2004, Public Law 108-362 of the 108th Congress. The law amends the Public Health Service Act. Islet cells are the cells in the pancreas that make insulin, and transplanting them is one line of work against diabetes.

One section helps the supply of research material: pancreata gathered by an organ procurement organization and used for islet cell transplants or research now count toward that organization's federal certification. Another section requires a yearly federal assessment of islet cell work. The report must judge funding, rules affecting the supply of pancreata, and the effect of organ sharing policies and animal-to-human transplant work.
plaw-108-363-2004:
Veterans' disability pay and survivors' benefits rise under the Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2004, Public Law 108-363 of the 108th Congress. The increase takes effect on December 1, 2004. It covers veterans with service-connected disabilities and the survivors of certain disabled veterans who have died.

The law directs the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to raise the dollar amounts paid under title 38. The raise reaches basic disability pay, added amounts for dependents, and the clothing allowance. It also lifts the pay that goes to survivors. Other lines cover new and old survivor rates, extra amounts for spouses with minor children, added amounts for disability, and payments for dependent children.
plaw-108-364-2004:
Help for people with disabilities is the subject of the Assistive Technology Act of 2004, Public Law 108-364 of the 108th Congress. The law rewrites the Assistive Technology Act of 1998. It supports state grant programs that deal with the technology needs of individuals with disabilities, from communication devices to tools for daily living.

Congress begins by noting that over 54 million people in the United States have disabilities, and almost half have severe ones affecting sight, hearing, speech, thinking, or walking. The rewritten act provides state grants for assistive technology and separate grants for protection and advocacy services tied to that technology. It also sets national activities, administrative rules, and funding levels for the program.
plaw-108-365-2004:
Breast cancer screening standards are extended by the Mammography Quality Standards Reauthorization Act of 2004, Public Law 108-365 of the 108th Congress. The law amends the Public Health Service Act. It revises and extends the federal rules that govern the quality of mammography, the X-ray screening used to find breast cancer early.

Much of the act deals with the certificates facilities need to operate. It creates room for a temporary renewal certificate when a facility's regular certificate is being renewed. It also allows a limited provisional certificate, a narrower short-term permit than the standard provisional one. The wording of the certification section is reworked so each certificate type is named and handled clearly in the inspection and approval process.
plaw-108-366-2004:
Federal college aid and other campus programs get a one-year reprieve in the Higher Education Extension Act of 2004, Public Law 108-366 of the 108th Congress. The short law simply extends every program under the Higher Education Act of 1965. Without it, those programs faced expiration while Congress worked on a fuller rewrite.

The extension runs through fiscal year 2005. Anything the Secretary of Education, a state, a college, a guaranty agency, or a lender had to do in fiscal year 2004 must still be done during the extension. Anything they were allowed to do may continue. Funding for each program stays at the greater of the amount authorized for 2004 or the amount actually provided that year.
plaw-108-367-2004:
A Civil War battlefield in Tennessee grows under the Fort Donelson National Battlefield Expansion Act of 2004, Public Law 108-367 of the 108th Congress. Fort Donelson is a unit of the National Park System. It marks the February 1862 battle and the campaign that ended with Union forces taking the fort.

The law revises the battlefield boundary to take in the fort site and associated land. Its purpose is to allow the government to acquire and explain lands tied to the campaign that led to the capture. That campaign was run by General Ulysses S Grant with naval support from Admiral Andrew H Foote. The added ground lets the park tell the story of the whole campaign, not just the fort itself.
plaw-108-368-2004:
Congress honors the leaders of the civil rights movement in Public Law 108-368, enacted in 2004 by the 108th Congress. The law authorizes the President to award a Congressional Gold Medal to Reverend Doctor Martin Luther King Jr, posthumously, and to his widow Coretta Scott King.

The findings call the Kings the first family of the civil rights movement. They recall that Dr King preached nonviolent civil disobedience against segregation and racial injustice. He led the 381-day Montgomery bus boycott, and led the 1963 march on Washington, where he gave the I Have a Dream speech. Congress credits his work with helping pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, and notes his assassination on April 4, 1968, in Memphis. Mrs King is honored for joining the movement in 1955 and raising four children while working beside her husband.
plaw-108-369-2004: Family farmers keep a bankruptcy option under Public Law 108-369, the Family Farmer Bankruptcy Relief Act of 2004, passed by the 108th Congress. Chapter 12 of the bankruptcy code, the part written for family farmers, had been set to lapse. The law extends the period for which chapter 12 is in force by eighteen months, moving the end date to July 1, 2005. The change is treated as having taken effect on January 1, 2004.
plaw-108-370-2004:
Groups that help return abducted children gain legal protection under the Prevention of Child Abduction Partnership Act, Public Law 108-370 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2004. The law amends the International Child Abduction Remedies Act. That act carries out the duties of the United States Central Authority, the office that handles international child abduction cases.

The new section limits tort liability for private groups that work for the Central Authority under a grant, contract, or agreement. Their directors, officers, employees, and agents are shielded for harm tied directly to that work. The shield falls away when a plaintiff proves intentional misconduct, malice, or reckless disregard of a serious risk of injury. It also does not cover acts done for a purpose unrelated to the assigned duties.
plaw-108-371-2004:
Satellite companies left over from the treaty era face new privatization terms in Public Law 108-371, passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. The law modifies and extends requirements in the Communications Satellite Act of 1962. It concerns successor companies to INTELSAT and Inmarsat, the old international satellite organizations.

One deadline moves from June 30, 2004, to June 30, 2005. The law then adds a new path: a successor company can skip an initial public offering and stock listing and still meet the act's goals. To use it, the company must certify that old signatory owners have been greatly diluted and hold no effective control. It must also certify that no intergovernmental organization owns more than a minimal stake in an Inmarsat successor. The communications commission must verify the claims after public notice and comment.
plaw-108-372-2004:
State courts keep a small federal support office under the State Justice Institute Reauthorization Act of 2004, Public Law 108-372 of the 108th Congress. The law reauthorizes the State Justice Institute, the body created by the State Justice Institute Act of 1984 to help state court systems.

Funding is set at seven million dollars for each of fiscal years 2005 through 2008, and the money stays available until spent. Technical changes let the Institute buy goods and services from the General Services Administration and clarify when its executive committee may act for the board. A final section amends a separate crime law provision dealing with law enforcement armor vests.
plaw-108-373-2004:
Poor regions get development help under the Economic Development Administration Reauthorization Act of 2004, Public Law 108-373 of the 108th Congress. The law reauthorizes and improves the programs of the Public Works and Economic Development Act of 1965. Those programs serve both rural and urban areas with weak economies.

Early titles set up economic development partnerships and coordination among agencies. The grant title then funds planning, public works, and economic development projects, with rules on cost sharing and extra grants for places in greatest need. Other grant lines cover training, research, and technical assistance, plus economic adjustment aid for areas hit by sudden losses. The act also guards against unfair competition and allows performance awards for strong planning.
plaw-108-374-2004:
Inherited Indian land is the problem behind the American Indian Probate Reform Act of 2004, Public Law 108-374 of the 108th Congress. The law amends the Indian Land Consolidation Act. It deals with probate, the legal process for passing trust and restricted land to heirs when an owner dies.

Congress traces the trouble to the Indian General Allotment Act of 1887, which barred allotment owners from leaving their land by will. Land instead passed under state inheritance law, so each generation split ownership further among more heirs as tenants in common. Different state rules could apply to one person's parcels in different states, and no single probate code covered trust land. The act improves the probate rules to fight that fractionation.
plaw-108-375-2004:
Military spending and policy for fiscal year 2005 are set by the Ronald W Reagan National Defense Authorization Act, Public Law 108-375 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2004. An authorization act approves programs and funding levels; separate spending bills provide the actual money. The act also fixes how many people each service may have that year.

The law is organized in three divisions. Division A covers Department of Defense authorizations, opening with procurement money for the Army, the Navy and Marine Corps, the Air Force, and defense-wide activities. Division B authorizes military construction. Division C covers Department of Energy national security programs and other authorizations. A long table of contents runs through hundreds of sections on weapons, operations, personnel, and construction projects.
plaw-108-376-2004:
Soldiers voting from overseas are protected by Public Law 108-376, passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. The law concerns elections for American Samoa's Delegate to the United States House of Representatives. American Samoa has held Delegate elections since 1980, in the first week of November in even-numbered years.

Congress found that the local runoff, held only two weeks after the general election, shut out service members and other overseas voters. Mail delays and limited air service made it impossible to send out and return absentee ballots in two weeks. Local law also required in-person registration, which conflicted with the federal absentee voting law for uniformed and overseas citizens. The act answers by requiring only a plurality of votes to elect the Delegate, as the states do for House members.
plaw-108-377-2004:
Children with asthma are the concern of the Asthmatic Schoolchildren's Treatment and Health Management Act of 2004, Public Law 108-377 of the 108th Congress. The law works through a funding preference: states that require schools to let students carry and use their own asthma or severe allergy medicine get favored treatment.

Congress supports the idea with findings about how common asthma had become. About 6.7 million Americans had asthma in 1980, and by 2001 the figure had risen past 20 million, including 6.3 million children. Rates ran 40 percent higher among African-American children than among white children. In 2000 asthma sent 1.8 million people to emergency rooms and caused about 14 million missed school days a year.
plaw-108-378-2004:
Guam's court system is clarified by Public Law 108-378, passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. The law amends the Organic Act of Guam, the federal statute that sets up the territory's government. Its subject is the local judicial structure, meaning which courts exist and what power each one holds.

Judicial authority in Guam is placed in two parts: the District Court of Guam, a court created by Congress, and a unified local judicial branch. The local branch has a Supreme Court of Guam at the top, a Superior Court of Guam as the trial court, and any lower local courts set up under Guam law. The Supreme Court may create divisions of the Superior Court, hears appeals from the lower courts, and supervises the whole local system.
plaw-108-379-2004: Pear growers lose a rule under Public Law 108-379, a very short 2004 law of the 108th Congress. It amends the Agricultural Adjustment Act, as reenacted by the Agricultural Marketing Agreement Act of 1937. Federal marketing orders set shared rules for selling a farm product, and an agency runs each order. For pears, processors no longer have to be members of the agency that administers the order. The law makes the change by striking two short passages, including the words or pears, from one sentence of the statute.
plaw-108-380-2004: One map changes under Public Law 108-380, passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. The law clarifies the boundaries of the Cedar Keys Unit P25 of the John H Chafee Coastal Barrier Resources System in Florida, along with its otherwise protected area P25P. Of the two maps for the unit, the northernmost one is replaced by a map dated February 9, 2004. The Secretary of the Interior must keep the replacement map on file and open for public inspection, as the Coastal Barrier Resources Act requires.
plaw-108-381-2004: A small church land problem in Florida is settled by Public Law 108-381, enacted by the 108th Congress in 2004. The law lets the Secretary of Agriculture give four small parcels of Apalachicola National Forest land to the Mt Trial Primitive Baptist Church of Wakulla County, with no payment required. The parcels, about ten acres, come from a 1983 survey, and the transfer resolves boundary errors. The Secretary sets the exact legal description and may add terms to protect federal interests.
plaw-108-382-2004:
A Utah water project passes out of federal hands under the Provo River Project Transfer Act, Public Law 108-382 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2004. The law authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to convey certain lands and facilities of the Provo River Project. The transfer follows a signed agreement among the United States, the Provo River Water Users Association, and the Metropolitan Water District of Salt Lake and Sandy.

Definitions fill much of the act. The Association is a nonprofit corporation under Utah law, and the District is a local political subdivision. One named parcel, the Pleasant Grove Property, covers 3.79 acres with an office building and shop complex built by the Association. Other defined features include the Provo Reservoir Canal, a key part of the project being handed over.
plaw-108-383-2004:
The nation's record keeper gets housekeeping changes in the National Archives and Records Administration Efficiency Act of 2004, Public Law 108-383 of the 108th Congress. The law amends title 44 of the United States Code. It aims to improve how the National Archives and Records Administration runs, and it reauthorizes the National Historical Publications and Records Commission.

One section eases the process for extending how long agencies must keep records, dropping the need to submit evidence of need and directing the Archivist to issue rules instead. Another lets the records center revolving fund pay for uniforms, or uniform allowances, for records center employees. A further section gives the agency authority to charge fees for public use of its facilities.
plaw-108-384-2004:
An invasive snake is the target of the Brown Tree Snake Control and Eradication Act of 2004, Public Law 108-384 of the 108th Congress. The brown tree snake, known by the scientific name Boiga irregularis, reached the island of Guam and harmed its wildlife. The law provides for controlling and wiping out the snake on Guam and for keeping it from spreading to other parts of the United States.

The opening sections define the terms the program runs on. Introduction means the snake spreading beyond the range where it naturally lives. Duties are split between the Secretary of the Interior and the Secretary of Agriculture, each acting within his own department's area. The law also ties the effort to the freely associated states of the Pacific: Palau, the Marshall Islands, and the Federated States of Micronesia.
plaw-108-385-2004: More land joins a California historic site under the John Muir National Historic Site Boundary Adjustment Act, Public Law 108-385 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2004. The boundary of the site is redrawn to take in the lands shown on an official map dated August 2001. The Secretary of the Interior may acquire the added land by donation, purchase, exchange, or other means. Once acquired, it is managed as part of the historic site, first established by an act of August 31, 1964.
