plaw-108-386-2004: District of Columbia government operations are the subject of the 2004 District of Columbia Omnibus Authorization Act, Public Law 108-386 of the 108th Congress. An omnibus act gathers many separate approvals into one law. Here the stated purpose is to authorize improvements in how the government of the District of Columbia operates. The sample text breaks off at the start of the early sections, so the specific improvements the act authorizes cannot be described from the text provided here.
plaw-108-387-2004:
Fort Clatsop National Memorial gains a new name and a wider reach under Public Law 108-387, passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. Title I is the Lewis and Clark National Historical Park Designation Act. The old memorial becomes the Lewis and Clark National Historical Park, with sites in Washington State as well as Oregon.

Congress says the park preserves the historic, cultural, scenic, and natural resources tied to the arrival of the Lewis and Clark Expedition in the lower Columbia River area. It marks the end of the expedition's crossing of North America and its winter camp of 1805 and 1806. The park boundary follows a map dated December 2003 and includes lands in Clatsop County, Oregon.
plaw-108-388-2004: Sergeant Riayan A Tejeda is honored by Public Law 108-388, a 2004 naming law of the 108th Congress. The United States Postal Service facility at 555 West 180th Street in New York, New York, is designated the Sergeant Riayan A Tejeda Post Office. From then on, any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record counts as a reference to the post office under its new name.
plaw-108-389-2004:
Land for a tribal cultural center drives the Chickasaw National Recreation Area Land Exchange Act of 2004, Public Law 108-389 of the 108th Congress. The recreation area is in Oklahoma, near the city of Sulphur. The law provides for land to be conveyed to the United States and revises the park boundary.

Congress recalls that 640 acres were ceded in 1902 to create Sulphur Springs Reservation, later Platt National Park, to protect water and give public access. In 1976 that park, the Arbuckle Recreation Area, and other lands were combined into the Chickasaw National Recreation Area, in part to honor Chickasaw history and culture. The Chickasaw Nation wants a cultural center on a site inside the boundary, and the park's 1994 management plan backs that site. The chosen land goes to the Nation in exchange for land of equal value, with Sulphur donating land as a partner.
plaw-108-390-2004:
Hiring paperwork goes electronic under Public Law 108-390, passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. The law amends section 274A of the Immigration and Nationality Act, the part that governs how employers verify that a worker is eligible for employment in the United States.

The changes are small but practical. An employer or worker attestation in the verification process may now be signed by hand or with an electronic signature. Records that employers must keep may be held as a paper, microfiche, microfilm, or electronic version of the form. The new rules take effect when final regulations arrive or 180 days after enactment, whichever comes first.
plaw-108-391-2004:
The seven astronauts lost aboard the space shuttle Columbia are remembered in Public Law 108-391, a joint resolution of the 108th Congress passed in 2004. The resolution states the sense of Congress in support of a Columbia Memorial Space Science Learning Center. The crew had devoted their mission to scientific research and to sparking children's interest in space flight and science.

Congress calls a learning center and museum a fitting tribute, since the crew carried out science projects made by American schoolchildren and gave their lives in that cause. The proposed site is the former shuttle factory in Downey, California, where Columbia and Challenger were built. City officials there had been working with NASA on the center. Congress says the Downey center should carry the Columbia Memorial name as a living memorial to the crew.
plaw-108-392-2004: Harvey and Bernice Jones are honored by Public Law 108-392, passed by the 108th Congress in October 2004. The Postal Service facility at 2811 Springdale Avenue in Springdale, Arkansas, takes the name Harvey and Bernice Jones Post Office Building. Under the law's reference rule, later mentions of the Springdale facility in any federal record are treated as mentions of the building under that name.
plaw-108-393-2004: Tribal housing loans get a firm guarantee level in the Homeownership Opportunities for Native Americans Act of 2004, Public Law 108-393 of the 108th Congress. The short law clarifies the loan guarantee authority under title VI of the Native American Housing Assistance and Self-Determination Act of 1996. It adds one rule: a federal guarantee under that title covers repayment of 95 percent of the unpaid principal and interest due on the guaranteed notes or other obligations.
plaw-108-394-2004:
A Missouri Civil War battlefield expands under the Wilson's Creek National Battlefield Boundary Adjustment Act of 2004, Public Law 108-394 of the 108th Congress. Wilson's Creek National Battlefield was established by a law of 1960, Public Law 86-434. The 2004 act amends that law to expand the boundaries of the park.

Six parcels totaling 615 acres join the battlefield, as shown on a map dated January 27, 2004. The Secretary of the Interior may acquire the land by donation, by purchase from willing sellers using donated or provided funds, or by exchange. The same methods may be used for personal property tied to the park and suited to explaining its story to visitors. The act also states protections so the expansion is not read against private property access.
plaw-108-395-2004: General William Carey Lee is honored by Public Law 108-395, a naming law enacted by the 108th Congress in October 2004. The Postal Service facility at 1115 South Clinton Avenue in Dunn, North Carolina, is designated the General William Carey Lee Post Office Building. Any later reference to that Dunn facility in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record is deemed a reference to the building by that name.
plaw-108-396-2004: Five acres join a presidential site under the Truman Farm Home Expansion Act, Public Law 108-396 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2004. The law modifies the boundary of the Harry S Truman National Historic Site in Missouri. The Secretary may acquire the added land by donation, purchase, or transfer from another agency. The parcel, about five acres including a structure south of the Truman Farm Home site, follows a map dated April 17, 2003. Once the land is acquired, the Secretary redraws the site boundary to include it.
plaw-108-397-2004: Anthony I Lombardi is remembered in Public Law 108-397, passed by the 108th Congress in October 2004. The Postal Service facility at 10 West Prospect Street in Nanuet, New York, becomes the Anthony I Lombardi Memorial Post Office Building. The law also carries the standard reference rule: mentions of the Nanuet facility in federal records are treated as mentions of the memorial building.
plaw-108-398-2004: Archie Spigner is honored by Public Law 108-398, enacted by the 108th Congress in October 2004. The Postal Service facility at 19504 Linden Boulevard in St Albans, New York, is designated the Archie Spigner Post Office Building. Under the law, any reference to that facility in a United States law, map, regulation, document, or other record counts as a reference to the Archie Spigner Post Office Building.
plaw-108-399-2004: Estuaries keep federal support under Public Law 108-399, a one-section law passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. It amends the Federal Water Pollution Control Act to reauthorize the National Estuary Program. That program works on the health of the nation's estuaries, where rivers meet the sea. The whole change is a date swap in section 320 of the act: the program's authorization end year moves from 2005 to 2010, keeping it alive for five more years.
plaw-108-400-2004: A Colorado landscape gets a new name in Public Law 108-400, passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. The law amends the Colorado Canyons National Conservation Area and Black Ridge Canyons Wilderness Act of 2000. Throughout that act, in its purpose, definitions, council, and short title, the words Colorado Canyons are struck and McInnis Canyons inserted. The area becomes the McInnis Canyons National Conservation Area. Any reference to the old name in a federal law, map, regulation, or record is read as a reference to the new one.
plaw-108-401-2004:
Federal rulemaking gets an advisory body funded again under the Federal Regulatory Improvement Act of 2004, Public Law 108-401 of the 108th Congress. The law amends title 5 of the United States Code. It authorizes funding for the Administrative Conference of the United States for fiscal years 2005, 2006, and 2007.

The act also rewrites the statement of purposes for the Conference. Agencies, helped by outside experts, are to study shared problems together, share information, and develop recommendations for action. The listed aims include fuller protection of private rights, wider and more effective public participation in rulemaking, and less needless litigation. Better use of science in the regulatory process and stronger laws for that process round out the list.
plaw-108-402-2004: Specialist Eric Ramirez is honored by Public Law 108-402, enacted by the 108th Congress in October 2004. The Postal Service facility at 411 Midway Avenue in Mascotte, Florida, is designated the Specialist Eric Ramirez Post Office. Later references to that facility in any federal law, map, regulation, or record are treated as references to the post office under its new name.
plaw-108-403-2004: Eva Holtzman is honored by Public Law 108-403, a naming law passed by the 108th Congress in October 2004. The Postal Service facility on United States Route 1 in Ridgeway, North Carolina, takes the name Eva Holtzman Post Office. The law adds the usual reference rule, so mentions of the Ridgeway facility in federal records count as mentions of the Eva Holtzman Post Office.
plaw-108-404-2004: Leonard C Burch is honored by Public Law 108-404, passed by the 108th Congress in October 2004. The Postal Service facility at 1001 Williams Street in Ignacio, Colorado, is designated the Leonard C Burch Post Office Building. Any reference to the Ignacio facility in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record is deemed a reference to the building by that name.
plaw-108-405-2004:
Crime victims and DNA evidence are the twin subjects of the Justice for All Act of 2004, Public Law 108-405 of the 108th Congress. The act states several goals. It aims to protect the rights of crime victims and clear the large backlog of DNA samples from crime scenes and convicted offenders. It also builds up the DNA testing capacity of federal, state, and local crime laboratories.

Title I is a crime victims' rights act named for five victims: Scott Campbell, Stephanie Roper, Wendy Preston, Louarna Gillis, and Nila Lynn. It lists victims' rights and adds resources to enforce them. Title II, the Debbie Smith Act of 2004, funds grants to cut the DNA backlog and expands the combined DNA index system. The act also backs new testing technology, training on DNA evidence, testing after conviction to free the innocent, and better lawyering in state death penalty cases.
plaw-108-406-2004:
Athletes with intellectual disabilities are served by the Special Olympics Sport and Empowerment Act of 2004, Public Law 108-406 of the 108th Congress. The law provides help to Special Olympics so it can grow. It supports expansion of the games, new education programs, and a Healthy Athletes Program.

Congress opens by honoring what Special Olympics stands for: a world where everybody matters and every person has worth. The findings say the nation is determined to end the isolation and stigma faced by people with intellectual disabilities. For more than 36 years, the findings note, Special Olympics had offered year-round training and competition in 26 sports to about one and a half million athletes. It planned to reach hundreds of thousands more within five years, at home and worldwide.
plaw-108-407-2004: Martha Pennino is honored by Public Law 108-407, a naming law of the 108th Congress enacted in October 2004. The Postal Service facility at 11110 Sunset Hills Road in Reston, Virginia, becomes the Martha Pennino Post Office Building. References to the Reston facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, and records are read as references to the building under that name.
plaw-108-408-2004: Evan Asa Ashcraft is remembered in Public Law 108-408, passed by the 108th Congress in October 2004. The Postal Service facility at 23055 Sherman Way in West Hills, California, is designated the Evan Asa Ashcraft Post Office Building. Under the law, any mention of that facility in a United States law, map, regulation, or other record counts as a mention of the Evan Asa Ashcraft Post Office Building.
plaw-108-409-2004:
Student loan costs and teacher rewards meet in the Taxpayer-Teacher Protection Act of 2004, Public Law 108-409 of the 108th Congress. The act has two stated aims: cut certain special allowance payments on federal student loans, and give teachers more loan forgiveness on their own federal student loans.

The detailed section in the text deals with the special allowance, a federal payment that tops up what loan holders earn. It targets loans made or bought with money from tax-exempt issues first sold before October 1, 1993, and with earnings on such funds. For those loans, renewed or refunded between September 30, 2004, and January 1, 2006, the quarterly allowance rate is reset under a new clause instead of the older, richer formula.
plaw-108-410-2004:
Washington's great concert hall is funded again by the John F Kennedy Center Reauthorization Act of 2004, Public Law 108-410 of the 108th Congress. The law amends the John F Kennedy Center Act, which governs the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. It authorizes money for the center and deals with the center's plaza project.

Two funding lines are set for the center's board. For upkeep, repair, and security, the act authorizes seventeen million dollars for fiscal year 2004 and eighteen million for each of 2005, 2006, and 2007. For capital projects, it authorizes sixteen million dollars for 2004 and eighteen million for each of the next three years. A later section has the Secretary set up a project team to push construction of the Kennedy Center Plaza forward.
plaw-108-411-2004:
Federal workers are the subject of the Federal Workforce Flexibility Act of 2004, Public Law 108-411 of the 108th Congress. The law reforms rules on federal employment across title 5 of the United States Code. Its three titles cover hiring management, career growth and benefits, and pay administration.

Title I reworks recruitment, relocation, and retention bonuses and streamlines the critical pay authority used for hard-to-fill jobs. Title II covers agency training, improvements to annual leave, and compensatory time off for travel. Title III makes corrections tied to pay administration, including technical fixes. The bonus section opens the act by replacing the older bonus sections of chapter 57 with new text.
plaw-108-412-2004:
Harmful weeds on public and private land are the target of Public Law 108-412, passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. The law orders the Secretary of Agriculture to set up a program of help for groups that fight noxious weeds. It works by adding a new subtitle to the Plant Protection Act, cited as the Noxious Weed Control and Eradication Act of 2004.

Help goes to weed management entities. Such a group must be recognized by its state and must show real skill and experience in controlling or wiping out noxious weeds and in teaching the public why the work matters. A group may cross local boundaries and fields of work, and it may include federal, state, local, and tribal governments along with private groups and individuals.
plaw-108-413-2004:
Ancient Southwest artifacts get a home under the Hibben Center Act, Public Law 108-413 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2004. The law authorizes the Secretary of the Interior, working with the University of New Mexico, to build and use part of the Hibben Center for Archaeological Research at the university.

The Secretary may lease space in the center for research on, and care of, the National Park Service collections tied to Chaco Culture National Historical Park and Aztec Ruins National Monument. The lease may run up to forty years at a nominal yearly payment. Once it is signed, the Secretary may grant the university up to 37 percent of the building cost. That grant is capped at one million seven hundred fifty thousand dollars. The Secretary may also add improvement costs of up to about two and a half million dollars. Cooperative deals may follow for care and study of Chacoan artifacts.
plaw-108-414-2004:
People with mental illness inside the justice system are the concern of the Mentally Ill Offender Treatment and Crime Reduction Act of 2004, Public Law 108-414 of the 108th Congress. The law aims to foster local teamwork so resources are used well within the criminal and juvenile justice systems.

Congress backs the act with hard numbers. Over 16 percent of adults in American jails and prisons have a mental illness, and about 20 percent of youth in the juvenile system have serious mental health problems. Up to 40 percent of adults with a serious mental illness will meet the criminal justice system at some point. Many adults in that group are homeless or near it and are jailed for minor, nonviolent offenses. The findings also note that most respond well to treatment joined with rehabilitation and support.
plaw-108-415-2004: The national debt ceiling rises under Public Law 108-415, a one-section law passed by the 108th Congress in November 2004. It amends title 31 of the United States Code, the part that caps how much the federal government may borrow. The limit on the public debt moves from about seven point four trillion dollars to about eight point two trillion dollars. That single number swap is the entire law.
plaw-108-416-2004: Government funding is extended again by Public Law 108-416, a joint resolution of the 108th Congress approved on November 21, 2004. It makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2005, keeping agencies funded while final spending bills are finished. The measure works on an earlier stopgap law, Public Law 108-309, and changes only its end date. The date in section 107(c) is struck, and December 3, 2004 is inserted in its place.
plaw-108-417-2004: A Georgia monument swaps land with a church under Public Law 108-417, passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. The Secretary of the Interior may convey about six acres inside Fort Frederica National Monument, next to Christ Church of St Simons Island, Georgia, to the church. In exchange, the church provides about eight point seven acres, shown as private lands for addition on the same 2003 boundary map. When the swap is complete, the Secretary redraws the monument boundary and manages the new land as part of the monument.
plaw-108-418-2004: A California water cleanup test gets more federal money under Public Law 108-418, passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. The law amends the Reclamation Projects Authorization and Adjustment Act of 1992. It raises the federal share of the costs of the San Gabriel Basin demonstration project. Under the new wording, the federal share may reach the regular amount for such projects plus an added six million five hundred thousand dollars.
plaw-108-419-2004:
Copyright royalty disputes get new judges under the Copyright Royalty and Distribution Reform Act of 2004, Public Law 108-419 of the 108th Congress. The law amends title 17, the copyright title of the United States Code. It replaces the copyright arbitration royalty panels, which had decided royalty fights case by case, with standing Copyright Royalty Judges.

Chapter 8 of the copyright law is rewritten around the new judges. The Librarian of Congress appoints three full-time Copyright Royalty Judges, naming one as Chief, after consulting the Register of Copyrights. Their job is to set and adjust reasonable royalty rates and terms and to handle how royalty money is divided. The rewritten chapter also covers their staff, how cases are started and heard, and the rule that voluntary agreements come first.
plaw-108-420-2004:
California's old Spanish missions get repair help from the California Missions Preservation Act, Public Law 108-420 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2004. The law backs the work of the California Missions Foundation. Its aim is to restore and repair the Spanish colonial and mission-era missions of California and to preserve their artworks and artifacts.

The act counts twenty-one historic Spanish missions and one asistencia, all California Registered Historic Landmarks built between 1769 and 1798. The Foundation is a nonsectarian charity set up in 1998 to fund mission restoration and run only for charitable purposes. The law lets the Secretary of the Interior enter cooperative agreements in support of that restoration work.
plaw-108-421-2004:
Four states share a highland region protected by the Highlands Conservation Act, Public Law 108-421 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2004. The states are Connecticut, New Jersey, New York, and Pennsylvania. The law helps them conserve priority lands and natural resources in the Highlands region, shown on a Forest Service map dated June 2004.

Congress states three purposes. First, to recognize the value of the region's water, forest, farm, wildlife, recreation, and cultural resources, and their national significance. Second, to let the Secretary of the Interior, working with the Secretary of Agriculture, give the Highlands states money to preserve high priority conservation land. Third, to continue Forest Service programs that help the states, local governments, and private forest and farm owners protect land and resources.
plaw-108-422-2004:
Veterans' health care is improved by the Veterans Health Programs Improvement Act of 2004, Public Law 108-422 of the 108th Congress. The law amends title 38, the veterans title of the United States Code. It raises the funding authorization for grants to help homeless veterans and improves how veterans' facilities and health programs are run.

Title I covers help for homeless veterans. Title II deals with long-term care. It covers help in hiring and keeping nurses at state veterans' homes, and how federal per diem payments to state homes are treated. It also extends authority for long-term care pilot programs, and bans collecting copayments for hospice care. Title III turns to medical care, with a sexual trauma counseling program, research and care centers for complex combat injuries, and better medical readiness in the Department of Veterans Affairs.
plaw-108-423-2004:
Supercomputing research is ordered up by the Department of Energy High-End Computing Revitalization Act of 2004, Public Law 108-423 of the 108th Congress. The law requires the Secretary of Energy to run a research and development program to advance high-end computing, acting through the Director of the Office of Science.

The act defines its terms with care. A high-end computing system far outperforms machines commonly available for advanced science and engineering work. A leadership system is a high-end machine among the most advanced in the world at solving such problems. The program covers both software and hardware development, and the act provides for High-End Software Development Centers at the heart of the effort.
plaw-108-424-2004:
Nevada land is rearranged by the Lincoln County Conservation, Recreation, and Development Act of 2004, Public Law 108-424 of the 108th Congress. The law deals with one county, Lincoln County. Its stated aims are to establish wilderness areas, promote conservation, improve public land, and provide for high quality development in the county.

Title I covers land disposal: the conveyance of Lincoln County land and how the proceeds are handled. Title II adds areas to the National Wilderness Preservation System and sets rules for running them. Its sections address how nearby land is managed, military overflights, Native American cultural and religious uses, and wildlife. Study areas not chosen for wilderness are released, and the act authorizes whatever funding is needed to carry it out.
plaw-108-425-2004:
Sewage flowing toward California beaches is the problem behind Public Law 108-425, passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. The law amends the Tijuana River Valley Estuary and Beach Sewage Cleanup Act of 2000 and extends its funding authorization. The cleanup work sits on the border with Mexico and follows Treaty Minute 311 to the 1944 water treaty between the two countries.

The amendments reshape how secondary sewage treatment is arranged. The boundary commission may sign a multiyear fee-for-service contract with the owner of a Mexican treatment facility, setting aside normal federal procurement law to do it. The contract terms protect the United States: neither the commission nor the federal government owes cancellation fees if the deal is ended. The facility owner may buy insurance for the work, and those costs may be spread across the contract term.
plaw-108-426-2004:
Congress reshaped transportation research in the Norman Y Mineta Research and Special Programs Improvement Act, Public Law 108-426 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2004. The law amends title 49, the transportation title. Its aim is to give the Department of Transportation a more focused research organization, with stress on new technology.

Section 2 creates the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration inside the department. The new administration must treat safety as its top goal in pipeline and hazardous materials transport. Its head is named by the President with the consent of the Senate. The head must have real experience in pipeline safety, hazardous materials safety, or other transport safety, and must report directly to the Secretary. A deputy, named by the Secretary, is also provided for.
plaw-108-427-2004:
Congress asks for two health research reports in the Research Review Act of 2004, Public Law 108-427 of the 108th Congress. The law aims to expand research information about projects that cross scientific fields and about epidemiological studies, the studies that track disease patterns in populations.

The first report, due February 1, 2005, goes to two named committees of Congress. The Secretary of Health and Human Services must explain, working with the head of the National Institutes of Health, how the Roadmap for Medical Research advanced team-based research across fields. The report also covers joint work among institutions, including work on spinal cord injury and paralysis. The second report, due May 1, 2005, comes through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It lists disease studies under way and planned, the rules for choosing which to run, delay, or drop, and work with patient groups, including a study of inflammatory bowel disease.
plaw-108-428-2004:
Rocket companies keep a federal safety net under Public Law 108-428, passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. The law extends the liability indemnification regime for the commercial space transportation industry. That regime, in section 70113 of title 49, shares the risk of launch accidents between companies and the government. Its end date moves from December 31, 2004, to December 31, 2009.

The act also orders a fresh look at the system. Within sixty days, the Secretary of Transportation must hire a nonprofit group to study the risk sharing regime on its own. The study must weigh ways to end the current system, and estimate how long each path would take. It must also ask whether other steps would be needed to keep an American launch industry viable and competitive against foreign providers.
plaw-108-429-2004:
Import duties on industrial chemicals fill the Miscellaneous Trade and Technical Corrections Act of 2004, Public Law 108-429 of the 108th Congress. The law amends the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States. It changes some duty rates for a limited time and makes technical fixes to the trade laws.

Title I holds the tariff provisions. Its first subtitle lists new duty suspensions and reductions, one chemical at a time. Early entries include bitolylene diisocyanate, 2-methylimidazole, hydroxylamine free base, prenol, and formamide. Dyes and related products follow, such as disperse blue 27, acid black 244, reactive orange 132, and vat red 13. Each named substance gets its own section, so importers can find the exact rate change for the product they ship.
plaw-108-430-2004: An Arizona park grows by a wide margin under the Petrified Forest National Park Expansion Act of 2004, Public Law 108-430 of the 108th Congress. The law revises the boundary of Petrified Forest National Park. The Secretary of the Interior may redraw the line to include about 125,000 added acres, as shown on a map titled Proposed Boundary Adjustments, Petrified Forest National Park, dated July 2004. The map is kept on file for public inspection in the proper offices.
plaw-108-431-2004:
Tribal self-rule is affirmed for the Osage Tribe in Public Law 108-431, passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. The law reaffirms the inherent sovereign rights of the tribe to decide its own membership and form of government. The Osage Tribe is a federally recognized tribe based in Pawhuska, Oklahoma.

Congress explains the problem it is fixing. The Osage Allotment Act of 1906 tied legal membership to the January 1, 1906 roll and to shares, called headrights, in the tribe's mineral estate. As a result, only Osage Indians holding a headright share counted as members, and adults without one could not vote in tribal elections or run for office under federal law. The act clarifies that the 1906 term legal membership covers allotment and mineral share rights only, not tribal membership for all purposes. The tribe may set its own membership, as long as no one's mineral shares are reduced.
plaw-108-432-2004:
A great winter battle is remembered in Public Law 108-432, a joint resolution of the 108th Congress passed in 2004. The resolution recognizes the sixtieth anniversary of the Battle of the Bulge, fought in Europe during World War II from December 16, 1944, to January 25, 1945.

The resolution recounts the German offensive through the Ardennes forest of Belgium and Luxembourg, meant to split the Allied armies, cut their fuel lines, and reach Antwerp. About 600,000 American troops fought, joined by 55,000 British, Belgian, Canadian, and other soldiers. The battle cost 81,000 American casualties, including about 19,000 killed. Congress recalls the Malmedy Massacre, where 86 unarmed American prisoners were gunned down, and the stand of the 101st Airborne at Bastogne. Victory in the Bulge, the resolution says, made the defeat of Nazi Germany possible four months later.
plaw-108-433-2004: A start date for Congress is set by Public Law 108-433, a joint resolution of the 108th Congress approved on December 3, 2004. The measure does a single thing: it appoints the day for the convening of the first session of the One Hundred Ninth Congress. That session is set to begin at noon on Tuesday, January 4, 2005.
plaw-108-434-2004: Stopgap funding is extended once more by Public Law 108-434, a joint resolution approved by the 108th Congress on December 3, 2004. It makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2005, keeping federal agencies running while final spending bills are completed. Like the earlier stopgap measures, it works by amending Public Law 108-309 and swapping one date: the cutoff in section 107(c) becomes December 8, 2004.
plaw-108-435-2004:
Internet taxes stay barred under the Internet Tax Nondiscrimination Act, Public Law 108-435 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2004. The act deals with the moratorium first set by the Internet Tax Freedom Act. Although its opening line speaks of making the ban permanent, the operative section grants a four-year extension.

From November 1, 2003, to November 1, 2007, no state or local government may tax Internet access. Multiple or discriminatory taxes on electronic commerce are barred for the same period. The act also sharpens the definition of a tax on Internet access: the ban covers such a tax whether it falls on the provider or the buyer, whatever it is called. Taxes measured by net income, capital stock, net worth, or property value are left outside the ban.
plaw-108-436-2004:
Forest land in Idaho may be sold or traded under the Idaho Panhandle National Forest Improvement Act of 2004, Public Law 108-436 of the 108th Congress. The Secretary of Agriculture may sell or exchange National Forest System parcels in the state. Money from any sale or trade goes to National Forest System purposes.

Named parcels include the Granite and Reeder Bay parcel at Priest Lake, about eighty acres, and the North South Ski area, about fifty acres. The Shoshone work camp, about nineteen acres with utility easements, is also listed. The Secretary may correct errors in the parcel descriptions or make small adjustments to help the transfers go through. The act also sets the terms for what the government must receive in return.
plaw-108-437-2004:
A flooded hospital is at last answered in the Three Affiliated Tribes Health Facility Compensation Act, Public Law 108-437 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2004. The law authorizes construction of a rural health care facility on the Fort Berthold Indian Reservation in North Dakota. It carries out the advice of the Garrison Unit Joint Tribal Advisory Committee.

Congress finds that in 1949 the United States took more than 150,000 prime acres of the reservation for the Garrison Dam and Reservoir. The reservoir flooded and destroyed key works on the reservation, including an Indian Health Service hospital. The United States promised the Three Affiliated Tribes it would replace what was lost. A joint tribal advisory committee studied the harm and reported in 1986 that the government owed the replacement, and a Senate committee urged that funding be provided.
plaw-108-438-2004:
A labor leader's home becomes a historic site under the Kate Mullany National Historic Site Act, Public Law 108-438 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2004. The law establishes the Kate Mullany National Historic Site in New York State. The site consists of the home of Kate Mullany at 350 Eighth Street in Troy.

The site is an affiliated area of the National Park System rather than a park run directly by the Park Service. The American Labor Studies Center owns, administers, and operates it. At the same time, the site is governed by the general laws for National Park System units, including the National Park Service Organic Act of 1916. Definitions in the act name the Center, the historic site, and the Secretary of the Interior as the key parties.
plaw-108-439-2004:
Dam safety work gets a large funding boost from Public Law 108-439, passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. The law authorizes added funding for the Reclamation Safety of Dams Act of 1978. That act governs repairs and changes to dams run by the Bureau of Reclamation.

Effective October 1, 2003, Congress authorizes up to five hundred forty million dollars more for the program, at 2003 price levels. A separate small-project cap rises from seven hundred fifty thousand dollars to one million two hundred fifty thousand dollars, adjusted for construction cost changes. The law also gives project beneficiaries, the users who benefit from a dam, a larger voice. The Secretary must consider their cost-saving ideas during repair work. The Secretary must also keep them informed about costs and progress.
plaw-108-440-2004: Mike Mansfield is honored by Public Law 108-440, enacted by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The Postal Service facility at 3150 Great Northern Avenue in Missoula, Montana, is designated the Mike Mansfield Post Office. Any reference to that facility in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record is deemed a reference to the Mike Mansfield Post Office.
plaw-108-441-2004:
Doctor shortages in underserved areas are eased by Public Law 108-441, passed by the 108th Congress in 2004. The law improves access to physicians by changing visa rules for international medical graduates, meaning doctors trained abroad who come to practice in the United States.

One change pushes a deadline in the immigration laws from 2004 to 2006, effective as if enacted on May 31, 2004. Another frees certain doctors from the H-1B visa cap. The numerical limits do not apply to a doctor whose two-year home residence requirement was waived at the request of a federal or state agency. The practice agreement wording is widened from practice medicine to primary care or specialty medicine. Special exemptions follow for doctors requested by the Department of Veterans Affairs and by state agencies serving patients in shortage areas.
plaw-108-442-2004: Fallen Nevada service members are honored by Public Law 108-442, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The Postal Service facility at 1050 North Hills Boulevard in Reno, Nevada, is designated the Guardians of Freedom Memorial Post Office Building. The law also lets the Postmaster General agree with Nevada's Office of Veterans' Services to install a plaque at the building. The plaque honors Nevada service members who lost their lives in the Global War on Terrorism and Operation Iraqi Freedom, with their names, ranks, and branches of service.
plaw-108-443-2004: Lieutenant John F Finn is honored by Public Law 108-443, enacted by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The Postal Service facility at 1475 Western Avenue, Suite 45, in Albany, New York, is designated the Lieutenant John F Finn Post Office. The law follows the standard form for such namings, with a designation section and a references section for later federal records.
plaw-108-444-2004: Livestock price reporting gets more time under Public Law 108-444, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The law amends the Livestock Mandatory Price Reporting Act of 1999, the act that requires packers to report the prices they pay for livestock. Its single section is headed Extension. The program's end language is struck and replaced with a firm date: mandatory price reporting terminates on September 30, 2005.
plaw-108-445-2004:
Pay for VA doctors, dentists, and nurses is reworked by the Department of Veterans Affairs Health Care Personnel Enhancement Act of 2004, Public Law 108-445 of the 108th Congress. The law amends title 38. It aims to simplify and improve pay rules for physicians and dentists and to allow alternate work schedules and executive pay for nurses.

Grades come first. The old Physician and Dentist Schedule items are replaced with two plain entries, Physician grade and Dentist grade, and a paragraph of grade rules is struck. Pay for doctors and dentists in jobs covered by an Executive order is moved under the pay subchapter of the veterans law instead. The act then rewrites that pay subchapter in full to set the new authorities.
plaw-108-446-2004:
Special education law is renewed by the Individuals with Disabilities Education Improvement Act of 2004, Public Law 108-446 of the 108th Congress. The law reauthorizes the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, the federal law that governs schooling for children with disabilities.

Title I rewrites parts A through D of the older act outright. The new Part A opens with findings and purposes, then definitions, and keeps the Office of Special Education Programs in place. Title II creates a National Center for Special Education Research. Title III gathers miscellaneous provisions. Because the whole text of the education act is replaced section by section, the law runs long and sets the framework schools and states work under.
plaw-108-447-2004:
Most of the federal government is funded in one package by the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2005, Public Law 108-447 of the 108th Congress, enacted in December 2004. An appropriations act provides actual spending money, and a consolidated act joins many yearly spending bills into one law. Its stated subject is funding for foreign operations, export financing, and related programs for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2005, and other purposes.

The act is built as a set of divisions, each a full spending bill. Division A funds agriculture, rural development, the Food and Drug Administration, and related agencies, with titles for farm programs, conservation, rural development, and food programs. Division B funds the Departments of Commerce, Justice, and State, the judiciary, and related agencies. Later divisions carry the same pattern across the rest of the government.
plaw-108-448-2004:
Help with Medicare premiums continues under Public Law 108-448, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The law amends title XIX of the Social Security Act, the Medicaid title. It extends Medicare cost-sharing for the Medicare Part B premium for qualifying individuals through September 2005.

States choose the qualifying individuals and give the help under rules modeled on the 2003 program. Congress fixes the total money for each period. Three hundred million dollars is set for January through September 2004. One hundred million follows for October through December 2004. A further three hundred million covers January through September 2005. Special rules apply to periods that begin after January 1, so the state selections stay within the set amounts.
plaw-108-449-2004:
A program tied to the Northern Ireland peace process is extended by Public Law 108-449, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The law amends the Irish Peace Process Cultural and Training Program Act of 1998. That program brings participants from Ireland and the United Kingdom to the United States for cultural exchange and job training.

New participant rules are spelled out. A participant must be a citizen of the United Kingdom or the Republic of Ireland, between twenty-one and thirty-five years old at departure. He or she must have lived in a designated county for at least eighteen months and been out of work for at least twelve months. Participants may not hold a degree from a college or university. The act also sets an end to the scheme: both the 1998 act and its visa category are repealed effective October 1, 2008.
plaw-108-450-2004:
Mental health commitment cases in the capital get a rebuilt panel under the District of Columbia Mental Health Civil Commitment Modernization Act of 2004, Public Law 108-450 of the 108th Congress. The law amends title 21 of the District of Columbia Official Code. It puts into effect parts of the District's own Mental Health Civil Commitment Act of 2002 that needed action by Congress, dealing with the Commission on Mental Health.

The Commission continues with nine members plus an alternate chairperson, all appointed by the Chief Judge of the Superior Court of the District of Columbia. One member is a magistrate judge of the court, a lawyer with at least five years of practice in the District, who chairs the panel and runs its hearings. The other eight members are psychiatrists or qualified psychologists, each with at least five years of work diagnosing and treating mental illness.
plaw-108-451-2004:
Water fights in Arizona are settled by the Arizona Water Settlements Act, Public Law 108-451 of the 108th Congress, enacted in December 2004. The act adjusts the Central Arizona Project, the great canal system that moves Colorado River water into the state. It also authorizes the Gila River Indian Community water rights settlement and renews and amends the Southern Arizona Water Rights Settlement Act of 1982.

Title I is the Central Arizona Project settlement. Its sections govern allowed uses of project water, how that water is allocated, and how firm the supply for Indian users must be. It also covers buying back farm priority water and the Lower Colorado River Basin Development Fund. Title II holds the Gila River Indian Community settlement itself. A link ties the parts together: Title I is repealed if Title II's terms fail to take effect by the set date.
plaw-108-452-2004:
Alaska land transfers are sped up by the Alaska Land Transfer Acceleration Act, Public Law 108-452 of the 108th Congress, enacted in December 2004. The law aims to facilitate the moving of land in Alaska out of federal hands. Huge transfers owed to the state, to Native groups, and to the University of Alaska had dragged on for decades.

Title I covers state selections and conveyances. It deals with community grant selections, the order in which land is handed over, and the settlement of what is still owed, including an entitlement for the University of Alaska. Sections also cover hydroelectric withdrawals, federal mining claims, and land mistakenly given up or left out. Title II works on the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, with rules on combined entitlements, conveyance by whole sections, cemetery sites and historical places, and allocations based on population.
plaw-108-453-2004:
Joint invention work is encouraged by the Cooperative Research and Technology Enhancement Act of 2004, known as the CREATE Act, Public Law 108-453 of the 108th Congress. The law amends title 35, the patent title. It promotes cooperative research among universities, the public sector, and private companies.

The change rewrites section 103(c) of the patent law. Work by one research partner may count as prior art only under certain parts of section 102. Even then, it cannot be used to block a patent. That bar holds when the work and the claimed invention were owned by the same person, or owed to the same person, when the invention was made. Team members count as one owner when they worked under a written joint research agreement. The invention must have grown out of that agreement, and the patent application must name the parties to the deal.
plaw-108-454-2004: Veterans' housing, education, and other benefits are improved and extended by the Veterans Benefits Improvement Act of 2004, Public Law 108-454 of the 108th Congress, enacted in December 2004. The law amends title 38 of the United States Code, the title that gathers the laws run by the Secretary of Veterans Affairs. The sample text provided here shows the title page, short title, and the start of the table of contents only. The act's individual benefit changes cannot be listed from the text at hand.
plaw-108-455-2004: Federal court sitting places are adjusted by Public Law 108-455, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The headlined change extends the power of the United States District Court for the Southern District of Iowa to hold court in Rock Island, Illinois. The end date moves from July 1, 2005, to July 1, 2006. Companion sections add Cleveland in Mississippi, Plattsburgh in New York, and Colorado Springs in Colorado as sitting places. They also let court sit anywhere in the Texarkana courthouse, which straddles the Texas and Arkansas line.
plaw-108-456-2004:
Toxic algae and low-oxygen water get renewed attention under Public Law 108-456, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. Title I, the Harmful Algal Bloom and Hypoxia Amendments Act of 2004, reauthorizes the Harmful Algal Bloom and Hypoxia Research and Control Act of 1998. Harmful algal blooms are overgrowths of algae that can poison water, and hypoxia means water with too little oxygen for sea life.

The interagency task force on the problem is kept in place. When it prepares assessments, reports, and plans, it must consult coastal states, Indian tribes, local governments, and affected industries such as fisheries, farming, and fertilizer makers. Universities and outside groups with coastal science skill are also named. Within twelve months, the President must send Congress a report judging how well the available measures protect the environment and public health from bloom damage.
plaw-108-457-2004: College tuition help for Washington students is renewed by Public Law 108-457, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The law amends the District of Columbia College Access Act of 1999. That act set up two tuition assistance programs, for public and private schools, to help District students pay for college. The wording stretches each program's run. Where the old text said each of the five succeeding fiscal years, the new text says each of the seven succeeding fiscal years. That adds two years to both programs.
plaw-108-458-2004:
American intelligence is rebuilt by the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004, Public Law 108-458 of the 108th Congress. The law reforms the intelligence community and the intelligence work of the United States Government. Title I alone is called Reform of the Intelligence Community.

Subtitle A of Title I establishes a Director of National Intelligence to manage the whole community. Its sections cover reorganization, a revised definition of national intelligence, and joint procedures for the Department of Defense and the Central Intelligence Agency to work together in the field. The new director gains a voice in appointing senior intelligence officials. Other sections deal with sharing information, testing rival readings of the same facts, and guarding the honesty and objectivity of analysis. Subtitle B turns to the National Counterterrorism Center.
plaw-108-459-2004: Henry Johnson is honored by Public Law 108-459, a redesignation law of the 108th Congress enacted in December 2004. The Postal Service facility at 747 Broadway in Albany, New York, until then called the United States Postal Service Carrier Annex, is renamed the United States Postal Service Henry Johnson Annex. References to the Albany facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, and records are read as references to the annex under its new name.
plaw-108-460-2004: A research station changes hands under Public Law 108-460, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The Secretary of Agriculture must give the State of North Carolina, at no charge, all federal right, title, and interest in about 4.28 acres at the Oxford Research Station in Granville County, North Carolina. The transfer covers the land plus all improvements, equipment, and resource materials at the station. A survey, paid for by the state, fixes the exact acreage and legal description, and the Secretary may add terms to protect federal interests.
plaw-108-461-2004: Tomochichi is honored by Public Law 108-461, a naming law enacted by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The United States courthouse at 125 Bull Street in Savannah, Georgia, is designated the Tomochichi United States Courthouse. Any reference to that courthouse in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record is deemed a reference to the Tomochichi United States Courthouse.
plaw-108-462-2004: F.H. Newell is honored by Public Law 108-462, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The shared facility of the United States Geological Survey and the United States Bureau of Reclamation at 230 Collins Road in Boise, Idaho, is designated the F.H. Newell Building. References to the Boise facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, and records are treated as references to the F.H. Newell Building.
plaw-108-463-2004: James V Hansen is honored by Public Law 108-463, enacted by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The federal building at 324 Twenty-Fifth Street in Ogden, Utah, is designated the James V Hansen Federal Building. Under the law's reference rule, mentions of that Ogden building in any United States law, map, regulation, or record count as mentions of the James V Hansen Federal Building.
plaw-108-464-2004:
Benjamin Franklin's three hundredth birthday is marked with coins under the Benjamin Franklin Commemorative Coin Act, Public Law 108-464 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2004. The law requires the Secretary of the Treasury to mint coins for the tercentenary, the three hundredth anniversary, of Franklin's birth.

Congress lists why Franklin fits a coin. He helped build the nation in government, business, science, communications, and the arts, and he was the only Founding Father to sign all of the nation's founding documents. As a printer he produced paper money for Pennsylvania, Delaware, New Jersey, and Maryland, wrote on paper currency in 1741, and designed the first American coin during the Revolution. His portrait later appeared on the half dollar from 1948 to 1963.
plaw-108-465-2004:
Fruit and vegetable growers get federal backing from the Specialty Crops Competitiveness Act of 2004, Public Law 108-465 of the 108th Congress. The law aims to keep an abundant, affordable supply of nutritious fruits, vegetables, and other specialty crops for American buyers and foreign markets. It does so by strengthening the position of United States growers.

Congress calls a secure home food supply a matter of national security. It finds that a strong specialty crop industry is needed for health, and that eating more of these crops would bring large health and money gains to buyers and growers alike. Growers, Congress notes, see many places where federal farm policy could help them. The findings also stress hard foreign competition: overseas producers often receive heavy government support, and American growers face steep tariffs and other trade barriers abroad.
plaw-108-466-2004: Joe Skeen is honored by Public Law 108-466, a naming law passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The federal building at Fifth and Richardson Avenues in Roswell, New Mexico, is designated the Joe Skeen Federal Building. Any reference to that building in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record is deemed a reference to the Joe Skeen Federal Building.
plaw-108-467-2004: Hipolito F Garcia is honored by Public Law 108-467, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The federal building and United States courthouse at 615 East Houston Street in San Antonio, Texas, is designated the Hipolito F Garcia Federal Building and United States Courthouse. References to that building in federal laws, maps, regulations, and records are deemed references to the building under its full new name.
plaw-108-468-2004: Jack Fields is honored by Public Law 108-468, a redesignation law of the 108th Congress enacted in December 2004. The Postal Service facility at 4025 Feather Lakes Way in Kingwood, Texas, known as the Kingwood Post Office, is redesignated the Congressman Jack Fields Post Office. Later references to the Kingwood facility in federal records count as references to the Congressman Jack Fields Post Office.
plaw-108-469-2004:
Federal workers gain year-round control of their retirement savings under the Thrift Savings Plan Open Elections Act of 2004, Public Law 108-469 of the 108th Congress. The law amends chapter 84 of title 5, which governs the Thrift Savings Plan, the savings plan for federal employees. Before the act, workers got a reasonable period every six months to choose their contributions.

The six-month window is struck. An election to make contributions may now be made at any time, and workers may also change or stop contributions whenever they wish. An election takes effect on the earliest date that is practical to administer, and it stays in force until changed or ended. One limit is kept: for certain new employees and members, agency contributions still begin only on the schedule the older rules provided.
plaw-108-470-2004: State farm fees may be collected through federal loans under Public Law 108-470, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The law confirms that the Secretary of Agriculture may collect approved state commodity assessments for a state out of the proceeds of marketing assistance loans. The assessment must be one a producer or the first buyer owes under state law or a federally run authority. Collection happens only under an agreement with the requesting state, and the power does not extend to collecting a state tax or other revenue.
plaw-108-471-2004: Adam G Kinser is honored by Public Law 108-471, enacted by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The Postal Service facility at 140 Sacramento Street in Rio Vista, California, is designated the Adam G Kinser Post Office Building. References to that facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, and other records are treated as references to the Adam G Kinser Post Office Building.
plaw-108-472-2004: Lieutenant General James V Edmundson is honored by Public Law 108-472, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The Postal Service facility at 560 Bay Isles Road in Longboat Key, Florida, takes the name Lieutenant General James V Edmundson Post Office Building. Under the law, any mention of the Longboat Key facility in a federal record counts as a mention of the building by that name.
plaw-108-473-2004: Bill Monroe is honored by Public Law 108-473, a naming law of the 108th Congress enacted in December 2004. The Postal Service facility at 25 McHenry Street in Rosine, Kentucky, is designated the Bill Monroe Post Office. Any reference to the Rosine facility in a law, map, regulation, document, or other record of the United States is deemed a reference to the Bill Monroe Post Office.
plaw-108-474-2004:
History teaching gets summer academies under the American History and Civics Education Act of 2004, Public Law 108-474 of the 108th Congress. The law authorizes grants to set up academies for teachers and students of American history and civics.

The Secretary of Education may award up to twelve grants, given by competition. Some grants create Presidential Academies for Teaching of American History and Civics, which may run workshops for both veteran and new teachers. Others create Congressional Academies for Students of American History and Civics. Applicants must show real skill in historical methods or in the teaching of history. Money for the grants may come from funds provided for a part of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, starting with fiscal year 2005. A third section covers the National History Day Program.
plaw-108-475-2004: Earl B Gilliam is honored by Public Law 108-475, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The Postal Service facility at 5505 Stevens Way in San Diego, California, is designated the Earl B Gilliam/Imperial Avenue Post Office Building. Any reference to that San Diego facility in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record is deemed a reference to the building under that combined name.
plaw-108-476-2004:
YMCA retirement plans gain church plan status under Public Law 108-476, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The law treats certain arrangements kept by the YMCA Retirement Fund as church plans for parts of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. Church plans are retirement plans with special tax treatment under the code.

For sections 401(a) and 403(b), any retirement plan the fund kept as of January 1, 2003, counts as a church plan run by the kind of organization the code describes. Plans that take salary reduction contributions get careful limits: their accounts count as retirement income accounts, but one church contract rule does not apply to them. A money purchase pension plan kept by the fund is treated as a defined contribution money purchase plan. It is also treated as having made an election that applies to plan years after December 31, 2005.
plaw-108-477-2004: Donald G Brotzman is honored by Public Law 108-477, enacted by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The Postal Service facility at 4985 Moorhead Avenue in Boulder, Colorado, is designated the Donald G Brotzman Post Office Building. References to the Boulder facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, and records are read as references to the Donald G Brotzman Post Office Building.
plaw-108-478-2004: Irma Rangel is honored by Public Law 108-478, a naming law passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The Postal Service facility at 103 East Kleberg in Kingsville, Texas, is designated the Irma Rangel Post Office Building. Any reference to that facility in a United States law, map, regulation, document, or other record is deemed a reference to the Irma Rangel Post Office Building.
plaw-108-479-2004:
A Pacific battle is honored in Public Law 108-479, a joint resolution of the 108th Congress passed in December 2004. The resolution marks the sixtieth anniversary of the Battle of Peleliu and the end of Japanese control of Palau. It urges the Secretary of the Interior to protect the battlefield sites and honor the Americans who fought there.

United States forces landed on Peleliu on September 15, 1944, after three days of naval shelling, aiming to take a key airfield. The battle lasted over two months and cost over 10,000 American casualties, including about 1,250 Marines and 540 soldiers killed. Two famous men took part. Future president George H W Bush flew as a Navy torpedo-bomber pilot in the softening-up operation. Future Secretary of State George P Shultz served with the Army division that took Angaur Island. The battlefield became a national historic landmark in 1985.
plaw-108-480-2004:
A Spanish fort in Florida gets a visitor center under Public Law 108-480, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. Title I is the Castillo de San Marcos National Monument Preservation and Education Act. The Castillo de San Marcos National Monument stands in St Augustine, and the law authorizes money for an educational center there.

If funds are provided and the project ranks in the Park Service five-year building program, the Secretary of the Interior may design and build the visitor center. Its site and design must follow the preferred plan in the monument's general management plan record, expected in 2005. The Secretary may work with the City of St Augustine, the Colonial St Augustine Preservation Foundation, other agencies, schools, and nonprofit groups to plan, build, run, and manage the center. A boundary expansion section covers buying land if the chosen site lies outside the monument.
plaw-108-481-2004:
A Hawaiian refuge grows under the Kilauea Point National Wildlife Refuge Expansion Act of 2004, Public Law 108-481 of the 108th Congress. The law provides for expanding the Kilauea Point National Wildlife Refuge on Kauai. The Secretary of the Interior may add the listed lands to the refuge.

Five parcels are named on a Fish and Wildlife Service map dated April 22, 2004. Kilauea Bay covers about twelve acres, Kilauea Vistas about forty, and Kilauea Falls Ranch about one hundred sixty-two. The Kahili Beach property adds about five acres, and one lot of Kilauea Garden Farms about fifteen. The Secretary may buy the land, receive it as a gift, or trade for it, and may adjust the parcel lines slightly to make buying easier. All purchases must be voluntary, never forced takings, and bought land joins the refuge.
plaw-108-482-2004:
Fake music and movie labels are targeted by the Intellectual Property Protection and Courts Amendments Act of 2004, Public Law 108-482 of the 108th Congress. The law aims to prevent and punish counterfeiting of copyrighted copies and phonorecords, the recordings covered by copyright law.

Title I is the Anti-counterfeiting Amendments Act of 2004. It widens the ban in section 2318 of title 18, the crimes title. The section heading now covers trafficking in counterfeit labels, illicit labels, and counterfeit documentation or packaging. The crime reaches a person who knowingly deals in a fake or illicit label. The label must be meant to be stuck on, enclosed with, or placed alongside a phonorecord or a copy of a computer program. Later parts of the act amend the courts side of intellectual property law.
plaw-108-483-2004:
Park land in the Everglades is swapped under Public Law 108-483, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The law authorizes the exchange of certain land in Everglades National Park in Florida. It works by amending section 102 of the Everglades National Park Protection and Expansion Act of 1989.

One part lets the Secretary of the Interior buy a small support site from willing sellers. The site may hold no more than ten acres outside the park, next to or near the East Everglades area. It would serve offices, housing, maintenance, or other park needs. Bought land is run as part of the park. A new land exchanges subsection then defines the trade partners, including the Administrator of General Services and Miami-Dade County. The county land in the swap is two parcels totaling about one hundred fifty-three acres.
plaw-108-484-2004:
Small loans to the poor are put under closer watch by the Microenterprise Results and Accountability Act of 2004, Public Law 108-484 of the 108th Congress. The law amends the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. Microenterprise programs give very small loans and business help to poor people in developing countries, and the act aims to improve their results and accountability.

Congress notes its past support in two microenterprise laws, the Microenterprise for Self-Reliance Act of 2000 and a 2003 follow-up. An outside review rated the United States Agency for International Development in the top tier of seventeen donors in microfinance. But a November 2003 report by the Comptroller General found the agency had met only some of the programs' main goals. The findings add that such aid can ease some effects of poverty, setting up the act's push for better measurement.
plaw-108-485-2004:
Ocean research space in Florida is shared under Public Law 108-485, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The Secretary of Commerce may make property on Virginia Key, Florida, available to the University of Miami. The land is run by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and the university would use it for a Marine Life Science Center.

The Secretary may hand over use by easement, lease, license, or long-term agreement. The university may build and run facilities for research across many fields on the environment and fisheries, plus assessment, management, and teaching. Use is allowed only under a written agreement. That deal must state the terms of non-federal use, the federal interests kept in the land, and rights of entry for federal workers. It must also cover shared use of buildings by the university and federal agencies and protect the ocean agency's work on the site.
plaw-108-486-2004:
The national bird is celebrated in coin form by the American Bald Eagle Recovery and National Emblem Commemorative Coin Act, Public Law 108-486 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2004. The law requires the Secretary of the Treasury to mint coins marking the recovery of the American bald eagle. It honors the bird's return to American lands, waterways, and skies, and the role of its endangered listing under the Endangered Species Act of 1973.

Congress recalls that the bald eagle became the national emblem on June 20, 1782, chosen at the Second Continental Congress. The findings call it the greatest visible symbol of freedom and democracy in the world. The eagle lives only in North America and stands for freedom, courage, strength, spirit, loyalty, justice, equality, and excellence. Its image sits at the center of the Great Seal and the seals of the President, Congress, and many departments.
plaw-108-487-2004:
Spy agencies are funded for a year by Public Law 108-487, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The act's own short title is the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2005. It authorizes money for the intelligence and intelligence-related work of the United States Government, for the Community Management Account, and for the Central Intelligence Agency Retirement and Disability System.

Title I covers intelligence activities. It authorizes the money, points to a classified schedule that holds the real figures, and allows changes to personnel ceilings. Other sections cover the community management account and fold in reporting duties. Title II funds the CIA retirement and disability system. Title III holds general provisions, including growth in employee pay and benefits already allowed by law.
plaw-108-488-2004:
A tree disease gets a national plan under Public Law 108-488, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The disease is Sudden Oak Death, a forest sickness caused by a fungus-like organism named Phytophthora ramorum. The law's one section orders the plan and lists what it must contain.

The Secretary of Agriculture, working through the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, must develop the national plan for controlling and managing the disease. The duty holds only if Congress provides money for the purpose. The plan elements begin in the section that follows in the text. A short law of this kind still matters: it puts one agency in charge of a shared national response instead of leaving the fight to scattered local efforts.
plaw-108-489-2004:
Retirement checks for capital workers are reorganized by the District of Columbia Retirement Protection Improvement Act of 2004, Public Law 108-489 of the 108th Congress. The law amends the Balanced Budget Act of 1997. It improves how federal pension benefit payments are run for District of Columbia teachers, police officers, and fire fighters.

Section 2 creates a new fund on the books of the Treasury, called the District of Columbia Teachers, Police Officers, and Firefighters Federal Pension Fund. The fund holds the assets transferred into it, the yearly federal payments deposited for it, and any other money provided for it. Earnings on the fund's investments also stay in the fund. A new chapter 9 is written into the District title of the 1997 act to hold these rules, and the old chapter 9 is renumbered chapter 10.
plaw-108-490-2004: Children's hospitals gain a counting change under Public Law 108-490, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The law amends section 340E of the Public Health Service Act, the section on federal payments to children's hospitals for the indirect costs of running approved graduate medical residency training programs. In the formula for those payments, beds and bassinets assigned to healthy newborn infants are now left out of the bed count. The change applies to payments for periods beginning with fiscal year 2005.
plaw-108-491-2004: Federal judges receive a pay adjustment under Public Law 108-491, a one-section law passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. Acting under section 140 of Public Law 97-92, the act authorizes Justices and judges of the United States to receive a salary adjustment during fiscal year 2005. The adjustment is the one set by section 461 of title 28 of the United States Code.
plaw-108-492-2004:
Private human space flight is promoted by the Commercial Space Launch Amendments Act of 2004, Public Law 108-492 of the 108th Congress. The law amends the commercial space launch rules in title 49. Its stated purpose is to help the emerging commercial human space flight industry grow.

The findings in section 70101 gain new paragraphs. Safely opening space to the American people and their private commercial, scientific, and cultural ventures should guide federal space spending, policy, and rules. Private firms have begun building launch vehicles that can carry people into space, and more private money in that work would strengthen the whole industry. At the same time, Congress warns that space transportation is inherently risky, and the future of crewed commercial flight depends on steadily better safety.
plaw-108-493-2004:
Archery gear is taxed in a new way by Public Law 108-493, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The law amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to change the tax on arrow components. It first repeals a subsection of the American Jobs Creation Act of 2004 on the subject, treating that change as if it had never been enacted.

A fresh rule then taxes arrow shafts. On the first sale by the maker, producer, or importer, a tax of thirty-nine cents falls on each shaft of a type used to make an arrow. The tax applies whether the shaft is sold alone or as part of a finished or unfinished product. Covered shafts measure eighteen inches or more, or are shorter but fit for use with a covered bow. After 2005, the thirty-nine cent figure rises each year with the cost of living.
plaw-108-494-2004:
Emergency calling is upgraded by Public Law 108-494, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The act reaches beyond one subject. It helps move radio spectrum from government to commercial users. It strengthens homeland security and public safety through enhanced 911 services. It also shields universal service funds from the Antideficiency Act for a time.

Title I is the Ensuring Needed Help Arrives Near Callers Employing 911 Act of 2004, or ENHANCE 911 Act. Congress finds that a universal 911 number with the most modern features possible should serve every citizen in every region, for the sake of homeland security and public safety. Building that system takes money and teamwork from federal, state, and local governments. Fees collected on phone bills for 911 should go only to 911 purposes, and Congress calls enhanced 911 a high national priority.
plaw-108-495-2004:
Secret filming of private body areas becomes a federal crime under the Video Voyeurism Prevention Act of 2004, Public Law 108-495 of the 108th Congress. The law adds a new chapter 88, titled Privacy, to title 18, the crimes title. The ban applies in the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the United States, meaning federal lands and waters.

The new section 1801 punishes anyone who intends to capture an image of a private area of a person without consent, and does so where the person reasonably expects privacy. The penalty is a fine, up to one year in prison, or both. Capture is defined broadly: videotaping, photographing, filming, recording by any means, or broadcasting. A private area means the naked or undergarment-clad genitals, pubic area, buttocks, or female breast.
plaw-108-496-2004:
Federal workers gain new benefit choices from the Federal Employee Dental and Vision Benefits Enhancement Act of 2004, Public Law 108-496 of the 108th Congress. The law amends part III of title 5. It sets up programs offering added dental and vision benefits to federal employees, retirees, and their dependents, and it widens the contracting power of the Office of Personnel Management.

Section 2 writes a new chapter 89A for enhanced dental benefits. Its sections cover definitions, who may get coverage, how the government contracts for plans, and what the benefits are. Further sections handle information for people who may enroll, choosing coverage, protection for restored survivor and disability annuitants, premiums, and the relation of the program to state law. Studies, reports, audits, court matters, and administration close the chapter. A companion arrangement covers vision benefits.
plaw-108-497-2004:
War and peace in Sudan are addressed by the Comprehensive Peace in Sudan Act of 2004, Public Law 108-497 of the 108th Congress. The act states the sense of Congress on the conflict in Darfur, Sudan. It provides help for the Darfur crisis and for a comprehensive peace across Sudan.

Definitions name the parties. The Government of Sudan means the National Congress Party government in Khartoum, formerly the National Islamic Front. It also covers a successor, other than the coalition government agreed in the Nairobi Declaration of June 5, 2004. The armed groups JEM, the Justice and Equality Movement, and SLA, the Sudan Liberation Army, are defined, as is the SPLM, the Sudan People's Liberation Movement. Congress then finds that a full peace deal could be at risk if the parties fail to act. The deal meant is the kind foreseen in the Sudan Peace Act and the Machakos Protocol of 2002.
plaw-108-498-2004: Conservation money is fenced off by Public Law 108-498, passed by the 108th Congress in December 2004. The law limits transfers of Commodity Credit Corporation funds between conservation programs for the expert help, called technical assistance, that makes them work. From fiscal year 2005 onward, corporation money for each listed program stays available for technical assistance for that same program. It may not be used for technical assistance for a different listed program. The change, to section 1241 of the Food Security Act of 1985, takes effect October 1, 2004.
plaw-2004: Private Law 108-3, approved on October 30, 2004 (H.R. 712), grants relief to Richi James Lesley. Despite the caps of the Immigration and Nationality Act, Lesley may seek an immigrant visa or adjustment of status to lawful permanent resident. His entry counts as lawful if it came before the filing deadline in the act. Filing with fees was due within two years, and one visa is then cut from his birth country's pool.
plos-pbio-0020004:
Tomoko Ishino, Kazuhiko Yano, Yasuo Chinzei, and their group traced a step in malaria infection for PLOS Biology in 2004. After a mosquito bite, malaria parasites travel to the liver. A sheet of cells lines the liver's blood vessels, and the parasites must cross it to reach liver cells.

The team found that the parasites need a cell-passage skill to make that crossing. They actively move through cells rather than slipping between them. Blocking that skill could, in theory, stop infection before the liver stage takes hold. The paper matters because the liver stage is a brief, quiet window. A drug or vaccine that works there could prevent illness outright.
plos-pbio-0020104:
Zhixin Xie, Lisa K. Johansen, Adam M. Gustafson, and a large team mapped small RNA pathways in plants for PLOS Biology in 2004. Plants use small RNAs to silence genes, fight viruses, and control growth. The team sorted the many small RNAs of the model plant Arabidopsis and traced how they are made.

They found that the pathways branch more than expected, with distinct sets of small RNAs doing distinct jobs. Some guard the genome against jumping genes, while others fine-tune growth genes. A full catalog of these RNAs gives plant science a working map. It also informs crop work, since the same pathways shape traits like yield and disease resistance.
plos-pbio-0020304:
Dennis R. Harris, Masashi Tanaka, Sergei V. Saveliev, and their team studied a radiation-proof bacterium in PLOS Biology in 2004. Deinococcus radiodurans survives doses of radiation that shatter its genome into hundreds of pieces, then rebuilds it. The authors focus on a protein called DdrA that appears after damage.

DdrA guards the broken ends of DNA, keeping them from being chewed away before repair starts. That protection buys time for the cell's rebuilding tools. The bacterium's tricks are of keen interest for cleaning up radioactive waste and for understanding DNA repair in general. Each named part, like DdrA, brings the full system closer to view.
plos-pone-0000004:
Douglas Strathdee, Helen Ibbotson, and Seth Grant asked a practical question about mouse genetics in work published by PLOS ONE in 2006. Gene engineers often park an added gene at the Gt(ROSA)26Sor locus, a safe harbor site in the mouse genome. The team tested whether the inserted gene works the same in either direction.

Their finding sits in the title: expression depends on orientation. A transgene facing one way at that locus behaved differently from the same gene facing the other way.
