The authors say grip alone is a poor sign of visual-motor skill.
pmc-13258604:
Elif Sertesen Çamöz leads a 2026 single center study of local ablation for breast cancer spread to the liver. Survival and tumor control were tracked from the first local treatment.

Smaller liver lesions were linked to notably longer survival. Results support careful patient selection for local treatment, while the tiny sample warns against broad conclusions.
pmc-13258704:
Yaren Aydın and colleagues teach image models to spot concrete carbonation in a 2026 study. Carbonation signals chemical change that can rust steel inside concrete and weaken structures. Four versions of a fast detection model family were trained and compared on a dedicated photo set.

Two versions reached near perfect scores on the test images. One of those also ran fastest, with the lowest delay per image. Other versions traded modest speed for similar accuracy. pmc-13259004:
Wenxuan Zhi and colleagues measure railway switch gaps by fusing deep vision with geometry in a 2026 study. Gap size reveals whether a turnout has locked correctly. Oil, glare, and vibration make ordinary camera measurement unstable in the field.

pmc-13260204:

pmc-13260304:

pmc-13260704:

pmc-13260804:

pmc-13262704:

pmc-13263304:

pmc-13263704:

pmc-13264204:

pmc-13264304:

pmc-13264404:

pmc-13264604:

pmc-13264904:
Keir E J Philip and colleagues link breathlessness with loneliness and social isolation in older English adults, in a 2026 cohort study. Breathlessness limits daily life and can be distressing. pmc-13265004:

pmc-13265404:

pmc-13265904:

pmc-13266104:

pmc-13266204:

pmc-13269404:

pmc-13269704:

pmc-13270704:

pmc-13271904:

pmc-13273204:

pmc-13273904:

pmc-13274104:

pmc-13274504:

pmc-13274604:

pmc-13275304:

pmc-13275504:

pmc-13276304:

pmc-13276504:

pmc-13279604:

pmc-13279904:

pmc-13280804:

pmc-13283204:

pmc-13283304:

pmc-13283404:

pmc-13283904:

pmc-13284604:

pmc-13285704:

pmc-13285904:

pmc-13286704:

pmc-13286904:

The network learned to reconstruct signals while also classifying diagnoses, a twin goal meant to protect clinical meaning. Rebuilt tracings correlated moderately with the originals and carried almost no systematic voltage error. Diagnostic accuracy from rebuilt signals was respectable across five disease classes. A second large database confirmed the benefit over a simple statistical baseline. The authors caution that chest leads remain too weak for fine heart attack screening.
pmc-13287204:
Michaela E Larson and co-authors compared blood immune markers and memory scores in 2026 among 238 adults in Durham, grouped by HIV status and regular marijuana use. Data were gathered from 2021 to 2023, when HIV treatment already controlled the virus in those infected.

Seven markers gave usable models. Adults without HIV who used marijuana had lower levels of one signalling protein, while untreated-looking inflammation was broadest in adults with HIV who did not use marijuana. Among adults with HIV, use did not clearly lower marker levels. Worse memory tracked modestly with higher tumour necrosis factor related markers, regardless of marijuana findings.
pmc-13287304:
Meriem Miyassa Aci and co-authors tested a shop-bought mix of two Trichoderma fungi in 2026 against Fusarium wilt, a soil disease that ruins melon crops. Treated roots were checked for disease signs, and gene activity was mapped to see which defence routes switched on.

Pre-treated plants showed far milder wilt. Root gene activity shifted toward building tougher cell walls and sending alarm signals. Several hub genes tied to stress response and wall building rose sharply. Defence chemical routes, including phenylpropanoid production, were enriched. The authors say the gene map can guide breeding and product design for greener crop protection that uses fewer chemical sprays.
pmc-13287804:
Noura K Ahmed and colleagues sampled 120 cheeses of four kinds in 2026 from shops across Cairo and Giza in Egypt. They checked for the hardy germ Pseudomonas aeruginosa and its resistance to antibiotics. Chemical and gene tests confirmed identity, and dish and tube tests measured slimy biofilm growth.

The germ turned up in eighteen samples, which is 15%. Every strain formed biofilm on plates, and gene markers for biofilm appeared in most strains. Over half the strains resisted nearly all drugs tested, and the rest resisted several. The authors call for tighter dairy hygiene, better cleaning, and careful antibiotic use to protect cheese quality and shoppers.
pmc-13288504:
Hyun Soo Park and Bumseok Jeong link metabolic syndrome to brain network costs in 2026. Scans came from UK Biobank. It holds 25,697 adults aged 40 to 70. Scores ran from zero to five. Waist, blood fats, pressure, and sugar set the score.

Worse scores meant higher subcortical energy costs. Visual network costs fell instead. Attention and executive networks also shifted. Brain aging looked faster in those profiles. Waist size was the strongest predictor. Effects grew with age. Memory and speed scores were lower. Spatial skills also looked at risk. The work ties body fat spread to brain energy use.
pmc-13288704:
Tori Demuth and Dennis Svatunek compute why benzene rarely joins a classic ring-forming reaction, in a 2026 study. In Diels-Alder chemistry, two partners click into a ring, but benzene's stable aromatic system resists breaking. Tetrazines are among the few partners reactive enough to engage benzene directly. The team modeled these rare reactions to find what makes them succeed.

Only strongly activated tetrazines could overcome benzene's poor orbital overlap, the calculations showed. Breaking the reaction energy into parts revealed a mix of orbital effects and charge control. Substituents changed the barrier a lot, especially when they pushed the transition state toward an uneven, polar shape. In that shape, one new bond forms ahead of the other. The authors say these rules clarify the electronic demands for coaxing aromatic rings into cycloadditions. Such insight may guide chemists hunting new reactions of stubborn arenes.
pmc-13288904:
Irem Pamuk and colleagues study vitamin K in dialysis patients. Their 2026 study follows 60 people on peritoneal dialysis. It runs for one year at one large center. Low vitamin K can let blood vessels harden. The team tracked plaque in neck arteries.

Plaque was present in 36 patients at the start. Vitamin K shortage was common in that group. Three blood markers ran high in plaque cases. Age and one marker each predicted plaque alone. A lower cut point caught more cases. New plaque grew over the year. One marker alone foretold new plaque growth.
pmc-13289004:
Miguel Garcia-Argibay and colleagues track ADHD drug use in Norway in 2026. Their register study covers youth under 18. All had a new ADHD diagnosis in clinics. Diagnoses ran from 2010 to 2012. Follow-up ran to the end of 2021 for the whole group.

The cohort held 8,961 young people. Most were boys, at 69 percent. About three in four started drugs. The wait to start was 106 days at the median. Older teens quit drugs the soonest. Girls quit sooner than boys too. Coverage fell faster with age at start. The authors urge close watch in late teens. They also urge support at the point of quitting.
pmc-13289104:
Ali Alghamdi and colleagues study herpes drugs and later Alzheimer's care in 2026. Their study uses Dutch pharmacy data. It spans 1994 to 2024. Adults aged 50 to 80 took part. None had past dementia or Alzheimer's drugs.

The set held 262,757 adults in all. Users of herpes drugs numbered 23,887. Each user was matched to ten non-users. In all, 2,495 people later started Alzheimer's drugs. Herpes drug use tied to far lower starts. The tie held in both time spans. All three herpes drugs showed the tie. The authors urge trials to test the link. Herpes flares may play a part in Alzheimer's.
pmc-13289304:
Kristoffer Staal Rohrberg led a 2026 first-in-human study of lomvastomig, a bispecific antibody for advanced solid tumors. The drug blocks two immune brakes at once, PD-1 and TIM-3, and was built to leave other antibody functions quiet. Lab and mouse work came first, then a phase 1 trial across many centers.

Dose escalation enrolled people with advanced or spread tumors, followed by expansion groups in four tumor types. Groups included melanoma and lung cancer after prior checkpoint drugs, plus small cell lung cancer and esophageal cancer without prior checkpoint care. Goals covered safety, highest tolerated dose, drug levels, target coverage, and early tumor shrinkage. Early human data like this set the dose and tumor types for larger trials.
pmc-13289404:
Courtney Franklin, Bernie Carter, David Taylor-Robinson, and Enitan Carrol analyzed a 2026 record cohort on fairness in children's emergency admissions in Northwest England. Attendances had risen before the 2020 lockdown, and social conditions may shape who gets admitted after arrival. Data covered every visit to Alder Hey Children's Hospital from 2016 to 2019, totaling 206 918 attendances in the file.

Admission followed about 16 percent of visits from poorer areas versus 24 percent from the richest areas in raw counts. More deprivation linked to slightly lower admission odds once a child had arrived, before other factors were added. Referral source, diagnosis, and urgency level were then tested as possible explanations for the gap. The pattern raises questions about thresholds and support by neighborhood wealth.
pmc-13289904:
Abdi Gari Negasa led a 2026 cost study on bubble CPAP for severe pneumonia with low oxygen in Ethiopian children under five. Pneumonia remains the top infectious killer in this age group despite being treatable. Bubble continuous positive airway pressure pushes air gently to keep airways open and can be built locally, but its value for money in Ethiopia was undocumented.

A decision tree compared locally made bubble CPAP with standard low-flow oxygen in general hospitals. Outcomes counted child deaths avoided and healthy life years gained, with costs from papers and local markets. Value was judged against thresholds tied to national income per person. Sensitivity checks varied key inputs to test how firm the verdict stays.
pmc-13290104:
How nursing students in Saudi Arabia feel about telehealth is linked to how well they handle digital health tools, report Muna Alharbi and colleagues in 2026. Their cross-sectional survey at one Saudi university measured digital health literacy and attitudes toward using telehealth in practice.

Of 273 students, about two-thirds showed high digital health literacy. Literacy strongly predicted positive attitudes toward telehealth, while male students were less likely than female students to report positive attitudes. Academic year, workshops, and informatics courses showed no clear link to attitudes. Alharbi and colleagues conclude that nursing programs should strengthen digital training directly, since current formal teaching did not move literacy levels.
pmc-13290604:
Injecting patients with their own blood, combined with other external Chinese medicine treatments, beat Western medicine for chronic hives in a 2026 meta-analysis by Jinchu Zhou and colleagues. Chronic urticaria is a recurring, stubborn skin disease, and the combined approach is reported to work with few side effects.

Searching 11 databases, the team pooled 20 randomized trials with 1,461 participants. The combined treatment raised overall response rates and cut recurrence sharply, with serum IgE also falling. Results for itch severity and wheal duration looked strong but proved fragile and showed publication bias. Zhou and colleagues credit the combination with real gains while warning that unclear randomization, mixed outcomes, and wide differences between studies mean stricter prospective trials must settle the question.
pmc-13290704:
An interpretable machine-learning model flags older stroke patients headed for pneumonia, Wen-Jie Chu and colleagues report in a 2026 modeling study. Stroke-associated pneumonia is a common, serious complication, and catching high-risk patients early is hard.

The retrospective study used 1,011 patients aged 65 and over admitted to Zhejiang Hospital between September 2018 and December 2023, of whom 18.79% developed the pneumonia. Feature screening kept 12 predictors, and eight algorithms competed on routine admission data. A support vector machine proved the steadiest, reaching an AUC of 0.794 on the test set, and explanation analysis showed which factors drove its calls. The team built an online platform around the model so clinicians can score new patients at the bedside.
pmc-13291004:
Two treatments for a broken finger bone are compared by Kemal Arda Col and colleagues in 2026. The breaks were Doyle type 4B mallet fractures. One group got a pin method with an orthosis. The other group got a splint alone. No best treatment was agreed before the trial.

Sixty-two patients were treated from 2022 to 2024. Checks ran for up to twelve months. Joint lag, movement, and bone healing were scored. The pin group ended with less lag at the fingertip joint. Bending range was also a bit better. Problem rates stayed alike in both groups. The pin method gains support from these results.
pmc-13291804:
Tiande Zou, with co-authors, reports a 2026 feeding trial testing potassium diformate in the diets of nursery piglets. Twenty-four weaned piglets were split into four groups receiving 0, 0.6, 1.2, or 1.8 percent of the additive for 28 days. The team tracked growth, blood and gut inflammation markers, intestinal barrier proteins, and gut microbes.

Feed conversion improved steadily as the dose rose, and the 1.8 percent group converted feed about 15 percent better than controls in early weeks. That group also showed lower interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor levels, less D-lactate and endotoxin in blood, and stronger barrier proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin. Microbe shifts accompanied the changes, including more Roseburia and less Lactobacillus.
pmc-13292104:
Tejal Patil and co-authors run a 2026 prospective study asking whether blood levels of growth and inflammation markers can flag oral cancer patients headed for recurrence. They followed 120 people with confirmed oral squamous cell carcinoma. Blood drawn at diagnosis, six months, and twelve months was tested for EGFR, interleukin-6, and TNF-alpha.

Thirty-four patients, 28.33 percent of the cohort, saw their cancer return, and their starting marker levels were far higher than those who stayed clear. The gap held at later draws too. Marker levels also rose alongside tumor size, overall stage, and lymph node spread. In adjusted analysis, all three baseline markers independently predicted recurrence. The authors suggest serial blood testing could sharpen follow-up for this common, relapse-prone cancer.
pmc-13292304:
Sanna Rotonen and co-authors ask a 2026 aging question in a Finnish cohort: does worsening insulin resistance raise the risk of mild cognitive impairment? Participants were followed from age 57 to 69 and sorted by their CERAD test score at follow-up. The team tracked changes in the HOMA-IR index and fasting insulin, alongside lifestyle, mood, and quality-of-life questionnaires.

Bigger rises in both insulin measures meant higher odds of impairment, with odds ratios of 2.20 for HOMA-IR change and 3.49 for fasting insulin change in adjusted models. Low baseline cognition, less education, and low physical activity also raised risk. Quality of life slid further in the group that developed impairment. The authors name insulin resistance a genuine risk factor worth acting on during aging.
pmc-13292604:
Leon B Hajdari, with co-authors, presents a 2026 case report of a giant retroperitoneal liposarcoma removed without sacrificing any organ. Their patient, a 61-year-old woman, arrived with a swelling abdomen, discomfort, nausea, indigestion, and breathlessness on exertion. MRI showed a mass measuring 28 by 23.6 by 24 centimeters behind the abdomen, first read as possibly dedifferentiated disease.

A needle biopsy instead indicated well-differentiated liposarcoma, the slower form. Through a midline incision the surgeons lifted out a 10-kilogram tumor whole, sparing every neighboring organ because clear dissection planes held. Final pathology confirmed the gentler subtype with clean margins and no vessel invasion, staged pT4. Scans found no leftover or spread disease, no extra therapy was given, and a three-month check stayed clear. The authors stress imaging, biopsy, and follow-up length.
pmc-13293604: Xiao-Wei Chen and co-authors issued a correction in 2026 to their 2013 study on how SEC24A shortage lowers blood cholesterol in mice. The notice removes one panel from Figure 1 after a lung image there was found to match an image in an earlier paper from the same group. Both lung samples had been judged fully normal by the pathologist who prepared both figures, so the findings do not change. One sentence in the results was reworded to drop its figure reference. The authors apologize for the error.
pmc-13294904:
Jiang-Wen Gui and a large team profile a new pain drug candidate that targets the kappa opioid receptor, in a 2026 pharmacology study. Kappa activators can relieve pain without the addiction risk of morphine-like drugs, yet older versions cause sedation and unease that limit their use. The candidate, SLL-022CCP, was built on a morphinan scaffold and had already shown tight binding to the kappa receptor, so the team ran a full battery of cell and animal tests.

In cells the compound activated the kappa receptor at extremely low doses, with far weaker action at the mu and delta receptors. In mice it relieved heat pain and chemical pain and calmed two kinds of itch at low doses, effects blocked by a kappa-specific blocker. At pain-relieving doses it caused no clumsiness or learned aversion, only brief sedation. The profile marks it as a promising nonaddictive analgesic lead.
pmc-13295004:
Rattaphol Seangrung and Rada Thitirangsee translate and validate a nerve pain questionnaire for Thai adults in a 2026 study. The Leeds scale helps clinicians spot neuropathic pain, but no checked Thai version existed. Work took place at a specialist pain clinic with adults in lasting non-cancer pain.

One hundred twenty patients took part, half judged mainly neuropathic and half mainly tissue based by an independent specialist. Raters agreed closely with each other and with repeat testing weeks later, and internal consistency was acceptable. At the standard cut-off score, the Thai version caught most nerve pain cases while rarely mislabelling the others.
pmc-13295104:
Mengping Zhang and colleagues profile a folk anti-inflammatory plant for animal feed use in a 2026 study. Staurogyne stenophylla has a long history in traditional practice, but its active ingredients and workings were unclear. Chemical profiling was paired with computer-based target hunting to fill that gap.

High-resolution liquid analysis found a very large chemical list, narrowed to 15 main active ingredients and 72 shared inflammation targets. Network work highlighted 16 core targets, including well-known control proteins for inflammation and cell survival. Docking and motion simulations showed strong, stable binding for several ingredient and target pairs, supporting a many-parts, many-targets action through two major signalling routes.
pmc-13295404:
Jiabao Hu and colleagues tune water flow for farmed silver pomfret in a 2026 study. The prized sea fish grows in recirculating tank systems where flow shapes health and growth. Gene and gut microbe profiling compared fish held at low, medium, and high flow rates.

Medium flow, at 600 litres per hour, gave the best growth and the calmest metabolism in the trial. Fish in that group also kept steadier gut microbe communities than fish in slower or faster water. The authors present the middle setting as a practical target for healthier, more sustainable pomfret farming in indoor systems.
pmc-13295804:
Eyob Akalewold Alemu and a large team map where pregnant women in sub-Saharan Africa miss HIV testing during antenatal care, in a 2026 study. The team pooled health survey data from twenty-four countries for 82,397 women who had been pregnant in the past two years. They charted how not taking the test spreads across space and which traits track with it.

Near forty percent of women who came for antenatal care had not taken an HIV test. Misses clustered in hot spots across much of Mali, Mauritania, Madagascar, Guinea, and Senegal, plus parts of Angola and northern Ethiopia. Being fifteen to nineteen, having no schooling, lacking health cover, and making fewer than four antenatal visits each tracked with a miss. The authors urge focused work in the hot spots.
pmc-13296604:
Mohammed M. A. Al Hussain and a large team make a plasmonic surface whose colour response can be switched electrically, in a 2026 paper. Their design places metal nanoparticles above a metal film, tethered by strands of DNA. Such surfaces normally keep whatever optical behaviour they were built with.

Applying a voltage moves the particles closer to or farther from the film, changing the gap that sets the optical resonance. Reflectance in visible light shifted strongly in response, at switching speeds above one kilohertz. Standard patterning methods could still place particles at chosen positions without losing the effect. Switchable surfaces of this kind could serve displays, sensors, and computing hardware that manipulates light.
pmc-13297604: Enza Maria Verde and co-authors issued this correction in 2026 to their 2025 review of protein clumping in ALS and frontotemporal dementia, centred on the protein TDP-43. The notice is a correction only. A reference tool misplaced one citation, so the whole reference list was revised. Two entries were removed, one was added, and two were swapped for better fit. Wording, grammar, and chapter layout were also adjusted, and a wrong sentence describing a figure on TDP-43 acetylation was fixed.
pmc-13297704:
Rut González-Jiménez and colleagues test whether eye-system faults can flag children their teachers judge to struggle in class, in a 2026 study. Reading, writing, and steady attention all lean on sound vision, yet which eye domains matter most was unclear. Five hundred eighty-one primary schoolchildren were assessed, with 506 full records entering the machine learning tests.

Five eye domains competed as predictors, from eye movement control to focusing power and eye length. Focusing faults classified struggling pupils best in cross-checks, with eye movement faults close behind. Alignment faults rarely flagged cases despite few false alarms, and eye length barely helped. The authors stress the results are exploratory: eye checks may add to school screening, but no model here can diagnose alone.
pmc-13297804:
Aitor Tejo-Otero opens a 2026 special issue of the journal Gels with an editor's tour of five papers on 3D printing with gels. Gels are soft nets that hold a lot of liquid. They act part solid and part fluid, which suits them for work in body-part printing, soft robots, drugs, and food.

Two review papers lead the set. One covers tragacanth-gum inks for printing living tissue, prized for holding water and being kind to cells. The other covers smart gels that react to heat, acid, or light for use in 4D printing. The research papers add a printed wound gel that senses acid by color shift while it gives out medicine, plus work on print methods for soft gels.
pmc-13298104:
Custom implants that sit on the bone can rebuild severely shrunken jaws when ordinary implants have nothing to grip, report Alberto Gasbarri and colleagues in a 2026 preliminary study. Their zero-gap protocol treated two cases of advanced jaw atrophy, one full upper arch and one partial, through a fully digital workflow.

Scans were mapped by mineral density to place screws in the hardest bone, reading +1200 to +1800 Hounsfield units, and printed guides plus check templates verified the fit during surgery. Alignment deviation was held to 0.2 mm. At two years, imaging showed no gap at the bone-implant surface, no bone loss, and healthy soft tissue in either case.
pmc-13298304:
Hongjian Wu and Xiangwei Kong engineer a foam fracturing fluid meant to stimulate coalbed methane wells without badly damaging the rock, in a 2026 study. Conventional foams harm formations through retained polymer. Their polymer-free design builds a gel-like network only at the gas-liquid interface, using a fluorosurfactant paired with nano-silica.

Screening and optimisation produced a formulation with strong foam quality and staying power, plus flow behaviour resembling crosslinked gels. Core flood tests showed far less permeability damage than reference fluids, and surface analysis linked protection to reduced adsorption of oxygen-bearing groups. Testing covered shallow reservoir temperatures, with hotter formations named as future work.
pmc-13298904:
Colin B. Shore and others ask patients what they think about drones carrying medical supplies, in a 2026 qualitative study. Scottish people from five health boards discussed chemotherapy items, lab diagnostics, and blood products in interviews and small focus groups. Drone trials exist across the United Kingdom, yet patient views were missing.

Eight themes emerged, covering acceptance, knowledge, concerns, and future hopes. Participants felt cautiously optimistic, welcoming better rural access, less travel, and environmental gains. Worries included reliability, red tape, privacy, and the risk of widening health inequalities. The authors advise transparent communication, co-design, solid rules, and lasting funding before routine integration proceeds.
pmc-13300204:
Spyridon Mantzoukas and co-authors report a 2026 laboratory study of a fungus as biological control for the Italian locust, a grasshopper pest ranging from Western Europe to western Siberia. Chemical sprays work fast but pollute the environment and harm non-target species. The team exposed locust nymphs, the young stages, to different doses of the fungus Beauveria bassiana, strain PPRI5339, and tracked survival.

The fungus caused significant death across all nymph stages tested. Younger and smaller nymphs proved more vulnerable and died faster than older ones, so susceptibility depended on developmental stage. The authors calculate lethal concentrations and lethal times to guide dosing. They present the results as a scientific basis for adding this fungus to integrated pest management programs aimed at the Italian locust.
pmc-13301304:
Which esophageal cancer patients fare worst after chemoradiation and surgery? Murat Yakin and colleagues answer from 155 cases treated at one center between March 2019 and November 2025, in a 2026 retrospective study. Response was judged by chest MRI and endoscopic biopsy, and survival links were tested across clinical and pathological factors.

Male sex, vessel invasion, adenocarcinoma type, weak treatment response, and advanced stage all tracked with shorter event-free survival. Stage IVa stood out in adjusted models, carrying roughly five times the risk of death or relapse. Squamous tumors did better, with median event-free survival of 18 months against 8.4 for adenocarcinoma. Careful surveillance may spare some complete responders an operation.
pmc-13301704:
S Pattu Valappil and co-authors dissect what makes an electrified guidewire cross the septum in a 2026 study. Twenty-five sheep hearts were prepared into septum models on a jig that mimics catheter push. Fifty-eight crossing attempts varied three things: how far the septum was pushed, how much wire tip stuck out, and which waveform drove the wire. Thermal cameras watched the burn.

One setup was perfect: a millimeter of tip with ten millimeters of push crossed every time. Longer tips and a slack, unpushed septum produced failed punctures, hotter tissue, and larger lesions. Waveform mattered. The coagulation setting peaked near thirty-four degrees, with a footprint under three millimeters. The cutting setting hit about sixty-nine degrees and spread past five. Crossing success was equal. The authors distill rules for operators: tent the septum, keep the tip short, and prefer the gentler waveform to spare tissue.
pmc-13302104:
G Viola and co-authors describe, in a 2026 prospective series, a nurse-led deep sedation routine for pulsed field ablation of atrial fibrillation and flutter. No standard sedation scheme exists yet for these procedures, which can be uncomfortable when the pulses fire. Their protocol used ketamine with small doses of other short-acting drugs while patients breathed on their own.

One hundred eight consecutive patients were treated at a busy centre using three different commercial ablation systems. Sedation needs did not differ between systems, and only one patient needed extra propofol from an anaesthetist to control movement. No complications occurred during the procedures, and both patients and operators rated satisfaction highly. The team presents the routine as safe and workable across platforms.
pmc-13302404:
J Gourraud and co-authors measure, in a 2026 study, how common a newly described inherited rhythm syndrome is among families struck by unexplained sudden death. In this condition, the heart's QT interval stays normal at rest but stretches abnormally during mental stress. Standard exercise and drug tests can miss it entirely.

The team examined 134 families with unexplained sudden death or cardiac arrest and no other diagnosis. The stress-test pattern identified the syndrome in fifteen families, about eleven percent of the total. Screening relatives found 43 affected people, a minority of whom had prior symptoms. Beta-blocker treatment was started in many, and over roughly seven years only one arrhythmia episode occurred, during a lapse in treatment.
pmc-13302504:
Careful screening before a heart pump implant kept right-heart failure at bay in a 2026 single-center study led by Giulia Elena Mandoli. Twenty-nine patients with end-stage heart failure, average age sixty-three and ejection fraction near twenty-three percent, were assessed under the SIENA protocol, catheter measurements included, then followed for a year after LVAD surgery.

Every patient scored zero or one on the protocol, and none developed the right ventricular failure the score is meant to predict. One catheter measure did stand out: a central venous to wedge pressure ratio above 0.63 tracked with death and rehospitalization. The authors offer that ratio as an extra mid-term warning sign.
pmc-13302704:
A Naraen and co-authors train, in a 2026 study, an artificial intelligence reader that can tell from a single heartbeat whether left bundle branch area pacing truly captured the conduction system. Judging capture on the ECG is tricky and slows adoption of this physiological pacing style. The team built a pipeline that isolates individual paced beats automatically.

Expert-labelled beat clusters from 225 British patients supplied nearly a quarter-million beats for training. The classifier reached about ninety-three percent accuracy in cross-checks within that dataset. Tested on an independent Chinese hospital dataset, it held up with similar accuracy and even stronger ranking scores. The authors say automatic capture checks could simplify implants and follow-up visits alike.
pmc-13303204:
A donor's stress-driven high blood sugar did not spoil transplanted pancreases, Luhao Liu and colleagues find in a 2026 retrospective cohort. Two hundred fifty-one simultaneous pancreas-kidney recipients were split by their donors' intensive care glucose history: forty-one from normoglycemic donors, two hundred ten whose donors needed insulin infusions for sustained high readings. Graft function, complications, and survival were compared for up to nine years.

Postoperative glucose, kidney markers, and complication rates matched between groups at every checkpoint. Death-censored graft survival and patient survival showed no significant gaps either. The authors caution that the single-center data cannot prove equivalence and may miss rare events, but the results argue against discarding such donors reflexively.
pmc-13304304:
Yuanchun Yue and co-authors isolate a helpful bacterium from fermented tofu whey in a 2026 study of natural antioxidants. The whey left over from tofu making is rich in lactic acid bacteria, but how those germs fight oxidation was unclear.

Six strains were screened for radical cleanup power and stress tolerance. One Lactiplantibacillus plantarum strain, MCS1903, gave the strongest activity outside its cells. Chemical profiling found many antioxidant-linked compounds in its broth. In gut cells the broth caused no harm at low doses and eased peroxide stress through a known defense pathway, marking the strain as a food probiotic candidate.
pmc-13304404:
Mikhail Yu. Dobryakov, Julia A. Buyuklyan, and Mikhail V. Biryukov describe, in a 2026 taxonomy study, a new soil Streptomyces species that makes a rare antibiotic compound. Hunting new species is a proven route to fresh drug scaffolds as resistance spreads. The strain came from soil in Russia's Yaroslavl region.

Genome comparisons against its closest relative fell well below the cut-offs for same-species status, confirming novelty. A fluorescent screening system flagged an unusual profile: growth stopped without triggering the bacterium's usual DNA-damage alarm. Chemical analysis pinned the activity on kinanthraquinone B, made by a gene cluster the strain apparently picked up from another organism. The compound class blocks bacterial DNA-handling enzymes, offering a scaffold possibly gentler on human cells.
pmc-13304804:
Wenjie Ning, Lingyu Hang, and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, licorice nanoparticles that carry herbal medicine through skin to treat eczema. Licorice decoctions naturally form such particles, but unruly assembly makes them unstable. By mixing water and alcohol extracts and boiling off the alcohol, the team produced uniform particles about two hundred nanometers wide.

Compared with plain decoction, the particles delivered all six tracked active compounds into skin far better. They slipped through follicles and lipid gaps on their own while nearby immune cells swallowed them, a dual-channel route boosting skin build-up. In eczema-model mice, treatment raised two key barrier proteins in the outer skin layer, tightening cell junctions. The work recasts a kitchen-style decoction as a well-described nanomedicine and a template for herbal skin products.
pmc-13306304:
Petronela Nechita coated packaging paper with modified xylan plus metal oxide particles in a 2026 materials study. Xylan, a plant fibre component, was acetylated with help from an ionic liquid to form a base that carries zinc and copper oxide particles.

One thin layer near 5 g/m2 on both sides raised water resistance, with surface angles reaching 83° and 97° for the two particle types in reported values. Coatings slowed a Bacillus bacterium and cut spore formation in a Penicillium fungus. The authors present the route as a promising step toward greener food packaging.
pmc-13306704:
Catalina Muñoz-Strale linked activity, muscle share and daily function in older Chileans in a 2026 survey study. A total of 129 community-living adults took part, with mean age 72.05 years in the reported sample.

Activity came from a standard questionnaire, body makeup from electrical impedance, and function from a timed stand-and-walk test, grip strength, heel bone scan and a health survey score. Total activity tied weakly to grip strength, with a correlation of 0.19 in the given figures. Muscle share did not carry the activity effect in mediation checks, so gains look modest and direct.
pmc-13306804:
Dingquan Huang and co-authors dissect in 2026 how a friendly root fungus protects gerbera plants against root rot. Roots from four groups, covering fungus alone, pathogen alone, both together, and untreated controls, were compared by gene activity profiling. The pathogen was Phytophthora cryptogea, and the protector was Piriformospora indica.

Nearly sixteen thousand genes changed activity across the comparisons, and hundreds coded for transcription factors that switch other genes on. One ERF family gene stood out across all comparisons; boosting it in tobacco leaves shrank pathogen lesions markedly. Plants holding both organisms switched on more defence and secondary chemistry genes than pathogen-only plants. Hormone and MAPK signalling also rose after colonisation. The authors present the work as a molecular map for breeding or treating gerbera against root rot.
pmc-13306904: A 2026 correction notice fixes a figure error in a 2016 rat study of diacerein protection against doxorubicin kidney harm. One panel was a zoomed-out copy of another despite differing labels, blamed on figure preparation mistakes. A replacement figure shows stained kidney cortex across control, treatment and drug groups with graded inflammation signals. The notice is short, carries an apology, and adds no new results, so readers should use the corrected figure only.
pmc-13307204:
Biniyam Tedla Mamo reported life-threatening skin peeling from phenobarbital in a young child in a 2026 case account. A six-year-old girl with epilepsy was referred with widespread shedding lesions covering eyes and mouth lining after starting the seizure drug.

Fever, red eyes, painful swallowing and dry cough accompanied skin loss over 90% of body surface in reported examination. Care stopped the drug and added intravenous antibiotics, steroids, twice-daily wound care, pain relief and feeding support. The authors stress fast recognition and drug withdrawal to limit harm from such reactions.
pmc-13307304:
Jhofree Einstein Briceño-Chavez linked household salt iodine to childhood anaemia in Peru in a 2026 survey study. Data from national family health rounds spanning 2014 to 2023 covered 110,561 children aged 6 to 59 months with valid blood and salt tests.

Anaemia meant altitude-adjusted haemoglobin under 11.0 g/dL, while weak salt iodisation meant under 15 ppm in the study definitions. Weighted rates, gaps and adjusted ratios compared homes by salt quality, place and wealth after allowing for age and sex. The work tests whether uneven salt programmes track uneven child blood health. The gaps by place and wealth show where salt checks and child care should go first in line.
pmc-13307704:
Mikayla Brown and co-authors study in 2026 gut symptoms in myalgic encephalomyelitis and chronic fatigue syndrome, an illness marked by deep fatigue, foggy thinking, and crashes after effort. They compared 116 patients with 80 matched controls across gut signs, 49 other symptoms, and blood markers of swelling.

Patients reported far more gut trouble than controls, and 53 percent had once been told they had irritable bowel syndrome, versus 8 percent of controls. Gut burden tracked with fatigue, pain, poor sleep, and flu like feelings in the patient group. A swelling marker also rose with gut burden, which points to a gut and immune link worth targeted study.
pmc-13309504:
Charles Wade and co-authors gather 2026 case data on a rare inherited disease that damages the white matter of the brain. Faults in the AARS2 gene cause the disease, which can mimic a related condition yet differs in genes and course. Fewer than 60 cases had been reported since 2014.

Fifteen new patients from several centers were added to 56 published cases, giving 71 people in total. Illness most often began in the late twenties with mental, mood, and thinking problems, followed by stiff movement and walking trouble. Most women affected also had early ovarian failure. Scans showed broad white matter change with a thin band linking the brain halves. The authors set out the full pattern to aid faster recognition.
pmc-13309904:
Rawan Aboud and co-authors review lab-grown mouth tissue for testing dental implant parts in a 2026 article. Implants anchor in bone well, but the soft tissue seal around the post guards against infection and gets far less study. Three-dimensional tissue models copy real mouth lining better than flat cell layers.

Searches of three databases screened over fifteen hundred records down to 14 studies using human tissue models at implant surfaces. All models paired surface cells with support cells and formed layered lining much like real mucosa. Some showed surface maturation over time. Gaps in shared methods stood out across studies. The authors map the field to guide tighter, comparable implant testing.
pmc-13310404:
Weihu Zhang and co-authors review scaffolds loaded with extracellular vesicles for spinal cord repair in a 2026 article. After the first impact, a second wave of harm follows: inflammation, chemical stress, nerve death, and insulation loss block recovery. Vesicles, tiny parcels shed by cells, carry healing signals but wash away fast and target poorly alone.

Placing vesicles inside scaffolds holds them at the injury and meters their release, with some scaffolds reacting to the injury environment. Reported gains include calmer inflammation, more nerve regrowth, renewed insulation, and better vessel growth. Large vesicle subtypes with roomy cargo get special attention. The authors map scaffold types and loading routes as a design guide.
pmc-13310504:
Laura M Periman and co-authors present two mite-driven eyelid cases that were first misread as other diseases in a 2026 article. Demodex blepharitis is chronic lid inflammation from mite overgrowth, and its signs overlap with common eye surface disorders. An expert panel has agreed on hallmark signs and first-line care.

The first case, a 75-year-old woman, showed collarettes, the waxy sleeves at lash bases the panel calls a sure sign, plus red lid margins. Treatment aimed at bacterial infection failed first. Re-reading the case under panel guidance led to lotilaner eye drops at 0.25 percent strength, the approved first-line therapy named in the report. A second misread case follows the same corrective path.
pmc-13310604:
Satoko Iwasawa and co-authors examine how Japan food safety intake limits are derived in a 2026 study. A tolerable daily intake sets the amount of a chemical judged safe to swallow each day for life. The mix of study types, safety margins, and harm thresholds behind those numbers had not been charted as a whole.

Ten trained reviewers coded 77 chemical risk reports from the Food Safety Commission of Japan, with 46 kept for final analysis under a standard template. Most limits, 73.9 percent of the set in the analysis, rested on animal studies with large safety margins of 100 to 1000. Human-based limits were fewer but carried smaller margins and higher values. The authors map where each evidence type dominates.
pmc-13311104:
Yaokang Xue and colleagues map proof on swallowing trouble after tube removal in sick children in a 2026 scoping review. The problem can cause lung infection, poor feeding, and longer hospital stays, yet child specific paths for checks and care are lacking. Past studies vary widely in how they define and time the issue.

Nine databases were searched through March 2026, yielding 15 studies, most recent and from China or Brazil. Reported rates ranged widely, from near one quarter to over two thirds of cases. Tube time, age, and a weaning score were the firmest predictors. No bedside tool had been checked against gold standard scope tests, a key gap.
pmc-13311204:
Yuexing Song and colleagues gather expert guidance on long term hyaluronic acid filler care in a 2026 paper. Juvéderm fillers are widely used for facial aging, yet proof and guidance over ten or more years of repeat care are scarce. Six seasoned clinicians shared written views and long treated cases.

Natural results over many cycles rest on three pillars in their account. Strong technique and deep anatomy knowledge come first, then right product choice by make, depth, and proof. Last comes long range planning: whole face review, a cautious start, mixed product plans, and photo tracking over time. Cases treated for a decade or more show the approach.
pmc-13311304:
Jocelyn Mueller and co-authors in 2026 present a survey of midlife women who swap prescribed drugs for cannabis to manage anxiety or low mood. The study asks what drives the swap for each condition.

The survey covered 172 women, of whom 88 swapped cannabis for antidepressants and 84 for anti-anxiety drugs. Both groups showed clear anxiety and low mood scores, and average early-life adversity scores passed four. Sleep trouble and alcohol use predicted swapping for both drug types. For the depression group, loneliness and lower schooling also played a part. The findings can guide safer counseling for women weighing this choice.
pmc-13311904:
Masaaki Yamamoto and co-authors report the 2026 case of robot-assisted salvage surgery for a rare esophageal sarcoma after chemoradiation. Sarcoma of the food pipe is extremely rare, and no standard treatment path exists.

The patient, an 82-year-old man, had trouble swallowing solids. Scans showed a mid-chest food pipe tumor with bulky lymph nodes pressing into the airway, so chemoradiation came first. The tumor and nodes shrank enough to allow surgery. A robot-assisted minimally invasive operation then removed part of the food pipe. The authors say this is the first such salvage case they know of for this tumor.
pmc-13312004:
Muhammad Farhan and colleagues report their 2026 case of a pseudoaneurysm in a rare groin artery branch after a heart catheter procedure, with a review of past cases. Such false aneurysms usually strike the main femoral artery.

The patient, an 86-year-old man, developed a right groin swelling after catheter work for cardioversion and ablation attempts. A first ultrasound missed it, but a CT vessel scan traced the sac to the superficial external pudendal artery. Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection closed it at once. The case backs CT checks when ultrasound is negative but suspicion stays, and shows the injection fix works even in odd locations.
pmc-13312504:
Sowmyashree Mayur Kaku writes a 2026 article arguing that the standard adverse childhood experiences framework fits rural India poorly. The ten-category tool, covering abuse, neglect, and household dysfunction, predicts lifelong mental and physical illness. It was built for wealthier settings and misses adversities that dominate poorer ones.

In rural India, where 65 percent of the country's children live, hardship grows from poverty, food insecurity, separation from parents, caste discrimination, and thin access to schooling and healthcare. Survey figures cited include 23 percent of women aged 20 to 24 married before 18 and domestic violence reported by over 30 percent of ever-married women. Kaku argues these structural and gendered harms cluster with weak nurturing environments and school dropout, and that frameworks for such settings must name them directly to guide prevention.
pmc-13313004:
Luis Martinez and co-authors publish a 2026 response to a letter faulting their crossover study of vibration anesthesia for injection pain. Two writers had raised doubts about the design, and the authors use the reply to defend their choices while granting where the study could be tightened.

They explain the trial was a real-world proof of concept. Every person received the plain procedure first and the DigiVibe vibration-assisted one second, so earlier vibration could not contaminate baseline pain scores. Pain fell a lot across all injection types, and for subcutaneous injections every single person reported less pain with vibration, a pattern the authors say order effects alone cannot explain. They accept that larger randomized runs, formal carryover checks over the five-minute gap, and a fuller account of anxiety would strengthen future work.
pmc-13313504:
Camillo Bechi Genzano and colleagues model, in a 2026 study, how the human immune system treats lab-grown insulin-producing islets, a cure hoped for in type 1 diabetes. Stem cell-derived islets from a patient's cells might dodge rejection, while donor-matched stranger cells likely cannot. Human evidence, though, was missing. The team transplanted self and foreign stem cell islets into mice carrying human immune systems. They examined the grafts fourteen to eighteen weeks later.

Foreign grafts drew heavy immune infiltration, cell proliferation, and scarring activity. Self grafts, by contrast, showed minimal infiltration and little fibrosis. They displayed features such as many glucagon-positive cells and cysts. Even when the researchers added self-reactive T cells known to target islet antigens, the self grafts stayed unmolested. The result is encouraging for personalized cell therapy. The authors caution, though, that their model cannot reproduce the spontaneous self-attack seen in diabetes.
pmc-13314104:
Aqsa Imtiaz and co-authors profile, in a 2026 study, two bacterial species carried by captive birds on farms in Kasur, Pakistan. Peafowl, pheasants, chukar partridges, turkeys, and quails supplied fecal samples, from which Escherichia coli and Campylobacter jejuni were cultured, confirmed by gene sequencing, and screened for virulence and drug resistance genes. Both organisms can move from birds to people, so their gene cargo matters beyond the farm.

Virulence genes proved widespread. In Campylobacter, two toxin genes appeared in every isolate, the motility gene in 80 percent, and a stress gene in 40 percent. In E. coli, an attachment gene was universal while toxin genes stayed at 10 to 20 percent. Resistance genes were highly prevalent in both species, and every E. coli isolate carried both beta-lactam and tetracycline resistance determinants. The authors argue that captive bird farms deserve routine molecular monitoring as part of public health protection.
pmc-13314204:
Peipei Li and colleagues test a muscle-made protein against sepsis damage to the heart in work published in 2026. Sepsis often weakens the heart muscle, a state with high death rates and no good therapy, and failing mitochondria sit at the center of the harm.

The protein, myonectin, also named CTRP15, guards the heart in other settings by calming inflammation, cell death, and scarring. The team made a lab-built form and gave it to mice before sepsis was induced by bacterial toxin or by gut puncture, and to newborn mouse heart cells in dishes. They then checked heart function and cell energy health, tracing the effect through the AdipoR1 and AMPK path named in the title. The work tests whether topping up a natural heart guard can shield the heart during sepsis.
pmc-13314404:
Mario Petretta, Giorgio Treglia, and Alberto Cuocolo introduce a journal research topic on brain connectomics in an editorial published in 2026. The field maps how brain areas link and pass signals, in health and in disease, and fresh imaging and network methods have pushed it ahead.

The editors thank the authors and reviewers who built the topic, named Brain connectomics, for work mapping brain connectivity in health and disease. They trace the rise of the terms connectome and connectomics to work by Sebastian Seung in 2012, as cited in the piece. Mapping these highways of signals, they write, shows how the brain harmonizes daily action. The collected papers span theory, methods, and clinical use, and the editors hope the set draws readers deeper into the field.
pmc-13314804:
Michael Griessmair and colleagues weigh bleeding risk from a platelet drug used during aneurysm care, in a 2026 report. Fixing a burst brain aneurysm from inside the vessel can need antiplatelet drugs, yet bleeding in a brain that just bled is a grave fear.

The team studied 99 patients treated from 2006 to 2024 for bleeding around the brain, with 51 given tirofiban and 48 matched controls, as counted in the report. Tirofiban courses were split into short ones under 7 days and long ones of 7 days or more. Bleeds were classed by a set scale as spontaneous or surgery-linked. Main endpoint data were on hand for 42 controls and 29 short-course patients, among others named in the report. The matched design gives a fairer read on whether long drug courses raise harm.
pmc-13315004:
Claudia Castro and colleagues study how five grapevine pathogens reshape the vine microbiome and chemistry, in work published in 2026. Vines are a high-value crop prone to vessel diseases from fungi and bacteria that cut yields and wine quality.

The five foes span trunk fungi such as Diplodia seriata and Eutypa lata and the bacterium Xylella fastidiosa, as listed in the report. For each infection the team sequenced bacterial and fungal markers and ran chromatography on phenolic compounds across vine tissues. They then asked whether chemistry shifts from one pathogen line up with microbe shifts in a local, specific way. Patterns that fingerprint each disease could aid early detection in vineyards, where pulling sick vines fast saves neighbors.
pmc-13315104:
Misganaw Gebrie Worku and colleagues study how forms of child undernutrition pair with common infections in Africa, in work published in 2026. Poor nutrition drives much illness in children under five, yet single and combined forms may not carry the same risk.

The team used health survey data from 2016 to 2024 across 27 sub-Saharan countries, with a weighted sample of 157,800 young children, as counted in the report. Nutrition was scored by a composite index that catches stunting, wasting, and underweight alone or together. Illness covered chest infections and diarrhea in the weeks before each survey. Layered models with country and village effects weighed each form. Sorting which failure pattern most raises infection odds can aim food aid where it cuts illness most.
pmc-13315504:
Md Mainuddin Hossain and co-authors screened plant chemicals from Ginkgo biloba in 2026 for dual action against herpes simplex virus type 1. The virus enters cells through two surface proteins, gB and gD, and has been linked to severe brain infection and to Alzheimer's disease, so blocking entry is an appealing strategy.

From databases the team took 39 plant chemicals and docked them against both viral proteins. Further computer checks covered drug-like behavior, toxicity, motion stability over time, and binding energy. The combined pipeline was used to rank which Ginkgo compounds might block both entry proteins at once, as a starting point for later lab work.
pmc-13315804:
Haixia Feng and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether a liver X receptor agonist can help newborn intestines regrow after bowel loss. Newborn short bowel syndrome often means gut failure and dependence on IV nutrition. Given the receptor's role in fat processing and mucosal repair, the team examined GW3965 in seven-day-old piglets after 75 percent bowel resection. They split six to control and four to treatment at 2 milligrams per kilogram per day by jugular vein over seven days.

Treatment improved gut barrier integrity and mucosal structure. Villus height rose in jejunum and ileum, crypt depth rose throughout the remnant gut and colon, serum gut toxin fell, and tight junction protein expression rose. Epithelial cell growth increased, and lab studies confirmed GW3965 stimulated growth of human intestinal organoids. It shifted colonic gene expression toward ileal identity. The authors suggest targeting this pathway may augment gut regeneration in short bowel syndrome.
pmc-13316304:
Kai Liu and colleagues present a 2026 dataset counting old and notable trees across Sichuan Province in China. Field teams visited all 183 county-level areas between 2016 and 2023 and logged each tree under a shared national standard.

The files hold 71,578 single tree records with 24 fields each, from species, age, and height to slope, soil, vigor, and local history or culture notes. One file gives the blank survey form with guidance, one holds the raw records, and one sums counts by city, growth site, age band, and ten other angles. Researchers can use the set to compare regions, study how trees, land, and people interact, and track how these valued populations change over time.
pmc-13316504:
Liang Liu and colleagues present a 2026 laboratory protocol for making more heart muscle cells and vessel lining cells from human stem cells, helped by placental growth factor. The factor normally drives heart and vessel growth before birth, and the method borrows that push in the dish.

Steps guide stem cell culture, coating plates with Matrigel, and steering cells toward heart or vessel fates with the factor added. The authors report yields two to two and a half times higher than standard methods, gained by boosting growth and fate change in early parent cells. Labs studying heart development or building cell supplies for research can follow the recipe and adapt its timing and doses.
pmc-13316604:
Clifford M. Marks leads a diagnostic study, published in 2026, comparing six large language models as screeners for missed diagnostic opportunities in emergency care. Electronic trigger tools already flag records at higher risk of harm, yet expert chart review is slow and many flagged cases yield no missed opportunity.

Two established emergency department trigger cohorts provided the test material. Models were judged against an adjudicated reference standard for sensitivity, specificity and predictive values. The authors also compared model judgements with those of individual physician reviewers. Such detail matters because a model used in safety work must fit human review, not just score well overall. Real-world record sets like these remain scarce in published evaluations.
pmc-13316704:
M García-Piqueras and a Spanish team report 2026 findings on pigeon medicine. Heavy use of nitroimidazole drugs in racing and show pigeons has blunted their power against Trichomonas gallinae, a parasite that causes a major pigeon disease. They sampled birds across eastern Spain to measure both infection and drug response.

Of 220 pigeons from 11 lofts, 63.6 percent carried the parasite in the sampled birds. Lab tests on 42 isolates found nearly half needed high drug levels to die, a pattern spread across most lofts. Birds bred for Pica contests carried harder-to-kill strains, and past metronidazole exposure linked with tougher parasites. The authors call for proven treatment plans, tighter loft hygiene, and new drugs before resistance spreads further.
pmc-13317304:
Esther Giehl-Brown and co-authors test, in a 2026 cohort study, whether waiting at least six weeks after drug therapy before liver surgery for spread colon cancer lowers complications without hurting cancer control. The best gap has been debated by surgeons.

The German center's records held 159 patients operated between 2018 and 2022, split at a 42-day wait. Serious complication scores hit 48.7 percent of early-surgery patients versus 31.3 percent of those who waited in the raw counts, and adjustment kept the wait protective, strongest for big liver removals. Survival and liver recurrence showed no clear penalty for waiting. The team backs the longer pause for complex cases, pending prospective proof.
pmc-13317404:
Qianqian Yu and co-authors pooled, in a 2026 analysis, genetic studies on four genes suspected of shaping risk for high myopia, the severe form of short-sightedness sweeping East Asia. Single letter changes in these genes might flag who needs early watching.

Searching two databases through December 2025 gathered 15 articles covering eight variants across the GJD2, ZC3H11B, MMP1, and MMP9 genes. One GJD2 variant, rs3743123, linked with lower overall risk of high myopia in the pooled math. All four ZC3H11B variants leaned the same protective way. The two MMP variants showed no clear signal in this summary. Larger studies and lab work must confirm the leads before screening use.
pmc-13318904:
Min Xu and colleagues present a 2026 multi-method study of oridonin, a natural plant compound, against cervical cancer. Network pharmacology, gene expression data, and single-cell sequencing were combined. Docking and molecular dynamics simulations tested binding. Laboratory experiments in cancer cell lines checked the predictions.

Analysis found 25 core targets tied to the shape-changing process called EMT. The PI3K/AKT pathway stood out in the enrichment results. Single-cell data placed that pathway mainly in epithelial tumour cells. Simulations suggested oridonin binds AKT1 favourably. In dishes, the compound slowed cancer cell growth, movement, and invasion. It triggered cell death and suppressed the shape change by dampening PI3K/AKT signalling. The authors call for animal studies next.
pmc-13319104:
Zhizhao Chang and colleagues present a 2026 Bayesian meta-analysis of trials testing protein plus probiotic supplements in adults. Protein alone is a standard aid for muscle adaptation. Probiotics might improve nutrient use and recovery, making the pairing attractive. Twenty randomised trials with 679 participants met the inclusion rules.

Physical performance improved under the combined supplements. The pooled estimate was a Hedges' g of 0.45, with its interval running from 0.21 to 0.67 in their model. Body composition barely moved, with an estimate near zero. Signals favoured muscle strength, endurance, and lean mass in particular. The authors caution that studies varied and quality was uneven. More rigorous trials should test whether benefits hold across strains, protein types, and populations.
pmc-13319204:
Hsun-Ming Hu leads a large team in a 2026 study of a sharp sea level rise near the end of an ice age about 340,000 years ago. Sea level rose as fast as about five meters per hundred years in that event, yet dated ocean records are too sparse to pin down why the melt was so fast.

A dated cave deposit from northern Italy gives a firm time line that the team lines up with ocean records from the North Atlantic. Their reading is that slow melt kept ocean flow weak and let heat build up below the surface. When flow picked up again, that stored heat sped up further ice loss.
pmc-13319404:
Rui Guo and co-authors study life timing in seven frog and toad types on Hainan Island in a 2026 article. Age at first breeding and total life span shape how each type splits its years between growth and making young. Warm steady rainforest life may favor a slow pace, with late breeding and long lives.

Most types first bred at age three and lived five to nine years in total. One river frog bred at age four and lived longer than the rest. Most split their years about half for growth and half for breeding, though two types spent more years growing. Stable warmth and rich food may let these animals take their time.
pmc-13319704:
Cayla Vila and colleagues present, in 2026, a diagnostic case involving a 77-year-old man who developed crusted scalp plaques four weeks after deep brain stimulation surgery for Parkinson's disease. The operation placed leads through two small frontal incisions, with wires tunnelled under the scalp to the chest. Skin complications after such surgery are uncommon but can threaten the implanted hardware.

At his first programming visit he felt well, with normal vital signs and healed incisions. Examination showed sun-damaged skin and thick golden-yellow and brown crusts on the crown, ringed by a red patch that extended over the tunnelled wires. The plaques lifted easily to reveal intact moist skin. The authors walk readers through a differential that includes erosive pustular dermatosis, sun-related growths, contact allergy and bacterial infections.
pmc-13320104:
Hanan Khalil and co-authors guide how to grade proof in umbrella reviews in a 2026 article on reviews of reviews. Such overviews pool many past reviews to guide big calls, yet grading trust across overlapping and clashing pools stays thorny. Past habits were mapped to find gaps, then grading frames were set side by side on fit, scale, and handling of clashes.

The best known grading frame suits trial proof but leans on personal calls and fits watch based overviews poorly. Score frames built on set number cut offs scale better and repeat more cleanly, though they need tuning by study type. Three traps get named advice, covering shared base studies, clashing trust grades, and clear pooling of proof.
pmc-13320504:
Salome Häuselmann and colleagues compare brain shape in a 2026 scan study of long-term pain that has no clear single cause. Thirty patients with chronic primary pain and 30 matched healthy adults had brain scans, pain tests, mood and life questionnaires, and saliva checks for stress markers. The aim was to link brain form to the wider burden of lasting pain.

Patients showed local changes in how the cortex folds, with more folding in left frontal areas and shallower grooves in right frontal and nearby regions. Links between brain wiring and daily traits were weak once strict checks were applied. A joint analysis still tied spread out brain patterns to combined pain and life measures.
pmc-13321204:
Worapan Sitthithaworn and Wullapa Jittachai build a DNA test to identify a prized plant cultivar in a 2026 study. Garcinia schomburgkiana, called Madan in Thailand, feeds food and cosmetic markets, and its Hero Green cultivar is valued for large fruit and factory use. Look-alike cultivars make raw material checks hard by eye.

Gene regions from chloroplast and nucleus were read across Hero Green and two other types. Chloroplast marks varied little, but one nuclear stretch held a single letter change unique to Hero Green. A melting test built on that change separated the cultivar cleanly, with a detection limit of 0.01 nanograms per microlitre. The cheap, fast assay suits factory quality control.
pmc-13321804:
Helen Helen and co-authors study why customers accept human-like AI in digital banking in a 2026 survey. Banks add AI to speed service and tailor offers, yet acceptance lags in high risk money settings where trust is vital. Survey data from 350 digital banking users were modelled to test trust, human-like traits, attitude, and social influence.

Trust and human-like traits each raised both attitude and the intent to use AI banking. Attitude was the strongest single predictor of intent. Social influence, though, did not clearly change the link between attitude and intent. Designing AI that feels trustworthy and personable may matter more than peer pressure for uptake in banking.
pmc-13322604:
Sangeeta Dhanger and co-authors compare two pain methods for frozen shoulder treatment in a 2026 randomised trial. Manipulation under anaesthesia stretches a stiff shoulder, usually aided by a steroid injection into the joint. The trial tested a pericapsular nerve group block instead in 130 patients aged 18 to 75 with stage 2 or 3 frozen shoulder.

Pain scores were lower in the block group at every check, from 15 minutes to 24 hours. At 15 minutes, mean pain was 4.1 in the block group against 5.2 in the steroid group on the study scale. Movement range and a shoulder pain and disability index were also better at 24 hours after the block, which supports it as the stronger option here.
pmc-13322804:
Meiyi Su and co-authors lay out the design of a multicentre trial of a traditional Chinese pill for small vessel heart disease in a 2026 protocol article. Coronary microvascular disease causes angina despite open main arteries and is often missed or undertreated. The Shexiang Tongxin dropping pill has shown protective signs in early work, but firm randomised proof is lacking.

Patients will be randomised evenly to the pill or a matched placebo for 12 weeks, with diagnosis set by stress ultrasound imaging. The main outcome is change in peak oxygen uptake on exercise testing. The trial also builds an AI assisted ultrasound tool to improve detection and sorting of this hard to spot condition.
pmc-13323004:
Chirapat Ukachoke examines whether conscious pain itself does causal work in the brain, in a 2026 neuroscientific analysis. The study sorts neural and behavioural events before, during and after a pain sensation and its awareness, asking which of them the sensation could shape.

Events before or at the same time as the sensation cannot be effects of it, and later events that carry no felt content may also run untouched. Acts that use felt content, such as experiencing, remembering or reporting pain, do depend on the sensation and its character. The author casts qualia as higher-level factors in stable counterfactual links, supplying information that neural circuits then carry into action.
pmc-13323304:
Na Yu and Fengqiang Wang present a pulmonary embolism case where heparin failure warned of a dangerous reaction, in a 2026 case report. Their patient, a 50-year-old man, also had deep vein thrombosis and a mass in the right ventricle.

Even as intravenous heparin doses climbed, clotting tests never reached target, and two episodes of instability on days 3 and 6 needed clot-busting rescue while clots grew. On day 8, falling platelets and a high clinical score pointed to heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, confirmed by antibody testing. Switching to argatroban hit target quickly, and later rivaroxaban followed platelet recovery. Three-month checks showed major clot clearing and a normal heart.
pmc-13323504:
Lin Chen and a large team build a spectral method to read plant traits in a rare tree under shade, reported in 2026. Young Hopea hainanensis, an endangered species, needs shade management in cultivation and restoration, yet changing light distorts leaf spectra and weakens standard retrieval models.

Their framework joins scale normalisation of spectra with a hybrid model mixing radiative transfer physics and deep learning. Chlorophyll retrieval reached high accuracy, while nitrogen stayed hard to recover from visible and near-infrared light alone in their tests. A new carbon-based index tracked measured dry leaf density in a consistent trend. The authors present the method as non-destructive monitoring for shaded nursery stock.
pmc-13323804:
Lukas Sveikata and co-authors relate long-term blood pressure swings to brain injury in cerebral amyloid angiopathy, in a 2026 prospective memory clinic study. Their cohort held 102 participants, 52 with probable amyloid angiopathy and mild cognitive symptoms, with pressure variability drawn from a median of twelve clinic readings over five years.

Higher systolic variability tracked worse white matter integrity on diffusion imaging in a dose-like pattern, independent of mean pressure and other risks. Amyloid angiopathy strengthened that link, and variability also tied to lobar lacunes, cortical microinfarcts and later cognitive decline in their models. The authors argue that steady pressure control may matter beyond average pressure in this fragile vessel disease.
pmc-13324104:
Sabrinna Wulandari and co-authors tested a greener way to recover value from red ginseng marc, the residue left after hot water extraction. Their 2026 study used dimethyl ether as a solvent, tuning temperature, pressure, and extraction time with response surface methodology. Conventional methods demand harsh conditions and extra solvent removal, raising costs, while the marc still holds useful lipids and bioactives.

At the best setting, 333 K, 7 MPa, and 80 minutes, yield reached 3.37%, with total ginsenoside content of 4.22 mg per gram of dry marc and strong antioxidant activity. The dimethyl ether oil beat ethanol and hexane extracts on antioxidant activity and fatty acid content, and it could be drawn directly from wet marc without prior drying. The authors highlight dimethyl ether as an energy-efficient solvent for food and cosmetic uses of ginseng oil.
pmc-13324304:
Allyson Quinn Ryan, Johannes Soltwedel and Carl D Modes present a topological skeleton tool for shape analysis, in a 2026 methods paper. Simple measures such as sphericity miss the detail of complex forms, so their software, napari-toska, turns shape asymmetry into a network for measurement.

Global neighbourhood rules, classic network metrics and spatial feature embedding build a profile for each segmented object, ready for direct reading or later classification. The tool follows shapes over time, picks out network features that separate experimental phenotypes and keeps true scale through absolute spatial measures. Emergence or loss of network cycles can even flag segmentation errors, a built-in quality check for imaging pipelines in biology and beyond.
pmc-13324704:
Fei Xu proposes a smarter library recommendation system that pushes resources to readers before they search. The 2026 paper diagnoses a dual dilemma: current services perceive user needs imprecisely and recommend passively, relying on single-dimensional borrowing data and collection metadata alone. The proposed system instead fuses user profiling with knowledge graphs that embed disciplinary ontologies and citation networks, then triggers proactive pushes through a gated aggregation mechanism.

Tested on a university library dataset, the method reached 16.02% on Recall@10 and 11.64% on NDCG@10, beating the best baselines by 4.87 and 5.23 percentage points. Proactive push acceptance hit 38.9%, far above random pushing, and ablation tests showed the knowledge graph module contributed most to accuracy, by mining cross-domain links that metadata methods miss. The author presents the design as a template for context-aware, proactive library services.
pmc-13325304:
Ivan A. Garces and team present a case report and literature review on Cutibacterium acnes infection of the acromioclavicular joint. Their 2026 paper pairs a single clinical case with a survey of the published reports on this uncommon joint illness. The pairing aims to give doctors a fuller picture than a lone case can offer, placing one patient's course against what prior reports have told.

By joining case detail with report synthesis, the paper addresses the test and care questions that arise when a rare organism infects a small joint. Readers gain both the specifics of an individual presentation and the patterns, pitfalls, and treatment considerations distilled from earlier cases. The authors frame the work as a practical reference for recognizing and managing a rare illness that is easy to overlook.
pmc-13325804:
This notice is an Expression of Concern issued by the journal for a 2010 paper by Compagnin and team. It covers cell proliferation and cell cycle changes in oesophageal p53-mutated cancer cells treated with cisplatin plus photodynamic therapy. The 2026 notice, agreed between the editor-in-chief and Wiley, follows third-party concerns and a study of Figure 9. It alerts readers to image problems while leaving the paper in place, with no new research findings of its own.

The team found duplications between two pellet band pairs in Figure 9, one for the cytochrome c panels and one for the BCL-2 panels. The authors were asked to comment and provide supporting data, but the original data were no longer available after years elapsed. Although the concerns cannot be fully resolved, the journal considers the paper's overall conclusions unaffected, and issued the notice to inform and alert readers rather than retracting the work.
pmc-13327404:
Aninda Debnath and co-authors pool Indian evidence on anxiety in people living with HIV in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. They searched four large databases through November 2024 for studies that used checked tools to measure anxiety. Fifteen studies covering 5,336 people met their rules.

Across studies, about 36 percent of people living with HIV had anxiety. Hospital-based studies gave 39 percent and community studies 23 percent, and women reached 46 percent against 36 percent for men. The measuring tool mattered a lot: self-report scales gave rates near 48 to 49 percent, while structured interviews gave far lower figures. The authors call for routine mental health checks in HIV care, with care in choosing how anxiety is measured.
pmc-13327804:
Dongchan Kim and co-authors find warning signs for cancer spread after chemoradiation in head and neck cancer in a 2026 study. They reviewed 210 patients with squamous cell cancer treated with focused radiation plus chemotherapy between 2009 and 2020. Two features stood out: spread into lower neck nodes at the start, and an incomplete response after treatment.

Distant spread appeared in 51 patients, 24.3 percent of the group, over a median follow-up of 59.8 months. Lower neck involvement roughly doubled the odds of distant spread, and an incomplete response raised them further, with both also tied to shorter survival without spread. Checking these two signs could help teams pick patients for closer watching or added drug treatment.
pmc-13327904:
Xinran Wu and a large team strengthen gel microtubes for growing mammalian cells in a 2026 study. Large-scale cell production matters for therapy making, yet current reactors suffer clumping, shear damage, and uneven batches. Their earlier alginate tubes grew cells well but lacked grip points for anchorage-dependent cells and broke too easily.

Weaving collagen nanofibers through the alginate mesh fixed both faults, giving strength plus adhesion sites in tubes kept at 400 micrometers wide for good nutrient flow. The hybrid tubes kept cells alive and dividing fast, reaching yields of 5 × 108 cells per milliliter in the reported tests. The design points toward steadier, larger cell manufacturing.
pmc-13330104:
Xingtong Li and colleagues hunt blood markers of poor tissue flow after stroke clot removal in a 2026 study. Some patients regain vessel flow yet brain tissue still starves, a pattern called no-reflow. The team profiled blood chemicals a day after successful treatment in 34 patients with large vessel blockage, 19 without no-reflow and 15 with it.

In total, 29 blood chemicals differed between the groups, most of them phosphatidylcholine types in the reported results. One type stood out and sorted patients well in accuracy checks. Pathways for fat-like membrane chemicals looked most disturbed. The authors suggest such markers could flag high-risk patients early and point to new treatment targets.
pmc-13330804:
Darya K. Polyanskaya and colleagues report the crystal structure of a modified BODIPY dye in a 2026 article. BODIPY dyes glow brightly, absorb strongly, and stay stable under light, which suits probes, imaging, solar cells, and light-based therapy. The new dye swaps the usual ring at its centre for a linked double thiophene unit.

Inside each molecule, weak carbon to sulfur contacts fold the shape into a six-membered ring pattern, the analysis shows. Between molecules, carbon to fluorine contacts link the whole set into a three-dimensional network. Centre swaps of this kind have drawn little study so far. Knowing the packing helps tune glow colour and strength for later uses.
pmc-13332004:
Jonathan Dounel and colleagues test a staged care pathway for fatty liver disease linked to poor metabolic health in adults with type 2 diabetes. The pathway sorts scarring risk in steps using tests that need no biopsy, aiming to find advanced scarring early. The team checked how it held up over two years against a scan that gauges liver stiffness. Participants were adults aged 50 to 79 drawn from walk-in clinics.

Of 626 people assessed at baseline, 209 returned for follow-up and entered the follow-up set. About seven in ten had the fatty liver condition at baseline, and roughly one in five had marked scarring. Each visit combined a blood-based scarring score, a second liver scan, and the stiffness scan. The study shows clinicians how well staged tests that need no biopsy track real change over time in a high-risk diabetes group.
pmc-13332404:
