Jamil Muqtadir and colleagues pooled United States hospital studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis from 2026 of rapid blood culture panels. These multiplex PCR panels name bloodstream germs and resistance markers within hours instead of the day or more that standard culture needs.

Twenty studies covering 4,587 inpatients with bloodstream infections met the review's rules. Adding the panels cut the time to suitable antibiotic treatment by 17.28 hours on average and shortened hospital stay by 1.25 days. Death rates did not shift significantly, with an odds ratio of 1.04, and cost results were also inconclusive. The authors conclude the panels speed correct therapy and support antibiotic stewardship, but only when clinical teams act promptly on the fast results.
pmc-13332604:
Alan N Engelman reviews 2026 how HIV-1 can resist dolutegravir without changes in the integrase enzyme itself. Modern HIV maintenance therapy often pairs one or two nucleoside reverse transcriptase blockers with a second-generation integrase strand transfer blocker. Dolutegravir, a leading drug in that class, is used worldwide. First-generation blockers in the class fail readily when amino acids near the integrase active site change, while second-generation drugs raise a higher genetic barrier to resistance.

Engelman focuses on resistance routes that bypass integrase altogether, a less familiar but clinically important path. The review explains how the virus's integration step works: integrase joins viral DNA ends to host chromosome DNA. It then weighs evidence for non-integrase mechanisms that blunt dolutegravir despite an intact target. Clinicians gain a fuller resistance map, helping them read treatment failure and choose next steps when standard integrase mutations are absent.
pmc-13333204:
Daniel Schrednitzki and colleagues report a 2026 case of peroneal nerve palsy from compression by an intramuscular synovial cyst. This nerve disorder is the most common lower limb nerve disorder, usually caused by external squeezing over the leg bone head where soft tissue protection is poor. Internal squeezing by cysts is unusual. Here a deep leg nerve was squeezed by an extraneural muscle cyst with acute symptoms.

A 45-year-old man developed sudden foot drop after knee distortion. Nerve studies showed severe axonal injury, and MRI revealed a multilobular cystic mass about 7.8 by 2 by 2.3 centimetres inside the peroneus longus muscle, arising from the tibioperoneal joint. Surgery removed the mucinous cyst completely including its stalk, and tissue examination confirmed a ganglion cyst without malignancy. Sensation and motor function recovered progressively within five days after surgery.
pmc-13333504:
Huan Liu and colleagues review in 2026 whether veterinary macrolide antibiotics still deserve a place against Streptococcus agalactiae. The bacterium is a persistent cause of bovine mastitis that drains herd productivity and milk quality. Lab data say many isolates stay susceptible. But they warn the picture is murkier than the petri dish suggests.

The review weighs susceptibility results from regions against the resistance gear in circulation, above all the erm(B) determinant. Drug-level evidence is friendlier: macrolides reach the udder well, persist in milk, and distribute into tissue, giving a plausible basis for efficacy. Against that stand obstacles. No mastitis-specific breakpoints exist, genotype and phenotype often disagree, drug rules restrict use, and milk residues raise concerns. Almost no trial data tie treatment to cure in this pathogen. The authors call for mastitis drug targets, outcome studies split by pathogen, and resistance surveillance before macrolides get a firmer role.
pmc-13334404:
Mar Álvarez and co-authors used CRISPR editing to remove a harmful pseudoexon from the PCCA gene in a 2026 gene therapy study. A deep variant switches this 84-letter segment fully into the gene's message, causing propionic acidemia, a dangerous metabolic disorder.

Working in liver cells, including a model homozygous for the activating variant, the team applied CRISPR-Cas12a cutting to delete the pseudoexon region or disable the splice enhancer the variant strengthens. Both routes raised activity of the propionyl-CoA carboxylase enzyme, with the enhancer-targeting guide performing best. Restoring normal splicing this way is a proof of concept for patients with the pseudoexon variant, and possibly for others whose weak enzyme variants could benefit from a modest activity boost.
pmc-13335104:
Sebastian Spencer and colleagues review 2026 IV iron safety and efficacy in people with kidney disease not yet needing dialysis who are iron deficient but not anaemic. The role of IV iron in this group remains uncertain. Iron deficiency in kidney disease is common and linked to impaired cell energy function, fatigue, thinking decline, and restless legs syndrome, even when haemoglobin levels are normalized.

Databases were searched for random trials and cohort studies involving adults with kidney disease not yet needing dialysis and kidney filter rate below sixty. Patients received IV iron compared with oral iron, placebo, or no treatment. The primary outcome was change in iron levels. Secondary outcomes included heart and vessel events, infections, physical function, symptoms, thinking, and quality of life. Six studies met the inclusion criteria, with pooled trial analyses showing improved iron levels.
pmc-13335404:
Antonio Di Lorenzo and co-authors tracked how a live flu vaccine affects children's daily wellbeing in a 2026 prospective study from Japan. No data existed on quality of life after the live-attenuated influenza vaccine, which children receive as a nasal spray.

Guardians of children aged 4 to 15 answered daily surveys for 16 days starting the day before vaccination, using standard EuroQoL youth measures plus a health scale and symptom reports. The final analysis included 92 children who completed at least half the surveys including days 7 and 14. About three-quarters of the children, 78 in the report's count, had at least one side effect, generally mild. Still, 30 had symptoms that disrupted daily activities, and one serious case reached an emergency room. Health scores dipped for two days, then recovered.
pmc-13336904:
Sungwoo Eo and co-authors teach an electronic nose to admit uncertainty in a 2026 sensor study. Sulfur gases behind bad breath and pollution are chemically alike, so metal-oxide sensors often confuse them. Their 15-channel array decorates oxide nanofibers with platinum, palladium, iridium, and cobalt catalysts, made by a flash light process.

Data across gases, doses, temperatures, and humidity trained a deep ensemble, a team of learning models that vote together. It names the gas, estimates its amount, and reports how unsure it is at the same time. A nose that knows its limits is safer for breath screening and field monitoring, where a confident wrong answer costs most.
pmc-13337004:
Xunjun Li and a large team uncover a self-amplifying loop that helps stomach cancer invade nerves in a 2026 study. Perineural invasion predicts poor outcomes, but the tumor-nerve conversation behind it was murky. Data mining plus surgical samples flagged high CXCL8 and VCAM1 in invasion-positive tumors, tied to spread and shorter survival.

Experiments showed CXCL8 raises a neuronal factor, MIF, which binds VCAM1 on tumor cells and drives still more CXCL8. That loop fuels tumor growth and invasion. Blocking the CXCL8-VCAM1 link or deleting MIF only in neurons shrank tumors and nerve invasion in mouse models. The axis offers both warning markers and drug targets for an aggressive cancer pattern.
pmc-13337704:
Umar G. Adamu leads a 2026 pooled analysis on timing of valve replacement for severe aortic narrowing without symptoms. Whether to operate early or watch closely has stayed unsettled. The analysis compares early aortic valve replacement against clinical surveillance.

Eight studies through August 2025 entered the pool, with 3,086 patients in total. Four were randomized trials and four used matched comparison groups. Early surgery linked to fewer major cardiac events and lower death rates, both overall and from heart causes. Hospital stays for heart failure and sudden death were also less common. Major vascular bleeding was more frequent after early surgery, so benefit came with a clear trade-off.
pmc-13338304:
Vasu Mehta, Khushwinder Singh, and Abdul Ahad study the paddy black beetle in Himalayan rice in a 2026 field study. The soil-dwelling pest has grown into a serious threat in mid-hill fields. Seasonal timing, rice variety resistance, and control options were tested together.

Beetles showed up as July ended and numbers topped out as August began, damaging up to 48.4 percent of tillers in the reported counts. Warm nights, humidity, and rain tracked with buildup. Among 60 rice types none was highly resistant, though two showed moderate resistance. Chlorpyrifos gave the lowest damage and highest yield among options, while plant-based sprays offered weaker but gentler alternatives.
pmc-13339604:
Nihan Izat and colleagues build virtual twin drug models for people with obesity in a 2026 study. A cholesterol byproduct ratio in blood marks activity of liver enzyme CYP3A4, which handles many drugs. Weight loss surgery changes that activity over time.

Blood marker data before surgery in 54 people and two years after bypass in 30 people fed personal models as reported. Predicted enzyme levels landed within twofold of biopsy truth in 85 percent of cases. Drug exposure forecasts matched observed values at a similar rate. Twins revised after surgery can guide dosing as bodies change.
pmc-13340404:
Keeping midge infestations in check inside a frog facility is the goal of a 2026 study by Maximilian Schwarzbach and Bastian Popper. Their Chironomid Quantification Tool uses AI-assisted image analysis to count adult non-biting midges in the aquatic frog housing that holds Xenopus laevis colonies.

The tool judged infestation levels and treatment effects within about a minute. Raising water exchange changed water chemistry but only modestly lowered midge numbers. Treatment with Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis instead wiped out adult midges almost fully within six weeks, with no harm seen in the animals. Objective counting like this helps facilities protect welfare, hygiene, and experiment quality.
pmc-13341004:
Ramtin Khanipour and colleagues reported an alpha-gal syndrome case in 2026 where meat allergy may have triggered dangerous heart rhythms. Alpha-gal syndrome causes delayed allergy after eating red meat following tick bites, with Lone Star and Ixodes ticks the common North American culprits. Most cases stay mild, but some progress to severe anaphylaxis.

A 64 year old man with coronary artery disease arrived with chest pain and suffered two episodes of ventricular fibrillation with successful resuscitation in hospital. After discharge he had episodic palpitations, belly pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea. An immunologist later diagnosed alpha-gal syndrome and raised its link to the fibrillation events. The case urges allergy workup after unexplained cardiac events.
pmc-13341304:
A small RNA that reins in an oxidative enzyme lessens bleeding after stroke reopening, in a 2026 rat study by Qiu-Yi Jiang and colleagues. Hemorrhagic transformation after recanalization worsens outcomes, so the team modeled it with 205 high-blood-sugar rats after 5 hours of artery blockage.

Giving a miR-383-5p mimic before recanalization suppressed NOX4 in tissue around the infarct and eased swelling, infarct size, and bleeding severity. Cell experiments under oxygen and glucose deprivation backed the protective pattern, with less reactive oxygen and neuronal injury. Shielding the blood-brain barrier this way could matter for patients treated after long blockages.
pmc-13341604:
Training body and brain together beats splitting them, in a 2026 randomized trial by Amanda Scott's team. The 12-week study assigned 107 young adults, average age 25, to cycling only, cycling with simultaneous cognitive training, or separate physical and cognitive sessions.

Cycling ran at 70 to 80% of each person's maximal heart rate, twice weekly, while cognitive work used a flexible multi-domain computer program. Fitness and cognitive test sets were scored before and after under intention-to-treat analysis. Doing both at once promises time savings for young adults facing heavy cognitive demands, and the trial design isolates whether simultaneity itself adds anything beyond doing both.
pmc-13341804:
Why self-driving tourists choose electric cars is modeled by Zhenzhen Xu and colleagues in the 2026 survey study. Using an extended planned behavior framework, the team surveyed 545 residents across six Chinese cities and tested the model with structural equation methods.

Attitude, social norms, and perceived control each lifted intention to rent or drive electric vehicles on trips. Price value worked through attitude, while range, charger availability, and incentives worked through perceived control, with range anxiety as a key mediator. Gender split the pathways: attitude drove men more, other routes mattered more for women. Destinations chasing low-carbon tourism get levers beyond price cuts.
pmc-13345904:
Preston J. Anderson and colleagues showed in 2026 that beta-arrestin proteins form liquid-like droplets that govern how a huge family of cell receptors works. G-protein-coupled receptors steer nearly every aspect of physiology and are among the most common drug targets, yet how beta-arrestins juggle so many different jobs at these receptors was unclear.

The team found that beta-arrestins undergo liquid-liquid phase separation, clustering near receptors to control processes such as internalisation and signalling. Condensation proved specific to visual and beta-arrestins, and breaking it changed receptor behaviour. The finding reframes these adaptor proteins as dynamic compartments rather than simple switches, opening new ways to tune receptor drugs.
pmc-13346804:
Yeshambel Asmare Mengist and co-authors built in 2026 a speech emotion spotter for Amharic, a language with few data sets where emotion spotting lags. Better emotion spotting could lift both human-computer links and talk aids. Yet most systems train on well-resourced languages.

The team made a data set of 1,650 three-second Amharic clips labelled as anger, fear, joy, neutral, or sad. They joined spectrogram images with local sound traits such as pitch, energy, and cepstral coefficients in a neural net. Spectral cleaning and wavelet denoising sharpened the signals. The model shows how careful trait design can bring emotion-aware tools to languages that mainstream work often skips.
pmc-13347304:
Mikhail Kuznetsov, Artemiy Okhotin, and Dmitry Sergeev set out a trial protocol, published in 2026, for Telegram chatbot support to help heart attack patients stop smoking. Many patients relapse soon after discharge where follow-up is thin. So a regional hospital in Russia will enrol adult smokers who use Telegram and split them evenly between routine advice with a passive bot and the same advice with active support.

The active bot sends motivation notes, craving tools, an SOS option, weekly check-ins, and relapse plans over six months, starting with recruitment in January 2026. The main outcome is 30-day abstinence at six months, checked by a blinded assessor and a relative, with results expected after follow-up ends in October 2026.
pmc-13347804:
Maemu P. Gededzha and a large team track COVID antibodies in blood and spit over a year in South Africa, in a cohort study from 2026. Sixty-seven confirmed cases from a point-of-care study gave 254 blood and 214 spit samples across entry, six, nine. Twelve months, tested for antibodies to spike and core proteins of the virus.

Spike antibodies lasted twelve months in most people, at 93.5 percent in blood and 90 percent in spit in the reported shares. Paired samples agreed in 80.5 percent of spike tests. Links between spit and blood levels were weak yet real, and vaccination after entry lifted blood spike levels against unvaccinated peers. While over half the vaccinated group later caught the virus again.
pmc-13349204:
Yukti K Agrawal and Suraj Kanase test watching-and-copying therapy after stroke. Their trial appeared in 2026. It targets the swinging leg gait. Thirty patients showed that gait pattern. They were split evenly into two groups. One group added action observation to standard physiotherapy. Videos showed normal gait patterns. Patients then tried to imitate them. The other group got physiotherapy alone. Footprints and motion software scored each walk.

The watching group gained more on every score. Gait symmetry improved the most in that group. Swing-out angle shrank further there. Strides grew longer and steps grew narrower. Each gain cleared the set significance bar. Mirrored learning is a cheap add-on. It helps the brain relearn straight walking. Daily mobility lifts as a result.
pmc-13349904:
Rong Wan and colleagues fed fermented mulberry leaves to weaned piglets in a 2026 feeding trial. Two hundred piglets aged 28 days were split into five groups, receiving a plain diet or the same diet with 5, 10, 15, or 20 percent fermented leaves over 28 days.

Growth did not differ clearly between groups, but feed efficiency improved at the lowest and highest doses. Diarrhoea fell in every supplemented group, most sharply at 15 percent, where gut acid levels and helpful fermentation products also rose. Gut microbe profiles shifted as well. Fermented leaves, prepared with bacteria and enzymes, could give pig producers a cheaper, gut-friendly feed ingredient.
pmc-13351904:
Jiefei Han and co-authors ask in 2026 whether TROP2 antibody-drug conjugates are ready for lung cancer that resists EGFR drugs. Targeted EGFR drugs changed first care for advanced disease, but resistance always comes. Standard chemotherapy after failure extends control by only four to five months at the median and carries heavy side effects.

TROP2 is abundant on resistant cells, and EGFR mutations may boost how well these linked drugs enter and kill tumours. Attention centres on the OptiTROP-Lung04 phase III trial in China, published online on October 19, 2025, which beat platinum chemotherapy on control time. The authors weigh patient choice, side effect care, and what comes next for the drug class.
pmc-13354404:
Sujan Dhakal leads a 2026 multicentre survey of anxiety before elective surgery in eastern Nepal. Preoperative anxiety is common yet under-checked, and it shapes surgical outcomes and wellbeing. Patients at two referral hospitals completed the Amsterdam anxiety scale in the holding area, while an anaesthetist added a clinician rating; scores of 11 or more counted as high anxiety.

Of 512 patients, mean age was 42.2 years and 59.8 percent were female. High anxiety appeared in 11.1 percent by patient scale and 14.3 percent by clinician rating. A high need for information was reported by 6.8 percent and 7.8 percent on the two scales. Younger age and female sex were among the predictors in adjusted models.
pmc-13354604:
Lianne Kearsley-Fleet and colleagues asked adults with childhood arthritis how they feel about sharing health data into adulthood, in a 2026 survey study. Under UK ethics rules, linkage of childhood cohort data to medical records must stop at age 16 without fresh consent. Many young adults have moved, left care, or changed hospitals by then, breaking long-term follow-up.

A survey built with patient partners and sent out in January 2025 drew 57 adults with childhood-onset arthritis, 93 percent female and 56 percent aged 45 or older. Respondents weighed continued use of their long-term outcome data and the terms under which they would agree. The findings help cohort stewards design consent that keeps life-course research going without losing trust.
pmc-13355604:
C. Elena Cervantes and others discussed joining medical choice support into chronic kidney disease care, in 2026. Kidney disease affects ten to fourteen percent of the people and causes major illness and death, yet care gaps persist. Albuminuria testing is underused, and proven care such as SGLT2 blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists, GLP-1 drugs, and renin-angiotensin blockers remain underprescribed.

Choice support built into medical workflows could prompt testing and giving at the right moment, closing gaps that education alone has not fixed. The paper sets out how such systems might fit kidney care, what barriers they face, and what evidence would show they work. Doctors and health systems gain a roadmap for turning kidney rules into routine practice.
pmc-13356504:
Saurabh Umrao and co-authors present a 2026 rapid farm test for porcine epidemic diarrhea virus, a gut virus that can kill most piglets in a litter. Farm tests are needed because lab tests are slow and need special gear. Their strip test uses net-shaped DNA structures that grip the virus far more tightly than single binders.

Results come within ten minutes from pig oral fluid, with no need to extract or copy viral genes. The test spotted very low virus levels and, on 102 farm samples, reached about 97 percent accuracy with no false hits from other swine viruses. The authors say the design can be adapted to other animal and shared human-animal diseases.
pmc-13358604:
Forrest Bethel and co-authors wrote a 2026 commentary on pancreatic cancer, one of the deadliest cancers. Even after full surgery and strong drug treatment, the cancer almost always returns, often in distant organs. The authors focus on the days around surgery, a window they argue is not neutral for the body.

Surgery stirs stress hormones, inflammation, and a brief dip in the immune cells that kill stray cancer cells. The PROSPER trial tested whether drugs given in this window can protect patients while leftover cancer is at its weakest. Bethel and co-authors draw lessons from that work for how future trials and care should be timed.
pmc-13359004:
Sahajal Dhooria and co-authors set test limits for a lung disease blood test in a 2026 study. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is an immune lung reaction to inhaled substances like mold. A blood test for antibodies against the trigger can support the diagnosis, but no one had fixed what level counts as positive. Guidelines suggest the test without giving cut-off values.

The team measured antibodies against four molds in 219 people: patients with the disease, patients with other lung diseases, and healthy people with and without mold exposure. They set cut-offs from the healthy group's top range and checked how well the values sorted the groups. Firm limits make the test far more useful in clinic.
pmc-13359104:
Isabel Vinterbladh and others brought in a fast rule for computing tiny heat science from between-molecule poses, in 2026. Exact heat maths are almost never feasible, yet heat traits matter across number physics, models, and tiny docking. A flexible, rapid estimate would serve many fields.

The method builds a quasi-regular grid in five-dimensional angular space between pairs of rigid objects. It scans radial-angular space fast, yielding the two-body partition function, related thermodynamic properties, and the second virial coefficient for anisotropic nanoparticles and proteins. The rule handles rigid-body systems broadly. Computer scientists gain a tool for heat estimates that were before too costly to compute.
pmc-13361104:
Miguel A Pesqueira Sanchez and co-authors studied tiny particles in the blood of Long COVID patients in a 2026 paper. Long COVID leaves lasting symptoms after the virus infection and still has no proven therapy. Cells shed small bubbles, called extracellular vesicles, that carry molecular cargo around the body. The team asked whether the sugar coating on these bubbles changes in Long COVID.

They separated large and small bubbles from blood taken after COVID illness. Large bubbles carried more mannose sugar marks than expected. A resin made from a snowdrop plant protein, which grabs mannose, was used to fish out the small bubbles. The team then read the tiny RNA cargo before and after this capture. Sugar-marked bubbles could become targets for tests or for clearing harmful cargo.
pmc-13362404:
Nadezhda Mitova and Zornitsa Lazarova wrote a 2026 review on the microbes that live inside decayed tooth dentin, the layer under enamel. Tooth decay is driven by films of bacteria that make acid and eat into the tooth. The review asks what germs stay behind when dentists remove decay gently, leaving some softened dentin in place to protect the tooth.

The authors find that dentin holds a rich mix of acid-making and protein-eating germs. Gentle removal cuts the germ count a lot but rarely clears every microbe. Sealed teeth still heal well, so care should aim to shrink and rebalance the germ mix rather than chase sterile teeth, which supports gentler, tooth-saving dentistry.
pmc-13363404:
Jacek Górka and colleagues report a 2026 study on laser-clad coatings of Inconel 625, a nickel alloy prized in harsh chemical and hot settings. The coatings were hardened with chromium carbide grains. They laid coatings with 20 to 40 percent carbide content at varied laser power on plain steel. They then read the layer makeup, hardness, and resistance to blasting by hard particles, a standard erosion test.

Even, well-mixed composite coatings formed across the tested range. The carbide grains raised hardness and cut erosion wear compared with the pure alloy coating. Laser power and carbide share both shaped the final quality, so the pair must be tuned together. The work supports laser cladding as a way to stretch the service life of steel parts in gritty, corrosive jobs.
pmc-13363504:
Yingjian Guo and colleagues report a 2026 mouse study on honeysuckle flower polyphenols against acute lung injury, a sudden, severe lung failure with few safe treatments. Mice were dosed for a week before a lung irritant triggered the injury, and some groups got fecal transplants from treated mice to test whether gut microbes carried part of the benefit. Lung tissue proteins and gut microbe mixes were read in depth.

The polyphenols eased lung damage, calmed the master swelling switch in lung cells, and raised antioxidant defenses, which curbed a rust-like cell death called ferroptosis. Gut microbes shifted toward helpful kinds that make protective fatty acids. Transplants alone also eased lung and gut harm, showing the gut-lung link shares the credit.
pmc-13363904:
Tianmin Li, Yuechao Wu, and Fengque Pei present a 2026 study on cleaning vibration signals from pumped-storage power units, the reversible turbines that balance the grid. Their signals twist and jump, and strong background noise buries the fault clues. The team's method pairs adaptive signal splitting, tuned by an improved swarm search, with wavelet threshold cleaning in two passes, screening split parts by how alike they look before the second pass.

Tests on simulated shaft signals and on real station data beat rival methods, lifting the signal-to-noise ratio and cutting error clearly. Cleaner signals give later fault analysis firmer ground. The authors frame the method as practical groundwork for watching the health of these large machines.
pmc-13371304:
Bilsev Demir and colleagues study spiritual well-being, anxiety, and resilience in liver donors in Turkey in a 2026 paper. The donors took part in a cross-matching system, where paired donors swap recipients so more transplants can proceed. The team surveyed 116 donors at a university liver transplant institute using scales for spiritual well-being, state anxiety, and resilience.

Donors reported high spiritual well-being, moderate resilience, and high anxiety. Spiritual well-being rose alongside resilience, and its meaning, peace, and faith parts each tracked with resilience. No clear link appeared between spiritual well-being and anxiety in the sample. The findings suggest that donor support should address anxiety directly, while also nurturing the sense of meaning that helps donors cope.
pmc-13371704:
Hwamin Woo and colleagues test whether carrying two copies of the APOE epsilon2 variant lowers breast cancer risk in a 2026 cohort study. APOE epsilon2 is linked to lower LDL cholesterol. Data from 234,857 women in the UK Biobank who were free of cancer and dementia were analysed, with new breast cancers tracked through national registries over a median of 12.3 years.

During follow-up, 7,961 first primary breast cancers occurred. Women with two epsilon2 copies had about 36 percent lower risk than non-carriers, and the protective link was stronger among those with a smoking history. The authors argue that genetically set lipid and inflammation control may shape breast cancer susceptibility, especially under inflammatory stress. The finding is observational and needs replication.
pmc-13371904:
Jay Yin and co-authors reshaped a cancer drug into a new tool in a 2026 study. They began with a drug that blocks a growth switch in skin cancer cells. The same drug also blocks a cell guard that fights virus attack and may aid memory.

With X-ray maps of the drug bound to its targets, they changed its shape step by step. The new form lost its grip on the cancer switch but kept its grip on the cell guard. Tests in cells showed clean, picky action. The new form is a start point for drugs that may one day help memory loss, and it must still pass many checks.
pmc-13373004:
Jeffrey Pannekoek closely examines the Montreal Criteria for uterine transplant in a 2026 article. Uterine transplant aims to offer the experience of carrying a child to people who cannot else carry a being pregnant. Existing guidelines treat uterine factor infertility in cis women as the reason, and the Montreal Criteria of 2012 and 2013 have served as the main ethical guide.

Pannekoek challenges how the Criteria frame that reason and their requirement for female genetics. He argues that, beyond the first experimental design, there are prima facie grounds to offer transplant more widely, and no overriding ethical reason to limit it to cis women. The article reframes the debate around who may seek carrying a child and on what grounds.
pmc-13373204:
Yan Zhang and co-authors tested a green tea part in stroke harm in a 2026 rat and cell study. Stroke care that reopens blood flow can itself harm the brain, and swelling adds to the loss. The tea part is known to calm swelling, but its role after flow returns was not clear.

Rats got the tea part in the brain before a blocked artery was freed. Brain scores, dead zone size, and cell marks were checked. Dish cells starved of air and food were also tested, with and without a blocker of the path in view. The tea part pushed brain guard cells to a calm state through that path.
pmc-13373604:
John J Santos and co-authors built a way to run immune studies from kids' urgent care in a 2026 study. Urgent care is fast and short, which clashes with the slow steps of study sign-up. The team ran a study of baby and mother immune replies to chest germs at four Seattle clinics.

The trick was to split the work in two. A short first touch in the clinic was split from sign-up and sample steps, which were done from home. That kept clinic flow smooth. So far 36 babies and 39 mothers have joined, with full sample sets. The plan may open a rich, missed site for child health studies.
pmc-13373904:
Khalisah Shoaib and co-authors report a blocked gut in late pregnancy in a 2026 case report. A first-time mother at 38 weeks came in with high belly pain, vomiting, and less baby movement. A blocked gut in pregnancy is rare and can be grave for both mother and child.

Her pulse and blood tests were fine, and a magnet scan showed a block low in the small gut. A planned surgery to birth the baby was done. In the work, the team found a scar band that pinched the gut, and cut it free through the same cut. Both mother and baby healed well. The case backs magnet scans as a safe guide here.
pmc-13376104:
Kezhen Shen and others rank plans to beat PARP blocker defence in breast cancer in a 2026 full review. Resistance to PARP blockers blocks durable benefit, yet many lab-stage plans lack a framework for choosing among them. Twenty-two lab-stage studies were synthesised, judging models, routes, results, bias with SYRCLE and ROBINS-I tools, and certainty with GRADE.

Epigenetic targeting through EZH2 inhibition and immune modulation through STING switching on showed consistently high-quality evidence for tumour suppression, survival benefit, and immune switching on in BRCA1-mutant models. Strategies restoring matching gene mixing showed strong lab synergy but limited animal translatability, constrained by drug behaviour and model limits. The review gives trial designers a ranked shortlist grounded in evidence quality, not only in lab promise.
pmc-13377804:
Anne J H Vochteloo and colleagues model whether 3D-guided wrist surgery is cost-effective in the Netherlands in a 2026 study. Distal radius malunion after fracture impairs function and quality of life, and conventional 2D-planned corrective surgery often misses optimal alignment, leading to revision. Three-dimensional planning with patient-specific guides improves radiographic and clinical outcomes but costs more upfront.

A health state transition model over five years from a societal view compared 3D and 2D strategies. Revisions for nonunion or implant failure fell by 179 per 1,000 patients with 3D planning. Overall, 3D gave slightly higher quality-adjusted life years, plus 0.007, at lower societal costs. The model suggests that higher upfront spending on 3D guides can pay for itself through fewer revisions.
pmc-13380704:
H Watanabe and colleagues describe a 2026 report on using sniffer dogs to confirm that bedbugs were fully cleared from a university hospital. Bedbug incidents in hospitals are uncommon, and no standard protocol exists. In 2018 bedbugs entered the hospital in a patient's belongings, and ten were found on a bed, wall, and floor.

Carpets were replaced and a specialist firm treated the area, following hotel hygiene guidance. Trained dogs then searched by smell for any survivors. The dogs found none, confirming the treatment had worked. The extra cost was modest. The authors suggest dogs are a practical extra check for early detection and for proving a hospital area is clear.
pmc-13383504:
Parsa Alijanizadeh's team reviews strategies to restore the NKG2D immune axis in head and neck cancer, in a 2026 review. Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma evades immune surveillance by crippling NKG2D on natural killer cells and killer T cells, shedding stress ligands and secreting suppressive cytokines such as TGF-beta1. The review surveys ways to rearm this axis.

Cytokines such as IL-2 and IL-15 boost NKG2D-driven natural killer activation, while antibodies against MICA, MICB, and ULBP ligands block shedding and trigger cell killing. Engineered NKG2D CAR-T and CAR-NK cells show potent preclinical activity, and pairing with EGFR antibodies or checkpoint blockers adds benefit. Tumor heterogeneity and suppressive signals remain hurdles to clinical translation.
pmc-13383704:
Chaynez Rachid and co-authors describe a woman whose lingering lung illness proved to be chronic eosinophilic pneumonia in a 2026 case report. The rare condition fills lung tissue with eosinophils and often mimics infection or tuberculosis. The 40-year-old patient had 40 days of worsening breathlessness, cough, and fever.

Scans showed spread-out shadowing in both lungs, while tests for tuberculosis came back negative. Further workup confirmed the diagnosis, and steroid treatment brought rapid clinical and scan improvement. The authors urge clinicians to weigh this condition when diffuse lung shadowing does not fit infection, since response to steroids is often striking.
pmc-13385004:
Shannon Desbiens, Katie Darabos, and Sean McHugh study how surroundings shape cancer-risk habits in young adults in 2026 work. Data came from a 2022 national survey linkage project covering healthy adults aged 18 to 29 years. Food and exercise surroundings, plus area income levels, were tested against behavior profiles.

Two broad profiles emerged, and both were notably unhealthy in different ways. Young adults with weaker access to exercise settings leaned toward the second profile in the analysis. Education and rural living each changed how place factors linked to behavior, which suggests prevention plans must fit local context rather than one national mold.
pmc-13386604:
Shubhransu Patro and colleagues test a simple blood index for judging severity in acute pancreatitis in a 2026 prospective study. The triglyceride-glucose index was compared with two established severity scores at a hospital in Bhubaneswar, India. The study enrolled 185 patients, with a mean age near 55 years and men making up about three quarters.

Values for pancreas enzymes, triglycerides, and fasting glucose fed the index calculation for each patient. The team's stated aim was to set thresholds for organ dysfunction and in-hospital death prediction. Full performance results sit beyond the opening sections, so the design and cohort form the clearest part of this record.
pmc-13388704:
Alice R Paine's team tested whether large volcanic eruptions helped trigger the cold snaps that broke Holocene climate stability in the northern hemisphere. They compiled eruption records, sulphate traces, climate data, and glacier histories across roughly twelve thousand years. They then checked the timing of eruptions against cooling events.

More than eighty percent of Holocene glacier advances fell within dating uncertainty of at least one major northern eruption, and simulations showed the match was unlikely by chance. Sea-ice growth, weaker Atlantic circulation, and a southward shift of tropical rains offer a route for effects lasting far beyond the lifetime of volcanic aerosols.
pmc-13389104:
Maram El Sabri and co-authors model a way to deliver the radioactive isotope actinium-225 directly into glioblastoma tumours using pressure-driven flow. This brain cancer recurs locally in over ninety percent of cases because surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy leave resistant cells behind. Alpha particles from actinium-225 kill powerfully but travel only a short distance, so delivery matters.

Their computer model combines diffusion, bulk flow, and the full radioactive decay chain in a simplified brain geometry, then converts the resulting doses into predicted cell survival. Convection-enhanced delivery reached therapeutic doses about 1.43 centimetres from injection points. A five-injection plan totalling ten megabecquerels cut the surviving fraction of tumour cells from one hundred percent to roughly 3.4 percent in the model, with higher activities reducing it further. The authors present the work as a feasibility study of both the promise and the limits of this approach.
pmc-13392404:
Haitham Helmy Sayed and co-authors survey, in 2026, Enterococcus infections in broiler chickens in Egypt, including resistance and virulence traits. These bacteria cause losses in poultry and can acquire and pass on antimicrobial resistance genes to other species.

One hundred twenty samples were collected from diseased broilers aged one to thirty-five days on thirty commercial farms in Qena and Sohag governorates. Birds were checked by eye and by lab culture. Each germ found was tested for drug resistance and for harm traits. Checks also spanned two classes of gene packets that jump between germs. Poultry vets gain local data on spread and drug resistance. The germ sits where farm, food, and health care meet.
pmc-13393804:
Nuoman Han and colleagues test a simple blood ratio for predicting leg vein clots after tibial plateau fracture in a 2026 retrospective analysis. Deep vein thrombosis is a common and serious complication of this fracture surgery, yet accurate early risk prediction has been difficult.

The study enrolled 1,582 adults operated on between October 2019 and December 2023, tracking clots within 14 days of surgery. Variable screening, spline modeling, and logistic regression tested the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio alongside demographic, surgical, and laboratory factors. Surgeons gain a cheap, routine lab signal that may flag patients needing closer clot prevention.
pmc-13393904:
Diklah Barak and others tie tongue motion in breast feeding to milk flow and reflux in a 2026 Israeli study of 21 pairs. Tongue motion shapes how well babies feed, but scan-based motion data and bedside checks had mostly been read apart.

Mothers and babies aged 3 to 6 weeks had tongue, nipple, and palate gaps and angles scanned, matched with reflux signs, nipple pain scores, and milk flow rates. The study asks which motion patterns track with smooth feeding and which with reflux or pain. Feeding advisers now have one joined view of tongue work and milk flow, not two split views.
pmc-13394804:
Liu and co-authors engineer, in 2026, platelet-mimicking nanoparticles designed to make tumor blood vessels behave normally, sooner. Tumor vessels grow chaotically, starving tissue of oxygen and blocking drug delivery. Drugs like apatinib can normalize them, but the beneficial window typically opens only after four to seven days of dosing, during which tumors keep growing. Their particle combines apatinib with the light-activated dye indocyanine green, wrapped in real platelet membrane.

Under laser light, the particles killed tumor cells through photodynamic therapy, which uses light-triggered chemistry, without over-pruning the vessels. Vessel structure and function normalized by day two of treatment, two days earlier than the drug alone achieved, and stayed optimal through day eight. Normalized vessels then delivered more drug, feeding a self-amplifying cycle between vessel repair and light therapy. The system also achieved its antitumor effects with lower dye doses than photodynamic therapy usually requires.
pmc-13395404:
Anne M. L. Nilsen and colleagues test, in 2026, whether heat training in young kelp passes to the next stock. Sugar kelp builds forests on North Atlantic coasts and anchors seaweed farming in Europe. Heatwaves now threaten both wild and farmed kelp. The team warmed the tiny gametophyte stage for three weeks, then bred those plants and heat-shocked their young sporophytes.

Offspring of warmed parents answered heat with stronger gene shifts, including a heat shield gene found only in them. Their light harvesting held up longer under heat. Untrained offspring lagged, then shut many genes down during recovery. The authors read the pattern as a stress memory passed across generations. Farms might prime seed stock this way.
pmc-13395904:
Dewi Yuliani, Romaidi, and Tatsuya Ueki report, in 2026, a sea bacterium enzyme that does two jobs at once. The enzyme normally helps build proteins by loading a building block onto carrier RNA. The team cloned it from a marine Shewanella strain and made it in the lab. Tests showed it also turns toxic vanadium, in its five-plus state, into a milder four-plus form.

Zinc and copper ions boosted the cleaning act by up to three quarters. Vanadium spills from industry threaten soil and water, so microbe cleaners draw interest. A dual-use enzyme could aid green clean-up rigs. The authors give rate figures for the new act. Field proof still lies ahead.
pmc-13396004:
Ester Eliyahu and colleagues asked doctors and nurses what stands in the way of treating blood cancer patients at home instead of in hospital, in a 2026 study from Israel. Home care can spare patients long stays, but staff must trust it is safe.

The group interviewed 23 clinicians, 11 physicians and 12 nurses, from eight hospitals and sorted their answers by themes. One theme cast the hospital as a safe haven, where close watching feels protective even when home care might suit the patient. Another covered what a home service needs to run well, from team roles to backup plans. Views gathered this way can guide services that staff will actually use.
pmc-13396304:
Nikolas Tauber and colleagues pulled together the largest European series yet of a rare and grave turn in breast cancer, where tumor cells flood the bone marrow. Their 2026 analysis draws on two large German university breast centers and covers cases found between 2010 and 2023.

Thirty-seven patients with metastatic breast cancer and marrow carcinomatosis were reviewed in detail. The authors chart blood count problems, where else the cancer had spread, which treatments were tried, and how long patients lived. Because single centers see so few cases, pooling records this way gives doctors firmer ground on how the condition presents and what outlook to expect.
pmc-13396404:
Wen and team design, in 2026, indium-based octahedral coatings that stabilize perovskite solar cells where they usually fail, at the surface. Halide perovskites degrade from the outside in, as defects build up and break the octahedral framework. The team built two coordination agents from phenylmethylammonium indium chlorides. One carried disordered octahedra. The other, co-containing sodium, had an ordered framework that locks coherently onto the lead-iodide termini of the perovskite surface.

That rigid coupling pinned the formamidinium cations and lead-iodide octahedra in place, relaxed interfacial imperfections, and aligned energy levels for better charge transport. Solar cells using the ordered coating reached 27.29 percent efficiency, certified at 26.84 percent by independent measurement, and minimodules hit 24 percent in the same testing. Devices kept over 98 percent of their initial efficiency after 3,000 hours of maximum-power tracking, addressing perovskites' notorious stability problem head-on.
pmc-13396504:
Zhang and co-authors identify, in 2026, a metabolic shield tumor cells use to survive immune attack: the enzyme HMGCS1, which starts cholesterol production. Killer lymphocytes punch pores in tumor cell membranes with perforin so that granzymes can enter and execute the cell. Screening 111 metabolic enzymes, the team found HMGCS1 is critical for repairing that perforin damage, resealing the membrane before the lethal payload lands.

Fresh cholesterol does double duty: beyond patching material, it directly binds the repair protein CHMP4B and recruits it to the membrane. Tumors with high HMGCS1 resisted natural killer cells, CAR-T therapy, and anti-PD-1 immunotherapy in their experiments. In lung cancer patients, high c-Jun activation, HMGCS1 expression, cholesterol content, and membrane CHMP4B all tracked with weaker responses to anti-PD-1 treatment. Blocking HMGCS1 improved immunotherapy effectiveness, making the enzyme a candidate drug target for resistant tumors.
pmc-13396604:
Kylie S. Andonian and John Strasswimmer tell of skin-and-mouth illness plus blood-gobbling illness after COVID-19 in a 2026 case tale. COVID-19 now counts as a whole-body flare illness, with skin tales at all ages, but this fierce flare pair was scant filed.

A sound young woman fell ill in January 2021, ere shots were out, with marrow showing blood gobbling and bold cell-in-cell nests. The case first ties cell-in-cell nests to fierce post-COVID flare illness. Doctors gain a rare post-virus shape to spot fast, ere it spirals.
pmc-13396704:
Zhi Liang and co-authors built tiny balls of human eye-surface tissue that can be produced in uniform batches for lab testing, in a 2026 methods study. The conjunctiva, the clear skin over the white of the eye, is a standard test site, but flat cell layers poorly mimic real tissue.

Using molds printed in fine detail and cast in silicone, the team formed arrays of microwells. In them, donor conjunctival surface cells and support cells gather into spheres of controlled size, with no scaffold needed. Such three-dimensional microtissues promise more lifelike, repeatable tests of eye drugs and irritants, and fit the push toward methods that reduce animal testing.
pmc-13398904:
Heng Wu and colleagues build a blood-test model to spot infected bone that refuses to heal, before surgery begins. Their 2026 study analyses 276 patients treated between 2018 and 2023 for femoral or tibial nonunion after fracture fixation. Hidden infection, with no outward signs, wrecks surgical planning, and standard inflammation markers alone judge it poorly.

A development group of 221 patients built the model, with 55 held back for testing. Four serum markers entered it: procalcitonin plus interleukin-6, C-reactive protein and sedimentation rate. The bet is that a newer marker layered on classics sharpens accuracy enough to change operations, and curve scores in the hold-out group grade whether the bet pays off.
pmc-13399304:
Matheus Daudt-Lemos and colleagues examined whether small inherited differences in immune and blood-pressure genes shaped how sick Brazilians became with COVID-19, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. The genes chosen govern inflammation signals such as interleukins and tumor necrosis factor. They also cover the ACE and ACE2 proteins the virus uses to enter cells, plus uromodulin, a protein tied to kidney function.

Participants were Brazilian patients from the first pandemic wave, assessed during acute illness and in the post-acute phase. Post-COVID-19 condition means symptoms appearing three months after infection and lasting at least two months. Genotyping covered ten variants across the IL1A, IL6, IL10, TNF, ACE, ACE2, and UMOD genes. The team compared variant patterns against disease severity and against persistent symptoms. They looked for associations that might one day help flag patients at risk of a long course.
pmc-13399404:
Hanna Rahimi and co-authors present the protocol for the NEONATAL trial in 2026, a Danish study testing whether immersive virtual reality practice added to standard mannequin training sharpens newborn resuscitation skills. Mannequin sessions are expensive to run and hard to schedule often. Virtual reality could let doctors and nurses rehearse more frequently at lower cost.

The multicenter trial recruits resident doctors and neonatal nurses at four hospitals in Eastern Denmark. Each person is assigned at random to mannequin training alone or mannequin training plus immersive VR sessions. Skills are measured before training and again at six to eight weeks, using standardized simulation scenarios, validated scoring tools, and questionnaires. Recruitment ran from October to December 2025 and enrolled 66 participants. Data collection finished in February 2026, with results expected in autumn 2026. The trial is registered as ISRCTN 43822066. Findings should show whether VR practice works inside routine clinical education.
pmc-13399504:
Aidah Nanvuma and colleagues evaluated a program at Uganda's Infectious Disease Institute that trains junior clinical researchers toward independence, in a 2026 mixed-methods study. Between July 2021 and February 2023 the team surveyed 80 current and former scholars of the institute's Capacity Building Unit and interviewed 20 of them in depth.

Satisfaction ran high. Ninety percent of scholars said they would recommend the model to others, 85 percent reported reaching their career goals, and 65 percent said it widened their employment options, as the survey reports. The overall scientific benefit score came to 48.7 percent, notably higher among continuing scholars, at 56.7 percent, than among alumni, at 25.0 percent in the comparison shown. Complaints targeted slow procurement, limited research funds, delayed supervision, and pandemic disruption of mentoring. The authors recommend fixing those administrative snags and spreading the model.
pmc-13399604:
Popper and co-authors survey, in 2026, how few American high school sports teams actually run ACL injury prevention programs, despite such programs being proven and well known. About 70 percent of anterior cruciate ligament injuries come from sports, usually noncontact cutting and jumping. The team surveyed athletic directors, trainers, and coaches covering 522 teams across 22 high schools served by a regional orthopaedic practice.

Only 18 teams, 3.5 percent of those surveyed, used a prevention program at the time of the study. Awareness was not the problem: 87.1 percent of representatives from non-using teams knew these programs exist. The leading barrier was lack of trained staff, cited by 43.6 percent of respondents, followed by time constraints during training at 33.0 percent in the survey. The authors call the barriers surmountable and argue that solving staffing and scheduling, rather than education, is the fastest route to fewer torn ligaments in teenagers.
pmc-13400504:
Marilia Silva Malvezzi Karwowski and co-authors test, in 2026, whether millet grain can carry helpful bacteria into dry-fermented sausage. Helpful bacteria must survive months of ripening and storage to benefit the eater. Trapping them in a grain matrix might protect them better than adding free cells.

Four sausage recipes were compared over 121 days: free bacteria, free bacteria with millet, and two levels of millet-trapped bacteria. Trapped bacteria kept higher counts through storage. Millet did not change acidity or water measures, but it did slow fat oxidation, guarding flavor. Forty-one aroma compounds were tracked; trapped-bacteria sausages kept the classic aroma profile, and storage time, not trapping, drove most aroma change.
pmc-13400904:
Fox, Zhu, and Sánchez-Ovando review influenza's double edged memory. Past infections and vaccines protect fast against familiar viruses, yet memory can crowd out responses when the virus drifts. This tension, once called original antigenic sin, decides how well the season's vaccine works. Their 2026 review weighs cohort, antibody, and vaccine data against mouse and cell fate mapping to sort when recall helps and when it constrains.

Three mechanisms do most of the constraining. Circulating antibodies can mask the spots new cells need to see. A receptor on B cells can brake activation. Battle tested memory cells outcompete naive ones when their aim is dated. Dose, antigen distance, formulation, and T cell help tilt the balance. The authors close with levers: higher doses, adjuvants that wake naive cells, displaying antigens, and strain choice. A universal flu vaccine, they argue, must be designed around memory, not despite it.
pmc-13401304:
Jostein Rødseth Brede wrote a 2026 article on electrostatic discharge during helicopter hoist operations, the static shocks crews know well but the medical literature barely mentions. Helicopters build up large static charges in flight, and rescuers lowered on a hoist can receive a discharge on reaching a patient or the ground.

Two nationwide Norwegian studies anchor the piece. A survey found every rescue paramedic and 73 percent of physicians had experienced a discharge, often repeatedly, and 23 percent rated an event as severe. A prospective study logged 28 events during 839 hoist operations. Reported consequences included severe pain, involuntary muscle or nerve symptoms, and falls. Brede argues the shocks should count as a clinical and operational safety risk, not a mere nuisance.
pmc-13401404:
Yang He and colleagues published a 2026 technical description of a new stitch for repairing the hip labrum, the cartilage ring that seals the hip socket, during arthroscopy. Preserving that suction seal matters, and older single-strand loop stitches can push the labrum outward and break it.

A vertical mattress stitch protects the labrum's free edge, but one strand may be too weak for large tears, and adding anchors is costly since anchors are a key consumable. Their inverted V-shape double-strand vertical mattress technique pairs the seal-preserving stitch pattern with a double-strand anchor arranged in a V. The result aims for stronger fixation of big tears with fewer anchors implanted, lowering both tissue distortion and the hardware bill for the procedure.
pmc-13401704:
Neda Ahmadzadeh Tori and co-authors produced a Persian version of the Social Participation Questionnaire and tested its measurement quality in a 2026 cross-sectional study from Babol, Iran. Joining in social life is tied to cognition, quality of life, well-being, and even lower mortality, so measuring it well matters.

The questionnaire was translated and culturally adapted by standard procedures, then given to 500 participants with a mean age of about 31 years between February and June 2024. A categorical principal component analysis found a two-component structure explaining about 68 percent of the total variance. The first component, carrying about 42 percent of variance, loaded strongly on four items representing general social engagement. Internal consistency was checked with Cronbach's alpha. The work gives Persian-speaking researchers a validated local tool.
pmc-13402104:
Reem K AlMealla and co-authors mapped the algae that live inside reef corals across three seas with very different heat regimes: Bahrain in the Arabian Gulf, the Seychelles, and Indonesia. These algae, from the family Symbiodiniaceae, feed their coral hosts, and some types tolerate heat better than others. The team sampled 11 coral species and kept 157 colonies that passed sequencing quality checks.

Sequencing of the ITS2 region found Cladocopium dominant everywhere, with Durusdinium and Symbiodinium also present. Hotter, more extreme Bahrain reefs held poorer, less varied algae sets than the other regions. A heat-tolerant type known as C3-Gulf turned up across Bahraini hosts and, at a trace level of 0.1 percent in one Seychelles sample, beyond its known range. The authors offer the survey as a baseline for tracking how coral partnerships shift as seas warm.
pmc-13402604:
Virgo and co-authors reveal, in 2026, how the cholera bacterium Vibrio cholerae reshapes its organization when it senses rival bacteria, readying its contact-dependent weaponry. Cholera bacteria can clump into aggregates held by pilus structures. That helps them survive host defenses but hurts attacks on competitors, since their type VI secretion system kills only on direct cell contact. The cross-species quorum signal AI-2, produced by gut bacteria, tips the balance.

On sensing AI-2 from competitors such as E. coli, the cholera cells partly break up their aggregates, freeing single cells to slip into the rival clusters. That intermixing multiplies cross-species contacts and lets the secretion system kill competitors more effectively in their tests. Tests ran in zebrafish up to five days post fertilization alongside culture models. The authors describe a shifting trade-off, toggled by eavesdropped signals, between hunkering down in aggregates and dispersing to fight.
pmc-13402704:
Pengcheng Gao and co-authors forge benzocyclobutenes, strained four-membered rings prized in drug and materials work, through gold catalysis that needs no added oxidant. Good routes to these rings are scarce, which throttles their use. The team runs a [2 + 2] annulation pairing common aryl halides with olefins under mild conditions, steered by a purpose-built N-heterocyclic carbene ligand that grips gold with both carbon and nitrogen.

The ligand shapes the gold center so it inserts selectively while blocking the beta-hydride elimination side path that ruins such couplings. Computer modeling traced the route and showed electron-withdrawing groups on the ligand frame doing key work. Many functional groups survived the reaction, and late-stage edits of complex molecules succeeded. The authors present the method as both a practical ring synthesis and a proof that smart ligands can unlock oxidant-free gold chemistry.
pmc-13402804:
Chen and co-authors report, in 2026, an encapsulated droplet array for running chemical reactions in parallel under harsh conditions. It fixes the flaws of microwell plates, which cannot take heat and pressure, and flow systems, which parallelize poorly. Each microliter droplet sits sealed inside an inert polypropylene pocket backed by an aluminum chassis, holding up at 105 degrees Celsius and 7 atmospheres, far beyond solvent boiling points.

A plate holds 48 reactions at once, thermoformed from a polypropylene sheet cut to the standard microplate footprint of 85 by 128 millimeters. Existing pipetting robots and analyzers accept it directly. Solvent loss stayed under 2 percent for all tested solvents heated at 50 degrees, where open formats bleed solvent badly. The team ran aminolysis, amide condensation, aromatic substitution, Buchwald-Hartwig amination, Suzuki-Miyaura coupling, and photoredox coupling on the platform, plus a fully automated end-to-end workflow from droplet preparation to analysis.
pmc-13403504:
Rongyu Li and Meihong Wu built a speech-based screening tool in 2026 for mild memory and thinking decline in Mandarin speakers. Brain scans and lab tests for such decline cost much and do not scale well. Speech is cheap to record, yet most tools use only part of what speech carries.

Their system joins three views of a voice sample: word meaning, rhythm over time, and how ideas link across a talk. A gate weighs the three views for each person. On one Chinese challenge set the tool reached about 89 percent correct calls. Results held up less strongly on a mixed second set, which shows both promise and limits.
pmc-13403604:
Rose V. Zach and co-authors described in 2026 a woman whose stubborn epilepsy eased only after two rounds of brain stimulation. The 51-year-old had a seizure type marked by sudden jerks, and more than ten drugs plus a nerve stimulator had failed her. Electrodes first went into one thalamic spot on both sides.

The first implants cut her large convulsions yet left daily jerks untouched. Those jerks made her fall and drop objects. A second set of electrodes went into a nearby thalamic spot. Seven months later jerks had become rare, her seizure class had improved, and daily function stayed better.
pmc-13403704:
YanLin Yang and Chao Wang detailed a 2026 case of a young man with fever and swollen glands that doctors first read as a simple chest infection. The 26-year-old also had fatigue, cough, and positive autoantibodies, clues that muddy the picture. Such signs can point to cancer, tuberculosis, or immune disease instead.

A lymph node biopsy finally confirmed Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease, a rare and usually mild gland illness. A like episode two years earlier, never biopsied, led the team to call the new one a return. Returns happen in a share of cases, so long follow-up matters, most of all with positive autoantibodies.
pmc-13404004:
Ishita Bhattacharya, Lisle Blackbourn, and Manajyoti Yadav reviewed in 2026 why Addison's disease so often hides for months before diagnosis. The fault lies in glands that make too little cortisol, and its signs mimic common stomach trouble. Fewer than half of patients get the right call within six months of first symptoms.

Their case follows a 55-year-old woman sent home with stomach remedies again and again. Salt shifts in her blood and low pressure slowly gave the true picture. One in five patients waits over five years for a diagnosis. Missed cases risk a sudden crisis that can kill, so wide thinking matters.
pmc-13404104:
Eyal Cohen and team propose a checkable alignment frame for medical artificial intelligence built on negative constraints. Their 2026 theoretical work, the AI Inversion Model, takes on the black-box snag in high-stakes triage, where standard alignment methods encode subjective morality through opaque pipelines and may amplify bias. Rather than computing positive virtues, the model sets strict anti-moral bounds.

A Genesis anchor system tunes those bounds from legal precedents and ethics writing, and the model tracks output kinematics, with vector angles included, to gauge good faith. A surgical simulation trace shows the filter flagging utilitarian bias and calling for human review when variance passes a 10 percent threshold. The authors present the model as a proof of concept for functional compassion, not a final fix, with real-world checks still ahead.
pmc-13404404:
Jan Yvan Verbakel and colleagues set out a trial plan in 2026 to test a digital prescribing helper for antibiotics in Belgian family practice. Poor antibiotic choices drive drug resistance, even with national guidelines in place. The helper turns guideline advice into a clickable tree inside patient record software.

Practices will switch from usual care to the helper in four timed steps over twelve months. The main question is whether practice-level antibiotic rates fall once the tool goes live. Logs and staff interviews will show how the tool gets used and where it snags. The plan needs about 36 to 48 practices to spot a five-point drop.
pmc-13404904:
Nataliia Ponzel and team gauged depression and anxiety among displaced Ukrainians inside and outside Ukraine. Their 2026 mixed-methods work surveys 462 adults displaced during or after February 2022, living in nine European countries plus Ukraine, using PHQ-9 and GAD-7 surveys and open-ended questions. War displacement raises mental health risk, yet rates by location had been little weighed.

Moderate to severe depression symptoms hit 37.0 percent and anxiety symptoms 51.5 percent, with most respondents women and only 13.9 percent previously diagnosed. After age adjustment, refugees outside Ukraine had higher odds of depression and anxiety than those displaced inside Ukraine, at odds ratios of 1.86 and 1.70. Free-text themes included war impact, broken networks, money strain, health woes, and integration blocks. The work urges open mental health support for displaced Ukrainians.
pmc-13405804:
Alina Maria Borcan and colleagues chart drug resistance in gut germs at a Romanian hospital over three years, in a 2026 lab record study. Diarrhoea often clears on its own, yet its germs show how resistance spreads. Past Romanian work tended to track one germ at a time.

Five germ groups were tracked: Salmonella, Campylobacter, E. coli, Yersinia and Shigella. Campylobacter shrugged off ciprofloxacin in over eighty percent of samples in the reported counts. It resisted tetracycline in about half. Erythromycin resistance stayed low and flat across the years. Salmonella resisted ciprofloxacin in 46 percent of cases. pmc-13406604:

Childhood airway infections and nasal inflammation drive many clinic visits, making a drug-free aid attractive.

Benefit depends on technique: the right solution, age-fitting delivery and caregivers taught properly. The authors frame irrigation as rational, non-drug management rather than a cure-all. pmc-13407004:
Nerea Blanco-Martínez and co-authors tested a movement-based programme for young children in a 2026 study of five- and six-year-olds. pmc-13407604:

pmc-13408204:

pmc-13408504:

pmc-13408604:

pmc-13408704:

pmc-13410304:

pmc-13410604:

pmc-13410804:

pmc-13412104:

pmc-13412304:
Cristina Mazzali and colleagues tested in 2026 whether an AI review tool, Elicit, can help build systematic reviews on air pollution and childhood lung infections. pmc-13412604:

Three years of follow-up are described in the report.
pmc-13413304:
Xiaojin Zou and colleagues test in 2026 whether farming soybeans under solar panels can rescue yield on the degraded Horqin Sandy Land. pmc-13414004:

pmc-13416204:

pmc-13418104:

Tailoring standard routines may sharpen performance and lower injury risk factors, though injury counts themselves were not the endpoint here.
pmc-13418204:

pmc-13418504:

It kept working in salty water, at near freezing temperature, and over 20 cycles. The contact route attacked a key DNA letter well but missed whole genes.
pmc-13418604:

pmc-13418704:

pmc-13419004:

The scans revealed strong regional differences, highest in occipital lobes, and a fall in a combined glutamate-glutamine signal of about 13 percent per decade. pmc-13419304:

Thirty-one patients developed venous clots, and all three ratios ran higher in that group, with neutrophil and platelet ratios standing as independent flags after adjustment. pmc-13420204:

pmc-13420304:

pmc-13420604:

pmc-13421004:

pmc-13421504:

pmc-13422304:

pmc-13422804:

pmc-13424004:

pmc-13424104:

pmc-13424504:

pmc-13425604:

pmc-13425804:

pmc-13426404:

pmc-13427504:

pmc-13427904:

pmc-13428004:

pmc-13429104:

pmc-13429904:

pmc-13430204:

pmc-13430704:

pmc-13431604:
