pmc-13432304:
Brierley and fellow members of the Union for International Cancer Control TNM committee explain the ninth edition of the TNM classification, the global standard for recording how far a cancer has spread. The system, maintained since the early 1950s and revised jointly with American and specialty partners, underpins treatment choices and outcome comparisons for most malignancies.

The review itemizes what changed between the eighth and ninth editions and sets out the evidence behind each revision for readers. Head and neck and lung cancers receive the deepest attention, reflecting major updates driven by imaging, pathology, and therapy advances in those fields. Newer elements across sites include imaging-detected extranodal extension, human papillomavirus status in throat cancers, and molecular scans for prostate disease. The authors stress that staging language must evolve as tumor behavior becomes better understood, while staying stable enough for worldwide use.
pmc-13433104:
Meredith Otley and colleagues surveyed caregivers about their role in easing children's pain during medical procedures such as needle sticks and blood draws. The 2026 cross-sectional study asked what caregivers know, what they feel, and what stops them from helping more.

Most caregivers were present during their child's procedures and felt broadly happy with how pain was handled. Yet many reported gaps in their own knowledge of best practice, which held them back from taking an active part. Their own distress, and their child's distress, also acted as barriers to helping. Otley suggests that coaching and support for caregivers could close these gaps and improve pain care for children.
pmc-13433804:
Philipp Sven Lars Schäfer and co-authors shipped a free Python kit in 2026 that scales a trade-off lens for cell data to millions of cells. Life runs on trade-offs: a cell cannot do all jobs at once, so it pours its stock into a few tasks and skims the rest. The lens finds the pure task poles that bound that spread.

Past tools for the lens stalled on big sets and sat apart from stock data flows. The kit leans on lean math tricks and core-set picks to keep speed as sets swell. Docs and pole portraits ride along. The team shows the kit at work on wobble inside one cell kind, read as task share drift. The frame swaps hard cell labels for smooth place on a trade-off map.
pmc-13433904:
Vishal Kumar and co-authors fired pulsed electron beams in 2026 at three frozen test samples to check a claim that pulsing spares samples from beam harm in cold-scope imaging. Beam harm caps the dose a scope can spend, which caps picture sharpness for life stuff. A radio rig on a top scope made the pulses while all else held still.

Wax sheets, a purple film from germs, and a plant virus in glass ice formed the test set. Harm read as the fade of spot patterns with dose, summed to a break dose per run. Pulsed and plain streams tied on break dose in all three samples, with no gap worth the name. The authors offer the null as a bench mark for future pulse source claims.
pmc-13434004:
Ke-ting Liu and co-authors built a point chart in 2026 for Parkinson's disease odds. Three plain reads feed the chart: smoke past, a blood swelling score, and a food state score. The brain disease climbs in China while early call tools stay thin. Swelling and food state both steer the disease's roots, yet joined calls lacked a frame.

Charts held more than two thousand people, split near even between patients and sound peers, then split again for build and check sets. A shrink sort picked the three reads from twenty-five hopefuls. Each read stood on its own in tuned math: smoke past cut odds, while the swelling score raised them. The chart split patients from peers at a strong rate in both sets.
pmc-13434204:
Sebastian Perrone and a large team examine Ser33 in 2026, a yeast enzyme that helps make serine, a building block for proteins and cell films. In some life forms this enzyme also makes a second product from a swapped partner molecule. The group asks how the yeast form does both jobs and how serine shuts it down.

Crystal images show the enzyme bound to its helper and to each key molecule in turn. Gene edits, lab rate tests, and computer motion studies pin down which parts grip each molecule. The work also shows how a short end piece tunes control in this enzyme family. The detail aids study of serine paths in health.
pmc-13434804:
F Arrouas and a large team catch a long predicted echo peak in quantum chaos in 2026. Cold atoms in a shaken light lattice stand in for electrons in messy matter. A forward echo peak was forecast for strong trapping but never seen head on until now.

The peak grows in step with how trapped the atoms stay. Its width reads out the trap length scale. Tuning two symmetries shifts both the old back echo and the new forward echo in distinct ways. Links between growth, contrast, and symmetry prove tight. Many body versions of the test now look within reach.
pmc-13437304:
Chao-Fu Chen and co-authors tested whether standing on a vibrating platform for one minute can sharpen a young baseball player's swing. Batting depends on a chain of motion that runs from the legs through the hips and trunk to the bat. Their 2026 study split thirty-two national-level teenage players into four groups. The groups stood plain, vibrated alone, or vibrated while holding loads of thirty or fifty percent of each player's best lift.

All groups trained in a half-squat calf-raise pose, then swung at full effort. Both vibration plans beat the plain group on leg speed and bat head speed. The heaviest load produced the fastest knee motion, the lighter load led on hip rotation, and vibration alone led on elbow speed. The authors offer brief vibration work as a quick warm-up tool before practice or games, .
pmc-13439104:
Kun Zhu, Qingchun Fu, and Muyun Liu review progress in measuring portal pressure for a rare liver vessel disorder, in a 2026 article. The disorder, porto-sinusoidal vascular disease, scars small vessels in the liver without causing cirrhosis. Raised pressure in the portal vein often follows, yet the usual vein-pressure test reads too low because the block sits before the sinusoids.

Newer options mix scans and direct checks. Stiffness imaging, CT, and MRI can help separate the disorder from cirrhosis and grade pressure severity. A scope-guided method now measures portal pressure more directly and may sort patients by risk. Lab markers, computer models, and AI tools add further paths to personal risk estimates. The authors favour care guided by several measures together rather than one test alone.
pmc-13439804:
Siraj Muhidin Degefa's team predicted clinic delivery in 2026 among Ethiopian women using machine learning on a 2019 national survey of 5,413 women with recent births. Clinic birth with skilled attendants cuts maternal and newborn deaths, yet many Ethiopian births still happen at home. Seven guided models were trained with careful cleaning and imbalance handling, and predictor importance was explained with SHAP values.

Random forest led with about seventy-four percent accuracy and eighty percent precision on test data, and top drivers included factors the paper details for targeting outreach. Health planners get a prediction tool plus a determinant map for lifting clinic births. The 2019 data and cross-sectional design mean current patterns need fresh confirmation.
pmc-13440804:
Dimitri T K Ndandja and colleagues measure what predicts a brain abscess bursting into the brain's fluid chambers, analysing 104 patients treated in Moscow between 2018 and 2023, in a 2026 study. Such rupture is among the deadliest turns a brain abscess can take. Records from two large hospitals covered patient traits, scans, germs, treatments, and outcomes, mixing past charts with prospective follow-up.

Rupture struck twenty-eight patients, just over a quarter of the group. Ruptured cases carried by far the highest odds of death and poor recovery. Distance dominated the risk maths: the closer an abscess sat to the chamber wall, the steeper the rupture odds climbed, dwarfing other traits. Weak immunity added independent risk. A five-millimetre cutoff separated danger well on accuracy testing. The authors urge early surgical drainage for any abscess within that margin.
pmc-13441204:
Hoo and colleagues measure how well a two part antibiotic design sticks to drug resistant Staphylococcus aureus, bacteria that cause hard to treat infections. The design joins vancomycin, a last resort antibiotic that grips the bacterial wall, to formyl peptides, small signals that summon immune cells. The hope is a conjugate that both marks bacteria and calls in the immune system. Their 2026 study uses flow cytometry, a laser counting method, to quantify binding on clinic isolates.

The conjugates bound less well than vancomycin alone. Their direct bacteria killing also fell, in step with the weaker binding. Binding still scaled measurably, which matters because the peptide cargo sets up a scent gradient guiding immune cells to the bacteria. The authors present the counting method as a tuning tool for balancing wall grip against immune signaling before body tests.
pmc-13441704:
Xiang Zhou and Changqing Ye sort patients recovering from acute COPD flare-ups into recovery paths and ask whether inflammation at admission foretells the path, in a 2026 study. Two hundred sixteen patients hospitalised between January 2023 and December 2024 were followed at seven time points, from admission to twelve weeks after discharge. Standard symptom and breathlessness scores charted each recovery, and blood markers CRP and procalcitonin gauged inflammatory burden on arrival.

Trajectory modelling found four paths: rapid recovery, slow recovery, persistent symptoms, and a fourth group detailed in the full report. Just under two fifths of patients recovered rapidly, while about a fifth stayed persistently symptomatic. Statistical models then linked trajectory membership to later repeat flare-ups, readmissions, and death risk, with regression hunting for traits that predict a non-rapid path. The authors argue that early symptom tracking can flag patients who need closer post-discharge care.
pmc-13442604:
Xiao Feng He and colleagues present a 60-year-old woman with early stomach cancer tied to Epstein-Barr virus in a 2026 case report. She had felt belly pain and swelling for more than a year before care. A scope biopsy showed poorly formed gland cancer, and surgery removed most of her stomach plus nearby lymph nodes.

Final lab work named the rare virus-linked subtype, with a lymph-rich growth pattern and spread along a nerve, a high-risk trait. Her team then weighed extra drug care after surgery, a point with no firm shared rule for early cases. She left the hospital in better shape, and a check one month later showed no spread, when a SOX drug plan enters the report. The authors pair her course with a review of cause, lab signs, and care paths for this subtype.
pmc-13443604:
Xinmiao Jia and colleagues tie a mouth germ, Fusobacterium periodonticum, to colon cancer growth through a fat acid in a 2026 study. Gene and chemical scans of patient groups found the germ enriched in cancer cases, hand in hand with high decanoic acid. Single-cell reads showed neutrophil crowds thick in cancer tissue, rich in a call signal, CXCL8.

Dish tests showed the acid can kill neutrophils late, yet also lure them through a toxin-sensitive G-protein path. Colonized mice grew more early gut growths and held more of the acid in the gut. Acid dosing alone sped tumor growth in mice by drawing neutrophils in. The authors cast the germ-acid pair as a driver pair that clinics might one day block.
pmc-13444004:
Charles van Wijk and Chris Muller test a 12-question mind health screen for extreme work posts in a 2026 study. Crews in isolated, confined, or harsh sites face strain that standard screens may misread. Two watch cohorts, with 730 and 128 workers, took the GHQ-12 beside proven scales for illness, grit, and mood.

Factor checks backed one strong general score, with thin side splits for plus and minus items. Scores rose with depression, worry, and adjustment strain, and fell as grit and mood rose. Repeat tests held fairly steady over time. A grey-zone plan with two cut marks sharpened triage for watch teams. The authors back the screen for field surveillance, while a few workers' sharp dips under stress show its watch value.
pmc-13444104:
Andrés F Bedoya-López and coauthors profile a 2026 epigenetic study of second primary breast cancers, which strike survivors and fare worse than first primaries for reasons still poorly mapped. The team set genome-wide methylation in 13 second primaries and 29 first primaries side by side, all estrogen-receptor positive and HER2 negative, then checked patterns in TCGA multi-omics data.

Second primaries carried 11,321 differentially methylated sites, with promoter hypermethylation hitting morphogenesis, hormone signaling, and cell adhesion genes, while hormone pathways fell in expression. Key transcription factor sites also shifted, and mitotic age ran higher by a wide margin. The scars point to prior malignancy and its treatment shaping later tumors, offering a base for tailored risk and therapy research.
pmc-13444304:
Yağmur Sürmeli Akbal and colleagues report a 2026 cross-sectional study of coffee habits and hot flush severity in 169 postmenopausal women in Turkey. The team recorded demographics, coffee type, amount, and drinking temperature alongside vasomotor symptom scores, testing links with ordinal regression.

Most women drank mainly Turkish coffee, and about half drank at most one cup daily. Coffee type and serving temperature linked significantly to some vasomotor symptoms, though the pattern varied by symptom. The authors present the links as suggestive rather than settled, calling for larger studies before advising women to change coffee habits.
pmc-13445504:
Laila Abu Madegam and colleagues map a switch that decides whether stressed cells recycle proteins from an inner compartment or move toward death, in a 2026 cell study. The compartment, the endoplasmic reticulum, folds proteins for the cell. Under mild stress it can send some proteins back to the cell body, where they gain survival roles.

Two helper proteins, DNAJB12 and DNAJB14, govern that return flow and sense the compartment's chemical balance. Mild stress keeps their inner bonds intact and the flow strong. Harsh stress floods the cell with a reducing agent that breaks those bonds, the helpers break down, and the flow stops. Cells then open a death path through two pore-forming proteins, a switch the authors tie to a third helper that recruits them.
pmc-13446204:
Po-Huang Chen and colleagues use a world health records network to ask whether a diabetes drug class, SGLT2 inhibitors, links to lower spread of breast cancer, in a 2026 study. The drugs lower blood sugar and show hints of anti-cancer action in the lab. The team mimicked a trial among women with breast cancer and type 2 diabetes who had breast removal surgery.

After matching, each arm held 3,569 women, new users of the drug class or of other diabetes drugs. Over five years, the drug group faced about a third lower risk of distant spread overall. The shield ran strongest for liver spread, then lung and bone, with no clear link for brain spread. Gene data from spread tumors fit the same gradient, though the authors urge caution.
pmc-13446304:
Rui Ma and colleagues map a partnership between two cell types that drives pancreatic cancer growth and shields it from immune drugs, in a 2026 study. Pancreatic tumors hide in dense scar tissue packed with fibroblasts, support cells that vary widely in kind. Single-cell and place-based gene reading singled out one fibroblast breed marked by the protein THBS2.

That breed crowds liver spread sites and helps wall immune cells out of the tumor. A master switch named PRRX2 steers its formation. The breed trades signals with malignant cells marked KRT17 through a THBS2 link, and tumors rich in both cell types mark poor outlook and weak reply to immune therapy. The axis offers both a warning sign and a target for breaking the shield.
pmc-13447004:
Maryam Mohebbi and colleagues review microneedle patches as a three-way tool in virology, for vaccines, virus drugs, and quick tests, in a 2026 paper. The patches press tiny points through the skin's top layer without pain, reaching a zone dense with immune scout cells. That route can rouse immunity with less antigen and wins better acceptance than needles.

Work now spans set vaccines, steady release of antivirals, gene payloads, and sampling of skin fluid for diagnosis at the point of care. Many patches stay stable without deep cold, which eases shipping to far places. The authors weigh the drags as well: mass making, rule sorting, dose exactness, and user spread, before judging clinic readiness.
pmc-13447304:
Maozheng Xuan leads a team appraising guidelines and consensus statements for congenital heart disease in a 2026 systematic review. Guidance documents shape care for children born with heart defects, yet their methods and reporting vary widely. Two standard appraisal tools were applied to judge how rigorously documents were built and how fully they were reported.

Thirty-three documents from Chinese and English databases up to late 2025 were scored by four independent raters. Clarity of scope scored highest, while practical applicability scored lowest by a wide margin. Reporting covered basics yet often skipped evidence summaries, benefit and harm balance, and update plans. Evidence-based documents, larger author teams and international groups scored higher, with Chinese documents trailing across domains. The authors urge patient involvement and stronger methods in future guidance.
pmc-13448104:
Avinash K and Harinakshi Karkera present a 2026 boosted steadiness number scheme for Poisson and Helmholtz math based on scale-3 Haar wave bits. The tool splits slopes by wavelet spread-outs stretched to two ways, sets edges through adding constants, and studies settling and balance.

Multi-grid pre-tuning won for scale-2 splitting, while Haar wavelet pre-tuning won for scale-3 with paired gradients, and a shifted Laplace pre-tuner paired with GMRES handled Helmholtz cases. Runs backed boosted steadiness and settling. Builders gain a robust solver for wave and possible problems at higher detail levels.
pmc-13448704:
Xinyi Xu develops a 2026 attention-based line for 3D human pose gauging and cartoon making, pairing a ResNet-Transformer backbone with modular SmoothNet smoothing. The backbone extracts image traits, encodes global links, and outputs 3D keypoints, while SmoothNet cuts frame-level jitter in guessed runs.

Tests spanned three benchmarks with joint, vertex, and speed-up errors, plus a fair match separating backbone gains from smoothing gains. Cartoon quality was proven through Blender and Unreal Engine use. The modular design suits cartoonists needing stable, in-time smooth motion without optical capture rigs.
pmc-13448904:
Wieslaw Dowjat and Yu-Wen Hwang ask in 2026 a focused question about Down syndrome: does having extra copies of the DYRK1A gene raise the enzyme's activity, or only its amount? The gene sits on chromosome 21, which people with Down syndrome carry in three copies. The encoded kinase helps regulate cell cycles, brain development, and immune balance, and its excess is tied to several features of the syndrome, including early Alzheimer disease.

Comparing matched control and Down syndrome samples side by side, they measured protein levels and kinase activity in parallel. Activity rose in step with protein amount, whatever the enzyme's own phosphorylation state. The authors conclude that catalytic activity in Down syndrome is governed mainly by how much DYRK1A protein is present. That finding supports dosing ideas aimed at trimming the excess protein or its production rather than only blocking the active site.
pmc-13449404:
Wanjiku Mathenge and colleagues apply in 2026 Normalization Process Theory to ask whether artificial intelligence screening for diabetic eye disease can settle into everyday care in Rwanda. Diabetes is rising across sub-Saharan Africa while eye specialists stay scarce. The team interviewed nine clinical staff and 67 patients involved in AI-based retinopathy screening at three clinics in Kigali. They sorted what they heard into the theory's four lenses: shared understanding, engagement, workability, and appraisal.

Participants understood the program's purpose and valued how it stretched scarce expertise against a growing disease burden. Friction came from workload, unclear division of labor, patients' early distrust of the technology, and organizational rules limiting who may operate it. The authors judge adoption positive so far and offer the framework as a way to surface fixable problems early. They caution that longer follow-up must still prove the screening preserves vision and speeds treatment.
pmc-13449704:
Qinquan Cheng and co-authors ask in 2026 whether a routine blood value taken early in pregnancy, serum uric acid, foretells gestational diabetes before the usual testing window opens. Their multicentre review covered 5,614 pregnancies at three Chinese hospitals, keeping each woman's earliest uric acid reading before twenty-four weeks. Diabetes screening normally happens at twenty-four to twenty-eight weeks, leaving an early blind spot this marker might fill.

Diabetes developed in 1,187 pregnancies, 21.1 percent, and hypertensive disorders in 275. Women in the highest uric acid quarter faced an adjusted risk 1.54 times the lowest quarter for diabetes and 1.89 times for hypertension. Each rise of ten micromoles per liter added about three to four percent risk. Curve analysis hinted at mild nonlinearity for diabetes only. The authors position uric acid as a complement to known risk factors, never a replacement for the standard glucose test.
pmc-13450004:
Yunyun Zhang and colleagues tested virtual reality drills for ear, nose, and throat trainees learning scope exams in 2026. Trainees need safe, repeatable practice for scope work, and virtual reality gives lifelike three-dimensional scenes to practice in. The question was whether it beats old-style model drills.

Forty-six trainees at a Beijing teaching hospital were split at random into virtual reality drills or model drills with plastic models and real scopes. Both groups took a knowledge test, a hands-on skills test, and a survey on how pleased they were. The virtual reality group scored better on the reported measures, hinting that lifelike practice can sharpen scope skills before trainees see real patients. Schools gain a head-to-head test to weigh the cost of new gear.
pmc-13451604:
Jodi Bullard and co-authors describe in 2026 a one-day boot camp that taught school nurses in northeast Texas to turn their data into clear messages. School nurses log visits, shots, and screens daily, yet few chances exist to learn data skills. Nursing faculty at a local university built an eight-hour program for fifteen nurses.

A keynote opened the day, then morning stations drilled data reading and message craft. In the afternoon, five small groups each took a set school health scene and a named audience, built slides, and presented them. Nurses rated the day highly and asked for a harder follow-up. The team frames the camp as a seed for a regional partnership.
pmc-13451804:
Taha Yasin Akin and a large team compare in 2026 seven ways to grade how bad a child's reaction is during a food test. Clinics feed a child a suspect food under watch to settle allergy doubts, and reactions need a shared grade. The team regraded 344 positive tests from one center under all seven systems.

About a sixth of the reactions counted as anaphylaxis, the severe full-body kind, and those children were older on average. Two systems caught every severe case when set against a world standard, while false alarms varied by system. Most gaps traced to how each system reads gut symptoms. One European system struck the best balance, the authors say, and shared grading would steady care.
pmc-13451904:
Junyi Zhang and co-authors check in 2026 whether magnetic heart readings track wall thickening in people with high blood pressure. Lasting pressure load reshapes the heart's main pump chamber, and early spotting of that change warns of later failure. The study sets a magnetic heart test, which reads tiny fields from heart currents, against ultrasound measures of wall and chamber shape.

Several magnetic values tracked wall thickness and the wall-to-cavity ratio that marks inward growth. Timing ratios from the magnetic trace also tied to that inward pattern. A four-value magnetic model held a steady link with the inward shape. The authors offer the painless magnetic test as a possible early flag, pending wider checks.
pmc-13452204:
Sousa-Pinto and colleagues present a 2026 task force review testing whether allergic rhinitis alone and rhinitis with asthma are truly two diseases, as a 2023 hypothesis proposed. The review gathers real-world data from the MASK-air app studies, in which patients log symptoms and medicines daily, plus a large French population cohort.

Four findings anchor the review. A combined phenotype of asthma, rhinitis, and conjunctivitis was confirmed as more severe than single diseases. Patients with rhinitis plus asthma used more rhinitis medicines and reported worse nose and eye symptoms in every country tested. In poorly controlled rhinitis clusters, combined patients more often stacked several rhinitis drugs.  The weight of real-world evidence supports treating the combination as its own disease, with its own management.
pmc-13452304:
Oh and a very large team report in 2026 how a targeted antibody-drug worked in two hard cancer groups inside a broad tumor trial. The drug aims at HER2, a growth mark, and was given to patients whose bile duct or pancreas tumors carried it after past care failed. The groups held 41 and 25 patients, followed for a median near six and five months.

Tumors shrank in about a fifth of the bile duct group by local reads, and in very few of the pancreas group. The bile duct reply rate ran far higher in the strongest HER2 group, past half. Most other patients held steady for a time. The authors read the drug as a live option for bile duct tumors, less so for pancreas.
pmc-13453004:
Haoyu Li and colleagues built a faster way to pull vanadium, a metal used in steel and large batteries, out of hazardous factory residue. Their method pairs ultrasound with iron powder and a strong oxidizer to break open grains that trap the metal.

The ultrasound kept stripping a rust-like coating off the iron, so the iron kept feeding the reaction instead of stalling. The new system leached out about 92 percent of the vanadium, beating about 82 percent for the same setup without ultrasound. It also cut the energy barrier for the reaction by nearly three quarters, easing the step that slows leaching most. Li presents the process as a greener route to reclaim a scarce metal from waste.
pmc-13453504:
Keti Mamillo and five co-authors count fainting episodes during treadmill exercise tests at Mayo Clinic, drawing on 40,715 tests. Their 2026 study covers tests run from 2006 to 2010 in 33,885 patients, with each serious event checked in depth to find its likely cause. Fainting during such supervised tests is rare but can signal heart trouble.

Eight patients fully fainted and five nearly did, rates of 0.20 and 0.12 per thousand tests. Only two events traced to a proven heart rhythm fault. Full faints clustered in younger women and tied to low blood pressure or the body's own faint reflex, while near faints hit older men with heart disease. The authors present the numbers as backing for the safety of supervised exercise testing.
pmc-13453604:
Lai and colleagues studied in 2026 a protein called USP8 in sepsis-related lung injury. Sepsis is a life-threatening body-wide response to infection, and acute lung injury is one of its earliest severe harms. The team traced how USP8 affects mitochondria, the energy-making parts of cells, and ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron and fat damage.

USP8 was found to block a partner protein, USP24, from protecting a growth regulator called PGC-1α. With that protection lost, mitochondria renewal faltered and ferroptotic death signals rose in lung tissue. Removing USP8 greatly eased lung injury in the models, but only when USP24 was present to act. The authors name USP8 and USP24 as possible drug targets for sepsis lung injury, pending further tests.
pmc-13453804:
Giovanbattista Gravina and four co-authors give a mobile robot a control system for moving safely through crowds in multi room spaces. Their 2026 framework splits the open floor into overlapping convex zones, then plans a route as a chain of zones. Sensors merge laser scans with camera meaning, and tracking filters forecast where each person is heading.

A predictive controller then picks each move while a safety rule, a barrier function, keeps a hard gap from every person. The setup ran both in simulation and on a real TIAGo robot, a mobile arm platform. Adding camera meaning to the laser geometry lifted success and cut collisions in cluttered rooms. The authors present the layered design as a path for service robots in hospitals and public halls.
pmc-13454204:
Saide Umut Zeybek Çakti asks whether social media addiction harms romantic relationships through a chain of stiff thinking and poor sleep. Her 2026 study surveys 466 adults across Türkiye, with 368 women and 98 men aged 18 to 72. She tests a serial model: addiction feeds psychological inflexibility, the inability to bend with hard thoughts, which then feeds insomnia, which drags relationship quality down.

Addiction tracked higher inflexibility and insomnia, and lower relationship quality, all in the expected directions. The full chain model fit the data well, with each link passing its effect along in order. Çakti suggests that therapies building mental flexibility, plus sleep repair, could blunt the relational damage of heavy social media use. The design is a one time survey, so the chain shows linkage rather than proven cause, a limit the framing keeps in view.
pmc-13454304:
Robin Urquhart and others found in 2026 that cancer survivors reporting sexual dysfunction concerns use primary care more often in Nova Scotia. Sexual health concerns are common ongoing effects after cancer treatment, yet their link to physician use was not quantified. The team linked survey responses to registry and administrative health data.

Survivors of breast, prostate, bowel, melanoma, and blood cancers diagnosed in 2012 to 2014, plus young adult survivors of any invasive cancer, were included, totaling 823 respondents. Nearly one-third reported sexual dysfunction as a big concern. Multivariable models tested links to primary care and oncology visit counts during follow-up. Primary care visits were higher among those with concerns, signaling unmet needs that primary care teams should address.
pmc-13454704:
Shotaro Komeyama and five colleagues report, in 2026, a case where debris inside a heart pump's outflow tube shifted position and suddenly choked the flow. Such external graft blockage is a known danger for people living on a left ventricular assist device, a mechanical pump that aids a failing heart. The patient was a 64-year-old man, four years after receiving his pump.

At a routine visit he felt fine, with pump readings at his usual levels. Scans, though, showed the graft pinched by half near the tube's guard sleeve. Later images told the real story: the near pinch eased while a new, severe pinch formed farther along the same sleeve. The debris had moved. The authors use the paired scans to show how a quiet finding can turn acute without any new material forming, only old material relocating.
pmc-13454804:
Junhao Wei, Yu Song, and Mingjia Guo critically review, in 2026, a decade of research on appearance anxiety, the lasting worry about how one looks under social scrutiny. Image-heavy culture and algorithm-driven feeds have sharpened this distress, above all among teenagers and young adults. The authors build a model that joins body, mind, and social forces.

Their review gathers studies from 2015 to 2025 across major databases. Social feeds serve a narrow, polished beauty standard again and again, which the authors liken to an exaggerated lure. Peer comments and family attitudes form a second layer of causes. Personal traits such as perfectionism and low self-worth form a third. The authors then grade existing help programs for real-world fit, finding many tested only in tidy lab settings. They close with practical directions for prevention that schools and platforms could actually run.
pmc-13455304:
Xia Chen and colleagues report a rare heart birth defect in a 2026 case study of a 44-year-old man. A thin membrane above the lung valve had fused with one valve leaflet, forming a pouch that choked blood flow out of the right heart, a shape not reported before. The man came in with growing breathlessness on exertion, and scans showed severe narrowing with a peak pressure gap of 170 mmHg across the valve.

At surgery the valve had three leaflets with thick, fused joins, and the team freed those joins to relieve the block. The patient recovered well and reported no symptoms at one month. Single cases cannot set a rule for others. The report gives surgeons a named shape to watch for when a membrane and valve appear joined. It shows that freeing the fused tissue can restore flow.
pmc-13455404:
Athinan Prommahom and colleagues describe rare chest and neck vessel variants found in a 2026 donor case. An aberrant right subclavian artery, the commonest arch variant, often runs behind the oesophagus. It can coincide with a non-recurrent laryngeal nerve, yet its pairing with missing chest wall arteries was barely recorded. Dissection of a 43-year-old Thai donor, embalmed with silicone-coloured vessels, mapped neck and upper chest anatomy.

The aberrant artery arose as the fourth arch branch behind the oesophagus, with no Kommerell pouch. The right laryngeal nerve ran directly from the vagus nerve. The right internal thoracic artery was absent, replaced by a superior intercostal artery from that vessel. A separate branch fed the left longus colli muscle. Surgeons gain a warning: image these vessels before thyroid, neck, oesophageal or bypass surgery, since a routine cut could injure an unexpected artery or nerve.
pmc-13456804:
Yimamu and colleagues test whether leftover cholesterol in the blood predicts artery re-narrowing after stenting in this 2026 retrospective study. Remnant cholesterol means the cholesterol carried in triglyceride-rich particles, and in-stent restenosis, renewed narrowing inside a stent, remains a stubborn problem after angioplasty. The team reviewed 548 coronary patients treated at a Sun Yat-sen University hospital between 2018 and 2023.

Fifty-six patients developed restenosis. Their leftover cholesterol levels ran significantly higher than those of the 492 patients who stayed clear of it during follow-up. Diabetes and alcohol use also independently predicted the outcome. When the cholesterol measure was combined with six clinical factors, the combined score separated the two groups with a discrimination value of about 0.72. Used on its own, the cholesterol measure scored about 0.62.
pmc-13457104:
Xingqing Long and nine colleagues review, in a 2026 article, immune-boosting nutrition for the mouth sores that radiation for head and neck cancer almost always causes. The sores strike eighty to nearly one hundred percent of patients, and over half suffer the severe grades, with pain, swallowing trouble, and weight loss. Ordinary feeding support fills calories but does nothing for the immune and tissue damage underneath.

Immunonutrition adds ingredients chosen to calm inflammation, fight oxidative stress, and help the mouth lining rebuild its barrier. Evidence gathered here suggests it can improve tolerance of radiation and chemotherapy and lift daily outcomes. Safety and tolerability look favorable across the studies. The authors are careful about certainty, since trials vary in formula and design. They frame immune nutrition as a promising partner to standard care, and they chart the trials needed to prove which blends help which patients.
pmc-13457204:
Antonio Moretti and colleagues review outcomes for critically ill patients whose lungs kept leaking air through abnormal connections into the chest cavity. Such persistent leaks complicate care for people on ventilators or high-flow oxygen, and sealing them with one-way endobronchial valves is one option. Their 2026 single-center study follows 38 adults treated this way, measuring how quickly chest drains could come out while treating death as a competing outcome.

The drain was removed in most patients quickly: cumulative removal reached 60.5 percent by day 10 and 94.7 percent by day 20, with a median of seven and a half days. Older age slowed removal, while air in the chest tissues around the heart predicted faster removal. In-hospital mortality was 10.5 percent, and no life-threatening procedure complications or emergency valve removals occurred. The authors say the results justify prospective trials in this high-risk group.
pmc-13457304:
H. Waldum, R. Fossmark, and I. Modlin argue that one hormone, gastrin, sits at the center of stomach cancer development. Gastric acid evolved to kill swallowed microbes, and the hormone gastrin, released when acidity falls, drives growth of the acid-producing lining and its enterochromaffin-like cells. Their 2026 perspective connects three roads to the same destination: infection with Helicobacter pylori, autoimmune wasting of the acid-producing tissue, and long-term acid-suppressing drugs.

All three lower acidity and thereby raise gastrin, sometimes for decades. Rodent studies showed acid blockers causing stomach tumors through exactly this hormone surge, and human tissue shows the early cell overgrowth. The authors contend that H. pylori causes cancer indirectly, through atrophy and high gastrin, rather than through any direct carcinogen, which explains why no such toxin was ever found. A drug that blocks gastrin, they say, is long overdue as a possible preventive.
pmc-13457704:
Lan Su, Xiaolong Pan, and Xinyao Duan study how virtual influencers turn human-like charm into good intentions. Brands and campaigns hire virtual activists more and more, yet how lifelike design produces goodwill was unmapped. Their 2026 survey asked 209 people who knew virtual activist content and modeled the paths with partial least squares, cross-checked by fuzzy-set analysis.

Making the influencer more human raised parasocial interaction, the one-sided friendship viewers feel, and warmed attitudes toward the influencer. Parasocial interaction fed attitudes, green self-identity, and a wish to do good. Attitudes and green self-identity each carried part of the effect toward doing good. The fuzzy-set results found several recipes for high intention, all built on green self-identity, while the recipes for low intention took another path. The authors frame activist anthropomorphism as open to design, offering guidance for building credible virtual advocates.
pmc-13458604:
Maciej Baron and colleagues systematically review two next-generation immune checkpoints in non-small cell lung cancer, VISTA and CD155, also called PVR. Checkpoint drugs have transformed this cancer's care, yet resistance is routine, pushing interest toward fresh brakes on immunity. Their 2026 review searches four databases through September 2025 and grades human, animal, and laboratory studies with standard bias tools.

Fifty-one studies qualified, 22 on VISTA and 29 on CD155. VISTA sat mainly in the stromal and immune compartments, plainly doing immune regulation, but its link to survival refused to settle in any consistent direction. CD155 decorated the tumor cells themselves, marked an immune-suppressed microenvironment, and more reliably predicted poor outcomes, especially when tumors also carried PD-L1. Study methods, scoring, and cut-offs varied enough to blur comparisons. The authors back CD155 as a prognostic marker and drug target worth advancing, while VISTA's clinical meaning stays an open question.
pmc-13458704:
Junchen Liu and colleagues test a porcine anti-T cell antibody in a rat model of multiple sclerosis in a 2026 study. Anti-human T lymphocyte porcine immunoglobulin, long used for aplastic anaemia and graft-versus-host disease, had unclear value against multiple sclerosis itself. The team tested P-ATG in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis rats, the standard animal model, after showing it binds human and rat T cells and curbs inflammatory cytokines in vitro.

Treatment eased behavioural and pathological changes, reducing spinal cord inflammation and demyelination, and cut interferon-gamma Th1 and interleukin-17 Th17 cell shares. The benefit came from blocking helper T cell activation toward Th1 and Th17 subsets, independent of T cell depletion. The study nominates P-ATG as a candidate multiple sclerosis therapy, pending safety and efficacy trials in people.
pmc-13459204:
Md Lokman Hossain and Derrick Y F Lai tracked two decades of plant growth across Inner Mongolia's grasslands to see how different grassland types withstand climate swings. Their 2026 study used satellite-derived productivity data from 2000 to 2019 for four grassland types, from lush meadow steppe to desert steppe. Productivity, measured as the carbon plants add each year, was compared against drought indices to separate resistance, absorbing a shock, from resilience, recovering after one.

Every grassland type grew more productive over the period, with meadow steppe gaining fastest and desert steppe slowest. Meadow steppe produced the most plant matter, at 251 grams of carbon per square meter yearly, against just 83 grams in desert steppe. Grasslands resisted wet extremes better than dry ones but recovered faster after drought than after wet spells. More plant species meant more productivity, suggesting diversity helps grasslands buffer climate extremes.
pmc-13459504:
Lhuaire and a large international team describe a hidden dissection plane in breast anatomy in this 2026 study. Tissue-preserving breast surgery depends on finding natural layers that open with minimal damage to glands and fascia, the connective tissue sheets. The team worked with fresh cadavers at two anatomy centers during 2024 and 2025. They performed 16 breast dissections. They compared standard and tissue-preserving approaches.

In every specimen they found a consistent posterior layer of stacked fat and fascia between the breast gland and the chest muscle's fascia. Gentle tunneling and balloon expansion preferentially opened exactly this plane, creating a workable space while sparing glands, fascia, and nearby nerves and vessels. Microscope staining confirmed the layer's laminated structure differed clearly from both gland tissue and the underlying muscle fascia.
pmc-13460104:
Li-Xi Gan and co-authors asked in 2026 whether involvement of the kidney arteries on a scan predicts how badly organs are starved of blood in acute type A aortic dissection. This emergency, a tear in the inner wall of the aorta, can cut flow to many organs at once. The study covered 471 patients operated on between 2020 and 2022, with 289 showing the tear extending to a renal artery opening.

Those patients had wider branch involvement, needed more extra procedures, and suffered more organ malperfusion and serious complications, even after matching. Renal involvement doubled the odds of malperfusion and more than tripled the hazard of death in adjusted models. The authors offer the scan finding as a simple, objective warning sign.
pmc-13460204:
Haikun Zhang and co-authors survey in 2026 how protein post-translational modifications, chemical edits made to proteins after they are built, drive acute respiratory distress syndrome. This catastrophic lung failure floods the air sacs and resists drug treatment, so attention turns to fast molecular switches. Classic edits such as phosphorylation and ubiquitination are covered first, as coordinators of the cytokine storm, vessel leakage, and failed fluid clearance.

Newer modifications then take the stage, including citrullination and lactylation, tied to neutrophil traps and amplifying inflammation. The review argues that the injured lung's rewired metabolism controls the enzymes performing these edits, making metabolism an upstream lever. Crosstalk between modifications and drugs targeting their enzymes close the discussion, with multi-omics studies proposed to bridge laboratory and bedside.
pmc-13460504:
Margaux Vandewalle and colleagues map the genetic structure of local and mainstream red-pied cattle breeds in a 2026 study. Pedigree completeness, common ancestors, pedigree and SNP-based inbreeding, multidimensional scaling and admixture were examined across five breeds from Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Germany.

Gene flow proved complex across all breeds, with the red-pied of the Ösling most connected to others, and the five breeds forming a genetic continuum rather than isolated groups. Inbreeding was not yet a problem overall, though some animals in the east Belgian and Meuse-Rhine-Yssel breeds ran above their breed averages. Breeders gain a basis for joint genetic evaluations, using mainstream breed data to strengthen local breed programmes.
pmc-13461504:
Ping Lai and colleagues analyzed in 2026 global atrial fibrillation deaths from 1990 to 2021 through the Global Burden of Disease study. They asked how age, sex, development level, and alcohol shape the toll across 204 countries. Atrial fibrillation, a chaotic heart rhythm, kills and disables millions, and alcohol's contribution had been comparatively neglected in global accounting.

Death rates rose worldwide for both sexes, climbing faster in women, with female increases concentrated at the oldest ages while male rates surged both young and old. Country stories diverged sharply: China's rates fell for both sexes, Sweden's rose, and Greenland's male rate declined. Alcohol weighed most heavily on fibrillation deaths in Europe and the Americas and far less across Africa, Southeast Asia, and the Eastern Mediterranean.
pmc-13461704:
Tianjiao Cui and colleagues compare, in a 2026 study, two steroid treatments for IgA nephropathy, a kidney disease. An immune protein builds up in the kidneys and harms them over time. One option releases budesonide in the gut, where much faulty immune activity starts. The other gives steroids body-wide, which works but carries wider side effects. 

The study followed 82 adults with biopsy-proven disease, 32 on the targeted drug and 50 on whole-body steroids, with checks over nine months. Both groups showed drops in protein leaking into urine. The main protein measure did not differ between groups at any point. A kidney function measure looked better for the targeted drug at six months, then faded by nine months. Serious infections and steroid side effects were fewer with the targeted drug, though events were few. The authors urge care with the short-term signals and call for longer follow-up.
pmc-13461904:
Sara N El Touliani and colleagues run, in a 2026 trial, a head-to-head test of two implant timings. One option places the implant at once. The other waits a healing period first. Each patient received both timings, one on each side, with custom-shaped healing caps. Twelve patients gave 24 implant sites.

Bone loss around the implant was the main measure, checked with 3D scans over a year. Immediate implants lost less bone early and felt stabler at three months. By twelve months, bone loss and stability no longer differed. Looks told a different story: gum and crown scores favored immediate placement at one year. Gum health improved in both groups, and no implant was lost. The authors conclude timing matters less for bone at one year when surgery and caps are used, while early placement may please the eye more.
pmc-13462404:
Tang and colleagues compared in 2026 high-frequency ultrasound and MRI for judging ankle ligament tears before surgery. The anterior talofibular ligament is the ankle ligament torn most often, and a second ligament, the calcaneofibular, is often hurt with it. The team reviewed 123 surgically treated patients from 2015 to 2025 who had both scans, and used the surgery itself as the truth standard.

Tang found ultrasound graded the main ligament's tear severity more accurately than MRI, at about nine in ten cases against about eight in ten. Ultrasound also scored higher for spotting complete tears. The picture flipped for the partner ligament: MRI caught nearly all its injuries, while ultrasound found only about two-thirds. The authors back a combined plan, ultrasound first for the main ligament and MRI when a fuller map of combined injury is needed.
pmc-13462804:
Shuo Shen and a large team build, in a 2026 study, an MRI-based prediction model for neck lymph node spread in thyroid cancer before surgery. Standard ultrasound and CT miss many involved nodes, yet the answer shapes the operation. The team enrolled 97 patients with thyroid cancer who had MRI scans and node removal at a hospital in Guangxi between 2017 and 2019. Sixty-three percent of patients had positive nodes.

Seventeen hundred image features were pulled from two MRI sequences, then winnowed into a signature read by a random forest model. The combined model, joining both sequences, beat each single-sequence model in training and checks. In the check set it caught almost all positive cases, yet its specificity was only one half, so many healthy nodes were flagged. The authors judge the model promising for sorting risk, though too trigger-happy to stand alone. Larger outside studies must come first.
pmc-13464104:
Zihan Su and Suowen Xu review inflammation as a driver of atherosclerosis, the artery-narrowing disease behind most heart attacks and strokes. Fat buildup alone no longer explains the disease, the pair argue. Vessel wall cells and immune cells keep a slow burn alive inside plaques.

Smoking, blood sugar faults, and fatty blood products all stoke that burn. A blood marker of inflammation now beats cholesterol at foretelling heart risk in some studies. Pairing fat-lowering drugs with inflammation blockers cut repeat events in trials, though infection risk needs care. Fresh tools, from stem-cell vessel models to rapid drug screens, close the survey of what care may look like next.
pmc-13464404:
Alaa A. Alkhateeb and five co-authors survey parents in Saudi Arabia on blocks to dental care for their children. The team questioned 351 parents of children aged one to eighteen between March and April 2023. Questions followed a known access framework that spans system and family factors.

A third of parents said needed dental care had been hard to reach in the past year. Children rated with fair or poor mouth health faced the steepest odds of access trouble by far. A child's general health troubles also raised the odds, as did having no clinic nearby. The authors call for wider, representative studies and for policy that spreads clinics where families actually live.
pmc-13464704:
Paynter and colleagues review in 2026 how communication problems in motor neurone disease, a progressive nerve disease also called ALS, can quietly strip patients of their say in medical decisions. Drawing on qualitative studies with patients and family carers, they map communication themes onto a team decision-making model and propose improvements.

Patients and carers do heavy hidden work to prepare for appointments and compensate for slow or effortful speech, work clinicians may not notice. When expression is slow, nuanced preferences get lost, and decisions can drift to others by default. The authors suggest clinicians state shared responsibilities openly and build communication support into every stage of care. They also give strategies for patients and families, and call for studies testing the revised model in practice.
pmc-13464904:
Yang and colleagues catalogued in 2026 the MAPK gene family in peanut. This family is a relay of signaling proteins letting plant cells react to stress and attack. Scanning the whole peanut genome, they found 32 family members spread unevenly across 14 chromosomes. The genes were sorted into four subgroups by evolutionary relatedness. The team checked which ones switch on across 19 tissues and under varied stresses.

Most family genes stayed modestly active everywhere. Two, AhMPK3 and AhMPK18, ran consistently high and surged further under environmental challenges. When those two genes were boosted in test plants, the plants mounted stronger immune alarms. They released a burst of reactive oxygen and switched on a defense marker gene called FRK1. The fortified plants also resisted a bacterial pathogen causing speck disease far better than ordinary plants. Because peanuts suffer heavy disease losses, the authors flag these two genes as prime candidates for breeding hardier varieties.
pmc-13465304:
Naved and co-authors reported in 2026 a heart valve procedure completed without general anesthesia in a high-risk patient. The patient was a 67-year-old woman with morbid obesity and severe obstructive sleep apnea, whose breathing falters in sleep. She also had poorly controlled diabetes and lung disease. Her aortic valve was severely narrowed by calcium. A catheter-based valve replacement through the leg was planned under monitored anesthesia care.

The risk was that sedation would let her airway collapse. The team preempted it with a mask delivering bi-level positive pressure ventilation throughout the case. A dexmedetomidine-based sedation plan and regional pain blocks completed the approach. She breathed on her own the whole time. No airway intervention or switch to general anesthesia was needed. Recovery was uneventful, and she went home on the fourth day after surgery.
pmc-13465704:
Chen, Liu, and Yang test a talking therapy for people with schizophrenia in this 2026 multicenter randomized trial in northern Taiwan. Not taking medication reliably raises relapse and hospitalization risks in schizophrenia spectrum disorders. The therapy combines motivational interviewing, which builds a person's own reasons to change, with cognitive therapy. A total of 120 patients received either eight therapy sessions spread over roughly six months or routine care with education.

Medication adherence scores in the therapy group improved by 2.56 points by the end of treatment, a clearly larger gain than the control group achieved during the same period. Insight into their illness also rose more in the therapy group at both mid-treatment and final checks. Positive symptoms, such as delusions and hallucinations, eased significantly more with therapy as well.
pmc-13466204:
Xiaomin Xu and Xiangyang Gong measure how well three systems move together across China: medical service capacity, residents' health, and regional economic growth, in a 2026 analysis. Panel data ran from 2012 to 2022, framed by the national Healthy China 2030 strategy. A scoring model combined the three parts into one coordination index for each place and year.

The overall system score crept upward over the decade, growing roughly half a percent per year. Coordination itself stayed low, with most regions sitting at a basic level of alignment. Mapping tools, inequality breakdowns, and machine learning with explanation methods traced where gaps cluster and which factors track them most closely.
pmc-13466504:
Birgit Linhart and twelve colleagues published this 2026 immunology study on how allergens switch on mast cells, the cells behind type 1 allergy attacks. These cells carry IgE antibodies on a receptor called FcεRI, and an allergen that links several receptors triggers the cell to release its chemicals. The team asked how the number of binding sites on an allergen, and how much IgE sits on the cell, shape that trigger.

Using a grass pollen allergen fragment, they built model antigens carrying the fragment in different counts and positions. The four-site version provoked stronger cell emptying and calcium signals than the two-site versions. It even signalled when IgE coverage was low and in cells missing a key signalling protein. Computer simulations predicted it forms large, tangled receptor clusters, while two-site antigens form simple chains. Microscopy and particle tracking confirmed the larger clusters, tying allergen shape to signalling strength.
pmc-13466904:
Manami Yamaguchi and co-authors report an orthodontics study, published in 2026. It tests artificial intelligence for marking facial landmarks. The images were side-view skull X-rays. Accurate landmark points underpin treatment planning. The team trained a ResNet50 neural network. It places fifteen landmarks directly on each image. Training used 669 X-rays from one Japanese centre.

Fifty held-out images tested the model. Its average placement error was a little over one millimetre. Over eighty percent of points landed within two millimetres of the expert reference. Some points fell outside that range, the authors stress. The output should assist orthodontists, not replace them. Outside testing is still needed.
pmc-13467204:
Esha Gupta, Moe Hein Aung, and Eileen Bowden review why glaucoma and diabetic eye disease stay hidden until too late in poor regions. Obstacles include few specialists, costly equipment, long travel, and low public awareness.

Scarce clinic slots can be assigned by risk, remote eye clinics extend reach, and focused teaching raises awareness. Programs using these tools have raised screening and follow-up at far lower cost than hospital-centered models. The authors propose combined packages fitted to each setting's own constraints rather than one global recipe.
pmc-13467304:
Oğuz Özakın and co-authors present a 2026 prospective study on predicting low blood pressure after spinal anesthesia for cesarean birth. Before the spinal injection, the team measured three shock indices from vital signs and used ultrasound to gauge how much the right jugular vein in the neck collapses with breathing. Low pressure after the spinal was defined by set cutoffs within the first 15 minutes.

Of 80 women enrolled, 76 were analyzed, and 36 of them, or 47.4 percent, developed low blood pressure after the spinal. The four prespinal measures were significantly higher in the women who developed the problem. The authors also tested combined prediction models and checked them with a resampling method, aiming at a simple early warning tool for delivery teams.
pmc-13467404:
Alves and a large team profile immune cells called macrophages as mouth cancers develop in this 2026 observational study. The researchers stained tissue samples to count macrophages. Three markers defined the groups. CD68 marked all macrophages, CD163 the tumor-friendly type, and CD80 the tumor-fighting type.

They examined 81 samples: healthy mouth lining, white precancerous patches called leukoplakias, and established cancers. Every marker rose step by step across the groups, with counts significantly higher in cancers than in healthy tissue and highest just beneath the surface layer. The tumor-friendly CD163 type dominated, climbing from about 79 cells per square millimeter in healthy tissue to about 301 in cancers.
pmc-13467604:
Junseo Lee and colleagues test in 2026 a road material that changes color in the cold to warn drivers about black ice. The team filled pavement grooves with a polyurea composite containing a reversible heat-sensitive pigment and silica sand, then measured its color response and strength.

A mix with 10 percent binder and 20 parts pigment per hundred was picked as the most balanced option. In the cold it turned darker and more reddish, a visible shift from its normal state, and it kept that color response at low temperatures. Its compressive strength reached 10.13 megapascals, with flexural strength at 6.20 megapascals. The study frames the material as a low-tech warning surface for known ice-prone spots.
pmc-13467904:

The hard part is spreading the tiny particles evenly before they clump. Using an optimized mixing method, the team made composites with filler loads from zero to 15 percent by weight and pulled them at both slow and very fast rates.

Under fast loading, the filler usually weakened the material, except that the heaviest loading recovered strongly at the fastest rate, reaching 78.49 megapascals through high-rate energy absorption. pmc-13469404:
Lisa Anna Limmer and co-authors explain in 2026 how listening for faint sounds inside wood can reveal whether insect larvae are actively feeding. The method uses acoustic emission sensors, which pick up structure borne sound made by chewing larvae.

Trials ran from single larvae in small lab blocks to big structural timbers with unknown damage. The team tested how warmth, sensor contact, and distance from the larva changed detection. A portable one channel device proved ready for field use alongside a larger lab system. The authors caution that judging what the signals mean for a building still takes expert assessment.
pmc-13469804:

The authors conclude that light alone suffices for trapping, and that local virus control needs strengthening.
pmc-13469904:
Jie Jiang and co-authors build in 2026 a camera based inspection method for the beveled edges, called chamfers, cut into glass panes. In trials the mean measurement error stayed under a tenth of a millimeter.
pmc-13470204:

pmc-13470504:
Xiaodan Chen and nine colleagues published this 2026 nanomedicine paper on a light-activated particle treatment for colorectal cancer. In a mouse model of colorectal cancer, the treatment drew more antitumour macrophages and effector T cells into the tumours.
pmc-13470704:

A matching framework pairs each technology with scenes such as wellbore integrity, reservoir movement, caprock faults, and surface facilities. The authors also fold in recent machine learning work on fiber data. Their recommendations split into near term and long term steps toward wide CCUS deployment.
pmc-13470904:

One carbon, YP-50F, completed nearly five hundred cycles, about twice the count of the weakest rival, showing faster charge and discharge behavior. The authors credit better transport through the particles and a closer match of electrical potentials.
pmc-13471304:
Hiratsuka and colleagues surveyed patients and staff in 2026 before launching diabetes screening inside a dental clinic for Alaska Native and American Indian adults. Patients were largely enthusiastic: most agreed the dental clinic is a good place for screening, expected it to help, and had few concerns about the setting. A minority worried screening does not belong in a dental visit, and about half thought results would help their own doctor. The coolest response came from primary care providers, who saw no need for dental-based screening at all. The authors say the pilot design must win over those providers, clarify roles, and use patients' openness as the engine of adoption.
pmc-13471404:
Yuan-Yuan Zeng, Yong Zhang, Feng Chen, and Yong-Jun Fang review in 2026 the nerve side effects of a leukemia drug in children treated at their hospital. Records covered sixty children treated across two years, with every neurological event logged by timing, severity, management, and outcome.

Thirteen children had eighteen events between them, mostly headache, dizziness, tremor, and confusion. Most events struck during the first treatment cycle, at a median of about nine days in, and lasted under three days. Nearly nine in ten were mild or moderate. Two children suffered grade four events, one with prolonged seizures and one with brain herniation. Older age independently predicted these events.
pmc-13471704:
Emma Filtenborg Hocke and twenty-three colleagues published this 2026 study of diversity in the hinge region of pfmdr1, a malaria parasite gene whose mutations tune resistance to antimalarial drugs. That variant correlated with resistance mutations at two codons, with odds of 12.6 for the pairing. Parasites carrying resistance mutations showed less hinge diversity, a sign in line with drug selection pressure since combination therapy rollout. The authors frame it as an evolutionary marker for tracking how treatment policy alters parasite populations.
pmc-13472204:

Their 2026 study peels flakes onto gold and reads electron patterns in three settings. These are single layers stuck to the metal, double layers, and layers lifted free over bubbles, where strain stretches them.

The lifted layer settled into a ripple geometry, one not seen in bulk. Charge transfer, bonding to the substrate, and strain were the control knobs. For device builders, the message is practical: in atom thin materials, the interface is not packaging, it is part of the physics.
pmc-13472804:
Wang and colleagues asked in 2026 which measures predict coronary heart disease in hospital patients who have type 2 diabetes but normal thyroid test ranges. In single-factor checks, insulin resistance, belly fat, one thyroid sensitivity index, age, and high blood pressure all tracked with heart disease. In the final model, the thyroid index, insulin resistance, belly fat, and age each stayed independent predictors. The model sorted patients with good accuracy, scoring near the same level in training and validation groups. The authors say adding thyroid sensitivity and belly fat measures could sharpen risk sorting in this common patient group.
pmc-13473104:

pmc-13473504:
Zachary B. Millman and co-authors probe how young people at high risk for psychosis learn from gains and losses in 2026. pmc-13473604:

pmc-13474004:
Gosse and colleagues in Australia asked in 2026 how country families rate the allied health care their children get for growth and handicap needs. Allied health spans speech, motion, and daily skill help. Town kids trail city kids on growth marks, and bush teams face long drives and thin staff. The team used warm, strength first talks, and heard from thirteen parents, one carer, and eight children in rural South Australia.

Folk prized teams who were part of town life, bent hours and rooms to fit, and walked them through the maze of funds. One mother said the team felt like a magic wand in hand.
pmc-13474404:

pmc-13474604:

pmc-13474804:

pmc-13476404:

pmc-13477004:
Sho Takagi and eight colleagues searched in 2026 for predictors of later aorta events after central repair of acute DeBakey type I dissection. They compared 51 patients who later suffered distal enlargement, new dissection, distal surgery, or rupture with 75 who did not.

pmc-13478604:

Early warning matters because delirium worsens recovery and lengthens hospital stays.

The model reached 92.0 percent accuracy on held-out patients, with discrimination scores of 0.76 averaged across classes and 0.96 pooled overall in the evaluation. Risk rose notably past age 60 years and past an injury score of 15 points on the severity scale.
pmc-13479404:
Sanskriti Iyer and coauthors published a 2026 survey study of what makes at-risk adults intend to check their own skin in depth. A layered statistical test then weighed which traits of age, mind, outlook, and habit best foretold plans to self-check. The authors aim to find the levers that skin cancer campaigns should pull, since knowing alone rarely turns into the habit of a full, careful skin check.
pmc-13479604:
Yuqi Yao and coauthors published a 2026 study of chemical tweaks to the first letter of gene-silencing RNA strands. Several modified strands silenced their targets significantly better than unmodified controls. Early safety checks found no detectable cell toxicity and no sign of the material inserting into the genome. The authors offer the modification as a general potency booster for RNA medicines.
pmc-13479704:

Blocking that signal or inhibiting PADI4 with a drug compound was tested as treatment in the mice. Cell culture experiments with irradiated lung cells and neutrophil-like cells confirmed the recruitment circuit. The authors nominate this axis as a druggable route into a currently stubborn complication.
pmc-13480104:
Kai-Hsiang Chang and colleagues report a 2026 case in which a heart catheter tangled on itself during a rhythm procedure. A 61-year-old man with persistent atrial fibrillation had a ten-pole diagnostic catheter guided toward the coronary sinus. The catheter slipped back, looped inside the right atrium, and tightened around nearby tissue with each pull, so standard withdrawal failed.

The team switched to a neck vein entry, used a steerable delivery tube plus a wire to steady the loop, and applied a snare pull from the other side. The catheter came free with no surgery and no damage to heart structures. The case gives labs a stepwise rescue plan for a rare but risky tangle.
pmc-13480204:
João Tiago Serra and co-authors describe a 2026 study of urinary tract damage in a worm infection zone in Mozambique. The infection, caused by Schistosoma haematobium, scars the bladder and kidneys over time. pmc-13482304:
Noureddine Elboughdiri and five colleagues tested in 2026 whether farm-waste ashes can replace Portland cement in geopolymer concrete. The article is flagged retracted, yet its experiments cover banana peel ash and sugarcane bagasse ash blends tuned for strength and handling.

Lab scans confirmed high silica content and cement-like behavior, with stronger activator yielding a denser matrix. pmc-13482504:
Kesia Esther da Silva and co-authors present a 2026 genomic study of tuberculosis spread inside Brazilian prisons, asking whether people without symptoms drive spread as much as those who feel ill. pmc-13483204:
Heather K. Bouzek and co-authors present a 2026 genome atlas of Gardnerella, the bacteria tied to bacterial vaginosis, a condition touching near one in three women of childbearing age. Drug and vaccine work gains a firm map at last.
pmc-13483404:

Of 65 people recruited, 61 finished all four days and gave feedback in group sessions. Residents liked reflecting on their food and suggested tweaks for sharper recall. Tallies showed women over the calorie guide and men under it, salt above healthy limits for all, and fruit, vegetable, and mineral intake running short. With the suggested fixes, the tool can serve diet studies across locked settings.
pmc-13483504:
Beiqi Yang and co-authors catalogue the temperature-sensing gene family of the red swamp crayfish in a 2026 genome study. Nine genes shifted under cold, twelve under harsh heat. Two lead candidates also changed how their messages were spliced. Breeders chasing hardier stock now have named targets.
pmc-13483704:

In 2026, the study looks at questionnaires and blood and urine samples collected in 2023 from 568 young people across five regions. pmc-13483904:

pmc-13486104:

pmc-13486504:

pmc-13486804:

Brain, blood, and peripheral organs are all sampled.

pmc-13487304:

pmc-13487904:

pmc-13489204:

pmc-13490604:

pmc-13491604:

pmc-13491704:

pmc-13491804:

pmc-13493804:

pmc-13493904:

pmc-13494004:

pmc-13495204:

pmc-13495304:

pmc-13500404:

pmc-13500604:

pmc-13500804:

pmc-13501004:

pmc-13501704:

pmc-13501804:

pmc-13503704:

pmc-13503804:

pmc-13503904:

pmc-13504004: Shawn S. Goodman and co-authors issued this 2026 correction for their paper on modeling ear emission growth. pmc-13506604:

pmc-13507204:

pmc-13508204:

pmc-13508404:

pmc-13508804:

pmc-13509804:
Zhiyong Han and co-authors ask in this 2026 study whether leaning on artificial intelligence at work can actually make employees more innovative, rather than dulling their thinking. They surveyed full-time employees in China between December 2024 and February 2025.

The benefit of flexibility faded, though, when jobs were highly complex. pmc-13511504:

pmc-13512904:

pmc-13514304:

pmc-13514504:
Giuseppe Guido Maria Scarlata and seven co-authors review, in a 2026 narrative synthesis, how gut microbes differ across the forms of metabolic syndrome. pmc-13518104:
Scott T Kilian, Samuel A Cerezo, and Rebecca L Sanchez review genetic ways to stop malaria mosquitoes in a 2026 article. Each also carries barriers the review weighs: ecological side effects, public acceptance, regulation, and the parasite's own talent for adaptation. pmc-13518804:
Hatice Eraslan Boz and five colleagues measure how rapid eye movements change across adulthood in 2026 research. Correct look-away rates also fell steadily, dropping most in the oldest group. pmc-13520504:
Khalid Abdullah Aljohani surveys in 2026 school health services across 242 public schools in Saudi Arabia, where no dedicated school nurses exist and teachers act as health advisors instead. Readiness for the national Healthy Schools Program was scored with an adapted index.

Boys' schools showed more funding gaps, while girls' schools showed stronger policy delivery and health teaching. Services leaned on outside workshops rather than steady clinical care. The author recommends a nurse-led model aligned with national reform goals, citing fragmented emergency and chronic care under the current setup.
pmc-13521504:
Sebastián Ayala and colleagues reported a stroke case in a young man living with advanced HIV infection. pmc-13522504:

pmc-13522704:

pmc-13523004:

pmc-13526104:

pmc-13527104:

pmc-13527504:

pmc-13527904:

pmc-13528004:

pmc-13528104:

pmc-13528904:

pmc-13529804:

pmc-13530104:

pmc-13530204:

pmc-13531004:

pmc-13531804:

pmc-13531904:

pmc-13532004:

pmc-13534704:

pmc-13536804:

pmc-13537504:

pmc-13539804:

pmc-13540104:

pmc-13540204:

pmc-13540904:

pmc-13542204:

pmc-13543704:

pmc-13546404:

pmc-13547204:

pmc-13547404:

pmc-13548604:

pmc-13548704:

pmc-13550404:

pmc-13550604:

pmc-13551704:

pmc-13551804:

pmc-13551904:

pmc-13553704:

pmc-13554304:

pmc-13557804:

pmc-13558304:

pmc-13558604:

pmc-13558704:

pmc-13560204:

pmc-13560304:

pmc-13561604:

pmc-13562204:

pmc-13562504:

pmc-13562704:

pmc-13563804:

pmc-13563904:

pmc-13569604:

pmc-13572504:

pmc-13574904:

pmc-13575004:

pmc-13575104:

pmc-13575204:

pmc-13576004:

pmc-13576104:

pmc-13576304:

pmc-13579904:

pmc-13580004:

pmc-13582704:

pmc-13586304:

pmc-13586604:

pmc-13587104:

pmc-13591504:

pmc-13591804:

pmc-13592304:

pmc-13592504:

pmc-13592604:

Timing, speed accuracy trade offs, and trial to trial wobble were recorded.

One neck measure, correct responses per second at the decision stage, best separated youths with multiple concussions from those with none or one. It also tracked tightly with response wobble, matching two parts of a classic decision model. Wilkerson and the team suggest the paired measures may flag a lingering deficit after repeated head injury.
pmc-13593704:
Ahmed Fageeri and Ousmane Hisseine review how to make ultra-high-performance concrete with a smaller carbon footprint, tying together published data on more than two hundred mixtures. This concrete is exceptionally strong and durable, but its recipes lean so heavily on cement that its climate cost is high.

Machine learning models predicted compressive strength from recipe details with high accuracy, though stretch resistance and permeability depended on fine structure the recipe alone cannot capture. Strength measures at different ages tracked each other closely and moved opposite to permeability. One striking pattern: pushing cement content past a certain level added almost nothing to performance while raising emissions steeply. The authors use these links to sketch recipes that keep the strength and durability while cutting the carbon carried by each batch.
pmc-13593804:
Athanasia Pappa and co-authors gathered every systematic review comparing the teeth and gums of children with type 1 diabetes against healthy peers. Their 2026 umbrella review covered eleven reviews built on eighty-two original studies, and they graded each review's trustworthiness while measuring how heavily the reviews overlapped.

For baby teeth, cavity experience looked much the same with or without diabetes. For permanent teeth, some reviews found more decay in diabetic children, especially where blood sugar control was poor. Gum inflammation and deeper periodontal damage were consistently worse in the diabetes groups. Five of the reviews carried a high risk of bias, and study methods varied a lot. The authors call for long-term studies with standard measures before firm claims about cavities can be made.
pmc-13594204:
Gangling Xu and co-authors published a correction to their review of extracellular vesicle-based drugs, fixing three descriptive errors about particle sizes that crept in during drafting. The review itself had appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy in 2025, surveying how these tiny membrane parcels might carry medicines, and how their quality and safety should be checked.

The corrected text now states that microvesicles span roughly fifty to one thousand nanometers. These bud directly from the cell surface. Exosomes, released after forming inside the cell, span roughly forty to one hundred sixty. A table entry giving the overall size spread was likewise adjusted to forty to one thousand nanometers, noting the overlap between the two types. The authors stress that the slips were clerical and that every conclusion of the review stands unchanged.
pmc-13595504:
Hao Qinqin and colleagues studied how the Musashi 2 protein differs between single and double corpora lutea in hybrid Mongolian sheep. The Xing'an black sheep grows fast and yields good meat, yet usually bears single lambs, limiting farm income. Their 2026 study compared gene and protein levels in single versus double corpora lutea, the hormone glands left after ovulation.

Musashi 2 ran higher in single corpora lutea, while two fertility proteins, GDF9 and BMP15, ran higher in double ones, with Musashi 2 levels falling as the fertility proteins rose. Double-corpus ewes also showed higher progesterone, LH, and oestrogen and lower FSH. The authors present Musashi 2 as a possible breeding target for larger litters.
pmc-13597504:
Yueyi Chen and colleagues found a brain-cell group that drives fentanyl withdrawal pain and drug seeking in mice. Withdrawal brings compulsive seeking plus heightened pain, yet the circuits behind it, above all for this drug, remain murky. Their 2026 study mapped whole-brain action during withdrawal, then probed GABAergic neurons in the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray with lab, gene, current, and gene-switch tools.

Quitting boosted action in these inhibitory neurons, and silencing them eased withdrawal pain. In males, silencing also blocked the usual climb in drug self-dosing across final sessions, an effect absent in females. Chen and colleagues propose targeting inhibitory signalling in this brain region to ease withdrawal pain and curb drug use.
pmc-13599104:
Li-an Liao and four colleagues report a 2026 case in which two heart stents became tangled and floated free inside a patient's aorta. The man, aged 70, had returned for a second planned procedure after an earlier heart attack. A wire passed through the mesh of his first stent, so a new stent pulled the old one out of shape as it moved. Both stents ended up loose in the ascending aorta, where loose metal could block blood flow or damage the heart.

Clinicians removed both stents with a snare device, a small loop passed through a tube, and then placed a fresh stent.
