Liao's account traces the mishap to the first stent sticking slightly into the left main artery and to the wire position going unchecked. Readers gain a clear warning: confirm where the wire sits before pushing a stent onward, and pause when movement meets resistance.
pmc-13606904:
Haorui Zheng leads a ten-author team profiling apple pulp chemistry and its antioxidant compounds. Twenty-five pulp samples from twelve cultivars were analyzed for free sugars, organic acids, and phenolic compounds. Fructose was the dominant sugar and malic acid the dominant acid. Clustering on seven key traits sorted the samples into four chemical types: acid-rich, sugar-rich but phenolic-poor, low-accumulating, and phenolic-rich.

Phenolic traits tracked antioxidant capacity in test-tube assays far more strongly than sugars or acids. To check the chemistry in living cells, extracts from five samples were applied to liver cells stressed with oxidants. At the chosen dose, the extracts significantly cut reactive oxygen buildup, with one sample, labeled TPGSH, protecting cells most strongly. The authors offer the combined sugar-acid-phenolic framework to characterize apple varieties and spot patterns tied to antioxidant activity, guiding breeding and functional food claims.
pmc-13612404:
Selene Berni leads a ten-author team squeezing nitrogen and water to pressures found inside icy moons in 2026. Nitrogen hydrate, a cage compound of water and nitrogen gas, matters for modeling Titan, Enceladus, and water-rich exoplanets, yet its high-pressure behavior was sketchy. Combining Raman spectroscopy, neutron diffraction, and crystal structure prediction, the team mapped the phase diagram to 16 gigapascals.

The known cage structures gave way in sequence: cubic clathrates yielded to a hexagonal phase, then a tetragonal one, as pressure climbed. Above 1.8 gigapascals something new appeared, an orthorhombic filled-ice structure matching no known ice framework. Its density sits roughly 30 percent below that of ice VII, pointing to unusual water-nitrogen bonding. Filled-ice forms then persisted all the way to 16 gigapascals. The authors argue such low-density, nitrogen-rich ices could store volatiles deep inside icy worlds.
pmc-13615904:
Kana Katakami and colleagues compared two operations for open-angle glaucoma in Japanese patients over one year, a 2026 retrospective study from Kobe University Hospital. Both operations lower eye pressure by draining fluid under the eye's outer layer, but the newer implant avoids cutting sclera or iris tissue, while the older trabeculectomy remains the stronger pressure-lowering operation. The team matched 102 eyes in each group on age, sex, lens status, glaucoma type, starting pressure, drug count, and vision.

At twelve months, average pressure was lower after trabeculectomy than after the implant, at 12.3 against 14.1 millimeters of mercury, though both groups improved from baseline and success rates looked similar. Drug-free rates, vision, and corneal cell counts also showed no clear gap between groups. Complications tied to very low pressure were more common after trabeculectomy and persistent low pressure appeared only there.
pmc-13616304:
Congwei Lu and Guancong Ma analyse a strange state of non-Hermitian physics called exceptional deficiency. Non-Hermitian systems gain and lose energy. In this state, every vibration mode of a lattice sits at a special merging point. All its direction patterns collapse in pairs. The authors work out the maths of how such a lattice answers a steady push and a sudden one, using tools called Green's functions.

Across the whole spectrum they find double poles, which give extra-wide, extra-tall resonance curves and a full double twist of phase at each peak. A surprise follows: adding loss can bring back surface-hugging waves that the defective state had erased, a revival they name and explain. Time responses grow in a straight-line pattern that can amplify the surface effects. The results hand wave engineers a new set of levers in acoustics, optics, and circuits.
pmc-13616404:
Mengting Zheng, Shangshu Qian, Meng Li, Shanqing Zhang, and Jun Lu study direct rebuilding of spent battery cathodes. The cathodes use lithium cobalt oxide. Their work shows that the choice of negative ions in a molten salt bath decides whether rebuilding into high-grade material works. Mountains of dead batteries using this cathode are coming, and recycling that restores the material beats shredding it for scrap metal. Salt choice until now was guesswork, with the anions' role ignored.

Ions that grip the cobalt oxide slabs tightly yet release lithium easily, such as chloride, proved best. The process rebuilt the crystal along a preferred axis and grew a lithium-and-oxygen-rich surface with a favourable face. The revived cathode kept over 95 percent of its original capacity. Picking bath salts by the anion's grip, not habit, turns battery recycling into materials engineering.
pmc-13617704:
Katelyn Brehon and eleven colleagues report a 2026 qualitative study of how the COVID-19 pandemic changed healthcare access for people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma in Alberta, Canada. Diagnoses of both conditions fell during the pandemic, and the team wanted to know whether illness truly dropped or patients simply stopped reaching care. Thirteen interviews with patients and clinicians were held between October 2023 and July 2024.

Two themes emerged. First, the pandemic reshaped care-seeking: entry points into the health system narrowed, and how people managed stress and symptoms at home changed when they decided to seek help. Second, participants saw a time and place for both virtual and in-person care, valuing each for different needs. The authors recommend that future virtual care include at least a visual element and protect the therapeutic relationship, rather than treating remote visits as a lesser default.
pmc-13617904:
Parzhin Moradi and four colleagues pilot a systems biology hunt for saliva markers of orthodontic root resorption, the shortening of tooth roots that tooth movement sometimes causes. Their workflow started with a literature review and a disease gene database, built a protein interaction network to find hub genes, and predicted which regulators sit upstream. Saliva from twelve affected orthodontic patients and twelve matched controls then tested two chosen candidates.

One hundred sixty genes linked to the process, with thirteen hubs at the network's center. A regulator called IRF4 was predicted to drive the two selected genes, CASP1 and SPP1. Saliva tests confirmed higher levels of both encoded proteins, caspase-1 and osteopontin, in patients with resorption, and caspase-1 separated the groups almost perfectly in this small sample. The authors frame both proteins as candidates only, urging large prospective studies before any diagnostic or treatment claims.
pmc-13618404:
Alex H. Lee and five colleagues spend six months inside acute care surgery teams studying how clinicians use the electronic health record when seconds matter. Acute care surgery spans trauma, emergency surgery, and surgical critical care, and no shared strategy exists for bending record workflows to that pace. The study combined interviews with fifteen surgeons and providers and one hundred hours of paired observation by a surgeon and a sociologist.

Two camps appeared. Some surgeons accepted information overload as inherent, leaning on generic templates and standard attestations, while others treated it as fixable, correcting errors and writing individualized summaries. Ambiguous billing rules drove note bloat that buried high-yield facts, and record use in decisions centered on risk checks, hampered by navigation friction. Clinicians wanted outcome forecasts and automated risk scores drawn from live data without alert fatigue, inside existing workflows.
pmc-13618904:
Graham Johnson and five colleagues scope the literature on breaking bad news in emergency departments, where urgency, crowding, and scarce privacy make hard conversations harder. Using Joanna Briggs Institute methods, they searched four databases and grey literature in July 2025 for work on adult patients, relatives, and clinicians. From nearly eight thousand records, one hundred fifty-six publications from twenty-six countries qualified, most from the United States and United Kingdom.

Twenty-five communication frameworks appeared, most borrowed from oncology, with SPIKES the most cited, and only three built for emergency practice. The literature is heavily clinician-centered and education-focused, measuring mostly confidence. Patient and family perspectives are uncommon, and no studies track long-term outcomes. Time pressure, lack of privacy, and too little training recurred as barriers. The authors call for emergency frameworks and research that follows patients and families, not just staff.
pmc-13619704:
Eduard Eiben, Robert Ganian, and Iyad Kanj settle open questions about coordinated motion planning, the problem of moving many robots on a grid to their goals without collisions, in a 2026 paper. Two goals compete: finishing as fast as possible overall, or keeping the total distance traveled small. The authors ask how the difficulty of each version depends on the number of robots and on the target value itself.

Both versions turn out to be solvable by fixed-parameter methods when the number of robots is the chosen measure, using new insight into the shape of optimal plans. When the target value is the measure instead, the distance version stays tractable while the speed version becomes genuinely hard. That hardness proof also yields a simpler proof that two classic path problems on grids are hard even with short fixed path lengths.
pmc-13621704:
Jana Willems and co-authors describe a 2026 forum where families helped make sense of quality-of-life scores for children with congenital heart disease, a heart problem present from birth. Scores from patient questionnaires often sit in reports that families never discuss. The forum, built with a patient organization and a university hospital, tested a shared way to read early results together.

Twenty families took part, viewing interim scores in a plain-language picture of life stages and talking in small groups. Families explained where the numbers matched daily life and where they missed context, raising worries about transitions, emotional strain, and knowing whom to contact. The meeting produced short joint notes, a ranked list of actions, and a family-friendly figure named the Quality-of-Life Tree. Participants found the format clear and useful, and the authors offer it as a model other studies can copy.
pmc-13623204:
Eszter-Anna Dho-Nagy and co-authors check whether people who say they use shop-bought medicines safely actually grasp the risks those habits guard against. The study reuses survey data from Romania on adults with no health training. Five pairs of questions matched a safety habit, such as checking active ingredients, with a test of the related risk.

Among 206 respondents, good habits did not always mean good understanding. Of those who said they always check ingredients, about one in seven still missed the danger of doubling up on paracetamol, a common painkiller. Gaps ran far wider for mixing antihistamines with alcohol, where most routine checkers failed the test. People were most consistent on knowing when symptoms lasting too long need a professional. After strict statistical correction, only the ingredient link held firm. The authors propose teaching the reasoning behind safety advice, not just the rules.
pmc-13624004:
Sayaka Shirai and colleagues published a 2026 study hunting for CT scan signs that predict when watchful treatment will fail in isolated dissection of the superior mesenteric artery. That is a tear in the main gut artery that appears without aortic involvement. Most patients settle with rest and blood thinners, but some keep deteriorating and need a stent or surgery. Knowing who is who, early, would sharpen monitoring.

The single-centre review covered thirty-two patients treated between January 2011 and September 2022, split into nine failures and twenty-three successes. In failures, the surviving channel of the artery was pinched far tighter, often completely closed, and a cut-off near two-thirds narrowing separated the groups well. A backup route vessel, called Riolan's arch, also showed up in every failure case and only about half the successes. The authors stress the signs flag patients needing closer watching rather than proving gut damage.
pmc-13624304:
Jiayin Ma and colleagues hand a hardy industrial yeast the genetic toolkit it has been missing. The yeast Pichia kudriavzevii shrugs off heat, acid, and other stresses that trouble factory fermentations, which makes it attractive for making proteins and chemicals. Genetic tinkering in it, though, stayed clumsy next to the standard laboratory yeasts, especially since it carries two copies of every gene.

The team built a CRISPR editing system that cuts both gene copies. It reached editing success in up to eighty-eight percent of attempts without leaving marker genes behind, so edits can be stacked round after round. They placed production genes at chosen addresses in the genome and had the yeast secrete two test proteins: a glowing red reporter and the tail fragment of a human antibody. Both came out. The authors offer the system as the foundation for turning this tough yeast into a programmable factory.
pmc-13626404:
Sifei Lu and colleagues systematically review what brain wave recordings can tell doctors about the earliest shades of memory trouble. Subjective cognitive decline and mild cognitive impairment can precede Alzheimer's disease, and electroencephalography, cheap, painless, and fast, might flag who is at risk. The team searched nine databases in English and Chinese for studies of group differences, computer classification, screening value, and forecasts of decline in these two states.

Twenty reports made the cut, covering up to 3,853 confirmed participants, and each study type was graded with a matching bias tool while overall certainty was weighed by GRADE. The review gathers a scattered field into one account of which wave patterns separate groups and which models predict progression. Such a map matters because cheap early warnings could focus costly scans and trials on the right people.
pmc-13628704:
Damiano Piovesan and six colleagues present Bluues2, an upgraded web tool. It computes the charge traits of proteins fast, right in a browser. Charge patterns govern how proteins fold, stay stable, and spot partners. Yet the strict equations behind them are costly to solve for large structures.

Bluues2 uses a faster shortcut method with refined surface modelling. It estimates charge-linked values such as acid strength, surface potentials, and solvation energies. The new version also handles pairs of proteins, and proteins bound to small molecules. It reports binding energies and how well charges fit at the contact face. A built-in three-dimensional viewer rounds out the tool. So does a job-handling framework. The authors aim it at specialists and newcomers alike.
pmc-13629804:
Ahamed Vilangalil and seven colleagues review triazole compounds as candidate treatments for triple-negative breast cancer, the aggressive subtype that lacks the hormone and HER2 receptors most targeted drugs exploit. Triazoles appeal because their ring structure is stable, versatile, and able to engage several biological targets at once.

The review organises the evidence on how these compounds kill tumour cells: triggering programmed death, halting the cell cycle, blocking blood vessel growth and spread, and interfering with major cancer signaling pathways. Natural and synthetic versions are compared through structure-activity relationships, and computational tools such as docking and virtual screening get credit for speeding the search. Remaining challenges include overcoming drug resistance in the clinic.
pmc-13630504:
Orli Weiser and three colleagues mined health records to rebuild how one airway disease declares itself over time. The disease bundles severe asthma, nasal polyps, and sensitivity to common painkillers. Its diagnosis typically arrives late. Their 2026 letter studies 181 patients in an Israeli health service. The diagnoses spanned two decades.

The team ordered the first appearance of each diagnosis code. The sequence varied across patients. It linked to age at onset, to the length of diagnostic delay, and to how heavily patients used healthcare. One pattern stood out. Nasal polyps plus painkiller sensitivity appeared before any asthma label. The authors flag that sequence as a high-risk signature. It warrants earlier specialist referral. Biologic therapy may deserve thought too.
pmc-13631404:
Lewis Johnstone and two colleagues study how younger people with Parkinson's disease live with a diagnosis that keeps announcing itself. Parkinson's is framed as an illness of old age. Those diagnosed at fifty-five or younger face decades of managing symptoms. Their workplaces and social settings are built for the healthy. Telling people is only the first step.

Stories from 22 participants show disclosure is not a single event. Tremor, stiffness, and slowness leak the diagnosis in daily encounters. This happens whether the person chooses it or not. It generates repeated social pressure to explain the body. The authors develop the idea of everyday exposure for this continual, partly unwilling revelation. Its costs include isolation that standard accounts of illness stories miss.
pmc-13631804:
Martina Rotondo and three colleagues built lab-made molecules aimed at a small RNA that helps cancers grow. The target, called miRNA-221, is often overactive in solid tumors. Their carriers are peptide nucleic acids, sturdy DNA-like strands that grip a chosen RNA tightly. The problem is getting such strands inside cells, so the team attached cell-penetrating peptides to them.

The group made the combined molecules in two ways, using click chemistry or a sulfur-based link. Tests showed the strands paired strongly and selectively with their target RNA. In lung cancer cells, the molecules slowed cell growth modestly when a helper drug aided entry, and they caused no sudden cell poisoning. The work shows that the kind of link used shapes how well these delivery systems perform.
pmc-13633504:
Nanako Hamada and five colleagues studied how an approved lung fibrosis drug works at the level of single cells. The drug, nerandomilast, slows a disease where lung tissue scars and stiffens until breathing fails. Trials proved it helps patients, yet its cellular actions stayed unclear. The team gave the drug to mice with chemically induced lung scarring. They then read gene activity cell by cell in the injured lungs.

Treated mice showed less fibrotic remodeling and better preserved air sac walls. The drug shifted the behavior of type 2 alveolar cells, the surface cells that repair air sacs and make the coating that keeps them open. Those cells became more numerous and more active in cell-division programs. Staining confirmed a larger area covered by their marker protein. The findings suggest the drug protects the lung partly by supporting these repair cells.
pmc-13634604:
Golnoush Saeidi and three colleagues asked whether dental scans could flag thinning bones elsewhere. Osteoporosis weakens the whole skeleton and is usually measured with a dedicated scan, called DEXA, that many patients never receive. Dental cone-beam scans are already routine, though. The team studied sixty-three women aged fifty to seventy who had both scan types. They measured brightness and pattern complexity at six spots in the upper and lower jaws.

About half the women had normal bone density on the reference scan, while the rest had thinning or full osteoporosis. The dental measures failed to separate those groups overall. Within subgroups, though, some jaw sites did track the spine results, most clearly the upper premolar region in women with abnormal density. The authors call the findings exploratory. Dental images may hold clues about body-wide bone health, but are not screening tools yet.
pmc-13637604:
C Fearn and eight colleagues present NanoDel, a software pipeline for finding large deletions in mitochondrial DNA using long-read sequencing. Deletions of big mitochondrial genome stretches cause disease, yet standard tests need prior knowledge of where to look, large DNA inputs, or give unquantified answers. The team combined a splice-aware alignment approach, borrowed from RNA analysis, with single long reads that can span a deletion junction.

Tested on artificial data, NanoDel proved more sensitive and exact than rival pipelines. Applied to samples from patients with mitochondrial disease, it found known deletions and new ones never described before, including mixtures within a sample. The breakpoints clustered near repeated sequences, certain folding-prone motifs, and a structural contact zone, hinting at shared weak points in the mitochondrial genome. The authors offer the free tool as a robust route to finding such deletions across tissue types.
pmc-13641704:
Dan Drecktrah and nine colleagues present a study of carbonyl stress in the bacteria that cause Lyme disease and relapsing fever. The pathway centers on methylglyoxal, a reactive byproduct that can tag proteins and change their behavior.

Signals such as glycerol and peptides switched the pathway on in the Lyme spirochete, and its activity required one gene, called mgsA. Relapsing fever relatives lacked the active pathway. In tick-mouse experiments the tagging was not lethal, and giving the pathway to a relapsing fever species lowered its peak numbers in blood. The authors treat the pathway as a lifestyle governor for these bacteria.
pmc-13642904:
Zhengxian Chen and ten colleagues present a 2026 dataset, called 3ITVP, for intelligent new energy vehicle research built on a high-fidelity digital twin platform. Public driving datasets usually cover perception alone, leaving control and energy behavior disconnected.

The dataset follows five vehicle types, from ordinary cars and light trucks to semi-trailers, buses, and logistics vehicles, with tightly synchronized data on surroundings, driving behavior, and powertrain response. Alongside long continuous drives it includes many special event cases. The authors aim it at research on planning, control, energy management, and transferring skills learned in simulation to real vehicles.
pmc-13644204:
Latesha K. Harris and four colleagues present a 2026 scoping review of how health research defines and measures police violence. The topic matters for public health, especially for Black Americans, yet the field lacks a shared concept.

From 1,692 references, ninety-eight studies qualified. The reviewers found more than one hundred terms in use, grouped into twenty-two categories, and only two thirds of studies defined their term at all. Police killings were the commonest definition, and self-report the commonest measure. The authors recommend an explicit common definition, better measurement testing, and systematic data collection backed by a public federal database.
pmc-13645604:
Yao Yin and four colleagues pool research on why young people who plan to exercise often fail to follow through, a puzzle called the intention-behavior gap. Their systematic review and meta-analysis use an extended version of the theory of planned behavior, a model that links attitudes, social pressure, and felt control to action. Twenty-eight papers covering 19,652 adolescents and college students qualified. The team also tested whether study features changed the links.

The model explained a large share of differences in intention and a smaller share of differences in actual activity. Intention carried the effect of attitudes and related factors into behavior, and making a concrete plan added a further step in that chain. Results shifted with participant group, culture, and how activity was measured. The work gives program designers a clearer map of where exercise plans break down for young people.
pmc-13645804:
Akiko Inujima and seven colleagues show in a 2026 study that RNA from plant chloroplasts can stir the mammalian immune system. Chloroplasts descend from ancient bacteria, so the team wondered whether their genetic material still carries bacteria-like alarm signals. Working with RNA from a small flowering plant, they used gene sequencing and cell reporter tests to hunt for active stretches. Mouse and human immune sensors were tested separately.

A short fifteen-letter stretch of chloroplast RNA switched on a mouse immune sensor known for detecting bacterial RNA. A longer human version of the signal worked through a different sensor, TLR7. The same short stretch turned up in radish, spinach, and broccoli chloroplasts. The authors suggest RNA in eaten greens might gently shape immune responses, much as helpful gut microbes do. The finding links plant biology with nutrition and immunity in an unexpected way.
pmc-13645904:
Nadia Botros and five colleagues survey 220 people five years after weight-loss surgery to test how anxiety and depression relate to gut complaints. Stomach and bowel symptoms are common after such surgery and can drag down quality of life. Participants filled standard scales for mood symptoms and for gut complaints. The group averaged about fifty years of age, and most were women who had a gastric bypass.

About four in ten reported moderate to severe gut complaints, and just over a quarter reported anxiety or depression symptoms. People with severe mood symptoms scored clearly worse on total gut complaints, belly pain, reflux, and constipation. Milder symptoms showed a similar, weaker pattern. After adjustment, severe symptoms went with more than double the rate of strong gut complaints. The authors argue that mood care deserves a firm place in long-term follow-up after weight-loss surgery.
pmc-13646104:
Xiao Luo and five colleagues recheck blood tests that might help diagnose acute ischemic stroke in its first hours. Biomarkers could support scans and exams when time is short, yet the test families differ greatly in method and quality. The team rebuilt its analysis from verified original studies found through earlier reviews and an updated search through July 2026. Seventeen reports from 2003 to 2025 supplied the data.

Tests based on cell-free DNA caught about seven in ten strokes while ruling out most non-strokes. Tests based on non-coding RNA looked stronger on average, though wide uncertainty ranges counsel caution. Two other families had too few studies to pool. Most original work used healthy controls and cutoffs chosen from the same data, which inflates accuracy. The authors present their verified rebuild as a firmer base for judging which blood tests deserve prospective trials.
pmc-13648304:
Tina Bagus and four colleagues examine in 2026 how moral views about animals align with eating behaviour across development, surveying German participants aged eight to seventy-four. Adults who eat meat often defend it morally, but whether children show the same alignment was unclear.

The sample held 571 people, analysed with Bayesian modelling. Children valued animals and condemned meat-eating regardless of their own diet. With age, meat-eaters grew more speciesist, meaning more willing to rank humans above animals, while vegetarians and vegans stayed consistent. Early adolescence emerged as the phase when diet and moral judgement begin to line up, a finding the authors link to efforts promoting sustainable diets.
pmc-13649404:
Chen Liu and seven colleagues built a tool to guess the risk of death within three years after lung cancer surgery. They used records for 350 patients from one centre and tested seven types of machine learning on routine facts such as tumour stage, body weight, and blood tests.

Six facts were kept in the final model, and a plain logistic model beat the fancier tools on held-out cases. The team turned it into a web tool and a paper chart for ease of use. They warn that the case mix may skew risk scores, and that no outside centre has yet tested the tool. It is meant for study use, not direct care choices.
pmc-13649504:
Judit Serrat and four colleagues built a lab model of the first contact between a liver fluke and the human gut wall. The worm's young stage crosses the gut soon after a person swallows it, but that step is hard to study in the body. Their model grows a flat sheet of gut cells from human organoids, tiny lab-grown tissue clumps.

Young flukes stayed alive on the sheets and pressed close to the cells. Tests of leak and strength showed the gut barrier weakened on contact with live worms or their skin proteins. A protein census flagged candidate players in cell links, immune signals, and stress. The authors offer the system as a test bed for how this infection begins.
pmc-13649704:
Julia Andronache and three colleagues applied a broad DNA scan, for the first time, to check which snail species hide in processed foods, in a study published in 2026. Food fraud swaps pricey species for cheap ones, and ground products defy checks by eye. Their scan reads a short gene stretch found in land, river, and sea snails alike.

In 17 of 18 known samples, the scan named the right genus or species, helped by a curated reference library. Test mixes gave few missed minor parts, likely from primer mismatch. Of 20 shop products, seven proved mislabelled. The authors offer the scan as a routine screen that fits beside assays for other animal groups.
pmc-13650004:
Jiayi Li and seven colleagues build a scoring chart to estimate which lung cancer patients face higher risk of radiation pneumonitis, a lung inflammation that can follow radiotherapy. Their chart mixes ordinary clinical facts with blood markers of body-wide inflammation and early swallowing-tube irritation from treatment.

Records from 726 patients who received radiotherapy were used to build and check the model, with serious pneumonitis as the outcome and unrelated death treated as a competing event. Alcohol history, treatment technique, a liver enzyme level, an inflammation score, and early esophagus inflammation each carried independent weight. The fullest model sorted patients modestly well and gave the most useful guidance in a middle risk range. A follow-up explanation method showed which factors pushed each score up or down, making the chart easier for clinicians to read.
pmc-13650704:
Ji-Hun Lee and seven colleagues, publishing in 2026, test a two-drug pairing against radiation-induced lung scarring in mice. High-dose chest radiation can stiffen lungs into fibrosis that resembles a serious human disease. Nintedanib, an approved antifibrotic, helps only partly, so the team added metformin, a common diabetes drug with protective hints.

Female mice received a focused dose to the left lung, then daily metformin, nintedanib, both, or neither for six weeks. Drug groups containing nintedanib showed cleaner lung tissue, less collagen buildup, lower injury scores, and better preserved air spaces, while the combination group carried the least of a collagen-related marker. A master scarring signal was suppressed by nintedanib treatments, and its natural brake rose only under the combination. A lung injury protein also eased. The authors see a broader protective profile for pairing, pending proof it truly beats nintedanib alone.
pmc-13650804:
Ali Mousavi and ten colleagues, publishing in 2026, build a heart-on-a-chip that carries a patient's own dilated cardiomyopathy, a disease where the heart stretches and weakens and often ends in transplantation. Existing models miss the living heart's complexity, so the team grew miniature beating tissues from cells reprogrammed out of patients' blood samples.

Healthy and diseased stem cells were turned into heart muscle cells, blended with cardiac support cells, and set in a gel studded with fluorescent beads inside chambers held by flexible pillars. The tissues compacted and began beating on their own. Diseased tissue showed poorer cell alignment and shorter cells, plus rhythm disturbances and abnormal calcium pulses after two weeks. A stress hormone challenge confirmed the tissues still responded to drugs. The bead mapping lets researchers watch contraction forces directly, suiting the platform for patient-specific drug testing.
pmc-13651104:
Wei Xu and seven colleagues hunt the genes behind salt tolerance in rice plants, a trait breeders need as salty soils spread and yields fall. Seedlings are the most salt-sensitive stage, so the team crossed a salt-sensitive Japanese-type variety with a tolerant Indian-type variety and raised 253 inbred lines from the pairing.

Lines were stressed with salt water and scored on several growth indices, then mapped against a genetic map built from whole-genome resequencing. Forty-three chromosomal regions influenced tolerance, eleven of them strongly. The team then layered gene annotations, variant patterns across lines, and gene activity networks. Direct expression checks singled out one candidate gene whose lower activity after salt exposure accompanied stronger tolerance in the lines carrying a particular variant form. Lines with that form tolerated salt better. The authors present the gene and its variant as breeding resources for salt-tolerant rice.
pmc-13651604:
Benjamin C Orsburn asks a workforce question hiding inside a booming science: where do proteomics people come from? Proteomics, the census of all proteins in a sample, was forecast to double in market size within a few years and eventually outgrow genomics. Growth is lagging those predictions, and training pipelines are his suspect.

Surveys and direct interviews covered more than two hundred working proteomics scientists. Over two thirds learned their technical craft during doctoral or postdoctoral training, the long apprenticeship stages of the life sciences. Only a tiny fraction picked up proteomics as undergraduates. With doctoral and postdoctoral cycles averaging many years, Orsburn argues the field's growth ceiling is set less by instruments or demand. It is set by how late and how slowly the field trains its own specialists. Earlier exposure, he implies, is the lever the community controls.
pmc-13652604:
Jignesh Joshi and colleagues report a 2026 case in which a benign cerebellar lesion, Lhermitte-Duclos disease, masqueraded as a malignant tumor in a thirty-two-year-old woman. She arrived with worsening headache, vomiting, vertigo, and right-sided imbalance. Imaging showed a large right lesion spreading into the vermis and brainstem pathways, with patchy enhancement and restricted diffusion that mimicked a high-grade tumor. Surgeons opened the skull base and relieved pressure.

Tissue study showed distorted cerebellar folds with loss of Purkinje cells and widening of the grain layer by small nerve cells, raising a dilemma with medulloblastoma. Staining for NeuN and synaptophysin, with very low cell division, settled the diagnosis as Lhermitte-Duclos disease. Later imaging showed subtotal removal and recovery was uneventful. Surgeons get a diagnostic warning: atypical imaging plus neuronal staining can spare a patient from excess treatment for a presumed cancer.
pmc-4455604:
Heberle, Meirelles, da Silva, and their team built InteractiVenn in 2015. Comparing sets is a step in a huge number of data workflows, above all in biology. Venn diagrams are the standard display for such comparisons, but existing tools were limited in what they allowed.

InteractiVenn is a web-based tool that lets users work with set diagrams in a flexible way. Users can build diagrams with several sets, edit labels, and pull out the members of any overlap. That interactivity turns a static figure into a working view of the data. It speeds the common task of finding what gene lists or sample groups share.
pmc-4531804:
Emms and Kelly made OrthoFinder in 2015, a tool for work on whole genomes. Genes in two species that came from one gene in a shared past form groups. Labs sort genes into such groups to compare species and trace how gene sets change over time.

The team found a flaw no one had seen in how old tools built these groups. Long genes skewed the groups and made them less true. OrthoFinder fixes that length bias with a new method. Tests showed the groups it builds are far more sound. Clean gene groups are a base step for work on gene birth, loss, and change.
pmc-4595904:
Wick, Schultz, Zobel, and their colleagues built Bandage in 2015 for genome assembly work. When a genome is assembled from scratch, the result is a graph of contigs, or nodes, joined by edges. Users found those connections hard to reach and inspect with existing tools.

Bandage draws assembly graphs in an interactive way, so users can navigate them easily. Seeing the graph helps spot tangles, repeats, and possible errors that tables hide. That visual check can rescue an assembly or explain why it broke at a point. The tool gave genome researchers a practical way to explore the structures their assemblers produce.
pmc-4756104:
Ríos-Covián, Ruas-Madiedo, Margolles, and their co-authors reviewed short chain fatty acids in the gut in 2016. The colon holds a dense population of microbes, the gut microbiota. These microbes break down carbs and proteins that the small intestine leaves behind.

Among their products are short chain fatty acids, which feed colon cells and signal to the immune system. The review links diet to the production of these acids and to human health. What people eat shapes which microbes thrive and what they release. That chain from diet to microbes to body chemistry is now central to nutrition science.
pmc-5576104:
Weiner, Lewis, Stanick, and their team tested new measures in 2017 for implementation research. Such measures track whether efforts to put proven care into practice are working. The measures in use lacked clear concepts, and their quality was largely unknown.

The team built three new measures and tested them for soundness. They cover how staff judge a new practice: whether it is acceptable, a good fit, and feasible to run. Tested tools let teams compare rollout plans on equal terms. Without them, a failed launch could be blamed on the care itself, when the true fault lay in how it was brought in.
pmc-7067204:
Jasper Chan, Kin-Hang Kok, Zheng Zhu, and coauthors characterized the genome of the new coronavirus in early 2020. A mysterious outbreak of pneumonia appeared in Wuhan in late 2019 and was linked to a seafood market. Within weeks a novel coronavirus was named as the cause.

The team sequenced the virus from a patient with atypical pneumonia and compared it with known coronaviruses. It proved closest to bat coronaviruses and distinct from the earlier SARS virus. Its entry protein suggested strong ability to infect human cells. The analysis helped confirm the outbreak's source family in the pandemic's opening weeks.
pmc-7418704:
Tyler Starr and co-authors measured in 2020 how every possible small change to a key piece of the COVID-19 virus affects its behavior. Their focus was the receptor binding domain, the part of the viral spike that grips the human ACE2 receptor. This piece is also a main target of the antibodies people make against the virus.

Using a method that builds and tests thousands of altered versions at once, they measured how each change affected the protein's folding and its grip on the receptor. The resulting map shows which spots cannot change without breaking the virus, and which can shift freely. Vaccine and drug designers use such maps to anticipate how the virus might evolve to escape treatment.
pmc-7779004:
Damian Szklarczyk and colleagues presented the 2021 edition of the STRING database, a resource for mapping how proteins work together. Life inside a cell depends on a web of partnerships between proteins, which pass signals, build structures, and run chemistry as teams. STRING gathers known and predicted protein associations from many sources into one network that researchers can explore.

The update adds flexible ways to customize the networks and a feature for characterizing sets of genes or measurements that users upload themselves. That lets a researcher move from a raw list of results to a picture of the processes involved. STRING is one of the standard first stops when making sense of gene level data.
podcast-dannyjones-Dwh6Oa-N_04:
Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 vanished in 2014, and a viral video years later claimed to show the plane surrounded by orbs and disappearing. Danny Jones hosts a contest over that footage: the visual effects artists of Corridor Crew against Ashton Forbes, the video's leading defender, arguing over what the clips actually show.

The format makes this episode unusual for the series: claim and forensic answer in the same room. The artists explain how the effects could be built, frame by frame, and Forbes answers their points. Listeners can watch a conspiracy claim tested by the people best qualified to fake it. Whatever verdict a listener reaches, the recording is a model of how such disputes should sound, and a rare case of the debunkers getting equal time on a believer-friendly show.
podcast-joerogan-hw-ibiz-M04:
Filmmaker Oliver Stone joins Joe Rogan for episode 1992 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Stone is the director of Platoon, JFK, and a string of films that fight the known tale of US power. His talks run long on war and lies.

Stone and Rogan talk film craft, the Kennedy case, and the tales the state tells of itself. Stone shares how his war years in Vietnam shaped each frame he shoots. Rogan gives him the long form to teach and rant. Listeners get a famed director in full voice. The library keeps the episode as a record of his stated views.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-158-19:
February 4, 1920, brought another front page of Charivaria in Punch, volume 158, where the London comic weekly packed its first column with short jokes on current reports. Ireland, money, and food supply the main targets this week.

A rumour of martial law in Ireland prompts the question of which army of occupation would declare it. A magistrate's claim that money requires hard work is called an improvement on raiding post offices. Cat skins wanted in Essex, a machine said to sound like Lord Fisher, and German horseradish sold dear in Manchester fill out the column's odd harvest of news.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: Nothing of Constant's memoir itself stands in the opening pages of its fourth volume. A publisher's header fills them instead, giving the title The Private Life of Napoleon Bonaparte, naming Constant as author, and noting the English language of the text. There is no contents page to map this part and no opening scene to quote or sum up. Anyone seeking what the fourth volume treats must look past these pages; from them alone only the title, the writer, and the volume's place in the set can be known.
reitzenstein-poimandres-1904:
Richard Reitzenstein published his study of the Poimandres in German in 1904. The Poimandres is the opening revelation of the Corpus Hermeticum, where Hermes receives a vision. Reitzenstein set that text inside its Graeco-Egyptian religious world.

He traced kinship between Hermetic writings, early Christianity, and Gnosticism. His method, the history-of-religions approach, treated texts as products of mixed cultures. The book founded a modern historical way of studying ancient mysticism. Scholars argued with his conclusions for decades, which proves his influence. Written for specialists, it changed how a whole field asked its questions.
reymont-peasants-1904:
Wladyslaw Reymont wrote The Peasants as a four-volume Polish epic, published in the first years of the 1900s. The Knopf English text of 1928 gathers the work in one volume. Life in the village of Lipce follows the four seasons. Land, faith, weddings, and feuds shape the peasants' year.

The Boryna family stands at the center, with land disputes and a tangled marriage plot. Reymont writes of soil and weather as forces in their own right. Village speech and custom fill the pages with color. The epic helped Reymont win the Nobel Prize in 1924. It remains Poland's great novel of rural life.
richard-carvel-volume-04:
Winston Churchill's Richard Carvel enters its fourth volume with A Man of Destiny, in which Richard is hauled from the sea. He is thrown into a brigantine's long-boat with a head full of salt water and a heart light with joy. A big, red-bearded man lifts his heels to drain him and pronounces him dead.

Richard answers that he is no more dead than the sailor, and springs up the ship's ladder before the captain. Asked if he is kelpie or pirate, he calls himself a young gentleman in misfortune. The captain drops his Scotch manner and bows like a French courtier. Later chapters promise a sad home-coming, London Town, and The Rescue.
russell-new-creation-vol6-1904:
Russell closed his own series with The New Creation, the sixth Studies volume of 1904, written for the consecrated. The book treats the calling, holiness, and discipline of the new creature, the believer set apart for God's work. Church order, conduct, marriage, and daily duty all fall under its careful, detailed rules.

Where earlier volumes mapped history and prophecy, this one governs a daily life from waking to sleep. Russell writes as pastor and organizer, shaping a people fit for the kingdom he expected very soon. With it his six-volume set stands complete, the full system of the Bible Student movement in its founder's words.
rutherford-radio-activity-1904:
Ernest Rutherford published Radio-activity in 1904, only a few years after radioactivity itself was found. Rutherford, a New Zealand physicist working in Canada and England, was the field's boldest experimenter. His book was the first full textbook on the new science.

Rutherford explains rays from uranium and radium, and how one element can change into another. He sets out half-life, the steady rate at which active matter decays. The work helped turn a strange glow in the lab into nuclear science, the field Rutherford would lead for decades. It also gathers the lab methods used to trace rays and count particles.
scheible-das-kloster-vol04:
In 1846 Johann Scheible issued band four of Das Kloster, holding cells thirteen through sixteen. The German anthology had grown past its first year into a known fixture of the trade. Scheible, its editor and publisher, hunted down scarce print that libraries had long ignored.

What he found, he reprinted whole: grimoires, Faust books, and grim Höllenzwänge among them. Folk charms, some meant for love and some for healing, share the binding with popular tales. The worth of such a band lies in survival. Texts that lived in a handful of copies now sat in one sturdy volume on many shelves.
schiller-wilhelm-tell-1804:
William Tell was Schiller's last completed play, finished in 1804, and Theodore Martin translated it into English. Tell, a Swiss marksman and quiet family man, refuses to bow to the hat of the Austrian bailiff Gessler. Gessler's punishment is cruel: Tell must shoot an apple from his own son's head.

Tell succeeds, yet vows revenge, and the Swiss cantons rise against their rulers. Schiller turns the old legend into a broad drama of a people's freedom. The play made Tell a worldwide emblem of resistance to tyranny. Rossini's opera later carried the tale further still. Schiller wrote it without ever seeing Switzerland, working from chronicles and maps alone.
scott-elliot-lost-lemuria-1904:
The Lost Lemuria, printed in 1904, gives Scott-Elliot's account of the sunken southern continent. Lemuria, in theosophical teaching, preceded Atlantis as a home of early humanity. Scott-Elliot marshals geological and biological evidence for the lost land. The spread of fossils and living species across oceans anchors his case.

Two maps trace the continent and its shrinking remains. He joins the science of his day to the society's clairvoyant records. The Story of Atlantis is the companion volume to this one. Together they set out the Theosophical Society's lost continent doctrine in full. The Gutenberg text preserves the argument entire. It remains the movement's Lemuria in chief.
serapis-volume-04:
Georg Ebers wrote this historical novel of Alexandria; volume four opens at chapter sixteen. Dada spends a bright day under the roof of Medius, charmed by costumes, scenery, and kind children. Her tricks and rhymes, stale to Papias by now, delight the new household.

Medius, a singer, buys any bargain that catches his eye. That morning he bought a whole tub of pickled fish at the harbor auction for a trifle. His wife rages that the last herring will outlast them all. Comic home strife gives this volume a warm, light opening amid the city's graver storms.
serge-panine-volume-04: Georges Ohnet's Serge Panine closes with a fourth volume, and these pages belong to it. The English issue joined a series of French romances crowned by the French Academy. Only the publisher's header appears in the pages at hand. It names the book, its author, and its series. No closing scene is shown. No death, wedding, or reckoning can be read here. The novel's end must stay untold in any account that rests on this header alone.
sketches-by-seymour-volume-04:
Robert Seymour's comic plates carry this fourth part of his sketches, opening with Watty Williams and a bull. Watty, a studious youth with a long nose and short trousers, loves green fields and finds sermons in stones. Deep in a book on solitude one day, he looks up at a loud moo.

A curly-fronted bull careers toward him across the meadow. Watty can laugh at an Irish bull and scorn a papal one, yet this breed alarms him beyond bounds. He scampered off at top speed toward a pollard tree. Pun-laden prose turns a country scare into a set piece of 1830s humor.
smith-wealth-nations-cannan-1904:
Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations appears here in Edwin Cannan's 1904 edition. Smith, a Scottish philosopher, first published An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations in 1776. Cannan, an economist, edited the text with notes that scholars used for a century.

Smith argued that the division of labor makes nations rich, and that free trade beats the old mercantilist controls. His famous invisible hand pictured each person seeking gain yet serving the public good. He also warned about monopolies, dull factory work, and business plots against the public. The book founded modern economics, and Cannan's edition remains a careful way to read it in full.
spr-proceedings-vol18-1903-1904:
Volume eighteen binds parts forty six through forty nine, for 1903 and 1904. Two decades in, the SPR Proceedings keep their founding bargain. Print the evidence for telepathy, apparitions, and mediumship, and print the criticism too. Fresh experiments try to close the gaps critics had found.

Trance cases, with Piper still central, receive long verbatim reports. The census tradition shapes new surveys of spontaneous experiences. Physical wonders appear rarely, and then under heavy guard. Volume eighteen sustains the journal of record through its Edwardian years. It offers historians a dense, dated file of the debate. The society's patience is its signature here.
steiner-theosophy-1904:
Rudolf Steiner wrote his Theosophy in 1904, while he still led the German theosophists. Its full title calls it a first step to knowledge past the senses. The book sets out man as body, soul, and spirit. It is the root text of the school he later built, Anthroposophy.

Birth anew and karma frame the tale of the soul's long growth. Three worlds stack up: flesh, soul, and spirit, each with its own laws. Steiner then maps a path by which a pupil can gain sight of those worlds. The book asks for slow, keen thought, not blind faith.
stevenson-the-zuni-indians-1904:
Matilda Coxe Stevenson was among the first women to do serious fieldwork in the Southwest, and she spent years at Zuni Pueblo. Her report, published in 1904 in the Bureau of American Ethnology's annual report, is the fullest early study of Zuni religion.

Stevenson describes the rain priesthood, whose prayers served the whole pueblo, and the kachina cult with its masked dancers. She gives detailed accounts of the esoteric fraternities, the secret societies that ran ceremonies and healing. Her access to restricted rites raised questions even then. Whatever the disputes, the record she left is unmatched in detail.
suess-face-of-earth-vol1-sollas-1904:
W J Sollas published his translation of Volume 1 of Eduard Suess's Face of the Earth in 1904. Suess, a Viennese geologist, wrote Das Antlitz der Erde as a synthesis of the whole science. Sollas, an Oxford geologist, carried the great work into English over many years.

Volume 1 treats the structure of the continents and the history of the Mediterranean lands. Suess argued that mountains rise as the cooling Earth contracts and its crust crumples, the contraction theory of mountain building. He also named Gondwana, a lost southern continent pieced together from matching fossils and rocks. The volume began the English form of the most ambitious geology of its age.
swift-battle-of-the-books-1704:
Jonathan Swift wrote The Battle of the Books while working as secretary to Sir William Temple, a retired statesman. A loud quarrel then divided scholars: were modern writers the equals of the ancient Greeks and Romans? Swift published his mock-epic prose satire in 1704, alongside A Tale of a Tub.

In the royal library at St. James, the ancient and modern books come alive and go to war. Bees and spiders argue the same case in a famous fable: the spider spins from itself, the bee gathers from every flower. Swift mocks pedants on both sides but saves his sharpest cuts for modern pride. The piece remains the wittiest shot fired in the ancients-versus-moderns war.
swift-tale-of-a-tub-1704:
Jonathan Swift published A Tale of a Tub in 1704, his first major work, issued with The Battle of the Books. Swift was then an unknown Irish clergyman in his thirties. The book's wild energy and strange digressions startled readers and made his reputation.

The tale itself is an allegory of three brothers who inherit coats they must not alter, standing for the Catholic, Anglican, and dissenting churches. Around it Swift piles mock prefaces and digressions praising madness and modern learning. The satire cuts at religious corruption and empty scholarship alike. Many call it the most savage and brilliant prose satire of its age.
synge-riders-to-sea-1904:
J. M. Synge drew Riders to the Sea from his visits to the Aran Islands, where the sea took men from nearly every family. The one-act play was first performed in 1904. It lasts under an hour and is often called the summit of Irish tragedy.

Maurya, an old widow, has already lost her husband and four sons to the sea. The play opens as her daughters identify a drowned man's clothing from far up the coast. Her last surviving son, Bartley, insists on sailing despite her pleas. When his body is carried in, Maurya reaches a calm, terrible acceptance. Synge's language, shaped by Irish speech, gives the grief a biblical weight.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
Jealous husbands and ill-matched wives rule the fourth volume of La Fontaine's Tales and Novels. It holds The Old Man's Calendar, The Avaricious Wife and Tricking Gallant, The Jealous Husband, and a Gascon tale. Jealousy and ill-matched marriage, La Fontaine's favorite themes, govern the set.

The Old Man's Calendar opens by marveling at weddings designed for riches alone. Sweet sixteen must learn to love sixty there. Yet the same parents match their carriage horses with exact care. They match their oxen for height and shade too. Such a marriage journey runs full of cares, the poet warns. The couples match in neither souls nor years. He tells one case in point. Quinzica indulged his wife at balls and shows. He hoped she would forget her other duties.
tales-and-novels-volume-04:
Castle Rackrent leads Volume IV of Maria Edgeworth's Tales and Novels. The volume was printed in 1857 with engravings on steel. It also contains her Essay on Irish Bulls. Her Essay on the Noble Science of Self-Justification follows. Ennui and The Dun complete the book. A motto from Lord Lyttelton's monody on his wife praises a prudence that believes neither too little nor too much.

Castle Rackrent opens on a Monday morning. Old Thady Quirk speaks. He has lived rent-free on the estate time out of mind. Out of friendship, he undertakes to publish the memoirs of the Rackrent family. His deadpan history of drunken, litigious, absentee landlords is the founding work of the Irish regional novel. The essays and the tales of Ennui and the Dun, a fashionable sponger, fill out Edgeworth's Ireland and her London.
the-a-b-c-of-phrenology-1904: A worn front page ties this phrenology handbook to Drane's ABC handbooks. Those books were small and fit the pocket. Each sold for one shilling. Each was bound in red cloth with white lettering. Henry J. Drane of Salisbury Square, Fleet Street, London, printed the set. The series ads make a plain promise. Each subject is set out as plainly as ABC. A specialist hand writes each book. The society heading above the ads is garbled. The author line is too garbled to read with trust.
the-arabian-nights-entertainments-volume: Contents alone list the fourth and last Aldine volume, printed at London in 1890 with pictures by S. L. Wood from Dr. Jonathan Scott's text. Tales include the enchanted horse, Prince Ahmed and the fairy Perie Banou, and the sisters who envied their younger sister. An abdicated sultan has adventures, and Mahummud, sultan of Cairo, gets a history. Two lunatics tell stories, among them tales of schoolmasters with broken backs and wry mouths. A sultan of Yemen and his three sons close the list.
the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-04:
Volume 4 of The Bride of the Nile, by Georg Ebers, opens at Chapter XIII in a house of sick and wounded men. Paula's report of the day's trial, and of Orion's conduct, angers the leech Philippus beyond measure. He backs her resolve to quit this cave of robbers, this house of treachery, false witnesses, and witless judges, as soon as she can. Told he can't see him till morning, the young giant sits up in his pillows, shakes his great head, and pours out abuse at the physician in his own tongue.

As Philippus tries to fix the bandage on his wound, Rustem flings his arms round him and tries, foaming at the lips, to drag him down. Paula stands by as witness. Philippus twists his ankles round the Persian's, forces his hands back, and pins him to the pillows till help can be called.
the-burgomaster-s-wife-volume-04:
Volume 4 of The Burgomaster's Wife, by Georg Ebers, opens at Chapter XX in the burgomaster's house. Henrica greets Maria with special cheerfulness. This morning has done her good, she says. If trust in recovery helps the physician, Doctor Bontius will have an easy task with her. The dead Castilian, she declares, must be the wretch who plunged her sister Anna into misery.

Maria, relieved, seeks her husband with the news. Peter only half listens. Talk turns to war business. Maria asks how communication with Delft is to be kept free of the enemy. Rotterdam also lies to the south, she notes. From Haarlem and Amsterdam, in Spanish hands, nothing can be hoped. Peter jokes that she has earned a place in the council of war, and asks where she learns her wisdom.
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume-04:
Part IV of the family novel The Caxtons opens a new stretch of Pisistratus's life story. He tells it himself, in the first person. The household he describes centers on his father, a scholar more at ease among books than in company.

The narrator praises early rising at length, calling each fresh morning a gift no late sleeper knows. Youth that dawdles over breakfast at noon, he says, looks worn and ghostly beside youth that sees the sun rise. Passing his father's study, he is surprised to find its windows open so early. The part opens in this reflective key, with habit and home routine carrying the scene.
the-celebrity-volume-04:
Volume 4 of Winston Churchill's novel opens at Chapter XV, in the thick of a morning effort led by Mr. Cooke. The narrator rates Cooke as having some gifts of a great general. His followers work under the threat of capture, which he holds over them in strong language.

Past campaigns, the narrator notes, often ran on hero worship more than on love of the cause. The same force works here. Cooke is everywhere at once, urging the group on and filling them with his own spirit. To his own surprise, the narrator finds himself working as hard as the rest. This late stretch shows how charm and command can move a whole party.
the-comedy-of-errors-pg1504:
William Shakespeare set this comedy at Ephesus. The cast list and scene headings here make that plain. Solinus, Duke of Ephesus, heads the personae. Egeon, a merchant of Syracuse, comes next. Two pairs of twins stand at the center. The twins do not know each other.

One pair is the two Antipholuses. They are twin brothers. Their parents are Egeon and Emilia. The other pair is the two Dromios. They are twins too. Each Dromio serves one Antipholus. Adriana stands by her husband, the Ephesian Antipholus. Luciana is her sister. Angelo is a goldsmith. Balthasar is a merchant. Pinch is a schoolmaster and conjurer. Emilia now lives as an abbess at Ephesus. The contents split the play into five acts. Each act holds short scenes. Two masters share one name in one city. Two servants share another. Mistaken identity is built into the cast list itself.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau:
Book IV of Jean Jacques Rousseau's Confessions stands here as volume IV of the twelve-book set, privately printed for members of the Aldus Society at London in 1903. An arrival brings grief at once: the woman Rousseau expected is not there to meet him.

Regret follows for having abandoned M. le Maitre, and the regret deepens with bad news. Le Maitre's box of music, holding all his fortune, had been seized at Lyons. Count Dortan, informed by the Chapter that the two had absconded with it, took the box by superior strength. Le Maitre reclaimed his property in vain: it was his means of existence, the labor of his life. His right to the music was at least open to litigation, but even that liberty was denied him, the affair being settled on the principle of force.
the-crisis-volume-04:
Volume 4 of Winston Churchill's The Crisis opens at Chapter VII, An Excursion, where the narrator jumps ahead two years. A nation, he says, has struggled in agony with a sickness it cannot throw off, a disease whose germs, he writes, a Dutch ship brought from Guinea to Virginia in 1620.

In the city by the Father of Waters, Stephen Brice has won leave to practice law in Missouri. He understands Judge Whipple better now and stays grateful to him for knowledge of Abraham Lincoln, the man of greatest influence on his life. Some of Stephen's income comes from newspaper pieces, in the blanket-sized papers of the day with no bold headlines. Talk of conventions fills the land, and the Freeport Heresy is not forgotten.
the-disowned-volume-04:
Chapter thirty-seven opens volume four of The Disowned, where Clarence pours out his grief to his friend Talbot. Lady Westborough has barred him from one room, and Talbot urges him to claim his true name at last. Clarence refuses with passion. Thrust from his father's home and blamed for another man's crime, he will rise under his assumed name or fall unknown.

Talbot, moved to tears, promises to stand as a father to him. The scene states the novel's core theme plainly: worth proved by conduct, not by birth. Dinner and guests then soften the mood.
the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustrated-h:
Cantos seven and eight make up part four of Hell in Dante's Vision, in the Rev. H. F. Cary's English verse. At the fourth circle, Plutus howls a strange cry, and Dante's guide rebukes the beast and calms his pupil's fear. The two then climb down to a shore that holds the woes of the whole world, where crowds push great weights and clash.

Greed and waste meet their match in this ring. Farther on, the travellers cross a foul marsh toward a tower with signals of fire. The part blends dread with strange, grim sights.
the-emperor-volume-04:
Volume four of Georg Ebers's The Emperor opens at chapter fifteen with Mastor, the emperor's body-slave. Since he ran to aid Selene when Hadrian's dog attacked her, strange words have echoed in his mind, and he does his morning tasks half in a dream. Before sunrise he cleans the gold on Hadrian's greaves, airs his clothes, and readies the bath at Lochias.

A slave's small round frames the emperor's vast power. Clara Bell's version keeps Ebers's eye for the gear of daily life. Selene's hurt and Mastor's awe pull the plot's threads tight.
the-follies-of-science-at-the-court-of-r: The front matter here is badly garbled by scanning. But the title can still be read in clear type at its foot. It is The Follies of Science at the Court of Rudolph II. A caption names Rudolph with his alchemist. A long number string stands above the caption. The author's name is too broken to read with trust. The rest of the page is broken too. So no more than the title and that caption can be stated from what is present.
the-great-events-by-famous-historians-vo: The Great Events by Famous Historians retells world history in the words of eminent historians. Rossiter Johnson was editor-in-chief. Charles F. Horne and John Rudd were associate editors. This record is Volume IV. The National Alumni published it in 1905. Only front matter is present here: the title page and the start of a contents list. The contents open with an outline narrative by Horne. The first set piece named is Visigoths Pillage Rome, A.D. 410, by Edward Gibbon. No further pieces are named.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1-part:
Cervantes' Don Quixote continues in Volume 1, Part 04, Englished by John Ormsby. Chapter nine concludes the terrific battle between the gallant Biscayan and the valiant Manchegan. The narrator first laments that the earlier history stopped mid-blow, with swords raised and no word of where the missing part could be found.

That break, the narrator says, turned pleasure into vexation. No good knight, he argues, should lack a sage to record his deeds and even his secret thoughts. He blames Time, the devourer of all things, for hiding or eating the tale, then weighs whether the story lived on in village memory instead.
the-innocents-abroad-volume-04:
Part 4 of Mark Twain's Innocents Abroad reaches chapter XXXI. The text comes from the 1869 first edition. The buried city of Pompeii is the subject. Twain first corrects his own picture of the place. No torches or damp stairways await visitors. Half the city stands exhumed in daylight. Roofless brick houses bake in the sun. Mosaic floors lie clean-swept. Frescoes of Venus and Bacchus brighten the walls.

His comedy turns municipal. Chariot wheels cut the streets with deep ruts. Some ruts run ten inches into the flagstones. Pompeii's street commissioners plainly shirked their work. Swindled taxpayers are an ancient tribe, he concludes. Merchant Street is cleaner now than in the city's prime. The joke measures ancient Rome by American city councils.
the-inside-of-the-cup-volume-04:
Volume 4 of Winston Churchill's novel opens with chapter XIII, Winterbourne. Hodder falls asleep from sheer exhaustion. Dreams caricature the day before him. Alison Parr talks with the woman in the flat. Eldon Parr romps with ragged children. The shoe factory's morning whistle rouses him at last. One object forms in his mind. He must go to Horace Bentley. Bentley's presence might ease the terror in his soul.

He climbs Tower street and avoids Dalton Street. Bentley is at home in the dining room. The old servant Sam has orders to bring him in. Churchill marks the turn plainly. The rector knows utter dependence on another man. He has not felt it since childhood. He feels no shame about it. The volume ahead holds a Saturday afternoon. The crucible and the encircling gloom follow.
the-last-of-the-barons-volume-04:
Intrigues at the court of Edward IV fill Book Four, the portion in this record of Edward Bulwer Lytton Warwick novel. Robert Hilyard, disguised as a cleric, picks through Thames side alleys where disbanded soldiers of both Roses wait for violent work. He reaches a poor religious house by the river.

Inside waits a foreign priest treated with saint like reverence, linked to Margaret of Anjou cause. Hilyard kneels and drops his hard manner into pity and awe. Conspiracy against the Yorkist court grows in rooms far from the throne, fed by men left idle by civil war.
the-memoirs-of-count-grammont-volume-04:
Volume 4 of Anthony Hamilton's Memoirs of Count Grammont, edited with notes by Sir Walter Scott, opens at Chapter Eighth. The chapter promises the funny adventure of the chaplain Poussatin, the marriage of the Duke of York, and Grammont's own story of the siege of Lerida. Grammont narrates that siege himself, describing how the Prince de Conde attacked a place defended by Don Gregorio Brice.

Brice, a Spaniard of the old stamp, let the French approach without molestation. Conde, elated by earlier victories, mounted the trenches at noon behind twenty-four fiddlers, as if going to a wedding. Night brought a cry of alarm, cannon fire, and a vigorous sally that cleared the trenches. Next day Brice sent the prince ice and fruit, politely regretting he had no violins to return the serenade. Readers get war retold as drawing-room comedy, with Spanish gallantry outfacing French glory.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
For Saturday, November 29, 1828, the Mirror's No. 343 illustrates the Admiralty Office in Whitehall. The building has few pretensions to architectural beauty, the article admits, but stands as a commanding pile. Its association with Britain's best bulwarks, her navy, earns it a representation. Ripley erected it under George II on the site of Wallingford House, adjoining the Horse Guards.

A lofty Ionic portico of four columns centers the brick front, with an anchor in bold relief on the entablature. Inside sit the offices and residences of the lords commissioners, and a semaphore telegraph on the roof signals the empire's principal ports. The most tasteful portion is Adams's stone screen before the court, decorated with naval emblems. Since the Duke of Clarence became Lord High Admiral, the house serves as his town residence. Readers get sea power housed in brick and signal flags.
the-parisians-volume-04:
Book IV of Edward Bulwer-Lytton's The Parisians opens with a letter from Isaura Cicogna to Madame de Grantmesnil. Isaura explains her long silence. She repeats words of M. Savarin, who said he would not intrude on the parting between an author and her finished work, that solemn moment before it leaves her hands for the world.

Isaura reflects that a book long cherished dies to its author once published. Fame itself may chill the writer's love, as strangers praise or blame her creatures like real people of the streets. She contrasts Savarin, who treats praise as food and dispraise as poison, and keeps a league of allies to defend his reputation.
the-right-of-way-volume-04:
Gilbert Parker's fourth volume opens after a great storm. A thunderstorm tears through the Chaudiere valley in it. Fences fall, and small bridges wash away below. Hail whitens the ground with pebbles of ice. Calm and sunshine return over the land afterward. Chapter twenty-nine takes the wild ride as its title.

Contents promise Rosalie warning Charley in this volume. Charley stands at bay in a later heading. Jo Portugais tells a story among the chapters. Ambush, barriers swept away, and a challenge follow. Paulette Dubois issues that challenge in the list. A scarlet woman closes the volume's headings. Storm damage sets a cleansed but dangerous stage here.
the-story-of-my-life-volume-04:
Volume four of Georg Ebers's autobiography opens at chapter thirteen. It tells of the founders of the Keilhau Institute. Friedrich Froebel, Middendorf, and Langethal taught at that school. The last two were Ebers's own teachers. Froebel, the master who planned it, was already sixty-six when Ebers arrived. He was a tall man. His face seemed cut from brown wood with a dull knife.

Yet his clear eyes beamed his motto, Come, let us live for our children, and his power over a child's heart was limitless. The shyest boy was won in a few words, younger pupils hung on his coattails begging for stories, and the boys called him only Oheim, since he detested the foreign-derived word Onkel.
the-thirty-years-war-volume-04:
Frederick Schiller begins Book Four of his History of the Thirty Years' War with the death of Gustavus Adolphus at Lutzen. The weak bond holding the Protestant allies together dissolved with the king, and the alliance had to be formed anew. Without union, Schiller argues, the allies would lose everything their bloodshed had bought and fall one by one to the Emperor and the League. Neither Sweden nor any single German state could match the enemy alone.

Peace on present terms would mean receiving laws from the victor, so the allies resolved to continue the war. Yet Schiller asks how the union could be renewed and where the means would come from. He notes that Sweden's influence in Germany had rested on its late king's talents, not its power, framing the crisis that drives this book.
the-wandering-jew-volume-04:
Volume four of Eugene Sue's Wandering Jew opens part second, The Chastisement, with a prologue called A Bird's-Eye View of Two Worlds. Contents chapters follow through a masquerade, a carouse, a farewell, temptation, burglary, and a penal code. The prologue invites readers to see like an eagle from a cliff, spotting what lies below unaided eyes.

In 1831, the prologue says, the Jesuit order began acting on long-digested information about a fortune of thirty to forty million francs. Its rightful owners are descendants of Marius, Count of Rennepont, from the reign of Louis XIV. Each heir carries a simple token in that year: a bronze medal stamped with legends, the visible word being Victim.
the-works-of-samuel-johnson-in-sixteen-v: An old Project Gutenberg header is what this record shows for volume four of The Works of Samuel Johnson. The header dates the electronic text to July 1996. It identifies the volume as number four of sixteen. The Rambler and The Adventurer are named as its contents. Johnson's essays themselves do not appear within the pages present. Nothing beyond the file header and its general notices can be read here.
thompson-devils-evil-spirits-babylonia-v:
The second volume of R. Campbell Thompson's Devils and Evil Spirits of Babylonia came out at London in 1904. Where volume one fought demons in general, this one turns to set sicknesses. Thompson again pairs English renderings with the cuneiform texts and full notes.

The chief series here are Asakki Marsuti, on fever sickness, Ti'i, and Luh-ka, plus mixed spells that fit no one series. Each spell treats illness as a spirit to be named and driven out. The volume rounds out the classic English source on Mesopotamian healing magic.
thomson-bible-1808-vol-04:
The fourth volume of Charles Thomson's Bible, from 1808, holds the New Testament. Thomson translated it from the Greek, as he had the Septuagint in the first three volumes. Jane Aitken printed the set at Philadelphia, and it counts as the first American translation of the whole Bible into English.

The four gospels, Acts, the letters of Paul and the other apostles, and Revelation stand in Thomson's plain, careful English. His renderings sometimes cut closer to the Greek than the King James text does. Thomson had been secretary of Congress through the war for independence. His Bible is both a work of faith and a monument of early American print culture.
thomson-electricity-matter-1904:
Lectures given at Yale in 1903 as the Silliman Lectures became J. J. Thomson's Electricity and Matter in 1904. Thomson had discovered the electron, a particle far lighter than any atom, in 1897. His lectures present the corpuscular theory, which treats electrons as the basic bits of matter. Cathode rays figure large in the evidence.

Thomson shows how his particles can explain electric charge, mass, and the build of atoms. He writes as a guide at the front of a new field. The lectures carry the excitement of a science remaking itself. Readers see theory built straight from lab results. The book fixed his views for a wide public.
tob-0004:
Presented in Edwin Arnold's English translation, the Bhagavad Gita is a Hindu scripture that forms part of the great epic Mahabharata. Tradition attributes the larger work to Vyasa. Its scene is a battlefield, just before fighting begins, where the warrior Arjuna must face relatives and teachers among the opposing army.

Arjuna hesitates, and his charioteer Krishna answers him. Krishna, revealed as divine, teaches duty, selfless action, and devotion, urging Arjuna to act without being ruled by the results. Readers meet questions about work, death, the self, and God in a tense conversation rather than a sermon, which helps explain its lasting place in Hindu life.
tob-0104:
Fifteenth-century Bavaria produced the Munich Manual of Demonic Magic, a working magician's handbook in Latin. Its unknown compiler cared little for theory. Conjurations, experiments, and lists of spirits fill the pages, aimed at plain results: treasure found, love won, enemies checked.

The raw, practical tone sets it apart from loftier grimoires that preach about angels. Scholars value it as a true picture of late medieval magic in daily use. The only English version is Richard Kieckhefer's modern translation, which remains under copyright, so no public-domain text is attached to this entry. The manual's fame rests on its blunt honesty.
tob-10804:
Lady Wilde, Oscar Wilde's mother, who wrote as Speranza, gathered Ireland's folk beliefs in Ancient Legends, Mystic Charms, and Superstitions of Ireland. She collected fairy legends, healing charms, omens, and keening songs from the peasantry she knew. The oral world she recorded was already vanishing in her lifetime.

Tales of the sidhe, banshees, sacred wells, and second sight sit beside practical charms for illness, love, and protection. Lady Wilde writes in vivid, sympathetic prose, treating storytellers as authorities rather than curiosities. Folklore collections like hers preserve, in print, what a culture once carried entirely in memory and voice.
tob-13504:
Henry Cornelius Agrippa, a German scholar and physician, issued his Three Books of Occult Philosophy in the 1530s. The work sums up the learned magic of the Renaissance in one system. The copy here follows the complete 1898 English edition.

Book one treats natural magic, the hidden powers of things; book two, the heavens and their numbers; book three, divine names and ceremony. Agrippa draws on Kabbalah, astrology, and ancient philosophy to argue that all levels of the world answer each other. The spurious fourth book often travels with it. Few occult books have been mined as long or as widely.
tob-4004:
Desiderius Erasmus published The Praise of Folly in 1509, and John Wilson's translation presents his mock-encomium in classic English. Folly herself takes the podium, robed and belled, to praise her own influence over human affairs.
